at first i was disappointed, but then i found more options to customize and control the game and saw that it is not so bad. i do not think it is one of the best games of all time.
it can be fun and there are many good things, but i just list some cons for now. (btw i completed civilization 2 and 3 in the past and played 5 for two or three rounds which amounted to about 40 hours).
con
* the graphics make the playing field look very cluttered. playing becomes mostly looking after the flags over the units instead of the actual unit graphics. (btw, different civilizations have different default colors). first round i played on max settings, second on min settings and i enjoyed it way more (the fog of war becomes black which could be a nice feature anyway)
* "a unit needs orders". you must give explicit orders to all units that are not sleeping/fortified or similar. there is no "skip" option. this means that when your are in/after/preparing a war or similar where many active units are involved, you have to command each unit even if for some turns you do not desire to command each one
* city states - i think it is pointless. those many city civilizations that compete for land and grow over the centuries but which are not countries. luckily they can be disabled
* the diplomacy - they keep backstabbing me so why deal with it. other leaders often do not seem to react appropriately. i just brace for war any time, trade a little for happiness and do my thing
* "happiness" - you win in a war and overtake a city, your whole empire becomes unhappy. and you get a lot of problems. unhappiness goes up also for every new city
* borders - if you do not claim all the land, then the other players will and then you are surrounded by them. it can be tedious and frustrating to get and keep good/safe borders when you want to have friendly relationships. other civilization may keep settling as much as they can around/between your cities, even at war
* the 3d leader portrays make me want to instantly declare war on some
* older civilization games had nice animations for wonders, here you get just a sketch image and a silly quote of a real life person (like george w bush for the final quote)
* to just besiege cities does not seem to be really effective. cities do not seem to starve even after 10 years
* why not make it look more realistic? cities look much unlike real cities for example
* the policy/ideology system feels a bit random. also you may suffer huge negative consequences if your ideology differs from another influential country, so you might switch from freedom to order just to be better off
It still works aful. Very badly optimized. I am extremley dissapointed

I've been a fan of the cyberpunk genre since William Gibson first published Johnny Mneumonic for Omni magazine.  I played the Shadowrun and Cyberpunk pencil and paper games and have been wishing someone would put out a game that did the genre justice.  Shadowrun Returns feels 'old school' in many ways.  The graphics are dated, there is no voice over (everything is text that must be read) and the interface lacks a lot of data that we've come to expect in modern games without the need to click a lot of menus to find out information about our characters.  The gameplay is slow and I just keep wishing it would go a bit faster.  I had flashbacks of days when we had to 'Insert Side 2 of Floppy 18'.  It is also entirely story driven and you'll feel like you have no choice except to do what is expected of you.  The combat is traditional turn-based tactics like X-Com and Jagged Alliance.  Even hacking into the net is basically the same combat system with Matrix/Tron-like graphics.
Don't get me wrong... I'm not saying that it is a bad game.  It just isn't a great game.  The saving grace are editing tools that allow anyone to create new 'runs' or scenarios to give the game some replayability.  But, really, all that entails are new text-based storylines to follow and the same 'goto next location, kill mobs, repeat ad naseum'.
It almost feels like the developers could not decide whether this should be a PC game or a console game.  It just feels clunky considering all of the other games out today.
Either way, I'll do my best to slog through to the end of the game.  But, I keep needing to take breaks to play something that is a bit faster paced and challenging.

Dead Space provides one of the most interesting stories I have ever heard. A heavily immersive third person horror with a well developed story, as well as unique characters and enemies alike. Weapons and pick-ups are a topic in game that can make your brain think. Health is a vital thing, so you need to think about what med packs you should carry; small, medium, or large. You also must make room for ammo, as you might run out of that in only two rooms! Once you have planned out your inventory space, you can now take in the atmosphere-or not. Incredible sound system and atmosphere has you on edge in every location. When those lights turn out, so do the sounds for a brief moment. Then...BAM! Roar! This kind of encounter brings the chills down your spine like no other! Last but not least, is the story. To be honest, the story was the true reason I kept playing, as every chapter kept getting more and more interesting. If you want a scary game to play loud and proud on a dark and stormy night, this will be a keeper.

Imagine going through Portal without the computer to keep you company.  Imagine stripping the story from Portal, and all you're left with is a mind-bending world to explore.  A world where spatial relationships don't always match up with what the eyes see.  Many reviewers describe this as an M. C. Escher mind♥♥♥♥, and that's probably the most succinct way to put it.
The artistic look of the game is what attracted my attention at first.  The graphics are so simple and clean.  They almost feel homemade.  Several spots reminded me of Mike Oldfield's Music VR (Tr3s Lunas), but that's just on the surface.
Rooms shift and move all around you.  Walking down a corridor may lead to a dead end, but then you walk back the way you came, and now you're in a totally different room.  Walking backwards down a corridor may take you to a completely different location verses walking forwards.  It's akin to being in a maze that's constantly changing, but even that isn't accurate because the world never actually changes.  It's all very logical, but totally unexpected.  The game is full of impossible spaces and corridors that wrap back around on themselves without curving.  It really does mess with the mind, but it's all logical, and if you learn the game's internal logic, everything does make sense.
As if that weren't enough, you're then given a device that creates and destroys cubes, so now you have to get used to manipulating those.  How you manipulate cubes depends on how far you've upgraded the device (I don't want to call it a gun).  More areas become open to you, and they're full of wonder.
Took me about 8 hours to finish the game, and I never needed a walkthrough.  It's superbly designed, perfectly balanced, and nearly flawless in every way possible.  Antichamber is the most satisfyingly mind-bending game I've ever played.  Everyone who likes games that are won by problem-solving and not by trigger finger needs to play this.

History changing game, either you have wanted to build Pyramids as China or Chichen Itza as Poland, now you might have a chance, or maybe you have decided to take in your own hands the Mayan calendar prophecy by nuking all the world. In Civilization V you have that chance.
Civilization V is a turn-based game, where the main goal is to survive countless wars, Gandhis betrayals and many more suprises. With no campaign, you make your own story with chosen Civilization, progress through game and either win or lose in five different ways, those being: Diplomatic, Cultural, Domination, Science and Time. Games replayability is infinite,  by giving you options to choose type of map, how many recources world has and is it hot or cold world, e.g., playing desert world or frozen where only on equador is lush, by choosing these options you also set the difficulty of your game, both desert and frozen maps will give you significant difficulties make rapid expansions or maintain high population, where as, lush world, filled with trees, rivers and grasslands will give significant boost to your population and expansion, but these options also increase difficulty for other Civilizations ( either players or AI ).
AI is somewhat interesting in this game, on lower AI difficulties, below King, game is easy, even too easy, on higher, Immortal and Deity, you must be skillful player, where city managment, right technological advancement, city placement and expansion will allow you to survive, where even then in many games AI will overpower you with numbers, but even then Human player is always better than AI, and depending on your knowledge and wits, you most likely will survive those countless wars and win that game by any chance possible.
Game is a fast time-travel, intended 5 mins can be 5 hours, and one fast game with friend can end your day quickly. Where for most casual players the game might seem boring, but for the player in game its the posibility to be a conquer or shrewd diplomat, showing the world you power and intelligence, very few games give players a certain feeling of power.
I've been playing from Civilization I to Civilization V, maybe at first I was disappointed in Civ 5, but after expansions and bug fixes it gives you the thrill and sense of power shrewd diplomat might need.
Better than Civilization 6, atleast I think so.
Civilization V: 8/10
Civ V + GK: 9/10
Civ V + GK + BNW: 10/10

This takes me back to games similar to SSI's 'Renegade Legion:Interceptor' from the late 80's, where control, defense and preservation of your ship was paramount and the core component of the game.
FTL is a basic looking, but fun game of sending your spaceship across a space 'map' - whilst battling enemies along the way, upgrading your ship and carrying out repairs. Even going as far as to repel enemy boarding parties - all while the Rebel fleet continues to hunt you down across the map.
It's simple, addictive and actually a lot of fun. The one slight issue I have is that even the Easiest setting, isn't that easy. You have the compulsion to rush from one side of your sector to the exit point in the most direct route possible - in order to evade the Rebels. But in doing so, you miss out on experience for your crew, upgrades and rewards from battles won. Rush ahead too quickly and the opposition crushes you with little effort.
A Super Easy patch would make this even better! 7.5/10

Antichamber is a game where you are given oblique hints to solve puzzles in something visually akin to a psychedelic maze. Oblique hints to the puzzlers are given in the form of riddles and sayings that require equal parts reflection, experiential practice and sudden insight to solve and understand. The experience of solving some of these koan-like puzzles is a game that can be characterised by a pattern of mind-bending expansion that sounds something like "huh... what?...oh... huh...why....oh okay... what the?... where? How? Oh I see! That's pretty clever... hrrm... what is that?". This pattern then repeats again to evoke feelings of confusion and disorientation before giving way to insight.

Super Hexagon is an awesome game. It may turn off many because of its initial difficulty, but once you understand that it's all just a series of patterns that you maneuver, you can understand and beat it. The best time you can have is when you're in a trance with it and you suddenly beat your high score without even thinking about it. And the numerous deaths you have become meaningless because it breaks the flow for less than a second, after which you can jump right back in. So very, very fun. And addicting.

Even so, I certainly got my money's worth from just one playthrough, and maybe I'll get past my annoyance and try it again later.

"RIP AND TEAR YOUR GUTS BECAUSE THIS GAME IS ALL ABOUT ZED DISMEMBERMENT AND GORE NOW, SO YOU'RE BASICALLY ♥♥♥♥ED IF YOU'RE FROM GERMANY OR AUSTRALIA, MAYBE EVEN JAPAN BECAUSE GIBS WERE THE MAIN PART OF KF, RIGHT?", also the maps feel a lot smaller than the ones in KF1

-PvP mode (in a PvE game that's barely even finished)

It is frustrating that i waited years (been with the arkham games from the start) for the conclusion to my favorite gaming franchise, only to later find out i had to force myself to play it in slideshow speeds. My build as of the time was an MSI GTX 970 4G Gaming, i5 3550 @3.3ghz and 8gb DDR3 1333mhz. The game would underutilise my GPU heavily, based on MSI Afterburner statistics. It definitely is the worst optimization i've experienced on a PC game, and i did begin the game the second it launched. Even with gameworks disabled, and tweaks by other users didn't help the game. It was possible to run the game at a locked 30fps, but 5-10 minutes in or so, you'd drop frames drastically to like 5fps. My assumption was that because the game offers no loading screens (aside from launching the game in the first place) it relied heavily on a good hard drive speed. This was why there were so many delays in the first place on consoles, and why the game was originally capped at 30fps on PC. It was because the game was designed to utilise your hard drive speed to sustain 30fps. IronGalaxy (who worked on the PC version) didn't bother to improve the hard drive streaming issues, and it's the reason why anyone's GPU could easily be under-utilised, even if you unlocked the frame rate cap. I waited patiently for the game to be patched, which took a few months. Performance definitely improved after the patch, but i still had poor performance. No way of sustaining 60fps on a well capable 970. I complained about the performance with a negative review and said we consumers were deserving of refunds. Good thing i was allowed to get a refund later, even if i put 20 or so hours into the game at the time. I forced myself to play the game at launch simply because i wanted to complete the story before anyone spoilt it, so it was a bit of a trap for me as i didn't think i would be eligable for a refund. I later upgraded my computer with 12gb of ram, and an SSD. I partially did this upgrade with Ark: Survival Evolved in mind, as that game also relies heavily on your drive speed and ram amount. I eventually decided to buy Arkham Knight again. I installed it on my SSD this time. The performance definitely improved, thanks to the fast drive speed. I do get drops to the 50s at times, but it's a CPU bottleneck that you can't blame the game for, and it only happens when gliding around the city. Graphical options are 'mehh', barely a difference between low and high settings in performance if you have the VRAM. Also suffers from a lack of actual options to tune you graphics. Ambient Occlusion options and other Anti-Aliasing methods would have been welcome. You can still modify the graphics settings in depth if you access the ini files. The default Anti-Aliasing method has to be the worst i've seen in a game. It's apparently a form of SMAA which surprises me, as it just seems like a blur filter. The aliasing remains horrible in the game unless you downsample from 4k. MSAA options would've definitely been nice, but all i've been able to do is force Reshade SMAA for a better anti aliasing setting than the default option. It's good way of tackling some of the aliasing without much of a hit to performance. I also use Reshade to inject the game with my own Ambient Occlusion settings (I recommend SSGI). The game is also capped at 90fps as your highest option, though you can unlock this cap in the ini files.
The game is solid underneath. Arkham City is still my favourite of the franchise, which surprised me as i expected the gameplay improvements Arkham Knight would offer to make it hard to go back. Arkham City certainly made Arkham Asylum feel a bit lacking after you played City, though both are still phenomenal games. What Arkham Knight ultimately suffered from, was the batmobile. The story is decent in my opinon, but the batmobile especially towards the end of the game feels like the biggest chore i've ever been forced into in a game. I understand that Rocksteady wanted to add a new gameplay option to keep the game fresh, but tank battles ultimately led to a lack of actual hand to hand boss fights in the game. It should've remained optional, and perhaps only as a driving mechanic too. There's no way you can expect all fans of the Arkham games to appreciate the batmobile, and i only notice about 1 in 5 people who are fans of the franchise actually like the batmobile. It's more likely you hate it rather than like it. I still however find fun in the game, This is because of mods and challenge mode in specific, which is why i've been able to dedicate so many hours into the game. As of 1st July 2016, the game is on sale and it's a steal for the price if your rig can handle it. It still remains a game that offers one of the higher end experiences that gaming can buy right now.

I love this game. It is a fairly simple space flight rogue-like game where you take control of a small star ship (think Millennium Falcon or Serenity). You control your crew from a top down perspective and tell them to operate systems, fight off intruders, or repair hull breaches. Meanwhile, you also control all the ship's subsystems by allocating power to them. Ship to ship combat plays a huge role, and is done by targeting an enemy vessel's subsystems and slowly firing away while trying to keep your own ship afloat. Once you lose your ship, it's game over.
This game is very hard. After hours of practice I normally manage a one in ten win to loss ratio. The difficulty, however, doesn't really make it frustrating.  Each play-through is like a different story for a doomed crew. One game may last an hour and a half if you go through the entire thing. There are also many ship unlocks that keep replayability high. I would have loved to see more crew and ship customization, but these are nitpicks. Buy this.

It is frustrating that i waited years (been with the arkham games from the start) for the conclusion to my favorite gaming franchise, only to later find out i had to force myself to play it in slideshow speeds. My build as of the time was an MSI GTX 970 4G Gaming, i5 3550 @3.3ghz and 8gb DDR3 1333mhz. The game would underutilise my GPU heavily, based on MSI Afterburner statistics. It definitely is the worst optimization i've experienced on a PC game, and i did begin the game the second it launched. Even with gameworks disabled, and tweaks by other users didn't help the game. It was possible to run the game at a locked 30fps, but 5-10 minutes in or so, you'd drop frames drastically to like 5fps. My assumption was that because the game offers no loading screens (aside from launching the game in the first place) it relied heavily on a good hard drive speed. This was why there were so many delays in the first place on consoles, and why the game was originally capped at 30fps on PC. It was because the game was designed to utilise your hard drive speed to sustain 30fps. IronGalaxy (who worked on the PC version) didn't bother to improve the hard drive streaming issues, and it's the reason why anyone's GPU could easily be under-utilised, even if you unlocked the frame rate cap. I waited patiently for the game to be patched, which took a few months. Performance definitely improved after the patch, but i still had poor performance. No way of sustaining 60fps on a well capable 970. I complained about the performance with a negative review and said we consumers were deserving of refunds. Good thing i was allowed to get a refund later, even if i put 20 or so hours into the game at the time. I forced myself to play the game at launch simply because i wanted to complete the story before anyone spoilt it, so it was a bit of a trap for me as i didn't think i would be eligable for a refund. I later upgraded my computer with 12gb of ram, and an SSD. I partially did this upgrade with Ark: Survival Evolved in mind, as that game also relies heavily on your drive speed and ram amount. I eventually decided to buy Arkham Knight again. I installed it on my SSD this time. The performance definitely improved, thanks to the fast drive speed. I do get drops to the 50s at times, but it's a CPU bottleneck that you can't blame the game for, and it only happens when gliding around the city. Graphical options are 'mehh', barely a difference between low and high settings in performance if you have the VRAM. Also suffers from a lack of actual options to tune you graphics. Ambient Occlusion options and other Anti-Aliasing methods would have been welcome. You can still modify the graphics settings in depth if you access the ini files. The default Anti-Aliasing method has to be the worst i've seen in a game. It's apparently a form of SMAA which surprises me, as it just seems like a blur filter. The aliasing remains horrible in the game unless you downsample from 4k. MSAA options would've definitely been nice, but all i've been able to do is force Reshade SMAA for a better anti aliasing setting than the default option. It's good way of tackling some of the aliasing without much of a hit to performance. I also use Reshade to inject the game with my own Ambient Occlusion settings (I recommend SSGI). The game is also capped at 90fps as your highest option, though you can unlock this cap in the ini files.
The game is solid underneath. Arkham City is still my favourite of the franchise, which surprised me as i expected the gameplay improvements Arkham Knight would offer to make it hard to go back. Arkham City certainly made Arkham Asylum feel a bit lacking after you played City, though both are still phenomenal games. What Arkham Knight ultimately suffered from, was the batmobile. The story is decent in my opinon, but the batmobile especially towards the end of the game feels like the biggest chore i've ever been forced into in a game. I understand that Rocksteady wanted to add a new gameplay option to keep the game fresh, but tank battles ultimately led to a lack of actual hand to hand boss fights in the game. It should've remained optional, and perhaps only as a driving mechanic too. There's no way you can expect all fans of the Arkham games to appreciate the batmobile, and i only notice about 1 in 5 people who are fans of the franchise actually like the batmobile. It's more likely you hate it rather than like it. I still however find fun in the game, This is because of mods and challenge mode in specific, which is why i've been able to dedicate so many hours into the game. As of 1st July 2016, the game is on sale and it's a steal for the price if your rig can handle it. It still remains a game that offers one of the higher end experiences that gaming can buy right now.

Risk of Rain is the most fun I have had playing a roguelike game.  You play until you die or until you beat the final boss.  It's punishing, and unless you play with friends, you'll find yourself dying quite a few times before managing to unlock any new characters.  You unlock items quickly, but there are so many that there is still a lot to unlock even 50 hours in.  You play as one of the survivors of a ship crash on a strange planet.  There is an awesome diversity of characters that play very differently.  All of them are very fun.  Play on "Drizzle", the easy mode, when you start.  My first set of lives I played on the normal difficulty, and I didn't get very far.  I unlocked all the characters about 45 hours in.  The bosses are a lot of fun, and this game gets tense as it starts spawning bosses a few at a time.  Even on easier settings, the difficulty of the game increases with time.  If you've collected enough items, you can keep pushing through to the final boss against overwhelming quantities of enemies.  Finally beating the game on the hardest difficulty was very satisfying, and you can unlock artifacts that change how the game is played.  I still haven't found them all.  Playing with your friends is a lot of fun, though this increases the chance of encountering one of the games common bugs.  In most single-player runs, you will not encounter bugs.  Every now and then, someone falls through the map in multiplayer.  The game has received some updates, and I believe the developers will continue to update the game, at least to address the bugs.  The art is beautiful.  The animation is cool and smooth.  The music is original and an awesome way of building as you trek through levels.  I find myself listening to it even when I'm not playing the game.  The maps are diverse and generate differently on different playthroughs.  You could end up in an entirely different environment, such as a underwater level or a snowy level, each time you take a teleporter, the bridge between levels.  Risk of Rain is inexpensive and absolutely worth getting.  A friend got it for me as part of a humble bundle that came with multiple copies.  Don't be discouraged when you die early on.  You unlock stronger items as you go.  This is one of the best games in my library.

It's a real shame that this game's launch was marred by technical issues because I think it's a great game. WB and the devs were rightly excoriated for the technical issues and I personally didn't expect this game to run very well on my system but it did run from day 1 without issues, and while I didn't get to play at max level graphics, the game still looks amazing at lower quality and I got a decent enough framerate for my personal taste.
That all being said, this is a GREAT game. GREAT. It's a refinement of AA's and AC's combat systems, which were already both VERY good. AK's combat is fantastic; the combos are better, the enemies are more varied and more challenging, integration with gadgets is better; if you played AA and AC you will LOVE AK's combat. I absolutely LOVED Batmobile assisted takedowns. That being said, the Batmobile was hit-or-miss honestly. I liked driving around the city to objectives, but the racing and obstacle courses didn't seem very fun or creative; they were more like chores I had to complete in order to finish all the quests. I enjoyed the side quests; the Mr. Freeze one was particularly good in terms of story. I enjoyed rescuing the firefighters, and beating up the Penguin is always great fun.
Let's talk about the Riddler. I'm DONE with the Riddler and his trophies and his mini-games and everything he brings to the series. If they ever do another game like this please - no more Riddler. AA and AC's Riddler stuff was fine, but this game took it to another level in terms of overkill. There was just TOO MUCH Riddler stuff. I think if they cut out all the racing it would have been a bit more tolerable, and honestly, they could have cut out about half of the collectibles and puzzles and that would have been tolerable. I actually quite enjoyed the 'co-op' parts with Catwoman, but that was about it.
Finally the story; I enjoyed the story quite a bit. I pawned off Scarecrow as a minor villain and didn't think he could bring much to the table, but boy he proved me wrong. The Arkham Knight story... well I saw the big reveal coming beforehand (I'm not sure how you could miss it, honestly), but that wasn't a bad thing. The issue I have is... considering the role the Arkham Knight played in the events of the game, why did he escape punishment while everyone else did not? That's probably my only big beef with the story.
Give this game a try. If you enjoyed AA and AC I don't doubt that you will enjoy AK which is a swan song to the series and Rocksteady's best Arkham game.

I love this game. It is a fairly simple space flight rogue-like game where you take control of a small star ship (think Millennium Falcon or Serenity). You control your crew from a top down perspective and tell them to operate systems, fight off intruders, or repair hull breaches. Meanwhile, you also control all the ship's subsystems by allocating power to them. Ship to ship combat plays a huge role, and is done by targeting an enemy vessel's subsystems and slowly firing away while trying to keep your own ship afloat. Once you lose your ship, it's game over.
This game is very hard. After hours of practice I normally manage a one in ten win to loss ratio. The difficulty, however, doesn't really make it frustrating.  Each play-through is like a different story for a doomed crew. One game may last an hour and a half if you go through the entire thing. There are also many ship unlocks that keep replayability high. I would have loved to see more crew and ship customization, but these are nitpicks. Buy this.

What more can I say that hasn't already been said? Half-Life 2 is the type of shooter that we do not see anymore. In an industry competing for who can have the most explosions and 10 year olds screaming, it is a breath of fresh air to play this game and notice all of the important things that are missing from most first-person shooters: atmosphere, level design, and most importantly, fun. Half-Life 2 manages to nail all three of these aspects and much more. A linear shooter, yes, but it has enough deviations from the typical FPS tropes to provide players with a unique experience that doesn't hold your hand to the next checkpoint. Graphically it is not up to par with today's major releases, but with an engine that has aged so well as Source, it is hard to put some of today's technologies up against it. Physics are still excellent, facial animations are terrific, and the overall art design, couple with the music, give the game a real sense of this strange and dystopian atmosphere that you are a part of. As we see some FPS now returning to this formula (e.g. Wolfenstein: The New Order, Bioshock Infinite), the reminder of the influence that this game has had on these newer releases is amazing. Easily my favorite first-person shooter of all time and a must play for anyone looking for a different experience.

What more can I say that hasn't already been said? Half-Life 2 is the type of shooter that we do not see anymore. In an industry competing for who can have the most explosions and 10 year olds screaming, it is a breath of fresh air to play this game and notice all of the important things that are missing from most first-person shooters: atmosphere, level design, and most importantly, fun. Half-Life 2 manages to nail all three of these aspects and much more. A linear shooter, yes, but it has enough deviations from the typical FPS tropes to provide players with a unique experience that doesn't hold your hand to the next checkpoint. Graphically it is not up to par with today's major releases, but with an engine that has aged so well as Source, it is hard to put some of today's technologies up against it. Physics are still excellent, facial animations are terrific, and the overall art design, couple with the music, give the game a real sense of this strange and dystopian atmosphere that you are a part of. As we see some FPS now returning to this formula (e.g. Wolfenstein: The New Order, Bioshock Infinite), the reminder of the influence that this game has had on these newer releases is amazing. Easily my favorite first-person shooter of all time and a must play for anyone looking for a different experience.

First let me emphasize that I am by no means a fan of the survival horror genre; particularly not games in that area since most of them rely on jump scares and cleverly placed music scores to frighten the player. In my opinion only a bad story, or a badly designed game need to constantly rely on jump scares. Back in 2008 when this was first released, I stopped at around chapter 3. I found it hard, my system was maxed out (bad performance equals bad reaction time which means dealing with the occasional jump scares was very difficult).
The other thing that really annoyed me back in 2008 was the horrible console port. Not so much the gameplay, but rather the inability to re-map controls. I'm left-handed, so WASD does not work for me. I ended up spending a good time researching a third party tool (which I still use these days) to make Dead Space playable. I guess that, to a good part, put me off the game back then. If you’re interested in this third-party tool, I wrote a guide for another game on how to use it.
Now, six years later, I guess we have accepted the existence of bad console ports, bad controls and having started the game again once more, I'm actually pleasantly surprised. I find it much more manageable now (granted, in part to better computer specs), and although the jump scares still annoy me somewhat, the balance between those, the sci-fi setting, the absolutely awesome zero-g sequences, and suspense is just right. I've also realized that I'm obviously making better choices when it comes to equipment this time around.
The overall "Aliens-meets-The Thing-meets-Event Horizon" atmosphere definitely works, the save point system allows you to access "consoles" in regular, fair intervals (and, should you die, the game won't force you to continue at the last manual save point, but also has an internal, temporary checkpoint system), and I think that overall the placement of enemies is largely very fair. The level design is clever and you're getting something new to play with, or see, just at the right moment when boredom, instead of another necromorph, is lurking around the corner. The feeling of being in a huge starship comes accross well.
On another positive note, the graphics can still hold up even today. Especially the light and shadow effects are top notch. They certainly provide the right atmosphere for a creepy sci-fi adventure. I'm not sure the full price is still justified, but if you can snap it up in a sale, definitely do so.
I want to provide another side note: Nothing against id software and their overall place in the Hall of Fame of computer games, but if I compare this game to DOOM III, I would prefer Dead Space. The additional features such as weapon and armor mods make all the difference and add just the right amount of depth to a shooter without making it cumbersome. Straight up FPS without a little bit of depth just doesn’t cut it anymore in my eyes. Dead Space got it right.

I'm surprised how divided people are on this game. At the very least, I would think that even if someone didn't like it, they could appreciate the storytelling and unique atmosphere and gameplay this game offers.
Granted, I can understand that the combat system is a straight clone of XCOM: EU, but the rest of the experience is diverse, immersive, and portrays a world with as much depth as any I've seen in a game.
Bear in mind, I was not a fan of the early Shadowrun games at all. While I could appreciate the concept, I think the final product was a little too abitious for the time. But in our current genration, this game succeeeds at taking elements we've seen before many times, and putting a twist on them to make them feel fresh and engaging, and at the same time, familiar and comfortable.
Like I said, there's some XCOM influence in there. But there's also a little bit of Baldur's Gate in there. There's a little bit of Mass Effect in there. There's a little bit of Fallout in there. There truly are some familiar elements to each aspect of Shadowrun Returns, and yet it still manages to place you in a world that feels fresh, and exciting. I can certainly tell that this game would not be for everyone... Specifically those who dont like to read large amounts of dialogue. But to someone who's read the desciptions and reviews, and feels on the fence about it, I can say  it's definitely worth a shot. It surprised me how quickly it hooked me in.

I have never played a game as perfectly designed and implemented as Super Hexagon before.
The game is as simple as it is brilliant: You move a triangle around a polygon (a hexagon in most parts of the game, hence the name) by pressing left or right, the only two buttons that matter.
The only goal is to reach 60 seconds in each of the 6 randomly generated levels which means that you can basically beat the game within mere 6 minutes. But trust me, you won't.
To beat a level you have to avoid hitting walls. And that's it.
However, it is not that easy. When I first started level 1 I died within 4 or 5 seconds. After more than 20 attempts I reached 10 seconds and thought "60 seconds? Nope, not possible.". Anyhow, you are never frustrated as the game is always a 100% fair and you will always come back.
Every situation can be beaten, each obstacle can be passed. The game hides nothing from you and is never unfair. If you die, it is you and only you to blame. And with each attempt you get better. In the meantime I am able to relax in Level 1.
The soundtrack fits perfectly and somehow never gets old.
The graphics are as simple as possible so you are not distracted (and that is good as the levels are rotating, pulsing and changing their colours all the time).
There is no story and no cutscenes (besides a ... let's call it "music-video" after beating level 6 that does not interrupt the game flow).
Even the achievements are simple: 1 for each level that is beaten (nothing useless as "die a hundred times" which would not add anything meaningful to the game).
There are no powerups and no enemies other than walls.
And after beating level 6, the final level, I felt rewarded like never before in my video game carreer.
Of course the game is not over yet as there are more records to be set (no level has an end, they are only beaten after 60 seconds but go on infinitely).
Also: After the first 60 seconds in the last level a "black and white" mode is launched. The music slows down and is relaxing, the rotations only happen rarely and everything seems to be peaceful ... until you die after 3 seconds.
And then you will hear something you will be used to by then: "Game Over ... begin!"

What more can I say that hasn't already been said? Half-Life 2 is the type of shooter that we do not see anymore. In an industry competing for who can have the most explosions and 10 year olds screaming, it is a breath of fresh air to play this game and notice all of the important things that are missing from most first-person shooters: atmosphere, level design, and most importantly, fun. Half-Life 2 manages to nail all three of these aspects and much more. A linear shooter, yes, but it has enough deviations from the typical FPS tropes to provide players with a unique experience that doesn't hold your hand to the next checkpoint. Graphically it is not up to par with today's major releases, but with an engine that has aged so well as Source, it is hard to put some of today's technologies up against it. Physics are still excellent, facial animations are terrific, and the overall art design, couple with the music, give the game a real sense of this strange and dystopian atmosphere that you are a part of. As we see some FPS now returning to this formula (e.g. Wolfenstein: The New Order, Bioshock Infinite), the reminder of the influence that this game has had on these newer releases is amazing. Easily my favorite first-person shooter of all time and a must play for anyone looking for a different experience.

​I'll preface this review by saying it is one of the best video games I have ever played.
This is a game where game-play is king. The mechanics are simple, with each class having four basic attacks, however the nature of game ensures that no playthrough is the same. As you progress you unlock new classes, all of whom have a unique play style, and new drops which are crucial to the variety in the experience you'll have during each of your playthroughs. Marooned on an alien planet you fight your way through each level in search of a teleport, which when activated releases a boss, or in many cases in the late game bosses. The longer you take to find the teleport and collect items the harder the game becomes, as indicated by an ever increasing difficulty meter. This introduces the dilemma of either speeding through everything with minimal gear against an easier game or stockpiling against a harder one. The basic layout of each respective level is the same with every playthrough, but the placement of the teleport and chests is random. Which levels you traverse are also random, with the exception of the last two (the second to last being my personal favorite) which are always the same. You can do an entire playthrough in about 45 minutes or less, or you can play for 3 or more hours continuously looping through the game again and again as the difficulty continuously ramps. While graphically simplistic, the stylized nature lends itself quite well to the melancholy atmosphere. Performance wise this game will run on anything more powerful than a TI-84, it runs smoothly even on my measly E5500 Dell work laptop with its 2.8 ghz Core 2 Duo, 4gb ram, and 400mhz integrated graphics; my gaming PC barely registers its existence. There is some slowdown when things get absurd (my weak laptop bottomed out at a still playable 28 fps while I was fighting against 3 magma worms and had more than 80 enemies spawned) which I'm guessing is engine related because I've seen improvements as the game has been updated. To be honest the slowdown was and still is rather helpful, like with certain NES games the drop in frame-rate gives you time to assess the chaotic situation you've gotten yourself into. The controls are tight and perfectly suited for the difficulty; I recommend playing with a controller. This leads into the challenge, which in this game is perfect. Never have I died and had it been the fault of the game or some cheap trick, each death is the result of my own mistakes which makes the game both humbling and satisfying.
I'm a fanboy, genuine 10/10.
Also: I got this game on sale for $2.49, and it is well worth the $9.99.

This is one of my first reviews, only my 2nd one in fact, which surprise surprise, it's on another rogue-like game.
At first, I did not have high hopes for this game. After getting the game and playing it for a while however, I couldn't really put it down. I did finally get bored however from some bugs like falling through the world constantly, but this usually only happened on the first level, the very moment you spawn. A more recent crashing problem also made me not play as much. The classes have a MOBA style 4 ability set. 1 of these are a normal attack like firing a gun or melee attack. The others have various things such as invulnerability, stronger attacks, nearly unseeable attacks due to their speed, or maybe even all 3.
But anyways, the game revolves around you surviving a planet you have crashed onto after an unknown humanoid creature destroys your transport ship. You must go through 6 areas, but to get to the next one, you must activate a teleporter, where you must survive for 90-120 seconds (depending on difficulty) until it is fully operational, and you proceed to finish off the enemies remaining. With time, the game grows more difficult, with enemies gaining more health, damage and also having increased spawn rates (as it seems) and more of the elite mobs appearing. Elite mobs can be approached the same way as the normal type, but you'll most likely get your bum handed to you on a silver platter if you do such a foolish thing. When playing for the first time, there is almost no chance of you beating it. If you do so, congratulations, this game is not going to be difficult for you. This game is fun in a Binding of Isaac way where you never know what you'll get. Gameplay usually is fun and intense, but after a while, the adrenaline stops pumping when you know you'll win, and it just gets a bit boring. Items you unlock with a slight bit of lore behind them in a way, in the form of order details. This makes sense, as you're pretty much were an intergalactic mailman in a way.
EDIT: As of recently however, I have been having major problems with the game, such as memory wipes, crashes, and the game messing with my sound. It is to the point where I cannot play the game anymore.

Doing neither too little nor too much is key to your survival in this game. If you spend too long leveling up, you will end up dealing with difficulty in the next area, due to a difficulty spike and new enemies to deal with. If you go to the teleporter immediately, with nothing but level 2 and 1 item, death will break down the door and slice your head off, which means, you die near instantly, or you just delay it by running, then die.
The soundtrack in this game is absolutely amazing, Chris Christodoulou did a great job with the different pieces. The soundtrack is one of the best I have heard in a long time.
New survivors are unlocked by completing various feats like killing a certain 3 bosses, or collecting this or that. Multiplayer is fun as hell, however, online can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to get working. Usually zoom scale 1x then resetting it to 2x makes it work, but other problems, sorry, can't help you there. If you get frustrated easily, this is not the game for you. If you hate difficulty, this is not for you. And last but not least, if you hate games where you only have a chance to get the items you so DESPERATELY need, this game is NOT for you.
And I have only skimmed the surface of the game for the most part. I leave you to figure out the rest and read other reviews.

FTL is my new favorite laptop game. By that I mean that you can play it with one hand. I love this game. I don't know where they get off calling it "roguelike," since it has absolutely nothing in common with rogue other than the top-down grid view.
In FTL, you command a starship on a trek across space (get it?). You have to get from point A to point B without getting blowed up. You fight other ships, send away teams, do escort missions and outrun the Rebel Alliance. So to speak.
The coolness of this game is (now that I think of it) its rogueness. The game has definite character development aspects, but you're only with your crew and ship for a couple hours and then never see them again. So you'll improve your ship's engines, and your pilot will get better at evading enemey fire over the course of a game.
UPDATE: THE ADVANCED EDITION
The Advanced Edition... definitely adds some stuff. I'm very satisfied with it as a free update. I'd be pretty disappointed if I'd paid for it as a DLC. There's some nice new music, a new alien race (or two?), some new random events and a bit of a UI tweak.
The hangar is now WAY easier to navigate and there's much less guess-work involved in "how do I unlock that ship?" I don't know if this was always the case, but in addition to the "unlock quests" there are now metagame achievement criteria for unlocking just about every ship and variant, and those are told to you right in the hangar while you're selecting your ship.
It seems to me that this update also came with a bit of a bump in difficulty. I recall pretty routinely making it all the way to the end boss (but not beating it very often), but in the dozen or so games I've played since the Advanced Edition went live, I don't think I've made it past map five.
So I'd have to say that all-in-all the Advanced Edition is awesome. For me, it has very effectively breathed new life into the game. This is once again my go-to laptop game, and also my go-to time waster when I'm waiting for a big dowload or something. and don't want to get into anything too involved or resource-intensive.
But don't agonize over your decisions because you'll be starting a new game with a new crew and ship very soon. Just play with it and see what works and what doesn't.

​I'll preface this review by saying it is one of the best video games I have ever played.
This is a game where game-play is king. The mechanics are simple, with each class having four basic attacks, however the nature of game ensures that no playthrough is the same. As you progress you unlock new classes, all of whom have a unique play style, and new drops which are crucial to the variety in the experience you'll have during each of your playthroughs. Marooned on an alien planet you fight your way through each level in search of a teleport, which when activated releases a boss, or in many cases in the late game bosses. The longer you take to find the teleport and collect items the harder the game becomes, as indicated by an ever increasing difficulty meter. This introduces the dilemma of either speeding through everything with minimal gear against an easier game or stockpiling against a harder one. The basic layout of each respective level is the same with every playthrough, but the placement of the teleport and chests is random. Which levels you traverse are also random, with the exception of the last two (the second to last being my personal favorite) which are always the same. You can do an entire playthrough in about 45 minutes or less, or you can play for 3 or more hours continuously looping through the game again and again as the difficulty continuously ramps. While graphically simplistic, the stylized nature lends itself quite well to the melancholy atmosphere. Performance wise this game will run on anything more powerful than a TI-84, it runs smoothly even on my measly E5500 Dell work laptop with its 2.8 ghz Core 2 Duo, 4gb ram, and 400mhz integrated graphics; my gaming PC barely registers its existence. There is some slowdown when things get absurd (my weak laptop bottomed out at a still playable 28 fps while I was fighting against 3 magma worms and had more than 80 enemies spawned) which I'm guessing is engine related because I've seen improvements as the game has been updated. To be honest the slowdown was and still is rather helpful, like with certain NES games the drop in frame-rate gives you time to assess the chaotic situation you've gotten yourself into. The controls are tight and perfectly suited for the difficulty; I recommend playing with a controller. This leads into the challenge, which in this game is perfect. Never have I died and had it been the fault of the game or some cheap trick, each death is the result of my own mistakes which makes the game both humbling and satisfying.
I'm a fanboy, genuine 10/10.
Also: I got this game on sale for $2.49, and it is well worth the $9.99.

This is one of my first reviews, only my 2nd one in fact, which surprise surprise, it's on another rogue-like game.
At first, I did not have high hopes for this game. After getting the game and playing it for a while however, I couldn't really put it down. I did finally get bored however from some bugs like falling through the world constantly, but this usually only happened on the first level, the very moment you spawn. A more recent crashing problem also made me not play as much. The classes have a MOBA style 4 ability set. 1 of these are a normal attack like firing a gun or melee attack. The others have various things such as invulnerability, stronger attacks, nearly unseeable attacks due to their speed, or maybe even all 3.
But anyways, the game revolves around you surviving a planet you have crashed onto after an unknown humanoid creature destroys your transport ship. You must go through 6 areas, but to get to the next one, you must activate a teleporter, where you must survive for 90-120 seconds (depending on difficulty) until it is fully operational, and you proceed to finish off the enemies remaining. With time, the game grows more difficult, with enemies gaining more health, damage and also having increased spawn rates (as it seems) and more of the elite mobs appearing. Elite mobs can be approached the same way as the normal type, but you'll most likely get your bum handed to you on a silver platter if you do such a foolish thing. When playing for the first time, there is almost no chance of you beating it. If you do so, congratulations, this game is not going to be difficult for you. This game is fun in a Binding of Isaac way where you never know what you'll get. Gameplay usually is fun and intense, but after a while, the adrenaline stops pumping when you know you'll win, and it just gets a bit boring. Items you unlock with a slight bit of lore behind them in a way, in the form of order details. This makes sense, as you're pretty much were an intergalactic mailman in a way.
EDIT: As of recently however, I have been having major problems with the game, such as memory wipes, crashes, and the game messing with my sound. It is to the point where I cannot play the game anymore.

Doing neither too little nor too much is key to your survival in this game. If you spend too long leveling up, you will end up dealing with difficulty in the next area, due to a difficulty spike and new enemies to deal with. If you go to the teleporter immediately, with nothing but level 2 and 1 item, death will break down the door and slice your head off, which means, you die near instantly, or you just delay it by running, then die.
The soundtrack in this game is absolutely amazing, Chris Christodoulou did a great job with the different pieces. The soundtrack is one of the best I have heard in a long time.
New survivors are unlocked by completing various feats like killing a certain 3 bosses, or collecting this or that. Multiplayer is fun as hell, however, online can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to get working. Usually zoom scale 1x then resetting it to 2x makes it work, but other problems, sorry, can't help you there. If you get frustrated easily, this is not the game for you. If you hate difficulty, this is not for you. And last but not least, if you hate games where you only have a chance to get the items you so DESPERATELY need, this game is NOT for you.
And I have only skimmed the surface of the game for the most part. I leave you to figure out the rest and read other reviews.

I first encountered xcom as a demo on xbox360. I also used to be a person who did not like the idea of turn based strategy games. Then I tried xcom, and fell in love with this game so much that when I got a computer I bought it on Steam too. What makes this game so good in my opinion? This game takes time to learn. You will make mistakes and lose. When you do not allow yourself to make the same mistakes and learn from them, the more you play, the better you will get. What I like most about xcom is the fact that when I first started this game, I was clueless. This is my first turn based strategy game. As I continued to play xcom, I became better and was able to finally beat classic difficulty with ironman mode enabled. This game requires you to make hard choices that are not always clear. That is why I like this game so much. It requires you to think about every choice you make in the base management side, and in the turn based tactical combat side. Every choice you make in base management has an upside and downside. The combat layer also has hard choices as well, requiring you to adapt and have backup plans, should your initial plan fail. Trust me, you will learn to hate this game and love it at the same time. The tutorial does a nice job of teaching you the basics, but it does not teach you some of the more unorthodox strategies that you have to learn on your own, or learn it from other players. Even though this game does have some bug issues from time to time, the main reason you will learn to like this game is simple. It will never be exactly the same twice. EVER. My main advice to new players or first time players of xcom, is to take your time. Patience and planning ahead will always be your most deadly weapon in this game. I hope that anyone reading this can give this game a chance as I did. I can honestly say that I do not regret playing this game one bit. If you like turn based strategy games, this game will give you a run for your money.

Having been a fan of Shadowrun for the SNES, this game had all the right touches to give me that old school nostalgic RPG feel to it.
First off, it's not marred by bad voice acting, mainly cause there is no voice acting.  Everything is text, so prepare to read.  This normally sounds like a bad thing (cause you ain't here to read, but you here to game!) but the dialogue is good enough where you actually don't mind it.  It really is well written and some of the conversational rebuttles truly are funny.  Which leads me to my next point.
The game is quite linear.  This is a classic case of a glass half full/empty.  I found this a refreshing change from all the latest RPGs as I tend to get lost in all the open world games because there's just too much to do.  I lose track of what exactly is the main storyline and almost never finish the game.  This one, I beat in about 14 hours, so know that there's an "end" to it.
While it may seem short, there are user made missions which you can do after, so the replayability is always there.  Plus, if you know your way around their editor you can make your own!  (I can't, I'm too dumb).
Also, the game plays out in sequences, or chapters if you will, and you can't save between them.  Some of these sequences are long, so it kind of becomes a pain if you need to go.
That said, here are my pros/cons to the game.
Pros
Battles are fun (you get to fight in the matrix!)
Dialogue
Character customization
Old school RPG feel
Cons
Too short!
Somewhat linear
Save points
Overall though, I enjoyed the game.  Its definitely not perfect, but it's definitely worth it's price.  I would say this gets a 7.5 out of 10 from me!  Enjoy!

While still "absorbing" up to a point, compared to previous Civilization games, this one is poorly designed.  Things "happen" for no apparent reason.  Example 1 is unhappiness, and you'll neither get a warning nor can you create an entertainer to take care of the problem.  Example 2 is ranged units; two units same distance and exact same setup, one will fire and the other won't.  Or one can reach the target but the other can't even though they're the same distance away.  Perhaps I'm missing some information but whatever it is, the game designers have certainly made it hard to find.  Example 3 is poor movement design.  Your units have no common sense; sometimes they refuse to move and other times they board ships and travel 47 spaces in order to move forward 2 spaces -- the latter is caused by the *&^&^% inability to stack.  Sometimes they can move "through" another unit; sometimes not, and I can't find any rhyme or reason to it.  Because of the inability to stack, cities on a peninsula are virtually impossible to capture.  Example 4 is the city-states.  While essentially harmless fluff, they're annoying and distracting and helping them adds little benefit, whereas hurting them is guaranteed to get you a war with someone.  Like I said at the beginning, it's absorbing -- so I'm going to try it one more time with some mods to see if the mods can fix or minimize these issues.

Definitely a horror classic at this point. Didn't invent the space-horror genre, but definitely one of the first to do it exceptionally well in modern visuals. Jumpscares, plot twists, mindf#@&s, and a genuinely creepy (but beautiful) atmosphere make this game a nail-biter all the way through. Which is a good thing, because the game tends to drone a bit toward the end. After a while you feel like you are running errands for the sake of running errands. The developers did a good job of keeping you on your toes, though, so don't expect to anticipate many of the scares. Quite a few of my favorite moments involve slow realization and horror of what is about to occur.
If I have to pick at it, I would say the controls could be improved a bit. There are some bugs with mouse and keyboard control sometimes, which is due to a lazy console port. The controls are much improved in DS3 (however that game is origin-exclusive).
Minor faults forgiven, Dead Space is definitely one of my top favorite horror shooters, close behind Alan Wake. It frequently goes on sale, so snag it during one of those times.

Everything is nice, from the crisp and colorful yet ominous colors, the music, the sounds and the animations.
After a successful Kickstarter campaign, the studio showed that all that money was not spent for nothing.

I honestly can't believe how the most playable, most polished, most focused early access title can get so much hate from "faithful fans". As a fan of the first Killing Floor i bought this game as soon as it appeared on steam. And with as little content as it had at the time (4 classes, 5 weapons each counting the knives), i still felt satisfied with my purchase. Great core systems and mechanics (The gore, persistent blood splatters, uniquely voiced characters and the phenomenal gunplay) gave me great hope for what might be developed for the game later down the line.
And the devs did not disappoint. Every major content patch brings great quality weapons, perks, maps and characters every 2-3 months. AND NO, JUST BECAUSE THEY CHOSE TO CALL THESE UPDATES "CONTENT PACKS" DOES NOT UNDO THE EFFORT THEY PUT INTO THEM. As this review is being written 8 out of the 10 planned perks are playable.
As for the microtransactions everyone are so mad about. Yes, there was no talk of them when the game launched on steam, which would be an excellent reason to be upset at the developers, EXCEPT for the BIG BLUE FU***** DISCLAIMER that says EARLY ACCESS GAME. Not to mention that the microtransactions are purely cosmetic, do not prohibit the use of clientside texture mods and are very discrete (do not interrupt gameplay). Considering there were no weapon skins before they were added, and that the cosmetic items which existed before them remain available to all, I simply cannot understand how so many people see them as pure evil.
Yeah, you get an item worth a few cents every week for playing one match. TOTALLY got shafted there people...
One thing that does however deserve some hate is the fact that apparently the VR version of the game will be exclusive to Oculus VR, which considering how similar all of those goggles are to each other seems like typical corporate do****baggery.
Oh and the Nvidia FLEX that some moro... people keep bit,,, complaining about is a totally optional, experimental graphical enhancement meant to entertain people with too much GPU processing power.
As for the game itself: It's no doubt the best wave based shooter/gun porn game in existence. Was worth buying in my opinion when it had 4 classes and like 3 or 4 maps, and is certainly worth buying now.

Dead Space is a Survivor-Horror game with a third-person view and great shooter elements from 2008. Developed by EA Redwood Shores (now Visceral Games) this game feature Isaac Clarke: a ship system engineer in the middle of the year 2508 into the mission to investigate one of the "planet-cracker" starships that send distress call during a mining operation. When the team (Isaac, commander Zach Hammond, and the computer specialist Kendra Daniels) suffer from a huge system faillure and crash into the planetcracker, called USG Ishimura. Then, without any hope, they try to explore and seek a way to know what happened to the ship, to the crew and -least but not less important- scape from there FAST. Because minutes latter after the forced arrive they witness that in that place there is something crawling, breathing, killing and inhuman. Now they must survive, releasing themselves from the same fate from the crew and stopping it right there. (10/10)
Besides what everyone knows about the future of this franchise (a.k.a Dead Space 3...) this game is almost flawless in every way. You will find one gitch or another that games with the same engine still had but it will never affect your gameplay - and sometimes it's hilarious (ANNNND you will need moments like these, trust me). Some parts of the history may seems unconnected because the way you see or read it; just pay close attention when you head hurts and calm yourself, nothing there happened without a reason.
Also, if you get really tired of any shooter or some so-called survivor-horrors: this game is for you. The monsters you get are all original and have a variety as you progress; and have more than one way to kill them. Yes, way more than one shot straight in the head.
DON'T SHOOT IN THE HEAD. YOU WILL ONLY MAKE THEM EVEN MORE HUNGRY AND MAD.
And, oh, don't think only the monsters had more than one wat to die, too. Just saying.
Dead Space is filled with an intoxicating atmosphere that will drawn you into fear in many ways; and sometimes you will not feel safe even when you are using a save point! - You know can stop reading and get the game to play until the end of this bloody mess. Satisfy your limbs, kid. Because if you want to get a true feeling of horror (in space!) Dead Space is for you.

TL;DR: Welcome to Risk of
Tears. It's a really hard rogue-like action platformer that you will die in repeatedly. 11/10 would die again.
What to say about Risk of Rain--how about we start with difficulty.
THIS GAME IS HARD AS BALLS.
If you're not looking for a challenging rogue-like game, then stop looking here right now. If you're still reading? Then please, check the other reviews as well. In Risk of Rain, you take control of one of 12 (not 10, 12!) survivors. Or four, if you've got friends (local and online co-op, anyone?). The object of the game is to survive each area and make it to the teleporter, grabbing loot and killing the boss for the level. If you die, you start over, but keep anything you've unlocked (for example, playable characters or game-mode modifiers called Artifacts).
You start the game with the Commando, a long range, high mobility character who does decent DPS. To unlock the others, you must complete certain objectives.
Each character has their own playstyle, which makes the diversity very interesting. If you can pay attention to it in the chaos of all of the enemies trying to gnaw/melt/rip/eat/burn/crush/disentigrate your face.
Perhaps the most interesting part of this game is the meter that you see on the top right of all the screenshots. The difficulty level is dynamic, raising every 5 minutes you last in game (it does pause when you pause the game, of course). So, it's not just a "oh my god, I can't die, gotta stay alive" type rogue-like, but also a race against time. As the difficulty rises, you could find yourself having to fight more than one boss in each level, or dealing with enemies who have multiple health bars.
All in all, I would highly reccomend this to anyone who enjoys rogue-like action platformers. Or even all those games separately, if you haven't played them together. I assume this is much more fun with friends, but I've yet to try the multiplayer.

Original core game review: Fun, feels like a little tabletop campaign. Decent result for a crowdfunded game. Don't expect a full game though (no cutscenes, short, limited sfx and gfx variety etc.). Patches have been slow and some big annoyances remain, but so far no gamestoppers. Can't wait for the DLC(s) and user-created content.
Post-Dragonfall: the first official DLC is a rather rich story experience, but mechanically the game remains unpolished. The UI is now seriously annoying, especially in combat, as almost nothing has been fixed - some functionality has been added, but what was previously bad or broken has not been repaired or even touched up. Nothing like loading a save because of a misclick, waiting and waiting for the goddamn click or hotspot or animation to register etc. There is also a very distinct staleness to the SFX now that I've rerun the main campaign a few times, as Dragonfall does little to introduce variety to the experience; what was charming minimalism in a crowdfunder is now becoming tiresome as time goes on and replays happen. The final, commercial product has not aged well.
Dragonfall is not worth its full asking price. Only adding a storyline and some maps is bargain bin stuff. The game needs a mechanical overhaul and fresh assets to stay enjoyable, otherwise it withers as replays and even new campaigns just feel stale and tiring.

Easily one of the best puzzle games ever created. This game pulls off the trick of creating a 3d environment out of an Escher drawing. The game takes place entirely in what is like a maze of puzzles and all the while twisting back on itself and bending the rules of reality to both mind boggling as well as enchanting levels. The puzzles do get challenging and while there is no real story, the cryptic messages found on the walls throughout the game sort of give the sense that you are being watched, not by some character but rather by the antichamber itself. It is a beautiful concept of creating a sort of relationship with the environment and unlocking its secrets and learning that there really are some rules, is an incredibly rewading experience. Do yourself a service as well as partake in the pleasure of playing this hallmark of game design.

Killing Floor 2 in a nutshell is basically a focus on CoD's zombie mode made so much better.
First of all, you have to give credit to Tripwire for making such a polished early access game. Yes, this game is not out yet but it feels like the game is already done and polished (and they polished it reaaaaal good). I have played for a number of hours and never have I encountered a bug before.
Something else you don't see much in zombie games is perks (pretty much classes in this game). Each perk has it's own strength and weakness (surprise, surprise) so having a variety of classes is actually quite important (especially the field medic). The perk system also encourages teamwork to make up for your weakneses and that lonewolves usually won't survive most of the time. So stick together and know your role and duty if you want to make it out alive.
My favorite part of this game is the slow-motions that occur in the middle of a multiplayer game. It's so satisfying to take out 5 zeds with 5 bullets all to the head and let those chunks fly all over the place.
It is, however, in this current state lacking contents but you gotta cut it some slack and remember that this is still early access. They did promise to have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of content in the game during the trailer and I'm confident they will deliver (eventually, I'm a patient guy).
As for the microtransactions, just ignore it. It's probably a way for the devs to make extra money and they probably need it as well and for a good reason. Developing games aren't exactly cheap and the better the games the bigger the budget required. You're here to murder zeds with extreme prejudice, looking good is just optional.
About the patches that take forever to come out, it's true. Yes it takes Tripwire months to release a new patch but I forgive them. Apparently they are also developing Rising Storm 2, a game I'm also looking forward to. So having your workforce split into half won't result the fastest of developments. Yeah I want KF2 to finish as quickly as possible but I want RS2 as well and for that I'm fine with.
After all, when's the last time you see a game about killing Zeds/Zombies while listening to deathcore music in slow motion? (Besides Killing Floor 1 obviously)

And honestly, I'm pretty great when it comes to setting up my router and finding open ports, but Risk of Rain makes it nearly impossible. For one thing, I've found it to be pretty unreliable (it will not detect my router's correct IP address, so I cannot input my router's open ports), and despite all the port forwarding methods I try, my friends and I have yet to have success in playing together unless we are connected to the same IP. But other than that, the game is fantastic.

While still "absorbing" up to a point, compared to previous Civilization games, this one is poorly designed.  Things "happen" for no apparent reason.  Example 1 is unhappiness, and you'll neither get a warning nor can you create an entertainer to take care of the problem.  Example 2 is ranged units; two units same distance and exact same setup, one will fire and the other won't.  Or one can reach the target but the other can't even though they're the same distance away.  Perhaps I'm missing some information but whatever it is, the game designers have certainly made it hard to find.  Example 3 is poor movement design.  Your units have no common sense; sometimes they refuse to move and other times they board ships and travel 47 spaces in order to move forward 2 spaces -- the latter is caused by the *&^&^% inability to stack.  Sometimes they can move "through" another unit; sometimes not, and I can't find any rhyme or reason to it.  Because of the inability to stack, cities on a peninsula are virtually impossible to capture.  Example 4 is the city-states.  While essentially harmless fluff, they're annoying and distracting and helping them adds little benefit, whereas hurting them is guaranteed to get you a war with someone.  Like I said at the beginning, it's absorbing -- so I'm going to try it one more time with some mods to see if the mods can fix or minimize these issues.

I will just start off by saying that this game is very good.  There are a few quirky controls and frankly that is the only big issue I can find with the game other than the overall length.
The characters and dialogue are 100% South Park so if you enjoy the show, this game will be more of the same type of jokes.  Most of the characters, even very minor ones, from the show make an appearance at some point.
The combat system is fairly well done.  Attacking is very easy and you will be performing non stop perfect attacks within the first 20 minutes of playing the game.  The defensive side of combat takes some getting used to though as each enemy has multiple different attacks that all need to be timed differently to get "Perfect" blocks which will greatly reduce the damage you take.  It only takes getting hit a few times though to get most of them down.  I played on normal difficulty and did not have much trouble with any of the fights.  I only had to replay three I think and only because my teammate died to an enemy attack and the enemy died to bleed or fire damage after it killed him which would have voided a playthrough long achievement had I kept going and not reverted to a prior save.
The quests in the game are not overly tedious and you are not really kept in any area long enough to get bored with it.  The downside to this was that I ended up finishing up the last of my playthrough around the 20 hour mark which is a bit short for an RPG.  If I had to add one thing to this game, it would have been about 10-15 more side missions.
The controls are good save for some placed where you must perform on screen commands.  I played using an XBOX 360 controller and some of these events were just brutal.  Learning the first spell from Cartman took me like 10 tries.  There is another part, towards the end of the story, where using a controlled will make you pull your hair out.  To remain spoiler free, you will know it when you get there and there are numerous threads discussing it.  When you have to spin the stick for this part, placing my palm on the stick and spinning it as fast is possible is the only way I made it.  Others have said that quitting and starting up the game with mouse and keyboard is much easier.
Overall, I would give this game a solid 8/10.  If it were another 15 hours or so longer, that score would be higher.

DISCLAIMER: I played this game on free weekends. Twice.
Both weekends I happened to have friends out visiting, and we managed to set up a few computers and murder things. And as far as the whole blood/guts/bullets thing goes, I haven't played anything better than this. The only thing more wonderful than the Zeds' beautiful textures and animations is watching them *POP* after pumping them full of microwave radiation. The environments were also gorgeous and varied, and the roaming shop ensures that you are able to fully explore each map. To be honest, I never found myself groaning at having to play through a map AGAIN, and lighting the last Zed on fire was almost as satisfying as the first.
The Nu Metal soundtrack features some big names from the scene, like Demon Hunter and Living Sacrifice, which feels right at home while beating the eyes out of Edward Sword-Hands and friends. The guns and sound design are a treat, make sure to bring nice headphones/speakers, and crank that volume up.
All in all, there's a lot of love being put into this game, and it shows. As of now, I think $20 for this much AAA content is a STEAL. No, this game is not finished. The classes aren't ballanced, there are only a few maps, like 2 bosses, and the levelling/perk system is very underwhelming. But you'll be having too much fun chopping mutants in half with a samurai sword to notice.

Really great game. Fast paced action roguelike semi-platformer. Challenges in the game unlock new items to drop and characters to play. Collectables can be found and activated to change the game experience making the game harder or easier, depending on which ones you choose.
While there are three distinct overall difficulties, the game's primary mechanic is that the longer you play it, the harder it gets (to a point, but it's a pretty crazy point). Rushing through isn't good unless you know how to do it right, because you'll not get any items and will be too weak later down the road. Slowing down and grabbing every chest, however, will ramp up the difficulty and make the game harder too. The skill is to do both. Harder global difficulties make this in-game difficulty clock speed up, among other things.
The game has six stages, ten levels, and at least twenty level varients. Each of the first four stages can be one of two unique levels. Each level has two or three varients, one of which will contain that level's unique collectable (every level has one) After beating stage five, you can keep looping through (levels and varients can change). The sixth stage is the final stretch to the end boss and the credits roll (but it ain't easy).
In each stage, you must find the teleporter and start charging it up (90 seconds in the first two global difficulties, 120 on the third). During this time a boss will spawn, enemy spawn chances are increased, and enemies are more likely to be elites. After time is up, remaining enimies must be mopped up. You're then free to activate the teleporter and move on to the next stage.
Each character (ten total) has a unique ability set, similar to LoL or DotA. The first always has no cooldown, the last has slightly longer cooldown. Enimies drop the cash you use to open chests which contain a random item. Most items are passive, and you can hold an infinite number of them (most of them stack, usually at a reduced effect). Like usual, whites are common, greens are uncommon, and reds are rare. Oranges are usable items, and you can only hold one at a time.
Full support for up to four player co-op, local and online. You respawn at the start of the next stage. Some items apply to all people who proc them, not just the one holding it. Money is shared, no additional chests spawn, and experience is duplicated. Everyone gets XP and cash for every kill, no matter who does it.
Complaints:
No servers for this game exist, you'll need to port forward.
Game speed is tied to framerate. This is not usually and issue, as it's not an intensive game. Only if you play for upwards of an hour in a single game (a really long time) will you start to see some issues, and only then if you're computer is lame.
Game is very RNG, (it's a roguelike) so if that puts you off then this game (the whole genre, really) isn't for you.
You'll probably need to use the wiki.
