The whole game is a puzzle game, no real story, but using a lot of spatial perception as the core mechanic. The key to this one is understanding its internal logic, and what's really interesting here is how consistent it all is. The more you play, the more you understand how it all works. There's a bit of a quantum theme going on, with perception mattering to the existence of objects. So if you look at a path while going down it, you end up in one place, but if you look away while travelling, you end up in another.
It's the sense of internal consistency which really is important here. The game has a map with waypoints that lets you travel around, and it uses a 2d projection of the 3d space to help you out. Some people have called the game 4d, which I suppose isn't totally inaccurate in some parts, but I prefer to look at it as non-euclidian quantum 3d. Yeah, I just made that definition up (I think?) but it fits to me.
Don't be mistaken by my postulation into thinking this is some hard sci-fi romp. If anything, it's a pensive meditation on reality. Existentialism if anything. All throughout the game, you are given hints of what to do by little wall panels with simple pictographs and fortune-cookie sayings. The interesting bit is how these are all extremely helpful, and also make you wonder about their statements. In real life, it can be hard to see why choosing the direction to walk can matter, but when extrapolated into this space, it becomes more visually apparent, and thus we are more susceptable to questioning why we act the way we do.
It's, perhaps, a little pretentious, you could say. I would say that misses the point. The game was once called Hazard: The Journey of Life, but I think Antichamber is more appropriate a title. The game uses the corners of your brain for a lot of puzzle solving, and requires you to think outside the box. Or perhaps, to reshape the box you think in. I dunno. It's neat.

Tactical gaming and magepunk at its finest. In this game, you can play as any of a variety of classic character types from the Shadowrun universe. You can play a Mage, a Shaman, a Street Samurai, a Rigger, a Hacker, or an Adept. You can interact with the Matrix, control drones summon spirits, use every sort of weapon, and more. Not only that, but after character creation your development is totally free form. You can even pick up magical skills if you didn't start with any. Beware of Essence expenditures, however; as always in Shadowrun canon, losing Essence makes magic harder to practice.
The game is tactical squad based combat. Not much in the way of noncombat ability is present. Even the Matrix missions focus on searching for things while engaging in cybercombat with IC. Noncombat skills that are featured are primarily noncombat applications of the hacking skillls, and the game's social aspect.
The story is full if twists and turns as any good Shadowrun plot is. Fans of the series will realize what the plot really is about halfway through, and your mind just might explode when you do. The plot was established a long time ago, but no one ever actually played it all out that I know of. Enjoy it!
What really makes this game complete, however is the mission editor. You can create your own custom adventures and then play them out and/or share them with others. I have a great deal of missions I could be playing through and simply haven't yet. I also have yet to play Dragonfall, the DLC sequel to this game.
Notable in its absence is the ability to play in Astral space, even though the original game concept included that as an option. This disappoints me greatly.
(Overall 9/10, Story 10/10, Gameplay 8/10, Graphics 7/10, Sound 9/10, Replayability 10/10)

I managed to finally get into this game after waiting a substantial length of time for a patch to fix PC issues as well as get a decent rig to start playing the higher up pc games in my library. While I haven't logged any hours on my profile, I played through on my relative's with 120% completion rate and unlocked all the endings.
Batman Arkham Knight is a great game, when you peel back some of the annoying layers covering it; from the horrid PC release to the seemingly rushed release, this game is still comparable to the first two games (I don't believe Arkham Origins really counts) and is a great conclusion to the Arkham series.
First, the good. The story; definitely, especially after having seen the animated series throughout and seeing how it came through to this end. The ending may confuse some people, but I think it was well done and quite satisfying. Moreover; the emotional beats this game hit compared to the others is worthy of praise. I was feeling very tense and emotional at key points during the story; the music definitely adds to this and is appreciated.
The cast of characters; with the Season of Infamy DLC, many villain arcs have come to a close and the quests were fun to play. The quest for Mr Freeze was especially heartwarming and one of my favourite sidequests. The other sidequests were... not so well done, but I'll get to that later.
The combat and predator encounters are improved upon further. Throw  counters and more special moves added to  Batman's arsenal and actually become very useful; especially fear takedowns, which you'll need to use against the improved mooks. They actually go to every length possible to beat you with new tactics including vantage point mining, sentry guns, scanning drones, better awareness of grates, and buddying up with each other. This makes the predator encounters more dynamic and challenging without being too frustrating, given the wider options Batman has as well.
Voice acting; as great as ever. And  Mark Hamill's addition was great and appreciated.
The visuals were definitely the best yet, but unfortunately require a decent computer to handle. Still, seeing Gotham in all its glory was breathtaking as you'll fly to the tops of huge towers and drive through vast plazas and streets; fully realising a big city like Gotham as the environment.
Now for the bad parts. Unfortunately, the tracking of sidequests was handled poorly, as most are more often than not fetch quests for extra objectives that span throughout the entire game. These become an annoyance because you can't always complete a quest the first time you receive it; most just end up piling up and getting annoying as I want to finish them off early, but you almost never can. Finding these objectives can be equally frustrating as only solving Riddler challenges lets you get map trackers on them.
Speaking of; Riddler challenges were not enjoyable here. Despite having less challenges than Arkham City; each one was overall more annoying than challenging as often switches you step on give you no feedback on what has changed; leaving you running around more than you should to find what you're supposed to be doing. The riddles were worse. In the open city, it only gives you the general area of a revealed riddle. Now this is a problem as there are so many things of interest to look at (which would otherwise be a good thing) to be annoying distractions as you often have little idea of what you're looking for. It could be a small poster in a whole city block; or a distant object that might have nothing to do with the riddle you're solving. This could have been alleviated by giving the exact location of the riddle in the open city like it was in Arkham City.
The Batmobile was kind of a mixed bag. At first, and especially throughout with car chases, using the Batmobile was refreshing and was always fun when chasing down mooks and APCs with tracking shots. However the tank battles got quite repetitive towards the end; not challenging enough or dynamic enough to keep my full attention for the whole thing. The more insulting thing about the Batmobile is that the majority of any boss battles are for the Batmobile. Disappointing, to say the least.
Still, I enjoyed Arkham Knight very much and it's clear now how much work was put into this game. Rocksteady still did a great job and I'm surprised by how hard many reviewers are being. Probably to do with the shoddy release, but this is a great conclusion and worth getting once you can get past the release problems and somewhat frustrating riddler crap (I had to resort to looking things up online). Thank you, Rocksteady.

I can't believe I didn't play this game sooner! But I don't mind having gotten it at a sale price. The Stick of Truth was way more fun than I ever expected, and I'm a huge fan of South Park. It just seems like games based on shows like this haven't done so well, but SOT is an exception to the rule.
For starters, it's a pretty solid RPG. You can customize your character to impressive levels of detail, and as you play you're constantly getting upgrades. There's at least one outfit for every level, and many of them match the missions you're playing, so your character is constantly changing over time, but still uniquely yours. Weapons and attacks are great, I found myself trying out all of them for all of the playable characters so I didn't miss any characteristic South Park humor.
And wow, there are a lot of references in this game. They managed to squeeze in a surprising number of characters from the show, and refer to some of the oldest episodes for some of the plot points. It is a really wild story, in true South Park fashion, and keeps you laughing from start to finish. As other reviewers have noted, some of the humor goes further than you might expect, with the game rubbing your nose in its most disgusting moments for extended periods. I thought it was hysterical. But of course, that's not for everyone.
Battles are really fun, and they always stay relatively challenging relative to your current level. With clever use of powerups, status effects, and items, you can finish off any enemy without too much effort.
Walking around South Park is pretty fun in itself, you can go to lots of places featured on the show and get a sense of where they are in relation to one another. Almost all of them serve a purpose in the greater story, or offer a side quest for you to take. There's also lots of collectibles, from equipment upgrades to Chinpokomon to people's underwear (go figure). Plenty to keep you busy in this town as you're progressing through the story. Some of the collectibles are missable which is disappointing, so keep an eye out during the main missions for pickups if that is important to you. For most that will be a minor issue.
My one big complaint is that the leveling up stops at level 15, and there didn't seem to be a dedicated outfit for that level - only a few level 14 ones to choose from. I got to 15 a few hours before the story ended, so I guess it just felt like it came too quickly. I would gladly have played another 5+ hours of this game.
Overall I really enjoyed SOT and look forward to enjoying this game again some day. For now, I've been inspired to rewatch South Park over from the beginning.

Having played the Shadowrun tabletop in the 90's, along with the SEGA and SNES games, I had high expectations for this game. I haven't enjoyed a Shadowrun game since the aforementioned titles, and this title was a long time in coming. If you're looking to reexperience the Shadowrun universe this is a great place to start. The campaign that shipped with the game itches that bug perfectly.  Additionally, there is a very active mod community churning out numbers of new campaigns for you to try. Where this title really shines, however, is in the ability for storytellers to create there own content to share with their friends and/or the world. The graphics aren't state of the art, there isn't any sleek cutscenes, nor is there any voice acting (thankfully), but I highly recommend this game to those of you looking to scratch that long festering Shadowrun itch. Really well-executed, mind-bending puzzler.  If you loved Portal but wished for more variety+difficulty in the mechanics and even less of a traditional narrative, then Antichamber is for you! :-)
The puzzles were challenging, engrossing, lateral-thought-provoking ... but still mostly "fair," if that makes sense.  I admit to getting hints online 3-4 times on the way to beating the game, and in most of those cases after seeing the solution I said "glad I checked; I wouldn't have noticed that in a million years."  But I weigh that against the 30-40 puzzles I solved that were "just right" in terms of novelty and difficulty, and the game is a clear winner.
If you like first-person  puzzle games, this is well worth your $15 and the 7-8 hours that an honest play-through will take.

When the game first came out it had its bugs and some framerate issues, nothing gamebreaking though. Recently though, the devs brought the game to a newer engine, and it caused LOADS of bugs and problems, even though the fps problems are mostly fixed now. I don't recommend it because even though it is loads of fun, the devs have abandoned it for the past weeks and haven't spoken to the community at all. It needs a big patch to fix the annoying bugs the game currently has and some balancing on some of the characters so that they become more viable and fun. I really like this game and I want it to thrive, but it raised more than 400% what it requested on kickstarter, and the developers NEED to address the problems it currently has, especially considering how much extra they raised.
If you're really interested in playing the game you should download the demo and try it out. If you really like it you can pick it up, the price is a steal for what the game offers anyway, but bear in mind that the current state of the game is very poor and the devs really need to put some work into fixing all the problems it currently has, and that's why my review will remain negative until the devs adress all that.

It plays a lot like the new X-Com on a more personal scale, and a lot more choice when it comes to combat. Since it includes a lot of RPG elements and the Shadowrun setting, you can create a character any way you like, from a run-and-gunner to a mage slinging fireballs, to a mage slinging buffs, to a mage with a pet, or something in-between.
Some things seem unpolished or foolish, however, like running a melee combatant or a physad; The few times I tried to melee an opponent, even with a physad NPC, I got chopped into hamburger. I'm also unsure why you'd want to stick with pistols when rifles and shotguns are available, no matter how good pistols get later in the game. Maxing out pistol skills seems silly. Similarly, some of the etiquette skills are nearly useless, while some are indispensable. I suppose that's true in life as well, but it's easy to feel annoyed that you've wasted your skill points.
But the setting is fantastic, and feels like it was written by people who know the game and want to make it as authentic and immersive as possible.

For $30, it's a decent deal. If you're a fan of these type of games, you will enjoy it.  The biggest issue is the difficulty balance and content, both not being accomodated in spite the game being "out of early access."
To those that don't know, this game isn't actually finished but rather it was a marketing move to say it is out of Early Access. It is still gaining new content, but the progress is very slow. New levels are slow, new weapons and characters are slow, everything is slow progression. However, the game still has enough content to be enjoyable and return to every so often there is a big update.
The biggest issue I have is much that I have had in the first one. It seems like a hard game at first, maybe even overwhelming to players unfamiliar with the formula. However, it's very easy once you learn how the game intends you to play. Those big scary zeds that are like tanks die in a few shots by sharpshooters or a few seconds by specific classes, camp spots are everywhere and kiting is still a thing, the game isn't by any means as easy as KF1 but it's still a bit disappointing they don't make Hell on Earth, the hardest difficulty, a bit more challenging. As someone that sucks at video games, especially these type of games, that has more responsibilities than gaming time and runs off to do his own thing more often than stay with his team mates, I feel I should be punished a bit more than I am. If I can run around without my team, there is probably a problem. I cannot imagine how dull this game is for someone that spends the time to get amazing at it.
Another issue is the quirks. The loading takes forever sometimes, it's inconsistent. Some startup launches can take as long as ten minutes for even high end computers, sometimes it's practically instant. Other issues is the zeds getting stuck in places on the map and the game sorta punishes you of all people for it, sometimes making players resort to suiciding if the zed is out of reach which often happens for specific maps. Some other issues like no way to remove community maps from your level menu or some clear way to make it official only when playing single player, no clear way to filter the games that consistently works, and the issue of looking at your perks in your escape menu is enough to change to them unlike the first game rationally requiring you to click a button to confirm your decision. The game also has a lot of weapons that are useless, classes that feel off, and the versus mode is a bit boring but some people enjoy it unless they're playing as the Zeds, which is mostly frustrating if the survivors are leveled up since zeds can't level up.
The game's balance is off with many things, bosses for an example has been a tad controversial so far, meaning Hanz is very powerful in comparison to the Patriarch unless in specific events. The game has no clear way to allow players to get cosmetic items, you simply wait for them to drop and you can recycle ones you don't want for a new one except the item drop speed is so slow that this will likely never happen in your benefit.
The graphics is amazing, the soundtrack is impressive, and the gameplay is excellent. There is not a whole lot to say. The graphics are a lot better than the first, but the atmosphere isn't the same. There is a lot more color in this game than the first, lot more lighting, meaning it's a bit less edgy and dark than the first game. There are maps that are completely day time which seems out of place for the game. Otherwise, the graphics are very good.
Overall, nothing else is needed to say. It is not something you will play a lot, maybe a good amount of hours here and there though. You definitely want to enter this with friends.
Do keep in mind it uses transactions and it will constantly nag you about them. Just when you thought you finally got a drop for something, it's something you already had or it is a chest. You can recycle item drops for a higher tier item, similar to Rocket League, but because you get one item every day I believe, it just feels unrealistic to expect to ever get those skins you really want for less than $10.

There is a feature which allows you to customize the aspects of your maps starting conditions.  These features include which era the game begins in, how many resources there are, and what the map looks like.  There are also many other aspects, but that is just to name a few.
Once you get all your settings finely tuned, the game play is very satisfying.  You can set the pace yourself.  Whether you like to take your time or rush thru all the messages, there is a setting for you.  The voice acting is minimal, there is not much need for it tho.  There are so many options for what direction you want your civilization to go in.
You can win by various types of victories as stated earlier.  To gain these victories, you must utilize different strategies.  Using terrain, leader abilities, and policies to your advantage.
Overall I would say this game is very worth giving a try, even if turn-based strategy is not your gaming style.

Let me start out by saying that this is the first Shadowrun game that I have ever actually played. Yes I have tried the 1993 Shadowrun for the Super Nintendo but I could never get into it due to it's... Interesting controls (read point and click with a controller). But the game concept and the universe intrigued me, Over the years I forgot the name of it several times but would bring it up every few years and try to find the name of it and feel that they should remake it for the pc where it ultimately belonged. Well a few months ago was one such time that It popped into my head, I did a quick search for it and what did I find but a new Shadowrun being made for its proper platform (psst its the PC). I instantly fell in love with the style and everything I say was just the best thing I have ever seen.
Flash forward to now where I have been given the ability to write this review and I am just stoked to be able to finally play a Shadowrun game without being hindered by a D-pad. Well I wasn't home when I got the Beta code but I had a 2 hour drive till I got home and then I had to download it and set it up. This just ate at me up inside but I managed to do it and when I first started it up I felt a chill as the dark and music (composed by Marshall Parker and Sam Powell from the 1993 SNES Shadowrun) started to play and the menu appeared.
When you start a new game your greeted with a fairly standard character creation menu. You can select your gender, race and choose between several preconfigured or a custom skill sets for your character as well as select from one of several portraits and player models. The models look nice but are lacking the level of detail that you see with other games though this low detail level just feels right in the world, fitting in with the 2D environments. Each race has specific traits that are more prominent then others, these usually have higher starting values and higher max values. After choosing a character model and skill set you get to pick traits and spend your skill points on your starting stats. As soon as you are done creating your character you start in a modest apartment. After looking around the apartment for a while you get a call from an old friend and are sent into a flashback where you learn more about yourself and your friend but more importantly you get to experience the combat system for the first time.
Shadowrun Returns is broken up into missions and uses an auto save feature that saves at the beginning of a mission. It uses a tactical combat system where you have your squad and each member has action points. Each action your characters take use action points and once they're gone then that character can't do anything till the next turn.
This is customary for tactical games like this and even new people to this style of play should get used to it rather quickly. The combat system uses cover and line of site as a tactic and shows you how good the cover is and to what side you have cover on. This system isn't perfect as it doesn't always show that you're in cover and at times it's hard to tell if your line of site is broken simply due to the layout of the room and the camera angle.
Shadowrun Returns comes with a full scenario editor that allows users to create whole new missions and stories and share them with the community. The editor has been out for many of the kickstarter backers for a while now so there is going to be plenty of user made content available. Someone is currently working on recreating the old SNES Shadowrun into Shadowrun Returns using the editor available here
Overall I feel that the 2D backgrounds and the 3D character models mesh very well together and unlike in some games they feel right together. The story is excellent and you don't feel like it's being force fed down your gullet so you can play the game for the story or the game play or both. The main story is quite linier and it tends to feel like there's some handholding going on but you can choose to help someone or leave them to their own devices and save your own skin. I am not a master of table top RPG's but this feels like how I would imagine a table top RPG should be on a PC.

For $30, it's a decent deal. If you're a fan of these type of games, you will enjoy it.  The biggest issue is the difficulty balance and content, both not being accomodated in spite the game being "out of early access."
To those that don't know, this game isn't actually finished but rather it was a marketing move to say it is out of Early Access. It is still gaining new content, but the progress is very slow. New levels are slow, new weapons and characters are slow, everything is slow progression. However, the game still has enough content to be enjoyable and return to every so often there is a big update.
The biggest issue I have is much that I have had in the first one. It seems like a hard game at first, maybe even overwhelming to players unfamiliar with the formula. However, it's very easy once you learn how the game intends you to play. Those big scary zeds that are like tanks die in a few shots by sharpshooters or a few seconds by specific classes, camp spots are everywhere and kiting is still a thing, the game isn't by any means as easy as KF1 but it's still a bit disappointing they don't make Hell on Earth, the hardest difficulty, a bit more challenging. As someone that sucks at video games, especially these type of games, that has more responsibilities than gaming time and runs off to do his own thing more often than stay with his team mates, I feel I should be punished a bit more than I am. If I can run around without my team, there is probably a problem. I cannot imagine how dull this game is for someone that spends the time to get amazing at it.
Another issue is the quirks. The loading takes forever sometimes, it's inconsistent. Some startup launches can take as long as ten minutes for even high end computers, sometimes it's practically instant. Other issues is the zeds getting stuck in places on the map and the game sorta punishes you of all people for it, sometimes making players resort to suiciding if the zed is out of reach which often happens for specific maps. Some other issues like no way to remove community maps from your level menu or some clear way to make it official only when playing single player, no clear way to filter the games that consistently works, and the issue of looking at your perks in your escape menu is enough to change to them unlike the first game rationally requiring you to click a button to confirm your decision. The game also has a lot of weapons that are useless, classes that feel off, and the versus mode is a bit boring but some people enjoy it unless they're playing as the Zeds, which is mostly frustrating if the survivors are leveled up since zeds can't level up.
The game's balance is off with many things, bosses for an example has been a tad controversial so far, meaning Hanz is very powerful in comparison to the Patriarch unless in specific events. The game has no clear way to allow players to get cosmetic items, you simply wait for them to drop and you can recycle ones you don't want for a new one except the item drop speed is so slow that this will likely never happen in your benefit.
The graphics is amazing, the soundtrack is impressive, and the gameplay is excellent. There is not a whole lot to say. The graphics are a lot better than the first, but the atmosphere isn't the same. There is a lot more color in this game than the first, lot more lighting, meaning it's a bit less edgy and dark than the first game. There are maps that are completely day time which seems out of place for the game. Otherwise, the graphics are very good.
Overall, nothing else is needed to say. It is not something you will play a lot, maybe a good amount of hours here and there though. You definitely want to enter this with friends.
Do keep in mind it uses transactions and it will constantly nag you about them. Just when you thought you finally got a drop for something, it's something you already had or it is a chest. You can recycle item drops for a higher tier item, similar to Rocket League, but because you get one item every day I believe, it just feels unrealistic to expect to ever get those skins you really want for less than $10.

Antichamber feels like the opposite of Portal, Quantum Conundrum and Q.U.B.E.
Those games make use of logical puzzles, Antichamber... does not. It will force you to think outside the box. And that is not an easy task for most of us.
The game itself consists of a mostly seamless world (until you get to a part where you're being forced to teleport out of it), with puzzles in every corner. Not all of these puzzles have to be finished for you to complete the game, but you do have to collect the 4 different guns in order to advance and finish the game. Once again, not an easy task.
I'd love to explain some of these puzzles to you but that would spoil them and it's too difficult to even try anyway. It's something you have to experience, if only for a short while.
Antichamber has another cool feature; the use of in-game achievements. The rooms use icons/pictures and text to act as in-game achievements. Seeing them lets you know if you've been there before and it might even give you a subtle hint on what to do. You'll have to solve every puzzle there is so fill up your wall.
It would've been nice if there were Steam achievements involved as well, but hey, you can't have everything I guess.
One annoying thing is that if you press Escape you have to start over if you wish to continue the puzzle you were working on. There's no pause button, if you press Esc you're back in the 'main menu' where you can select which puzzle you want to solve and see your achievements. Quite annoying if you want to take a little break.
Oh, as you may have noticed the graphics are a mix of simplistic, artistic and futurustic styles, and while they're not always hi def, they're cool to look at. It's really something special.
Hmm, I don't know what to say to you. I wish I could recommend this game to anyone out there, but I think it's a 'love it or hate it' game. As a game though, it's a success !

What can I say? It's Half-Life 2, pretty much the perfect game. It has an interesting story that remains tightly focused on a core group of characters while never revealing too much to the player. It has ever-evolving gameplay mechanics that all use the same basic controls so it never gets too complicated. Everything from the environment design to the characters to the enemies looks absoutely beautiful even though the game was released a decade ago.
The only downside is the fact that Half-Life 2 was so revoultionary, so innovative, that if you still haven't played it yet, it might actually seem quaint and boring to you.
Yes, Half-Life 2 unfortunately suffers from the "Seinfeld is Lame" problem in that since its release, almost every first-person shooter released afterwards has copied the game's mechanics in one way or another. So even though you've never played Half-Life 2, you've almost certainly played some sort of derivative.
But don't let that discourage you. Half-Life 2 is still one of the greatest first-person shooter games ever made. I suggest you buy it on sale for the 2014 Steam Holiday Sale and play it all the way through in one day, preferably with some good headphones plugged in at 1080p with full settings on. You won't regret it, unless you're ♥♥♥♥ing stupid.

I'll start by saying that a lot of the criticism of this game is well-founded, but that doesn't mean it's not worth playing.  If you're just looking for another RPG, Shadowrun may not be for you.  It is extremely linear and the included campaign is not what I would call replayable.  The biggest negative aspect of the game lies in persistent UI problems.  None of them are game-breaking, and most are simply irritating, though once in a while you might have to reload.
On the other hand, if you like Shadowrun, cyberpunk, or if a game world that includes tech and magic interests you, you should give the game a look.  The storyline may be linear, but it's well written, full of believable and interesting characters.  So much so, that I was immediately looking to see if someone had created a follow-up campaign to continue the story.
Makes me want to find a local gaming group and play some old-fashioned pen and paper Shadowrun.

XCOM: Enemy Within: Enemy Unknown was a great game. Enemy Within makes a great game even better in every way. A new resource adds to character development, new maps add a great deal of variety, and the new enemies really round out areas that were lacking before. Don't even bother playing classic Enemy Unknown, because Enemy Within gives that much more of a complete experience and integrates seamlessly into the original game. This is by every definition an expansion, rather than a continuation or sequel, rounding out the early and middle of the game rather than altering the late game.
Introduced right at the start, MELD adds further specialization to your soldiers, allowing deeper development and forcing additional choices. As you progress you obtain abilities that alter the entire experience, from being able to turn invisble to rivaling the large mechanical enemies. The entirely new EXALT questline adds an element that really rounds out the mid-game, something that could seem to drag on previously while waiting for research or money to accumulate.
The quintessential XCOM experience is obtained by turning on Ironman mode, for two reasons: Your progress is continuously saved while preventing reloads if things don't turn out your way. Until you've lost a veteran of 30 missions due to a single poor choice, you haven't played XCOM. The higher difficulty levels are much higher difficulty as well, so enter them with caution, they can be extremely unforgiving.
The only glitch I encountered was enemies teleporting around the map or seeming to enter from a weird angle. Other than that and a crash that may have been driver related, the game is extremely polished, allowing you to focus on having fun.
Overall, XCOM:Enemy Within is a fantastic game. It approaches a level that is hard to match despite a couple minor glitches that shouldn't have a major negative impact on gameplay.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a 2012, turn-based tactical strategy game released by Firaxis Games (the company that is responsible for the well-famous Civilization franchise) and published by 2K. Enemy Unknown is a remake of the classic 1994 game of the same title. Enemy Unknown takes you into a long and brutal journey to fend off the alien invaders and the hefty responsibility to command your troops to victory. The game was a huge success to Firaxis Games. This review will also extend to the expansion pack, Enemy Within. Is Firaxis Games’ vision of XCOM a true successor to the original franchise?
The story is very simple. The aliens invade Earth and you play as the Commander, who leads the XCOM organization to fight off the aliens via commanding your troops and facilitate limited resources to your advantage. One of the main features for the game is character customization that brings in strong, “emotional” investment to your created characters. Admittedly, I found the character customization limited but it did little to prevent me from caring about the created characters. A few reasons why a person would be invested in fictional characters. Field promotions and experiences in combat will put you in intense situations. The feeling of victory and triumph or the tragedy of mission failure and a character’s (or characters’) sudden death will put you in an emotional ride. Such emotions makes this game very addicting.
The game brings a good challenge to the player and the difficulty levels are appropriate for any player who have some experience on understanding basic tactics or “complex” strategies to win over the enemy. The best features for the game are the unpredictable nature and improvisation to withdrawal from battle or fight to the bitter end. Even with “common sense”, aliens can hit you based upon chance and random critical hits. The commander’s (or your) decision will determine if your soldier will fight another day or take a huge risk to kill the biggest threat to your squad.
The game certainly has some of the best features, but there are some minor annoyances and criticisms that needs to be addressed to potential buyers. First, I find Dr. Moira Vahlen a tad annoying due to her “accent” or the voice acting for the character. Second, the game’s unpredictability can be a turn-off for some players who felt “cheated” by sudden critical hits on your soldiers. Essentially, the outcome of each mission is based on a “gamble”, hoping that the enemy won’t hit you or at least won’t “cheat” on getting a sudden kill shot on someone who has full health. Honestly, I like this unpredictability but not for some players. The map designs are “limited”, meaning that there is a chance that you will play the same map design more than one mission. Since the missions can take place in anywhere on the world, there are no “cultural distinction” on any maps. For example, if the mission takes place in Egypt, China, Germany (and elsewhere) there are no cultural icons or specific cultural features in the maps that take place (besides the introductory mission in the Slingshot Pack)
Lastly, the spoken languages are very limited and disappointing. The game only offers English and various European languages (like Spanish, French, Polish, Russian, etc). Ironically, the addition for European languages comes from the expansion pack, Enemy Within. Worse, the European languages pack comes from the base game (for European players who played in his or her native language) only to be packaged to the expansion pack for American audiences. Since XCOM is an international military and scientific organization, the lack of more languages (Arabic, various African languages, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin and Cantonese, and various others) in the game was a bitter disappointment to me.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown and its expansion pack, Enemy Within, is worth your money and your investment. An excellent mod, The Long War, raise the replay value into new heights and is a worthy addition for any XCOM player to have (depending if you want a very brutal and a marathon campaign). The game’s optimization is very good mainly because the system requirements is very affordable for any PC player at this point of time. However, this game might not be everyone’s favorite cup of tea if the person does not like turn-based combat. Regardless, the high replay value, intense firefights, and emotional attachments to your created character makes this game unique. A must buy for any PC gamer even with the minor issues at hand. This game has my highest recommendation.

Out of all of the games I played in 2014, I think Risk of Rain was one of the few that I truly fell in love with. Something to be rivaled only by Smash Bros. 3DS/Wii U and Saints Row IV.
Don't let the mention of those games make you think this is anything like that. Risk of Rain is a unique experience where you find yourself as one of a unique roster of warriors fighting against creatures on an alien planet. The story is minimal, and you're only given a vague idea of whats going on and the personality of the characters, but every aspect of this sci fi universe that you're given a peek at is truly a joy.
Soon after you crash on one of a handful of randomly generated planets, enemies begin spawning in. You use 4 different attacks, some long range, some short range, to kill your enemies as quickly as possible, because the longer you take to progress in the game the higher the difficulty gets. The game manages to convey a vague sense of each character's personality through the minimalistic pixel art and unique attacks that each character has. It has light roguelike mechanics where you level up and acquire items as you progress through the game. Some may be intimidated by the difficulty, but I personally loved learning the mechanics of each character and improving my skill in the game. While there are randomized items that will give you big advantages at times, this game is still heavily skill based. I loved knowing that I was becoming more skilled at the game while doing cool atacks, taking down massive bosses and playing with friends.
Oh yeah, and did I mention there's up to 4 player co-op, both local and online? Yes, this game is a blast to play by yourself or with friends. Buy it now. For me, the game is only held back somewhat by some of the glitches and the clunky IP method for playing online, but these things can hardly detract from one of my favorite games in recent years.

What can I say? It's Half-Life 2, pretty much the perfect game. It has an interesting story that remains tightly focused on a core group of characters while never revealing too much to the player. It has ever-evolving gameplay mechanics that all use the same basic controls so it never gets too complicated. Everything from the environment design to the characters to the enemies looks absoutely beautiful even though the game was released a decade ago.
The only downside is the fact that Half-Life 2 was so revoultionary, so innovative, that if you still haven't played it yet, it might actually seem quaint and boring to you.
Yes, Half-Life 2 unfortunately suffers from the "Seinfeld is Lame" problem in that since its release, almost every first-person shooter released afterwards has copied the game's mechanics in one way or another. So even though you've never played Half-Life 2, you've almost certainly played some sort of derivative.
But don't let that discourage you. Half-Life 2 is still one of the greatest first-person shooter games ever made. I suggest you buy it on sale for the 2014 Steam Holiday Sale and play it all the way through in one day, preferably with some good headphones plugged in at 1080p with full settings on. You won't regret it, unless you're ♥♥♥♥ing stupid.

I LOVED KF1!
Played it a lot. Over three hundred hours. All through college it was the game me and my mates would play when we should have been studying. It was great. It had open levels, encouraged teamwork, was hard as hell, but always felt fair. In a way, like Dark Souls. It beat you but you kept coming back.
KF2?
Its...okay. I mean, I play it but there is just something ...off.  Not as is ‘not KF1’. But as a shooter in general.  I think part of it is that the maps are not very interesting in their design and they are rather small. Some maps alleviate this by being vertical with multiple levels but overall the levels are just cramped and give you this weird feeling of being in a corridor shooter even though you can go anywhere. Imagine if Call of Duty made you play a whole campaign mission on one of its multiplayer maps.
Not that you’ll really explore much of the map because it sort of becomes a tower defense game. Unlike the first game that encouraged movement, or at least holding up somewhere where you could escape (and often you would need too on the hardest difficulties) this game encourages you sit in one place (and most levels only really have on good place to defend) with your team and just shoot down hallways. Honestly, it becomes mind-numbingly repetitive because you never feel the need to haul♥♥♥♥♥cause you can take down anything.
I could go on. I mean it’s a pretty game. And the sound effects and the recoil of the guns are great. But there is just something so 'meh' about this game that just follows you the entire time.  Not to mention Tripwire is micro transaction the hell out of its game. Sure, if people want to buy new outfits, that's great. But its been a year Tripwire.  The game is still in Early Access. How about you focus on -finishing- the game, fixing its known bugs and issues, and releasing it; THEN try to nickel and dime your customers to death?
Overall, I'd say get the game on sale and then only get it if you have friends who want to play. It CAN be enjoyable with friends but the friends are doing the heavy lifting.  But even then, in my mind, I can't shake the feeling that there are more rewarding games we could be playing.

In this game, upon first start, are three basic modes, nicknamed
(the easiest, apparently),
(medium difficulty), and
(the first hardest). Your time on these stages is your overall score, and after lasting one minute in the first three, you unlock a much more harder mode of the same stage (
). And if you wish to "practice" for one of these difficulties, there's an Acrade mode under Options.
Restating what I said earlier: Super Hexagon is
. If you enjoy hypnotizing yourself as you try to move a triangle through an infinitely rotating hexagonal labyrinth, this is a worthy game to play. With the leaderboard, the purpose of the game can be to beat friends by lasting longer than they did in these six stages. Only six achievements? Though it might not do much, but the game could be give me more worthwhile challenges to reach, like an achievement for lasting 120 seconds in the third stage

This game is deceptively impossible and endlessly fun.
Risk of rain gets a whole bunch of things right. It takes the same addictive qualities of Flappy Bird, being that each game starts from level one with no powerups and only 15 coins. You earn coins and EXP by killing enemies, which you can later turn in for power ups, drones that follow you and help you fight, or keep till the end of each level to exchange for EXP. But the deceptive part of this game is that it gets more difficult as time goes on. Every decision you make effects how long it will take you to beat certain levels. Rather than making it through the levels, this game is more about how long you can last.
To be honest, I didn't expect much of Risk of Rain when I bought it. I got the four pack while it was on sale and gave it to three of my friends, and we've all been playing it non stop. It's the most frustrating game I've played in a while but it's also probably the most fun. Buy it, even if it's full price. You won't regret it.

What makes this game great for me is the variety of gameplay for each chapter. No two chapters feek alike. One chapter feels like a survival horror game. Another chapter feels like a tower defense game. Some chapters have you driving vehicles around at high speeds taking out enemies as you drive by. There's a chapter that has you commanding a squad of allies similar to a game like Pikmin. But even with the huge amount of variety in each chapter, one thing stays consistent: the quality of the game. It's amazing from start to finish and it's definitely a must play.

Shadowrun Returns had the potential of being a great game, however, they fell painfully short. First off, the game is incredibly linear. Make sure you complete EVERY task as you come across it because you can't go back to do it later. Second, there is no save feature other than a waypoint system that autosaves the game when completing quests and changing areas. So if you need to step away from the game you either let it sit open until you come back, or you lose playtime when the game reploads your last autosave. Third, the game was on the short side. I was able to complete the entire game in about 12 hours.
Now on to the good stuff...
I really like the skill based system that lets you pick and choose what you want to do with your character. There really needs to be more games with this function. The game also had some interesting characters (I especially liked Dresdan). I like that NPC attitudes changed based on how you responded, and that your skills actually swayed them one way or another.
I would recommend the game to others, but to be honest, I'd wait for it to go on sale first. $20 for a 12 hour extremely linear game is a bit on the steep side in my opinion.

GTA in its purest form. It was the first GTA game I ever played and probably the best. Vice City has everything - a managable map; memorable characters; a killer OST; great sense of humour and inch-perfect controls. It's much cheaper now than back in the day so there's no excuse to not pick it up. Listen out for the celeb cameos (Debbie Harry and Jenna Jameson to name but two)!

It's ♥♥♥♥ing Early Access.
A company is making it, they want money. There are microtransactions for cosmetics that *ding*ding*ding* DON'T ACTUALLY MEAN ANYTHING. They took it from CSGO because it's obviously working. Just ignore it.
Anywho, it's a fun game even for early access. I enjoyed it even back when there were only 4 perks (yes I bought it that early). It's a slow EA, but whatever. I've more than 100 hours into this and I'm not even close to bored. Even through the Zed teleporting or... whatever, the game is still relatively smooth and killing zombies feels stangely therapudic (especially when you get a headshot with high gore and their eyeballs go flying out... never gets old).
The perks do need a bit of balancing and the vs. mode (although fun) needs to fix some stuff that can make certain Zed players impossible to kill. Also there need to be a few more songs. The ones they have are good killing music, but after 100 hours you get a bit used to them.
All in all, I thuroughly enjoy this game. People who gripe about it are justified but still are really butthurt even though they decided to back this endevour. To me it doesn't even seem like it's the devs fault. Most of the stuff they add has the air of being forced into production by some money grabbing higher-ups, and it took the community rioting almost for those higher-ups to let the devs actually get to work.
If you want to kill hundreds upon hundreds of zombies, get this game. If you want a polished masterpiece that won't waste any of your time, wait for its official release, it's as easy as that.

The single best puzzle game since 'Portal 2'. Confusing, Intriguing, Captivating, and still Fun.  Very similar to Portal in its presentation (a basic white 'testing' environment), however - game play mechanics are a bit different.  The best description I've found is a cross between Portal and Minecraft. Each new puzzle 'room' forces you to re evaluate what is being presented versus what is possible, forcing you to constantly re-analyze your possibilities. Walkthroughs are not recommended, just patience - as leaving the game to come back with fresh eyes is the BEST way to overcome that obstacle, and reap the benefits of being proud at your own abilities. Sound FX are good and interesting, providing environmental specific background noise, but it is not intrusive. There are no themes to sing along with, no dialogue to pay attention to. In the end, the audio sets a relaxing, unobtrusive mood, and nothing more. Graphics are simple, yet refined. Due to the amount of individual 3d 'objects' you can have in the game at once - perhaps a simple graphic presentation is by design. It took a while, but with some effort, Ii WAS able to eventually crash the game by spawning enough objects to overwhelm my video abilities. Lots of enjoyment for any puzzle enthusiast. If you liked Portal, then this game is for you - and at the right price too!

Any fan of Portal is going to be a fan of Antichamber. It's quasi-physic world is not only a bit of a mind-trip at first, but a rewarding adventure that shouldn't be missed.
The game has Braid-like life lessons along the way that are relevant to each puzzle that have just been completed. In a world where the door you just entered could turn into a hallway once you look away from it, there's almost to the amount of creativity that Alexander Bruce, the designer, put into the world.
Meshing nicely with the game's "antiphysical reality" is a block gun that shoots little cubes that the player needs in order to both complete puzzles and navigate the rooms.
While the game is missing a direct narrative, it doesn't subtract from the experience at all - immersed in the simplistically stylized, but mechanically complex world is an inward journey of self discovery, one that adding a centralized character or plot element to would only serve to distract from the focus of the game.
Definitely don't regret putting money down on this one.

I am torn on wither or not to recommend this game or not.  It is about a year after its famously bad release and a lot of people are saying the game is running a lot better for them. My experience though is that even on my fairly high end set up, I have to set all the graphics to low to have anything playable in the Batmobile sections because it runs about 12FPS in those sections otherwise.
Maybe it's just some conflicting software, maybe its just a certain driver causing issues, but my experience is even a year after release the game runs and feels like how many alpha games run, not optimized at all.
All in all not a good PC port even after a year. With that said though the game has a fantastic story to play through and for the most part runs at a tolerable (but not great) framerate apart from those batmobile sections which does not run at a tolerable framerate but mearly but a playable framerate.
The Batmobile sections get really old after a short time, but the rest of the game is fairly good. Would I pick the game up at full price? No, I don't care how great the story is and how well the combat flows in a majority of the game, its got major major flaws that does not deserve rewarding a full price for. If the game is on sale 100% worth your time to play despite the major flaws, but at full price I would say WB needs to show a lot more care for PC and to not reward them with money for a terribly unoptimized game. WB needs to learn that sub par PC ports are not acceptable From Software learned that sub par ports are not acceptable, WB needs to learn the same thing, I mean its one thing to launch broken and be fixed in a few days, that's still pretty bad. But this has been a year and its still not up to PC expectations.
Gameplay and story are fantastic, runs not that good on my rig but that could just be me (I doubt it, but it could). And since the biggest negitive might just be my rig seeing as a lot of people are saying its better, I will go ahead and give this a reccomended, but only if its on sale.

I pre-ordered KF2 and I don't know why people are so angry. I love the game. Graphics are great, gore system is awesome, weapons do their jobs, and you can play as a zed!
It's taken them a while to get the perks up and running for sure, but so what? The original perks from KF1 are here. Just need to wait a bit for the rest to come out. Map selection is small but you can go with player created maps if you're sick of the original maps. Weapon selection is small for each class, but i actually prefer it this way because dosh has been rebalanced and it's tougher to get.
The VS gameplay needs more balancing. They are continually working on this, and it makes sense that it would be tough to get right. You need to be tougher than the original zeds but not overpoweringly so. The point system in VS mode is COMPLETELY borked. My team managed to win the game by being destroyed in all 4 rounds as zeds and one person wiping the other team as the Patriarch. Then we switch sides. Our team was wiped out in the first round as humans, but somehow we still won the game? The other team did far better than we did and were deffinately better players. They should have won. It's still great fun to play as a Scrake or Fleshpound though, even if they are pretty squishy.
There's and in-game store! ~GASP~ So what? It's just for weapon skins and character cosmetic items. There are no added benefits to using ANY of the store items aside from character customization. I've made over $110 selling all the skins from crates and usb sticks. That seems like a major plus imo. You have to purchase keys to unlock the crates and usb sticks for $2.49. Nearly every one I've opened has had an item that sells for over $5.00 on the market. I've sold some for over $40.
Maybe the devs haven't lived up to their "promises". But I would rather wait for devs to fine tune their content before releasing a broken mess to meet deadlines. If you've played any of the BF games you know what I'm talking about. I simply love KF. It's the one game I always come back to when I'm bored with everything else. i know this game has huge technical flaws and issues, runs like crap on many systems, fps drops and so and so, i preordered this and i really wanted it, but came around playing it just lately, so most of the problems were already "softened"
That being said this game is a MASTERPIECE.

The new mechanics like the car, the coop puzzles and combat, the more complex gadgets like voice distraction and such are very brilliant and fun to use, as to vary the fights greatly.

To be honest, I never had any doubts that this game would definitely appeal to me. It's ♥♥♥♥en non-euclidian puzzle FPSing, so it slots into all the little niches that I enjoy. It fulfilled my expectations and more.
The little tips and quips about life as a whole which act as both the hints and central source of feedback and structure in the game go a long way to make you feel like the game doesn't want to make things hard for you. It wants you to learn and it wants you to improve and every new room presents a different trick or application that helps broaden and extend the tools you have. Often, the way it gets you to expand what you can do is so subtle that you feel like you cheated the system in some way, you're never explicitly told you can do anything. Then you go online and watch a playthrough or something and see that everybody else thought of the same thing as you and it's amazing that the game got you to do that without ever telling you anything and a little disheartening that you didn't do anything innovative at the same time.
The game perfectly conjures up intense cranial carnage of a beautiful ilk through every asset available to it. My favourite example of this being the sounds you hear. You'll hear beautiful ocean soundscapes while looking at a sterile white room, which turns to the roaring of an underground stream as you descend into an equally sterile dark tunnel. Bright colours and stark white walls clash and compliment at every turn and, obviously, impossible spaces will become second nature to you. Glass observation rooms will encircle a room on the other side of the map and deep chasms will drop you mere steps away from the precipice you fell from.
One complaint, if you can even call it that, of the game is that its focus changes about a third of the way through the game. The Euclidian ♥♥♥♥ery takes a back seat to a nifty gun which can be used to manipulate small cubes. While the gun is excellent, the puzzles are even more challenging that before and the mechanics for the cubes are really, really fleshed out, it seems like past this point no new advances are made with the Euclidian business, it would have been more interesting to see the manipulation of the cubes and the twisting of Euclidian space interact  more, and to develop the traits of both simulateously, rather than having one peter out as soon as the other arrives. I understand why this is the case though, as making non-euclidian environs is incredibly time consuming.
Overall, I'd recommend this as a must buy. It is masterfully crafted and comes as a milestone in many areas, but most of all in its lack of handholding. The game gives you the barest ingredients to cook up success and makes you feel like a genius when you figure it all out, without ever revealing the cogs and wheels that went into giving you that satisfaction on both a mechanical and personal level.

One of the best sci-fi horror games out there. It's a Third Person Shooter, with an emphasis on aiming for the
of enemies rather than the body itself or the head. It is scary, but it's mostly just suspense, although very gruesome. This game's UI (User Interface) takes place as bars on the back of your suit (easy to see though), and windows are "2.5D" and they're on the world rather than on your HUD.
If you are not okay with scary games, or you have a weak stomach, or you simply dislike gore, this game is likely
for you.
The game has a very deep storyline, centering on a "Maintenance Mission" over at a wrecked spaceship, overrun by alien lifeforms which turned the spaceship's crew into mutants.
As for gameplay, you are given "cutting" weapons, with a sort of laser sights so you can see the cutting area, and you have to aim at body parts like the shoulders, arms, hands, legs... Some enemies have other "parts". You need to learn how to kill each and every enemy efficiently in order to conserve ammo and health, as items are limited in this game. In this game there is also zero gravity areas where you'll be able to move around more freely (but not float around), and stand on most walls you see. Some areas have no oxygen, and your Air meter will run down per second, until you reach an area with oxygen. You are also able to use "Stasis", used for slowing down objects and enemies, giving you a better chance at doing certain things, especially saving ammo.
Almost everything is upgradeable, including your HP, Air meter, Stasis, the damage/capacity/reload/speed of your weapons, Etc. This is done by consuming Power Nodes at an Upgrade Bench. You can buy those at stores, finding them around the ship, or receive them for killing powerful enemies.
If you decide to play on Hard Mode, this is where the game truly shines. You'll need to be
careful on how you use your weapons, and you need to be aware of your surroundings. Items are used up quicker on Hard Mode, and you might see yourself going around with low HP often. I myself reccommend to play on Hard Mode, since this is a not-so-short game and Hard Mode makes it even longer and more interesting.
Stability wise, this game isn't so good for that. It is rather old, but not too old, and normally plays well on most computers. There is, unfortunately, a "mouse lag" glitch, where aiming will never actually be smooth. It's easy to overcome this glitch though, and keep playing on while ignoring it.
Disable V-Sync (Vertical Sync) on the in-game video options before you start playing, as it will only cause a lot of trouble and it'll increase the mouse lag further if left enabled.
Replayability is okay, but the game is always interesting and fun no matter what.
TL;DR: Really nice semi-scary game, lots of gore, very immersive and promotes aiming strategically. My rating is 9/10, almost the best game I've ever played.
While it is short, I really enjoyed the game play. Not too complex, yet satisfying. The dialogue was what really made it, along with the soundtrack.

It's one of the most evil games I've played in the last few months, and addictive. It'll make you swear like a sailor for hours while you desperately try to beat your score, even by a fraction of a second; all of this is in the name of 'progression'. It's made worse when you set your sights on that ambitious score your friend got earlier. The music isn't bad either, and it's very retro-chiptune in style. But if you dislike it, you can also choose to mute the music and play your own in the background and rock out to something while you die over and over again.
Visually, the game screws with you, horribly. You'll feel completely dazed and confused while you're trying to navigate away from the impending death-blocks flying towards your cursor. It takes several attempts before you get a solid handle on how to move and avoid the blocks. It's a very neat game to break out at a gathering of friends and watch them struggle and curse at it while they try to last beyond 12 seconds.
I rate this game highly, and I still have yet to plumb the depths of the harder difficulty settings. I only just recently went beyond a minute at the easiest setting, and I shudder to imagine getting good enough at the game to last as long on the upper echelons. I've even purchased copies for family and friends. Get this game and give it a shot, especially if you're hankering after some good old fashioned classic gaming.

I pre-ordered KF2 and I don't know why people are so angry. I love the game. Graphics are great, gore system is awesome, weapons do their jobs, and you can play as a zed!
It's taken them a while to get the perks up and running for sure, but so what? The original perks from KF1 are here. Just need to wait a bit for the rest to come out. Map selection is small but you can go with player created maps if you're sick of the original maps. Weapon selection is small for each class, but i actually prefer it this way because dosh has been rebalanced and it's tougher to get.
The VS gameplay needs more balancing. They are continually working on this, and it makes sense that it would be tough to get right. You need to be tougher than the original zeds but not overpoweringly so. The point system in VS mode is COMPLETELY borked. My team managed to win the game by being destroyed in all 4 rounds as zeds and one person wiping the other team as the Patriarch. Then we switch sides. Our team was wiped out in the first round as humans, but somehow we still won the game? The other team did far better than we did and were deffinately better players. They should have won. It's still great fun to play as a Scrake or Fleshpound though, even if they are pretty squishy.
There's and in-game store! ~GASP~ So what? It's just for weapon skins and character cosmetic items. There are no added benefits to using ANY of the store items aside from character customization. I've made over $110 selling all the skins from crates and usb sticks. That seems like a major plus imo. You have to purchase keys to unlock the crates and usb sticks for $2.49. Nearly every one I've opened has had an item that sells for over $5.00 on the market. I've sold some for over $40.
Maybe the devs haven't lived up to their "promises". But I would rather wait for devs to fine tune their content before releasing a broken mess to meet deadlines. If you've played any of the BF games you know what I'm talking about. I simply love KF. It's the one game I always come back to when I'm bored with everything else. Killing wave after wave of zeds in brutal, gory, sickeningly splattery ways never gets old. As always, with ANY game, I recommend waiting for it to go on sale. I pre-purchased the game and don't feel ripped off, but I leave the game for a few months and come back to it for a few months and their is always something new to try out.
This is only my opinion. If you disagree, fine. If you agree, fine. I just hope I get the chance to dismember zeds with you all one day.

Simply put if you enjoy South Park the TV show you will enjoy this game. A lot. Being a fan of RPGs or not will have zero effect on your enjoyment if you enjoy the show.
There are some negatives though, most having to do with it being a bad console port;
-Price. I got it 66% off and that's pushing it when it comes to gameplay value. But well worth the entertainment value of the story and comedy.
-Loading screens between nearly every single area or transition.
-The controls are pointlessly clunky in parts; You will go through a tutorial learning a move one way only to find out it is completely different in combat and then different yet again in the World Map.
-It was admittedly very easy but I did grind and explore quite a bit.
-Menu system for equipment modification "patches" is clunky.
-I had an audio clip drop during one part but had subtitles on luckily. Only happened once.
Things that didn't bother me but might bother others;
-30FPS cap.
-Shop menus are slow when it comes to selling junk.
-Some cutscenes are a pixel off to the right and down.
Basically it really is a horrible port to the PC.
BUT!
The good far outweighes the bad if you're a fan of the show. Endless references. Nearly every character makes a cameo. Well written. Very very often laugh out loud funny. My feelings towards this game are bittersweet but overall I would recommend it. The core game isn't too long but it is an interesting storyline in a great setting. It is a more "on rails" type of game as opposed to the expansive open world sort that many mainstream role-playing games have leaned towards in recent years. Sometimes it can feel as though your choices are less about your actions and more about your dialogue choices. The character classes initially harken to the tabletop game (Street Sam, Phys Adept, Decker, Rigger, Shaman, Mage) but this is a classless game so you can pick and choose from an array of options that sometimes boil down to "should I put give +1 to X or Y and maybe unlock a new attack". The replayability of the core scenario isn't that great and subsequent play throughs feel more about trying a different build in order to see other dialogue options. Since you can hire various runners throughout the game, one play through will likely let you try out a large combination of character builds so second and third play throughs are really more about seeing what "Eitquette: Academic" or "Decking 5" does when talking to that NPC as opposed to experiencing new tactical aspects. Some of the mods and scenarios for download are pretty good which helps enhance further playing. Overall I'd say if you're a Shadowrun fan and/or like tactical grid-based combat then its a good purchase. If you prefer games like Skyrim over ones like Ogre Tactics, maybe not a first pick for you then.

Shadowrun returns tries *really hard* to be a great game. It's got a great history in tabletop roleplay, and the super nintendo shadowrun might be the most overlooked RPG of all time. The framework is definitely laid to make this one of the best retro gaming experiences of the last few years. Sadly, a lack of attention to detail often holds it back. Simple things, like healing kits in the store before the last fight, have been flat out overlooked or left out. It may be intentional, however there are enough times that it happens that it really feels like the game was slightly rushed. Another great example of this is the decking system. Decking itself is fun, if a bit tedious at times. However, there are 3 missions in the entire game that actually allow you to deck. And the times there are decking quests? One requires you to take an npc along as a sidekick (not bad, all things considered). The next decking mission? The npc *has to* do it, you don't even help. I realize there may be plot reasons, but where it ends up is that there's an entire skill tree that they literally only let you use twice. My first run was a decker, and I got through 3/4ths of the game before I got to actually use the skills I built for. Frustrating doesn't describe it. Another issue is how healing magic only heals the last attack to hit you. Mobs love throwing a big hit, then pinging you for 1 damage. This wouldn't even be an issue, except for the fact that you have limited medkits, and can't force your helpers to pick em up on the fly. Either you get them, or they go to your stash. This isn't an issue in combat mode, but you can't toggle combat mode manually, so if you're out of a fight? Hope you're the medic, because you're the one getting the health packs. Movement can be equally tricky, especially when it starts getting crowded. Misclicks, clicks in wrong places, moving instead of attacking (the worst of the bunch, as it's pretty easy to die if you're not behind cover) are commonplace if you're not careful. Add the ability to manually enter combat mode at any time (so npcs can pick stuff up), or inventory management on the fly, mixed with a bit of an easier way to move to a specific location in a crowd? A lot of my problems would immediately go away.
Shadowrun combat is fun and engaging. There's a deep variety of skills and abilities that all influence the battle field in different ways. Mage-based spellcasting feels powerful, especially if you beef yourself up to be able to take a hit (you'll have to) and stand on a ley line. Rigging is a *blast*, if a bit frustrating as they only allow one of each drone type per tier. This means, if you want 2 attack drones? One's gonna suck a bit. Summoning, similarly, is a ton of fun and feels really powerful. They put quite a few free summoning points in the game, it's one of the few ways you can use the environment against your enemy. As for Adepts? They are a bit under-utilized, IMO. Right now they're heavily melee focused, and take a lot of finesse to get full use out of, because you're so skill-thin. Body for HP, Quickness because Dodge, Strength for melee attacks and the attack focus skill, Will for Chi Casting. Late bloomer doesn't describe them, even the supposedly super-awesome npc you pick up near the end isn't all that impressive. And, without spoilers, he's one of the strongest characters in the entire Shadowrun canon.
The campaign's difficulty is incredibly well balanced. I was thrilled when even my biggest indestructible troll still had to take cover from time to time, because becoming fully immortal is impossible when your enemies have fully automatic machine guns. Some of the UGC (actually, most of it I've played to this point) doesn't have the same light touch, though, making swapping from the official campaign a pretty steep learning curve. The only real issue with the main campaign is length. It's incredibly short, especially for this style of game. Lots of people lament the fact that it's a fairly linear experience, but I personally enjoyed that. Not every game needs to be a sandbox, and Shadowrun Returns has a very distinct story to tell. Some may feel shoehorned, but I just enjoyed going along for the ride. The writing in the main campaign is *fantastic* and easily the strongest thing about it. They paid a lot of attention to detail, and really worked a lot of the flavor of the shadowrun world into their story. I *love* the big bad, as well. They definitely swung for the fences with the nemesis in dead man's switch. This is a great touch, since I know a lot of us pnp shadowrun players have fond memories of them. As well, major and well known players in the shadowrun universe make cameos, and some may even join your team. There's a great early nod to the snes shadowrun game that really set a great tone. This game pays obvious respect to what came before it. The fact that Jordan Weisman was responsible for this is very apparent in the plot and tone. Also, for those wanting a sandbox style adventure? Dragonfall is very much along those lines.
The graphics, as well, are spot on. The game feels fun, and cartoony, and really captures the essence of the shadowrun universe. Hyperkinetic neon and chrome, with a touch of Tolkien fantasy, blend together oddly well. None of it feels out of place. My only qualms about the background art boil down to there not being enough of them, which becomes a problem with UGC as it all starts to look exactly the same. The sprites are also well designed, if a bit generic at times (I'm looking at you, every troll in the game), and the game wouldn't hurt for the option of using different faces/body types. The sound? Meh. The soundtrack is fun at first, but quickly gets repetitive. I tend to turn off the music and put on some industrial while I play, or other music suitable for shadowrun. After the first playthrough, or even the first few hours? You probably will too.
UGC... It's the elephant in the room. UGC is a great idea in theory, and supposedly a high selling point for the game. The ability to create your own worlds, and play the worlds other people create, is *fantastic* on paper. And sometimes, it even works in execution. This is seeming to be the exception to the rule. UGC suffers from the same thing it does in most other games that feature it. It's uneven, balance is often lacking, the plots are frequently very weak, and... Well... It was made by the community, with all of the lack of polish that entails. There are a few *strong* exceptions to this rule, but it seems overall like the ones with the great plot lack any semblance of combat balance. As well, and as mentioned, the art assets get rather repetitive. A lot of the UGC just looks cut-and-paste, which is probably because they are. On the upside, sourcebooks from the original pen and paper game being fully converted into the game, and heavily fine tuned. Some of the creators have done a lot of work adding even more customization options, which is *amazing*. The major downfall to UGC is already becoming apparent post-Dragonfall, however. A few of the people responsible for large conversion kits or well known adventures have walked away, because the expansion completely broke their work. It's the same problem the UGC community of the first Neverwinter Nights faced, with every new expansion comes 10-20 hours of work to put your mods back together again.
Overall, this game is fantastic. It's got some quirks, but Dragonfall cleaned up a lot of bugs or issues that were once holding it back. This is solid retro gaming.
