I quite enjoyed this game. The main story is well written and takes about 15 hours worth of gameplay. You'll need to not be bothered by text as you'll be served quite a lot of dialog and story. If you hate that kind of thing, I won't recommend you picking this game up. But if you don't have a problem with reading, you can get quite a nice Shadowrun experience of it. Dialogues are nicely written and I really like them taking the time to also write about body language of the characters. Good move! While I didn't really mind it my self, but the story line is linear. You don't really have alternative appoaches to reach the same goal, nor do you roleplaying options really seem to have an impact. So for those that like to actually play a role: the main story doesn't really give you that opportunity. But I have to admit, I was actually too busy figuring out the plot of the story that I did not really miss side-questing even for the slightest bit (and it's almost nonexistant by the way).
Personally I like the art style of this game, but I can image it might be a bit offputting for some. Animation quality is not too great, but only the melee attacks really bothered me. Those just looked unrealistically floaty and slow, and don't even look remotely deadly.
The game is about 65% combat oriented, and 35% story telling and roleplaying oriented. The combat itself is not too spectacular. I've played as a hacker & droid controlling character, so I think I actually got the most out of the combat options the game has to offer. But if you would have gone the Street Samurai type of character, you might get bored with it before the end. Combat is turnbased, featuring 2/3 moves per character each turn. You can get into various degrees of cover, there a 4 gun types (each with a few special attacks), 2 melee weapon types, 3 types of spell casting you can spec into, there is cyber combat (hacking, aka running the Matrix) and you can bring combat drones into the battlefield. If you've played XCom Enemy Unknown, you'll recognise this as a light version of that combat system.
There are no stealth mechanics to speak off, which I missed a bit as I always liked to play a stealthy character in the paper based RPG of Shadowrun. But I don't hold it against the game, as such a system would put even more strain on this kickstarted project. Where I might add: they did a hell of a job: good playable game, good story, finished in time and within budget and with level editor to boot! I also like that they implemented the Matrix from the paper based RPG, the realm for hackers together with combat against AI hacking counter-measures. One thing that did bother me from time to time, was that the point and click controls just don't feel that responsive. I often feel I have to click 1x too many to speak to a character.
One last important note: this game does not allow you to save at your whim. It uses a checkpoint system, which are often about 30 to 45 minutes of gameplay apart from each other. This might be something for you to take into consideration.

Before Divinity and Dragon Age came out this year, I would have pegged this as the best traditional RPG of 2014. Now, it doesn't neccesarily hold a candle to those two games in terms of depth and gameplay, but if you are a fan of South Park, it absolutely holds a candle in terms of appreciation of fans and the lore built up over the last 18 years of South Park.
I'm a large fan of the show, and watched the series again before booting this up for the first time. Everywhere you turn, there is additional lore and references to the show that would be lost on most players. Even if you haven't watched the show a ton, the combat is very solid, and the writing is genuinely funny. It's, in a sense, like playing through one of the more epic episode trilogies that have come out in recent years. It's short (around 13 hours if you do mostly everything), but absolutely worth a purchase if on sale. Combat is similar to Paper Mario, in that it is turn based with quick time events to add damage to your attacks and add a layer of depth to combat. I had a lot of fun with it.
I didn't have a moment of dullness with this game, and I look forward to going through it again. However, don't expect to want to do multiple playthroughs, as once you see the jokes once, I don't assume that it'll be as fresh the second time.

A fully-refined end to a great series.
If your computer can play it, it's a wonderful buy. I am fortunate enough to be able to say that mine can play it without issues.
Combat mechanics are tight, and everything feels even more fluid than from previous installments. Where Arkham Origins was (in my opinion) a step backward in fluidity, Arkham Knight takes the great gameplay of Arkham Asylum and Arkham City and refines it even more. Rest assured, if you liked the combat in Arkham City, it's even better here.
A common complaint one might here is that the batmobile feels 'forced' or out of place. I used to feel the same, but it's grown on me significantly. Pay attention to what the game hints say regarding the possible actions in the batmobile, and you'll enjoy it. I play on mouse+KB, and have since the first game, which made 'critical' shots with the batmobile quite easy. If you lack the accuracy with your given control scheme, then you might find the batmobile battles more challenging.
The story is 'comic book good'. Which is to say, it's hammy, often has plot holes that are unsatisfyingly explained away, or even bizarre at times. But conversely, the story & mechanics that are used to explore the psyche of batman and what it means to go 'too far' in his mind is so satisfying to experience. If you can ignore the warts on the skin of the story, there's some great stuff inside.
Some of the side-quests feel tacked-on. For instance, the firefly sidequest consists entirely of chasing him in the batmobile 3 times for about 5 minutes each. After which you capture him and he's locked up. I think this sort of thing is chiefly where the "batmoblie feels forced" complaint comes from.
There's a batmobile component to many of the sidequests, and there are times where it's a batmobile battle rather than a predator encounter or on-foot combat. Personally I didn't mind if I had to use the batmobile to defeat an enemy instead of my fists-- You're still batman being batman, bringnig down the enemy with an (in?)appropriate amonut of force. I can understand why people would be disappointed with not being able to use stealth or other means to take down some of the more iconic bosses though.

Unfortunately, the game uses direct IP connect for multiplayer and zero mod support, but other than that and some latency, I've had no issues with it. You unlock something on every playthrough, even tens of hours later. The characters are unique and play very differently from one another, synergizing well with different skills. Artifacts (togglable game modifiers) are an interesting touch that change the game too. Risk of Rain is easily worth your time, and remember to play with a controller.

This is literally my favorite game of all time. A lot of games come very close but if I have to name a number one, It's Half Life 2.
General:
Ok, let me tell why I think this highly of the game. In my own words I would call HL2 a FPS/adventure/puzzle game. It follows the 1998 game Half Life. It takes everything that made the first a great game and improved on it. The pacing of the game is perfect. It balances exploration, puzzle solving and action/gunfights very well. The cut-scenes never leave the first person perspective and don't remove you from the experience.
You will not get bored or stuck very quickly and the game doesn't feel like it's holding your hand. For most puzzles you really feel like you found the solution yourself instead of it being placed there by the devs. The physics play a major part in this. The game was groundbreaking on this front and allowed you to play with your environment like never before.
The story continues from the first, so really read up on or play the first Half Life before playing this one! You will not be disappointed.
Presentation:
The graphics aged very well, but can be improved with the HL2 "Update" mod. There's also a Cinematic Mod which overhauls the game to give it a Hollywood blockbuster feel and improves the graphics a lot. This puts it more in sync with modern shooters but does affect the atmosphere of the game. It makes it more dark, and characters less believable. I suggest playing it in it's original form before playing it with the Cinematic Mod.
The audio is awesome. The ambient sounds and the chatter from the combine really help sell the experience. The weapons sound very good but can be bland compared to modern shooters. I think this is done on purpose however. They never take away from the other aspects of the game. Like I said, gunplay is not the most important aspect of the game. It's just a part of the whole and the sound of the guns helps sell this. If you have a nice audio-set or headphones, they still have enough punch. :)
Arsenal:
Your primary "weapon" will be the gravity gun. This gun allows you to manipulate objects in the environment. It can be used for problem/puzzle solving like pulling down a ramp, getting your car unstuck, stacking objects, etc. It can also be used as an actual weapon by picking up sawblades, explosive barrels, toilets, etc and flinging them at your opponents.
All the other weapons in the game are your standard fare for early 2000s shooters. Two handguns (a 9mm pistol and a Magnum), an SMG (with grenadelauncher), a shotgun, a crossbow, RPG and grenades. The more exotic weapons are the pulse rifle (not the one from aliens ;) ) and bug bait. The pulse rifle acts like a more accurate and damaging SMG with energy orbs instead of grenades. Bug bait can be tossed at enemies and they will be attacked by Ant-Lions if they are in the area. Squeezing it will attract them to your location and they will sort of protect you.
You will also get the HEV (Hazardous EnVironment) suit that acts as armor and protection against, well, environmental hazards. This can be charged with batteries or at charge stations.
The game is still very much worth the 10 bucks, but I recommend getting the game in the Orange Box. This will also give you access to both followup episodes (a must play if you like this one) and also holds the amazing game Portal and the premium version of Team Fortress 2!
Lastly I want to debunk two "negatives" about the game i see in the reviews.
The first is that the game has no ADS. But this game is from 2004. Barely any game had ADS and was just implemented for the first time months prior in Vietcong. To be honest, I never had any doubts that this game would definitely appeal to me. It's ♥♥♥♥en non-euclidian puzzle FPSing, so it slots into all the little niches that I enjoy. It fulfilled my expectations and more.
The little tips and quips about life as a whole which act as both the hints and central source of feedback and structure in the game go a long way to make you feel like the game doesn't want to make things hard for you. It wants you to learn and it wants you to improve and every new room presents a different trick or application that helps broaden and extend the tools you have. Often, the way it gets you to expand what you can do is so subtle that you feel like you cheated the system in some way, you're never explicitly told you can do anything. Then you go online and watch a playthrough or something and see that everybody else thought of the same thing as you and it's amazing that the game got you to do that without ever telling you anything and a little disheartening that you didn't do anything innovative at the same time.
The game perfectly conjures up intense cranial carnage of a beautiful ilk through every asset available to it. My favourite example of this being the sounds you hear. You'll hear beautiful ocean soundscapes while looking at a sterile white room, which turns to the roaring of an underground stream as you descend into an equally sterile dark tunnel. Bright colours and stark white walls clash and compliment at every turn and, obviously, impossible spaces will become second nature to you. Glass observation rooms will encircle a room on the other side of the map and deep chasms will drop you mere steps away from the precipice you fell from.
One complaint, if you can even call it that, of the game is that its focus changes about a third of the way through the game. The Euclidian ♥♥♥♥ery takes a back seat to a nifty gun which can be used to manipulate small cubes. While the gun is excellent, the puzzles are even more challenging that before and the mechanics for the cubes are really, really fleshed out, it seems like past this point no new advances are made with the Euclidian business, it would have been more interesting to see the manipulation of the cubes and the twisting of Euclidian space interact  more, and to develop the traits of both simulateously, rather than having one peter out as soon as the other arrives. I understand why this is the case though, as making non-euclidian environs is incredibly time consuming.
Overall, I'd recommend this as a must buy. It is masterfully crafted and comes as a milestone in many areas, but most of all in its lack of handholding. The game gives you the barest ingredients to cook up success and makes you feel like a genius when you figure it all out, without ever revealing the cogs and wheels that went into giving you that satisfaction on both a mechanical and personal level.

Simply put if you enjoy South Park the TV show you will enjoy this game. A lot. Being a fan of RPGs or not will have zero effect on your enjoyment if you enjoy the show.
There are some negatives though, most having to do with it being a bad console port;
-Price. I got it 66% off and that's pushing it when it comes to gameplay value. But well worth the entertainment value of the story and comedy.
-Loading screens between nearly every single area or transition.
-The controls are pointlessly clunky in parts; You will go through a tutorial learning a move one way only to find out it is completely different in combat and then different yet again in the World Map.
-It was admittedly very easy but I did grind and explore quite a bit.
-Menu system for equipment modification "patches" is clunky.
-I had an audio clip drop during one part but had subtitles on luckily. Only happened once.
Things that didn't bother me but might bother others;
-30FPS cap.
-Shop menus are slow when it comes to selling junk.
-Some cutscenes are a pixel off to the right and down.
Basically it really is a horrible port to the PC.
BUT!
The good far outweighes the bad if you're a fan of the show. Endless references. Nearly every character makes a cameo. Well written. Very very often laugh out loud funny. And the gameplay itself is way deeper than I could have ever imagined. And although it was easy, it was also rewarding. I grinded and explored the town multiple times over the course of the game just for the pure enjoyment of the easter eggs.
Any South Park fan has to play this. Pick it up if it is 66% or more on sale. DLC's can and should be skipped entirely even when they're on sale for pocket change. Best enjoyed spoiler free, so no 'Cartman Brahs' kiddos!

I think the key thing that people are misisng here is that TWI are now actively engaged with the community and are putting work in to resolve issues. I've been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at them myself before; the resistances patch mentioned prior, poor community outreach, implementing things such as the versus mode (which I'm sure some people want, but most of us don't care about) and microtransactions before bug fixing/completing perks, releasing the EA version and stating the price would be fixed, then dropping it in a flash sale a fortnight later etc. TWI have not really done the best job of implementing this title into the community, but the key thing players who don't own this should take from this review is that they seem to have learnt a valuable lesson about ostracising their player base.

Before Divinity and Dragon Age came out this year, I would have pegged this as the best traditional RPG of 2014. Now, it doesn't neccesarily hold a candle to those two games in terms of depth and gameplay, but if you are a fan of South Park, it absolutely holds a candle in terms of appreciation of fans and the lore built up over the last 18 years of South Park.
I'm a large fan of the show, and watched the series again before booting this up for the first time. Everywhere you turn, there is additional lore and references to the show that would be lost on most players. Even if you haven't watched the show a ton, the combat is very solid, and the writing is genuinely funny. It's, in a sense, like playing through one of the more epic episode trilogies that have come out in recent years. It's short (around 13 hours if you do mostly everything), but absolutely worth a purchase if on sale. Combat is similar to Paper Mario, in that it is turn based with quick time events to add damage to your attacks and add a layer of depth to combat. I had a lot of fun with it.
I didn't have a moment of dullness with this game, and I look forward to going through it again. However, don't expect to want to do multiple playthroughs, as once you see the jokes once, I don't assume that it'll be as fresh the second time.

This is one of the best puzzle games I've played in quite some time. I've heard it compared to portal, but I wouldn't say that. Portal makes some sense. This game is full of illusions, endless hallways, changing rooms, and of course puzzles. Difficult puzzles. As far as the Portal comparison, what was a portal gun is now a minecraft-style block pickup, placer, and mover gun, what were deadly lasers are now just sensor lasers that have to be blocked and avoided, what were turrets are now nothing. No death, you just end up in another room you don't know how it could have connected to the one you were just in, or get stuck and have to return to the hub. Another notable thing are the notes you'll find on the wall. Little words of wisdom that are hints for some puzzles, or work as hints for puzzles but are really just tips for life in general.
Overall, I love AntiChamber. It's challenging, beautiful, and enjoyably confusing.

This game is brutal. It punishes you for being slow. It punishes you (slightly less) for being fast. First of all, Risk of Rain is a platformer with roguelike elements that never gets old. Every new game you start will be different from the last one you played.
Now, Personally I really loved this game because of its genre: survival-esque combined with perk-gathering. Your goal is to survive for as long as possible through levels while opening chests containing perks (items that will 'boost' your character, whether it be a goat hoof that increases your movement speed to a flask of liquid that boosts your health regen, there are just a ton of different items with different abilities).
As for gameplay, the game itself isn't that hard. It only takes about 90 minutes, give or take, to beat the game, solo. But what makes you come back to it are all the unlockable items, classes and artifacts that completely change a game that you think would be unchangable.
This the perfect game for fans of survival/scavenging/platformer -esque games

A very good game. When I first played it in 2014 I didn't like it since I hadn't played the first game first and I was trying to rush through everything, instead of actually listening to people.
But after replaying it after completing the first game, I realized how great this is. There's a great story, but it's in the background and not shoved in your face. The pacing is great because, for most of the game, you go at your own pace. There are entire areas you can skip if you want to. The replayability is massive, and even after 3 playthroughs, I'm still finding new things. And the game oozes atmosphere. Just standing still sometimes to watch and listen is entertaining.
Like the first game, It's hard to believe this was made when it was, in 2004. It's definitely not perfect (gimmicky physics puzzles and some cheap deaths for example,) but it's definitely a worthy sequel to the genre-redefining Half-Life.

I quite enjoyed this game.
At first glance, this game seemed like an electronic spinoff of the board game Risk. However, after playing the game and getting to know and understand the game's mechanics and complexity, I am very impressed.
With beautiful graphics and sounds, the game has many different units of many different classes, a balanced 'economy' system that juggles around the features of citizen happiness, city production, and gold income/expense.
You can play in a randomly-generated map, or on a scenario-pack, in several different languages. There is a vast variety of mods available in the Steam Workshop for more intensive gamers who are easily bored.
Each individual AI civilisation (and there are many) has it's own tendencies towards behavior, social policies, and trade agreements. The detail on the "Leader Screen" (the screen where you speak to the AI leaders" is rather impressive.
Great detail can be found on the terrain map, everything from the animals running around to steep mountians jutting out from acrossed the sparkling ocean, this game leaves nothing to be desired.
I did pay full price for this game, but it was definitely worth it.

This used to be one of my favorite multiplayer games. I've purchased multiple copies for friends, who have in turn purchased copies for other friends. Current bugs include (but are certainly not limited to):
*If you are playing online mutiplayer and get to the last level, all clients will crash.
*All abilities are supposed to do random amounts of damage, and little random "damage numbers" pop up over enemies' heads, but as you can see by watching boss's health bars when you attack them, the numbers are lies and you are actually doing the exact same amount of damage with every shot.
*Sometimes you will get stuck one pixel below the platform that you are supposed to be standing on, and you'll never be able to move again.

I'm going to make this super short so I don't end up writing a long, winding novel of ups and downs. There are some really good reviews on both sides, I'm just throwing my 2 cents in the pot.
The game looks GREAT, and feels so good (when your Perk isn't on the current list of things nerfed at the moment), but in the way of weapons, maps, Perks, and a few other things- the content is just a bland dish with lots of garnish to make it LOOK good- and doesn't satisfy. On the postitive side, though, I'd like to add that the sound effects are awesome as well, and the character banter is usually pretty hilarious, even after hearing it a lot.
So, I guess what I'm saying is, "awesome lights, sounds, and buzzers"? Check.
But honestly, it feels like a cash grab. Post poned release dates, "high and mighty" mods and devs, lackluster content, and microtransactions. At it's core, it lacks that special, from the heart magic that was Killing Floor 1.

After the official release, there have been some modifications. More maps, more classes (Surivialist is really awesome), more reception to player feedback, and many other changes. It feels better- but it honestly did take way longer than quoted (and frought with problems along the way). However, I'm changing my recommendation to a postitive one, as the finished product is a fun, exciting, and stable game. If it continues on this trend of positive improvement, I think it will end up being an excellent sequel worthy of the name "Killing Floor".

Hired by your dead buddy, you go on a quest to find his murderer and bring him to justice. The game quickly evolves in true Shadowrunner style into a story of grand conspiracies and demonic spirits bent on making the world their plaything.
The game is very enjoyable and I suspect is one of the few games which actually does have some replay value -- all styles of combat appears to be valid and different enough to warrant a replay on that account alone, combined with the decision to pick up a deck or not, use magic or to go the social way, I'm pretty sure I will enjoy my second playthough.
The game is among the best RPGs (for starters, it actually -is- an RPG, which most "RPGs" of today aren't) that's been released since Fallout (the original), which in my book means it's one of the best I've played.
The game does have some big flaws -- the complete linearity of the main campaign is a big minus. With that in sight however, the main campaign is very enjoyable. The only other -real- negative I have to say about the game is that you will get an abundance of karma (XP for the uninitated) which means you will be able to fill out at least two roles in your squad, possible more with a bit of build tweaking. I wasted a very large amount of karma on non-essential stuff (my guess > 50%) and was still able to finish the main campaign without any problems at all -- playing on normal might have been the problem. I'll have to investigate in a future playthrough.
At no point did I think any character was out of place, didn't behave in a sensible manner or would say or do something that I thought just didn't fit the situation. That's pretty much a first for me in terms of games. Too often do games have NPCs which do not fit in the game, spout gibberish or in some other way make me feel like they don't belong in the game (at all or in that situation).
It took me ~16 hours (16 hours + a bit of sleep = 21 hours) to complete the game and I didn't find a single seriouse bug (Linux with free drivers) in version 1.10. The only bugs I stumbled upon was some 2-3 second spinning (animation didn't progress at all) for a when my character performed actions in combat -- the problem disappeared when I loaded a new map and never reappeared.
A solid game with very few and only (really) minor flaws.

Very good turn-based game, but not so good as an rpg, I expect more of the next campaings since I cant use the workshop (it simple crashes after i try to make a new content). As for my opinion concerning the rpg genre, the thing is: in the main story your choices doesnt really matter, because it is pretty strait-foward you do as your told, or you cant progress. It is like a GM that doesnt know really how to embrace multiple possibilities. For instance, you cant change alliances, jobs, take a lot of side quests (almost none, almost), fully specialize your character (obs.: it will cost you a lot of patience, since you always need to explore, out of combat, in the front lines - a support mage doesnt explore in the front lines, period). The same problem about specialization happens in player-made content, not to mention that ranged combat is far superior than melee in this game, to have a good melee combatant, on par with a ranged, you need twice as much karma and money, I think it is pretty unballanced, but possible to fix it.
One important thing to mention is: browsing through the player-made content it became pretty obvious that the publishers can make the game much more interesting in terms of choice, exploring, loot, etc. They did a very good job on the writing, but not so much on the rpg.

It was great while it lasted, but man was it SHORT. In case you don't already know, be aware - you WILL beat this entire game inside of about 12-15 hours (and that's assuming you take your time and do a lot of the optional side quests) and once you beat it there is no replay value. There aren't really different choices or paths through the game, it's more like a 15-hour interactive episode of South Park. So playing again is not really enticing - it's the same exact thing again.
The game itself is hilarious and pretty fun, although some of the fighting mechanics can get repetitive and it relies heavily on things like pressing a button really fast or pressing the next key they show on the screen (think Mario Party,) timing clicks / button presses with on-screen cues (think Paper Mario for N64,) or occasionally pressing keys as they scroll up the screen (think DDR.)
For the actual content, I'd give it an 8 or 9 out of 10, but it is way too short - when I was fighting the last boss I was thinking I was maybe 20% through the game. As I said above, after you beat it, there isn't really any enjoyment in playing again. So overall I'd have to say 6/10. Too bad really, because if it was 3 or 4 times as long and/or had some kind of replay value, it'd be way higher.

Remake of a classic squad based tactical strategy. They wiped away a huge amount of the original's complexity, and replaced it with more or less passable gameplay. For example instead of a team of raw recruits that you specialize as you wish, characters become one of four standard classes. Instead of action points during combat you get 2 moves.
The fear of the aliens technological superiority and a sense of overwhelming odds is totally there, building the intensity. If a character dies, they're dead, and you need to replace them.
My biggest criticism of the game is the sloooooooow tactical combat. They introduce the concept of AI getting a free move when you uncover them, which is totally ridiculous. The enemies basically wait around to be discovered, then get free shots on you. You are severely penalized for letting your squad get separated. Which makes tactical sense, but it simply isn't fun to spend 30 minutes herding your commandos around the map looking for that last batch of enemies.

Overall I would say that playing SR was a good experience. It took a bit of getting used to going back to the old school type rpg layout reminiscent of the early Baldur's Gate and Fallout titles. Most of the story unfolds through heavy dialogue either from a narrative between areas on the loading screen or from conversation between your character and NPCs.
PROS: *Great Story, the writers did a good job mixing the scifi and fantasy elements to create a game that has an almost noire detective story feel.  *Decent graphics (considering the game type), *Extensive character development through skills and equipment. Very immersive, the world of shadowrun is a cross between cyberpunk and D&D. Good music, it fits right in with the feel of the game.
Cons: *Very linear, I would have loved to have the opportunity to explore this world or to go to other cities. *The top down narrative rpg system is kind of dated, unless  you are ready to read what amounts to a small novel this game may not be right for you. *Too short, I would imagine this has to do with the budget since this was a kickstarter but typically rpgs like this should take 40-60 hours to complete, not 15-20. The shortness also affects your character development since, unless you dump all your points into one area, there is no way you can explore all the options available to you.
NITPICKS: I really feel like it would have been better to have characters on your team that you can develop and equip yourself. You can hire needed teammates from a merc pool and sometimes story characters go with you but you never get the chance to really develop them. For my playthrough the cred to equipment was unbalanced. I had way too much money by the end of the game. I would have spent it on equipment or implants for party members but you cant.
FINAL SAY: Definitely play this game if you can afford to. Overall it was good, just very short with a few minor issues. 4 out of 5 rating.

It's basically System Shock 2 with Resident Evil 4 style gameplay... only not nearly as good as either. This isn't a bad game by any means, just mediocre.
All the "horrors" are pretty much just jump scares, which I'm not really into, and they are pretty predictable. The AI being terrible doesn't really help there. It has "got me" a couple of times, but mostly it's just boringly linear and predictable. I find the added clanking sounds everywhere to be just annoying as well (not creepy either, you can EASILY tell if it's just background noise or an actual monster by turning); silence would've made the monster sounds way more tensing. Even with all that, and a weapon that mows down enemies, the environment still keeps me at least a little tense, so there's that.
The story is... well... it's ok. Only because it's CLEARLY "inspired" by System Shock 2 (with a dash of Alien tossed in). And that's kind of a nice way of saying it's almost a ripoff. Though at least they managed to make me care at least a little about a silent protagonist. Unlike "Goggles" from SS2, which nobody even knows his name.
I found the graphics to be quite good for the time though, and the UI is pretty neat. The textures all look reasonably sharp and it runs perfectly even on my 460. The art direction is pretty uninspired for the most part, however.
The upgrade system is interesting as well. The level of customisation is nifty. I dislike how there are empty upgrade nodes though, but whatever. I wonder how many upgrade points you get through the game though.
This is all putting aside the fact that it is a mediocre console port. Controls are passable at best, unplayable at worst. The UI controls are even broken beyond belief. You know it's a bad console port when saving is hard because of the controls. Also, the worst vsync integration I have ever seen in a game. Holy cow. Makes the game almost unplayable. If you do buy this, turn it off.
Half the "horror" in this game is because you are playing a guy who has less agility than a guy in a wheelchair, who walks around like he's in a tank. I very much dislike games that use this scheme (I'm looking at you, Resident Evil 4). There are far better ways to instill fear in the player than to just cripple there movement. Give me some agility and melee capabilities, and up the AI's reaction and speed and you could achieve the same effect, and you have a games that's *gasp* fun to play.
I'd say skip it unless it's a genre you are really into (tank control third person "horror" game). Even with that, go play System Shock 2 and get over it's old graphics, because it's a far, far better game that defines how you do a space horror game. If this game scares you and System Shock 2 doesn't even phase you then you are quite the simpleton, I'd have to say.

Let me preface this by saying that this isn't a bad game. It's just sort of medicore.
There is a great deal of attention to detail at the beginning of the game, but you get the feeling that EA contracted these people to develop a game that was longer than it needed to be.
A lot of the objectives are pretty much, "We need to do this one big thing during this chapter, so you need to do this thing 1 and this thing 2 in order to do the big thing." It wasn't very compelling.
The ship itself has a great interior but you don't feel like most of it was meant for people to live on. It is cold and uninviting, which, while forboding, wasn't exactly great at connecting the player to this environment. This detail was better addressed in Dead Space 2.
The combat is novel. The problem is that they give you these cool weapons to purchase in the game, but you don't actually need them. I completed the game using nothing but the default weapon.
The pacing of the scares was, again, great at the beginning, but became rather predictable the longer you played. It felt like a lot of action and almost no suspense. A detail which was also addressed better in Dead Space 2.
There was an aggravating bug in one section using zero-G that made my character die immediately. It was made more aggravating because it was a puzzle section and each time I died I had to start over.
Don't get me wrong, Dead Space does do some things great that other games don't do very well. The need to conserve ammunition for instance is pretty good and balanced out by the in-game store. It really does have a survival horror feel.
Lastly, it runs very well with my Radeon HD 7770 and 2.9 ghz x4.
Overall, it's just okay. I had a bit of fun, but it was sort of hampered by a few poor design choices.

This is a review for gamers who aren't gamers - like me.  I'm a weak gamer, so I'm always worried a game will be too hard for me.  This game isn't in the slightest.  I play on easy mode, and I've never lost a battle.  I don't know what else is affected by easy mode, but I'd guess the quests are easier, too.  This is probably the first non-Mario Bros.-related game that that I've ever played without needing a walkthrough to guide me.  I've actually considered raising the difficuty level.  It's not so easy that it's not fun, though.  The quests are fun to work through, and the strategy aspect adds a challenge that's stress-free.  If you're the kind of player that gets stuck early, and ends up too frustrated to keep trying, have no fear here.
I've never played a turn-based game before, but I like it.  I'm not competitive, so I mostly like watching how the various characters fight, and the battle animations.  Even if you think you're terrible at fighting games, you'll find yourself getting better in these battles.. The turn-based style gives you a lot of time to think about, and learn from your own gameplay.
The South Park world is excellently represented.  All the characters you'd hope for, or expect are here, and they have their proper voices.  No cheap knock-off voice actors!  That said, you don't need to have watched South Park to enjoy this game.  If you don't watch South Park, you won't be lost in story, but you will be confused by some of the elements.  Just roll with it!  It's worth it.
Finally, on the subject of worth, I paid $13 for this game, and it's worth every penny.  If I had paid full price upon release, it would still be worth it.  It's a big game that will provide countless hours of excellent play for the very casual gamer.

my experience with shadowrun is not from the pen and paper game, but from the snes and sega genesis games. and my oh my, does this feel very familliar.
while it isnt anywhere near as difficult as the oldschool games were (they could be notoriously cruel, and extremely cryptic), it still has quite a bit of fun for a fan of the older games, as well as newcomers. the writing style truly draws you in to the grimy, futuristic, cyberpunk-infused-with-magic world that shadowrun does so well.
there's a large amount of options in terms of what kind of gameplay style you want (several different fantasy races to play as, elves and orcs and trolls oh my), as well as several different character classes (do you wanna be a big, buff street samurai troll? a smooth talking elf shaman? a human street-mage? a dwarven hacker? there's tons of possibilities and the level up system further expands on that by allowing you to build a character with abilities that might not be typical of your class, so experimentation is endless).
the game also has a wide variety of user created campaigns and other extras available for free in the steam workshop, adding near limitless replay value for those who enjoy running the shadows and dealing with the vast corruption and filth that comes with a world ruled entirely by corporations.
i would very much recommend this game for anybody who enjoys rpgs with a touch of tactical, turn-based gun combat (the actual gameplay itself reminds me very strongly of fallout 1 and 2).
all in all this is a fantastic game, and if $20 is too steep for you (which is very understandable), definitely pick it up on sale. and if you're a hardcore cyberpunk/ magic fantasy/ crime mystery/ rpg fan, you may want to consider buying at full price.

Remake of a classic squad based tactical strategy. They wiped away a huge amount of the original's complexity, and replaced it with more or less passable gameplay. For example instead of a team of raw recruits that you specialize as you wish, characters become one of four standard classes. Instead of action points during combat you get 2 moves.
The fear of the aliens technological superiority and a sense of overwhelming odds is totally there, building the intensity. If a character dies, they're dead, and you need to replace them.
My biggest criticism of the game is the sloooooooow tactical combat. They introduce the concept of AI getting a free move when you uncover them, which is totally ridiculous. The enemies basically wait around to be discovered, then get free shots on you. You are severely penalized for letting your squad get separated. Which makes tactical sense, but it simply isn't fun to spend 30 minutes herding your commandos around the map looking for that last batch of enemies.
Such a refreshing experience. Buy this! NAO!

I like this game in principal; however, in execution there are a number of flaws.
The worst of these is that the gameplay is a railroad. While this is always somewhat true of video RPGs in comparison to table-top RPGs, this game is particularly obvious about it. Unlike the version for Sega Genesis I grew up with, quests happen on the game’s schedule. No more wasting zombies in the Redmond Barrens or hacking random mega-corps for paydata until you feel like doing Mr. Johnson’s dirty work.
Less devastating are an annoying slow combat movement system that persists between combat at times and poor usability of hired deckers within the matrix.
I love the setting of Shadowrun, and the story is good, but the linear gameplay grinds on my table-top gamer nerves. If linear gameplay doesn’t bother you, buy this game; if it does, buy this game on sale.

Let me preface this by saying that this isn't a bad game. It's just sort of medicore.
There is a great deal of attention to detail at the beginning of the game, but you get the feeling that EA contracted these people to develop a game that was longer than it needed to be.
A lot of the objectives are pretty much, "We need to do this one big thing during this chapter, so you need to do this thing 1 and this thing 2 in order to do the big thing." It wasn't very compelling.
The ship itself has a great interior but you don't feel like most of it was meant for people to live on. It is cold and uninviting, which, while forboding, wasn't exactly great at connecting the player to this environment. This detail was better addressed in Dead Space 2.
The combat is novel. The problem is that they give you these cool weapons to purchase in the game, but you don't actually need them. I completed the game using nothing but the default weapon.
The pacing of the scares was, again, great at the beginning, but became rather predictable the longer you played. It felt like a lot of action and almost no suspense. A detail which was also addressed better in Dead Space 2.
There was an aggravating bug in one section using zero-G that made my character die immediately. It was made more aggravating because it was a puzzle section and each time I died I had to start over.
Don't get me wrong, Dead Space does do some things great that other games don't do very well. The need to conserve ammunition for instance is pretty good and balanced out by the in-game store. It really does have a survival horror feel.
Lastly, it runs very well with my Radeon HD 7770 and 2.9 ghz x4.
Overall, it's just okay. I had a bit of fun, but it was sort of hampered by a few poor design choices.

Risk of Rain features many neat ideas wrapped into a pretty poorly designed and balanced product. The gameplay itself, hectic running and gunning, using a character's abilities and items to defeat hordes of enemies works very well. Generally, you'll be able to take on any threat you face if you use the right tactics and use your character correctly. However, the way the game presents its core gameplay and the difficulty issues with the game just make it a total chore to get through.
I understand that indie developers think they're being cool and novel when they make a game that's supposed to be nigh on impossible, but it's been done, and done far better than you could ever hope to do. See Faster Than Light. The game needs to create a sense that the player is at fault, and that a few key decisions would have resulted in an entirely different outcome, and Risk of Rain just fails miserably at this.
Far too much of the game is randomized, and while that might be a hallmark of roguelike games, it doesn't work here. Beating the game, or even getting more than a third of the way through it, is entirely dependent on getting certain items that may or may not spawn into chests, which also may or may not spawn in locations that are feasible to reach. If you don't get the right items to synergize with your character, you lose when the difficulty starts to ramp up in level four. Period. The randomness might be acceptable if not for the way difficulty scales in this game: The longer you play, the harder it gets. Not per level. Per game. This would be interesting and fun if getting items weren't so critical. Considering the teleporter you need to advance to the next level also spawns into the world randomly, it might spawn on the one side of one of the game's gargantuan maps, while most of the loot necessary to win spawns on the other, in some cases taking the player a whole three minutes to get to the loot, then get back to the teleporter. Again, this would not be terrible if the game didn't exponentially increase in difficulty every 5 or so minutes. This makes camping one level and farming items an unviable strategy as the game will soon become far too hard to beat. As it is, the game is a mad dash to the teleporter, then a mad dash to all the items and loot, then a mad dash back to the teleporter. 90% of the time, it'll take too long to get to the items, so the difficulty will increase, or the player will rightly assume that it will take too long to the items, and they'll soldier on unprepared. To me, the game's randomness just creates too many playthroughs that are simply dead on arrival by the third level. This is not good game design. As a side note, some characters are just unviable. This is okay in a competitive multiplayer game where a developer can't predict the metagame. This is not okay in a singleplayer game where the developer knows what challenges the player will face.
The amount of platforming in the game is also totally unacceptable. Most characters are just slow and clunky unless you get the right combination of items that may or may not appear in your game. The platforming controls work just fine, but when you're trying to platform with a slow character with a short jump, and with a swarm of 10+ enemies trying to get you, frustration becomes the first thing one feels, not challenge. In a game that thrives off of its fun, frantic run and gun gameplay, platforming is just not really necessary. And it's unaccpetable when you spend 50% of your play time scaling ladders, timing pixel perfect jumps, and navigating huge levels trying to find where the hell the teleporter spawned this time. Did I mention that your character is slow yet? You character is slow. The levels just aren't interesting enough to spend 2 minutes wandering around while you agonize over the imminent difficulty scale up.
The audio and visual presentation of the game is pretty solid. The pixel art style chosen for the game is visually pleasing and clear, and the soundtrack is an interesting fresh fusion of chiptunes, guitar riffs, and soft electronic sounds. However, there are about 12 tracks in the game, and they loop far too often.
A minor gripe of mine is the minimalist story presentation, done through item descriptions, and monster descriptions, mostly. It provides and interesting picture of a hostile world in a pristine state of nature, which is a good setting for the gameplay, and it also hints at the protagonist experiencing profound loneliness and being shaken by many of the enemies he faces. However, there's just one picture. No more. The world the game takes place on could use a bit more fleshing out to make it seem more like an entity in itself instead of a series of badly designed level to slog through, and the universe of RoR could do with a bit of fleshing out.
Overall, this is an ambitious indie game that certainly has some strong points, but it's just torpedoed by a desire to bow to trends. This game includes far too much randomness, just because the developers want to make it more of a rogue-like. Also, the platforming totally sucks.

The final installment in the Arkham series, Knight.  This game certainly did not go off without a hitch, as many of the reviewers will mention and the media slung around a little over a year ago.  However, a year + after release, this game has taken its foothold, and while it's too little too late to win back the people who abandoned it during the launch fiasco, if you've yet to try it out, know that there is essentially no more problems with performance, so now is the time to give it a shot, if there ever was.
On launch, this game was plauged with a 30 FPS cap, among a myriad of issues running on even the most high end systems with crashes, buggy gameplay, stuttering and tearing frame-rates and drivers issues galore.  Since then, it has been taken off storefronts and patched fairly extensively and reworked and put back on the store at a loss essentially.
As of 2016, there will obviously be no more patches to the game, but the patches that were installed seem to have fixed everything that most people complained about.
As someone who did not play during this time period, I cannot elaborate on the effects of the patch directly, but I can tell you that it now runs just as smooth as any other game I own.
Knight expands on the formula that has made the previous three Batman games so popular: Semi-open-world, great voice acting, stellar graphics/animations, myriad of auxillary and primary villains and support characters, extensive backstory availability as well as side-quests, and a pretty flawless combat system.
The world is open, as it was before in the previous games, as well as the fact that some of the areas are restricted until you've reached a certain amount of story progression.
The combat is the same, with fluidity tweaks and new gadgets and abilities.  "Press Y to counter", score multipliers, combo attacks, etc...
Voice acting and characters present are phenomenal.
Graphics are very well done.  I can't speak for performance on low end systems (I run a 4690K OC'ed w/ GTX 980Ti), but on my system everything ran buttery smooth.
There is still the enourmous number of collectibles present in the game geared towards the Riddler storyline, and they are still over the top with the amount, in my opinion, making them more of a chore than an intersting collectible system.
That said, the collectibles, among a few other items, will give backstory to characters and the universe, as well as concept art, challenge maps, etc... same as before.
The new addition of the BatMobile/BatTank fighting sequences does get a mite repetitive after a bit, but really never to the point of wanting to quit playing because of it.  For the most part, this was an amazing addition to the game and brought a new level of gameplay to a series whos only real gameplay mechanics were the hand-to-hand combat systems.
The story was...alright.  It wasn't amazing, or something I really wish to experience for the first time again.  It was just good.  The gritty, darker side of things was shown more, which is a nice reprieve, but some of the story directions were a little poorly chosen, I think.
A great addition to the franchise overall and definitely worth a play for fans of the series.  I highly recommend playing all the games in the franchise for the total feel, however, the games (minus City -> Origins) don't really build much off each other, so I don't think you'd be missing out on a ton if you were (for some reason) wanting to jump right in at the end of the series with Knight.

The world of Shadowrun Returns is based on the tabletop RPG Shadowrun. As such, the lore is well established and will certainly please many cyberpunk fans. When you purchase Shadowrun Returns, don't expect to be satisfied with "Dead Man's Switch", the campaign that comes pre-installed with it. With that said, "Dead Man's Switch" is around 6 hours long and features a rather linear but interesting story. In this campaign, a fellow shadowrunner that you knew hires you to avenge him for a hundred thousand nuyen, through the use of a dead man's switch. You travel to Seattle in order to find the killer and get paid, but as luck would have it, it involves plenty of jumping through hoops. Once you complete the campaign, you'll find yourself wanting more and that can be easily solved through a quick browse in the Steam workshop.

In-dpeth review. After wasting probably $50 on different games trying to find one I really enjoyed playing, I found Shadowrun. I am very picky about everything, and while other RPGs weren't able to hold my interest, I became addicted to SRR every since I created my first character. As of this review, I have made one character, played it a couple hours, then made a new one once I learned fully how the game works.
First off, let me talk about the character and skill system. One word: perfection. You have a choice of races, with each race having different starting stats. The race is kind of a class system in itself since different races have max skill limits on certain skills, which means certain races can level up certain skills higher than others. Then there are the base class archetypes. I say "base" because once the game starts, you can easily become whatever the ♥♥♥♥ you want to be. Want every kind of skill/fighting option possible? Fine. You can have it. Want to focus on one skill tree? Fine. Do it. Want to level up a couple of similar skill trees or two totally opposite skills for an epic complementary combo? You can do that too. This game probably has the best skill system I have ever seen in a game (Don't hate, I'm a "casual" RPG player). I have had this for two days and I am in love with the class/skill system.
Then, you've got the storyline. Nothing that will make you cry in awe or worship the pc on which this game runs, but the plot/story is entertaining. It holds my interest well as opposed to many, many games which haven't, and has a dark style to it that I really like. There are sidequests throughout the game which can earn your character more cash and skill points. Once you ahve completed the main storyline of the game, there are player-created mods and episodes you can play. I have not yet completed the main storyline so I'm not quite sure how this works and I'm excited to try it.
The battle system also isn't the best, and usually I have a few annoying moments in the game when I cannot click or misclick something due to the view/way the battle system maps out. But nothing major at all, and as you can see from the first part of my review, the strength of this game is it's skill system which is so good it makes all the tiny little minor flaws worth it.
Overall, I give this game a 9.5/10.

You may have or may not figured from the screenshots but : this is a game where you control a little triangle and dodge whatever is closing in to you , coming from the margins to the centre.
This game has 6 levels (hence hexa) , each being beaten after you survive 60 seconds (hence hexa) , maybe this sounds easy , or if not easy , at least a game which does not last long , well the acual gameplay when you win is 6 minutes , but you will be failing so much in the meantime , wich can drive you crazy , but it still gives you an ache to play it more , rather than just making you ragequit. But it is true you will ragequit sometimes , it's unavoidable.
There is a lady announcer that tells you your current level when you reach it , the level being just a reference to the time in one level (0 seconds=point 10 seconds=line 20 seconds=triangle 30 seconds=square 45 seconds=pentagon 60 seconds=hexagon).She also tells you 'Begin' at the start and 'Game Over' when you fail to avoid the obstacles , (wich trust me , you will hear a lot) and 'Excelent' when you beat your record , you will be happy when you hear this , but most of the times you will die shortly after.
Controls are left and right arrow keys , A and D , left and right mouse buttons , and gamepad.
The soundtrack is amazying , in my opinion , and it fits the game realy well.
The visuals are like you see in the screenshots , also the game is a little bit flashy and fast , and may give some problems to epileptics.
I could detail more , but do you realy need so much reason to buy a 3 euro game that will surely entertain you (but how much is based on your motivation) , and if you have doubts get it at a sale , definately worth it :)

I'm very surprised by how rigid and linear this game is, given the deep and complex nature of the source material.  Shadowrun is supposed to be an RPG, but despite being able to upgrade your character, there is very little of the game which the player truly controls.  The environments are richely decorated and look very interesting.  It is clear that the art team clocked many hours making things look pretty.  Sadly the same areas are so dreadfully linear and barren that even the 16-bit Sega Genesis version of the game seems more mysterious and interesting.  The story progresses with little to no input from the player except clicking diologue choices that make no discernable changes to the way the game behaves.
Speaking of the dialogue, it seems that for every hour that was put into the art, one was taken away from the crafting and then editing of the torrential downpour of text that the player is faced with.  Besides comitting the faux pas of presenting the player with only a single style of speech for a multitude of characters with widely-varied backgrounds -- a problem that nearly every game that is faced with the necessity of a script commits -- the game is also riddled with grammatical errors, wrong word use, punctuation mistakes, hair-brained metaphores (oh the irony), moronic similies and other slip-ups that make it seem as if the text were hastily translated from an obscure foreign dialect.
Combat is so rare that I almost feel like buying weapons is a waste of money... the other reason for that is probably because my chracter is so overpowered fromt he beginning that I can literally punch every enemy to death that I do encounter in the first 5 hours of the game.  All ten of them.  If I wanted to go overkill and throw grenades at the enemies until my inventory was empty, that would be fine too as money (nuyen) is to abundant that it becomes meaningless.  The guns don't even require you to purchase specific or even a general category of ammunition from them.  In fact, you don't have to purchase ammo at all.
I was concerned that there was no map on the HUD.  I searched a while for it, but then I realized why there's no map.  The game is so incredibly inflexible and anti-freeform that it will instantly transport you to the next area of the storyline without even the option to walk out of a building onto the street.  There is absolutely no intermediate time where a mercenary (Runner) could... what's it called... oh yeah... go do a Run.  The game shoves you into every job that comes your way and there isn't any opportunity or need to do side jobs for extra cash... unless you actually wanted to play around in the Shadowrun univese, parish the thought.
Look up at the synopsis of the game in the steam store.  It says "Adventure" and without action, suspense or danger that's what this is.  It's an adventure.  A text-and-portrait dialogue-clicking adventure.  I just hope you have a good imagination because there's an awful lot of whitespace to fill in if you want to make this a true Shadowrun adventure.

First I have to say: Civilization V is a very good game. I didn't like the predecessor, so I stuck with Civilization III for a long time. I got used to that game, and, if you like Civilization III, you will definitely like Civilization V. The good things about this game are some fairly well made new game techniques, such as the culture, happines/unhappiness and the social policies. This allows smaller empiries to survive better, it's less nessecairy to have a large amount of cities. The hexagrid map works nicely and it brings the strategy to a new level, you can't put in more than one combat unit into one hexagon. Siege becomes difficult, you need to build more defensive buildings in a city to make it strong, the garrison is not so important anymore. The result of battels depends on the units used in it, it makes a difference now which units you use to conquer. A large amount of artillery is needed as well as strong offensive ground units. The skill system has been taken from Civilization IV, but it has improved. It is very neat. The annoying and useless sea transport units in Civilization III have been replaced by an embarking system. every unit can cross water tiles after researching a technology. This makes the game better. Founding cities at good spots has become an important defensive strategy, if you choose wisely, your cities stay invincible in early eras. But the game also has some disadvantages. If you have a large amount of cities, your army grows with the time. Caused by the fact that it is impossible to stack units, you have to move them around the map precisely. And if you have ten combat units, placing them well is fun, but if you make mistakes you simply can't keep track of all your combat units. It's very annoying to move them around. So I tend to use only a few ground units in the later game era, but lower the cities' strengh with heavy air strikes. The game is designed to use aircraft carriers to carry the bombers, but you can also garrison bombers in cities. Aircraft is stackable, but it can't be moved in a stack. So moving eighty bombers from one city to another is very annoying. Cities can have a building queue, but you can put only five things into them. And buildings which require another building (such as Bank, Stock Exchange etc.) can't be put into the queue, even if the required marketplace is being constructed. This makes it difficult again to keep track of the cities' construction orders. The AI in the game is also a bit weird, they tend to declare at certain points. You suddenly have to face multiple enemies declaring war on you randomly. At the same time. Their reasons are mostly, that you are too powerful already. But the enemies declare war, even if they don't have any chance. Stronger enemies tend to not use their military strengh at all. You see them placing units around your cities, "preparing and attack", but they only attack with a single unit and struggle to place their units out of the water. Embarked units are very vulnerable to city bombardment, which makes it too easy to kill strong enemy units. So, the most annoying point is, that the game is either too easy or just too random. It doesn't make sense at many points, nothing is really predictable. This occours on every diificulty level, and, I have to say that in general, the game is too easy. The AI is too stupid. But nevertheless, the game is good and makes fun ín the end. It is worth spending money on it. I'd not say it's better than Civilization III, but it gets close to it and the concept works nicely.

When I first saw this game, I was just about ready to make physical love to it, that's how amazing I thought it looked. Ad while I would be greatly exaggerating to say I was disappointed, this game still wasn't quite what I expected. Really, my only big problem with this game is that it is exactly that: a game. Purely and simply. There is absolutely not plot, story, character, nothin'. It's just a big ol' labyrinth of puzzles with no well-defined beginning or end. That aside, this game excels in every other aspect. The puzzles and logic are just as mind-bending as the trailer implies, and I legitimately found myself stuck on several occasions. One reviewer put it extremely aptly that "your greatest enemy in this game is yourself." Puzzles with seemingly obvious answers will leave you baffled as you throw yourself at them again and again, until you realize the answer was indeed simple and obvious, but the approach you assumed was right and then got stuck on, was wrong. Even with it's lack of linearity or storytelling, there is still a strong sense of progression and, dare I say, personal development, as you wander the non-euclidian geography of the game. The puzzles continue to challenge and interest the player throughout, and even when you think you're done, there are bound to be some you missed. The asthetic look of the game is really stunning. Imagine Borderlands meets Portal, and you have this game's graphics. The stark white environment, spiked with occasional splashes of coklor and a few swaths of darkness, really lend to the gameplay too, putting you into a calm, introspective mindset as you play. I say I was stuck several times, but with this game's atmosphere, I was never frustrated. Speaking of atmosphere, the sound design was equally well-done, always giving just the right amount of background noise for the situation. With all it's branching paths and mental workouts, I think this game will have me coming back many a time. I found a door marked "the end," but I don't know if I'll ever truly reach it.

Killing Floor 2 started off as a much loved and potentially amazing game, but even the most fervent fanbase can only take so much abuse.
I've had KF2 pretty much since it was released on early access. This game was supposed to be the game that "did early access right". And I know, obviously in retrospect, this is completely untrue, but there were very few red flags that presented themselves in the beginning of the development cycle, and the game was fun! I mean, it was real fun. My friends and I all had a great time blasting zombies (or 'zeds', as they're called in this game), and it was great, although it got a bit stale after a while.
"But that's okay!" I told my friends. "More classes, guns, and maps will be added shortly! After all, the full game will be released November 2015!"
Or so we'd thought. But that gives you some perspective on how stretched out this development has gotten. It is now July 2016 as of writing this.
And I know. Developing a game is not easy. I code things myself, and it's not easy. But the delays aren't the only issue.
Besides extremely long gaps (and I'm talking 2-3+ MONTH long gaps of SILENCE) between updates, the other bad thing TWI did was offer almost no communication at all for their player-base, outside of vague, "we promise it's coming soon(tm)!" updates. Not only did they not communicate with the player-base, they also refused to listen to what the players (the people funding this game) wanted. Instead of a new perk, we got crates a la CS:GO for weapon skins, which would have been fine if they had just talked to the community a little more! Told us what was coming! Instead they only revealed new content through press releases to the press (like GameSpot), leaving the players confused and frustrated because, again, we were the ones giving them money and backing this project. Why would they not just let us know directly what was coming?
Finally, the gameplay. The game plays well for the most part. Which is cool. But it lacks content, so it gets stale after a while to everyone but the most diehard fans of the game.  Another lame thing is that TWI (the developers) constantly release new balance patches without any communication to the players, and when the players don't like them, TWI gives nothing but silence in return (except for the most egregious changes). As of now, there are many widely disliked changes that have been implemented that TWI still refuses to change.
The thing is, it's 2016. Developers can no longer go the "Valve route", which means be completely silent on future content (think Half Life 3), and somehow still have people worshipping them. At best, it's disrespectful to the player-base, because they were promised this when they bought into the episodic game series. At worst, well, your target audience gives up on development and writes bad reviews on the game's Steam page.
Perhaps this game will be good in the future. Mechanically, it's decent now. But since this is an early access game, you're probably purchasing this with the question, "is it worth getting this game in the state it's in, and what is the road map for future development looking like?"
The answer to the first question is - No, it's not worth getting at the moment.
Second answer is - No one knows, and that's why it's not worth getting at the moment.

There are definitely multiple decisions that TWI have made during the development of KF2 that made me incredibly frustrated and regretful in buying the early access game (microtransactions in particular, resistances**Which were reverted**).
But when I actually play the game I'm not fighting against microtransactions, I'm fighting waves of mutated creatures that want to rip my face off. This game makes you vulnerable and powerful at the same time. The way the gore system works makes every kill feel exhilarating and the levels show increasingly more bodies and blood on the ground as the game continues.
There are currently 8 different perks (with two more on the way) which specialize in a certain type of weaponry or playstyle that you level up to gain more power and choose a "skill" every 5 levels up to level 25 to further tailor how you want to play. You can choose to level up perks that specialize in shotguns, assault rifles, team healing, handguns, explosives, melee weapons, and accurate rifles/crossbows.
There are approximately 10 official maps so far and many many custom maps that are extremely well made and more fun to play. I have played KF2 almost as much as I've played KF1 and soon I will have played more.
People were right to be mad about TWI's practices, but quite recently they have been listening to community feedback and responding appropriately (like reverting resistance changes). It sucks when they make big changes without even asking for community feedback, but I still REALLY like playing this game despite all the drama that's been going on, and I'm sure if you liked the first Killing Floor, you will like this one as well.

When I first saw this game, I was just about ready to make physical love to it, that's how amazing I thought it looked. Ad while I would be greatly exaggerating to say I was disappointed, this game still wasn't quite what I expected. Really, my only big problem with this game is that it is exactly that: a game. Purely and simply. There is absolutely not plot, story, character, nothin'. It's just a big ol' labyrinth of puzzles with no well-defined beginning or end. That aside, this game excels in every other aspect. The puzzles and logic are just as mind-bending as the trailer implies, and I legitimately found myself stuck on several occasions. One reviewer put it extremely aptly that "your greatest enemy in this game is yourself." Puzzles with seemingly obvious answers will leave you baffled as you throw yourself at them again and again, until you realize the answer was indeed simple and obvious, but the approach you assumed was right and then got stuck on, was wrong. Even with it's lack of linearity or storytelling, there is still a strong sense of progression and, dare I say, personal development, as you wander the non-euclidian geography of the game. The puzzles continue to challenge and interest the player throughout, and even when you think you're done, there are bound to be some you missed. The asthetic look of the game is really stunning. Imagine Borderlands meets Portal, and you have this game's graphics. The stark white environment, spiked with occasional splashes of coklor and a few swaths of darkness, really lend to the gameplay too, putting you into a calm, introspective mindset as you play. I say I was stuck several times, but with this game's atmosphere, I was never frustrated. Speaking of atmosphere, the sound design was equally well-done, always giving just the right amount of background noise for the situation. With all it's branching paths and mental workouts, I think this game will have me coming back many a time. I found a door marked "the end," but I don't know if I'll ever truly reach it.

I've played this game for ten hours before I eventually got too frustrated and uninstalled.
What I thought when I first encountered it was a misstep, (the lack of any save/load game feature), turned into a death knell -- you WILL reach moments in the game, where despite your best planning you are left in the worst condition you could be and are unable to continue.
In a typical RPG, you would restore to an autosave or a quicksave or otherwise from somewhere earlier on and roll the dice again, presumably to try and get a better result from a combat sequence -- you'd be free to because a regular game recognises the mutability of each instance of combat and provides you that opportunity. That is NOT the case in this game: if you get to the penultimate area of a mission with no health, dead team members, or no supplies, you must either run through the situation over and over from their awkwardly placed checkpoints, or start the entire mission over again from BEFORE you initiated it. This includes talking to all the NPCs, watching unskippable cinematics, recruting new team members, purchasing supplies, levelling up, and travelling to the mission area. Depending on how much preparation you require, you may spend more time in preliminary prepping than actually playing the game, going over the same (admittedly clever and consistent) dialogue, losing its significance each time.
This surely seems like an issue that one shouldn't harp on, but consider how elemental even a rudimentary save system is to any RPG you've ever played, and then remove it. How many opportunities are there to say that it was a universally good choice? In this game, the absence is so notable that it almost renders the game worthless.
As for the positives, the game is set in the legendary Shadowrun universe, fully realised in video game form! The writing is quite often witty and on point. There is a potential for infinite content with the open authoring tools.
It's worth buying if you think you can deal with the big drawback, but it is a big one.

FTL is the poster child for Kickstarter and crowd-sourced funding in general. It also happens to be a damn fine roguelike In Space.
The game has a distinctly retro pixelly feel, but looks really clean and functional. Gameplay-wise it plays out like a real time table top RPG as you move your crew around and divert power to your ship's systems. It's punishingly difficult, even on 'Easy', and has a huge amount of depth for what initially appears to relatively linear game.
I can't recommend this enough for fans of roguelikes and that difficult to pin down genre of action/strategy/sim. The dev team behind this seem like a bunch of excellent guys who care about their fans and deserve the success that this project has already received.
The addition of new races and ships in the patches since release have only made this a more enticing proposition. Add to this some very lovely ambient music and you have yourself a game worthy of your time.

To understand why I am not recommending it, you need to first understand in what time it came out, and what time we are now.
It could be safe to say that, while Dead Space did not invent the shock horror genre, it did give it a very strong boost.
That said, we are now in a time and year where we've been frequently exposed, if not overexposed, to shock horror and quick scares. Horror in gaming has had to evolve and those that didn't or failed to do so obviously got left behind.
With this little bit of perspective, you should understand that Dead Space (at all times I am talking about the first instalment, I haven't tried the sequels yet) no longer offers any real scares any more. Only those not accustomed to this kind of horror would still feel the dread. And quite frankly, that can't be a whole lot of people any more, let alone 'Gamers'.
(if you do happen to find that rare person, videotape it. Those tend to be a real hit on Youtube)
Everything that this game throws at you feels like it 'once' was scary and impressive. Especially as it, if my knowledge doesn't fail me, came in a time when it did a lot of impressive things. It's visual quality was top notch and people hadn't tired fully yet from QTE's.
But that's the thing (and I know I'm harping on it way too much), it just doesn't scare me any more. And you can also see where the concept had it's flaws. Sure, getting grabbed by that huge tentacle and having to timely shoot it's weak spot before it consumes you is a shocker the first time, but when you die... It just starts all over again once you've gotten to that point from your last checkpoint, and the scare factor is completely devoid of it.
In fact, because I was playing on the Hard difficulty, I've had to attempt the second encounter of said tentacle for over TWENTY TIMES. This is partly thanks to the fact I was trying to do a Plasma Cutter only run. Suffice to say I was nothing short of annoyed and bored, eventually. Modern games nowadays tend to include some kind of compensation or balancing so the challenge remains fair but largely doable, unless the game's whole deal is to be unfair.
And that is why I am not recommending it. Not because it would be bad game, not because it would happen to be unfair or brutal. I simply don't recommend it because it's no longer adhering to the standards of modern Horror. Which is largely to blame for the genre itself evolving and drastically changing recently.
If you would get the game, get it for the nostalgia and to understand where the genre 'used to be'.
Just don't expect a product that will knock you off your socks.

It kind of felt like RE4 with a slightly better control scheme, meaning I liked it quite a bit. The whole idea of cutting off the limbs of the Necromorphs instead of just shooting them to death adds slightly more strategy than most shooters, which I found cool. It does get a bit repetitive after you kill/curbstomp these things 1000 times.
Horror-wise, the enemies and the story can be quite disturbing and quite frightening at first. However, I felt Dead Space relies far too heavily on enemies jumping out of vents and going "BLARGHLARGHLARGH!" to scare you 90% of the time, which gets old really quick. Plus, by the time you curbstomp these things 100 times, you'll be desensitized to the disturbance factor of the Necromorphs, and they'll just be like typical mooks to kill like in other games.
In terms of music, I felt the soundtrack did a very good job of keeping the player tense at almost all times. Scare chords were used to great effect in the presence of enemies, though they can get a little repetitive if you're in a fight for too long.
One nitpick I have is that this game runs a bit slower than Dead Space 3, which is very interesting. It's not a game-breaker, by any means, but it can be a bit jarring at first. I've also heard that aiming with the mouse is really sluggish in this game, but I have never tried that out. Instead, I played with a gamepad, which controls the game very nicely, and which I would highly recommend for any game of this genre (like Resident Evil 5, for example).
All in all, I had fun with this game as an action title. As a horror game, it does its job quite nicely, especially through the first playthrough, but there are better games out there for the sole purpose of scares.
