I dunno what it is about this game, but it's just so...captivating.
The gameworld just feels so alive. I know it's supposed to not be, but the physics engine really does a great job making everything fling around after explosions, how grenades echo throughout the coast, how the score is used so sparcely (even though I don't particularly like the score that much.)
The gunplay is solid. You've got a standard selection of guns that all feel smooth to use, but they are very limited. How convenient we have the Gravity gun, then! The maps are littered with physics objects, so it's easy to make an improvised weapon. A barrel, a bench or even a pipe can be flung at the enemies to bash their brains in, and it's all so rewarding.
The graphics, while not the best, still hold up to today. Other 3rd party games today still struggle to compete with Half life 2's facial animations. The community update also does the game a few favors.
The voice acting is pretty great, though I felt  the voice actor of Alyx could've done a greater job. Not that she was bad, but some of her lines just felt a little unenthused. (I know she's gotten better with The Last of Us, so hopefully she will come back in Half life 3.)
So yeah, I really like this game. I just hope someday there will be a sequel, though I doubt it with Valve's current work policy.

I just purchased this during the Autumn sale and I have greatly enjoyed it.  The art style, sound, and gameplay are all great.  The combat is turn-based and very similiar to X-Com: Enemy Unknown.  The story is engrossing and well presented, always leaving me wanting more.
I have a few gripes with the game, however.  First, there is no way to currently save your game during missions, which can make for some long and frustrating gameplay sessions.   Secondly, there are some bugs with melee combat.  On one mission, I would use a melee attack and it would not register for 10 seconds.  It's a minor bug but after enough times, it is an annoyance.
All and all, for the price, I recommend it and certainly look forward to checking out some of the Steam Workshop mods.
EDIT:  Be forewarned, the lack of a quick-save feature can be a major annoyance in missions.  For example, during missions where you go into the Matrix, if you trigger the alarm, you will forever be hutned by more powerful foes.  It is extremely annoying and chances are once you trigger it, you will not be able to overcome the alarm.  The ability to save and reload would have easily negated unnecssary frustration.

Shadowrun Returns is an amazing adaptation of my favorite game world.
Absolutely beautiful maps...  Faithful adaptation of the game rules...  Evocative effects and voices...  Dramatic models...  It all does a wonderful job of re-creating the world of Shadowrun.
The only thing is...  Shadowrun Returns feels more like a framework for others to build their games atop, than an actual game in itself.
Shadowrun Returns ships with a campaign called "Dead Man's Switch" that does a terrific job of introducing the world of Shadowrun...  And it's got a good chunk of gameplay to it.  And there's actually a good amount of replay-ability with different classes and abilities.  But, ultimately, it feels a little short.
You can build your own campaigns from within the game...  And you can download what others have made through the Workshop...
But I'm still kind of waiting for the developer to release some more "official" campaigns.

I got this game for free with my graphics card last year, and was at first tremendously dissapointed with the quality of the port.  Even with a GTX 970 card, the thing ran like a cat stuffed in a bag full of rocks and pistachios.  It having been free, I wasn't able to 'return' it during the Great Batman AK Return event of 2015, and since my purchase of the Season Pass had techincally happened before any content came out, I was denied a refund by Steam.
This ended up being a blessing, because over the course of the last year, Rocksteady not only made the game playable, but tremendously enjoyable.  I was recently shocked to discover it holds the #2 spot on my list of games I've pent the most time playing, second only to Elite: Dangerous.  I think I've played through this game 3-4 times now, and played the DLC even more.
The story is very true to the core Batman mythos, and it truly conveys the raw emotion and sensation that you'd expect from being the bat.  The action is solid, engaging, and exhilerating, with the co-operative moments with other members of the Bat-family being a particular gameplay highlight.  The addition of the patched in challenge maps immensely increases replayability.
It still suffers from some hitches.  For the love of pete, don't turn on any of the NvidiaWorks BS or you'll watch your framrate nosedive into an ocean of chug-pain.  Also, while I personally didn't have any issues during the Riddler Batmobile sections, I can entirely sympathize with those who see them as irritating and superfluous.
I reccomend this game wholeheartedly now, and I think it's a shining example of a company holding to a promise to fix something they shipped broken, even if it takes a year to do it.
Yes the game is short. Yes it is outdated. But in truth it is still one of the best if not THE best game ever created. 9/10.

When life poisons your lemons, by Jove you need to take back your orchard with overclocked power tools that can only be set to eleven (you destroyed the other settings with a  gore-encrusted soldering iron).  The Ishimura--the massive, city-sized ship that is the setting for your wondrously haunting nightmare-- is that metaphorical, blood-soaked orchard, and it's up to a plucky engineer to save the day.
The coms are down, the marines are dead, and your flashlight is the last thing on your mind when all the oxygen is being sucked out of the room by malevolent organisms that have calcium-based bone-blades for hands.  Grab an industrial saw, flamethrower, or plasma cutter and show that thing wearing your best friend's skin as a party favor what the labor movement truly means.

This is a really tight, well made squad based strategy game. Everything about it is well made. The graphics, the plot, the gear, the combat, the enemy progression, the difficulty scaling, it's all pretty much perfect. It's also easy to play how you want to play, with options that allow anything between an old school xcom 'half your squad dies from friendly fire after a rookie panics' game to some sort of action move where aliens die in their hundreds and nobody on the good guys side gets scratched.
The early game is suitably hectic as you struggle to build gear and satellites and run missions but that trails off towards the endgame where you can pretty much slaughter any aliens that stick their heads up, and the heart thumping sense of 'oh god not more attacks not now oh god' pretty much vanishes and you can get to the end of the tech tree way before the final few missions. The missions themselves are pretty good, with a healthy amount of variety so it doesn't get stale. The only issue I had was with the expansion pack storyline and the main game storyline - the xp one kicks in late and lasted longer than the main game storyline did, so I was stuck twiddling my thumbs staring at the big red GO FIGHT THE END BOSS button while I waited for more of the expansion stuff to happen.
The support cast are all pretty good, and honestly they are all much more fleshed out than I would have expected considering they are stuck in a few soundbites and cutscenes, but they do add a lot to the game, even if you never do quite shake the suspicion Vahlen is a little bit too into dissecting things alive.

Shadowrun Returns is in many ways a half-baked game. It's short, not terribly deep, not particularly pretty, and often reminds you that it's a game. Despite this, there's a fantastic deal to like about Shadowrun Returns.
Shadowrun Returns (SR) is the second of the major profile video games funded via crowdfunding platform Kickstarter while still in the pre-planning stages to be released. The campaign ran in April 2012, and pulled in about 1.83 million dollars, well over its minimum funding goal of 400,000 dollars. SR is the fourth video game based on the pen-and-paper roleplaying setting Shadowrun, and is the first to not be called simply by its setting's name. The game builds on the story of the first two Shadowrun games - the first released for the SNES, the second on the Genesis - and disregards the third one - released for the 360, PS3 and the PC - on account of it being a multiplayer game with no story.
At first glance, Shadowrun is one of the most archetypical cyberpunk settings available in tabletop gaming. It's perpetually rainy, everything is owned by soulless megacorporations, poverty is widespread and the Internet is a world in itself. In a market saturated with these kinds of settings, you need a special something to stand out, and what makes Shadowrun one of the most popular games in the genre is its overlap with standard fantasy. In 2012, magic unexpectedly returned to the world, transforming many humans into dwarves, elves, orcs, trolls, and more. Many were gifted with magical abilities, while dragons awakened from their deep slumber. Two generations later, magic and technology coexist in a society rife with racial (specieal?) tensions and little hope in sight.
The game casts you in the down-on-your-luck shoes of one of the eponymous Shadowrunners - a sort of mercenary-slash-master criminal that lives in the cracks of society. Work has been scarce lately after a botched shadowrun, and you are down to your last saved Nuyens when a colleague contacts you about a job. Or, more specifically, the recording of a colleague - as it turns out, your old acquaintance got himself killed, and is contacting you to let you know that his life insurance payout is yours if you will bring his killer to justice. Having no other options, you accept, taking the first step towards unravelling the convoluted mystery behind his death.
The simple motivation of trying to get at a former coworker's insurance money is a great story hook. Even the best Shadowrunner is little more than a pawn on the big corporations' boards, and, to mix metaphors, you're little more than a deuce in the Suit of Pawns at this point. As a result, the story is largely personal, and it's up to you if you're just in it for the money, justice or revenge. The interaction is reminiscent of Planescape: Torment, in that much of the environmental interaction is done via dialogue trees or by reading text hovering over the environment, although SR never comes close to Torment's sheer verbosity. All in all, the story is excellently told - it's well-written, has good twists, ups the stakes at the right spots, and has interesting characters. That said, the last third isn't as interesting as the preceding material, as the focus starts to move away from your own story, and it must be noted that there is a complete absence of voice acting in the game - a shame, as the dialogue is superb.
Who your character is is up to you - the character creation system is open-ended, and doesn't restrict skills to certain character classes like many RPGs do. Although you may opt to choose one of the ready-made decks, such as the melee-centric Street Samurai or the hacking-oriented Decker, there is no penalty for distributing skill points according to your own preferences instead. You can pick your own name, be male or female, and may choose to be human, elf, dwarf, troll, or orc. The choice of race (species) gives certain minor bonuses and affects the maximum level a particular stat can reach (each skill or subskill is tied to a particular stat, and can't be higher than the stat or skill it's nested under), and you will be treated differently in-game depending on your choice of race (species) and gender. All in all, it's pretty standard stuff for an RPG, but the system is very open, and if you feel like playing as a troll Decker who dabbles in shamanism, go for it.
The game is controlled from an isometric perspective, and is divided into two discrete sections: exploration and combat. While exploring, you can only control your own character, and mostly click on objects or non-playable characters to interact with them. There is usually not a lot to interact with, but there is usually just enough to keep exploration rewarding, even if it's just in the form of another description of the environment. Skills and stats are frequently used to solve problems in ways that give better results, although since the game is fairly short, most skills are only used once or twice each. The game is also fairly rigid; the player has little input on how the story plays out, aside from the details. Interestingly, SR does not use an experience point-based system; instead, "karma points" are doled out after completing certain tasks. These points are then spent in the skill tree, improving your character directly. Oddly, "evil" decisions will apparently not yield karma points, which is a strange design choice. That said, there are more than enough karma points to go around.
Unlike most CRPGs, SR is a very linear game. Each level is its own microcosm that can't be exited until the game tells you to, and while there are a number of recurring levels throughout the game - most notably the Seamstresses Union, the town-equivalent you visit between missions - most of them occur in sequence; as such, it doesn't feel as if you're returning to places already visited, but rather to different versions of them. This plays into how the game rewards the player as well: on certain levels, skill checks will have become noticably harder, and equipment upgrades will usually by straight numerical improvements. It's somewhat immersion-breaking, as it feels as if you're just being rewarded for the sake of it.
In combat, the game switches to what might be termed XCOM-lite mode. The combat is turn-based, with each participant moving their entire party on their turn. Each character has two or three action points, and each point allows you to move a certain amount of squares or perform some other action, such as attack or cast a spell. Scattered throughout the environment are walls and objects that can be used for partial or full cover. If a character is outfitted with a "datajack" they may access the Matrix (the Internet); however, Matrix gameplay is little more than an underdeveloped version of normal combat, and it is a mixed blessing that it is used only maybe half a dozen times, mostly in the second half of the game. Overall, the combat is not outstanding, but it does the job, and it can be rewarding to successfully play off each character's attributes to achieve optimum results.
Graphically, the game looks alright. The backgrounds are high-res images, and while not fantastic-looking, they do contribute a great deal artistically to the atmosphere. Sound effects are what you would expect, and the music is mostly moody synthesizer tunes that complement the setting well.
Shadowrun Returns may have its rough edges and be a fairly shallow experience at times, but the superb writing, great atmosphere and satisfying gameplay makes it well worth the low price that matches its length. Finally, since tradition dictates I say it: never, ever, cut a deal with a dragon.

This is a really tight, well made squad based strategy game. Everything about it is well made. The graphics, the plot, the gear, the combat, the enemy progression, the difficulty scaling, it's all pretty much perfect. It's also easy to play how you want to play, with options that allow anything between an old school xcom 'half your squad dies from friendly fire after a rookie panics' game to some sort of action move where aliens die in their hundreds and nobody on the good guys side gets scratched.
The early game is suitably hectic as you struggle to build gear and satellites and run missions but that trails off towards the endgame where you can pretty much slaughter any aliens that stick their heads up, and the heart thumping sense of 'oh god not more attacks not now oh god' pretty much vanishes and you can get to the end of the tech tree way before the final few missions. The missions themselves are pretty good, with a healthy amount of variety so it doesn't get stale. The only issue I had was with the expansion pack storyline and the main game storyline - the xp one kicks in late and lasted longer than the main game storyline did, so I was stuck twiddling my thumbs staring at the big red GO FIGHT THE END BOSS button while I waited for more of the expansion stuff to happen.
The support cast are all pretty good, and honestly they are all much more fleshed out than I would have expected considering they are stuck in a few soundbites and cutscenes, but they do add a lot to the game, even if you never do quite shake the suspicion Vahlen is a little bit too into dissecting things alive.

The sequel to the critically acclaimed Half-Life, Half-Life 2 breathes new life into the series.
After the cliffhanger of the original Half-Life, Gordon Freeman is once again thrust into an alien invasion. This time, however, the invaders have effectively taken control of every resource and major population center on Earth. The prowess of the invaders is staggering, at least until Freeman manages to obtain another crowbar. After meeting with some old allies,  a terrible mistake exposes Freeman to the dictatorship in control of Earth, which leads to the mobilisation of all available units with the sole purpose of destroying Freeman.
Without giving too much away, mayhem awaits.
The plot of Half-Life 2 really is quite impressive, especially when considering that Half-Life had only a simple story. Half-Life 2 branches off from the original in an impressive manner, showing off the impressive writing talents of the Valve team. The plot is discovered through typical Half-Life fashion: your surroundings. While it's no Dark Souls in terms of plot, it doesn't obviously point out all the plot points, nor does it pause your game to tell you insignificant amounts of information.
Gameplay in Half-Life 2 is similar to the original, except with a new arsenal and significantly larger environment. While restrained to the Black Mesa facility in Half-Life, Freeman is free to explore the world in the much largr sequel. This leads to more epic fights, environments and strategies.
The new space is well utilised in most cases. Helicopters must be shot down, yet can do significant damage to any areas where you may hide. The Combine will attempt to ambush you whenever possible, which leads to surprises.
The enemies and environment are impressive. The environment depicts what happens to Earth after being completely dominated by atechnologically superior force, and the aliens fit into areas apropriate for them, such asthe Antlions whom live under sand in beaches.
Overall, I would say that Half-Life 2 builds on the original game in every way, yet it does not replace it. It creates an amazing world and great cast of characters that you will feel attached to, even the silent protagonist Gordon Freeman and the seemingly omnipotent G-man. I highly recommend this game, for its story, gameplay, characters and everything else that makes it amazing.

As someone who has occasionally delved into strategy games, I can say that this is the best strategy game i have ever played- hands down. I played the vanilla edition for about a year and on the whole was pretty satisfied; my one gripe was that diplomacy wasn't immersive enough, by that I mean that you can tell Montezuma to get the ♥♥♥♥ away from your territory, and you can become friends with Gandhi and he will probably stab you in the back with that goofy smile, throw in some trading... and that is your vanilla Civ V. Enter 'Brave New World' and 'Gods & Kings' DLC.... Suddenly ideologies and religions are as key to success as dominance on the battlefield. It makes end-game so so interesting as the world unfolds at the scale it did IRL. have you reached a stalemate with a neighbouring Civ and you can't just make up and be friends? Perhaps you both choose the 'order' ideology and become best buds hell bent on painting the world red. Or did your neighbour choose an opposing ideology? Well form an alliance with another Civ like yourself and paint the hexes red with your enemies blood. Check this game out, I couldn't win a game for about a month, and a year on I still often lose or decide to quit (a game can take from 3-10 hours) from my experience; a game you'll come back to is a challenging one. Very easy on the eye with a great soundtrack.

Shadowrun Returns is a fun, enjoyable game with an engaging story. The story and graphics will push you towards the finish line. That said, it lacks the ability to further engage and explore this aesthetically pleasing and memorable world. Some community patches allow you to further explore this dystopian Seattle.
While I am looking forward to the next stand-alone chapter in Berlin, I would have liked for there to be a Seattle continuation once you finish Dead Man's Switch. Hopefully there will be one other time. It would also be nice if the game provided a bit more freedom and sidequests as the Shadowrun Return environment matures, as well as the ability to develop a crew that is customizable to the same degree as the main character.
While the team you can hire improves throughout the game, you cannot manually improve their abilities or manage their Karma points. You only fully customize the main character. I wish there were more options available.
In a nutshell, its a engaging story, and fun to play, which reminded me of Crusader: No Regret, as well as Jagged Alliance 2 with its top-down isometric approach, yet it falls short of the freedom provided by Fallout 2 or similar CRPGs.
If you like player controlled team-based strategy games, this is a pretty fun game.

***I originally wrote this review on 11-04-2008***
Creating a successful horror game is tricky. There needs to be just enough of a blend tension, fear and scare tactics so the game does not fall to mundane generic enemies jumping out at players. Dead Space not only creates the one of the best atmospheres in a horror video game, it’s full of enough puzzles, frights and dilemmas to make even the most jaded 3rd Person Shooter player sit up and take notice.
You play as Isaac Clarke, a space engineer, traveling to the USG Ishimura, a “Planet Cracker” which is emitting a distress call. After a tense opening sequence, Isaac boards the ship with his coworkers, Lt. Zach Hammond, security officer, and Kendra Daniels, a computer expert, and soon realizes this is no ordinary distress call as the ship has been overrun by an alien race. Isaac gets separated from his coworkers and must fight his way through the alien monsters to bring the ship back online and find a way off the Ishimura.

Dead Space has taken every great piece of third person gameplay in the history of video games and combines it together to deliver an entertaining, enjoyable journey. You navigate Isaac from an over-the-shoulder view. There is no Heads Up Display (HUD) in Dead Space. Your health is indicated by the light meter embedded in the spine of your suit spine. Your ammo is displayed above your weapon when you aim and your stasis meter is also located on the back of your suit. What is stasis? It is a piece of technology that gives you the ability to slow down objects and enemies for puzzle solving and reaction time. You can recharge your stasis by accessing stations located throughout the ship or by finding portable stasis packs. Isaac also has the ability to use Kinesis, which allows him to move heavy objects or acquire objects that are out of reach. Stasis becomes available to Isaac a few minutes into the game, and Kinesis becomes available for use when entering the second chapter and has unlimited use.
The game's most unique and striking appeal is operating in zero gravity or a vacuum. When entering a Zero-G zone, Isaac has the ability to jump from one side of the area to another. This opens up an new realm of puzzle solving and is some of the most fun sequences in the game.
The enemies in Dead Space are deformed humans that were killed and turned into monsters by a race of alien creatures. There are a dozen or so different styles of enemies that navigate their way through the ships ventilation system, which means you may encounter an enemy at any given time. As many enemies as there are, they all can be taken out with the same technique: begin by shooting off their limbs first. Direct hits to the body will waste ammo, especially during fights with the tougher, more advanced enemies. Some of the more memorable enemies are the epic boss fights that also combine a little Zero-G action. The threats on the ship are sometimes not always enemy related. Dead Space shifts gears twice for a little Han Solo, “Don’t Get Cocky” turret action.
So how do you take out all the enemies? With a wide range of weaponry of course. Isaac begins the game with a Cutter, an extremely accurate “laser” that fires a wide beam either horizontally or vertically. There are tons of lockers and chests to explore during the course of the game. Some lockers may contain ammo and others may contain credits, which can be used in Stores. At these Store locations, Isaac can store, ammo and items. Isaac is limited in the number of items he can carry, however the number of items can be increased if he upgrades his suit. Usually near by a store, is a Workbench, where Isaac can upgrade his weapons and gear.
There is a lot of backtracking in Dead Space. At the beginning of each chapter, Issac exits a tram which carries passengers from one section of the ship to another, and at the end of each chapter he makes his way back to the same tram to journey to the next section of the ship. Isaac visits some sections of the ship more than once. There are tons of save points throughout Dead Space, probably more than there should be. Even if you don not save, Dead Space autosaves so much that you really do not have to save once through the entire game, unless you want to exit out of Dead Space or turn off your PS3. To make the game even easier, the developers also added in a feature that actually maps out the direction Isaac needs to travel to complete his next objective. This feature is displayed by a blue outline on the ground. (see pic below)
The problem that most avid gamers will notice is that everything, aside from the zero gravity gameplay, has been borrowed from past films, novels, or other games. The over the shoulder view bares a striking resemblance to Resident Evil 4, the monsters are mere replicas of John Carpenter's The Thing, parallels in Event Horizon are seen throughout the entire game including some obvious set design rip offs and features in Doom 3 and System Shock are also used in Dead Space. It is at this point where we stop and think: are these references by the EA Readwood Game designers an homage to their favs or are they simply thefts? No matter, the similarities are not enough to take away from the Dead Space experience which delivers a terrifying story, but the influences are definitely obvious.
Dead Space does everything right graphically. It looks beautiful in full 1080p when staring out into the vast ocean of space, blowing an enemies head off, or playing through some beautiful level designs of what a 'Planet Cracker's' engine room, maintenance bay and mining section may look like.
The sound effects are also top notch in Dead Space. As Isaac communicates with his team, a 2D holograph image appears before Isaac, which the player can rotate. The static overlaid onto the video and audio logs is incorporated nicely, and the creeks and cracks heard throughout the broken ship add much to the atmosphere. Listen for the lullaby.
Players may pick up quickly on how Visceral tries to scare its players. They use the same formula that Hollywood does, during a tense or critical moment in the game they play loud music like the typical brass pieces you hear in most horror movies. More often than not this takes place when a player looks in the direction of an enemy. So this tactic may help a player in certain areas rather than scare him or her. If a player is not paying attention and some random horns start playing, that is a pretty good indication that there was probably a monster that ran past the door that they probably missed.
: controls work extremely well on the PS3, terrifying boss battles, graphics and sound are gripping,
: : unoriginal enemies, predictable but engaging story, very easy to beat, lots of backtracking
: I recommend this game in spite of my criticism of the unoriginality of some of its elements but it is defendable to question why this game has been so highly touted. Some have labeled Dead Space as the ‘Worlds Scariest Game’ and people are shouting from roof tops to “Buy this game immediately!”. The game isn’t perfect, but what is? It has a wonderfully smooth flowing story, a great environment, near perfect controls and graphics that can make a grown man cry. Dead Space is solid game that should be experienced by as many players as possible. There are striking resemblances to a dozen pieces of work, but they are forgivable. Expect a sequel.

Honestly? It ain't that good - but it is still hell a lot of fun. Especially for those who cannot stand the overly complex, doomstacking micromanagement nightmare of its predecessor.
If you are new to the series, do not even bother reading further, this game is the simple greatest possible introduction you could have to Civilization and that is actually by far the strongest argument I have here: it is simple enough to make newcomers accustomed to the feel of it and when they get bored with it - which is, mind you, highly unlikely anytime soon, you can trust me on that - they can go hardcore and try one of the more... complex Civ games that are still around.
If you are coming from Civ4 however...
Civ5 got rid of some of the (sometimes really complicated) features of Civ4 like espionage or the pop health system and also overcame some others which (in my opinion) made that game less realistic and really annyoying sometimes - so military units do not stack anymore and cultural borders of cities no longer grow in a circular way. Well at least not always.
There are also a lot of really good innovations like the replacement of the old square-based map with hexes, a bit more realistic religion system FINALLY independent of technology, a consistent generation of Great People, the introduction of strategic and luxury resources etc.
And also the leaders/civilizations: the unique buffs each civ gets are great and diverse and offer different strategies indeed not mentioning the miriads of possibilities different maps / resources / enemies / luck could provide you.
But.
In the end all those did not make it a better game. Of course not everybody is obsessed with micromanaging dozens of cities each with dozens of pops or finding a way to get rid of dozens of enemy units being doomstacked on a single tile. But the simplification has its price: it makes the game far less challenging than its predecessors were. It is not just about the AI, which is seemingly incapable of mounting a sane attack and is generally wasting its armies in futile battles, but the game itself lacks one core thing I like: deep planning. Things are a lot more straightforward now and once you have put your civilization on the right track you cannot really mess it up anymore...
All in all I still recommend it because it offers you to taste the wonderful meal called Sid Meier's Civilization and it tastes great indeed - but again: why would you stop at the appetizer?

Running this at 2k 60 fps on a 980 ti and it's really doing well. Exceptionally better than before for sure. Frame rate drops are rare and only slightly appear during some cut scenes and when the batmobile shows up. But this is only by 2-3 frames most of the time.
The story can be engaging, even if predictable for harcore comic fans. But that is to be expected and shouldn't be a complaint since most movies based on books SURPRISE follow the book. Batman is struggling mentally with visions of the past and an old villain comes back as hallucinations that are done in a really unique way. You are going up against the mysterious "arkham knight" whom shares a striking resemblance to batman, trying to take over gotham. Many villains make a return whether it be in the main story or many of the sidequests. Other allies of batman join in too.
Gameplay is fluid and has nearly gotten down to perfection combat wise. You feel like you really are getting a big glimpse into what being batman really is like. Glide and traverse the city with the help of you batclaw or take the road in your bat mobile. Their are collectables, sidequests, challenges and of course main story missions, or if you so choose a plentiful supply of thugs to beat up  causing mayhem in the streets of gotham. Combat wise can be stealthy or a full on brawl with tons of bad guys. Or a mix of both. Batman has a huge assortment of tech, martial arts, and stealth capabilities at hand and even more to unlock upon leveling up. Their are also quite a few sections with the batmobile which can transform into a tank. Some people had complaints on this but at the end of the day it didn't ever come off as offensive. Some times there can also be small "detective sections" where you solve crimes and it can be really fascinating and engaging, sometimes making me feel incredibly satisfied for solving them. I can't go way too in depth here but their are plenty of things to keep people entertained.
Graphics and detail are great and sometimes even incredible to look at and the sound design is pretty good as well. Ragdoll physics can be kinda silly but nothing too crazy. This game is incredibly more stable than the initial launch.
If I were to put this game into summary it is a free roaming, beat em up, stealth, action and mystery game.
I won't put a stupid number to rate this but who would i recommend this too?
People who like comics and batman? - HELL YES
People who love stealth games - Yes and there is a lot of it but it isnt entirely stealth
People who like beat em ups - Hell yes
People who like free roaming games/ sandbox games - Yes, BUT don't expect gta free roaming. There are many things to do but they are things batman would do. There are so many possibilities with all of the tech he has at exposal. But don't expect batman to go murdering people in the street and jacking cars. You get around with the batmobile or running across rooftops and gliding around with your batclaw. I would say absolutely try it.

I like these old style turn based games.  And Shadow Run Returns tries to take after the best (though it just misses it in my opinion).  The thing that I really appreciate about this game is that the developers went for simplicity.  Most games of this nature have a learning curve that takes weeks to get used to.  I'm not complaining about those games in the least it's just sometimes I'd like a game thats simple to learn and play.  SR (Shadowrun Returns) can have a beginner used to the layout in a matter of 2 hours.  That doesn't mean that there is no strategy, or depth, actually it's quite the opposite.  Though it's not super deep like say Fallout 1 and 2 or Baldur's Gate it still has a style that is often overlooked in modern games.  Fans of Shadowrun would hopefully love it, as for me I never played the original SR games, but I always loved cyberpunk stories.  This game has an interesting combination of leveling and skill learning, it's a good pick.  This is definitely worth the small investment, plus you get the workshop on top of it and player created content can sometimes beat out the developers story lines.
So what I am saying is this.  Expect a simple game that has just enopugh depth to entertain and make different characters and combinations of playthroughs.  Player content makes it worth more as well.  It's cheap enough to try out and when Steam has a sale it's most certainly worth the buy.

Shadowrun Returns is a turn-based cyberpunk themed strategy R.P.G. developed by Harebrained Schemes and published by Harebrained Holdings. Shadowrun has gained a huge cult following since its creation nearly 25 years ago. Now, creator Jordan Weisman returns to the world of Shadowrun, modernizing this classic game setting as a single player, turn-based tactical roleplaying game. The year is 2054 and magic has returned to the world awakening powerful creatures of myth and legend as technology merges with flesh and consciousness. As a shadowrunner, you're a mercenary living on the fringes of society, in the shadows of massive corporate arcologies, surviving day-by-day on skill and instinct alone. Shadowrun Returns harkens back to the classic old school roleplaying games from back in the day. The top-down isometic view, intense turn-based combat and non-voiced dialogue of a traditional R.P.G. are expertly blended in this fantastic indie title from Harebrained Holdings. The story is divided into campaigns which can range from solving murders to battling corporate espionage and a number of other different situations and once you've finished the games main storyline you can download new user created campaigns from the Steam Workshop or the Nexus which further extends the replayability of this great title.
Besides the excellent story, the turn-based combat of course is one of the best features of this game. Progressing through the narrative will reward you with experience points and allow you to grow your character in any direction that you choose. Want to summon spirits as an elven shaman, be an expert hacker or go guns and blade ablazing as a Street Samurai? The choice is up to you. As the leader of the group, it's also up to you to choose the right balance of combat, tech and magical abilities in order to have a successful run. The gripping tactical combat system is quick and responsive and just a fun alternative to the combat of today's more popular roleplaying games.
Graphically the game looks terrific in full high definition with its futuristic cyberpunk setting. The environments are also quite varied as you will travel from the slums of the Redmond Barrens to the extravagant offices of powerful corporations and beyond. The character portraits presented during conversations have a unique style that lends itself well to this title and I find the isometric backgrounds and set pieces delightful to view. One of my favorite things about these types of games are the small details in the world around you and this title is chock full of them and add to that some excellent sound effects and a terrific musical score and Shadowrun Returns delivers big time.
If you're a R.P.G. fan looking for something a little different to add to your library or just enjoy old-school or retro games then I HIGHLY RECOMMEND Shadowrun Returns! You will not be dissapointed with this title.

===============Risk of Rain Review==============
Upon starting up risk of rain, I was hit with a bit of a nostalgia trip. The graphics are deliberately 8-bit and the overall aestheic of the game is tailored towards an "old school" feel. This game is very similar to sword and scorcery in its graphical appearance. To some, this may appeal, but to others, it may not incite any excitement. However, the game itself is a survival platformer whereby you must find a teleporter on each level. You can initially only choose 1 character (the commando) however, unlocks are plenty in this game and eventually you will unlock all 8 characters.
The difficulty in this game ramps up about 15 minuts in and you must buy items that appear in the world in order to survive (and gain useful buffs). Sessions of Risk of Rain will usually last about 30minutes and the gameplay is satisfying and fun. Although difficult, it's rewarding when you finally wipe all the monsters (that randomly spawn) from each area.
As far as I can tell, each map is randomly generated so that replay value remains high. Couple this with both local and online multiplayer, and you have a satisfying survival 8-bit platformer with an above average music score.
======Pros=====
+Great replay value
+Music score suits the game/atmosphere
+Satisfying gameplay
======Cons=====
- 8-bit may not appeal to everyone
- Heavily dependant on starting zone
- Online needs more optimisation

Ridiculously addictive and fun to play. Its one failing is claiming that it's fun to lose - games *can* be fun to lose, specifically games with an incredible amount of variables and procedural elements allowing not only emergent gameplay but emergent catastrophe. Dwarf Fortress comes to mind as one such example. The problem with FTL is that it *doesn't* have that many variables. There are too few actions to take and too few ways to die to make it *funny*. In Dwarf Fortress, you might say such and such dwarf caught a fever, went mad and killed his cat, no one cleaned it up so the miasma from the corpse made all the other dwarves vomit and the last one ran out and got trampled by an elephant. This is fun, this is funny and you want to tell your friends. "Derp, just died from a hull breach again" is considerably less interesting.
Nonetheless a very entertaining game and well worth the price.

Updated Review - after installing Enemy Within "DLC".
Enemy Within is a highly recommended change to this game. It's not DLC in the sense as its not really an "addon" to the game, but rather more like a complete overhaul, and a totally different game.
If I was to compare it to a "mod", it would more like a total conversion rather than a small change to the game.
There's tons of different maps (this will help with the boredom that.. oh its one of those maps again), in addition to the maps that are in the original X-Com, and there's a lot of extra storyline missons/Council missions.
In addition to that, there's loads of new items to research and the whole new concept of "Meld" which will allow you to mutate your soldiers to have special powers, or even change them into Battlemechs.
In addition to this, there a a few more different enemy types (those new steath squid things are nasty!) - I don't want to spoil all of the new stuff in the game, but there is plenty to keep you busy.
You just must get the Enemy Within, it's the best purchase I bought so far this year, and I got it at 75% off, which was a bargin!
Some things you should be aware of: Known (annoying) bugs:
- Mouse bug - aiming explosives (rockets or grendades) the target area often jumps about making it extremely difficult to aim accurately and often makes you misclick. The workaround is to try to change the camera angle or position. The mouse bug also affects movement selection.
- Frequent random crashes - game often crashes (3 - 4 times a session for me) there is no known fix or workaround.
- Save file corruption - this can happen if your PC powers off during a save. No fix for this, extremely annoying if you play Ironman - only way to circumvent is to make frequent backups of your save games.

Aside from the old SNES game, which I quite liked for its bewildering strangeness back in the day, I had little previous engagement with the Shadowrun world. But expected great things from this.
As it stands, I can't say they were warranted. Shadowrun Returns is very atmospheric, the steam-punked noir world is very well rendered, the script is well written, and the game is fun enough to play. But it's also rather shallow and very straightforward: not a single choice to make and barely three sidequests through the whole game. Also, don't expect too much from the turn-based combat: a strategy-RPG this is not! As is, the game is pretty much the corridor shooter of modern day RPGs. It'as an action-packed thrill ride in a suggestive world that leaves little time or space for thought, but does what it sets out to do confidently and a fair amount of gusto. Here's hoping expansions give the game the depth it sorely lacks.

Although I had some doubts about Shadowrun Returns - Mitch Gitelman basically had to apologize for the 360 game that he helped produce a few years ago - the final product was certainly a pleasant surprise.  For one, it actually came out and mostly delivered what was promised during the Kickstarter campaign (the extra module is still forthcoming), which is a bit of a win in and of itself.
As for the game, it plays very much like a modernized version of the isometric RPGs of old.  It's linear and completely segmented into levels, to the point where the game only saves when you enter a new area, so there is no room for exploration or choice.  Yes, there are dialog options that can slightly change how characters react to you, but you are being guided through the game's main storyline by the developers.
Where the game shines is the combat system, which is very evocative of the many turn-based SRPGs that have had a bit of a Renaissance in recent years.  It's not quite Xcom or Fire Emblem, of course, but many of the same ideas apply.  Play smart and tactically or watch as you and your party members fall to the enemy.  As an aside, I'd also recommend rolling a Decker, because it gives you a chance to play through some exclusive missions with your own character rather than rely on a party member.
If you are looking for a true throwback to the CRPGs of old... let's be honest, you probably backed Wasteland or Torment.  Heck, you probably own this game already as well.  But if you are curious about looking back into a time when RPGs were a bit more numbers-focused and "grognardy", Shadowrun Returns gives you a taste of what that experience was like without being too overwhelming.  It's polished, pleasing to the eye, and supported by a good community.  Give it a shot!

Ridiculously addictive and fun to play. Its one failing is claiming that it's fun to lose - games *can* be fun to lose, specifically games with an incredible amount of variables and procedural elements allowing not only emergent gameplay but emergent catastrophe. Dwarf Fortress comes to mind as one such example. The problem with FTL is that it *doesn't* have that many variables. There are too few actions to take and too few ways to die to make it *funny*. In Dwarf Fortress, you might say such and such dwarf caught a fever, went mad and killed his cat, no one cleaned it up so the miasma from the corpse made all the other dwarves vomit and the last one ran out and got trampled by an elephant. This is fun, this is funny and you want to tell your friends. "Derp, just died from a hull breach again" is considerably less interesting.
Nonetheless a very entertaining game and well worth the price.

I have nothing to say other than this game is truly amazing - in terms of both atmosphere and the gameplay itself. Before I go into that in detail, though I shoud probably first discuss the issues. Firstly, Dead Space is certainly not a PC game but a (poor) console port. The controls may sometimes feel fiddly, and are somewhat disjointed in feel. There is no way on earth you are ever going to be able to play this game with a trackpad - regardless of which way you look at it. The controls to fire require that you have both mouse buttons pressed at once. Failure to do so will leave you aiming, but doing nothing, or simply performing melee actions. That's not to say that it doesn't feel sophisticated in its workings, but it certainly is restrictive to some users. Another point is that in-game menus are not controlled via mouse, and it feels simply ridiculous to navigate expansive menus with arrow keys when you can clearly see the button is RIGHT THERE.
Another issue to consider is that the game doesn't play particularly nice with newer hardware. Your choices are either to experience frequent screen tearing or to have severe control issues with the mouse - V-Sync off or on respectively. I do note that I said 'frequently' but it's really not so bad as it sounds (at least on my own setup) and generally doesn't happen at any key moments (in fact, I've never experienced tearing at any point where there was any action going on). There are ways around it written Steam Guides, but note that they seem pretty time-consuming to set up and thus far I've not seen a fix for anything other than AMD/ATI chips. It may be that NVidia cards don't have the issue, but it may also be that users of those cards pretty much have to like it or lump it. The final noticable technical issue is that it doesn't play particularly well with the Steam overlay (or application switching in general), and the system mouse cursor will be permanently visible during gameplay once you've switched back. Seriously, consider appearing offline and making sure you've no background process that'll pull you out - the inconsistency between the cursor speeds is just downright confusing and offputting.
So that's the technical downsides dealt with.
The game itself is nothing short of a joy (or not so) to play. Suspence is kept even in places where you're pretty convinced you're safe from harm, and throwing in the occassional threat in such an area leaves a certain feeling of uneasiness. Unexpected events also add to this feeling of suspense, leaving you with something incredibly atmospheric. There are some moments where you do lose this sort of feeling - but the feeling of panic is kept by the developer's amazing ability to predict when you're going to be low on resources - you've really got to be conservative where you can afford to be.
Having a futuristic setting really played to the developer's advantage: the mind-boggling zero-gravity areas of the game serve not only to confuse the hell out of you, but also to instill that little bit of extra fear as it makes tracking enemies incredibly difficult. Overall, the gameplay is incredibly fun, and you will likely not be disappointed in the respect. Particularly considering that new enemy types are introduced continuously, and new puzzles (yes, puzzles, both environment and enemy based), really make the game feel like there's something to work to all the time.
In terms of story everything seems to be well-considered: characters, backing, events timeline. Everything fits together quite nicely. Out of your characters you could say that they're pretty generic: the by-the-book commander gone desperate, the mistrusting female companion and yourself. That's a fault, by the way. You. Your character, Isaac, seems to have a bad case of Valve syndrome. You're one of three things: a sufferer of atrocious selective mutism, completely mute or so unbelievable uncooperative that it's just not funny. You won't even say a word about key events - it's just plain silly. That said, many games of the time seemed to have the same issue - so it'd be unfair to judge it based solely on that.
All in all, Dead Space is a unique experience that's particularly difficult to put into words that (graphically speaking) aged particularly well. I'd honestly say that it's well worth a go if you're into zombie shooters but want something other than 'the corpses got diseased!' or 'do I look like I care about a reason?' for a plot.

First of all, I never played the boardgame or the SNES game before I tried Shadowrun Returns. I guess this is important because some people say it doesn't have that old-school appeal. However, I can tell you this is an amazing game with great storytelling and some of the coolest atmospheres I've ever seen in a game. Basically it's noir fiction set in a cyberpunk multiracial world (elves, humans, dwarves, orks, trolls) where magic and technology are used everyday.
The gameplay is very flexible: in many missions you can choose a team and you can include hackers, drone masters, berserkers, spirit summoners... so if you want, you can go and shoot all the enemies with your team members, or you can send some drones and spirits to do the dirty job. The character progression is decent: everytime you accomplish an objective you win some points that you can use to upgrade your skills. In my gameplay I had an sniper shaman with a decent amount of healh points and some basic mage skills, so as you can see you can have any combination you want.
The main flaw is the checkpoint/save system: you can only save after you finish a mission (and it's an automatic save). In average, each of the missions can last from 20 to 40 minutes, so it can be pretty frustrating to die in the middle of a battle and have to repeat all over again. Apparently, this issue is going to be fixed by the developers with the release of the new campaign next year (2014). Also, you could find some minor bugs in the game. For example, I had to repeat a  battle because at end of it there was a conversation and suddenly it stopped and I couldn't advance to the next mission.
Finally, you have to take into account that the game has Steam Workshop support! There are some projects with new campaigns. For example, some people are trying to bring back the original Shadowrun SNES campaign. I haven't tried them yet because I'm waiting for the finished version. However, I believe the user-generated content will increase the value of the game in the medium/long term.

The graphics desperately cried out for an increased zoom - far too often I had problems making out what I was looking at because of my stories-high viewpoint. The story was surprisingly solid (at least until the last-level bug-hunt, which was a rather mundane dungeon-crawl) with some unexpected twists and decently capturing the feel of the cyberpunk genre. Alas, the game also featured and unfortunate - and unexpected - difficulty spike at end that made the final battles tedious grinds. Still, I suppose I must have enjoyed the game somewhat, as I did play it to the end. On the other hand, I feel no need to return or replay the game anytime soon; it is just too unpolished and lacking in content to pull me back into its shadows.

We huddle together search for that yellow light(please don't be red yet), and when we spot it, we unleash everything. Bullets, rockets, see of flames. My fellow's both died. I somehow managed to kill them. Or get away. My heart pounding, not knowing what is still alive what isn't, I run inside the building, spraying fire on everything that moves. Running low on ammo, so I go on a search for more. But all I find are more monsters.
A random message in the message window notifies me that my ENTIRE team is watching me play now. A quick look on the counter reveals I have yet 70 monsters to kill. Heart racing even faster, I keep running from room to room. Quick look behind me and I see a whole plethora of monsters behind me. The lack of a save feature is not the only thing this game is missing.
When I saw it on sale I knew it was time to get it.  I had heard that there was no concrete save feature and was prepared to deal with the autosaving from place to place.
What I didn't realize is that you cannot backtrack at all.  The story happens linearly and doesn't allow you to explore or make mistakes.  Everything is set and put into a "hallway" where you run through a series of events rather than a vast metropolis I'd expect of shadow run.
The noir side of things boils down to speed reading the dialogue.  Any character you like, or get attached to ultimately leaves  doesn't involve themselves past a point of the plot.  There is no option to hire mercenaries or additional team members for cash.  So your money sits when you aren't bribing plot points.
There is no variety of meele weapons outside of magic, guns, grenades and shaman summoning spells.  Needless to say as a meele street samurai I've got little more than a machette and a baseball bat going for me.
The main redeeming portion of this game are the portraits.  The banter itself is the usual filler from bioware or blizzard to fill space between plot hooks, but the portraits at least stand out and are pleasing.  Voice acting would not have saved the experience for me.
If you get it for under 10 bucks it's a lesson learned.

My opinion of the game in various prespectives:
I am running this game on GeForce 780, i7 and 12GB RAM. On launch, the game did have framerates issues especially with the bat-mobile. Over time it got better.
Nvidia's graphical features (such as the fog/smoke physics or rain physics) do not run smoothly on my 780. So set them off if you do not own a high-end 900 series card from nvidia. Not sure if AMD card can even activate these features.
Combat is the same but this time feels more solid and a bit challenging because of the variety of enemy types this time around. There are interesting sidequests where other characters will come to aid Batman and you get to play with them as well (catwoman, nightwing...). It does feel awesome to glide in the sky and dive into the batmobile.
However, what ruin all the fun is some of the Batmobile missions.
Story is exciting but also disappointing in some areas. Try to enjoy it without setting any high expectations. If you are playing it simply to reach the ending, you will get disappointed and ruin your whole experience.
Yes. This is still a must have for every batman fan.
Is it better than any previous Arkham game? It is a yes and no. Arkham Knight does take step forwards in some areas and at the same times it takes steps back in others. It does not prevent it from being a good game.
It is a good round-based game and everyone, who is playing the Total War Series too, will understand. Sometimes it has some kinds of bugs but all in all it is worth buying.

What can I say? It was the chosen one... it was said Knight would blow the other games away - not join the triple A shame crowd. Bring balanced DLC - not leave us with a bad taste of buyers remorse in our mouths. The most depressing part is that - shortly before Knight - there was another game called Shadows of Mordor that actually did a better job than Knight itself of living up to the feeling of the original Arkham games. So, where do you start in a situation like this? Well, the most obvious problem to start with would be the number of glitches and bugs and stability issues present in the PC version. Of course - to be fair - we shouldn't focus on those issues. Judging a game by ONE bad port is hardly fair.
So we will focus on the other issues that plague Arkham Knight - such as the story. First we have the number two to the main villain (Arkham Knight) and even if you don't know who he is (clue, yes you do) he comes off not so much as a villain - but as a pathetic crybaby. He was tortured - he hates Batman - this fact will be ground into your head within the first hour of the game. The problem with Knight is that (with the removal of Joker) the motivation he SHOULD have had for coming to Gotham is gone. So an ornate (and in some cases crappy) plot has to be contrived to explain his presence in Gotham and his willingness to work with Scarecrow. The rest of Batman's villains are okay - some of them even good - but none of them are ever really great. Not even villains like Penguin or Two-Face (both of whom made some of the most memorable contributions to AC and in Penguins case AO) are ever really anything more than good because you never really FIGHT them. They never SEEM like a threat because you've always got your tank or there's always a cutscene where Batman solves the problem for you.
Let's try and be honest here - when the majority of the best story moments happen when Batman is talking to Alfred, his pet teenager(s) or his new imaginary friend SOMETHING is wrong. In fact; some of the only real classic boss battles in the whole of the game can be experienced ONLY if you're willing to shell out some cash. And there we come to the next problem.
The DLC for this game.
Ignoring the fact that 'challenge mode' was locked behind a paywall, with features and characters that should have been in at launch. We instantly come up against the fact that the batmotank (with all it's iterations) is what you'll be stuck with for the majority of the game. Because Rocksteady couldn't be bothered to work weapons or features for the tank into all the other Batmobiles. And the MAJORITY of the game is what we're talking about here. Every few seconds you have to stop what you're doing or leave where you're fighting to go get the tank and do something in some other part of Gotham. Then you have to come back and - surprise surprise surprise - a bunch of TANKS have shown up while you were gone. Rinse and repeat as needed.
Tired of the tank yet? Tough♥♥♥♥♥♥- because now the Riddler wants a piece of you and he's decided the only way to bring your♥♥♥♥♥down is to challenge you and your batmotank to a perverted weird♥♥♥♥♥green version of Speed Racer that will leave you actively cursing your screen. Moving on past the mess that is the Batmobile and the DLC we come to the basic non-tank gameplay. The combat in this game is faster than its predecessors - and the number of enemies are through the roof. But - again - we come to a corner that Rocksteady cut. You'll be impressed with the NUMBER of foes... but not only do most of them look exactly the same - but they all FUNCTION the same.
Unlike City and Origins and even Asylum (to an extent) the enemies are always the same low-level goons you encounter at the beginning of the game. There are all these new types of enemies - all these new abilities they have - but unless you're playing a mission you won't encounter them. The streets are full of the same cardboard cutout thug and that is what you'll be facing seventy to eighty percent of the time when you aren't cruisin for chicks and suckin face in your batmotank. Worst of all - under all this steaming mess - you get the feeling throughout the game that this SHOULD be fun. You hear that kid in the back of your head saying how much fun this SHOULD be - and if you haven't played another Arkham game it's VERY likely you won't even notice the flaws (unless you're on the PC) until you're running around in your tank... again.

When Batman: Arkham Knight first released, I was hesitant after hearing so many problems being shared with the game that I didn't install the game for a long period of time. Come time to play, I only experienced minor lagging and after a few updates there were no more issues in the performance department. Nevertheless, the wait was worth it! Batman: Arkham Knight has everything you could have asked for with the colossal and dark Gotham City. The Batmobile is integral to the majority of the game but I'd say it struck the balance between gliding and driving just right (besides, those combat sequences in Battle Mode are a lot of fun and break up travel, and never unnecessarily). The Gotham City Police Department is the Batman's rock in this game where Commissioner James Gordon's character steps into the spotlight the most out of the rest of his appearances in the series. Nods to the previous titles involving certain villains are made and some new faces will come as a surprise. The beginning is eerie and the graphics throughout the game are the best I've seen in a superhero game. Batman: Arkham Knight dwells on the the theme of fear and shows us that fear in many ways isn't a weakness at all. It's the only thing that keeps us wary, not weary. In being aware, we're not really afraid at all, not even of who we are and what we've come to be. If you've heard rage about this game, don't worry; most of that is from people who severely underestimated the cost of video games development.  A $2 million Kickstarter campaign (which worked out to about $1.2 mil after Amazon and Kickstarter's cuts, which then also had to cover the physical rewards for the backers as well as the game) doesn't mean AAA quality - it means a shoestring budget.  Keep that in mind, and this is a fantastic game and a worthy addition to the Shadowrun universe.
Set in the dystopian, cyberpunk future of 2050, in a world where magic and the races of fantasy have returned.  Unlike the last two good Shadowrun games (the FPS should only be considered a Shadowrun game in the context of how NOT to make a Shadowrun game) back on the SNES and Genesis, Returns hews more closely to the turn-based nature and feel of the original pen-and-paper game.  It doesn't exactly port over the ruleset - merely uses a whole new one inspired by the rulesets used by the PnP game's 2nd and 3rd editions.  It's a classless system, meaning you can spend your Karma (what the game calls XP) on whatever aspect of your character you want.  Think your AK-97-totting ork needs some skill with a blade for when the enemy gets up-close and personal?  No problem - just drop the Karma into the relevant stat when you have the chance.  What if you feel your chi-wielding Physical Adept needs a bit of extra ranged oomph but you don't want to spend the money on guns?  Sink some Karma into spellcasting and you can add some fireballs and lightning bolts to the mix.
The game does provide a set of Archetypes to pick from during character creation, each one fitting one of six roles in the SR universe - the Street Samurai, who follows a code of honour but mostly focuses on combat and augmenting himself with a lot of cyberware; the Mage, who lashes out with powerful spells; the Decker, who uses his cyberdeck to hack into the Matrix (the internet's successor... no, no relation to the films; Shadowrun was using the term way back in the late '80s); the Shaman, who manipulates the energies of the natural world to aid his companions as well as calling up spirits to fight alongside them; the Rigger, who remote-controls a series of combat drones and the Physical Adept, who focuses his magic inward and make strikes with his fists or a blade more devastating.
The Archetypes spend most of your starting Karma for you and (in the included campaign, Dead Man's Switch) set your starting gear.  If you want to spend all that starting Karma yourself, be prepared to start the game with a few guns (I think a pistol, an SMG and an assault rifle) and no spells/drones/cyberdeck/etc.  In addition to the archetypes, you also have five races, or metatypes as the game calls them, to choose from.  In the 2050s, humanity is now metahumanity and consists of humans, elves, dwarves, orks and trolls.
Most of them are pretty much what you'd expect - elves are agile and smart, dwarves and tough and stubborn, orks can snap you in two like a dry twig, etc.  Trolls, though, can basically be seen as orks on steroids (an analogy that doesn't quite work as well when there could literally be orks taking steroids) - they're even bigger, even stronger and have bony growths on their skin that act like armour.  Each metatype's drawback is limits on how high certain stats can go - most can raise them to about 10 or 11, but trolls, for example, can't raise their Charisma above six.
The combat has something of an XCOM feel to it, save that you can't rotate the camera.  HBS took some of the elements from XCOM Enemy Unknown that worked - the assumption that your team brought more than enough ammo for the job (infinite ammo, but needing to reload) and the high-low-cover system (though flanking doesn't give a bonus to critical hits, just makes them easier to hit).
I'll get the negatives out of the way now - at the time I'm writing this, there is no manual save feature.  It only auto-saves on loading screens and there will be times when those are spaced far enough apart to be a pain.  Good news on this front - they're working on a manual save system that should be done at the same time as the first expansion, Dragonfall, but will be applied to the base game and campaign without you having to buy that.  That won't be til about January, though.  Secondly, the included campaign is rather short - tops out at about 12 hours or thereabouts and is rather linear.  Don't go into it expecting the freedom most other RPGs have; Dead Man's Switch is a very story-driven campaign and the events in it only cover a few days.  This next one I don't see as a problem, but there were a lot of people raging about it on the Steam forums after launch - the game has zero voice acting.  They couldn't afford it.  Yes, sadly; this means that you will have to read.  But for the added freedom this gave them in NPC dialogue, I have no problem with that.  There is also very little to actually interact with in the environments (or at least in Dead Man's Switch, this may not be the case in Dragonfall or some user-generated content) so they can feel rather empty at times.
The graphics have an interesting, stylised look to them.  It was a big jarring for me at first (I'd binged a bit on the various 4th edition books during the Kickstarter campaign where most of the art's a bit more realistic) but eventually I came to enjoy it.  The character models aren't exactly high-grade, but the camera never really gets close enough for it to be annoying.  You'll be getting a better feel for a character's look from their portrait.  The overall character designs fit the SR universe, though; Detective McKluskly is a good example of this - they've taken an almost stereotypical design of a corrupt detective and turned him into an ork and it works.  Even with the lower-quality of the character models, they still found ways to add little details to them.  Jump over to Google and do a quick image search with "Shadowrun Returns McKlusky" and find an image of his character model.  You might notice a tattoo on one forearm.  It's never mentioned anywhere in the game, but that's a tattoo from the UCAS Marines - he's ex-military.
This game does come with a full editor that is, relatively, user-friendly.  I say 'relatively' because any editor that involves more than placing terrain and hostile NPCs is going to be complex, no matter how you slice it.  But the coding side of this one is a lot simpler than any other I've seen - using If/Else statements and the like.  It takes some getting used to, but there are tutorials for it on the HBS youtube channel and there's bound to be plenty of fan-made tutorials out there by now.  Most of this game's life will come from the campaigns published on the Workshop, but like any game driven by fan-made content (ARMA, Elder Scrolls, even ol' Neverwinter Nights) it will be at least a year before that side of the game comes into its own.
I'd say more about Dead Man's Switch itself, but most of the negatives I feel players could be warned about (or at least worth mentioning here) come with some serious spoilers.  These aren't massive ones, really just mention on why one NPC isn't as tough as the PnP game's books suggested.  What I will say is that it has some phenomenal writing that pulls you into the setting.  There are perhaps some things mentioned that may not mean anything to someone new to the setting, but HBS has a Shadowrun Primer on their website for free download that should help in that respect.  Regardless, they made great use of Shadowrun's iconic slang and the various setting elements (although that does mean anyone familiar with the setting may know what's coming once you start having to deal with the Universal Brotherhood).

If you hate South Park, don't play this game. That should be a no-brainer, because if the show's brand of abrasive, offensive humor isn't to your taste, you'll find that same humor turned up to the max in The Stick of Truth. There are jokes that will make some uncomfortable or worse, though if you're the type of person who doesn't care for that style of humor, you probably already know that a South Park game isn't for you.
On the other hand, fans of the show and those who sit somewhere in the middle (like myself) will find an engaging turn-based RPG with nothing-is-sacred writing and scenarios that will both disgust and amuse. The level of care spent in capturing as many in-jokes as possible, both for South Park fans and for long-time gamers, is staggering. Every one of the many objects in the game has unique (and often hilarious) text to describe it, and all manner of gaming tropes are brought into the spotlight and then bludgeoned for comedic effect. The world design is hilarious and creative and puts the whole of South Park (and its surrounding environs) at your feet. There's more to talk about than I ever could in the space of one review, but suffice it to say this is absolutely the definitive South Park game and one of Obsidian's best games in years.
The story finds you, the New Kid (or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, as you'll be quickly named for voice-acting's sake), as the freshest face in the mad Colorado town of South Park. In a matter of minutes, you'll be swept up into a clash between the "humans" and "elves" over the legendary Stick of Truth, which grants its owner the ability to control space and time. Over the course of the 10 to 15-hour storyline, you'll switch alliances, witness (and perpetrate) betrayals, and fight aliens, Nazis, hobos, dogs, rats, and still stranger creatures as you quest after the Stick.
There's a kind of glee in the double world at play here. The game is absolutely South Park in its humor and delivery, but it's also an incredible display of the childlike wonder and drama we all once found in playacting. The children's fantasy world Zaron and its war over the titular Stick bleeds into the real South Park's "actual" danger, and what the player is left with is a bizarre meta-narrative in which kids hitting each other with plastic swords are also murdering Nazi zombies and blowing up houses with "magic." It's hard to articulate, but it's wholly compelling and always pushes you forward. The pacing of the game is utterly fantastic, with new and insane things happening constantly, making a strong argument for the game's relative brevity being a positive rather than, as certain sectors of the Internet have decided, a negative. Additionally, unlike many similar games, this is an adventure that picks up steam as it goes along, rather than petering off. The final day of the storyline is packed so full of insanity and hilarious betrayals (and a trip to Terrance and Phillip's homeland of Canada) that I found myself laughing almost the entire time.
The presentation is dead-on. The game looks and sounds like the show, which is to say that it's not exactly pushing any technical limits, but it's one hundred percent successful in doing what it sets out to do. The music satirically apes recent big-fantasy scores and even offers a few catchy tunes. More importantly, the requisite Latin chanting and choir vocals are replaced by Cartman's voice making up his own words, which sound like something along the lines of "jews, sanctus," in a fashion that is both funny and demonstrates that there's a real understanding of the kinds of tropes we accept as fans of high fantasy.
Attacks and enemies in the turn-based combat are consistently hilarious, and, most importantly, fun to wrestle with. Each of the game's character classes offers a unique set of skills, and the various party members whose aid you'll enlist have unique dialogue for combat situations and story beats, so there's definitely some replayability here. You might skew towards your favorite character in the show, as I did — perpetual victim Butters Stotch is irresistible to me as a paladin who gives his friends a comforting pat on the back for his special healing skill. The game also makes use of a number of different traversal powers during exploration, both your own and those of your buddies. This adds a lot of incentive to send you back to earlier areas or scour the far reaches of the town looking for colored cracks, alien satellites, or hurt friends in need of a little pick-me-up, since following up on these leads usually results in a side quest, secret weapon, or some otherwise hilarious exchange of dialogue.
Unfortunately, while the role-playing elements, which include lots of exploring, talking, side-questing, and secrets to uncover (along with tons of in-jokes, jabs, and references), are great, the game becomes a bit too easy a bit too quickly. Even on the hard difficulty, I was killed only once in the game, and by the end I was laying waste to bosses in a matter of two or three turns with my explosive firework attack. Additionally, I did experience one game-breaking (but amusing) bug in which Cartman lowered his pants to light a fart on fire and the game stopped responding. There I sat, Cartman's♥♥♥♥♥hanging out in the enemy's direction, for about thirty seconds until realizing that the game had locked up while still animating and playing music.
South Park isn't a world I'm especially in love with. The creators are adamant that they do not set out specifically with a point of view to push on viewers , but rather aim to take nothing as sacred and spear anything with comedic potential. As a result, there are jokes in the game that even I found occasionally a bit much; likely by design. And yet I was completely engrossed in The Stick of Truth. I had a blast from start to finish, with not only the humor, but also the Mario & Luigi-style combat, the dense world, and the varied story line scenarios. If you're at all open to the idea of Trey Parker and Matt Stone's world, Obsidian has given you the best vehicle yet to go on down to South Park.
