A huge disappointment.  I was really looking forward to this game since it showed up on Kickstarter.  Fallout 1 & 2 are among my favorite games ever, and this was touted as a return to that style of RPG.  It...isn't.
I find the combat enjoyable.  It's basically a simplified version of XCOM:  Enemy Unknown.  One problem with it is that once combat starts, it doesn't end until you move to another map, even if there are no enemies around.  So after a fight ends, you'll have to move your party through the map in turn-based mode until you get to an exit.
The story is good by video game standards.  You receive a recorded message from an old friend who's been murdered and are tasked with tracking down his killer.  For the most part, dialogue is well-written.  There's no voice acting, which some may take issue with, but it allows for more robust dialogue.  Unfortunately, this game doesn't take advantage of that benefit.
The game is extraordinarily linear.  There's exactly one path through the story.  A handful of situations where you may be able to get from point A to point B by a slightly different route exist (i.e., bluff your way past a guard vs. hacking through an unguarded door), but these are so few and so insignificant that they don't make any real difference overall.  Dialogue is pretty much the same no matter what:  Ask about story-related stuff, ask about general backround/setting information.  Very little opportunity to employ your character's personality.
Sidequests are almost nonexistent, and the few that the game does have are simple "go over there and get me that thing," or "while you're on this run, see if you can find a thing I want" sorts of things.
The whole game is designed entirely around mobile devices and it suffers for it.  The UI is a bit clunky and unintuitive for PC, limited to what would work on a touch-based interface.  The save system is simply unacceptable.  The game has no manual save option.  Not even a save and quit function.  It's entirely based on reaching checkpoints.  This is supposed to be fixed with the DLC scheduled for January 2014, but until then, if you screw up a fight at the end of a mission?  You're replaying the whole mission.  Have to leave before you finish a mission?  You're replaying the whole mission.  As I understand it, this is because the game cannot save the current map state, which explains some of the linearity.  When you return to a location, you're actually loading a completely different map of the location with its own triggers, different versions of NPCs with dialogue appropriate to that point in the story, etc.  This means that the player can't affect any change in the game as every change or combination of changes to a location would require its own unique map, and I'm not even sure if the game is able to load different versions of the same map based on variables.
I can't really speak to the user-generated content as I haven't used the editor or played any user-made campaigns yet, but from what I've heard from those who have, the editor is very, very limited in what it can do.  As a result, a lot of people who were planning on making content for the game have given up.
Maybe the upcoming DLC will improve the editor, maybe (probably) it won't.  Either way, I wouldn't suggest paying more than about $5 for Shadowrun Returns.

What can I say? It was the chosen one... it was said Knight would blow the other games away - not join the triple A shame crowd. Bring balanced DLC - not leave us with a bad taste of buyers remorse in our mouths. The most depressing part is that - shortly before Knight - there was another game called Shadows of Mordor that actually did a better job than Knight itself of living up to the feeling of the original Arkham games. So, where do you start in a situation like this? Well, the most obvious problem to start with would be the number of glitches and bugs and stability issues present in the PC version. Of course - to be fair - we shouldn't focus on those issues. Judging a game by ONE bad port is hardly fair.
So we will focus on the other issues that plague Arkham Knight - such as the story. First we have the number two to the main villain (Arkham Knight) and even if you don't know who he is (clue, yes you do) he comes off not so much as a villain - but as a pathetic crybaby. He was tortured - he hates Batman - this fact will be ground into your head within the first hour of the game. The problem with Knight is that (with the removal of Joker) the motivation he SHOULD have had for coming to Gotham is gone. So an ornate (and in some cases crappy) plot has to be contrived to explain his presence in Gotham and his willingness to work with Scarecrow. The rest of Batman's villains are okay - some of them even good - but none of them are ever really great. Not even villains like Penguin or Two-Face (both of whom made some of the most memorable contributions to AC and in Penguins case AO) are ever really anything more than good because you never really FIGHT them. They never SEEM like a threat because you've always got your tank or there's always a cutscene where Batman solves the problem for you.
Let's try and be honest here - when the majority of the best story moments happen when Batman is talking to Alfred, his pet teenager(s) or his new imaginary friend SOMETHING is wrong. In fact; some of the only real classic boss battles in the whole of the game can be experienced ONLY if you're willing to shell out some cash. And there we come to the next problem.
The DLC for this game.
Ignoring the fact that 'challenge mode' was locked behind a paywall, with features and characters that should have been in at launch. We instantly come up against the fact that the batmotank (with all it's iterations) is what you'll be stuck with for the majority of the game. Because Rocksteady couldn't be bothered to work weapons or features for the tank into all the other Batmobiles. And the MAJORITY of the game is what we're talking about here. Every few seconds you have to stop what you're doing or leave where you're fighting to go get the tank and do something in some other part of Gotham. Then you have to come back and - surprise surprise surprise - a bunch of TANKS have shown up while you were gone. Rinse and repeat as needed.
Tired of the tank yet? Tough♥♥♥♥♥♥- because now the Riddler wants a piece of you and he's decided the only way to bring your♥♥♥♥♥down is to challenge you and your batmotank to a perverted weird♥♥♥♥♥green version of Speed Racer that will leave you actively cursing your screen. Moving on past the mess that is the Batmobile and the DLC we come to the basic non-tank gameplay. The combat in this game is faster than its predecessors - and the number of enemies are through the roof. But - again - we come to a corner that Rocksteady cut. You'll be impressed with the NUMBER of foes... but not only do most of them look exactly the same - but they all FUNCTION the same.
Unlike City and Origins and even Asylum (to an extent) the enemies are always the same low-level goons you encounter at the beginning of the game. There are all these new types of enemies - all these new abilities they have - but unless you're playing a mission you won't encounter them. The streets are full of the same cardboard cutout thug and that is what you'll be facing seventy to eighty percent of the time when you aren't cruisin for chicks and suckin face in your batmotank. Worst of all - under all this steaming mess - you get the feeling throughout the game that this SHOULD be fun. You hear that kid in the back of your head saying how much fun this SHOULD be - and if you haven't played another Arkham game it's VERY likely you won't even notice the flaws (unless you're on the PC) until you're running around in your tank... again.

When Batman: Arkham Knight first released, I was hesitant after hearing so many problems being shared with the game that I didn't install the game for a long period of time. Come time to play, I only experienced minor lagging and after a few updates there were no more issues in the performance department. Nevertheless, the wait was worth it! Batman: Arkham Knight has everything you could have asked for with the colossal and dark Gotham City. The Batmobile is integral to the majority of the game but I'd say it struck the balance between gliding and driving just right (besides, those combat sequences in Battle Mode are a lot of fun and break up travel, and never unnecessarily). The Gotham City Police Department is the Batman's rock in this game where Commissioner James Gordon's character steps into the spotlight the most out of the rest of his appearances in the series. Nods to the previous titles involving certain villains are made and some new faces will come as a surprise. The beginning is eerie and the graphics throughout the game are the best I've seen in a superhero game. Batman: Arkham Knight dwells on the the theme of fear and shows us that fear in many ways isn't a weakness at all. It's the only thing that keeps us wary, not weary. In being aware, we're not really afraid at all, not even of who we are and what we've come to be. Batman: Arkham Knight may not be the best superhero game but there's no reason not to settle for being one of the greatest in a series of great superhero games.

I'm not a big gamer, but when I watched PewDiePie play this before its release, I laughed so hard and I just wanted to play so bad. I was worried it would be way too hard with too many complicated controls. However, that's not the case. This game is actually really smooth and fun to play. GRAPHICS:  The difference between the 3D character models and the 2D backdrops and portraits really couldn't be greater.  The backgrounds of this game really help set the ambiance, being very dreary, weathered, and overall unpleasant.  The game occasionally contrasts this with very nice areas, but only to emphasize the feel of how dirty and unkempt the rest of the game world is.  All the praise and honors I give the 2D artists I would take from the 3D designers.  The characters are incredibly low-poly.  Think somewhere around Goldeneye for the Nintendo 64.  There definitely could have been improvements in the quality of the models.  That being said, you walk into this game knowing it isn't exactly Crysis.  The game's focus is in getting you into the story.  And it does that exceedingly well.
REVIEW:
Overall, I am having a lot of fun playing this.  The game has a really good story and a fantastic environment that really holds itself together, even with new plot points and characters introducing themselves.  It's very reminiscent of Deus Ex in it's view of the not-quite-near future, and I found myself wandering all around the game, talking to the people because I wanted to, not because I had to.  Conversations options are plentiful, not just a "Yes, I will do the mission" or "Not now".  You can be an♥♥♥♥♥to people, or you can kiss it.  Conversation options unlock if you have a certain amount of skill points in that specific area, much like the Fallout series.  If you are able to say the unlocked option, it usually helps you out with better prices or more specific information.
One of my favorite aspects of the game was the fact that not all of the game was accessible because of the class I chose.  I am a hacker class, but I poured too many stat-points into combat.  This locked me out of rooms I could have gained access to if I had more hacking skill.  It enhances replayability by quite a bit.  Another element was the different fighting styles and the enhancements you can unlock.  The game seems designed to cater to specializing in one or two unique skill paths, or else you don't really get many fun abilities in combat and conversation.  This is not a bad thing by any means, but there is that feeling of regret when you see a skill you really want in a skill tree you haven't invested in.
The combat is tile and turn-based.  It found quite a bit like the new X-COM combat, but without permadeath, and more weapon options.  It also resembles Fallout combat in some ways.
I have always found point-and-click games tedious and fetch-questy.  Many of these games say to the developer "Hey, we have a game that you could reasonably complete in a couple hours.  Milk three more hours out of it." Shadowrun Returns respects the player's time.  I never noticed myself retracing my steps or stopping playing because I didn't want to "go all the way back there" in-game. It's much more movie-esque, where the next big scene/event is at the destination, not right where you are after you collect the three Orbs of Annoyance and Plot Forgetting from three obnoxiously far-apart places in game.  I'd really recommend this game, and for people who really enjoy a good story, you can't miss it.
Personally I enjoy taking my time and soaking in the game.  The story is great, and I really enjoy the conversations as well as combat.  This may not be your cup of tea, though.  If you power through the game, you'll miss all the good stuff and find it lacking polish.  But the fun of this game does not give itself away, you have to lose yourself in it to find it.
For me, 9/10.

If you hate South Park, don't play this game. That should be a no-brainer, because if the show's brand of abrasive, offensive humor isn't to your taste, you'll find that same humor turned up to the max in The Stick of Truth. There are jokes that will make some uncomfortable or worse, though if you're the type of person who doesn't care for that style of humor, you probably already know that a South Park game isn't for you.
On the other hand, fans of the show and those who sit somewhere in the middle (like myself) will find an engaging turn-based RPG with nothing-is-sacred writing and scenarios that will both disgust and amuse. The level of care spent in capturing as many in-jokes as possible, both for South Park fans and for long-time gamers, is staggering. Every one of the many objects in the game has unique (and often hilarious) text to describe it, and all manner of gaming tropes are brought into the spotlight and then bludgeoned for comedic effect. The world design is hilarious and creative and puts the whole of South Park (and its surrounding environs) at your feet. There's more to talk about than I ever could in the space of one review, but suffice it to say this is absolutely the definitive South Park game and one of Obsidian's best games in years.
The story finds you, the New Kid (or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, as you'll be quickly named for voice-acting's sake), as the freshest face in the mad Colorado town of South Park. In a matter of minutes, you'll be swept up into a clash between the "humans" and "elves" over the legendary Stick of Truth, which grants its owner the ability to control space and time. Over the course of the 10 to 15-hour storyline, you'll switch alliances, witness (and perpetrate) betrayals, and fight aliens, Nazis, hobos, dogs, rats, and still stranger creatures as you quest after the Stick.
There's a kind of glee in the double world at play here. The game is absolutely South Park in its humor and delivery, but it's also an incredible display of the childlike wonder and drama we all once found in playacting. The children's fantasy world Zaron and its war over the titular Stick bleeds into the real South Park's "actual" danger, and what the player is left with is a bizarre meta-narrative in which kids hitting each other with plastic swords are also murdering Nazi zombies and blowing up houses with "magic." It's hard to articulate, but it's wholly compelling and always pushes you forward. The pacing of the game is utterly fantastic, with new and insane things happening constantly, making a strong argument for the game's relative brevity being a positive rather than, as certain sectors of the Internet have decided, a negative. Additionally, unlike many similar games, this is an adventure that picks up steam as it goes along, rather than petering off. The final day of the storyline is packed so full of insanity and hilarious betrayals (and a trip to Terrance and Phillip's homeland of Canada) that I found myself laughing almost the entire time.
The presentation is dead-on. The game looks and sounds like the show, which is to say that it's not exactly pushing any technical limits, but it's one hundred percent successful in doing what it sets out to do. The music satirically apes recent big-fantasy scores and even offers a few catchy tunes. More importantly, the requisite Latin chanting and choir vocals are replaced by Cartman's voice making up his own words, which sound like something along the lines of "jews, sanctus," in a fashion that is both funny and demonstrates that there's a real understanding of the kinds of tropes we accept as fans of high fantasy.
Attacks and enemies in the turn-based combat are consistently hilarious, and, most importantly, fun to wrestle with. Each of the game's character classes offers a unique set of skills, and the various party members whose aid you'll enlist have unique dialogue for combat situations and story beats, so there's definitely some replayability here. You might skew towards your favorite character in the show, as I did — perpetual victim Butters Stotch is irresistible to me as a paladin who gives his friends a comforting pat on the back for his special healing skill. The game also makes use of a number of different traversal powers during exploration, both your own and those of your buddies. This adds a lot of incentive to send you back to earlier areas or scour the far reaches of the town looking for colored cracks, alien satellites, or hurt friends in need of a little pick-me-up, since following up on these leads usually results in a side quest, secret weapon, or some otherwise hilarious exchange of dialogue.
Unfortunately, while the role-playing elements, which include lots of exploring, talking, side-questing, and secrets to uncover (along with tons of in-jokes, jabs, and references), are great, the game becomes a bit too easy a bit too quickly. Even on the hard difficulty, I was killed only once in the game, and by the end I was laying waste to bosses in a matter of two or three turns with my explosive firework attack. Additionally, I did experience one game-breaking (but amusing) bug in which Cartman lowered his pants to light a fart on fire and the game stopped responding. There I sat, Cartman's♥♥♥♥♥hanging out in the enemy's direction, for about thirty seconds until realizing that the game had locked up while still animating and playing music.
South Park isn't a world I'm especially in love with. The creators are adamant that they do not set out specifically with a point of view to push on viewers , but rather aim to take nothing as sacred and spear anything with comedic potential. As a result, there are jokes in the game that even I found occasionally a bit much; likely by design. And yet I was completely engrossed in The Stick of Truth. I had a blast from start to finish, with not only the humor, but also the Mario & Luigi-style combat, the dense world, and the varied story line scenarios. If you're at all open to the idea of Trey Parker and Matt Stone's world, Obsidian has given you the best vehicle yet to go on down to South Park.

Risk of Rain comforts me in a way that one wouldn’t expect from a perma-death/rogue-like experience.  The more I die (and believe me, you will do a lot of that in this game), the more compelled I become to push on and dig deeper into this indie gem.  On its surface, Risk of Rain may seem simple enough.  You start out as a Commando Class character; shipwrecked on a deadly planet, which you in turn need to briefly explore to find a portal that forces you to fight a boss once activated so that you can then leave the current geographical region for another one, and repeat ad infinitum (ok, maybe not forever, but you get the point).
There are a number of readily available and unlockable items that you can pick up along the way, either as drops from boss enemies, or by using cash monies dropped by lesser enemies on chests and shrines interspersed throughout the game’s varied environments.  Each location has a unique look and feel, accompanied by music that not only works well for said environment, but in my opinion is incredible for this type of game – much more catchy and compelling than I would have expected from a relatively cheap (only $10 regularly) indie title (seriously, I want the soundtrack!!).  There are a decent number of enemies to contend with and each character class (there are multiple to  choose from as they are unlocked, something like 10 classes) has its own unique set of weaponry and special abilities that may prove more or less beneficial for certain enemy types, adding for a great amount of replay value.  I mentioned ‘unlockable’ earlier for some of the items.
These are items that won’t become available in game, either as a regular drop or for purchase, until you successfully complete one of Risk of Rain’s ‘in-game’ achievements (think Borderlands to get a better understanding of what I mean).  You can confirm what these are and how to unlock them by looking them up in the title menu’s varying selections, one of which relates to items and unlockables, etc. Sure, there are Steam achievements as well, and some will even result in a special item unlocking for in game use, but this further adds to replay value.
If none of these features compels you to download a copy of this game for yourself or a friend, then perhaps the fact that the player characters are amongst the smallest ever in a game will (for reals, they’re like 6-12 pixels in size….yeah, I may be over exaggerating just a tad but they are still freakishly small, which is awesome though I know not why that is).
Do yourself a favor, pick up a copy of this game right now while it’s on sale and don’t forget to bring an umbrella. Lame joke, I know, but I have no idea what the hell the title means…..and I don’t care!

Shadowrun Returns was an astoundingly addictive game. As a long time of fan of tabletop RPGs this game provides all that traditional character customization that I desire in a game. Each race has an area where it will excel as a focus. By investing in skills you can open new dialogue options and earn extra rewards. You won’t always know what you are about to get into when you enter a new area. There are normally several ways to solve any particular problem. As a result, building a well balanced team is imperative to completing missions.
Players of games like XCOM: Enemy Unknown and other grid based tactics games will feel right at home during combat. Combat requires you to think carefully about your moves and one wrong click can get a character killed. However, the game is somewhat more forgiving as you can revive any fallen character in the middle of battle as long as you have the right item. Combat can be problematic at times because the chance of hit seems to have some hidden values that you aren’t told about. I have missed way too many 80% hit chances for that to be the correct number. The world design and art style are high quality for the price of the game and the music is great to listen to.
There were only three major problems I had with the game. First the save game system in the main campaign is unpleasant at time. The game will auto save every time you enter an area. The problem is that there are certain levels where you have to do a 2-5 minute dialogue conversation before you enter combat. If you’re main character dies in combat you have to start the entire area over again. That includes the dialogue segment. This game needs to have a way to quick save before you go into combat so you don’t have to do the same dialogue segment multiple times.
Second, in some of the combat segments I ran into problems where an enemy would be behind some piece of terrain. Even though I could make a shot I had to hunt for the few pixels where the enemy was visible in order to select them for an attack. I would love it if there was a drop down menu of enemies that you could use target attacks.
Third, it was very frustrating that you could control your teammates outside of combat for two reasons. First you couldn’t take any items that you find on a mission (outside of combat) and give then two your teammates. As a result, I had lots of health packs I wanted to give to teammates but had to send to stashed instead. Second the player controlled characters is the one responsible for opening doors and will be the one blasted when an ambush is triggered. I want to order my companion street samurai to open the door for me.
The main campaign will probably take between 12-16 hours. There is also an active steam community producing additional campaigns. I strongly recommend Shadowrun Returns to anyone who enjoys an RPG with some heavy strategy elements.
EDIT 3/8/2014:
After Finishing Dragonfall on hard mode, I am happy to say that the developers have fixed the few reservations I had about the base game. First and foremost: they have finally implemented a save game system. In the base game I became majorly frustrated with the way the fact that if you lost is a battle you would have to restart the area from the beginning, including any dialogue segments. The ability to save at will (outside of battle) is a major improvement from the base game. (Though I do have some concerns about the ethics of making such a game necessary feature DLC.)
Story wise, Dragonfall is an all new full length campaign. It is in fact longer than the base game. I beat base game story in about 14 hours, Dragonfall took about 20. I was a little disappointed that you couldn’t import your old character at first, but after a few hours I realized that rolling up a new character made the story feel like it can stand on its own. The campaign itself feels very reminiscent of the story of Dragon Age: Origins. After the initial two missions, the world opens up to you and you have much more choice in what order you want to do the quests in.
I only have a few reservations about Dragonfall. First, while playing on hard mode I found the AI’s strategy was to through everything against your character and completely ignore your squad mates. I suppose this comes down to personal preference but I for me this seems like a pretty week strategy, though it certainly does make the game more challenging. In addition, points two and three is original review are still problems.

This is a game for people who are already familiar with Shadowrun. When you have some reference you're more likely to forgive what you are filling in of the gameworld yourself, because this game has some emptiness to it.
It has some fun writing, it's descriptive and written well enough. It's used well in conjunction with its general aesthetic to describe the environments and people you deal with.
Its interface is clunky, but useable. It was very clearly designed with an handheld-sized touchscreen in mind, which means it's very unstreamlined and doesn't display as much information as it could on a single screen.
The skills and abilities feel extraneous, and while not poorly designed they are certainly not designed well within the restrictions of the levels and gameplay. Or perhaps the levels are not designed well around the skills of a Shadowrun skillset.
I think it's a really nice looking game.
Combat plays out like an XCOM-lite, but it's not nearly so strategic; you will tend to stand/crouch somewhere and shoot, moving around isn't really necessary to win.
The items and item progression don't seem very well integrated into the game. Weapons and armor and such don't have a lot of (or interesting) upgrade paths, so it's not really exciting or anything to level up. The combat is simple enough that you don't really gain too much of an edge if you do, anyway.
It does have some nice multiple paths to accomplish goals, whether through conversations or through the environment, which is nice.
You will never sit back after playing a piece of this game and think, 'Yeah, that was amazing,' but you'll have some decent fun out of the whole thing.
There aren't very many new or interesting mods out their either, if you're thinking of that. They're mostly very...amateur, in a perjorative sense.

You may notice at the top of the page that the Overall Reviews are Mixed but the recent reviews are Overwhelminhly Positive. At first, I thought this was a joke the internet was playing, like how the Cory in the House DS game has a 9.5 user score on Metacritic, but then I read some of the reviews and some forum posts and saw that people are saying the game is playable now. So, I picked this game up cheap (the game's reputation has lowered its price on third party stores) and I played it. Let me tell you, it was definitely worth it.
Is the game playable? Yes. Is it well optimized now? Oh God no. There was a lot of stuttering when I first loaded up the game, or when I go to new areas in the open world. But, I'm a patient man so I was able to deal with it. It should be noted that I have a 4 year old card so some of the higher end GPUs will probably have better performances. Other than that, the only other bugs I encountered were small texture bugs. I never experienced any game breaking bugs.
Now on to the actual game. How is it? Well, my recommendation should tell you that I very much enjoyed the game. I think it's the best in the series (which is not an opinion shared by many). I felt the story was extremely well done. I don't want to spoil anything, but I will say that the other Arkham games were really focused on the plot and the supervillians that Batman goes up against, but this game really explores Batman himself as a character. Again, some people were a bit disappointed by the story, especially with the reveal of the Arkham Knight, but I was fine with it. I was never a die-hard Batman comic book fan so I don't share the same point of view as those people.
The gameplay is where the game really shines. I loved everything about it. Even the Batmobile. I had a lot of fun driving around Gotham. At first, the driving controls felt really wonky, but once I got used to it, it felt really great. Now the tank mode. A lot of people hated it, but I found it very enjoyable. You can probably notice a trend here...
How about the ground combat? They improved nearly everything from AC. No longer can you "spam Y to win". They have added many new enemies into the game, such as electricty covered enemies and medics, that require you to change up your tactics. There is also a "Fear Takedown" ability that allows you to take out multiple enemies in one go without the enemy being able to react, which helps makes Predator Mode faster and more enjoyable. Finally, when travelling around the city, it is mostly unchanged, but they did buff the grapple boost since the city is MUCH bigger this time around.
This game is a great conclusion to the trilogy. The story is very well done (but the ending was a bit weak), the presentation is godly (well, when everything is working properly), the gameplay is the best it has ever been, and the music OH THE MUSIC. The PC version is playable now and you can get it for cheap during a Steam Sale or on a third party site. If you are a fan of the Arkham series, you should get this game. If you are new, play AC first, then come to this.

If you are a fan of the X-com series, you should strongly consider getting X-com: Enemy Unknown, the latest incarnation of the classic game. I would consider it a spiritual successor, rather than a reboot of the original, since it is not X-com: UFO defense with new graphics; rather it strives to keep the flavor and style of the original game with new gameplay style.
The geoscape and research sections of the game are, IMO, much improved over the original. This includes greater options on buildings for your base, which open up different improvements and stategies for your X-com Soldiers and teams. The game also provides incentives and reasons to research fallen alien soldiers, as they provide materials and information that is directly useful.
The battles and combat are where the game deviates from the original. It is still a turn based strategy game, but instead of time units your soldiers get a certain number of moves and actions that are measured by the game. This means you spend far less time micromanaging every single action that all of your soldiers can take, but on the downside, you cannot always get your soldiers to do exactly what you might want them to do. Your soldiers also have classes which are assigned (seemingly randomly) as they level up, which gives them different abilities and make the soldiers distinct from each other. It also makes your veterans much more powerful and valuable, if you are using them correctly. The game features a greater variety of missions your teams can undertake, but the maps are slightly less diverse than the original.
In conclusion, if you were a fan of the original, or want a challanging turn based strategy game, then you should consider giving X-com: Enemy Unkown a play.

Dead Space is the classic definition of horror. This game made me feel so uncomfortable and disgusted, yet so attached and interested. It has a good story, filled with mistery and conspiracy. Everything about the game feels right and natural. It delivers a solid gameplay, which consists of exploring and fixing a huge ship, fighting an endless variety of necromorphs, playing with gravity, crafting and upgrading equipment, uncovering the truth about what happened, and just trying to survive. You get to be Isaac Clarke, the "speechless" protagonist of the game, who slowly goes insane while under the effects of a "relic" called - The Marker.
The game's name is the perfect description of how the game feels. Everything seems so cold, so lifeless, diseased and abandoned. Everywhere you look, it's just cold metal walls, dry blood spilled on the floor and doors, rotten bodies everywhere and flickering xenon lights. Aside the ship, there are also times when you have to go "outside". The space looks gorgeous. It's dark and dangerous, but also endlessly beautiful. All of these create an unforgettable atmosphere, full of terror, shock and dementia. I wish I could say "Don't worry, it's not that scarry." But I can't. You will get scared. Even when you tread carefully, trying to notice the vents or ducts from where the necromorphs might come, you'll still get surprised every time. The developers have scripted the game so well, that it's impossible not to get scared. You'll start getting used to the monsters after a while. And when you're letting your guard down for a minute, just when you least expect it, you get a instant heart attack and a broken chair.
Dead Space makes you feel absolutely stranded, alone, but not helpless. The player can choose from a variety of weapons and tools. Which not only look cool, but also behave differently. And each of those weapons can be found and upgraded at the Work Benches. You also get to use Kinesis, which is totally awesome. Especially when combined with the Stasis. But what I liked the most most, was the suit. The RIG, as they call it, can also be upgraded and augumented. I just loved it. It looked so armored and heavy, and cold. But also so very cool and protective. The game becomes more challenging as you progress. There are new types of monsters lurking the corridors, wishing to get their... hands/paws/claws/teeth/blades/tails/tentacles/quills/proboscis/pustules and other limbs around your neck. But besides all those gruesome and brutal deaths, there are also other things that can and will kill you if you're not careful enough. Such as getting hit with some massive spinning tethers, getting electrocuted, running out of air, being hit with a meteorite, jumping into open space, and my personal favorite - getting crushed by a door. That's just what I remember anyway. But I'm sure there's a lot more to choose from.
Another absolutely great feature of this game is the sound and music. Everything sounds just right. Shooting sounds awesome. Stomping and punching the necromorphs feels so very satisfying, because I always found myself crushing every body I saw. Which is a little strange come to think of it... Oh, and the music. I don't know if you can really call it music, because it's mainly a series of very well done ambient soundtracks. Always tensionate, rhythmic, and terror-inducing. Nothing scares me more than a rotten-baby-tentacle-monster jumping on me, while some extremely loud and terrifying chimes are playing on the background. But it was also... fun. I liked to be scared. And if you like to be scared too, this is it my friend.
Although this game was made back in 2008, it looks fantastic. It has got awesome lightning, good-looking models and a most satisfying dismembering system. You can literally tear someone's limbs apart, one by one. And a good physics engine that allows you to do a lot of crazy stuff with those gravity boots.
Finally, a must play. It's a shame I haven't played this a long time ago. This game delivers an amazing experience, full of horror and action. With a good story and lovely sound design.

Ooops... Shadowrun returned, kind of. Sadly they messed it up.
1.) Graphics
For me it's been a questionable descision to go with bitmap graphics in this game. It looks like they tried to copy the style from the old Fallout games and they did a good job with that. Still it's a mess. Playing this game on a modern system with an HD monitor leaves you with text you can barely read, scenes with tiny characters and objects and so on. There is a zoom which is pretty pointless because it hardly does zoom.
It's clear that zooming in further wouldn't improve things anyway because the resolution of the bitmap graphics is too low. Still, at least an option for the font size would be a great improvement.
2.) Gameplay
The gameplay is as linear as a laser beam. You exactly have to follow the story line, sometimes that leaves you locked into an area searching for that one switch / item / ... to be able to continue. Creating an individual character is pointless. The creators may have noticed that, because you can't play all Runs with your one unique character (like in the pen & paper game) but have to trash your character and make a new one for every Run. Dude. Further more the character generator is worse than anything I've seen before, including home brew Shadowrun character generators back on Windows 95. On top of that they kinda mixed up skills, attributes, specialisation etc. in a really confusing way.
Fights are as boring as f***, as the rest of the game is. I could never even feel the original Shadowrun roleplaying system behind any action.
The only valuable feature of this game is the possibility to create own runs.

If you hate South Park, don't play this game. That should be a no-brainer, because if the show's brand of abrasive, offensive humor isn't to your taste, you'll find that same humor turned up to the max in The Stick of Truth. There are jokes that will make some uncomfortable or worse, though if you're the type of person who doesn't care for that style of humor, you probably already know that a South Park game isn't for you.
On the other hand, fans of the show and those who sit somewhere in the middle (like myself) will find an engaging turn-based RPG with nothing-is-sacred writing and scenarios that will both disgust and amuse. The level of care spent in capturing as many in-jokes as possible, both for South Park fans and for long-time gamers, is staggering. Every one of the many objects in the game has unique (and often hilarious) text to describe it, and all manner of gaming tropes are brought into the spotlight and then bludgeoned for comedic effect. The world design is hilarious and creative and puts the whole of South Park (and its surrounding environs) at your feet. There's more to talk about than I ever could in the space of one review, but suffice it to say this is absolutely the definitive South Park game and one of Obsidian's best games in years.
The story finds you, the New Kid (or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, as you'll be quickly named for voice-acting's sake), as the freshest face in the mad Colorado town of South Park. In a matter of minutes, you'll be swept up into a clash between the "humans" and "elves" over the legendary Stick of Truth, which grants its owner the ability to control space and time. Over the course of the 10 to 15-hour storyline, you'll switch alliances, witness (and perpetrate) betrayals, and fight aliens, Nazis, hobos, dogs, rats, and still stranger creatures as you quest after the Stick.
There's a kind of glee in the double world at play here. The game is absolutely South Park in its humor and delivery, but it's also an incredible display of the childlike wonder and drama we all once found in playacting. The children's fantasy world Zaron and its war over the titular Stick bleeds into the real South Park's "actual" danger, and what the player is left with is a bizarre meta-narrative in which kids hitting each other with plastic swords are also murdering Nazi zombies and blowing up houses with "magic." It's hard to articulate, but it's wholly compelling and always pushes you forward. The pacing of the game is utterly fantastic, with new and insane things happening constantly, making a strong argument for the game's relative brevity being a positive rather than, as certain sectors of the Internet have decided, a negative. Additionally, unlike many similar games, this is an adventure that picks up steam as it goes along, rather than petering off. The final day of the storyline is packed so full of insanity and hilarious betrayals (and a trip to Terrance and Phillip's homeland of Canada) that I found myself laughing almost the entire time.
The presentation is dead-on. The game looks and sounds like the show, which is to say that it's not exactly pushing any technical limits, but it's one hundred percent successful in doing what it sets out to do. The music satirically apes recent big-fantasy scores and even offers a few catchy tunes. More importantly, the requisite Latin chanting and choir vocals are replaced by Cartman's voice making up his own words, which sound like something along the lines of "jews, sanctus," in a fashion that is both funny and demonstrates that there's a real understanding of the kinds of tropes we accept as fans of high fantasy.
Attacks and enemies in the turn-based combat are consistently hilarious, and, most importantly, fun to wrestle with. Each of the game's character classes offers a unique set of skills, and the various party members whose aid you'll enlist have unique dialogue for combat situations and story beats, so there's definitely some replayability here. You might skew towards your favorite character in the show, as I did — perpetual victim Butters Stotch is irresistible to me as a paladin who gives his friends a comforting pat on the back for his special healing skill. The game also makes use of a number of different traversal powers during exploration, both your own and those of your buddies. This adds a lot of incentive to send you back to earlier areas or scour the far reaches of the town looking for colored cracks, alien satellites, or hurt friends in need of a little pick-me-up, since following up on these leads usually results in a side quest, secret weapon, or some otherwise hilarious exchange of dialogue.
Unfortunately, while the role-playing elements, which include lots of exploring, talking, side-questing, and secrets to uncover (along with tons of in-jokes, jabs, and references), are great, the game becomes a bit too easy a bit too quickly. Even on the hard difficulty, I was killed only once in the game, and by the end I was laying waste to bosses in a matter of two or three turns with my explosive firework attack. Additionally, I did experience one game-breaking (but amusing) bug in which Cartman lowered his pants to light a fart on fire and the game stopped responding. There I sat, Cartman's♥♥♥♥♥hanging out in the enemy's direction, for about thirty seconds until realizing that the game had locked up while still animating and playing music.
South Park isn't a world I'm especially in love with. The creators are adamant that they do not set out specifically with a point of view to push on viewers , but rather aim to take nothing as sacred and spear anything with comedic potential. As a result, there are jokes in the game that even I found occasionally a bit much; likely by design. And yet I was completely engrossed in The Stick of Truth. I had a blast from start to finish, with not only the humor, but also the Mario & Luigi-style combat, the dense world, and the varied story line scenarios. If you're at all open to the idea of Trey Parker and Matt Stone's world, Obsidian has given you the best vehicle yet to go on down to South Park.

Risk of Rain comforts me in a way that one wouldn’t expect from a perma-death/rogue-like experience.  The more I die (and believe me, you will do a lot of that in this game), the more compelled I become to push on and dig deeper into this indie gem.  On its surface, Risk of Rain may seem simple enough.  You start out as a Commando Class character; shipwrecked on a deadly planet, which you in turn need to briefly explore to find a portal that forces you to fight a boss once activated so that you can then leave the current geographical region for another one, and repeat ad infinitum (ok, maybe not forever, but you get the point).
There are a number of readily available and unlockable items that you can pick up along the way, either as drops from boss enemies, or by using cash monies dropped by lesser enemies on chests and shrines interspersed throughout the game’s varied environments.  Each location has a unique look and feel, accompanied by music that not only works well for said environment, but in my opinion is incredible for this type of game – much more catchy and compelling than I would have expected from a relatively cheap (only $10 regularly) indie title (seriously, I want the soundtrack!!).  There are a decent number of enemies to contend with and each character class (there are multiple to  choose from as they are unlocked, something like 10 classes) has its own unique set of weaponry and special abilities that may prove more or less beneficial for certain enemy types, adding for a great amount of replay value.  I mentioned ‘unlockable’ earlier for some of the items.
These are items that won’t become available in game, either as a regular drop or for purchase, until you successfully complete one of Risk of Rain’s ‘in-game’ achievements (think Borderlands to get a better understanding of what I mean).  You can confirm what these are and how to unlock them by looking them up in the title menu’s varying selections, one of which relates to items and unlockables, etc. Sure, there are Steam achievements as well, and some will even result in a special item unlocking for in game use, but this further adds to replay value.
If none of these features compels you to download a copy of this game for yourself or a friend, then perhaps the fact that the player characters are amongst the smallest ever in a game will (for reals, they’re like 6-12 pixels in size….yeah, I may be over exaggerating just a tad but they are still freakishly small, which is awesome though I know not why that is).
Do yourself a favor, pick up a copy of this game right now while it’s on sale and don’t forget to bring an umbrella. Lame joke, I know, but I have no idea what the hell the title means…..and I don’t care!

Shadowrun Returns' turn-based, old style XCOM-esque gameplay is solid and set in the fascinating mix of cyberpunk and high fantasy that is the Shadowrun world. The vanilla storyline is compelling the first time around, but loses much of its appeal on replays due to the lack of meaningful choices or varying narrative paths. Ultimately, no matter what you do or say, you always end up at the same place and talk to the same characters. However, the diversity in the character building/class system does much to keep the game interesting across multiple playthroughs, with Deckers, for example, playing much differently from Mages or Street Samurai. EDIT:
For a $60 AAA title, I could not recommend this game, but if you've got the teraflops and the time, it's a steal for $10. Definitely $10 worth of value if you have at least a 6th gen i5 or i7 and a 2 GB graphics card. I still stand by it being subpar.
GAMEPLAY:
I think it's fair to say this game is bothersome. Talking from a PC gamer standpoint, the operability is disappointing. True, you *can* run it, and I didn't really complain with my ability to do so, but for the average gamer, I cannot recommend you buy it. There's a lot of intuitive bugs here. However, the fighting mechanics are in their prime here. I think I had the most fun in the challenge room. But there's only a handful of maps, so that was a bummer. The car was more annoying, by 3 hours in, than cool. SPOILER:
So on gameplay, it gets a big "meh" which is not really enough to recommend a purchase.
STORY:
Horse crap. I'm not gonna lie, I really did not like the story. Lots of moving parts and no real enjoyable substance. It was more frustrating than interesting. You know in Arkham City when
Yeah, there's nothing emotionally comparable to that here. Lots of homages to Batman comics, movies, and the game series, as well as several
but overall, it still gets a "no" from me. The only wonderful moment was the return of the sweet serenading of Mark Hamill. That was really the only positive to my three-night binge of Batman. Maybe I was just so shocked with the idiocy of the story that I thought less of it, so I might give it another go later on, but I would definitely say it is sub-par when comparing it to its older brothers.
CONCLUSION:
Arkham Knight? No. If you're a completist, I guess? But you probably would have this game anyway. If you're starting new, stick to Arkham Asylum, City, or if you need better graphics, Origins. All are solid games and have merits in their own respect. The only reason you might *like* this game is if you genuinely enjoy the source material (not my favourite stories, frankly), and you want to be the most intensely violent Batman ever presented (including Batman v Superman). I bought it on sale and would in no way recommend buying it for any less. In the end, yeah, I guess I was entertained. I never thought I would say it, but Arkham Origins looks REALLY good right now.

Dead Space is a rare kind of game and one of the best linear singleplayer games I've ever had the tremendous pleasure to play. It has profoundly affected me as a gamer and has shown to me that you can do a lot with a little and make a game that not only plays good, but looks good. I feel it is a classic no one should go without, even if one is faint of heart.
Dead Space has been out for many years and, by now, it has been thoroughly explored by player and developer alike. Even still, its well-balanced gameplay, mixing satisfying weapons handling, unique dismemberment mechanics, and survival elements that pressure the player throughout the game, leave it as one of the most entertaining third person shooters I've ever played. Interesting balancing of the player's enemy-slowing stasis module and object-manipulating kinesis tool make for unusual puzzles and gunplay that's more than just gunplay. Weapon balance, level design, and enemy variety all make for challenging combat scenarios that can vary greatly in execution with every combination of weapons, stasis use, and kinesis use.
Graphically, Dead Space is unusually high in quality for its technical fidelity. While the game has relatively low detail models and textures, its good aesthetic direction, breathtaking animations, and clever manipulation of lighting and effects make for a game that will remain visually pleasing for a long time. Voice acting by its cast and atmosphere by its audio team continue to blow me away in sheer quality, even after nearly a dozen playthroughs between console and PC that have solidifed nearly every turn in my memory. Overall, I feel Dead Space has such cinematic and aesthetic quality that some live action movies fall short in comparison.
A linear game such as Dead Space would be little but an on-rails third person shooter without a good story and, with all its great aesthetic traits in mind, it does not fail to disappoint. While not immensely groundbreaking, its often psychologically-oriented horror, novel take on otherwise run-of-the-mill space zombies, and interesting backstory woven into audio and text logs make it thoroughly enjoyable.
No game is without its failings somewhere and, while I feel Dead Space's are relatively few, this game most certainly has some. While understandable as part of its placement in the horror genre, movement feels unusually clunky at times. Physics oddities and interaction with moving objects can make for some very bizarre moments, ranging from comically confounding and common ragdoll spasms to infrequent, but frustrating random deaths and object disappearances. Puzzles are often simple and blatantly obvious, usually relying overwhelmingly on the threat of death rather than true complexity.
Additionally, Dead Space was made for consoles first, PCs second. Many users have run into issues with gamebreaking bugs resultant from their setup or PC-specific options and other port problems - such as control scheme modification being difficult at times - and, as with any console port, be ready for a little bit of work to get it to play nice. I, personally, did not experience many issues, but caution and patience are advised regardless.
Modding in Dead Space is essentially non-existent, to my knowledge, as with many other Electronic Arts-backed titles. I feel the lack of support for a modding community is an incredible shame, as its gameplay and atmosphere could have been ripe candidates for talented and amateur modders alike.
In the end, if you don't own Dead Space, whether you prefer action or horror, I strongly urge you to change course and pick it up. It is a title that has thoroughly impressed me and, for a time, restored some faith in Electronic Arts. It is a game that spooked me, challenged me, and satisfied me enough to buy it for both Xbox 360 and PC. It is an experience that I honestly believe you would do yourself a disservice not to try. It has earned every little penny I spent on it and thensome, and I will remember it fondly for years to come.

Civilization V it's an natural progress to the series. It really makes a lot of things better, but it's not too flawless, so improvements can be made.
PROS
- Good graphics without going over the top with 3D part
- Hexagons
- 1 unit per hex - if kinda change the whole concept of flooding the production queue with units that previous titles had, but also bring some more strategic diversity on the table
- Great interface. Once you get used to it, everything it's simple, very intuitive.
- Map/resource display. Things are just displayed clearly. You know what resources you have on a hex and what yeld without having to hover too much.
- Gandhi.
CONS
- Religion not so deep. They do not influence diplomacy as much.
- Warmonger penality. The concept it's understandable, but the way it's applied it's not so good. It's sometimes too strict and it does not take into account past actions. If you are getting attacked and manage to win over the civilization that attacked you in the first place, you get as much penality as if you attack Gandi in first 30 turns.
- AI and diplomacy as a concept. Basically, you do not need to be friend with anyone for a diplomatic victory. You simply need to take care of city states, to make sure to have them friends and you will get the diplomatic victory. Getting friends with other civilizations it's very abnoxious. They will turn their backs on you with every chance they've got. You have a friendly Civ that's not doing too well, so you decide to be good guy and ask for a declaration of friendship, they will probably decline. You ask for an defensive pact or open borders while they have only one city left and you want to help them out, they might decline you.
- End turn. I don't see any reason that have something to do with gameplay that require you to issue orders to every single unit and to pick your research/build before finishing a turn. I think it got something to do with the way the enemies calculate their moves, as they might be calculated during yours, so things might go faster when you actually hit "end turn". But it should be optional.
- Gandhi. He's still a psycho.
Even if there might seem a lot of cons, i actually highly recommend this game. It's addictive, it's a pleasure to play, it's a great game overal.

Dead Space is a rare kind of game and one of the best linear singleplayer games I've ever had the tremendous pleasure to play. It has profoundly affected me as a gamer and has shown to me that you can do a lot with a little and make a game that not only plays good, but looks good. I feel it is a classic no one should go without, even if one is faint of heart.
Dead Space has been out for many years and, by now, it has been thoroughly explored by player and developer alike. Even still, its well-balanced gameplay, mixing satisfying weapons handling, unique dismemberment mechanics, and survival elements that pressure the player throughout the game, leave it as one of the most entertaining third person shooters I've ever played. Interesting balancing of the player's enemy-slowing stasis module and object-manipulating kinesis tool make for unusual puzzles and gunplay that's more than just gunplay. Weapon balance, level design, and enemy variety all make for challenging combat scenarios that can vary greatly in execution with every combination of weapons, stasis use, and kinesis use.
Graphically, Dead Space is unusually high in quality for its technical fidelity. While the game has relatively low detail models and textures, its good aesthetic direction, breathtaking animations, and clever manipulation of lighting and effects make for a game that will remain visually pleasing for a long time. Voice acting by its cast and atmosphere by its audio team continue to blow me away in sheer quality, even after nearly a dozen playthroughs between console and PC that have solidifed nearly every turn in my memory. Overall, I feel Dead Space has such cinematic and aesthetic quality that some live action movies fall short in comparison.
A linear game such as Dead Space would be little but an on-rails third person shooter without a good story and, with all its great aesthetic traits in mind, it does not fail to disappoint. While not immensely groundbreaking, its often psychologically-oriented horror, novel take on otherwise run-of-the-mill space zombies, and interesting backstory woven into audio and text logs make it thoroughly enjoyable.
No game is without its failings somewhere and, while I feel Dead Space's are relatively few, this game most certainly has some. While understandable as part of its placement in the horror genre, movement feels unusually clunky at times. Physics oddities and interaction with moving objects can make for some very bizarre moments, ranging from comically confounding and common ragdoll spasms to infrequent, but frustrating random deaths and object disappearances. Puzzles are often simple and blatantly obvious, usually relying overwhelmingly on the threat of death rather than true complexity.
Additionally, Dead Space was made for consoles first, PCs second. Many users have run into issues with gamebreaking bugs resultant from their setup or PC-specific options and other port problems - such as control scheme modification being difficult at times - and, as with any console port, be ready for a little bit of work to get it to play nice. I, personally, did not experience many issues, but caution and patience are advised regardless.
Modding in Dead Space is essentially non-existent, to my knowledge, as with many other Electronic Arts-backed titles. I feel the lack of support for a modding community is an incredible shame, as its gameplay and atmosphere could have been ripe candidates for talented and amateur modders alike.
In the end, if you don't own Dead Space, whether you prefer action or horror, I strongly urge you to change course and pick it up. It is a title that has thoroughly impressed me and, for a time, restored some faith in Electronic Arts. It is a game that spooked me, challenged me, and satisfied me enough to buy it for both Xbox 360 and PC. It is an experience that I honestly believe you would do yourself a disservice not to try. It has earned every little penny I spent on it and thensome, and I will remember it fondly for years to come.

To start: I used to add a longer header to these reviews, but since it often made the review™ too long to submit™, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery™. In case you can't tell, I'm poking fun at the amount of trademarks™ in the title™ of this game.
Gameplay™: Oh neat, a South Park™ (alright, I'll stop) game that's actually good. The Stick of Truth is a turn-based RPG very much in the line of something like Paper Mario just with bigger numbers. While you select moves in a turn-based setup, the moves themselves have associated QTEs that will either do more damage, hit more enemies, block attacks, etc. etc. It's about the same level of depth as Paper Mario as well, so don't expect something insanely detailed like Trails in the Sky. It's pretty fun, but it does suffer from a lot of the same problems that I find myself having in a lot of RPGs in that the beginning of the game is the hardest part, and the game tends to get overall easier from then on. In fact, here's another comparison: the game is about as hard as Paper Mario, so you don't need too many RPG skeelz in order to beat it. There are three difficulty options; I just stuck with Normal because I wasn't sure how the difficulty level of this game would be.
Enemies line themselves up in a "non-linear" grid, which can sometimes allow you to hit multiple enemies with one attack. I never needed to concern myself with that deep of tactics, but I could see it becoming useful in Hard mode. There's a decent amount of side-quests as well, but even a completionist file shouldn't take any longer than 20 hours. Also, there are some things that you can end up missing if you don't do them early enough, so if you're into completionism, I'd consult a guide. Apart from that, there's really not much else to talk about on the gameplay front. It's a very competent RPG that I could see being fun for maybe a couple of playthroughs more at most. It's nothing that you'd probably want to go back to year after year, though. 8/10.
Story: The real meat and potatoes of the game here, and they really nailed the South Park feel with this game. Admittedly, this feel is more along the lines of the Song of Ice and Fire parody they did a season or two ago, so if you didn't like those episodes too much, you might not be too hot on this game's plot. There's a ton of stuff for the really crazy South Park fan as well (the strength potion is Weight Gain 4000, for example). There were a few jokes that fell flat, but considering you get about 8-12 hours worth of South Park content, that's really no surprise. Plus, there's plenty of other great stuff in there to make up for it. Of course, if you don't like South Park at all, you won't be enjoying this one bit. If you do like South Park, you'll feel right at home. Really great stuff on this front. 9/10.
Graphics: It's kinda silly to knock the graphical fidelity of this game, as it's meant to look really tacky. I will say that the compression on the cutscenes are kinda obvious, even with just a 1080p monitor. It did fullscreen to my native resolution of 1080p, which I always appreciate. Apart from that, there really isn't much else as far as graphical options, but as mentioned in the top of the paragraph, there doesn't need to be. It looks like a South Park game and it runs without any (unintentional) "framiness." What more can I ask for? 5/5.
Sound: Voice-acting is great, as you would hope from a game like this. The OST is pretty alright, even if I don't really remember any of the tracks, save for a couple of them. One day, your friends tells you “you HAVE to play super hexagon! it’s like the best game in the history of ever!” This then makes you want to do some research on this game.
Most YouTubers you’ve found ragequit on the game never to pick it up again, with the exception of nerd cubed who said (and I quote) “This is NOT a fun game.” You’ve seen replays of the game, and you think it’s too fast for you. You have lost all hope in the game being good.
You tell your friend that “it’s just not my style,” and go back to playing Team Fortress 2.
A few months later comes another huge steam sale, and Super Hexagon happens to be 66% off, making a mere $0.99. You think “ah, what the heck. I’ll buy it.” So you do.
You then boot the game up.
You are greeted with a robotic female voice that says nothing more than two, simple words: “Super Hexagon” Seeing that the only three options are Start Game, Options, and Exit, you just decide to dive head-first into it.
You have three levels unlocked out of six. Hexagon, Hexagoner, and Hexagonest. Their difficulties are correspondingly: Hard, Harder, and Hardest. considering there is no “Easy” difficulty setting, you reluctantly select Hexagon.
the robotic voice comes once again.
“Begin”
“Game Over”
You last...three and a half seconds.
You think to yourself “I-I-I-I wasn’t ready that time. Lets try this again…” You press your A button once more.
“Begin”
“Excellent”
“Game Over”
You lasted five and a quarter seconds this time. “I think i’m getting the hang of this now…” you reassure yourself. You press A again.
“Begin”
“Game Over”
“Begin”
“Game Over”
“Begin”
“Game Over”
“Begin”
“Game Over”
You look up at the clock, and find that an entire hour has passed with you playing this...thing. Your new highscore has gotten to 46.38 seconds somehow. Your controller is sweaty, your adrenaline is still rushing, your fingers are twitchy, and you have the best techno ever looping over and over in your head.
You now understand why your friend wanted you to buy this.
You suggest this game to your other friends and wait a fair 15 minutes for a reply. They eventually get back to you and say:
“it’s just not my style.”
and they go back to playing Team Fortress 2.

Looking for a truly frightening horror-survival experience? Crave to feel truly desperate and alone trapped on a forsaken space vessel in the furthest reaches of uncharted space, while hellish alien-mutant montsrosities are closing in on you from every angle? Looking to♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants every time you turn a corner and be too distracted by pure terror to feel it all running down your leg?
In that case, you'll likely be sorely dissapointed by EA's "Horror" title, and yet I found that I genuinley had alot of fun with Dead Space. While rarely genuinley scary, the game creates enough atmosphere to draw you in, and gives you enough aliens to splatter all over the wall to keep you interested until you're through.
The gameplay is solid and really quite fun, and the weapons available complement this prety well. Unfortuantely, it's not exceptionally difficult on the normal setting, so hardcore players will likely breeze through the game until they unlock the Impossible Mode, by which point they'll have completed their first playthrough and potencially lost interest. On the other hand, players who aren't quite skilled enough to beat Ghosts and Goblins while blindfolded will probably find the game a decent challenge without being overwhelming (albeit, there are a few "BS" moments when you'll be killed simply because you weren't clear on what to do, or you walked into a trap that first timers would never have seen coming.)
On the whole, the story is a bit lacking, and the characters, while interesting enough to keep you paying attention while in the moment, rarely do much you'll remember later. Text and audio logs are scattered around like candy, but they don't really do much to further develop the stroy once you've pieced together what's going on. And the finale: weak.
Overall, Dead Space is no diamond among games, but it's definately worth a second look. While not the "Horror" game it was advertised to be, you'll likely have plentyof fun with it your first time through, and might even be persuaded to attempt a sceond run so you can try out a harder difficulty and some new weapons.
Bottom line question: Should you buy it? Well, it's a few years old now, meaning it's normally fairly cheap, and if you can wait until sale time (which I reccomend), you'll be getting several hours of fun for a few bucks, and I have no regrets buying it myself.

Just finished Dead Space on Medium (Normal) difficulty. So far the title has been an absolute thrill, with tension and terror at every turn, some physical and some psychological. The backstory of the game is very deep, with you being able to control the character Isaac in an attempt to escape a ship  filled with the undead alive, preferably with his allies and his wife, who is lost onboard. The background is explored through lost recordings, some video, audio, and text, as well as the environment itself.
The title itself is very unsettling, as even bumping into a beer can will startle you. Undead can appear behind you, in front of you, above you, all around you. It was fairly challenging on medium, with an option for Easy, Hard, and an unlockable Impossible mode, which I haven't tried out yet. Items can be found through schematics, bought in the store, and then upgraded through the use of nodes (items which you insert into others to make them better). The story is long, around 8-10 hours if you spend time collecting everything. The replayability factor is large enough for maybe 1 or 2 extra playthroughs, which can be spent using your fully upgraded arsenal, or upgrading it to that, and collecting logs you may have missed.
The downsides to this title are mentionable, although they don't detract from the experience very much. No steam achievements, cards, or DLC for this title. I cling to hope that EA may port their dlc to the pc, preferably in a package, although its small. I encountered a glitch, which I read is very common for pc gamers. That glitch is called the "Continue glitch", where if you start the game on any difficulty other than medium, save, exit, then click continue instead of load game, it will change your save to medium difficulty with no way to go back. I started on Easy the first play through, and it happened to me on chapter 2. This can be avoided though, although it hasn't been patched out yet. The aim is also sort of slow, but I can't tell if its a bug or if its part of the games' unique aiming itself.
All in all I rate this game a 9/10. Its a great game to start off a series but it is hindered by an almost unavoidable bug, no steam extras, and no pc DLC, although the other two versions of this game recieved it. Get it on discount and you won't regret it.

Shadowrun Returns capture very well the atmosphere that the Pen and Paper version have, that whole crazy idea of fantasy and cyberpunk mixed together. The 2d art is really well done and the music is fitting, this game is recommended for people that really like the Pen and Paper RPG or anyone curious to know a world where orks, elves, dragons and magic coexist with cyberpunk as this is a good introduction to it. Experienced and long time RPG veterans might be disappointed as the combat is easy and uses a streamlined version of the Pen and Paper rules, the story while with good dialog for the most part, suffers from pacing issues and isn't going to blow the minds of any Shadowrun veteran.
If having a sand box experience is fundamental for you in any RPG, you could be disappointed as well because the story is linear and railroaded with you not being able to return to previous areas or explore the city freely. The game has an easy to learn editor as well, so if you have aspirations to be a modder it could be a good place to start. I recommend this game in general but except for those that really want a really challenging turn based combat or sand boxy exploration but if you like a good adventure in Shadowrun universe that is a really reasonable price.

So Shadowrun Returns, the kickstarter-funded project by Harebrained Schemes has finally come out. I had high expectations for this game, so how did it fair?
Dialogue:
Pretty good. Some of the more eccentric characters are quite interesting. You won't find anything on the level of Planescape: Torment, but then again it's hard to find that anywhere.
A minor gripe, and one that I am fully aware is entirely due to personal preference, is that I did not enjoy the usage of "drek" instead of actual swearing. I realize this is in accordance to established lore, but I still thought it detracted from what could have been far more genuine lines. "Drek" means nothing to me, and even if it's obvious after a couple of minutes that it is profanity, it doesn't come across that way. It's proprietary lingo that adds nothing. Again, my opinion.
Story:
Good. You'll see what few twists it has from a mile away, but that's just about the only thing I could criticize. The characters, while not particularly memorable, are still relatable enough to give you some motivation to carry on, helping them along the way and finding out the truth behind Sam's murder.
Combat:
Enjoyable enough, but it could have been better. The blatant homogenization of classes across the board does little beyond creating an illusion of variety. It's hard not to think of XCOM or Fallout, and this iteration of the tried-and-true tactical system works okay.
Visuals:
Pretty darn beautiful. Nice job on the pre-rendered backgrounds, and the models, simple though they may be, blend in well with anti-aliasing maxed out. The portraits are nothing short of perfect. Great artwork.
Music:
This would have been "audio overall" if there were any voice acting, but understandably so the budget constraints did not allow any of it. That's okay, really.
The music is pretty fantastic. It fits the setting. Not sure what else can be said here.
Interface:
Looks sleek, but functionally it's garbage. Painfully obvious it was made primarily for tablet devices. Who needs a right mouse button or context menus, right? Some things, like healing outside of combat, are buried so deep you'd think the goddess of non-intuitiveness herself made this.
And really? No manual saves? Some checkpoints are ridiculously far apart. The developers claim they average at about 15 mins. Maybe if you skip all the dialogue.
Replay value:
Very small as it currently stands. You have no real choices, nothing that will change the course of the game in the slightest. As previously mentioned, the different classes offer little beyond some flavor that wears off early. And I don't think that will change much in the coming months. The game engine is rudimentary and even the more creative and talented modders will be stuck using dialog triggers for basic features not included in the game. Unless somebody out there has a really interesting story to tell and wants to do so through this game's editor, you should probably keep your expectations low.
Final thoughts:
As an RPG, Shadowrun falls short. It lacks depth in almost every way you would expect it not to: the narrative is solid, but you can't steer away from it; the combat feels great on the surface, but you can't get very creative even after you have a good grasp on it; the characters are interesting, but you'll never get the opportunity to build a real relationship with any of them or find out more about their past; you play a shadowrunner but you can't take on any jobs that aren't directly tied to the story - there's a whopping two of them, and though inconsequential, they're both required to progress; you're told mugging is ridiculously common, but there's no loot system. Frankly, I could go on but this is already longer than I expected it to be.
Ultimately, this game feels unfinished. I understand the reasons behind it, but it doesn't change the reality of the situation.
The game is worth the money, provided you really like what little it has to offer. There's quality here, and the setting is very unique. I hope it succeeds commercially, at least enough to see a sequel with all the problems ironed out.

FTL is probably going to go down as my favorite indie game of 2012. Almost a perfect combination of Master of Orion, Star Control, and the essence of Star Trek, FTL is a DOS-style space "exploration" game where you control one ship and its crew, as you try to outrun the persuing enemy force on your way to your home system to deliver vital info (which triggers the final series of boss battles). Along the way there are many different random encounters, most being some kind of ship-to-ship combat. You find new equipment and crew members to outfit your ship, and eventually you unlock new ships and outfits for ships as you play through the game. A few words of warning however: FTL is crazy-addictive, you'll find yourself playing until sunrise if not careful; also FTL does not have a save/load feature that allows you to turn back time - your decisions matter and a few bad choices will quickly spiral into your ship, crew, and the entire mission being lost. Overall 10/10.
