Just finished Dead Space on Medium (Normal) difficulty. So far the title has been an absolute thrill, with tension and terror at every turn, some physical and some psychological. The backstory of the game is very deep, with you being able to control the character Isaac in an attempt to escape a ship  filled with the undead alive, preferably with his allies and his wife, who is lost onboard. The background is explored through lost recordings, some video, audio, and text, as well as the environment itself.
The title itself is very unsettling, as even bumping into a beer can will startle you. Undead can appear behind you, in front of you, above you, all around you. It was fairly challenging on medium, with an option for Easy, Hard, and an unlockable Impossible mode, which I haven't tried out yet. Items can be found through schematics, bought in the store, and then upgraded through the use of nodes (items which you insert into others to make them better). The story is long, around 8-10 hours if you spend time collecting everything. The replayability factor is large enough for maybe 1 or 2 extra playthroughs, which can be spent using your fully upgraded arsenal, or upgrading it to that, and collecting logs you may have missed.
The downsides to this title are mentionable, although they don't detract from the experience very much. No steam achievements, cards, or DLC for this title. I cling to hope that EA may port their dlc to the pc, preferably in a package, although its small. I encountered a glitch, which I read is very common for pc gamers. That glitch is called the "Continue glitch", where if you start the game on any difficulty other than medium, save, exit, then click continue instead of load game, it will change your save to medium difficulty with no way to go back. I started on Easy the first play through, and it happened to me on chapter 2. This can be avoided though, although it hasn't been patched out yet. The aim is also sort of slow, but I can't tell if its a bug or if its part of the games' unique aiming itself.
All in all I rate this game a 9/10. Its a great game to start off a series but it is hindered by an almost unavoidable bug, no steam extras, and no pc DLC, although the other two versions of this game recieved it. Get it on discount and you won't regret it.

While I never played classic XCOM this was my first entry into this series. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a turn based action/strategy game through and through. While you will also be doing some base/weapon/squad/research management as well, the real meat and potatoes lies in your ability to effectively manage your squad through some tough battles with strategic movements while being able to adjust your tactics on the fly when danger rears its head. The real fun lies in your squads. You can personally name them and then progress them down skill trees growing to hold dear to their abilities and what they bring to your team. You grow to depend on your team and when it comes to a bad decision or something in your tactics gone wrong, and when one of your team mates die (and they will die), you actually feel a sense of lose for losing that squad mate. The tactics make this game so much fun. Don’t be turned off by “turn based” if that is a normal red flag for you. It is a strategy game that uses a turn based model, but it is filled with action that keeps each turn something to anticipate. Add this in with a good sci-fi story, having to build your base while researching weapons, technology, and alien corpses while also trying to keep everyone around the worlds panic level down and have them still help fund your XCOM project gives you lots of reasons to play and enjoy this awesome game. Hands down one of the best games I have played in years if not all time.

Civilization V it's an natural progress to the series. It really makes a lot of things better, but it's not too flawless, so improvements can be made.
PROS
- Good graphics without going over the top with 3D part
- Hexagons
- 1 unit per hex - if kinda change the whole concept of flooding the production queue with units that previous titles had, but also bring some more strategic diversity on the table
- Great interface. Once you get used to it, everything it's simple, very intuitive.
- Map/resource display. Things are just displayed clearly. You know what resources you have on a hex and what yeld without having to hover too much.
- Gandhi.
CONS
- Religion not so deep. They do not influence diplomacy as much.
- Warmonger penality. The concept it's understandable, but the way it's applied it's not so good. It's sometimes too strict and it does not take into account past actions. If you are getting attacked and manage to win over the civilization that attacked you in the first place, you get as much penality as if you attack Gandi in first 30 turns.
- AI and diplomacy as a concept. Basically, you do not need to be friend with anyone for a diplomatic victory. You simply need to take care of city states, to make sure to have them friends and you will get the diplomatic victory. Getting friends with other civilizations it's very abnoxious. They will turn their backs on you with every chance they've got. You have a friendly Civ that's not doing too well, so you decide to be good guy and ask for a declaration of friendship, they will probably decline. Almost all reviews of this game appear to deal with Tripwire's marketing policies and MTX system, which in actual fact is a carbon copy of CS;GO's MTX system.  It is not required to play the game or have access to all of it's content (With one notable exception being the "sidegrade" weapons you can unlock by owning a different game, only one currently implemented being the Berserker's Zweihander from owning Chivalry)
Whatever your opinion of such a system, it is important to understand that Tripwire is a small company trying to produce games with AAA graphics, and that is both expensive and takes time.  And the content they have release for KF2 has been of exceptionally high quality.
So with that out of the way, lets reveiw the actual game:
Gameplay - 8/10
If you have played KF1 or any other horde shooter you will probably catch on pretty quick here.  However Killing Floor 2's Perks, skill customisation and different weapon loadouts as well as it's leveling system gives this game an amount of replayability many other horde shooters lack.
Compared to KF1 where the classes were hard counters to certain ZED (Read: Zombie) types and having the correct amount of each type of Perk was a requirement for success, KF2 takes a Soft-counter approach, where every perk is as equally valid as the next for both dealing with trash as well as the big scary ZEDs, but some perks lean more towards one than the other.  They can also be specialised (or generalised) further using the skill system, as well as choosing a different weapon loadout.
In my opinion this leads to a much healthier multiplayer experience where people arn't shouting at each other to choose perks you may dislike or have not have leveled yet.
The recent Resistances patch made the game considerably harder, but many of it's changes were reverted based on feedback (All those negative reviews you probably saw before mine were based on this patch.)
The game is now pretty much as difficult as it was before the patch, and certain classes (namely Berserker) received a huge buff as a result.
Overall the playerbase's response to balance changes has been extremely reactionary and often not based in fact.  Take anything you hear about KF2s balance with multiple grains of salt.  People have claimed that Berserker has been nerfed extremely by these changes, but because of them I can now clear Hell On Earth (the hardest difficulty) on solo with Berserker.  Same with Firebug.  The best way to see how balanced the game is is to watch a skilled player play the game.
Appearance - 9.5/10
Gore flying everywhere, fluid enemy animations that react to everything you do to them, guns animated in 300FPS so that in ZEDTIME you can even see the barrel of your gun shake, reloads based on actual techniques used by trained soldiers.  Killing Floor 2 is a gun nerd's wet dream, and has enough blood and guts to literally paint entire levels red.
If you want to know why each update for this game takes so long, you only need to look at how beautiful this game is.  Each weapon is an equisite piece of animation work and attention to detail.
This game looks GOOD and it knows it.  If it takes 4-6 months to produce content of this high quality, I would say that time is very well spent.
Audio - 8/10
The grungy heavy death metal is back in full force.  If this sort of music is your cup of tea then you will love this games soundtrack.  And if not, the music still sets the tone of the game extremely well.
Guns sound like guns and have a satisfying punch to them, Heads explode with a satisfying crunch, the warcries of Scrakes and Fleshpounds fill you with dread as the sound of the heavy footsteps haunt your dreams...
You get the picture.  Sound in a game is important and Killing Floor 2 delivers on that note, and with good 3D virtualisation you will be relying on each ZED's unique sounds to avoid being flayed from behind.
Conclusion - 9/10
Killing Floor 2 is an excellent horde shooter that with a good group of friends can keep you entertained for months.  Despite all the flak they receive, Tripwire has done a good job with this one so far, their only fault being the speed of their updates, which considering the quality of them is time well waited.
On that note however, now is an extremely good time to get this game:  We now have 8 unique Perks compared to the 4 at release, and with 2 more in store the game is almost done.
Alternativly you could wait a year for when the game will be done, but even then with the MTX system Tripwire has an income to work with on delivering more content for KF2 even after its actual release.
For £20 this game is well worth the cost, and on sale its a steal for something that so far has given me 300+ hours of entertainment.

FTL is probably going to go down as my favorite indie game of 2012. Almost a perfect combination of Master of Orion, Star Control, and the essence of Star Trek, FTL is a DOS-style space "exploration" game where you control one ship and its crew, as you try to outrun the persuing enemy force on your way to your home system to deliver vital info (which triggers the final series of boss battles). Along the way there are many different random encounters, most being some kind of ship-to-ship combat. You find new equipment and crew members to outfit your ship, and eventually you unlock new ships and outfits for ships as you play through the game. A few words of warning however: FTL is crazy-addictive, you'll find yourself playing until sunrise if not careful; also FTL does not have a save/load feature that allows you to turn back time - your decisions matter and a few bad choices will quickly spiral into your ship, crew, and the entire mission being lost. Overall 10/10.

The graphics are hipster retro, but the game world feels true to the cyberpunk genre - even with the addition of magic.  Once I got past the premise that allows magic, there is a lot to like from a story point of view. Thus, the edition of the game with the downloadable sound track and collection of background stories turns out to be a decent buy - but heed the warning . . . there be spoilers in the backstories.  The turn-based tactical combat portion of the game is a lot of fun, and is more varied than what is on offer from the XCOM revival game.
There are some negatives.  The check point based save games are pure suck, but not enough so to completely ruin the game. The leveling system may prove too limited to sustain really large community DLC projects, but that may be by design as the module that ships with the game is a little too short to justify the game's price on its own merits.  This is the most legitmate criticism of the game in my opinion.  There is just too little on offer for the price of the game.
Put another way, the game design lends itself to modules that are more like short stories and less like full lengh novels.  Since the game only ships with one relatively short module, one does get the feeling that one has paid for full lengh novel and only received a short story in return.  This is also bad news if you would prefer to carry the same character through from module to module - this just doesn't seem possible as you would effectively need to start skill development over with each module. There are hacks around this limitation, but then play balance is shot to heck.
Speaking of play balance, decking does not seem like a particularly viable solo class and the adept class is only marginally better.  If you want to play as a decker or an adept, try a multi-class design instead.  Longer modules might yield enough levels for the adpet class to be viable, but there is no such hope for the poor decker.  There were other balance issues that have been fixed in later patches.
My impression is that the DLC community may not be large enough to produce enough quality DLC to even the "value for dollar spent" score.  However, I am not comfortable saying that community DLC won't get there . . . it just may take a very long time.  If you are a frugal gamer, check back in a year or so.

Kickstarter has proven itself to be an exciting tool for gamers disenchanted with the the games being pushed out be major publishers. Last year Kickstarter exploded with projects promising to revive classic gaming franchises and bring new releases that embrace classic gaming conventions. Shadowrun Returns is one of the first major kickstarter releases to come to market and it's success or failure to impress will inevitably shape gamers trust of the kickstarter. Based on a pen and paper RPG, two completely different Shadowrun titles were released for the Super Nintendo and the Sega Genesis. The shadowrun universe is a unique combination of high fantasy races like elves and dwarfs and a cyberpunk world. Shadowrun Returns offers an original campaign, turn based tactical combat and a robust editor that allows players to create their own campaign.
Your created character has struggled after a shadowrun gone bad and is contacted by one of your old crew members from that run named Sam Watts. The catch is that Sam has been murdered and his message is pre recorded, in it, he offers you 100,00 nuyen if you are able to bring the person who killed him to justice. As it turns out, Sam has been slain by a notorious serial killer, the Emerald City Ripper. The quest to identify the ripper takes you through drug dens, shadowrunner bars, the National Transportation Safety Board, a mental hospital, a cult's worship center and into mega corp territory. The narrative is very noir inspired with its femme fatals, seedy locations and nihilistic denizens. The script is peppered with slang that is simultaneously ridiculous and enriching. This is especially important since Shadowrun Returns features no voice acting. The regulars of the Seamstress Union, your quest hub for much of the game, are usually up for a little chat and even the merchants are on the loquacious side, sharing their personal stories before hocking their wares. Oddly enough, most of the shadowrunners that accompany your character on missions are mute. There are a handful of optional tasks and even fewer optional missions to pad your coffers. It's ultimately a refreshing experience since your character and the supporting cast are fueled solely by their own personal gains and vendettas instead of high-minded, self aggrandizing world saving exploits.
Tackling your missions involves navigating isometric maps, extracting information from the locals and of course engaging in turn based tactical combat. Exploring the sections of Seattle that host your missions isn't often rewarding. On occasion you will run across a grenade or a med kit for taking the trouble to look around before chatting with the next NPC that points your party in direction of the critical path. Fortunately, Shadowrun Returns often makes finding the way to your next objective engaging by asking you to so some puzzle solving, detective work and smooth talking. When the need to fight arises, combat starts immediately without any transition screens and props that litter the environment becomes all important cover. The turn based combat will have you analyzing the positioning of your units, managing action points and deciding which skills and spells to use. There are also elements in the environment to take advantage of, Riggers can send their drones through vents and Deckers can enter the Matrix to hack turrets, security cameras and swipe information to fence for funds. Turns in Shadowrun Returns are not governed by stats; there is simply a player phase and an enemy phase which makes streamlines planning. A large emphasis is on ranged combat since firearms are generally more powerful though melee attacks provide secondary effects like taking away a target's action points in addition to health. A wide range of buffs and debuffs can also swing the conditions on the battlefield in your favor.
Where much of the difficulty in Shadowrun comes in is through the use of overwhelming numbers. Often enemy encounters are lopsided and several missions have you face down endless waves of enemies until a given task is complete. Careful planning and making use of the environment makes these missions more than manageable. In fact, on the whole, Shadowrun is a bit on the easy side if you build an offense based class. Instead of gaining levels, completing actions earns your character karma. Karma can be spent on stat increases that progressively become more expensive as they increase. In addition there are base stats that must be leveled to level a subset of stats that are associated with that particular stat. All of the other shadowrunners that your character hires are not customizable in any way. While this fits into the lore of Shadowrun, it can make the game more difficult if you choose to play as a specialized support character.
The futuristic Seattle rendered in Shadowrun Returns is quintessential cyberpunk with hand painted interiors and cityscapes. The hand-painted aesthetic is very attractive and distinct and most of your surroundings are packed with details.  Most everything not associated with the Mega corporations are dingy and filthy and bathes in neon light. Unfortunately, some of the miliue can feel lifeless since there are few animated assets present. A few particle effects would have gone a long way toward making the streets of Seattle much less static. Characters are very minimalistic and their animations are modest. Detailed character portraits make up for this and do a commendable job communicating some personality. The music is handled by the composers of the original soundtracks for the Genesis and SNES games and as one would expect it has a large electronic influence. It's a catchy soundtrack that pays homage to it predecessor while properly aiding the tone of Returns.

Shadowrun Returns is one of several games that has to shoulder the heavy burden of gamers expectations from Kickstarter funded games and it has held up it's part of those expectations admirably. Harebrained Schemes has delivered several balancing patches and has offered excellent support for Shadowrun Returns and it's quality is quite exceptional. It's cyberpunk noir narrative is highly enjoyable with it's cast of characters motivated by very personal circumstances rather than the need for glory and heroism. Combat is simple but flexible, offering an appreciable degree of options for taking down foes. It's also a bit easy, linear and has a modest presentation but all of this is easily forgiven since it's price is a third of a tiple A game. Shadowrun Returns is an excellent example of what made classic RPGs special while reminding us how far the genre has come. Now, let's hope that Wasteland 2 and Broken Age also impress.

Almost all reviews of this game appear to deal with Tripwire's marketing policies and MTX system, which in actual fact is a carbon copy of CS;GO's MTX system.  It is not required to play the game or have access to all of it's content (With one notable exception being the "sidegrade" weapons you can unlock by owning a different game, only one currently implemented being the Berserker's Zweihander from owning Chivalry)
Whatever your opinion of such a system, it is important to understand that Tripwire is a small company trying to produce games with AAA graphics, and that is both expensive and takes time.  And the content they have release for KF2 has been of exceptionally high quality.
So with that out of the way, lets reveiw the actual game:
Gameplay - 8/10
If you have played KF1 or any other horde shooter you will probably catch on pretty quick here.  However Killing Floor 2's Perks, skill customisation and different weapon loadouts as well as it's leveling system gives this game an amount of replayability many other horde shooters lack.
Compared to KF1 where the classes were hard counters to certain ZED (Read: Zombie) types and having the correct amount of each type of Perk was a requirement for success, KF2 takes a Soft-counter approach, where every perk is as equally valid as the next for both dealing with trash as well as the big scary ZEDs, but some perks lean more towards one than the other.  They can also be specialised (or generalised) further using the skill system, as well as choosing a different weapon loadout.
In my opinion this leads to a much healthier multiplayer experience where people arn't shouting at each other to choose perks you may dislike or have not have leveled yet.
The recent Resistances patch made the game considerably harder, but many of it's changes were reverted based on feedback (All those negative reviews you probably saw before mine were based on this patch.)
The game is now pretty much as difficult as it was before the patch, and certain classes (namely Berserker) received a huge buff as a result.
Overall the playerbase's response to balance changes has been extremely reactionary and often not based in fact.  Take anything you hear about KF2s balance with multiple grains of salt.  People have claimed that Berserker has been nerfed extremely by these changes, but because of them I can now clear Hell On Earth (the hardest difficulty) on solo with Berserker.  Same with Firebug.  The best way to see how balanced the game is is to watch a skilled player play the game.
Appearance - 9.5/10
Gore flying everywhere, fluid enemy animations that react to everything you do to them, guns animated in 300FPS so that in ZEDTIME you can even see the barrel of your gun shake, reloads based on actual techniques used by trained soldiers.  Killing Floor 2 is a gun nerd's wet dream, and has enough blood and guts to literally paint entire levels red.
If you want to know why each update for this game takes so long, you only need to look at how beautiful this game is.  Each weapon is an equisite piece of animation work and attention to detail.
This game looks GOOD and it knows it.  If it takes 4-6 months to produce content of this high quality, I would say that time is very well spent.
Audio - 8/10
The grungy heavy death metal is back in full force.  If this sort of music is your cup of tea then you will love this games soundtrack.  And if not, the music still sets the tone of the game extremely well.
Guns sound like guns and have a satisfying punch to them, Heads explode with a satisfying crunch, the warcries of Scrakes and Fleshpounds fill you with dread as the sound of the heavy footsteps haunt your dreams...
You get the picture.  Sound in a game is important and Killing Floor 2 delivers on that note, and with good 3D virtualisation you will be relying on each ZED's unique sounds to avoid being flayed from behind.
Conclusion - 9/10
Killing Floor 2 is an excellent horde shooter that with a good group of friends can keep you entertained for months.  Despite all the flak they receive, Tripwire has done a good job with this one so far, their only fault being the speed of their updates, which considering the quality of them is time well waited.
On that note however, now is an extremely good time to get this game:  We now have 8 unique Perks compared to the 4 at release, and with 2 more in store the game is almost done.
Alternativly you could wait a year for when the game will be done, but even then with the MTX system Tripwire has an income to work with on delivering more content for KF2 even after its actual release.
For £20 this game is well worth the cost, and on sale its a steal for something that so far has given me 300+ hours of entertainment.

This game is not like any other pzzle game out there. The puzzle games we know and love is more or less, put block here and it will open a door there. This game takes that and throws it out a 100 floor building, then proceeds to jump with it. The people behind this game really naild it with the puzzle aspect as well as to blow the mind of the player. Countless times i was amazed by the simple complexity of some of the puzzles you incounter. For example Imagine you’re walking down a series of hallways, one after another. Every turn you take only results in another hallway. You don’t even know where you’re going, but you do know that you don’t want to be there anymore. In an act of desperation, you turn around. Suddenly, the area behind you is completely new. It is most certainly not where you came from, but it is where you are going now. Around each corner in Antichamber awaits a complete mystery; you never know what you’re going to get. Even when viewing something, it is hard to be certain what is there and what isn’t. It's because the game succeeds in using non-Euclidean geometry, or a set of geometric rules that aren't consistent in logic. After each puzzle there are brief hints accompanied by a picture. The starting area contains a map of all the rooms and how they connect, each room revealed only as it is encountered. This main lobby area can be accessed at any time by pressing the Esc key. This becomes useful in a handful of situations, since it shows the room you were last in. It also allows you to teleport to any previously visited area, without traversing the maze and puzzles again. Dont let me get started on the gun you get, that can remove or place blocks at will. All and all this game is amazing and should be checked out. 10/10 in my book.

Like every game, this isn't for everyone. The default campaign is short (took me slightly north of 10 hours without skipping sidequests), it has a check point system instead of save anywhere (getting changed in Berlin DLC, unsure if being ptached in to cover default game too), lack of lootable corpses, and no voice acting. My main complaints are as an RPG, it's kind of lacking content. The campaign is very linear, not a lot of tactical depth to combat, no ability to customize anything except a handful of consumables on party members, nearly all hired runners lack any personality, and reactivity is pretty sparse (i.e. special dialog for race/gender is rare). However, where this game will really shine is future content. It shipped with an ugly but powerful editor that allows modders to fix certain things (more open world questing and lootable bodies for starters). The Berlin DLC is also planned to be more open ended.
Overall, a shallow but solid default campaign. The best of this game will come to the surface in the coming months.

Shadowrun is an RPG set in a future version of Earth where Elves, Orcs and magic exist. It has a strong story, involving murder investigations, corporate espionage and supernatural rituals. There are many interesting NPCs and good dialogue choices, although sadly no voice acting. The stats/skills level up system has some nice depth, and some stats can influence dialogue options. Combat is like Xcom, turn based with a squad of 4, with action points to spend on moving, firing guns or using items/magic. Some squad members are hired temporarily before each quest, have no dialogue, and you can't customise their stats/gear, so unfortunately they lack personality. Levels are small and the whole game is quite linear, with not much scope for exploration. But the campaign lasts around 11 hours so value for money is good. The music is fantastic and really adds to the atmosphere. Although some things could be improved, its still very enjoyable and well worth checking out.
Review update: Dragonfall
Dragonfall takes the formula established in the original release, and improves on it in several ways. Its actually misleading to describe this as "DLC". These days, particularly in the RPG genre, that term conjures up thoughts of short quests and meaningless item packs. Dragonfall is more like the good old days of expansion packs, where you got a meaty chunk of gameplay to sink your teeth into.
The story is excellent, one of the best I've played through in any game for quite some time. The action has shifted to Berlin, where you've joined a crew of shadowrunners on a contract to extract some data from a vault. Predictably, the mission goes wrong, dragging you into another deep conspiracy full of twists and turns, that also helps to explain more of the world's lore.
Because your crew are fully fleshed out characters, instead of the original's mostly hired help, each character has much more depth to their personality. They have a past, they have feelings, and the story is given increased emotional weight through conversations with these characters.
The gameplay mechanics, tactical turn based combat, and level up system all remain intact, and we now have the ability to save anywhere, rather than being limited to the original's checkpoint only system. Quest structure is less linear than before. You have some control over which order to play certain quests, and most quests have optional objectives that, if completed, provide greater (or alternate) rewards. You'll also have some tough moral choices to consider which affect quest outcomes, and many areas allow for the use of non combat skills, including talking your way past guards or hacking computers to gain information.
Dragonfall took me 19 hours to complete, which is significantly longer than the original game, and represents excellent value for money at full price. I don't recall encountering any bugs at all.
Overall Dragonfall is amazing, and I rate it as an absolute MUST BUY.

In terms of horror these days, zombies seem to be a key mechanic in attempting to instill fear in the player. Naturally, with so many people harboring a fear of death and the unknown, a creature that comes back from the dead is a remarkably effective means of accomplishing and setting a fear-striking atmosphere. But with so many games applying this mechanic, it does tend to become broken and repetetive, leaving the recipient jaded and unamused.
To help add a new spice to the genre is Dead Space, a game whose name will take on numerous meanings throughout your playthrough. "What is this new spice?", you may ask. Simply put, it's the spice of a heavier science fiction attitude set in place by making the zombies into alien zombies. Where dark and stormy nights have succeeded in the past amongst the decaying ruins of a dilapidated house, or the whole of a city burning in the night as it dies, Dead Space attempts the same by replacing that all with rough static metal and the suffocating, inescapable reality of being marooned in space.
And, it succeeds magnificently.
Now, we're all in the horror genre because we enjoy the morbid, rushing thrill of being scared, or we've been press-ganged by our friend(s) into playing one of the games. If you're one of the latter, then godspeed. If you're one of the former, however, you're definitely in luck no matter what kind of thrill you seek. Dead Space presents a level of horror for each kind of player, ranging from the intense jump-scares to the underlying, bone-chillingly creepy logs written by crewpeople on the spaceship while the horror unfolded around them. To put it quite simply, Dead Space is a people-pleaser that performs its job exceptionally well; If you're playing the game for the quintissential fear factor, you'll definitely not be disappointed.
But why does it work so well? What exactly combines with and works well with the game's other parts to make it what it is?
Part of it comes from the interesting graphical take it presents to the player. While most horror games are typically set in darkness, Dead Space tends to forego this in preference for, on the most part, a decently well-lit stage. Strangely enough, it works out as a whole. Since the player is so used to everything being visible, it's so much more shocking when you -are- thrust into darkness for a few moments, or when the lights go on the fritz and start flickering, adding to the uncertainty of exactly how safe the next room will be. Of course, the light is neccessary most of the time, because without it, we wouldn't be able to see the multitude of blood streaks spattered on the industrial metal bulwarks.
Another part of the atmosphere is built by the sounds. Now, we're all used to the ambient sounds in horror games: the whistling wind, the low groaning in the distance; Sadly, I've learnt to tune most of them out at this point. Dead Space has an interesting way of recapturing my attention. It decides to be silent a lot of the time. No atmospheric music. No orchestral cues except for when enemies pop out to attempt another throat-gouging. Pure silence. And it's legitimately unsettling to me. I'm used to music trying to set the stage for some heart-straining anxiety, but Dead Space won't give it to me, preferring to let me sweat it out on my own terms. It plays the same role as the lighting, really, so that it's shocking and powerful when it -does- change dramatically. Of course, it can't always play the same card, and toys around with ambient metallic scratching noises and, in one particular part, a deep lowing that rivals most other groans in the horror genre, making it truely chilling to hear.
Naturally, flickering lights and distant sounds (or lack thereof) can't do it alone for the horror genre. Every good (and sometimes bad) horror game has a control scheme that is simple, yet just confining enough to make the player feel helpless in some ways. The early Resident Evil titles did this by making the most ridiculously convoluted camera angles to try and trip us up, and it worked. A lot of people who played it were enthralled by it, and tried over and over again to beat the game in its entirety. While not as extreme as Resident Evil, Dead Space's controls are just hampering enough to lend a feeling of desperation when it comes to traversing the tight, metal hallways, and to add salt to the wound, players are punished for trying to rush through most sections, so you're forced to take it slow and steady. Isaac Clarke's (the main character) movements are akin to the movements of driving a tank, though with the added benefit of feeling slightly as though you're being impeded by molasses. What I'm trying to say is that Isaac doesn't run very quickly, his aiming is relaxed at best, and the arm-flailing and foot stomping melee attacks feel as though Isaac is wearing some form of a suit of armor. And it all works out. The player really gets the feeling that Isaac isn't a war-hardened army veteran or a muscle-bound powerhouse, but instead just a regular joe who was sucked into the whole, nasty event against his will.
However, above all that comprises the game, the unlock feature helps to drive the playablity of the game. Beat the storyline once and you get access to harder difficulty levels more items to use in-game with a nifty "new game plus" feature. Because, while it's certainly enjoyable playing it over to feel more capable, and, in some circumstances, like an absolute god, it's refreshing to be punished heavily for breathing improperly in "Impossible" difficulty.
So, to sum it up, Dead Space is there to gouge your eyes out, disembowel you, and beat you to death with your own limbs, and all the while, you're being urged to do the same to it. And you'll enjoy every second of it. I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone wanting to get into the horror genre, and to anyone already in the genre who wants something new. I'll recommend it to everyone else as well, since no one should be left out.

I liked both its sequels - yeah, the 3rd part has more action, so what? The story continues, so this was needed so those of you who prefer the scary parts can easily play the first game again.
Pros:
--- hologram-like ingame menu: your inventory, the map, and even your objectives are projected in front of you
--- the concept of dismemberment: forget everything you learned from FPS games - headshots this time will not work, at all
--- amazing graphics and equally high-quality audio: my favourites are the zero-g scenes where you hear your breathing more than the surrounding sound
--- high replayability due to the unlockable items, difficulty modes
Cons:
--- not much to say here, really, perhaps that the game can be difficult at times, but not because it truly is challenging but because fighting in close-quarters can only be difficult (you cannot really come up with any proper tactics)
The sequels only improve upon the experience by expanding upon the story and giving the protagonist a face and voice.

I thought this was great, from start to finish. Excellent. It is difficult to know what else to say... I just thought this was great. I'll just ramble as follows.
As an RPG it was the perfect amount of complexity, deep but easy to understand.
The artwork is lovely, everything is well animated and it is just generally a really attractive game.
It is VERY well written IMHO, the characters come to life through the text and written dialogue, it's great! I honestly felt like I was enjoying an interactive book, which is a feeling I tend to get when I am fully engaged. The locations, the people, the story.. all of it is vivid and believable, not so much due to the on screen action, but more through the filter of my imagination which the writing nutures throughout, things playing out in my mind's eye as I read the next interchange between characters, or digested the description of the place I'd just arrived at.
The narrative is solid, and makes sense (within the world it is told) and pans out well, I thought the pacing was excellent.
Some might dislike the linear nature of the game, I personally love it. Side missions are available, but they are in direct relevance to the main storyline at all times which keeps things moving, and therefore aren't always available for you to come back to tidy up and complete later, so bear that in mind. I am a fan of a well told story, and "sandbox" games are never as good as experience for me as being told a well crafted story. Shadowrun Returns nails this.
I really enjoyed this game, took me 17.2 hours to complete but it felt like a lot less purely because I was enjoying every minute of it and was just waiting to turn the next page in this electronic short story and learn what was going to happen next. Like a good book, it was tough to put down.
It has it's flaws here and there, like checkpoint saves (due to be changed in a patch or via the next DLC I understand), some sections keeping you in turn based combat mode when there aren't any enemies about and on some of the longer battles the combat music can get a little tiring, but those are small complaints.
Excellent and I'm looking forward to see what they do next! Recommended.

I have wanted this game since the moment I heard about it but just couldn't justify spending $40 for it. And I'm actually kind of glad that I waited until it was steeply discounted because this game is nowhere near being worth full price. It almost hurts to give this game a thumbs down and if the rating system here were a little more finely tuned, I'd probably give it a more lukewarm than negative rating because there is a lot to love about it but I can't help but to feel a little bit ripped off.
There are definitely positive things about this game. Trey and Matt wrote the scripts and were very heavily invovled in it and you can tell that. There are plenty of cutscenes which are bascially just scenes from an episode of South Park. They're funny and enjoyable. You never find yourself wanting to skip through them (unless you're prompted to). The plot of the game itself is very South Park. It's a mixture of the Black Friday Triology with Night of the Living Homeless and some anal probing and Nazi's thrown in for fun. It's tasteless and everything you want from a South Park game.
The fighting is turned-based which I usually don't care for but I actually really enjoyed it in the game. You almost always have a buddy to fight with and their weapons and special attacks are highly customized so it's interesting to go through and see what each of them can do. You also update your armor and weapons from fighting with a plank with nails in it to fighting with a vibrator. On top of that you can add patches to most of your weapons to increase their damage. You find most of the armor and weapons along the way on your various quests so you usually get upgraded items as you level up without having to take a detour to get them.
However, the game is really short. It's been advertised as this sprawling and epic adventure RPG and it has the price tag to match it but it really doesn't take that much time to beat it. I think that's why some of the achievements are so random and specific so you'll have to play through it more than once. But there's not enoguh to do in the game and nothing really depenedent on your choices that make it a game that warrants another playthrough. There's a lot of padding in it and at times they're clearly making fun of it but just because they make fun of it doesn't mean they get off on having you pop to one place, then pop back and then back again. It feels cheap. And not in the beloved way that the show feels cheap.
The map is not very expansive. It's pretty annoying when you're on a fetch quest and you keep having to fight villains in the same place you were just at because they keep respawning every time you leave the area by going off the edge of the map. Another way they pad out the game but it all the villains are essentially the same outside of the main bosses of a certain area and once you get better loot, it's pretty easy to beat them. So it just ends up being more padding. Of course, there are a lot of loading screens when you go off the edge of the map as well. Which kind of just comes across as more padding.
Also, if you're a mouse-and-keyboard player...you can't remap any of the keys so you're going to have to use W,A,S,D even if you're left-handed.  Not a big thing but for a game that had a decent budget...you'd expect something like that. And there are a few quicktime events and special moves where you're just supposed to mash certain buttons and they're just...they're just awful. But they're thankfully full and far between so it's not that game breaking just really annoying.
All in all, I would suggest this game to someone who is really a fan of the serious but I would not recommend putting down the full price on it. Even half off would still be somewhat of a rip-off but you'd at least have a few days with a funny game out of it. And Matt and Trey will get more money.

I have wanted this game since the moment I heard about it but just couldn't justify spending $40 for it. And I'm actually kind of glad that I waited until it was steeply discounted because this game is nowhere near being worth full price. It almost hurts to give this game a thumbs down and if the rating system here were a little more finely tuned, I'd probably give it a more lukewarm than negative rating because there is a lot to love about it but I can't help but to feel a little bit ripped off.
There are definitely positive things about this game. Trey and Matt wrote the scripts and were very heavily invovled in it and you can tell that. There are plenty of cutscenes which are bascially just scenes from an episode of South Park. They're funny and enjoyable. You never find yourself wanting to skip through them (unless you're prompted to). The plot of the game itself is very South Park. It's a mixture of the Black Friday Triology with Night of the Living Homeless and some anal probing and Nazi's thrown in for fun. It's tasteless and everything you want from a South Park game.
The fighting is turned-based which I usually don't care for but I actually really enjoyed it in the game. You almost always have a buddy to fight with and their weapons and special attacks are highly customized so it's interesting to go through and see what each of them can do. You also update your armor and weapons from fighting with a plank with nails in it to fighting with a vibrator. On top of that you can add patches to most of your weapons to increase their damage. You find most of the armor and weapons along the way on your various quests so you usually get upgraded items as you level up without having to take a detour to get them.
However, the game is really short. It's been advertised as this sprawling and epic adventure RPG and it has the price tag to match it but it really doesn't take that much time to beat it. I think that's why some of the achievements are so random and specific so you'll have to play through it more than once. But there's not enoguh to do in the game and nothing really depenedent on your choices that make it a game that warrants another playthrough. There's a lot of padding in it and at times they're clearly making fun of it but just because they make fun of it doesn't mean they get off on having you pop to one place, then pop back and then back again. It feels cheap. And not in the beloved way that the show feels cheap.
The map is not very expansive. It's pretty annoying when you're on a fetch quest and you keep having to fight villains in the same place you were just at because they keep respawning every time you leave the area by going off the edge of the map. Another way they pad out the game but it all the villains are essentially the same outside of the main bosses of a certain area and once you get better loot, it's pretty easy to beat them. So it just ends up being more padding. Of course, there are a lot of loading screens when you go off the edge of the map as well. Which kind of just comes across as more padding.
Also, if you're a mouse-and-keyboard player...you can't remap any of the keys so you're going to have to use W,A,S,D even if you're left-handed.  Not a big thing but for a game that had a decent budget...you'd expect something like that. And there are a few quicktime events and special moves where you're just supposed to mash certain buttons and they're just...they're just awful. But they're thankfully full and far between so it's not that game breaking just really annoying.
All in all, I would suggest this game to someone who is really a fan of the serious but I would not recommend putting down the full price on it. Even half off would still be somewhat of a rip-off but you'd at least have a few days with a funny game out of it. And Matt and Trey will get more money.

As limited my experience with the Shadowrun Universe is, I actually enjoy this as it stands. However, the highlight of this game is not the content which came with it. The highlight is essentially making this as a platform to participate in user designed content. This is not a game that deserves full price, nor does it ask it. $20 is not terrible when it comes to getting a few hours of gameplay for a linear story.
There is plenty of potential through the Workshop, leaving this to feel more like a Tabletop RPG set-up than an free standing game. The game was designed specifically for users to creat their own campaigns, their own missions, their own content in such a way that I've yet to see of other games. When it comes to tabletop games, there are some pre-set stories, but DMs are often given the tools to make their own within a set of rules. This is a cRPG equivalent, even if it is limiting compared to the actual tabletops capabilities. The users get to play pseudo DM, designing tales and stories to be uploaded with others to enjoy.
It's not perfect either. More than once a bug or two is encountered, and both times potentially game-breaking. IE: Cannot progress issues. One time I had to restart to the last checkpoint almost a half hour behind. There is no real manual saving system, auto-saves only happen as the story is progressed. This means that if you just finished a leg, you have to keep going until you progress to the next stage, or you lost all your work from when you started the mission of sorts.
It is worth noting that this game /will/ let you screw up. Horribly building a character can have dire consequences, just like in a tabletop. You can spend money poorly, losing out on ability to hire help, get overwhelmed, and unable to proceed. The shadows are a dangers place, and the game allows for them to consume you for tripping. There is no hand-holding on how to advance your character, or to manage your money.
For the price, it was worth it to me. If you are interested in cRPGs at all, it's fun. Don't expect a completely fulfilling experience right off the bat, as I mentioned... This game was designed for user content, coming with only one rather linear campaign. If you are a fan of Shadowrun, and unable to get into a tabeltop group, this just may scratch your itch.

Killing Floor 2 doesn't have more content to give than the original, but certainly a lot of replayability just by having different Perks (and roles to fill), leveling them up and trying to unlock all of the Achievements. After that, the most fun for me is to try out many different tactics, seeing what's working the best during certain situations.
Graphically, the game isn't bad at all. The Audio is great and the Soundtrack is authentic, very fitting.
Plus, the game can be modded, isn't that fantastic? That means tons of maps are being played on Servers, and that's not counting the Custom Servers. Some have a Prestige System where you can level up you Perks as you want, put attribute points wherever you like, they have new Zeds, Weapons, etc.
For only 43.99$ CAD (Digital Deluxe Edition) that I paid, I have clocked over 450+ hours (not hours of tedious gameplay) on the game, way more than AAA bs games for 80$.
So just to resume:
-Lots of Perks to play with
-Achievements
-Good Graphics
-Good Audio
-Mods
I hope this will help somebody out there, thinking if they should buy the game.

A damn fine remake of a damn fine classic RPG. As its predecessor in the 16bit era (SNES and Sega Genesis/Mega Drive) did, Shadowrun puts a very unique twist on the time-tested cyber-punk formula.
Imagine if you took the fantasy elements of elves, orks, trolls, dwarves, magic use, summons...and blended it seemlessly with a corporate controlled, dystopian, near future. Well, that's the gist of Shadowrun's world and aesthetic.
Now throw in turn-based strategy combat, the ability to "deck" into cyberspace for info gathering and alternate combat, a boatload of cybernetic upgrades, magic upgrades, weapons, armor, character customization, and a dark noir-esque story.
Shadowrun...and now...Shadowrun Returns!

Addictive, challenging, emergent, complex, yet easy to grasp. FTL is the very definition of the phrase "more than the sum of its parts", and it's one of those games that shows respect for the player's intelligence by throwing curveballs at them and standing back expectantly. The fact that you can play this on virtually any PC makes it even better, although this means Steam Cloud support is glaringly absent.
A huge steal at the launch price of $9.

Cyberpunk and fantasy mixed together in a tactical RPG with a main campaign set in and around Seattle.  If that sounds good, check this out.  You customize your character’s gender, race, and class and spend points on improving stats, which adds to the potential variety and number of playthroughs.
There are a few issues that I take with the game.  For instance the turn based combat has animations that aren't too flashy, they get the point across but won’t wow you; there is no quicksave system, which can be quite rough if you fail a particularly long section between checkpoints; and the campaign is quite linear, though I do feel this serves this game well.
The writing has a noir feel to it that I enjoyed considerably, which was good because there is a lot of it.  Hopefully you enjoy reading.  It should also be noted that Harebrained Schemes have been working on the save system, though nothing has been implemented yet.  There is also a second campaign, set in Berlin this time, in development with new art assets, systems, and a more flexible story structure, which I am very much looking forward to.
In addition to the main campaign, the game includes a fairly powerful editor which can be used to create custom missions or campaigns.  These custom games can be shared and downloaded through the steam workshop.  Check this out if you like tactical RPGs.

text:
Imagine a riot cop with thallium-lined bullets, the horn of an infernal monster, the tentacle of an overlord, the eye of a giant magma worm, a necklace made of monster teeth, a giant missile launcher and a drone army.
That is Risk of Rain.
The perfect blend of old school UFO:Enemy Unknown with an up-to-date graphical makeover that's a feast for the eyes.

Strongest point of Shadowrun Returns is its writing. In best tradition of older RPGs, game describes what you character sees in flowery language. Character introductions, location descriptions and dialogues are smart and charming. The setting of Shadowrun is a blend of cyberpunk and urban fantasy - don't think I knew something like this exists before. I wouldn't mind experiencing Shadowrun Returns in book or graphical novel form.
As a game, however, it is not so magnificent.
SR was made by relatively inexperienced developers on tight budget using Unity and it shows. Graphics are mixed bag - wonderful character portraits, bright and detailed, if somewhat cartoony 2D backgrounds, but awful character models and awkward animations. Sound direction feels cheap overall - music are fine, but forgettable and there is absolutely no voice acting. Combat mechanics ripped straight off X-COM: Enemy Unknown.
The biggest flaw of SR is its linearity. I just didn't have the opportunity to explore the world of Shadowrun - game kept railroading me on one story after another, with brief breaks in same   small hub. All two side missions are one chance affairs - go on them right now or miss it forever. While writing itself is great, spending points to improve charisma and get new dialogue options felt like total waste - game is too short and there is almost no opportunity to use your mad speech skills - I think I used each etiquette only once or twice in whole game. Story starts as a noir-like murder mystery, but after halfway point abruptly turns into "save the world" scenario and ends with series of boring battles against bugs. Absolutely unnecessary twist, in my opinion.
My final impression: SR is an enjoyable short RPG; not without flaws but if you are able to overlook them, you will have a great time playing it.

The first Dead Space takes place on one large spaceship on a general forward path with the ability to return to a few hubs to unlock more rooms, very much like a deliberate Resident Evil in space, with the doomed spaceship taking place of the haunted mansion. The aliens are evolved versions of The Thing, mutating dead flesh into gross killing appendages. Its easy to write off Dead Space as any number of influences mashed together, but it continually strives to be more, with extra care taken to make certain room entrances and boss queues unpredictable.
Yes, its Resident Evil + The Thing + Event Horizon + Aliens + Metroid, and other source material, but its the best parts all wrapped up in one.

Antichamber debuted about 3 years ago as a student project called Hazard - The Journey Of Life.  Then it disappeared for 3 years.  Now it has FINALLY been released and it was well worth the wait.  While it is another manipulate-cubes-in-first-person sim, this is a very well made MCIFPS.  The puzzles are laid out in a metroidvania sprawling map that is full of secrets, easter eggs, and very unusual geometries.  Oh yeah, the map isn't Euclidian.  Not even a little bit.
Bottom line: great puzzle game.  It's rather short (I beat it in 3.5 hours, but I skipped a few areas), but it is a wonderful experience on par with the likes of games like Portal.  Just be prepared to be very confused at how you got to where you were when the hallway you were walking down is now a cliff to nowhere.

For only 43.99$ CAD (Digital Deluxe Edition) that I paid, I have clocked over 450+ hours (not hours of tedious gameplay) on the game, way more than AAA bs games for 80$.
So just to resume:
-Lots of Perks to play with
-Achievements
-Good Graphics
-Good Audio
-Mods

My shields are down. I've got a man trying to fix them, but he's running out of oxygen and I can't get him anymore. He's about to die. I'm about to die. And this is only my lunch break.
FTL is a game of death. Ok. Ok. Actually, it's a game about captaining your own starship. However, unlike Cpt. Piccard or Kirk, your time spent in the captain's chair will be rather brief. You will die. Often. But as you die, you get better at the game and you earn enough to buy new ships and start with new races.
A full game can be played rather quickly. Just pick it up, play it, put it down and go back to work. Although, that may not be recommended because the entire time you're working you'll be wondering just what choice you could have made to get closer to beating the game. It'll eat away at you. You'll be clawing at your scalp by day's end. Your eyes will be blood red. The experience will engulf you and ruin you for the rest of your life. At least that's been my experience. Your mileage may vary.
This means do not play this game if you get frustrated when you die. It's not about if you will die, but when. This is a rogue-like. That means it is a tough game and that sometimes the "roll-of-the-dice" will mess you up no matter how good things are going.
You have been warned.

Shadowrun Returns is a top-down RPG-type pretty much as the title describes.  It is based within the 'world' of Shadowrun, which was born as a Pen-and-Paper role-playing game in 1989.  Throughout the years there have been a
video games produced within the setting as well such as the classic SNES game made in 1993.
Like its roots, Shadowrun Returns contains at its core every bit of what makes this setting and series unique.  That is to say it is still a mix-up of several genres in one:  horror, mystery, cyberpunk, fantasy, conspiracy.

As a disclaimer, I'm fairly new to the Shadowrun universe itself (shame on me!)  Its a world where practically everything fantastical co-exists, in a bleak futuristic world with Mega-Corporations dominanting the world.  Corporate Espionage with Magic and Elves, awesome right?  You are the Shadowrunner - a gun for hire.
Overall this game certainly sets out what it intended to do - a Shadowrun game within the spirit of the original PnP.  It is bit linear for a classic RPG setup, in that you go from one setting to the next, but it worked for what it intends to do with lite-tactics turn-based with a decent story.  The art style and music certainly set the mood for the general theme as well.  A no brainer, and by now pretty cheap addition to your steam library.
A common question is whether or not to play this or simply purchase the Dragonfall Director's Cut.  Like many first iterations of games, I think its always a good idea to experience it from the beginning, if at least once.

So, maybe I'm over 5 years, 2 sequels and god knows how many spin-offs late, but I've finally played the very first Dead Space. Now, I know what you're thinking ''Why don't you play Dead Space 3? Being the newest, it most certainly ironed out the issues with the first two and must be technically the best, right?''. Actually, no, you didn't think that, unless you're a madman with no notion of progression or how game sequels work.
Anyway, you are the very cutely named Isaac Clarke, a generic short-brown-haired hunky space marine who thankfully carries a ridiculous helmet around so he looks a little less boring. He and he's crew, a token black guy whose name I can't remember, a token chick whose name I can't remember, and two expendables who aren't even given names because they die right away, are called over to space station to fix a technical problem, and I almost feel like copying Yahtzee's review word by word on how it all turned out to be something as mudane as a broken lightbulb and they call it a day, because of course the place looks like a butcher shop after an earthquake,♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan and you spend the rest of the game fixing stuff. The plot is largely uninteresting; it's kinda predictable and the characters are either unlikeable or downright insane, and that includes the silent protagonist. Oh yeah, Isaac is mute, and while this is usually meant to make the protagonist a blank slate you can put any personality you feel like on, it doesn't particularly work on this game. Isaac just seems to make the worst decisions a human being can make. There's a part where you're ordered to go kill the mothertruckin' shoggoth that's hanging out in the food court and Isaac obliges without as much as a sigh. If I was him, and had the capability of speech, I would go ''Are you F*cking kidding me!? Why don't YOU go kill the eldrich abomination for a change? I've been down here cleaning this sh*t up while you were up there picking your nose! Why must you keep dumping this sh*t on my shoulders, is it because I was the only one sensible enough to bring a helmet to outer-f*cking-space!?''
Gameplay wise, Dead Space is actually alright. It resembles Resident Evil 4, most notably the over-the-shoulder perspective and being able to buy supplies and weapons from a store, which I really wish would have an automated voice to say ''I've got a selection of good things on sale, stranger!''. What's really interesting is that instead of the usual ''shoot anywhere, but headshots are worth extra points'' strategy, you're actually encouraged to shoot off limbs and make them a much more ineffective murder weapon, so that's a bit of a breath of fresh air. In addition to that, you have two special abilities: Slowing down time, which, although you've seen it in pretty much every game ever created, can actually manage to get you out of a pickle, and it kinda feels badass to stop a monster midair and chop him into pieces before he falls down on the floor. The other ability is an anti-gravity system that helps you lift objects, and quite frankly you'll only use it to solve puzzles, considering you won't have much time to look for stuff to fling at the horde who wants a piece of your delicious butt. There are also zero-gravity segments that are really entertaining that consist of you walking over the walls and ceiling and constantly jumping from one to another while changing perspective. And one more minor thing to add, you can press a button to make a line guiding you to your next objective appear. This might seem like a minor thing, but it really annoyed me how in Doom 3 you're never told exactly where the bloody hell you're supposed to go and I just kept walking in circles until I figured it out.
Now. I guess it's time for the big question. Is Dead Space scary? And the answer is a resounding nooooooo. This game relies heavily on jump scares, and jump scares can only work so many times before they get predictable. And that's the mood for the failed attempt to scare you: Predictable. You know that, when you reach the objective, a monster will either burst into the room, show up on the way back or both; you know that large open spaces mean a whole horde will attack you soon; you know that dead body with the suspicious extra limbs that look like scythes is probably just faking it. And let's be honest, having a gun that shoots mothertruckin' buzzsaws really kills the mood. Oh, didn't I tell you? There's a gun that shoots buzzsaws. And there's more, it not only shoots buzzsaws, it hovers and spins then for a little while so you can dismember more efficiently. And it's not like you ever run out of ammo either, I swear you can easily kill a monster with a single buzzsaw, maybe 2 and sometimes even 3 if you're lucky, and nearly every one of them, their mothers and every container ever drops sets of 4 of the things. I was piling up so much ammo I actually started selling the stuff to make money and room for medkits, which is the stuff I actually needed seeing as those horde fights really eat away your health. If the game was designed to make you rely much more on inventory management due to scarce ammunition, it would've been easily a lot more scary, considering the melee is one of the most ineffective I've ever seen since the knife from Resident Evil 2 and most of the time you'd have to use the millennia old technique of running really really fast. But nope, lucky you the local hardware just exploded and now there are buzzsaws everywhere.
All in all, is Dead Space worth a try? Well, not if you're looking for something scary, but overall it's actually a fun experience. if you go back in time and read the paragraph on gameplay, you'll see I said it plays kinda like Resident Evil 4, and if you go even further back in time you'll remember that Resident Evil 4 was really good. It might not be the deepest game out there, but it's decent enough to entertain, it looks good, it's visceral and it has a gun that shoots buzzsaws, so why not give it a try?

I have finished the main story, so I guess it's time for a review.
Disclaimer: I did not check my grammar while writing this, please excuse me as English is not my first language.
TL;DR version:
Should I buy this game if I'm a batman fan? Yes. Absolutely.
Should I buy this game if I'm not a batman fan? If you like the trademarked "Arkham combat" gamestyle and a good, enjoyable story, yes.
Is it as badly optimised as they say? I run an nvidia GT 740M, 12 GB RAM, 4th gen i7m series and I can run this in ~20 fps at lowest graphics and reduced resolution. Judge for yourself.
Is the tank gameplay as bad as they say? Yes and no. It is repeated a lot of times. Although it is kind of enjoyable, sometimes it gets straight frustrating.
Does it deserve all the hate it got? No. It is terribly optimised, but they are making up for it by cutting the price and releasing free dlcs. It is by no means a perfect game, but overall, I don't think it deserves all the hate.
Long version (includes spoilers, read at your own risk.)
Arkham knight is a game that perfectly ends the Arkham series. It pays sufficient homage to previous games, some nostalgic feeling here and there, but they don't shove it up your face to make it obvious. As usual, they are very true to the characters as they are potrayed in the comics, animated movies, tv series etc etc. Batman and the Joker is exceptionally nicely written. A huge chunk of the story is dedicated to the mentality of the batman. How he is haunted by his previous mistakes, how he is afraid to lose more of his loved one. His decent to madness as a product of both the new fear toxin and overall mental trauma. Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill did astoundingly well in the voice acting of the game. That being said, not all of the characters are delivered satisfactorily. The most obvious gripe I have with the character design is how Barbara Gordon is in a romantic relationship with Tim Drake, not♥♥♥♥♥♥Greyson. While I respect the storywriter's freedom to make changes in the overall Bat mythos, it simply grinds my gear.
Combat feels satisfying, as usual. I dislike the new particle effect that flies off batman's fists as he is punching people in the face greatly. Thankfully, there is a mod that removes them (along with the counter icon etc) so there is no huge problem there. Some people might complain that there are insufficient improvement over the last Arkham games (Origins and City) in terms of combat. Basically what they did is made a few changes on which gadget is quick-usable and some animation improvements (except the remote detonator, it is very much easier to use here). There is a new sound effect on the throwing of the batarangs which is very satisfying to the ears. And of course, they throw in more enemy types to confuse you even further, including the new medic type, the huge grunt guys, improvement on the ninjas, etc etc.
The puzzle element in the game remains mostly satisfying, with an addition of batmobile-related puzzles and the return of the riddler trophy (yay). What I dislike is that the riddles, which is still present in the game, will go mostly unnoticable as they removed the pop up that appears when you enter a new zone. I am not sure if this is configurable or not, but I am definitely not seeing them. Be prepared to feel inadequate to fill in the batman's shoes as you take too long to solve an incredibly obvious puzzle. I have not attempted the Riddler's most wanted quest yet, so I can't really comment on that.
The freeroam in the city feels more alive than in origins, but less than city. A lot of thugs and militias roam around the street, you can do chases with the batmobile or tank fights with them to clear some side quests. Speaking of side quests, Knight is filled with them, and they are almost all the time very satisfying and interesting to play. Doing side quests give you upgrade points, which you will need a lot if you are keen on making the game easier, as the upgrades are a lot more branching and numerous than in previous installments. Better implemented as well.
Some of my gripes are quite minor. The biggest one is that the challenge map packs are unlocked not by solving puzzles or progressing in the story as City is, but unlockable via DLC (correct me if I'm wrong). This not only feels very greedy, but extremely unsatisfying to play and solve riddles without unlocking any of the challenge maps. Other than that, there is little choice of robin/catwoman/harley/whatever skins available. Which is not that big of a deal, because they aren't unplayable in the free roam anyway. Also, you can only equip the sweet sweet batmobile skins in free roam once you clear out all the tanks etc.
As an addition, huge props to Rocksteady for doing the extra animation for the skins. Though they are not present in the last bit of the game, it is still highly appreciated.
I won't make a judgement on sound, texture, graphics, etc. I can't judge the graphics as I am running the game in a potato and I'm not a good sound judge. They sound good and they look good. That's it.
Overall score: scores are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It's a good game. It's cheap. If you have a decent PC, get it.

If you're a fan of South Park, then you probably don't need me to tell you to play this game. It's certainly more than a lame RPG with a South Park skin, but it's less than an a masterpiece that elevates the genre and the source material.
Pros:
*Funny story from start to finish
*Fun to explore the South Park world on your own
*Fun, somewhat-deep combat system that even non-rpg fans can enjoy
*High quality cut scenes and writing
*Good environment variety
Cons:
*Brings nothing new to the table
*No real reason to return to the game after you've completed the main story
*NOT for people who have never seen South Park
I feel like the pros are self explanatory, so I'll elaborate on the cons. The game does not introduce any new ideas that do not already exist in the South Park universe. Almost every single joke in the game is a reference to something that is in the show. For fans of the show, like myself, this is a good thing. But this completely closes the door for any non-SouthPark fans. Even in terms of combat, which I found to be very engaging as an RPG-enthusiast, there is nothing new here. The combat is good overall, and much deeper than I expected it to be, but it's still not as deep as what you might find in your typical RPG. There's a good tutorial and scalable difficulty, so even people new to the RPG genre can jump right into the game and have a good time. It comes off as RPG-lite, which is understandable as the game needs to appeal to a broad spectrum of South Park fans.
The main story is high quality all the way through, and the writing is solid, but once you've completed the main quest and side quests, there is nothing else to do. You can achievement hunt and look for collectibles, but many of the previous mission areas are inaccessible, and there's no real reason to explore. You won't find a secret side quest that you never knew about, or a mini-boss that you'll have to grind to level 99 to beat. As an RPGer, I found this to be a detriment, as even the old school Final Fantasy games had this.
Overall, I had a great time with this game, and I highly recommend to any and all South Park fans. Even those who aren't interested in RPGs. Non-South Park fans would do best to stay away, as there's not enough new things to appeal to people just looking for a good RPG, and almost all the jokes are show-referential.

After many hours spent in Gotham I can say this: Arkham Knight has succeeded.
It may have cost Warner and Rocksteady an amount of time to fix what was broken, but lets face it, mistakes happen, apologies have been made and free DLC was given to compensate.
Although the game has its flaws, the overall experience as the Batman is satisfying. The combat still stands, with some new shiny gadgets and a new Batsuit. There were some point during game when I thought that some gadgets from previous games would have been a warm welcome. When I was faced with some breakable walls, I wanted the improved Batclaw for example. Instead I had to fly trough it, which let to some frustration when my speed wasn't fast enough for the third time.
The Story is a direct sequel to Arkham City, I will not spoil any major plot points here, but if you are really spoiler sensitive skip to the next paragraph. **MILD SPOILERS AHEAD** The story begins around Halloween and this time Scarecrow takes the lead together with his new angry army general The Arkham Knight. Scarecrow really takes all the credits when it comes to charismatic villains, while the Arkham Knight mostly sounds like a spoiled child.
I found a lot of enjoyment in all the little side stories, but overall I was disappointed in some resolutions at the end of the chains. Especially if you invested 15 hours to defeat the Knight and the real battle isn't really face to face.
The second story I was disappointed about was Deathstroke, I really expected a Arkham Origins epicness, but after all the taunts the story arch felt flat.
Overall the conclusion of the Story (or at least the Scarecrow story) was satisfying and imo, better than Asylum (where are talking about the ending).
If you are a gamer who decides to buy a game depending on the length, than this game is worth it. The amount of side objectives is immense, the main story takes about 15-20 hours, and along the way there are many extra missions you can take up like saving firemen crew, stop bank heists, chase villains and of course the infamous riddles.
These riddles are not always as fresh and new as they felt in Asylum, and I think Rocksteady over did it a little.
Although some are very clever created, a lot of them feel as extra fluff to keep you going, especially as you need them all to get the real ending. YOU READ IT RIGHT, you need ALL THE RIDDLER TROPHIES to get the real good ending.
With 243 trophies on the counter, it takes a enormous grind to complete.
Of course you can always watch the ending online if it suits you, but if you are like me, you want to earn it by doing it.
If all the Riddler challenges and trophies were interesting enough it would be less of a chore, but they aren't, at least not all of them. 150 would have been a better mark.
This game introduces you to the full advanced Batmobile. Although I really like to drive around and felt all powerful in this handsome Wayne toy. The shine wears off after hours of gameplay. It has to fit in the story, fit in the game. But to many times it felt as if the game has been built around the Batmobile and thus makes it "so convenient." You use it for: Boss battles, challenges, Riddler trophy locations, reaching areas etc . It's like everyone knew Batman was gonna bring his car, so they prepared for it, which feels odd. In the end, it is so overused that the real boss battles from Asylum, City and Origins have no place here, because the Batmobile saves the day every time.
Conclusion, Although the city is deserted again and the story tries to sum up a reason for it to happen, it kinda feels lame. It would have been such an enjoyment to finally be the hero for Gotham's civilians, but again we are stuck with thugs only.
In the end the game really delivers on fan service, almost every iconic Batman character has to come pass, all the little stories within Gotham are well executed. I think it's sad that some characters haven't got more screen time this time around. The gameplay is solid, but the Batmobile is overused. The pacing could have been a bit better with a bit less of the trophy hunt. The story delivers, the graphics are outstanding and the soundtrack makes the experience complete.
