If you're a fan of South Park, then you probably don't need me to tell you to play this game. It's certainly more than a lame RPG with a South Park skin, but it's less than an a masterpiece that elevates the genre and the source material.
Pros:
*Funny story from start to finish
*Fun to explore the South Park world on your own
*Fun, somewhat-deep combat system that even non-rpg fans can enjoy
*High quality cut scenes and writing
*Good environment variety
Cons:
*Brings nothing new to the table
*No real reason to return to the game after you've completed the main story
*NOT for people who have never seen South Park
I feel like the pros are self explanatory, so I'll elaborate on the cons. The game does not introduce any new ideas that do not already exist in the South Park universe. Almost every single joke in the game is a reference to something that is in the show. For fans of the show, like myself, this is a good thing. But this completely closes the door for any non-SouthPark fans. Even in terms of combat, which I found to be very engaging as an RPG-enthusiast, there is nothing new here. The combat is good overall, and much deeper than I expected it to be, but it's still not as deep as what you might find in your typical RPG. There's a good tutorial and scalable difficulty, so even people new to the RPG genre can jump right into the game and have a good time. It comes off as RPG-lite, which is understandable as the game needs to appeal to a broad spectrum of South Park fans.
The main story is high quality all the way through, and the writing is solid, but once you've completed the main quest and side quests, there is nothing else to do. You can achievement hunt and look for collectibles, but many of the previous mission areas are inaccessible, and there's no real reason to explore. You won't find a secret side quest that you never knew about, or a mini-boss that you'll have to grind to level 99 to beat. As an RPGer, I found this to be a detriment, as even the old school Final Fantasy games had this.
Overall, I had a great time with this game, and I highly recommend to any and all South Park fans. Even those who aren't interested in RPGs. Non-South Park fans would do best to stay away, as there's not enough new things to appeal to people just looking for a good RPG, and almost all the jokes are show-referential.

I've only bought AK on a sale (20.99€ for the base game and all downloadable content) in February, so I haven't really had the opportunity to experience its launch issues. What I got to play was a beautiful, well-optimized masterpiece of a game.
Arkham Knight is much more cinematic than its predecessors, with the cutscenes being in-engine and, at some points in the story, giving you control over other characters, like Gordon.
The main story is alright, nothing too special about it, but it is realized so wonderfully that it left a lasting appeal. Along with the side missions, it does a great job of wrapping up each character's personal story.
The combat is the best it's ever been, with added environmental interaction and Batmobile assists. I found the much-disliked Batmobile sequences fun, but I guess it's different for each person. Predator is fun and the enemies are more lethal than ever - they make for a challenge even with the added Fear takedowns. There are plenty of challenges and eight different playable characters (with DLC included).
I recommend getting the full edition with all the content, if not then at least the Most Wanted missions, as they are a worthy (if not necessary) addition to the game.
With all these in mind, Arkham Knight truly stands as a crown to the series, and a worthy sendoff for Batman as we've come to know him since Asylum.

I have to say, I am becoming increasingly disappointed with big gaming website critics. They have let me down far too often. This game's praises were sung across all major gaming sites, and yet it's just not that good. Is it beautiful to look at? Sure, but that's about all it has going for it.
This game was scary for about the first hour, but after I accumulated a few strong weapons and the "jump scares" started becoming repetitive, I was no longer surprised by anything. So maybe the story is where this game shines? Sorry, no. I get the sense that this game's story was trying to be Aliens, but after a couple hours of play, I rarely cared what my next objective was since they were all such mundane meaningless tasks anyway (such as going around an obstruction, or restoring power to some section, etc).
Finally there's the combat. While I thoroughly enjoyed the look and feel of the weapons, this game gets sci-fi technology right, the actual combat was mediocre and repetitive. The dismemberment mechanic was a nice touch, but not enough to keep me engaged. So while the major gaming websites gave this game an 8-9/10, I would give it a 6/10.
I bought this game on sale along with the second one, so hopefully the sequel will be better.

This game was created so that other player can create their stories on this platform.  Some very good mods already exist for it.  If you love Fantasy mixed with Science Fiction than this is the perfect game for you!

Dead Space was released 6 years ago, yet is still capable of immersing you into the dark atmosphere of the Ishimura.  Taking inspiration from films like Ridley Scott's Alien, it weaves a tale of horror and survival.
You play as Isaac Clarke, an engineer.  Issac is completely mute throughout the game, which adds to the affect of putting your own self in Issac's shoes.  The story is largely played out through your general completion of objectives, and also through text and audio logs left behind by the Ishimura's unlucky crew.  The graphics are a little dated, yet still hold up well and I was impressed by the visuals still.
You battle creatively designed abominations known as Necromorphs.  Probably the most brutal and unforgiving enemies ever encountered in a video game.  Weapons are varied and interesting, allowing you to give brutal effect to your killings.  All weapons are upgradable by collecting tokens known as "power nodes" giving you another feeling of progression and power.
Dead Space is an awesome and much needed addition to the survival horror genre.

I've only bought AK on a sale (20.99€ for the base game and all downloadable content) in February, so I haven't really had the opportunity to experience its launch issues. What I got to play was a beautiful, well-optimized masterpiece of a game.
Arkham Knight is much more cinematic than its predecessors, with the cutscenes being in-engine and, at some points in the story, giving you control over other characters, like Gordon.
The main story is alright, nothing too special about it, but it is realized so wonderfully that it left a lasting appeal. Along with the side missions, it does a great job of wrapping up each character's personal story.
The combat is the best it's ever been, with added environmental interaction and Batmobile assists. I found the much-disliked Batmobile sequences fun, but I guess it's different for each person. Predator is fun and the enemies are more lethal than ever - they make for a challenge even with the added Fear takedowns. There are plenty of challenges and eight different playable characters (with DLC included).
I recommend getting the full edition with all the content, if not then at least the Most Wanted missions, as they are a worthy (if not necessary) addition to the game.
With all these in mind, Arkham Knight truly stands as a crown to the series, and a worthy sendoff for Batman as we've come to know him since Asylum.

For me the biggest best part about this game is that it's
, and I love
.  And I mean this is actual, proper SR too, not like some of the dribble that's carried the SR name in the past.  It's made by some of the folks who created SR in the first place, and it definitely shows by how deeply entwined with the actual lore it is.  If you like - or, like me, love - SR, you owe it to yourself to get this game.
But that's not all!  The writing is top notch, with great characters and a great story with lots of neat twists and turns.  The art is beautiful, making the game look like a painting come to life.  And the turn-based tactical combat - while not exactly original - is very well-executed and fun to play.
Further, it's set up so you can make your own campaigns, which is pretty dang cool in my book.
Though I understood pretty much everything that was going on in the story, understanding almost every reference and technical term that came flying my way, I'm not entirely certain it would be nearly as accessible for anyone who doesn't already know the SR rulebooks forwards and backwards or is at least somewhat familiar with the setting.  This may be a foundless fear, but I figure I should mention it just in case.
Character stats were greatly simplified from the original systems, and even compared to at least one of the previous SR video games, which I do understand to a degree.  But I feel they may have simplified a little bit too much, and would have welcomed a little more depth.  That may be just me being a rules lawyer, tho'.
If my comments above don't speak plainly enough for themselves, I don't really have much bad to say about this game, but I fully realize that that might simply be my own pro-
bias.  The game does have its faults, and I do wish it had a bit more depth than it does, but overall I feel that its pros far outweigh its cons, so I feel very confident in recommending it to folks.  And if you can, play the SNES and Genesis games first!

The Half-Life series is like the Beatles of FPS gaming in the way that playing Half-Life or the Beatles now, you find yourself thinking that they're somewhat dated. Upon further playing you realise why they feel dated: it's because everyone since then has, either consciously or unconsciously, been influenced by them. While other games go for flash, Half-Life 2 goes for subtlety both in narrative and in gameplay. This results in a game that is brilliant in its minimalism. While it's easy to be put off by the lack of cutscenes, some form of guide to objectives, or even a talking player character, you begin to realise that all this culminates in an experience that immerses you in the environment. The lack of cutscenes deprives you of exposition- a thing we have come to expect in video games, literature and movies- and instead creates a narrative as if you were actually there. Think about it, if any scenario in video games were to happen to us, would we have an opening cutscene with a monologue? The lack of clear guides further solidifies this immersiveness, without a shining marker or dot on a map telling you how to progress, you are forced to look at the environment to figure out how to progress, whether it is noticing a small gap in a fence or a tiny piece of graffiti that hides a resuply cache. The fact that Gordon (the guy you play as) doesn't talk again is a slight put off but you realise that with this, his opinions don't change your own and you fill in with your own quips, in my case an NPC was congratulating me after winning a particularly tough fight and I found myself muttering "No thanks to you". This narrative style results in game that is constantly flowing. While in most games, there is a clear distinction between "Killing Time" and "Story time", Half-Life 2 melds these two in such a way that keeps the momentum going, as opposed to the "stop-start" feel of games that have a more conventional narrative style.
I'd recommend this game to people who are looking for something beyond the brainless gloss of mainstream games, I believe that it's my Call of Duty to not mention the titles of the games to which I am referring and I uphold that promise as my Medal of Honor, even though it feels like crossing a Battlefield to acheive this. In short, a game that is brilliant without the inclusion of Kevin Spacey

I, as a fan of the Arkham games, wasn't disappointed by this last installment of the franchise. It had everything I love about previous Arkham games for- enjoyable fighting system, atmospheric environment, interesting characters (villains in particular), world that you can explore (this time with references to villains we haven't even seen in the Arkham games and also references to Superman and The Green Arrow) and last but not least the story, but it also added some new stuff as Batmobile and Fear Mode.
Should you buy the game? You like Batman or enjoyed the last two (three if you want) games? Then yeah, buy it, I think it will be worth your money and time.
But if you are still here, then I would like to talk a bit about the main story, because I think that it was a good and a bad story at the same time. Arkham games always had this ONE big villain (Joker in Asylum and City) and the rest of the villains were there to fill up the story. This time  the big bad guy is Scarecrow. But you may say- "But there is a guy in the game who is called Arkham Knight! His name is in the tittle of the game!". And yeah... He is also a big villain, but he is not the last villain you face in the story. The Arkham Knight has his own storyline that is nearly not connected to the Scarecrow storyline. Yes, they are kind of allies, but their stories aren't really connected. And it felt like they pushed a great story about Arkham Knight (okey, maybe a bit obvious story, but still) into the Scarecrow story just to get a longer game.
By all that I meant to say that they had two different things in one game and it didn't feel as a single great-structured story.
Still if you take the stories one by one- they are both good.
Still 8.5/10 for the game as a whole.

Shadowrun Returns succeeds primarily by harnassing the creepy, cybepunky/fantasy setting in a way that is neither too expository nor too assuming - this really is one of the best RPG settings out there, and this is the first PC version of the game that's brought that to the forefront. The turn-based combat is solid, if not the most technically sound I've ever seen. The characters are quite cool within the Shadowrun paradigm. The story, of course, is ridiculous, but I wouldn't call it anything worse than average.
If I have one complaint, it's that Shadowrun Returns gives you a taste of the rich, well-developed setting...and then yanks a lot of it away by making the game so linear. While the user-generated content will add a lot to this game going forward, it'll take some patience/real urge to play a different kind of character to want to replay the main campaign. Also, the decision to leave out some kind of co-op option is freaking mindboggling, given the audience that they were targeting with this game.
Long story short, it's quite good despite significant shortcomings.

Back in June 2016, after many poorly made decisions by Tripwire I gave this game a negative review, the details of my decision are down in the review.
Now as of August 2017 I think it's about time I change it to positive.
You see, back then it was not the game itself that was bad, it never was, it was Tripwire prioritizing the wrong things and acting bad towards the fanbase, fortunately that has changed and now not only the game is even better, but things are going smooth and Tripwire is doing a lot better, so it's only fair I change my review.
So my positive review:
• Graphics: Tripwire did a great job on the graphics, the game is beautiful (as much as a gory and bloody game can be xD).
• Optimization: Despite it's beautiful graphics, the game runs really well both on decent and more simple computers.
• Gameplay: Not much to say here, it's a known style that works well enough. Lots of options of maps, classes, weapons etc.
• Workshop: You can download a ton of cool stuff made by the players, community made maps are a great way to make this game even more diverse.
• Microtransactions: Crate/Key gambling is a cancer in the modern gaming scenario and no matter how good a game is, I will
list microtransactions as negative.
• Setting up servers: Back in Killing Floor 1 it was really simple to set up a server for you and your friends, you could just open the game, set things up and click either listen for a quick play or dedicated if you wanted to leave the server running even if you weren't playing, max you'd have to do was set up router ports in case they were closed, unfortunately Tripwire changed this and now it's a lot more troublesome to set up servers, you need to download an external tool and dedicated server files and set them up manually in a much more complex process (to be honest it isn't really that hard and Tripwire does provide a step-by-step tutorial on their wiki page, it is however much more complicated than it was on KF1 and takes a lot longer to properly set it up).
That's about it, if you wish to understand my previous negative review, please read it below.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Where to start..
Well, the first Killing Floor
an amazing game even today, it's great, so I figured I'd give a chance to this one despite my own "
" rule. Sadly it was a HUGE disappointment and I've come to decide that I will never break this rule again and here's why:
• They are
slow to develop this game, they had said the game was going to be finished by the end of 2015, but by that date, they haven't even finished the perks they initially promised.
This review is being written in June of 2016 and as of now, the game is FAR from being finished.
• At some point, after telling everyone they didn't plan to add microtransactions to the game, not only they did exactly what they said they would not do, but they completely stopped the development of the game and it's core content to focus in the creation of the in-game store, so a game that was already late in development is was put aside so they could focus on something else (in the meantime, they even made a COMPLETE VR GAME so you can see how they care with those waiting for KF2 to be finished).
• They censor pretty much anyone who complains about these things and developers are pretty salty to the community when they don't agree with what is being told.
• Class balance is a joke, not to mention the last perk, which they delivered 7 months late is simply terrible.
• Game went on sale like a couple of weeks after it was initially released, which is a complete lack of respect with those who purchased it on release.
So, while the game itself IS good and it CAN be fun, the developers of this game are lazy, salty and doesn't respect what their customers want.
While I could recommend the game, I won't, I don't think Tripwire deserves, they have a lot to learn, sadly I thought they'd have experience thanks to KF1, seems I was wrong, it almost feels like it's a completely new group of people under the same name.
Want to have fun? Buy Kf1, it's good and already finished, they can't screw it up as they're doing with KF2.

There are very few games like XCom Enemy Unknown made today. Strategy games apart from sims are far and few between, especially made by AAA studios and publishers. This game was no different, as it took a very long time to get developed since the publisher originally wanted to make it a first person shooter.
Instead what we got is a delightful return to form for the series. XCom Enemy Unknown is a game where you play as the commander of a team that specializes in stopping an alien invasion of the planet Earth. The game is a turn based strategy game and heavy in things like cover and approaching carefully. Your squad of soldiers likewise is heavily customizeable, and as you complete more missions they grow identities of their own.
What amuses me is how the game likewise punishes you for failure. There's a setting in the game called "Ironman" mode which disables quicksaving. What this does is force you to either restart an entire mission from the start, or bite the bullet and move on if one of your favorite squad members dies. Because you can only level up soldiers by completing missions, this mode makes you play extra carefully so you can get everyone out alive.
Enemy Unknown is a refreshing change of pace from the nonstop first person shooters we get every few months. A title that injects a little humanity into an otherwise drab and faceless genre. Where your unwilling to make redshirts out of your pawns.

This is not a review of the base game. This is a review of the popular mod, The Long War.
Short version: It is terrible, do not play it.
Long version:
Long War adds a load of depth to xcom. Here's a list.
- It fleshes out the Geoscape with a more complex and interesting alien metagame (they have missions, resources, etc).
- It adds many new soldier classes, all of which are very useful and distinct
- It makes the psionics a real part of the game, rather than a weird, largely ignored late game add on
- It rebalances many things (SHIVS are buffed, flying units are massively buffed so that they aren't automatically flanked anymore).
- It adds loads more small items, giving the player far more tactical options
- It stretches the campaign out, so that you can't just skip right over mid game tech
- It modifies the difficult curve so that late game isn't a procession anymore
There are probably a few dozen other things that I have forgotten about, having been so long since I played Vanilla, but that should give you a good heads up. At first, all of this new content looks really enticing, but I've played a few hundred hours now and I can tell you it is one of the worst experiences I've ever had video gaming, an excercise in suffering prolonged by my determination to complete it. So, onto the bad:
- Long War has 'fixed' the difficulty curve problem of vanilla (too hard at start, far too easy late game) and made it so that the first few months is a easy as♥♥♥♥♥♥and mid late game is utterly absurd.
- Long War adds two extra soldiers to the game (6-8 instead of vanillas 4-6), and consequently adds more aliens as well to compensate for the fact that your squad has all this extra firepower. Which sounds perfectly reasonable. The trouble is the base game was never designed to have this many units on a map. The maps (particularly the abduction/terror maps) are designed for 4-6 soldiers and 15-20 aliens. Not 8 soldiers and 35+ aliens. The end result is an overcrowded nightmare where just about every single mission has you overwatching at the lz desperately trying to avoid triggering the 3-4 pods that are just out of sight. Does this sound like fun? Because it's not. Btw, don't even think about using that Assault aggressively, it's a squad wipe waiting to happen.
- You can't just jump into the game and explore it. If you haven't read copious amounts of details before you start playing, you're going to get wrecked. It took me three tries when I started before I finally realised that a big part of the air war was that scout and raider ufos that are flying very low will land, and you didn't have to risk interceptors to shoot them down. Not knowing stuff like this will end your campaign.
- If there's anything you missed before you started (like the above) that becomes relevent in the midgame, you're probably going to have to start over. Didn't realise psionics are essentially free once the lab is built? Missed a detail about the air war? Got your research order wrong? Start over. Trouble is in Long War 'starting over' after about the third month means goodbye to 20-30 hours of play time.
- The expanded rng is really problematic at times, and just encourages hugely defensive play. Do not run your Assault up expecting him to end that big Mectoid, its completely unreliable and you are just throwing away that troop. Hunker and suppress til you die of boredom, the way of Long War.
- The base game is still really, really ♥♥♥♥ing buggy, and in a game that runs as long as this ironmanning is basically impossible. I have seen snipers grapple across the map into the enemy command pod, I have had saves corrupted, I have had pods on the other side of the map, well outside of vision range, activate and bum rush me. Sometimes it's minor, sometimes it's campaign ending. Remember what I said above? Have fun grinding through the tedious first few months again when that happens. Don't worry it's only 20 odd hours of gameplay. My current playthrough I'm almost at the Gollop chamber and suddenly I can't save anymore. What fun!
- The game throws so many missions at you that half the time you feel as though you are making no progress at all. Half the fun of this game is the sense of reward when new gear is rolled out. I'm all in favour of making the campaign longer to make mid game tech more relevent but this is absurd.
- The late game is an incredibly tedious grind, and the problem of all the good tech only showing up pretty much just before the temple mission is still present and correct. This is particularly problematic with the airgame, where you sit on laser cannons for months on end, and firestorms, emps and plasma all show up in the last few months of the game.
- The game provides tools to counter the stronger enemies that you will face, but some aliens are countered by everything and some by almost nothing. It's a mess. Mutons are countered by blowing up their cover, floaters are dealt with by psionics, mechtoids and sectopods don't like chem grenades, sectoid are beaten by psi inspiration, all of which is great. Chrysallids, however, are still a joke (they just cluster up and get ruined by grenades or assaults, just like they always did). They aren't the real problem though. Oh no. For some reason, the Cyberdisk (which shows up in like month 3-4, reasonably early on in the campaign) gets extra special treatment. Can't be psionically disabled, can't be chem grenaded, yet it still gets huge armour reduction and flying unit evasion. What?
- The devs say that if any part of the game is bothering you, you can edit the INI file. Well, many people aren't comfortable doing that, because they either dont want to diddle with it, or in my case, just regard it as another form of cheating. Having a problem with the game? Edit the INI file. Or just type in a cheat code I guess. Not a rewarding experience to play a game for a hundred hours, realise you made a mistake around hour 50 and have to cheat to get around it.
- The maps have been modified to have new start locations! Some of which are obscenely unfair, with little to no cover available! Or they dump you right in the middle of the map (surrounded by pods, remember) with no option but to either abandon or get smashed! Sound like fun? It isn't. Particularly bad culprits are the Graveyard map that has you start behind the shed (my god), the truckstop lz in the middle of the map, and the roadway one at the bottom of the hill. On the flipside, the Doorn map has a a new lz on the opposite side of the pit, which is laughably easy if you brought a sniper and a concealment scout.
- You will fail many missions in this game. That's the way it's supposed to be. You are not supposed to take large landed ships in March/April. Only, the missions you are most likely to fail are the critical, game ending ones. It's not the landed battleship or the alien base (god the alien base is easy) that will give you grief, it's a terror mission with a terrible lz and a million aliens on contact that you have to abandon/squadwipe, causing a nation to leave the council. This happens a lot. Feel like starting this hugely long grindy game all over again after getting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tted like this? No? Better start save scumming then. Again, map size is the problem here.
- The length of the game makes it super duper god damned boring, repetitive and tedious. No normal human has the time to sit through the whole thing. I've seen multiple people start streams and LPs of Long War and I found only a handful that ever bothered to actually finish this thing. Not even Beaglerush could be arsed actually completing his LW youtube LP, he taps out after about 140 hours and early pulse weaponry IIRC.
I'm out of space. In short, it's filled with great ideas but the end result is total crap. Be thankful the devs took note and added much of that stuff to Xcom 2, and play that instead.

Awesome RPG, mixing Tolkien's 'Lord of the Rings' with William Gibson's 'Neuromancer'.
The gameplay is spot on for those who like exploration, turn-based combat and skill-levelling. The amount of weapons, abilities, magic spells and creatures to use is huge, and the characters have a lot of depth to their personalities and dialog that every time you interact with them is quite engaging.
The art design for the characters is a little lackluster during play, but the amount of detail used to create your character and level their skills, abilities and weapons makes up for it. The environments are mostly dark and gloomy (with a few key exceptions) and give off a gritty, troubled, desperate atmosphere, making you want to explore every crack and crevice of the city.
The story for the main campaign starts off with a kick and gets you deeply involved with the characters and the environments, but around 3/4 of the way through, it gets a bit absurd and doing the main mission becomes a chore.
Still, if the main campaign is not enough, there is always new user-created content to try out. And you can also use the Shadowrun Returns Scene Editor to create your own stories. However, if you're not familiar with using logic and triggers for events, then good luck creating your own levels with story.

Happy Birthday Half-Life 2. Can't believe it's been ten years.
Did not think it was going to turn out this way.
When this came out I considered it to include the most intrusive form of DRM at the time, Steam. It's funny how time changes things. In Steam's wake, it's competitors started using limited installations or require a constant internet connection. Suddenly, Steam became the lesser of other evils.
The end of physical media for PC should have been much more obvious to me at the time. I was worried they would gain to much control as we moved away from it. They've gain a lot more than they used to, but they don't control everything. The age of DRM didn't kill mods or dedicated servers (though it did severely wound them in many cases!) and it definitely did not kill piracy.
What it did do though was fundamentally change the consumer relationship. Sales psychology is much more aggressive and access to product is at an all time high. Having been a long time fan of the original XCOM: UFO Defense on both PC and Playstation, hearing about the re-release under the umbrella of XCOM: Enemy Unknown was exciting news.
I took time to play through this, piece by piece, chipping away at it each night until I completed it to my satisfaction.  XCOM keeps true to its roots by making the player suffer for their mistakes.  A full turn based strategy game with base building elements, the player guides their troops in individual battles while managing the design, construction, and research of their base.  Do you hire more scientists to research alien weaponry faster, or do you focus on more mechanics and engineers to build space ships and robots with lasers?  The choice is yours, and each you make will have consequences.
It's a delicate balance of gameplay to ensure that all countries are satisfied, protected, and happy.  If a country becomes too unhappy, it pulls itself out of the XCOM project, which can have devastating results.
Should you invest in XCOM, be prepared to save a lot, save early, and save often.  You'll form a squad of your elite soldiers, people you cannot live without.  Men and women that are so skilled that should anything happen to them, you will be devastated both emotionally and game-play wise, because they are seriously the backbone of your operations.  Swapping out your veterans for a team of rookies is a sure fire way to get annihilated at the hands of some experienced aliens.  It's far better to keep 3 veterans in the team along with some rookies, who can help mentor and hand-hold the newbies until they have enough experience and rank to become useful themselves.
I found that keeping the game on normal difficulty and playing through one time was satisfying enough for me, and I enjoyed the difficulty that the game had -- only having to reload a few times.  Once you get your key soldiers and some special psionic abilities, the game really starts to get fun.  Without giving spoilers, the game deviates slightly from the original XCOM game around the ending, but it's still an interesting and unique way to end the game and give closure to the player.
For some parting thoughts:  When you get your soldiers, try and personalize them.  Make them look and feel like your family and friends.  Make a soldier after yourself.  I found that by doing this, I was extra careful with my soldiers, never taking un-needed risks because I was so afraid that I'd do something that might lose them.
If you end up getting XCOM, good luck -- it can be a difficult, but rewarding game.

The Stick of Truth is, on its own legs, a hilarious romp of an RPG; it is the fantasy adventure that occurs when a collection of kids play make-believe, and it plays with the theme heavily; at some points reminding you that it's all made up and at others diving completely into the fantasy.  If you're a South Park fan, this game is a must-own. It has nearly 20 years' worth of comedy references that date back to even the earliest seasons, managing to cram pack references everywhere you look. Most of the time, you don't even realize it, as the references are often seamlessly merged with the fabric of the fantasy story; no easy feat. My favorite gag was when I had to use the skip cutscene function to make Jimmy stop stuttering.
If you're not a South Park fan, this is still a great game to own, but you should understand that a minor amount of the humor will be lost on you. As a game aside from its theme, it's fantastic, but only about 30-35 hours long at the most, even if you're one of the every-nook-and-cranny-types. That being said, there are multiple classes to replay the game as, each providing their own gags.
One point of warning: This game is not family friendly. It's not even adult-friendly, actually. It's for the most purile juvenile in all of us. For example, one of your regularly used weapons is a broken♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of spoilable origin that resides in your♥♥♥♥♥♥permanently and gives you the ability to teleport. There is even a level set in the town's planned parenthood, which dives headfirst into all of the dark comedy tropes we never wished to explore regarding abortion. If you find distaste in the show, the game will make you call Tipper Gore. Just don't tell her that her husband is in the game.

Many players will dive into this game expecting the definitive South Park experience, but you won't get it.
Pros:
-Fantastic voice acting
-Funny script
-Fun gameplay
Cons:
-The game is short.
-In terms of the sheer amount of material they could have drawn on from the show, you see only a fraction of it in the game.
-There is little replay value.
-The total game area is actually tiny.
-Surprisingly bad performance.
-Unlike other RPGs, there is very little variation in the story. At a couple points you get to make choices, but they have the same results and so are meaningless.
Overall it's an okay game, but chances are you'll play through it once or twice then drop it forever. Get it while it's on sale because it is most definitely NOT worth $40. For that much you're mostly paying for the brand name.

Happy Birthday Half-Life 2. Can't believe it's been ten years.
Did not think it was going to turn out this way.
When this came out I considered it to include the most intrusive form of DRM at the time, Steam. It's funny how time changes things. In Steam's wake, it's competitors started using limited installations or require a constant internet connection. Suddenly, Steam became the lesser of other evils.
The end of physical media for PC should have been much more obvious to me at the time. I was worried they would gain to much control as we moved away from it. They've gain a lot more than they used to, but they don't control everything. The age of DRM didn't kill mods or dedicated servers (though it did severely wound them in many cases!) and it definitely did not kill piracy.
What it did do though was fundamentally change the consumer relationship. Sales psychology is much more aggressive and access to product is at an all time high. Weighing how much money I have wasted compared to the games I might not have played if Steam didn't exist, I don't know if I would do the same thing again. But that is of little consequence considering how things are now.
Sorry for rambling on about stuff that likely does not matter for a purchase decision. But, today is this game's birthday and it changed the game, whether I liked or not. So it deserves some recognition today, at least more than Valve is giving it.

Starting this game, my immediate sense was it forces me to use the batmobile WAAAY too often.
After finishing it, here are a few takeaways.
-The riddler is seriously the worst part of this game, hands down. The racing is bad enough (oh yes, there are racetracks), but 243 riddles need to be solved to 100% the game and essentially get the true ending. This is so mind numbingly boring that I just youtubed it. It ends up feeling like it was just to pad out the play time, and that kind of grinding shouldn't ever be a thing.
-Batmobile default controls. On the pc it seriously wants you to use left control by default to trigger riddler blockades. I suggest you change this immediately to something that isn't terrible. Also first person view makes the wall driving you are required to do during the racing sections far easier, and a lot more fun. The game should suggest this during these sections.
-The stuff using batman and not the batmobile was pretty fun, and generally what I expect of a batman game.
-Story was okay. There are a few parts where I went uh that isn't how that works, and a few parts that were downright confusing, but all in all decent.
-Regular tank battles aren't bad. There are too many of them, but still. Somewhat fun, just not really batman-y. Stealth tank battles are painful to watch, and/or play. Kind of boring.
- It would have been nice to see a little more line launcher use. It's barely used at all, and most of the destructible wall puzzles are instead solved with the batmobile, rather than with explosive gel and the launcher (since you can't use both at once, which is silly).
-Some of the Dlc storylines were great. The Mr. Freeze storyline being particularly great.
I still can't say I recommend it. The frustrating and bad parts of this game just ruined the entire experience for me. Though I can definitely say if I knew about first person on the batmobile in the very beginning that would have solved some of my major problems with it. I also wouldn't even have bothered starting to collect the riddler trophies. There really isn't any point unless you are going to grind through to the end, and it really isn't worth it.
If you love Batman games enough to overlook it's flaws, I'd suggest getting it. If you aren't a major fan though and you are leaning towards buying it, nab it on a deep discount (shouldn't be hard) and you'll probably be satisfied.

Civ V is a very complex game and even after hundreds of hours one can still discover new tactics and learn new civilizations. But Civ V's complexity is a double edged sword, the best and the worst part of the game  at the same time. The complexity may be great, but it desroys the game's balance. Some civilizations, like the Babylonians, are far too strong, others, like the Ottomans or Venetians, are far too weak. This can be a problem if you want to play with friends,  but it hasn't to be, depending on your friends.
The bots are programmed reasonably, but on higher difficulties they get unfair advantages instead of playing better. This bugs me everytime when I play Civ V, but it is how it is.
Another thing I love about this game is, that you learn lots of things about history. The game is full of information. Every civilization, every leader, every world wonder, every building and even every unit has an entry in the so called 'Civilopedia'.  You want to know more about Washington? About the Ottoman Empire? About the German tanks or the Temple of Artemis? No problem! Just look it up! (Preferably when your friends take far too much time for their move again...)
But there is one more important thing: This game is hard to learn and even harder to master. You will need some time and much patience until you understand every game mechanic, but the satisfaction when you beat the game on the highest difficulty is totally worth it.

This game has great concepts behind it, but is not executed well. The storyline might be a fascinating read, but does not engage the player at all. The best scripted fight, the last fight of the game about 8 hours in, is almost as fun as the prologue of Neverwinter Nights. Almost.
My biggest complaint is with the story, but the game has potential to give the community what they are thirsty for. I'm not overly impressed with the graphics, and I really wished I could have changed angles from the point of view on the field, but for the most part the combat and character navigation is easy enough to manage. The equipment is very simple, though not explained well (*cough cybernetics cough*), and you don't have to put much thought into micro-managing your character or your hire-by-mission squadmates. It's impossible to get attached to characters as they're just a portrait to represent the mathhammer you wield as the gamer.
I did really like the etiquitte aspect to your character. The game gives you more conversation options if you have a higher Charisma stat, and with a higher Charisma you learn new jargon by which to speak with the appropriate factions (ie shadowrunners, security, corporate, or gang). Unfortunately, the dialogue is still linear and it only provides introductory ports for the equifinality of the storyline.
Pros: cheap, potential for community contribution, non-demanding of hardware, neat concepts.
Cons: easy, impersonal, clunky, and inconsequential.

Shadowrun Returns is a cRPG in the Baldur's Gate or Planescape Torment style, set in the Shadowrun universe.
For those that don't know, Shadowrun is basically a cyberpunk setting (think Blade Runner) mixed with your standard fantasy races and magic (elves, orcs, dwarves, etc).
The game itself is fantastic.  The turn based combat is perfect, and the storyline is quite good.  Everything runs fluid and its all very fun to play.  The character customization system is great, leading to what appears to be many different ways to play through the game.
The game comes with an editor and supports Steam Workshop, so there is no dearth of content to download and play with.
If any of that sounds remotely interesting to you I highly recommend checking this game out.
If I were to say something negative, I'd have to say that the graphics are simple and the animations basic.  However, depite relative simplicity, the art style is fantastic and makes the Shadowrun universe real.  Also understand that despite being relatively simple, the graphics are by no means poor.  There is great detail in the world, and all the characters are distinct from one another.  Nothing feels out of place, and the graphics never hinder the experience.
All-in-all I would highly recommend Shadowrun Returns

and take on alien invaders in
.
A 2.5D third person squad tactical game with percentile resolution system, where you are the commander of an elite anti-alien taskgroup that is fighting back against a force of technologically superior enemies intent on eliminating humankind.
I would recommend XCom if you enjoy being challenged by strategy games.  The game design is interesting, with full use of cover, concealment, panic, rage, etc. You can benefit from flanking targets, from being on higher ground, out of direct LOS, etc.
The UI is workable, with a simple interface and tutorials to cover what isn't obvious at first glance.  Weapons upgrades are interesting, with a range of specialisations and abilities within those specialties that can make for some very varied and useful combinations.
The AI has a good range of conservative and aggressive units, with a variety of tactics expected from each, as well as a medium of threats both close and ranged.
The graphics level is decent, and care has obviously been taken to ensure a quality product is presented to the screen the moment you start the game.
The game promises the native languages of their multicultural soldiers; so a French sniper will reply in French, a German heavy gunner will reply in German, a Russian assault gunner will reply in Russian.  For the most part, this actually adds to the game effect.
The RNG is
punishing. It's a system that favours chance over choice, and about 90% of the game's success depends purely on luck. While this can make some combat hair-raising, the majority of the time you'll be wondering what happened when a tiny alien basic grunt waltzes through 5x 95%-to-kill cover fire and then kills 4 of your men in succession with less-than-10%-hit.
That's not to say that it is imbalanced, or that the numbers display the wrong chances. This is the sense that you'll be hurt, badly, when those %s aren't perfectly covered.
The game promises "native languages of soldiers" - which really entices when you realise some of them are from Iraq, or Nigeria.  Then anyone not from a French, German, Russian, or Spanish lingual group begins speaks in a blaring American accent and fluent English; a bit jarring hearing a Yankee twang from a Brit, South African, New Zealander, or Aussie.
The missions get a bit 'samey' after a while - there needs to be a bit more variety with mission types.
The game glitches, though not as badly as other franchises can be held to on inspection. Freezes are common, but not unrecoverable, and the autosave negates most of the sting that brings.
The RNG can apply to more than just combat - it can also apply to panic levels in various countries, and you have to sometimes choose arbitrarily which of three countries is going to not hate you after a particular mission.
In a modern day military, apparently only one squad can be deployed at a time, and no ground troops are available for reinforcement.
Cover the "native languages".
Code patching for those glitchy AI moments.
More variation on missions - say, a 'king of the hill' where you aren't defending, or puzzle maps where you have to position soldiers at points a, d, and y to open the door and let the big bad alien out.
Did I mention the languages? I think I mentioned the languages.
A different ending would be nice -
.

"Risk of Rain," also known as "Risk of Buttclench" and "Ragequit Simulator 2015" is a permadeath sidescrolling shooter with decent controls and a constantly stable 60 FPS, two essentials for a roguelike.
In it, you play as a guy who just crashlanded on a planet.  You have to find the teleporter on the map (it moves around each session), activate it, survive for 90 seconds, and clear off any remaining enemies before you go to the next area.  Here's the catch: the game slowly increases in difficulty the longer you're on a level and doesn't reset, meaning you might see things as easy when you're in beginner-level difficulty but the longer you take to complete the level, the harder the enemies will be, so it might all be fun around Very Easy, but♥♥♥♥♥♥gets sour around Easy and if you reach Medium or higher before you've at least found and started the second teleporter... may God have mercy on your soul.
The maps themselves won't change much.  It's alright, though, because the teleporter can be anywhere on it, they're huge, and the game cycles between different sets of maps with around 10 in total across 4 tiers (plus UES Contact Light), so it doesn't really get old.  It's also got good netcoding for co-op, so you can bring along a friend without any out-of-sync issues.
Overall: 9/10.  $10?  Worth it.  $2.50?  Get it, or you're just stupid.

"Risk of Rain," also known as "Risk of Buttclench" and "Ragequit Simulator 2015" is a permadeath sidescrolling shooter with decent controls and a constantly stable 60 FPS, two essentials for a roguelike.
In it, you play as a guy who just crashlanded on a planet.  You have to find the teleporter on the map (it moves around each session), activate it, survive for 90 seconds, and clear off any remaining enemies before you go to the next area.  Here's the catch: the game slowly increases in difficulty the longer you're on a level and doesn't reset, meaning you might see things as easy when you're in beginner-level difficulty but the longer you take to complete the level, the harder the enemies will be, so it might all be fun around Very Easy, but♥♥♥♥♥♥gets sour around Easy and if you reach Medium or higher before you've at least found and started the second teleporter... may God have mercy on your soul.
The maps themselves won't change much.  It's alright, though, because the teleporter can be anywhere on it, they're huge, and the game cycles between different sets of maps with around 10 in total across 4 tiers (plus UES Contact Light), so it doesn't really get old.  It's also got good netcoding for co-op, so you can bring along a friend without any out-of-sync issues.
Overall: 9/10.  $10?  Worth it.  $2.50?  Get it, or you're just stupid.

First off. Let me say this. I enjoy the game. I do. Even if it's samey.
But Killing Floor 1 does everything better sans the movement and gun play.
The balance feels...strange? I'll go over the classes first. Then onto the other things,such as gameplay,difficulty,maps,micro transactions and other things.
The Firebug has problems killing things due to the fact that what it's class is about,burning everything,tends to take an abusrd amount of ammo to kill. But with the tier 3 weapon,the microwave gun,you shoot the floor at their feet and you kill them,but again,you don't have the ammo to actually be effective in longer waves or higher difficulties. The trench gun is trash as well. On Normal to possibly hard(with a decent support with ammo) you might be alright. But this is not a perk to take into Suicide or Hell On Earth.
The Commando. I honestly don't know what to feel about this perk class. An M14 Sharp Shooter has more ammo(if you take damage perks over ammo perks) and can stun enemies. You get to see cloaked enemies,like the Stalkers and the Patriarch. Other than that,there's no real point to this class anymore. Other classes can kill and clear minor mobs faster than you can with less ammo spent.
The Demolition perk is a funny one too. It falls into a similar problem the Firebug gets. Not enough ammo,but it's compounded by the fact that everything for this class is very expensive,and you don't get the full use out of it until at least wave 4 in longer maps. Heavy weaponry(Tier 2+3 weapons don't leave you room for a backup or a meidpistol to help your medic.) is fun,but you have to aim your shots and hope a Zed doesn't decide to spin you as you fire a rocket at a raging Scrake. There is a required perk,the one that lets your weapons resist Siren screams. But the perks feel half baked and not well thought out(I.e Less ammo for slightly more damage on a direct hit?)
The Medic. Can carry all his weapons at once without the need to carry dual 9mms. But the AR has funny recoil to me(this is subjective). The shotgun,I abseloutly love it. But it lacks ammo and stopping power compared to the Supports M1014. The SMG is pretty much pointless as it burns through ammo far too quickly to be useful(less ammo than the rifle the class gets.) and the pistol is overall a decent backup or off perk weapon for any class if you can carry it(sorry Demo!) YOu heal stuff,drop fart bombs and heal and poison. You're an essential player in harder difficulties. But if you're the last one,and you don't know what to do,you will get swamped quickly,especially with how quickly the weapons burn through ammo.
The Sharpshooter. Do the Commandos job but better! Carry an M14 if you want to be killing anything that moves. It's less powerful than any of the other weapons,and is about equal to the top tier weapon for the Commando,the SCARH. It's more accurate,and can penetrate or stun nearly any Zed you fight. Coupled with a high rate of fire,it's a stellar weapon. The Railgun is laughably overpowered if you can aim. If you can gather a group togeather you can freeze them with a grenade making easy pickings.
The Gunslinger,in KF1 was rolled into the Sharpshooter. These guns were your backups. They're all pistols. The only major downside to the Gunslinger is reload times. You have to plan ahead for this class,or risk getting swamped. This class,with Deagles,or 1911s is just as effective as a Commando at trash cleaning. The nail bomb is only effective in very small hallways.
The Support is all about the shotguns. Usually working with the Firebug and behind the Beserkers,they are all about keeping people stocked with ammo(once per wave) and killing anything that moves. A double barrel with the AA12 means you have won the game.  One of the strongest classes in the game. Even without a beserker to take the heat off,you can easily hold back the tide until you run out of shells.
The Beserker...well...I feel really bad for zerker drivers. This perk has been nerfed into the dirt. It's not useful at all as the support class can do it's job better and faster. Can't parry or block a boss or enraged Scrake or Fleshpound,so your formerly strongest abiltiy is rendered moot. Any other class with better weapons than you can do your job better than you. This class is pointless now.
Sharp Shooter,Gunslinger,Medic and Support are the main classes. The others aren't that great anymore in higher tier play,and often have problems in some way(i.e ammo,cost or weight) that hinder them more than they can help a team. If you were thinking about picking a perk,go with the 4 I mentioned if you want to play higher levels,and the others for Easy or Normal.
Now onto the maps. They're tiny,and dark for the most part. While they are well designed, I feel like they are overly cramped and the official maps number while much better than it was,still feels too few. There's tons of custom maps that range from awesome,to crap. At times, I do with that there were additional ammo spawns due to some classes needing more ammo.
Now, TWI has done some questionable things to balance the game well. Between the long times between patches,sometimes it feels like TWI doesn't do anything at all. For example,the reistances feel strange and awkward. But the gameplay itself feels solid. The graphics are great.  But the balance between classes is still in a strange place.
There is a PVP mode. It sucks. Don't bother with it.
Now,for microtransactions.
There's tons of problems with them,crates not opening,infinite loading so you can't open them,or the fact that you need to spend nearly 3$ an item to open it. There seems to be no point, If you get a crate or usb stick,I'd just sell it on the market,or not even bother.
Overall?
It's fun,but there's not much meat here. Theres no charm that makes it stand out compared to KF1. If you really want the game,get it on sale. But certainly try before you buy on a free play weekend.

Note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
Shadowrun Returns is an isometric turn-based cyberpunk RPG. The game's setting is based on the Shadowrun universe, and it is perhaps best summed up as "Fantasy meets Sci-Fi, or as one official tag-line put it: "Magic meets Machine". This isn't an idyllic world, megacorporations are the real powers, and those who aren't corporate wage-slaves try to make a living in the Shadows. The game itself features one campaign, but several more is avaliable from the steam workshop as Harebrained Schemes (the developers) have made the game design system and assets freely avaliable. I would say the mechanics are reminiscent of XCom, though with a fixed angle of view.
Pro:
*A fascinating setting, which will probably leave you wanting to learn more about the Shadowrun universe.
*An interesting main campaign, with more avaliable from the community.
*Excellent character portraits deserving of special mention.
*The Developer fully supports modding and new content.
*Possible to build a character's ability points the way you want it.
Con:
*The in-game character models have limited customization options and at times, this makes them clash badly with the exellent character portraits.
*Only one campaign, which is fairly limited in an A-to-B way, even if it IS well-written.
Summary:
This is a very good TBS, the characters are interesting if not as interesting as in its successor, Shadowrun: Dragonfall. The real attraction here is the cyberpunk world of Shadowrun, but it is well supported by good, solid mechanics and a developer that clearly cares about both the community and the game itself. 7/10 -Recommended.

A 2.5D third person squad tactical game with percentile resolution system, where you are the commander of an elite anti-alien taskgroup that is fighting back against a force of technologically superior enemies intent on eliminating humankind.
I would recommend XCom if you enjoy being challenged by strategy games.  The game design is interesting, with full use of cover, concealment, panic, rage, etc. You can benefit from flanking targets, from being on higher ground, out of direct LOS, etc.
The UI is workable, with a simple interface and tutorials to cover what isn't obvious at first glance.  Weapons upgrades are interesting, with a range of specialisations and abilities within those specialties that can make for some very varied and useful combinations.
The AI has a good range of conservative and aggressive units, with a variety of tactics expected from each, as well as a medium of threats both close and ranged.
The graphics level is decent, and care has obviously been taken to ensure a quality product is presented to the screen the moment you start the game.
The game promises the native languages of their multicultural soldiers; so a French sniper will reply in French, a German heavy gunner will reply in German, a Russian assault gunner will reply in Russian.  For the most part, this actually adds to the game effect.
The RNG is
punishing. It's a system that favours chance over choice, and about 90% of the game's success depends purely on luck. While this can make some combat hair-raising, the majority of the time you'll be wondering what happened when a tiny alien basic grunt waltzes through 5x 95%-to-kill cover fire and then kills 4 of your men in succession with less-than-10%-hit.
That's not to say that it is imbalanced, or that the numbers display the wrong chances. This is the sense that you'll be hurt, badly, when those %s aren't perfectly covered.
The game promises "native languages of soldiers" - which really entices when you realise some of them are from Iraq, or Nigeria.  Then anyone not from a French, German, Russian, or Spanish lingual group begins speaks in a blaring American accent and fluent English; a bit jarring hearing a Yankee twang from a Brit, South African, New Zealander, or Aussie.
The missions get a bit 'samey' after a while - there needs to be a bit more variety with mission types.
The game glitches, though not as badly as other franchises can be held to on inspection. Freezes are common, but not unrecoverable, and the autosave negates most of the sting that brings.
The RNG can apply to more than just combat - it can also apply to panic levels in various countries, and you have to sometimes choose arbitrarily which of three countries is going to not hate you after a particular mission.
In a modern day military, apparently only one squad can be deployed at a time, and no ground troops are available for reinforcement.
Cover the "native languages".
Code patching for those glitchy AI moments.
More variation on missions - say, a 'king of the hill' where you aren't defending, or puzzle maps where you have to position soldiers at points a, d, and y to open the door and let the big bad alien out.
Did I mention the languages? I think I mentioned the languages.
A different ending would be nice -
.

When this came out I considered it to include the most intrusive form of DRM at the time, Steam. It's funny how time changes things. In Steam's wake, it's competitors started using limited installations or require a constant internet connection. Suddenly, Steam became the lesser of other evils.
The end of physical media for PC should have been much more obvious to me at the time. I was worried they would gain to much control as we moved away from it. They've gain a lot more than they used to, but they don't control everything. The age of DRM didn't kill mods or dedicated servers (though it did severely wound them in many cases!) and it definitely did not kill piracy.
What it did do though was fundamentally change the consumer relationship. Sales psychology is much more aggressive and access to product is at an all time high. Weighing how much money I have wasted compared to the games I might not have played if Steam didn't exist, I don't know if I would do the same thing again. But that is of little consequence considering how things are now.
Sorry for rambling on about stuff that likely does not matter for a purchase decision. But, today is this game's birthday and it changed the game, whether I liked or not. So it deserves some recognition today, at least more than Valve is giving it.

Batman Is Not The Night
Arkham Knight, the long awaited conclusion to the Arkham trilogy. Bigger than ever, it dwarfs Arkham City's size, detail, and scope but much like City it feels bloated and too open for Batman.
Batman is the night, he is stealth, he is not destruction on a rampage in a tank causing what must be billions of dollar’s worth of collateral damage by the end of the game. What Arkham Asylum got so right were the tight spaces, small amounts of enemies, closed off areas. This pushed you to be "the night" so to speak, sneaking around as Batman, taking down goons one at a time. Forcing you to think ahead, plan out your attack, making you to stick to the shadows, heights, or grates.
Arkham Knight like most open games lets you tackle obstacles (namely goons) for the most part anyway you damn well please. Take out a dozen (an all too common occurrence) goons in one fight, relying on mashing buttons till all that remains is Batman and a sea of bodies on the floor. Stealth? do whatever you please, attack, fly away, attack, brawl your way through or tease them with a variety of the all too well known bat-gadgets from previous games. Or role play the stealthy Batman if you so choose although while doing so it never feels that satisfactory since the level design never really makes it challenging.
Easy Mode Engage
In one section of the game, a character is playing sniper on a perch but his vision of the area in front of him is so narrow and limiting you can literally walk in a straight line towards him provided you're not coming from the centre. This is one of the dumbest "avoid the sniper and sneak up on him" objectives I've ever seen in a videogame. But then again the Arkham games have always been simplistic in design and challenge, once you figure it out (normally takes all of 10sec) you're set.
The game tries to keep the pace in check (unlike City) by changing up the missions styles instead of beat up goon after goon until you get to your objective. The biggest of these are the Tank missions that change it up though they are a bit dull (most turning into beat up tank after tank) but the controls make it enjoyable nonetheless. Riddler's missions are amusing albeit not very riddler-like, more Saw crossed with racing/simplistic puzzles. And Catwoman in the Riddler mission is always a welcome character making a nice change from the gloom & doom of most of the Batman characters.
FUN For All The Bat-Family, Cripples And All!
The game provides almost no challenge (like many AAA titles nowadays) but it does make up for it in FUN. All the animations, old moves, and new moves are all shiny & improved and most importantly feel "cool" when you pull them off. Flying or better yet falling with style is as fun as ever and I'm pretty certain is still the fastest mode of travel than driving around the city in the...
The batmobile tank for all its ridiculousness is pretty fun to slide around the city while shooting up tanks, vehicles, goons, and the city itself in the form of partly destructible environments (pillars, supports, corners of buildings, almost any inanimate object). All the while you somehow avoid killing one single person which is greatly amusing, the tank even has a built in auto-taser feature that electrocutes people and sends them flying as soon you mow down somebody with the tank.
The Good Narrative, The Bad Narrative, And The Ugly
The story is a mixed bag in Arkham Knight, at times providing the punches a final story should but then chickening out and resorting to classic comic book troupes and clichés. Making you wish for what could of been. The characters are the characters you've come to know but finally get to see more of, most notably Oracle & Robin. It pulls lots of reference from the source material and has oodles of nods for fans of the comics.
The core storyline is pretty weak for the most part, Scarecrow taking over and gassing the now mostly deserted Gotham except for criminals and police. His reasons for doing this are almost non-existent and he is so poorly explored as a person you don't care about his overarching plan. He is however masterfully voiced by John Noble (Fringe) who fits the character perfectly, a voice to truly be afraid of, you believe every threat he makes.
The occasional acts of Scarecrow & the Arkham Knight are where it shines and the various sub plots, all too few moments of great drama, the tiniest glimpse of romance (mostly hidden thanks to the riddler trophies), and conflict which makes you route for Bats, Robin, Gordon, & Oracle. Almost every moment of sadness though is expertly ruined by the writers towards the conclusion of the game showing they themselves have been affected by Scarecrow’s fear toxins.
The ending is perhaps the game’s biggest misstep, the fact you can't even access the proper ending till you've completed 100% of the game (including riddler trophies) otherwise the game leaves you with an ending that doesn't even feel like one and doesn't even cut to credits leaving many like me feeling a little cheated since the rest of the game to get to 100% isn’t story based for the most part.
And then when you do get the full ending it is disappointing at best, adequate at best being very short, feeling a little rushed, and leaving some ambiguity which seems a little random considering what came before it.
TL;DR
A fun game which improves upon City's pluses but also showcases the negatives even more so  but at least makes them FUN. Gorgeous to look at even with little in the way of improvements over the console versions. A story that is very up and down but good characterization across the park (except for Harley as usual) but it’s an Arkham game not a Naughty Dog or CDProject Red game after all so we can’t expect that level of quality. Arkham Asylum still rules supreme in this series. 7/10

In space, when you're all out of missiles, the fire from the engine room consumes the life support system, and the hull of the ship is crumbling around you, no one can hear you scream. That is, if any of your crewmates were still alive. They've been eaten by insectoids.
Game over.
FTL is a mix of roguelike-alike and chaos management, in space, aboard a fragile ship that looks remarkably like the previous n million that were sent to their doom in some horrible, regrettable fashion. You'll love it regardless - you're saving the galaxy, fighting the rebel scum, as you plot a galactic (escape) course to ultimate (unlikely) victory... you'll love it right up until it's fiery gibs explode and float off to join the growing debris of your many failures.
Depth of mechanics and instant high replayability make FTL a winner. There's no doubt lots of successful strategies, but appropriately for the genre, uncovering them is both challenging and fun. Even when you're screaming.

XCOM puts you in the shoes of a base and battlefield commander, taking on missions around the globe with a team of 6 operatives to combat the unknown alien threat. It is equal parts turn-based strategy and base operations planning, the former being a glorious slugfest against ever increasingly potent enemies and the latter an easy to understand base set-up game that encourages planning ahead to maximize building adjacency bonuses and tech tree unlocks.
The game is infinitely replayable thanks to alternative upgrades, dozens of maps, mutators to the campaign, and variable difficulty modes that are mitigated somewhat by the ability to quick load a save every time an operative bites it.
Your choices on soldier abilities have impact because choosing one route usually locks out the other. You have limited funding and have to juggle weapons and armor production and research and base expansion.
With the upcoming Enemy Within expansion set to release, now is a great time for anyone who fancies turn-based action RPGs to hop in and see what the fuss is all about.

Risk of Rain has the potential to become one of your favorite games if you have the stomach for its challenging gameplay and incredible difficulty. This game has been one of the harder titles I've attempted to play in recent years, and the satisfaction of having completed even a marginally successful run is immense.
Graphics: 9/10
Pixel art is the oldest tool for 2d games, it's great and you can tell how much effort was put to it. RoR has some pretty damn good Pixel art, with great palette choices going from gloomy colors to vibrant ones. While the backgrounds are not the best, they do not bore and thanks to the variations on the maps and the random spawn system, this game is far from tedious. The enemies on this game is where the Graphics shine though, the designs are awesome and Bosses are quite memmorable.
Sound: 10/10
Beautiful chip tunes and synth notes with a dark mood that perfectly adorn the atmosphere of the game. It mix-matches different genres, including prog rock, metal, drum 'n' bass and industrial, giving it a great "psychedelic trip" feel that helps the player become immerse in this concept of exploring a vast and hostile strange planet.
Playability: 9.5/10
Controls are simple and responsive, in both, the keyboard and Joypad. And thanks to the multiple playable characters, you have a ton of strategies to tackle the game with. The difficulty on this game is... Let's just say it's not for the faint of heart, but it remains fair all in all. It is also part of the unique game mechanics that it offers, being that it get's more difficult as time passes, this is relevant because you can skip the last level and keep revisiting the previous ones to farm items and XP at the cost of a higher challenge and putting all your progress at risk.
Replay Value: 10/10
Tons of items and a dozen of playable charaters to unlock + An insane difficulty that will foil your plans, make this game replayable to the point of addiction.

Buying the Humble Origin Bundle with the knowledge that 2/3rds of the Dead Space series was included, my feelings were probably akin to a royal food tester's: I love the banquet, but the thought of that one deadly dish is absolutely terrifying. I've played my share of Survival Horror (starting with the granddaddy of them all, Alone in the Dark), but there's just something about Dead Space that's truly terrifying - the same reason Amnesia still sits on my digital shelf collecting digital cobwebs.
But then the backlog starts piling, and a man's gotta do what a man's gotta do. I finished Dead Space, and that should count as something when I get to Purgatory. The worry of absolute terror never ended - that's really something considering the game clocks in about 12 hours; and most survival horror/action games usually lose the terror after a few hours of collecting heavy weaponry. I was hooked with the atmoshpere and story that borrows a lot from scifi horror greats, but somehow puts its own stamp of uniqueness on what it steals.
Speaking of uniqueness, there's a lot of it in Dead Space. The gameplay twist that enemies go down easier by shooting off their limbs instead of the head sounds wonky in the beginning, but a few encounters with the necromorphs made me a believer. It's perfect because arms and legs tend to move more erraticly than one's head, which adds to the tension when aiming. Also, as a result, probably the most unique weapons I've handled in a game were created for this Dead Space. The cutter, the linegun, the ripper, all have their special use when it comes to dismemberment, with just the right amount of frustration to give them character - give them a sense that these are real tools.
Another thing to note is the game's inventory system. Very much like Resident Evil's limited slot-based  inventory, complete with external storage nodes that transfer excess baggage from one spot to another, Dead Space ups the ante by adding money to the mix. This actually made inventory management fun instead of frustrating, as I was figuring out how much of which ammo I should have, I should sell in exchange for Power Nodes (basically upgrade points). It became a mini game in itself. I'd be sad to hear if this lead to the adoption of microtransactions in Dead Space 3, but for this humble begging, it's very much welcome. (It also helps that plot items have their own inventory space, so need to worry about not having a crucial item when you need it).
That's Dead Space in a nutshell. A rancid, mutating death nutshell. I'm still getting that same sense of thrill/dread about sampling the next two installments, so maybe I'll give the other gut-friendlier dishes in my buffet a try for the time being.

I'm pretty sure this game is a big part of why Steam updated the review system to show "overall" and "recent" reviews.  Upon launch this game was apparently unplayable due to how poorly it was ported to PC, and hopefully the flack WB Games got for it will teach developers in the future to show more care for their PC releases...however, the game itself (once the bulk of the bugs were worked out) is actually pretty fun.
As usual, the storyline is solid.  The Arkham games in general have been some of the best adaptations of Batman from the comics ever.  And Batman rarely translates well from the comics.
After Scarecrow got his face chewed off by Killer Croc in Arkham City, he's come back for revenge on Batman, and this time he's brought along a new player, the Arkham Knight.  The Arkham Knight is someone we haven't seen in the Arkham series before, but if you're familiar with the comics, you'll have fun trying to figure out who it is behind the mask, and why they're hell bent on destroying Batman.
As with every other game, Riddler's been leaving trophies and graffiti around town, but this time he's got a hostage, you have to complete various challenge levels with Catwoman to help her defuse an explosive collar, and you're able to switch between the two in real-time to help them work together more efficiently.  This feature is also present whenever you're fighting alongside Robin.
There are more toys, this time around.  The Batarangs, Batclaw, Line Launcher and Explosive Gel are still there, but this time you also get a voice synthesizer to command henchmen around for Predator challenges (until they inevitably catch on to the deception), a disruptor (which I think may have also been in Arkham City, I'm not sure), the Remote Hacking Device has more utility this time around and you can even call in the Batmobile to whereever you are in the city, even if you left it way on the other end of the map, it seems to always conveniently be just around the corner.  But I won't complain.
There are street battles against the Arkham Knight's tanks, there's environment takedowns during fight sequences, there are car chases, there's an even wider variety of takedown methods...there's just so much more to the (presumably) final installation of the Arkham series...so if you liked the previous games but are worried it's just more of the same, worry not.  It's totally worth it.  And if you're apprehensive because of how buggy everyone said it was at launch, don't worry, it's fine now.  I only had one issue my entire time playing it, and I'd practically beaten the game by the time it happened, I started clipping through buildings.  Just reloading from a previous save fixed it, I only lost a couple minutes of gliding through the city, no big deal.
I give it an 8.5/10, I really liked this damn game.
