A decent game, but more of a final cash in on the Arkham series, than the ode to Batman offered in the first two.  The only truly new feature here is the Batmobile, and it makes the overall experience worse.  Arkham City recommended over Knight.
+ Impressive smoke and water graphics
+ Bigger, taller, and more interesting city
+ Improvements and additions to combat and stealth
+ Destructible environments, but only to the Batmobile
+ GCPD is a neat collectibles hub, though lacking a Batcave
+ Online scoreboards make AR challenges a bit more interesting, though the highscores are blatantly hacked, with top combos of 30,000 to 1,000,000,000
+- The new non-FPS tunnel/grate outline system is a bit strange, especially since you can't see yourself highlighted under the floor
+- Graphic performance comes and goes, sometimes hitting the 90 FPS cap, other times falling below 60
- Gadget swapping is more intrusive, instead of more intuitive
- Alternate Batmobile skins break the game by disabling combat mode
- I find it strange that Batman can use bats (and other enemy melee weapons)
- Only basic thugs when freeroaming post game, no armed patrols, or even advanced melee
- You get very few upgrade points from the main story, mostly from side missions, and most upgrades require multiple points.  This makes progression feel slow and unrewarding.
- Various minor bugs throughout the game
- The freeze grenade is on a random table?  Rather uneventful gadget acquisition
- Dear Batman, stop pausing my adventure every 5 minutes to facetime with Alfred
- The slowmo cinematic cam is absent on most final takedowns
- Combat sounds like you're smacking somebody with a soggy toaster
- Environmental takedowns seem very picky about when they'll work, almost random
- Batman's walking is now locked in the direction of the camera.  In Arkham City you could walk towards the camera, cool guys don't look at explosions
- The controls for sliding and detective vision were nonsensically changed for no reason
- Hit X 5 times for grappling boost?  If anything, this should have been reduced to once
- SMAA is the only AA option.  Its blurry, mutes details, and doesn't effectively fix jaggies.  Chromatic Aberration, another blur filter?  Film Grain, yet more distortion?  Its like they don't want you to see the graphics.
- Adaptive vsync doesn't work properly, and tries to sync the game to 30 FPS.  The point of adaptive is to only sync above the monitor's refresh rate
- The normal ending of the story is unsatisfying, it feels rushed, if not unfinished.  The first additional ending doesn't help whatsoever.  I haven't unlocked the final final ending yet, as it requires collecting 100% of the universe.
- So, let me get this straight... They went through all the trouble of adding combat systems and combo animations for 2 people, but didn't bother adding actual multiplayer/coop?  And sidekicks aren't even available in free roaming.  GG, Rocksteady, GG
- I hate the new art style, and am not sure why it was changed.  The new batsuit looks like a cosplayer's attempt at making ironman-batman, by taping random bits of plastic to a tracksuit.  All of the villains look worse as well, the main villain looks like a cosplayer of the keyblade wars.  The Arkham City costume is the best batsuit design of all time, and shouldn't have been scrapped.
- Endless TazerMedics in the endless AR modes, like Iceburg Lounge, are gamebreaking.  Though they are a nice addition in most normal modes.
- The Batmobile (tank) is more of a hindrance than anything, its like a persistent escort quest.  It isn't well integrated into gameplay flow.  Its combat isn't well thought out or balanced.  It isn't fun to drive, partially because it feels 2x too slow, and shooting mechanics don't work on a controller.  If it simply had some automated systems, autopilot, autolocking on tanks, and countering missiles with Y, like you can in melee combat, perhaps it would have felt more a part of the game, instead of a quickly thrown in, barely functional minigame, that constantly plagues main story progression.  Batman can infinitely sprint, dodge, counter, use his gadgets, etc, but the Batmobile has a cooldown on every one of its equivalent features.  It feels like an afterthought, and I never once found myself using it, unless required for progression.  You know what the Batmobile's most useful feature is?  Slingshotting you into a super glide, so that you don't have to use the Batmobile.

Shadowrun Returns is a return to CRPGs with some modern squad-based combat touches. Imagine taking the setting of Blade Runner, placing Tolkien's mythical creatures, classic Pen & Paper feel, XCOM combat, and a Starcraft Editor (maps, additional features and dialog for user-created stories.) The combination you can imagine is what is offered for this game.
SRR's emphasis on immersing you into this lore filled Sixth World is the game's greatest strengths, even if you know nothing but drek about the source material. Dialogue holds that prosy, to the point content; character descriptions help build bonds with all the NPCs; and the game uses its characters to help relate to the inhuman lore, especially when it comes to the idea of its stats (ex. the Essence for Cyberware.)
The 12 to 15 hour main-storyline is compact with memorable moments with some optional objectives to reward your exploration into databases and completing smaller tasks. Some might see its content's length as a downside. After playing the classic Infinity Engine games, the following Shadowrun games, and other modern CRPGs like Wasteland 2, I can understand this issue but I don't think the game's brevity is entirely bad. Games like SRR cuts out padding to give you a reasonable blank slate while providing a servicable story.
Self-destruction is the game's theme. Your character is a retired Runner who is brought back from a friend who's lifestyle of detachment from reality lead to his demise. There are spirtual, moral degregation from individuals, corporations and the world itself. All of which is maintained by the dialogue system keeping character. In other games where you question an as*hole being the savior it is very believable here because the character can be as corrupt as everyone. Or he can be someone who honors a friend by seeing justice to the end. It's one of those qualities of a game's lore that gets you more engaged.
Difficulty is another positive. Unlike a lot of RPGs there are no random encounters and traditional leveling up system. You will purchase new equipment, use Karma points (stats) and currency to improve your character. Every battle you fight becomes a matter of mind over stats and guns, which do not degrade and don't require you to purchase ammo--but you will have to reload for an action point! Also, you have to purchase your squad members before each mission (and you can only outfit them with consumable items). There are plenty to chose from and if they die, which I imagine on higher difficulties will happen a lot. Even if you do not have a full party you can still finish missions.
The last thing I have to say are to the complaints given to this game. I already stated how I felt about the length of the game: Quality over quantity. SR's checkpoint system is the other "problem". I never had any issue at all with the checkpoints. It is not as simplified as some say. Almost every time you move to a new area the game will autosave. If you get into an impossible situation you can revert to a prior checkpoint. This is far more extensive than some AAA titles. It is an odd change for cRPG fans but it is not a detriment to the game itself.
For those who didn't want to read, do not buy this game. You will spend far more time reading than fighting, which makes combat feel more like punctuation. If you are new to cRPGs, try this game out. Shadowrun fans will enjoy the Deluxe Edition for an extra $15. This is easily one of my top games for this year and I'm anxious to explore more in the Workshop's content.

This game is amazing. I played it during the free weekend, first on solo mode before moving on to multiplayer. I'd like to start off my review with the pros of this game first, then move on to the cons.
First off (And *OBVIOUSLY* the most important aspect of the game), I loved the comments of the various characters. In Killing Floor, every character had the same comments. In the sequel, Mr. Foster has different quips than the Reverend. He's cocky, and I quite like it ("You're doing good, kid. Just keep doing what I'm doing", "All still alive? You can thank me later"). The varied grenades for the different perks was interesting, Molotovs for Firebug, Dynamite for the Demolitionist (The EMPs for the beserker were a bit strange, though. In my opinion). I would have loved the ability to use other perks' grenades, but it's not a big concern of mine. I loved the addition of a new boss, Hans Volter, in addition to the Patriarch. If they added more bosses, I don't think I'd complain (Those fleshpounds, though. They might as well be minibosses...). There were plenty of online servers to choose from, as well (So many...they just came out of nowhere...), from Great Britian to Hong Kong, Germany to United States. And the players? The players are great, (especially the finely tuned killing machines). It's even better when you find a server full of people working together, watching each other's back (Looking at you, Aussies!).
Now, the concerns I *DO* have, though, feel like they need mentioning (Of course, what's a review without complaints?), such as with the weapons or the maps. The maps they have are fun, but not nearly as many as they had in the original. There aren't many weapons as the first, either. For instance, the Firebug as only three or so weapons (I do miss the Flare Revolvers). Admittedly, Survival mode can get a little repetitive, and Versus mode seems to lean heavily in the favor of the Zeds. Regardless, this doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the game. Additionally, I've heard complaints about the new resistance system, and while it is a nuisance, it adds to the challenge of the game (Hint, shotguns deal some decent damage to Fleshpounds, in my opinion). Surprisingly, I didn't mind the TF2 microtransactions as much as I thought I would; they had their own little store, if you want the goods, they're there. I will say, though, I didn't like having crates and "USBs" (Essentially crates for weapons skins. I think. I didn't open them) dropped into my lap, with the expectation fo me to open them. I *DID*, however, like that they're quietly dropped in my inventory. No grand announcements or popup windows telling me to open the mystery box; I found out I had crates only after exiting the game and seeing that green envelope.
Overall, I think all the many negative reviews, while they have good points, need to remember; this is an Early Access game, and requires time, effort, and support from all ends. The developers are working as best they can, and attempting to make this game as entertaining as possible for a wide range of people.
I give the game, as is, a high rating 8/10, and hope to see the game become greater.

Event Horizon, Pandorum, Alien, even 2001. All of these films and many other great Sci Fi traditions act as a healthy source base for Dead Space. The game features a distress call, a seemingly silent ship which we quickly realize is dark and full of monsters. Something has gone terribly wrong.
The game's carefully crafted atmosphere and surprisingly good voice acting are really what draw you in. Although the plot is very transparent, and the character development (especially for Kendra) is a little weak, the game isn't really about that. It's about living out some version of the space horror fantasy you've had in your head ever since the first time you saw say, Event Horizon. The game has it all, spooky lighting, creepy cultists, a wide array of frightening monsters, and a slowing unfolding backstory involving a typical breakdown of the chain of command and descent into chaos.
Playing this game with headphones and in the dark, while alone, even a second time through, is quite an experience. Your heart will pound and you will jump out of your seat.
Graphically speaking the game isn't much to look at, and the necromorphs aren't very inspired in their design, although they are scary. Nevertheless, the lighting and audio more than make up for the game's low resolution textures and low poly models.
Apart from really wonky object physics, the game feels very good to play as well. The slow turning speed of Isaac, your avatar, contributes to the sense of the game as being about horror/survival, and scavenging is essential. You aren't incredibly vulnerable, especially after upgrades, but you feel like you are, and that's what counts.
Ultimately, Dead Space is a surprising and fun guilty pleasure of a game that will remind you of nights spent watching sci-fi horror movies scaring yourself senseless in the dark.

A lot of people are going to write hate about the microtransaction system. There's a legit complaint there as Tripwire focused development resources on that system rather than gameplay content which was already beyond its promise date. My guess is that their hand was forced due to not having the necessary funds to complete development with the current rate of purchases being made, but they could've at least been honest with fans and customers who already purchased the game.
Aside from all that, my real gripe was just how dumbed down the combat got. In KF1, thanks to subtle mechanics like mini-stuns and such, you could do some amazing strategic plays even by yourself or with few team mates left standing. In KF2, it's just point and click, do some damage, hope it dies before it reaches you. The biggest problem there being with the Berserker (read: melee) class. The weapons became homogenized, and are barely differentiated in a way to make clear tiers stand out among the different weapons. The same uninspired, homogenized type gameplay is only further reinforced by the maps and the boss (though the later re-added Patriarch may not suffer as much).
As time went on, even before microtransactions, my weekly play time was dropping consistently until one day I realized I hadn't played in over a month. The game's fun factor just wasn't there for me like KF1. I was looking forward to coming back to it when new content was released, but that's been so little so often, I'm barely bothered to even do more than glancing at patch notes anymore.
With the announcement of everything else Tripwire is now spending development resources on, I'm left with even less hope that this game will reach the glory of its predecessor. This is not the same Tripwire that developed KF1, and it shows not only in their business decisions, but far more importantly in the drab and lackluster gameplay in KF2.
Bottom line, while the game may look fun from the trailers, it's a level of enjoyment that wears thin fast and leaves you with unfinished content. You'll be left waiting for balance and more emergent game mechanics to arrive with new patches only to find that it never comes.
If you're really eager to try this game out, at least wait for it to leave Early Access such that you understand what the game really has to offer. Because right now, what it does offer is woefully short of what's promised, leaves a bit to be desired, and how much better it may ever be is a question that no one knows the answer to, likely not even Tripwire themselves.

The Stick of Truth is an endearing homage to South Park. While the gameplay gets a little repetetive with time, the funny dialogue, characters and environments keep you interested. There's something slightly magical about interacting with characters you've been watching for close to 20 years now, and I'd recommend it to any fan of the show.
Without spoiling too much, the story will let you revisit many jokes and storylines from the show, and in adition, the game lampoons games and game tropes throughout the campaign. The main campaign took me around 15 hours to complete, and there's still a bunch of sidequests and collectables left to take part in.
Gameplay consists partially of exploring south park and solving environmental puzzles or talking to people, as well as a great deal of turn-based combat. You select the attack that you and your party members use, and then execute them with QTE in order to score better hits. You can find/buy weapons, armor and equipment to modify them (as well as clothes, disguises, etc) throughout your game, and managing your inventory is a considerable part of the fun.
CONCLUSION:
All in all, if you are a fan of south park, the game is definitely worth getting just for the fan service. That's what carries the game. The gameplay isn't bad, but I wouldn't be enjoying it nearly as much if I didn't get to fight manbearpig with Butters at my side.

This rather simple yet addictive, often hectic game packs a lot of punch despite it's somewhat downgraded graphics (although the retro look in my opinion suits this game and the background is usually quite colourful and good-looking) the gameplay itself varies greatly thanks to a wide selection of characters with multiple abilities both melee and ranged, various items with different effects, most of which can stack (some infinitely as far as I'm aware) there's a decent selection of monsters (although I hope a few more are released in future updates) and added extras in the game known as "Artifacts" which you usually aquire through obscure methods, these extras are activated before starting a game and persist throughout the game and can change the style of play completely (item drops not being random, items not spawning in chests but instead dropping from monsters etc) the bosses are generally quite epic, my first encounter with a Magma Worm actually shocked me as I wasn't expecting something quite so collosal, most of the bosses have a decent degree of difficulty as well with some of them clearly built to be effective against either a ranged or a melee character (e.g. Collosus being easy on a ranged character.)
Onto downsides/potential improvements:
First thing to mention is a rather persistent glitch I've noticed, I'm not sure if it's a combination of circumstances which causes this but sometimes you can spawn into the first level and either be falling infinitely because the ground isnt solid or you might find an area that isnt solid ground, this is obviously a bit game breaking but unfortunately not too bad an issue as starting a new game usually fixes this and its only on the first level as far as I'm aware so you wont have made much progression, this should hopefully be patched soon but this has been happening since I started playing about a month ago and there's been an update since then.
The local multiplayer is a nice feature, with a controller and a keyboard two people can play on the same system, the xbox controller feels responsive and is easy to map and I'd recommend a controller for anyone playing this game however the issue I find with the local multiplayer is that you have to play zoomed out making it difficult to see things and sometimes distinguish between your characters, the screen seems to try and follow both players simultaneously and doesn't go into split screen once youve gone out of range of each other.
Online multiplayer doesn't seem to work for me, not sure why, I can get it working with virtual local area network software but me and my housemate couldn't seem to connect over the same network, many people seem to have similar issues so I think this is something that might need fixing or at the very least explained how to host a game within the game itself if there isn't an issue with it, having said all of this, the multiplayer doesn't rely on servers hosted by the games publisher, instead you host the server (which can cause issues depending on internet connection/system specs) but this means there's never a risk of (rain) the servers being closed down.
Some of the items require being unlocked before they will drop and the achievements to unlock the items vary greatly with some having, in my opinion, far too high a difficulty to achieve and the achievement for aquiring the Soldiers Syringe doesn't seem to work, the item is unlocked and it says the achievement is unlocked ingame but it doesn't appear in your achievement log ingame or on Steam - quite an annoying bug for any perfectionists.
Overall I think this game is good and worth playing, a few tweaks here and there, a bit more new content (maybe even some sort of open sourcing so people can create there own content?) and I think this would be a great indie game.

Pros:
-Some good writing
-Turn based combat is great, slightly better than Fallout with cover system.
-Beautiful hand drawn world
-Game editor and User Generated Content. (from what I read, the editor is quite restricted.)
Cons:
-Clunky user interface, clearly meant for touchscreens
-No voiceover.
-Non interactive world. Everything that you can interact with is highlighted with the hand icon. Anything not highlighted is just a background. Makes the world feel empty.
-Non practical inventory system: cannot trade items between party members. You can only manage your inventory during start of a mission and at the safehouse.
-Too little choice of weapon and armor.
-No lootable corpse. Perished enemy will simply disappear into the thin air.
-Moving and clicking is a bit off, particularly because it's a tablet game in the first place.
-Extremely linear campaign and no sidequests.
On tablet this game easily score an 8 out of 10. The game was designed for tablets in mind, making the developers overlooked some of its flaws and ignored many of the aspect of a good RPG other than writing. In fact, Harebrained Schemes (HBS) is a tablet game developer, has only released mobile games.
Bear in mind that Shadowrun Returns comes with an editor and a default campaign made by HBS. The campaign is restricting and painfully linear. You cannot go back to previously visited place and there's only a few sidequest that you can do for extra cash. Right now there is some user made campaign available on the workshop which was designed better than the campaign made by the devs.
Shadowrun Returns is a disappointing RPG lacking of real depth with so many unfullfilled potentials. If you're really looking up for this title and has already run out of RPGs to play, just wait for a sale.

If you happen to be reading this review, you are likely aware of the current playerbase response to the direction Killing Floor 2 developers have taken the game. I agree with the playerbase. Currently, as of writing this review, 2,512 reviews of this game have been written in the past 30 days with 56% of them being negative reviews. I will just assume that you are already aware of the forum censorship, unwanted updates, slow updates, etc. concerning the development of KF2, and I will jump right to my main issues with the various mechanics of the gameplay in its current state.
UPDATE: some listed issues have been corrected or improved. Recent reviews are up to about 75% positive, which is a major improvement resulting from the last few patches actually being mostly positive changes to the game. The exceptions are boss health/damage on various difficulties, where I would still argue that they made the boss health too high and compensated by providing more ammo crates. 20-30 minutes of 1 or 2 surviving players running in a giant circular path around a map while collecting ammo crates is NOT a fun boss fight. The duration is too long unless mechanics are being borderline abused (DoW, I'm talking to you). <3
PHYSICS:
1. Scrake lunges can no longer be dodged by physically running/jumping to their side while they attack. Now, along with crawlers, stalkers and fleshpounds, they have invisible jetpacks which allow them to do a full 180 degree turn mid air to get free cheap shots on any players attempting to physically avoid a physical impact. This is counterintuitive, and it feels generic and cheap.
v IMPROVED
2. Essentially all enemies now have a knockback mechanic added to their physical impacts on players. This generates serious issues when combined with issue 1 due to the fact that an enemy can jump at you, do a full 180 turn mid air and impact you, sending you flying TOWARD the direction it jumped FROM (into more zeds). This can even knock you on top of other zeds/cars/obstacles or into corners or against obstacles where you will become "clipping locked", as I like to call it.
3. Physical impacts from zeds do not generate feedback in their movements or animations. This results in stalkers physically impacting players with cartwheel-like maneuvers and simply sliding against them as if players were coated in WD-40 or something of that nature. This means that stalkers can continuously flip at point blank range, damaging players and obscuring their own headshot hitboxes with no repercussions.
v CORRECTED (mostly returned to normal)
4. Zed resistances to weapons. A single round from the weakest commando weapon can impact the toe (or anywhere) of a stalker and kill it outright. 4+ body shots from a M14ebr sharpshooter weapon would be required to kill the same stalker. Even a headshot from the M14ebr would leave it headless but still moving and attacking. This is completely counterintuitive to how caliber, bullet speed and impact locality actually works.
BEHAVIOR:
v IMPROVED? (I believe tripwire thought this was the "teleporting zeds" issue, because zeds still frequently teleport several feet during attack animations)
1. Zed movements defy continuity. Aside from the boss, virtually all zeds have the passive ability to dematerialize from any position in a map and rematerialize ahead of the direction players are running. With 6 zeds remaining on the map, and all 6 zeds visually accounted for in a single field of view, a player can then run ahead through the next doorway and encounter one of those previous zeds dropping right in front of them from the catwalk above. This is gamebreaking for at least 2 reasons. Firstly, continuity of zed movement is destroyed, resulting in a generic atmosphere. Secondly, running "away" from something isn't practicable.
v HUGE DECLINE (Zeds now intentionally put their weapons in front of their heads to deflect bullets. This could be a cool mechanic if bullets were able to jam/break/destroy things like drills/blades/chainsaws as they do when exploding husk backpacks. However, enemies are simply invincible in their vital points by mere cointoss probabilities now. This is true garbage which eliminates the prospects of SKILL being a factor in success, and it's easily the worst idea since resistances.)
2. Zeds movements are sporadic. In addition to the previously mentioned, zeds also "protect" themselves via sporadic flailing of metal objects (imbedded blades, chainsaws, etc.). This results in unpredictable moments where a bullet is simply deflected and no harm is done to the zeds.
AMBIENCE:
v IMPROVED (flashlights last longer and recharge quicker, but ambient lighting issues remain)
1. Lighting is too sparce. Initially, flashlights were limited as a default mod to a select few weapons. Since, the flashlight has been added as a default body mod so that all players have the ability to use one. These flashlights are still operating on a battery timer and must be recharged frequently. The problem here is that the ambient lighting on most maps is simply too dark to maneuver properly. I have, on multiple computers, maxed out the brightness settings in every conceivable way only to still be unable to see things directly in front of my player.
2. Many maps continuously rain zeds. There are many maps which have zed spawnpoints on top of buildings, allowing essentially endless raining of zombies. This also gives husks the advantage of firing multiple shots accross a huge area before even making themselves vulnerable to (reachable by) many players, noteably berserkers. This feels generic and cheap.
WEAPON HANDLING:
1. Attempting to fire while out of ammo results in an "automated" weapon switch. However, if a player attempts to manually switch weapons at the same time, the result is a too-quick-for-animations switch to a good weapon and then BACK to the weapon with no ammo.
2. Reloading animations are incredibly deceptive. There are weapons where, while attempting to reload, a player drops the old mag, pulls out a new mag, places the new mag into the weapon and chambers a round, only to then realize that by switching weapons, the amination hadn't "finished", and the entire process must again be repeated from the beginning. The unfinished part of the animation is simply the player lowering the weapon a few inches over the course of a fraction of a second.
//// I will add more on this later \\\\
I would like to add that Tripwire has been adjusting boss damage/health for various difficulties based on win/loss ratio for those difficulties. Is a coin toss really their goal here when it comes to success? I will try back in a few months when the new enemy blocking mechanic has surely been voted out of existence by the community.

Fantastic game.  The whole way through, the experience feels like watching a really good South Park episode or South Park movie, and the game is a *really* solid RPG, to boot.
But the game isn't without its flaws.  I want to spend a few paragraphs on some criticisms of the game, and then we'll talk about what makes the game awesome.
The game feels heavily "consolized."  Loading screens are far more frequent than they should be and the controls often don't make much sense.  Throughout the game your character will be taught "magic spells" from various NPCs.  Each time you learn a spell, you are taught a series of controls to use that spell.  However, these spells can be used both in and out of combat, and in both situations the controls are different from one another—and in neither situation is the spell invoked the same way the game inititally taught you!
Your out-of-combat utilities (like firing a ranged weapon at something in the environment or sending a buddy to perform a task) are equally awkward to select and use.
Now, here I should note that I played with a controller attached to a PC.  I started the game with a keyboard/mouse but changed very, very early on to give my normal gaming posture a rest (I play games a lot with the keyboard/mouse), and also because South Park: The Stick of Truth seemed to be tailored more toward a controller.  Perhaps the controls are better with a keyboard/mouse, but using a controller felt awkward in many parts of the game.  But not in combat.  In combat the controls felt great.  More on that later, though.
On top of that, the game's humor can be off-putting in some parts.  This isn't a real criticism so much as it is a warning—it IS South Park, after all!  The show has a reputation of making comedy material out of even the most sensitive of topics, and this game also doesn't hold back.  I like to think of myself as a fairly easy-going guy and I try not to take many things too seriously, but there were parts in this game that I felt myself somewhat rushing through or avoiding just to get away from an uncomfortable topic.
There's a lot of back-and-forth running around the map in this game, and loading screens are absolutely everywhere.  The loading screens are a real slowdown.
So let's see.  The loading screens, the really iffy controls in much of the game, and the warning about how the game remains very South Park in its humor are all the things I wanted to make sure to mention.  So, now we can talk about the stuff that makes this game a fantastic one!
While moving on the map and navigating menus is often awkward with the game's controls, combat is something the game gets very, very right.  As I mentioned earlier, this game is a very solid RPG, and The Stick of Truth's turn-based combat is airtight.  This isn't your typical "select an ability and watch what happens" kind of turn-based combat.  Here, you'll select an ability, and then you'll influence the outcome of the ability with some simple, but fun controls.
For example, Butters the Paladin has a "Hammer of Justice" ability.  To use it, you select it and then choose a target.  The game then has you rotate the left control stick in circles to make Butters spin (think Olympic discus tossing), and at just the right instant, press the A button.  Succeed, and you'll deal bonus damage to the enemy!  If you mess up, Butters will still deal damage, but not as much.  Again, this is coming from the perspective of using a gamepad to control the game; I'm sure this is different for a mouse/keyboard, but the principle is the same.
Combat is filled with awesome stuff like this.  When you are attacked, most of the time you are given the chance to block some of the enemy's damage by pressing A at just the right time.  Some enemy attacks strike multiple times, requiring multiple well-timed blocks!  Different enemy attacks have different timings as well, so you'll always need to be on your guard.
These combat mechanics make even turn-based combat a very active affair.  The action is fast and challenging, so you'll need to be spot on with your controls.  Thankfully, controls in combat are responsive and intuitive, and anytime there's some ambiguity about what to do in battle, there are useful tooltips and pop-ups to remind you of how to use an ability.
While combat is great fun, the game also very often presents you with multiple ways of dealing with foes.  Sometimes you can distract them and sneak by.  Other times you can use the environment to defeat your foes without having to confront them.  Keen awareness of your surroundings and appropriate use of your abilities out of combat can speed up your progress and yield satisfying results.
It should be noted that if you sneak by enemies, you probably won't get experience for dealing with them.  But in the cases where you can use the environment to defeat them, you'll be awarded experience as if you had battled them!
There are many quests to accomplish throughout the game, and a few side quests can be completed as you progress.  As far as questing is concerned, it's your typical RPG fare—pick up a quest, complete the objectives, turn the quest in.  The game does nothing to revolutionize questing, but it handles questing very well.
The story-based quests, however, are always greatly satisfying to accomplish because you are awarded not only with experience and often loot/money, but also with story exposition done in only the way South Park can.  It really does feel like you're earning a little piece of a South Park episode or South Park movie when you complete a story quest.
The writing in the game is spot on.  You'll get to watch the South Park characters you're so familiar with do the things they do, in the way they do them, while interacting with one another and with your character.  I found the story largely fun and interesting.
I was often quite pleased with the developers' efforts to include as many South Park characters as they could in the game.  This could not have been an easy task to accomplish, but the game is solid through-and-through with the show's characters, and because the show has been running so long, these characters bring with them their histories, backdrops, and references that the South Park fan should thoroughly enjoy.
Character customization is very in-depth for a game with such a simplistic visual style.  You'll begin the game by choosing a class, and then customizing your looks.  As the game progresses, you will find, like, a bajillion different ways to customize your charcter's costume ("gear"), hair, facial features, makeup, and accessories.  You'll even find "strap-ons" (for weapons) and "patches" (for armor) that let you add significant bonuses to your gear, letting you really specialize or round out your character and playstyle.
I did make a warning above about the game's humor, but for South Park fans, that (most of the time) means you're in for more of what you enjoy about the show.  There were plenty of times I found myself actually laughing out loud at the characters' antics; or at the writing; or at the timing of a joke; or just at South Park being South Park.  It's a funny game.
There is also a difficulty slider bar.  Early in the game I cranked the difficulty to max and didn't look back, and for me, it was quite rewarding.  The window of opportunity to block enemy attacks seemed drastically smaller, necessitating more precise timing, and enemies often didn't go down without a fight.  I had to stay on top of my gear choices and customize appropriately.  Which buddy to bring into battle with me was also a serious consideration, and more than once I had to stock up on potions.
Overall, it's just a really solid RPG, and I'd strongly recommend it to any South Park fan.  I could go on about it, but I feel I've covered most of the relevant aspects of the game, and apparently Steam has a character limit for reviews.  :)

As a huge DC and Batman fan, I've religiously 100%ed the previous Arkham games with the exception of Batman: Arkham Origins (I gave up on the Predator Paragon achievement). It seems Batman: Arkham Knight will be another exception but for different reasons. I actually loved Origins despite its flaws but the more I think about this title... the more I realize it was a chore to play. Keep in mind that I got the premium edition (base game + all DLC) for ~$24 USD off of Bundlestars when they were having a sale too. Before I cover the issues that annoyed me though, I'd like to go over the positives first.
For starters, this game looks amazing -- there's no doubt about it. I've never seen an Unreal Engine 3 game that looks like this and I'm not just talking about the facial animations and expressions, I'm talking about everything. Another area the game excelled in was voice acting. Most characters were well cast and Kevin Conroy as Batman and a certain someone definitely were at the top of their game here. Also worth mentioning is the good twists and "gotcha!" moments that totally caught me off guard. The soundtrack was similarly great and hit most of the right notes, making me almost cry in one scene. Building off what Arkham City gave us, we get even more combat moves and ways to initiate a silent takedown. Not only that, we finally get to drive around in the batmobile and tear down the streets in it. I can't downplay how exciting it is to hop into this awesome vehicle the first time and then find out it's a tank! Yes, the batmobile can transform in a matter of seconds into a tank which the game calls "Battle mode". There's tons of stuff you can do while in this mode and it's all really exciting stuff.
Batmobile aside, there's no shortage of side missions and other little diversions happening while you fly around the map such as: thugs driving around in cars like hooligans or riots happening on the streets. If you've got the season pass there's also a ton of different batmobiles that you can test drive with authentic sounds and multiple characters you can play as in the AR challenges. My fondest memories are of playing the Adam West race tracks while hearing the TV show's theme song and playing as characters like Harley Quinn and Red Hood because of how unique they are. The best part of this game would have to be Photo Mode though. This wasn't even part of the base game upon launch but it was later added as a free update. A good 1/4 of my screenshots for this game were done in photo mode and what makes it great to use is that you can pause the game at any time, choose "Photo Mode" from the pause menu, manipulate the camera angles, slap on a filter, zoom in or zoom out, choose a border, and do it all in a way that's really easy to use. You end up getting some great looking screenshots like the one below. But unfortunately... all of this isn’t enough.
Even though I’d say this is the best Arkham game for role-playing as Batman... there's such a thing as less is more. The batmobile's undoubtedly great but because the story mode over relies on it, the fun factor disappears. Tank battle after tank battle and the game doesn't give up.
Winch this, dodge these tanks and blow them up (it feels like an arcade game at times honestly), drive around and use this feature from the batmobile… and repeat. I really think the batmobile should've been optional and not forced in the way that it is. The batmobile just feels a bit too destructive at times as well. I laughed as I mowed over people and slammed into buildings leaving nothing but debris. In addition to all of what I've said, the batmobile reduces the rather cool boss fights that we had in previous games to... yep, you guessed it... tank battles.
Want to battle Deathstroke? Tank battle. Want to battle the Arkham Knight? Tank battle. Want to battle Firefly? Batmobile pursuit (okay it's a bit different but still not much fun). It just shows a lack of creativity. Other side missions? Disabling bombs safely and destroying APC military vehicles. How? I won't even go there. Even some of The Riddler missions - one of my favourite Batman villains - are almost crippled because of this. I won't spoil anything but The Riddler has basically set up race tracks for your batmobile and you have to get to the finish line in time. Yay? Writing this just makes me upset at all the lost potential here (even a lot of the non-batmobile missions and sidemissions lack fun for some reason). I get Rocksteady wanted to spoil us with the batmobile as well as a large cast of villains but it came at the cost of quality and most of the game just feels extremely repetitive.
Next is the story. The writing here is noticeably weaker than any of the other Arkham games (might be because Paul Dini left) and the story has too many plot holes for my liking. Not to mention the identity of one of the villains in this game is incredibly easy to guess. There's a ridiculous amount of foreshadowing and what could've been a powerful reveal is mostly uneventful. Besides that, to get the “True Ending” players are forced to beat every side mission and get 243/243 riddles. The true ending doesn’t even answer a lot of questions or provide much closure but locking something like this behind riddles is a very silly move. Thankfully there’s a 242/243 savegame on PCGamingWiki if you don’t feel up to the task. On the port side of things, the game runs mostly decent but I had some issues that need to be addressed. The first: unlocking certain Steam achievements will actually make the game freeze for a second or two every time you satisfy the criteria once more for that achievement. I’m not joking. It’s all to do with the PCEngine.ini file. The second: I had around 13 crashes total across my playtime but 8 of those were in the same part of the story (analysing the crash site of a vehicle for someone that was kidnapped). You might not experience it, but it too has been another reported issue that remains unfixed.
Other negatives include the "Arkham episodes". 6 characters have a DLC mission made for them but 5 of them can be finished in less than 10 minutes. I could probably forgive this but these missions are divided into 3 sections with 3 short cutscenes usually. Combat room, predator room, combat room or the other way around, but I don't think that's worth applauding. Batgirl's DLC is fortunately 1 hour and man is it a good piece of DLC in the way that Cold, Cold Heart was for Batman: Arkham Origins. Season of Infamy is also good but not worth the $10. Moving onto AR challenges… most of them aren't tailored for every character. You'll notice this with someone like Harley Quinn where there's a lack of things for her to climb or jump up to. When it comes to combat, a lot of characters share a ridiculous amount of moves. Lastly, thug voiceovers are reused for most of the characters and maybe one line for some is changed. A good example would be "Batman's not going to save you now
!". For Nightwing? "Batman's not going to save you now
!". It's especially bad when these lines repeat over and over more than they ever did in Arkham City. Certain AR challenges have bugs where thugs stand still and do nothing. Other maps are just unfair and weren't made in mind with the current combat system (Iceberg Lounge and Catwoman's Revenge). I’ll stop here….
I've written an essay but all I’ll say is this: the PC port's better now but this game is easily the weakest in this series. If I wasn't a person with a lot of patience and/or a hardcore achievement collector, I don't think I would've made it far into this game. 4.5/10.

A lot of people are going to write hate about the microtransaction system. There's a legit complaint there as Tripwire focused development resources on that system rather than gameplay content which was already beyond its promise date. My guess is that their hand was forced due to not having the necessary funds to complete development with the current rate of purchases being made, but they could've at least been honest with fans and customers who already purchased the game.
Aside from all that, my real gripe was just how dumbed down the combat got. In KF1, thanks to subtle mechanics like mini-stuns and such, you could do some amazing strategic plays even by yourself or with few team mates left standing. In KF2, it's just point and click, do some damage, hope it dies before it reaches you. The biggest problem there being with the Berserker (read: melee) class. The weapons became homogenized, and are barely differentiated in a way to make clear tiers stand out among the different weapons. The same uninspired, homogenized type gameplay is only further reinforced by the maps and the boss (though the later re-added Patriarch may not suffer as much).
As time went on, even before microtransactions, my weekly play time was dropping consistently until one day I realized I hadn't played in over a month. The game's fun factor just wasn't there for me like KF1. I was looking forward to coming back to it when new content was released, but that's been so little so often, I'm barely bothered to even do more than glancing at patch notes anymore.
With the announcement of everything else Tripwire is now spending development resources on, I'm left with even less hope that this game will reach the glory of its predecessor. This is not the same Tripwire that developed KF1, and it shows not only in their business decisions, but far more importantly in the drab and lackluster gameplay in KF2.
Bottom line, while the game may look fun from the trailers, it's a level of enjoyment that wears thin fast and leaves you with unfinished content. You'll be left waiting for balance and more emergent game mechanics to arrive with new patches only to find that it never comes.
If you're really eager to try this game out, at least wait for it to leave Early Access such that you understand what the game really has to offer. Because right now, what it does offer is woefully short of what's promised, leaves a bit to be desired, and how much better it may ever be is a question that no one knows the answer to, likely not even Tripwire themselves.

First things first, the graphics aren't the best and there is no voice overs to tell the story, everything is read. From a story perspective the story kept me interested throughout, I read every conversation because the people and world were interesting. In certain parts where it got kind of crazy it didn't take itself too serious. Overall it was a well written story. This, to be honest, wasn't really expected when I first got it because I was mainly interested in the combat gameplay, but it exceeded expectations in story.
Now for the combat you can expect similar gameplay to Xcom Enemy Unknown. I think it has more options than enemy unknown as far as abilities go though. I played a melee character with some adept abilities. That is one weak spot of the game, you level your character and choose his path, but you can't really customize your entire team outside of choosing pre-made allies for missions and on some missions certain story characters will just come along. While there are a lot of abilities it felt to me that the character I was making didn't get all that many abilities, not that they don't exist, but it takes too many prerequisite points to unlock them. When I finished the game I was only about half through the various tech trees, and there isn't a way to get more experience than what the game provides, at least not substantially more.
The game takes a little while to get started, at least for those people that are playing it for the combat more than the story. The first 3-4 hours is a lot of story and very easy, 2-3 enemy battles that aren't very exciting. It isn't until mid to late in the game that you start to encounter battles that take a little bit of thought and strategy. The game really shows how good it can be in the final 3 or so battles.
The game comes with a scenario creation kit that the community can use to create new stories and publish them to the Steam workshop. While this is a great plus I can't really be that excited for it until something of quality is released. So with that said, the base game without the possibility of those added campaigns is a pretty good game on its own as long as you're into turn based strategy games with moderate depth and don't mind reading through the story through character conversations.

I could pretty much live without every game in my inventory except Civ 5. If I had to take a game to a desert island and play only that game it would be Civ 5. The simple reason being that it's time sinkingly enjoyable, well-polished and has fantastic replay value. Digest the negative reviews but don't be put off, no other game in my inventory has seen as much play time as this true classic of the genre.
You simply must buy the complete edition, many of the mechanics criticised by fans when the game first came out have been fixed and improved by all the DLC and on sale it's quite frankly a bargain. The DLC adds more depth, victory conditions and replay value making what was a good game a superb game.
The graphics and atmosphere are perfect for this type of game and everything is clear and easy to read, the UI is straight forward and easy to use and also well laid out. The combat is straight forward but still enjoyable and I much prefer the single unit to a hex tile system to earlier versions of stacked 'power tiles'. If you read through negative reviews for this game, people will complain about certain aspects (for example diplomacy could work better) and some people think the combat is too simplistic. However the simple fact of the matter is as a complete package Civ 5 is arguably one of the best turn based strategy games you can currently buy. I honestly don't believe it does anything badly, what it does do is lots of things brilliantly and a couple of things well and the odd thing (diplomacy mainly) averagely.
This game for me is a 9.5/10 and if you are even remotely interested in turn based strategy games and don't already own this then you need to buy it right now... if right now is a Steam sale because it's on sale like... always!

I bought this game pretty much on a hunch, a hunch that it would be something I would enjoy immensely, and I was right. As soon as I step into the Main Menu I came across a great tune which got me into the right mood. The character creation is overall pretty good in my honest opinion, having a set of difference races, classes and ettiquets to choose from and then the usual skill "tree". If you enjoy turn based combat games I'm positive that you'll enjoy this one, as soon as I got my first encounter it reminded me of the XCOM: EU and Omerta, mainly due to the cover system and because I've played those too fairly recently. The combat ranges from a variety of standard guns, hand to hand combat and spells to the deploying drones and summoning spirits to fight by your side, it also uses the standard chance to hit per attack with a somewhat medium variety of skills and abilities to use. The world is really well put together and the writing does a tremendous great job of putting you inside the game world where magic meets cutting edge tech and when the Earth is a total mess. As I said the writing is pretty good, atleast I thought so, and that made me enjoy this game much more than I was expecting to. I'm looking foward to the user created content and the upcoming DLC and I HIGHLY recommend this to any fan of classic party RPGs or turn based combat.

While I am enjoying this game so far, I cannot recommend this game to anyone except die-hard Shadowrun fans. The gameplay is quite shallow and almost completely linear, the interface is clunky and designed for tablets. There is no exploration, poor documentation, and equipment selection is limited. Dialog choices are meaningless for the most part, and you cannot save the game except for advancing checkpoints, which also means no going back if you missed anything. Fallen enemies disappear and cannot be looted, and class/skill balance is poorly implemented. For a 2 million dollar budget from kickstarter alone this is a disappointment.
What Shadowrun Returns really is, is a game engine and development toolkit, whose true merit has yet to be seen, with a short adventure included. This could be a good thing, but only time will tell. I see the potential for great things with this game but in my opinion that is not a selling point at this time for anyone but modders.
However, as a Shadowrun fan, I am thrilled to be back exploring the neon lit slums of 2055 Seattle. The level artwork is the highlight, with the music adding to the atmosphere. The 3d character models are quite crude but fit in with the world when you are actually playing, just don't expect to get interesting looking armour for your character. There is no voice acting, but for a video game the writing is a pleasant surprise though that isn't saying much.
All said and done, I don't regret preordering Shadowrun Returns, but if you are curious about the setting I recommend picking up one of the books until this game goes on sale.

As a huge DC and Batman fan, I've religiously 100%ed the previous Arkham games with the exception of Batman: Arkham Origins (I gave up on the Predator Paragon achievement). It seems Batman: Arkham Knight will be another exception but for different reasons. I actually loved Origins despite its flaws but the more I think about this title... the more I realize it was a chore to play. Keep in mind that I got the premium edition (base game + all DLC) for ~$24 USD off of Bundlestars when they were having a sale too. Before I cover the issues that annoyed me though, I'd like to go over the positives first.
For starters, this game looks amazing -- there's no doubt about it. I've never seen an Unreal Engine 3 game that looks like this and I'm not just talking about the facial animations and expressions, I'm talking about everything. Another area the game excelled in was voice acting. Most characters were well cast and Kevin Conroy as Batman and a certain someone definitely were at the top of their game here. Also worth mentioning is the good twists and "gotcha!" moments that totally caught me off guard. The soundtrack was similarly great and hit most of the right notes, making me almost cry in one scene. Building off what Arkham City gave us, we get even more combat moves and ways to initiate a silent takedown. Not only that, we finally get to drive around in the batmobile and tear down the streets in it. I can't downplay how exciting it is to hop into this awesome vehicle the first time and then find out it's a tank! Yes, the batmobile can transform in a matter of seconds into a tank which the game calls "Battle mode". There's tons of stuff you can do while in this mode and it's all really exciting stuff.
Batmobile aside, there's no shortage of side missions and other little diversions happening while you fly around the map such as: thugs driving around in cars like hooligans or riots happening on the streets. If you've got the season pass there's also a ton of different batmobiles that you can test drive with authentic sounds and multiple characters you can play as in the AR challenges. My fondest memories are of playing the Adam West race tracks while hearing the TV show's theme song and playing as characters like Harley Quinn and Red Hood because of how unique they are. The best part of this game would have to be Photo Mode though. This wasn't even part of the base game upon launch but it was later added as a free update. A good 1/4 of my screenshots for this game were done in photo mode and what makes it great to use is that you can pause the game at any time, choose "Photo Mode" from the pause menu, manipulate the camera angles, slap on a filter, zoom in or zoom out, choose a border, and do it all in a way that's really easy to use. You end up getting some great looking screenshots like the one below. But unfortunately... all of this isn’t enough.
Even though I’d say this is the best Arkham game for role-playing as Batman... there's such a thing as less is more. The batmobile's undoubtedly great but because the story mode over relies on it, the fun factor disappears. Tank battle after tank battle and the game doesn't give up.
Winch this, dodge these tanks and blow them up (it feels like an arcade game at times honestly), drive around and use this feature from the batmobile… and repeat. I really think the batmobile should've been optional and not forced in the way that it is. The batmobile just feels a bit too destructive at times as well. I laughed as I mowed over people and slammed into buildings leaving nothing but debris. In addition to all of what I've said, the batmobile reduces the rather cool boss fights that we had in previous games to... yep, you guessed it... tank battles.
Want to battle Deathstroke? Tank battle. Want to battle the Arkham Knight? Tank battle. Want to battle Firefly? Batmobile pursuit (okay it's a bit different but still not much fun). It just shows a lack of creativity. Other side missions? Disabling bombs safely and destroying APC military vehicles. How? I won't even go there. Even some of The Riddler missions - one of my favourite Batman villains - are almost crippled because of this. I won't spoil anything but The Riddler has basically set up race tracks for your batmobile and you have to get to the finish line in time. Yay? Writing this just makes me upset at all the lost potential here (even a lot of the non-batmobile missions and sidemissions lack fun for some reason). I get Rocksteady wanted to spoil us with the batmobile as well as a large cast of villains but it came at the cost of quality and most of the game just feels extremely repetitive.
Next is the story. The writing here is noticeably weaker than any of the other Arkham games (might be because Paul Dini left) and the story has too many plot holes for my liking. Not to mention the identity of one of the villains in this game is incredibly easy to guess. There's a ridiculous amount of foreshadowing and what could've been a powerful reveal is mostly uneventful. Besides that, to get the “True Ending” players are forced to beat every side mission and get 243/243 riddles. The true ending doesn’t even answer a lot of questions or provide much closure but locking something like this behind riddles is a very silly move. Thankfully there’s a 242/243 savegame on PCGamingWiki if you don’t feel up to the task. On the port side of things, the game runs mostly decent but I had some issues that need to be addressed. The first: unlocking certain Steam achievements will actually make the game freeze for a second or two every time you satisfy the criteria once more for that achievement. I’m not joking. It’s all to do with the PCEngine.ini file. The second: I had around 13 crashes total across my playtime but 8 of those were in the same part of the story (analysing the crash site of a vehicle for someone that was kidnapped). You might not experience it, but it too has been another reported issue that remains unfixed.
Other negatives include the "Arkham episodes". 6 characters have a DLC mission made for them but 5 of them can be finished in less than 10 minutes. I could probably forgive this but these missions are divided into 3 sections with 3 short cutscenes usually. Combat room, predator room, combat room or the other way around, but I don't think that's worth applauding. Batgirl's DLC is fortunately 1 hour and man is it a good piece of DLC in the way that Cold, Cold Heart was for Batman: Arkham Origins. Season of Infamy is also good but not worth the $10. Moving onto AR challenges… most of them aren't tailored for every character. You'll notice this with someone like Harley Quinn where there's a lack of things for her to climb or jump up to. When it comes to combat, a lot of characters share a ridiculous amount of moves. Lastly, thug voiceovers are reused for most of the characters and maybe one line for some is changed. A good example would be "Batman's not going to save you now
!". For Nightwing? "Batman's not going to save you now
!". It's especially bad when these lines repeat over and over more than they ever did in Arkham City. Certain AR challenges have bugs where thugs stand still and do nothing. Other maps are just unfair and weren't made in mind with the current combat system (Iceberg Lounge and Catwoman's Revenge). I’ll stop here….
I've written an essay but all I’ll say is this: the PC port's better now but this game is easily the weakest in this series. If I wasn't a person with a lot of patience and/or a hardcore achievement collector, I don't think I would've made it far into this game. 4.5/10.

Shadowrun Returns has the unfortunate "honor" of being a modern reboot of a classic series. I say unfortunate due to the fact that bringing back an old franchise can have significant repercussions on the validity of the entire series if the new game doesn't happen to live up to the standards placed upon it by rabid, nostalgic fans (see 2011's Deus Ex Human Revolution, 2012's Syndicate, or 2013's The Bureau - XCOM Declassified).
Thankfully I can't count myself among the older generation of gamers who enjoyed the original Shadowrun titles and thus I believe that makes me and those like me more able to approach SRR with much more objectivity.
That being said how does this game stack up?
Older and/or retro gamers will be happy to see that SRR embraces the old school RPG feel. Beautifully crafted, high resolution 2D environments (with 3D character models), turn-based combat (recognizable to anyone who has played XCOM - Enemy Unknown), text-based conversations and descriptions, and even a retro-sounding soundtrack harks back to the "good ol' days" of early '90s PC roleplaying games.
The game sports five different races, six different classes, a wide (yet rather shallow) assortment of weapons/armor/items/etc, and a rather robust skill point tree that you allocate your XP (called Karma) into. Furthermore the game even allows you to create your own class where you can combine any of the different skills into whatever combination you desire.
On the surface everything seems right where it belongs but its when you start getting into the actual content that things start to lose their shine.
SRR shipped with one campaign that will take a typical gamer somewhere between ten and twenty hours to complete. However the game's length is not the most concerning but rather the fact that it is, without a doubt, one of the most linear experiences I've encountered in an RPG. Aside from a single optional mission everything you do in the campaign is devoted to moving the story along. The effect of this is made even more painful as there is no game world to explore and move about freely - instead once you reach the main hub you automatically teleport to the mission area and back to the hub when your objective is completed. The icing on the not-so-fantastic cake though is the save system which is automatic and only saves when you enter a new area. Although this wasn't much of an issue for me there were instances where a manual save system would've been much appreciated.
Aside from a linear, albeit interesting and enjoyable, campaign the game comes with a editor that allows gamers to create their own campaigns. Much like Skyrim though, the good stuff won't start coming out from the community full swing until a few months down the road.
All-in-all SRR isn't a bad game by any means. For $20 it's a nice throw back to the classic RPG era that promises to deliver much more content once the UGC (user generated content) starts rolling out as well as additional campaigns from the developers themselves. If you like RPGs Shadowrun Returns isnt a terrible investment, just one that will improve with time. I would definitely recommend this to anyone interested in the whole cyber-punk/future fantasy vibe.

And there are some characters from the old game as well as Shadowrun lore that make an appearance. The game also necessitates that you hire shadowrunners yourself to complete jobs, thus creating a team party. This is fun.
On the negative side, there is only an auto-save feature after you complete a run. So if you're in the middle of an hour+ jaunt and you gotta leave for work - guess what - either leave the game running or start over. The game also ignores some of the major mechanics of the pen-n-paper game such as essence and magic. Cyberware (machine augmentation in a character's body) lowers essence in the old game. Low essence means that one's magic rating starts reducing as well. Put in too much cyber and you'll eventually be such a weak mage that you can't light a candle with a fireball spell. In Shadowrun Returns, you can do both with only a spell cooldown modifier.
The mixed side is that the game is rather short and has a fairly linear story. A good story, but it's pretty straight to the point. I wanted more when I was done. This is a good compliment in reference to how fun the game is to play. It's a negative though in the sense that there isn't more. But for $20 (or $18 that I got it for on sale), the game ended up costing me $1/hour to play from start to finish. Of course I can download user-generated content or make my own if I so wish, so at least there's that.
Ultimately though, if you liked the old SNES version, this will be a nostalgic blast from the past. If you're a fan of the pen-n-paper game, this might annoy you, but overall it encompasses the feel of the original game.. so, give it a shot. You'll probably like it.

This game is... it's just...
Let me put it this way. If people say your reaction time is slow, play this for a few minutes. Which isn't hard. You die repeatedly, and in some cases literally every two seconds. But it hooks you to try to beat it. To beat that record you set. From 5 seconds, to 7, to 10. Time burns when this game is running. But trust me: when you beat that first level, you know you can beat the next, and next in turn. It's addictive. Ridiculously. I've seen other reviews that say "sensitivity adjustment" or "insane moving game", and even "you need perfect timing to get anywhere." I say to you; be not deterred. This game is brilliant.
Super Hexagon is, as shown by the teaser video, a game involving a triangle (which you play as) dodging a world of imploding six-sided polygons. You need to use speed and precision to get to where you need to be in time to not get hit with a wall, and killed. That part itself causes the game to lose players, but I say this; the more you play, the better you get, and the better you feel when you beat that next level.
This game is, as I see it, centered around two things: Mastery and Achievements. Look at that teaser. I mean, you can't just sit down and start beating these levels one day. It takes time. Practice. And when you get good enough to beat level one, level two is in it's shadow, waiting to challenge you again.
In terms of achievements, look at the percentages. Truly, 1.8% of owners have beat this game? How would you feel to be one of the few who raise that percentage? To be a part of the few victors? Because trust me, it's awesome.
Really, the game itself is worth more than the tiny price it's up for. The colors, the gameplay, ect. But one of my favorite parts is the music. Really, the soundtrack alone should be for sale for the same price the game is worth.
...All in all, I say this: If you want this game, don't hesitate. If you don't, you're missing out. If you have it, and have yet to beat it, don't give up. That victory is a few seconds away. And if you have it, and have beaten it... you have every right to call yourself a reaction master.
I recommend this game to everyone I know. It's crazily fun. Just... don't rage. Hehe.

Anyway, my story. I was a pre-order of this game, I downloaded day one and tried to start playing. Those of us that remember what that was like, will remember the agony and disappointment. But I knew the problems that the game had, I also knew what a .ini file was. A couple notepad edits later, the game was fixed.

I loved the game, it was fun. Tank combat was a little out of place but I enjoyed it. One of the few I suppose. It still had a LOT of problems: texture popping, hit detection, combo keys not registering, not to mention stuttering, screen tearing, FPS drops, and Nvidia's additions screwing us AMD users over.
Anyway, I beat it a while back, and moved on. Until recently when all the DLC had come out, and I had a $20 steam code burning a hole in my pocket. So I bought the season pass. I started playing the new game plus. I realized that it was still kinda fun. Then the different realization. NOTHING had changed. My modifications to the .ini file had been overwritten by some of the updates so it ran like a monkey in a bat-diaper. Tank combat was still kinda nice. Combo keys (alt-# is terrible to use as combo's, especially when it takes the blood of a virgin on a blood moon to get them to trigger) were still broken.
When trying to make a person happy, you give them control. Too much control can make people feel overwhelmed, but some control is better than none. New Game plus (NG+ from now on) was going fine. Until I got trapped in a corner repeatedly when special combos refused to execute (my usual virgin was out on buisness, moon was only a blue moon).
Could not change difficulty, could not reload save, could not reset NG+, unable to skip death cutscene (probably my biggest peve of them all, once or twice is alright, makes you madder I get that. However at the five mark it is just annoying)
Not exactly happy, then I noticed something else. Game crashes if you hit too many keys trying to find the key to skip death cutscene.
Thought I would try the Arkham episodes. Broken as the rest of it and even more frustrating (that catwoman robot fight "boss" is absolute dolphin crap). And the default control hints for the Red Hood story pack were in Play station form.
This may seem like a rant of a frustrated casual. And in part it is, I mostly play the arkham games for story anyway. But when a developer promises support, fails to give it (I know what WB said to all the articles, at about half a year since launch, then it faded away) and then just moves on? Makes me hesitant about future games on the PC, let alone from WB or Rocksteady. Games SHOULDN'T launch buggy. You are not buying a complete product (like a kettle without a handle, I mean it will work but... not what you were looking for), you are buying some big wigs desire to get something released to the ravinous wallets (I was guilty of this, love me some batman, but pre-ordering is not a good thing, but that is another rant).
My point is, I gave you a chance to fix it, I gave you my faith. I have a pile of kettle code that compiles without a handle. And I have a request for a refund from steam (for the seasons pass). PC players are getting shafted of late with buggy console ports and rip-offs. I know we may not be as lucrative as we once were, but we are still a player base.
Don't release dolphin crap, train or release your monkeys, find a PC division and let them work on it with time and dedication (maybe not Iron Galaxy next time) they might produce something that is worth a buy.

If you read through negative reviews for this game, people will complain about certain aspects (for example diplomacy could work better) and some people think the combat is too simplistic. However the simple fact of the matter is as a complete package Civ 5 is arguably one of the best turn based strategy games you can currently buy. I honestly don't believe it does anything badly, what it does do is lots of things brilliantly and a couple of things well and the odd thing (diplomacy mainly) averagely.
This game for me is a 9.5/10 and if you are even remotely interested in turn based strategy games and don't already own this then you need to buy it right now... if right now is a Steam sale because it's on sale like... always!

First, let me start this review by stating... I have never played the original Killing Floor. I will not be attempting comparisons to the original.
This is one of the most satisfying game experiences for me in a long time. I have over 500 hrs on this game and I never tire of it. The game is absolute fun. This game is what co-op play is meant to be. We either succeed as a team or we are ground up as a team. Some players are better than others, but nobody can simply carry the team. The victories are sweet because the defeats are so bitter. If you're the lone wolf type, save your money for another game. There is a single player option, but it is hard and it isn't really fun. Teaming up with five other random players and praying they have your back is a fun, hilarious, and intense experience. You will learn to develop eyes in the back of your head, because the zeds show up out of almost any place. If you are cut off from your team, your odds of survival decrease rapidly.  You will be angered by your team leaving you when you weren't paying attention, and you will be thankful when they come back and save you. Both experiences are common.
As with any online game, some players are friendlier than others. If you join a game with four players all named after dead presidents, don't take it personal if they kick you... just like every other online game of this sort. The majority, in my experience, are friendly and will offer help. The community guides are a wealth of good info and tips. There are sevaral playstyles (perks) to fit your taste. The more you play the better you get both leveling and playing your character to the team's advantage.
The visuals are pretty good. The zeds blown to bits, dismembered, burned, and generally gibbed in hilarious violent ways. For me, it's the headshots. They never get old, that's why the commando is my fav. The settings are varied, and the community maps mostly good. Some levels (maps) are open and some are claustrophobic. Some are well lit and some are dark. I guess the soundtrack is pretty good, but honestly, I get so drawn into the battle at hand, I never really hear it.
Finally, There has been a lot of mixed views on this game recently. Some people complain about the microtransactions, where you can buy "cosmetic only" changes to the look of your character. Others complain about the developers being too slow on releasing updates. And still others complain the game is too different from the original. While some of these may be legit to the person complaining, many are simply complaints by individuals whos favorite perk got nerfed this month in the developers ongoing effort to balance the classes and the zeds. Some online games have been on the market for over a decade and they are still constantly dealing with balance issues... get used to it.
The learning curve on this game seems difficult, but it really isn't. Accept death and try to give as much as you get. It gets easier as you get better, and the majority of players know this and wont hold it against you.
Have fun, heal often!

text:
If you're looking for a professionally made game that will give you hours of entertainment with it's packaged campaign: Shadowrun Returns is not for you. If you're looking for a great set of tools to create your own stories, or play through stories created by other players, then you *should* get Shadowrun Returns.
The "game" itself, at least at this point in time, is more of a taste of things to come. The packaged campaign is extremely short, offering, at best, 10-12 hours of play time from start to finish. There are almost no side-quests, little to no exploration, and pretty basic combat scenarios. The included campaign doesn't even show off a fraction of what the editor is capable of.
Fans of the Shadowrun pen and paper game that are looking for a faithful recreation of the PnP rules into a CRPG will also be disappointed, as the game itself does not really use the PnP rules. It does, however, faithfully recreate the setting and gives a good idea of how a PnP campaign might play out, but it is a far cry from a true port of the PnP system to a computer game. Neverwinter Nights was more faithful to the D&D 3.5e ruleset than Shadowrun Returns is to any version of the Shadowrun PnP rules.
The story within the Dead Man's Switch campaign is, at least, well written and pretty decent. There are various differing branches of dialogue you can read through, but ultimately, your choices don't alter the outcome of any given situation.
Looking at the editor, things seem a little brighter. Everything I've read about the tools before launch seem to be there. Everything is simple to use, and fairly easy to understand, though some more thourough documentation would be nice (the entire documentation for the editor is a user maintained wiki with, at this time, very little information). I was able to create a basic little one scene quest in only about 15 minutes (sans learning the basics of the editor).
For those that are looking for just a game to play, I can not recommend Shadowrun Returns at this time. That is not to say I wouldn't recommend it in the future, once the bigger campaign releases as DLC or when good, complete UGC is released. For those looking to create and share their own campaigns, stories, and content, however, I highly recommend Shadowrun Returns for it's simple and powerful editor.
