Half Life 2 was an amazing game when it came out in 2004, and is still a great game today. Its graphics can still compete with the most high-tech games of our time, and the Source engine's physics turn this game into an architectural masterpiece, the epitome of computer game engineering. Its satisfying soudns and visuals let you feel like yu're living the adventure, and the mechanics and structure are flawless. Valve clearly put much care and dedication into this gem.
But while all the technical stuff is definitely a defining factor in the initial and continuing popularity of this game, that's not what left me feeling sad when I realized the game was over, and why I was so joyful when I discovered Episodes One and Two. It was the amazing strory, the dialogue, and the so well-defined characters which really pulled me into this game, let me feel like I was Gordon Freeman. I genuinly hated Dr. Breen, even though I had never technically seen him do anything bad. I hated him because I knew that Gordon's comapnions — namely, Eli Vance — hated him, and I had developed an attachment to these chracters, more so than in any other game I have played. The only other games I have played that have allowed me to really pull me into the game like Half Life 2 did are Portal, Bioshock, and to an extent, Skyrim. But what really struck me was that all the information you get comes from the speech of the chracters you encounter. There is no pre-game intro which gives a back story, and your character never speaks. In short, you, the player, grow into Gordon Freeman, become him in a sense, as you progress, and how other characters react to you helps you understand who you are controlling and guiding through this dystopian future.
I throughly enjoyed my experience with Half Life 2 and I eagerly await my completion of its episodic sequels. without hesitation, I give this game the only perfect score I am likely to give to a game.

text:
HL2. The game that got me gaming :) Once upon a time many dark moons ago I didn't own any games. Instead I played free demos. I did this for about a year. And one demo I played about 60 times was Half Life 2. We don't go to Ravenholm so it is said. But I did. I practically lived in bloody Ravenholm.
And lets face it - the rent is cheap there. The zombies drove the prices way down. No more yuppies just one bizarre preacher with amazing shotgun skills. Sure there's a lot of blood and headcrabs and killer traps and weird noises... but nowhere is perfect right?
Out of all the demos this one was the most visceral, interesting, scary, intense and fun one to play. But I needed to know what came before - and what happens after, the amazing Ravenholm section.
So I bought HL2. Got into gaming. I think this is about 6 years back. And learned that HL2 is indeed an epic story and gameplay experience. The amazing thing is, I still get a rush - a brain rush - when I load it up again. Because I know I'm going to experience an entire gamut of locations, combat, feelings, enemies, friends, and puzzles, (And don't listen to Duke Nukem who said - "I hate valve puzzles" - ♥♥♥♥ you big guy you don't have the mind-set :)
I love how varied the game is from start to finish, including the two Episodes that come after HL2. It's a treat. It still looks Ok. It runs perfectly. I've never experienced a bug. And getting a chievo for getting through the Ravenholm section using only a crowbar and gravity gun, felt like full circle for me. Goddamn zombies I'm back - and I'm badass.
My review isn't about plot. It's about something deeper, that I can't put into words because I don't have that ability. If you don't have this game, pick it up. And sink your brain and time into it. Let it build. It may not be for everybody, but those who like it, love it.

So let's get the obvious out of the way - this game had an utterly unforgivable launch. I will not buy from Rocksteady again. The only reason I had to purchase this game was the investment I had in the universe itself.
NEGATIVES:
- Tank warfare... Like really? Weak.
- Major boss fights end up being car fights, utterly ridiculous.
- Performance issues, regularly skips frames
- They ruined freeflow and combat in general. By adding ridiculous amounts of enemies who you can't just up and attack, they make maintaining flow almost impossible. On top of this, the prioritizing for which enemies you attack (i.e. the game assumes I intend to instant takedown a brute instead of an unarmed goon) is also botched. I will try to disarm and destroy a shield and end up attacking someone with a baseball bat. Just in general, the combat has taken a huge step down in playability, enjoyability, and flow.
- FEAR takedowns are way too important. I get it, Batman has a new gimmick. Don't make it a necessity for stealth.
- Instead of locking a Riddler cutscene to his quest line, the actual story's conclusion in its entirety is locked until you 100% all the default missions. Including 240 riddler trophies...
- DLC is very short, but because I bought this so long after release, I felt the lower price was fair.
POSITIVES:
+ Still an Arkham game. The story, as botched as the intro is, ends up being fairly fun. It's no where near as good as City or Asylum, however.
+ Batcomputer data is fun to read, even though it isn't as extensive as City's batcomputer data.
+ The batmobile is actually pretty fun. It's just not the right game or universe for the kind of combat they shoehorned in.
+ Voice acting is, for the most part, on par with the other games. It's not phenomenal, but it doesn't distract.
+ The batmobile riddles are mostly pretty good. Some are cheap as hell though. I spent twenty minutes working on a riddle only to discover I needed an upgrade that is unmarked and unmentioned by anything, and you only get it by doing certain riddles - but that's not enough for me to consider them all bad.
+ You can play, provided you have the DLC, as a lot of characters in AR mode (new challenge mode)
+ Dual team combat is a blast. I wish they had focused more on this than FEAR and batmobile combat. They could have made the game co-op with a little more work.
+ Graphics are superb when the game isn't dropping frames
+ Satisfying ending mission, use youtube for final cutscene (which is less satisfying to the point of being frustrating)
All in all... Lots of mixed elements here. Overall I think I got my money's worth, but I'm really invested in the franchise. For someone who just wants to play an Arkham game, I suggest City.

Overview: This is a 3rd person survival horror game set in the future on a interstellar mining ship.  You play as Isaac Clarke, a ship systems engineer, who was sent along with a team to investigate a distress signal sent out by the ship.  You soon learn that the entire crew is dead and has been turned into Necromorphs.  They appear in many forms and require strategic dismemberment to defeat.  To defeat the Necromorphs, the player must shoot off various limbs.  Removing the head is not enough to stop these creatures.  After crashing into the ship, Isaac must make his way through the ship and find some way to escape.
Pros: This game really lives up to its survival horror genre.  The game is dark and scary with monsters continually jumping out from the shadows and walls.  The story is decent and presented well.  It never really interupts the gameplay as most storytelling is done in real time.  The game is also very immersive.  All interfaces are displayed holographically in game and in real time.  So, opening up a menu doesn't break the players immersion.  There are a wide variety of enemies each with a decent range of player death animations.  It can actually be quite entertaining just to watch all the ways Isaac can die.  The gameplay presents a good mix of action, platforming, and simple puzzle solving.  Never did I feel bored playing through the game.
Cons: The biggest con to me is the game balance.  I had to be extremely careful to manage my resources well.  Even though this genre encourages good resource management, I felt it was a little off.  This wouldn't be a con for me if the game was tailored for this type of extreme resourch management.  Many times would I come to a room where I had to kill a horde of enemies with a handful of shots.  Even if I managed to defeat them all, if I didn't do it efficiently enough I would have to reload the game and try it again.  This continues to be an issue throughout the game as ammo and money is scarce.  Whenever you get to a shop, you have to spend all your money on ammo, which isn't cheap.  To me, this game was all about the action and the lack of resources just hindered that action.  The perspective and controls also may be difficult for some people to adjust to.
Conclusion: If you're looking for a good survival horror game, look no further.  This game is challenging and quite fun.  Even though I think the game balance is a little off, this really is my only major con with the game.  It's worth a playthrough.
Score: 9.1 / 10

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a fantastic reboot from the old days of XCOM. Its complexity may have been reduced and it could probably add more game mechanics to make it feel more organic, but XCOM: Enemy Unknown really does work with less.
You pick a team of elite soldiers on a mission to figure out the alien threat through a project known as XCOM. As you play the game you will slowly level up the soldiers you command on the battle field making them specialize such as Support, Sniper, Assault, or Heavy giving each their own set of abilities that make each of them very useful in their own situations.
Throughout the game you will also find upgrades through certain story events allowing you not only upgrade your soldiers but be able to give them more advanced gear.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a hard hitter. Every mission can end in victory or utter elimination of your units. Units dying feels like you lost someone close and are definitely cemented by the Memorial wall that can be viewed back at base.
XCOM: EU does it all right. It makes a very engaging and rewarding experience finding more difficult enemies and game play requiring more and more strategies to ensure your soldiers get out alive and ultimately destroy the alien invaders.

The patched version of the game ran perfectly on my 980, at max settings.  If you have a medium to high-end computer, I think you'll be fine running this. Honestly, it looks more natural and fluid at 30 FPS than at 60.
As for the game itself, the story is really good. They focus on less villians and make it mostly about Scarecrow messing with Batman's family. They found a brilliant way to bring the Joker back into it too. I think this is the single best Mark Hamill Joker performance ever. The Arkham Knight stuff is stupid and too predictable, but he's honestly not even in it that much. Just ignore him.
The gameplay is solid. The batmobile is way over used, but I like how fast it makes the combat. There are less "Batman beats up 30 guys" sequences than in Arkham City, which my thumb is thankful for. The biggest downgrade is the crappiness of the boss fights. Most of the time it comes down to a tank battle with incredibly dumb AI. I managed to kill the Arkham Knight by circling the same building twenty times and shooting him repeatedly in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ till he gave up.
It's totally worth playing, even if it's not quite as good as Arkham City.

You know how they say that sequels aren't as good as the original... The Rocksteady Arkham Trilogy is the exception to the rule. This game is pure f*****g magic. After Arkham City I thought its gonna be hard to top... With AK, Rocksteady succeeds in giving you the most action packed, heart and mind thrilling conclusion to a nearly perfect game trilogy.
Sure the PC version got of to a rocky start with performance problems... but those problems are now fixed and the game looks and feels so goddamn amazing.  I'm running it with full graphics and physics options enabled and it maintains a smooth 60fps with a possibility for 90fps if you own a high refresh rate monitor... This is with a i5-6600k, 16gb ddr4, gtx 980 ti and 950 pro m.2 ssd.
One of the main complaints i've read most ppl have is with the batmobile and how it has to be used for some portions of the game. After 2 games solely on foot, i find the batmobile action very refreshing. There's still heaps of stuff to do and places to explore on foot. But the fact remains that Gotham is in a state of war with heavy artillery roaming the streets... Having a machine of destruction in your arsenal is very logical and convinient. I wouldnt want to spend hours trying to slap explosive gel on the side of a tank actively looking to gun me down.
If you're really into the story like me, then this is THE game for you. By the end of this you might shed a manly tear or two. I couldn't recommend this game enough... so good.

I would say "don't bother. Just start with DS2." But you really do miss a lot of the plot (not that it's very good), and DS2 is a lot easier to get into if you've played DS for at least a couple hours.
In Dead Space, you play a space janitor with the "clever" name of Isaac Clarke (anybody who doesn't get the references in the name, go read a book). But you're not a very good space janitor. In fact, Isaac is not even functional enough to walk and reload his plasma cutter at the same time. And when something goes wrong on the derelict ship that Isaac's crew is investigating, he's actually fairly useless, needing directions from the science officer (or was she the XO?) to tell him where to go.
To put that in perspective, that's essentially Mr. Spock telling Scotty how to repair a ship. It's Riker telling Geordi how to restart the warp core. Isaac is supposedly the engineer, but when he needs to reboot the systems of the derelict, it's up to everyone else to tell him how.
But let's not let a silly thing like "plot" or "continuity" get in the way of a "good" game. Good things about Dead Space. Atmosphere. This game just sucks you in. At least, it sucked me right in. At first. But more on that later. Dead Space is just dripping with little nifty touches to make you feel uneasy. It's wonderful in that regard.
The weapons are... interesting, if difficult. Some of them take a lot of trial and error to figure out exactly when you should use the alternate fire mode, and that gets frustrating. but nevertheless, the weapon selection is very interesting, and none of the weapons are very similar.
The bad. Oh, where to begin. The controls are awful, the plot is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (as previously mentioned), the main character is a hunch-backed halfwit who somehow graduated space high school and went through some sort of space vocational training to become a master of the space janitorial arts. But again, I try not to let a horrible plot ruin a game.
Navigating is a chore, which is more hampered than helped by the glowing "follow me" trail, because you basically become completely dependent on it.
If you see a space zombie lying on the ground, it is going to jump up when you get near. Shoot it all you want before you walk up to it. The only thing that triggers them is proximity, and nothing you do before waking them up will actually damage them. The first time one jumped up at me, it was startling and very cool. After the tenth time, it was just tedious. If there was some randomness to it, that would be another story. Maybe this one really is dead. Nope!♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ But no. Every single "corpse" you find lying on the floor is going to wake up and attack you.
Despite all the cheese and awfulness of the controls, I actually enjoyed Dead Space for a few hours until it just became tedious. If everyone hadn't told me how awesome it was, I would have played it for a bout five minutes and wanted my money back. The controls are that bad. Mouse or gamepad, it doesn't matter. It's just very clumsy and finnicky.

The Batman series has taken me along for the ride. I should probably explain upfront the elephant in the room; the thing that everyone needs to know and yet somehow no one seems to be talking about.
In between Arkham City and Arkham Knight, the game was handed to an Ipad Factory developer and Warner Bros.-owned Warner Montreal. Warner Montreal has never made a blockbuster to save their life, so basically what that team did was copy Arkham City almost exactly, and try to bring back a few old faces from the Batman comic. They failed spectacularly. Arkham Origins was a complete flop.
The reason for this decision was simple. Rocksteady is a great developer, and Warner Inc is greedy. Rocksteady said, after Arkham City: "We're not really happy with our engine. You need to give us a few years to improve our code." Not able to compel Rocksteady into action, they redeployed Rocksteady's secondary assets to Montreal. The problem with this is it stymied development of Arkham Knight, causing the game's PC release to be glitchy and unfinished when it finally arrived.
TLDR: A lot of these negative reviews reflect poorly on the publisher, not on the game.
Arkham Knight is the natural progression of the Arkham series. If you haven't played the other games, you won't understand the story of this one. If I wasn't a Batman fan, I would probably be confused with the time skip even after playing the previous games. It was rather jarring after seeing Oracle in a supporting role in City, and then being bumped up to a major recurring character in Knight. A lot of the story was left out and I think it might have been more evocative to see what happened with the supporting cast. Oh well.
Functionally, I like this game. It feels very very smooth. When you call the batmobile, it's like the game intelligently decides how to cinematically drop Batman's model into the cockpit. If you're in the air, the car will drive beneath you and try to land you seamlessly in your seat. On the ground? The car will drive past you and the Batman model will take a quick hop in the air. Want to get out quickly? The model will eject and the car will drift to a halt. It's very well done. A lot of effort went into asthetics.
Combat is pretty nice. Improvements were made on the counter system. Now trying to fit your strikes in with blocks isn't such a big deal.  I was disappointed with a lack of innovative level up incentives. The ability to use one specific gadet while flying costs 4 tech points? Also, some of the upgrades didn't unlock in normal mode until you were way past used to dealing with certain annoying enemies.
All of the gripes I have with Knight are with production choices. Scarecrow's voice actor ISN'T SCARY. He sounds too much like Hugo strange. Hearing his voiceovers as I'm driving around makes me want to yawn. Jonathan Crane is supposed to be a spindly little doctor with a sadistic streak. Where is that character? Production turned him into a generic-o-matic villain. The character is flat and not fun.
On the flip side, there is a certain surprise actor who does an amazing job, as always, and the production team did a great job of standing him up. I wish they had spent a little more time on Scarecrow.
Where is Jervish Tetch? The mad hatter is my favorite villain. All I get is a little sidenote in the evidence locker? shame.
All in all? 8/10. It's a great game. It certainly has my vote for GotY

Horror probably isn't the right word here. The game doesn't really go for good scares, mostly just sudden "oh my god it's an alien coming straight for you suddenly have a loud noise" and they just got incredibly predictable after a while. But it can be quite creepy at times - probably helped absolutely humonguous amounts by the absolutely incredible sound design of this game. I think that this might the only time I max out one of the score categories for a game.
Seriously, the sound design is just amazing. Incredible ambient noise, with really creepy nuances and fantastic utterly disgusting music for when you get under attack. Every single sound made is absolutely perfect.
Also the UI of this game is just amazing. Everything makes sense in the game world, it's all projected out of your suit or from screens on everything. It's fantastic, and it helps increase the tension because you can't pause the game by opening the map screen/inventory screen.
The gameplay is pretty good, though I didn't feel it got tough enough on Normal difficulty so perhaps Hard difficulty is the right difficulty to play it on. The weapons are all satisfying to use, and can be very effective when upgraded correctly. I liked the way most of the enemies had weak points you could exploit to kill them quicker and conserve more ammo. The design of the aliens was fantastic, and the ship design was quite good (I liked how you had to revisit some levels for good reason, and some things had changed and that actually made it slightly creepy and foreboding).
The story wasn't particularly impressive, but a few bits of it were quite good. I was quite disappointed by the very end of the game though, like literally the last few seconds [if you've played it you'll know what I mean] because it just felt incredibly cheap.
Other than that, this game was very good. A definite play, if not for the perfectly adequate gameplay then just for the mindblowingly incredible sound. Seriously, someone give the guy who did all that all the awards. Ever. All the awards.

It was all in that moment when I just sat back and laughed. I couldn't believe it was quite this good. I chuckled in muddled disbelief, expectations utterly defied. My nervous fingers reloaded the level, knowing that I had to see that breathtaking sequence one more time. It was then that I knew for certain: Valve had surpassed not only themselves, but everyone else too. Half-Life 2 is an astounding accomplishment. It is the definitive statement of the last five years of first-person shooters. Everything else was just a stopgap.
Half-Life 2 is a near perfect sequel. It takes almost everything that worked from Half-Life and either improves on it, or keeps it much the same. But that simple summation undersells how the Valve team have approached this task. Half-Life 2 is a linear shooter with most of the refinements one would expect from years of work, but it is also a game of a higher order of magnitude than any of the previous pretenders to the throne. The polish and the stratospheric height of the production values mean that Half-Life 2 is a magnificent, dramatic experience that has few peers.
It would be madness for me to spoil this game by talking about the specific turn of events, so spoilers are going to be kept to a minimum. We're going to talk about general processes and the elements of style and design that make Half-Life 2 such an energising experience. Key to this is the way in which Gordon's tale is told. Once again we never leave his perspective. There are no cutscenes, no moment in which you are anything but utterly embedded in Gordon's view of the world. Everything is told through his eyes. And what a story it is. Gordon arrives at the central station at City 17—a disruptive and chilling dystopia. And from there? Well, that would be telling. This is not the contemporary America that Gordon seemed to be living in during the original Half-Life. The events of Black Mesa have affected the whole world. The crossover with Xen has meant that things have altered radically, with hyper-technology existing alongside eastern bloc dereliction.

Desde o começo Dead Space dá um certo receio de ser jogado, e isso se deve principalmente pelo clima obscuro apresentado no jogo, o qual te faz ter medo durante praticamento o jogo todo. Esse clima tenso transmitido pelo jogo é causado principalmente pela ambientação: uma nave gigantesca, a USS Ishimura, cheia de corredores escuros e estreitos, com buracos abertos por necromorphs em todos os lados, e você, sozinho, com suas armas, tendo que dar um jeito de sair daquele inferno. Além da ambientação, o som é um fator que aumenta ainda mais o clima de tensão durante o jogo: a maior parte do tempo, você anda na nave em total silêncio, e é pego totalmente de surpresa quando algum necromorph aparece, simplismente pelo fato de não saber de onde e quando ele vai vir. Os efeitos visuais do jogo são ao mesmo tempo magnfícos e bizarros, desde a mutilação dos mutantes pelas suas armas, as partes fora da Ishimura, até a sua própria mutilação, quando um necromorph te finaliza de um jeito grotesco, fazendo sua morte uma cena cinematográfica. O arsenal é bem variado, e cada arma tem suas características e pontos fortes. Os gráficos são muito bonitos pra época, e até hoje agradam os olhos. E além de tudo isso, a história de Dead Space dá o toque final para o jogo se consagrar como um excelente survival horror: é macabra, extremamente imersiva, e cheia de revira-voltas. Finalizando, Dead Space é sem sombra de dúvidas um dos melhores survival horros da geração, e merece muito ser jogado, mesmo após anos de seu lançamento. 8.5/10

Half Life 2 was an amazing game when it came out in 2004, and is still a great game today. Its graphics can still compete with the most high-tech games of our time, and the Source engine's physics turn this game into an architectural masterpiece, the epitome of computer game engineering. Its satisfying soudns and visuals let you feel like yu're living the adventure, and the mechanics and structure are flawless. Valve clearly put much care and dedication into this gem.
But while all the technical stuff is definitely a defining factor in the initial and continuing popularity of this game, that's not what left me feeling sad when I realized the game was over, and why I was so joyful when I discovered Episodes One and Two. It was the amazing strory, the dialogue, and the so well-defined characters which really pulled me into this game, let me feel like I was Gordon Freeman. I genuinly hated Dr. Breen, even though I had never technically seen him do anything bad. I hated him because I knew that Gordon's comapnions — namely, Eli Vance — hated him, and I had developed an attachment to these chracters, more so than in any other game I have played. The only other games I have played that have allowed me to really pull me into the game like Half Life 2 did are Portal, Bioshock, and to an extent, Skyrim. But what really struck me was that all the information you get comes from the speech of the chracters you encounter. There is no pre-game intro which gives a back story, and your character never speaks. In short, you, the player, grow into Gordon Freeman, become him in a sense, as you progress, and how other characters react to you helps you understand who you are controlling and guiding through this dystopian future.
I throughly enjoyed my experience with Half Life 2 and I eagerly await my completion of its episodic sequels. without hesitation, I give this game the only perfect score I am likely to give to a game.

HL2. The game that got me gaming :) Once upon a time many dark moons ago I didn't own any games. Instead I played free demos. I did this for about a year. And one demo I played about 60 times was Half Life 2. We don't go to Ravenholm so it is said. But I did. I practically lived in bloody Ravenholm.
And lets face it - the rent is cheap there. The zombies drove the prices way down. No more yuppies just one bizarre preacher with amazing shotgun skills. Sure there's a lot of blood and headcrabs and killer traps and weird noises... but nowhere is perfect right?
Out of all the demos this one was the most visceral, interesting, scary, intense and fun one to play. But I needed to know what came before - and what happens after, the amazing Ravenholm section.
So I bought HL2. Got into gaming. I think this is about 6 years back. And learned that HL2 is indeed an epic story and gameplay experience. The amazing thing is, I still get a rush - a brain rush - when I load it up again. Because I know I'm going to experience an entire gamut of locations, combat, feelings, enemies, friends, and puzzles, (And don't listen to Duke Nukem who said - "I hate valve puzzles" - ♥♥♥♥ you big guy you don't have the mind-set :)
I love how varied the game is from start to finish, including the two Episodes that come after HL2. It's a treat. It still looks Ok. It runs perfectly. I've never experienced a bug. And getting a chievo for getting through the Ravenholm section using only a crowbar and gravity gun, felt like full circle for me. Goddamn zombies I'm back - and I'm badass.
My review isn't about plot. It's about something deeper, that I can't put into words because I don't have that ability. If you don't have this game, pick it up. And sink your brain and time into it. Let it build. It may not be for everybody, but those who like it, love it.
Maybe not up there with the original form the 90's but still one of the best games of 2012 and definitely the best turn-based shooter!

The Batman series has taken me along for the ride. I should probably explain upfront the elephant in the room; the thing that everyone needs to know and yet somehow no one seems to be talking about.
In between Arkham City and Arkham Knight, the game was handed to an Ipad Factory developer and Warner Bros.-owned Warner Montreal. Warner Montreal has never made a blockbuster to save their life, so basically what that team did was copy Arkham City almost exactly, and try to bring back a few old faces from the Batman comic. They failed spectacularly. Arkham Origins was a complete flop.
The reason for this decision was simple. Rocksteady is a great developer, and Warner Inc is greedy. Rocksteady said, after Arkham City: "We're not really happy with our engine. You need to give us a few years to improve our code." Not able to compel Rocksteady into action, they redeployed Rocksteady's secondary assets to Montreal. The problem with this is it stymied development of Arkham Knight, causing the game's PC release to be glitchy and unfinished when it finally arrived.
TLDR: A lot of these negative reviews reflect poorly on the publisher, not on the game.
Arkham Knight is the natural progression of the Arkham series. If you haven't played the other games, you won't understand the story of this one. If I wasn't a Batman fan, I would probably be confused with the time skip even after playing the previous games. It was rather jarring after seeing Oracle in a supporting role in City, and then being bumped up to a major recurring character in Knight. A lot of the story was left out and I think it might have been more evocative to see what happened with the supporting cast. Oh well.
Functionally, I like this game. It feels very very smooth. When you call the batmobile, it's like the game intelligently decides how to cinematically drop Batman's model into the cockpit. If you're in the air, the car will drive beneath you and try to land you seamlessly in your seat. On the ground? The car will drive past you and the Batman model will take a quick hop in the air. Want to get out quickly? The model will eject and the car will drift to a halt. It's very well done. A lot of effort went into asthetics.
Combat is pretty nice. Improvements were made on the counter system. Now trying to fit your strikes in with blocks isn't such a big deal.  I was disappointed with a lack of innovative level up incentives. The ability to use one specific gadet while flying costs 4 tech points? Also, some of the upgrades didn't unlock in normal mode until you were way past used to dealing with certain annoying enemies.
All of the gripes I have with Knight are with production choices. Scarecrow's voice actor ISN'T SCARY. He sounds too much like Hugo strange. Hearing his voiceovers as I'm driving around makes me want to yawn. Jonathan Crane is supposed to be a spindly little doctor with a sadistic streak. Where is that character? Production turned him into a generic-o-matic villain. The character is flat and not fun.
On the flip side, there is a certain surprise actor who does an amazing job, as always, and the production team did a great job of standing him up. I wish they had spent a little more time on Scarecrow.
Where is Jervish Tetch? The mad hatter is my favorite villain. All I get is a little sidenote in the evidence locker? shame.
All in all? 8/10. It's a great game. It certainly has my vote for GotY

With Risk of Rain, patience isn't only a virtue. It's a matter of survival. The game is certainly fun, but new players should bear in mind that when they first start playing, they will die quickly and often, even at the lowest difficulty setting.
In Risk of Rain, you play as one of several spacefaring warriors who have crashed on a mysterious planet and must attempt to escape while fighting off hostile local wildlife. Although the basic premise and gameplay doesn't exactly break new ground, the game does introduce some unique mechanics that keep things interesting. Among these is the fact that the game's difficutly level starts off relatively low, and gradually increases the longer the player remains in the game, regardless of how far they've actually progressed. Each level has a randomly-generated teleporter that the player must find in order to progress to the next stage.  But simply running straight to it is a poor strategy since the player also needs to fight monsters and collect power-ups in order to become strong enough to face the later levels. This forces the player to manage their time well and creates a nice bit of tension that underlies the morally ambiguious nature of the game's story; the planet's background is slowly revealed to the player through a series of "Monster Logs" and it quickly becomes clear that the player is more of a genocidal invader than a lost astronaut (I know, moral ambiguity in an indie game? How absurd!).
The big problem with Risk of Rain (one of many in a game that was written by two guys in a ♥♥♥♥ing basement) is that it only starts out with one playable character. And although the possibilty of unlocking more creates incentive to keep playing the game, the difficutly level makes unlocking more characters something of a grind, espcially when the starting character gets old pretty fast.
If you do end up buying RoR, you'll probably want to beat the game at least once on the lowest difficutly setting before you try anthing tougher. You'll save yourself a great many broken keyboards and monitors in the process.

South Park fans rejoice! This game is fanservice at its best. As an unabashed South Park fan, this game had me literally laughing out loud for most of the game. If you are a South Park fan, do not hesitate to buy The Stick of Truth! If you're not, I'm afraid that the RPG-style gameplay may be a bit dull and a bit too easy to keep you interested. You'll find yourself spamming the same couple of attacks in every battle. The timed button presses make it a bit more engaging, but once you're doing them by muscle memory... battle kinda becomes a chore.
There are a fair amount of collectable elements that make exploring all the nooks and crannies of the seemingly shrunken town of South Park more interesting, at least on the first playthough. Absolutely no grinding, very few fetch quests, and the game doesn't draw anything out unneccisarily, making it short but sweet. It's sort of like an RPG for people who don't play RPG's, but honestly the gameplay is just there to add a 'game' element to what is otherwise a long episode of South Park.
Be wary of the autosave system! Reloading a game may mean you have to go back and re-do something because it doesn't save your exact moment of progress! Pay attention each time you load your game, as there are some missable collectables! I missed out on a major achievement because of this wonky system. TALK TO CLYDE AS SOON AS YOU ENTER KUPA KEEP! You'll thank me later!

This happened to be the first turn based strategy that I ever laid my hands on, but now I realized the charm that lies in this particular genre. I haven't played the older xcom, so I have nothing to compare against. Overall, the game did a stellar job of managing the tense combat situation, as you follow the alien sounds, inching your way through the fog of war not knowing when the next move is going to activate a set of aliens, and make your grunt a sitting duck to enemy fire while he has no moves left to get back.
The other part of the game is base management. You have a single base, where you build various upgrades, satellites, laboratories and workshop where you can build/upgrade weapons and armours. There is a satisfying progression there as you unlock more advanced weapons one by one. Your soldiers level up as they gain XP and soon you will find the right mix of talents and the kind of soldiers you want to take which works for you.
The game has difficulty modes, thus not too difficult for the novice. It sports a ironman mode, and it is frequently touted that the way to play this game would be in ironman mode with classic difficulty. Having played it on easy without ironman and survived in the really really terrifying terror missions, I would advice against that to everyone but the most experienced/masochist of you. May be for second/third playthrough if I decide to give this another shot. While there is a narrative, it is barely there as a glue to make you do the various research required for the story to progress.
Among the cons, the game can be frustrating at times. Sometimes it can take as much as half an hour to find the one remaining alien on the map, the map themselves start repeating pretty soon. And once your soldiers are upgraded, the combat can feel a tard repetetive. The statistical probablity to hit an enemy sometime appears to be random, with no visual indicator before actually moving into position, but I guess this was a game design decision.
The game has a enjoyable multiplayer where you can build up your squad of alien types as well.
Overall I would definitely recommend the game, it is scary at times, but when you see an alien burst out into green goo which had only 15% probabibility to get hit, it is definitely worth it.

The Following Statements are solely based on the official Seattle Campaign of the game as i have yet to play any of the user created content for the game.
What the drek do i say about Shadowrun : Returns ?
I guess what i can say are the following things regarding what i consider to be my Game Of The Year 2013
First lets start with the music it is absolutely phenomenal and really makes me regret not buying the soundtrack edition because it is the kind of music i would probably play a lot of it if it was available on spotify because it is that damn good plus it matches the mood of the game perfectly.
Second lets talk about the sweet sweet combat it is so satisfying to get crits when attacking the enemy but i should back up a bit and explain that yes it is turn based combat that has a cover system in place to reduce incoming damage if you are positioned right and it is downright brutal at times but at the same time is very rewarding when you succeed in a fight and with a nice arrange of attacks both ranged and melee as well as a nice assortment of spells and abilities so in short i would say the combat is very good and meaty.
Third i would like to discuss the story and probably my most fav thing about the game the dialog options. Okay so in short without spoiling anything regarding the story it is very much a solid Cyberpunk story that is really dark and has some WTF moments that had me in shock during those moments and most importantly hooked and wanting to know what will happen next but even then i may be saying too much so i will be quiet for now regarding the story.
Okay now onto one of my favorite parts of the game the Dialog options. It is very well written and sticks true to shadowrun`s tone through and through with terms like drek, slotting in, chummer and my favorite fraggin. Depending on what skills you have you can sometimes avoid a fight entirely or open up dialog options you normally could not without the required skill or receive mission items that may help you later on in the game i mean come on this is a dialog system that while is not as deep as lets say Planescape Torment but is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton deeper than any modern “AAA” game to come out in recent years with the exception of Witcher 1 and 2.
Fourth lets talk about character creation which while it is nice and they have a decent amount of portraits for you to use and there is a little bit of customization. I really wish there was a lot more to it then the game offers but i think this may be a limitation due to the engine and how the game was made.
Conclusion i highly recommend anyone to buy this game if they are a fan of cyberpunk or shadowrun or both i really mean it when i say it is so damn good and at a price of $19.99 how can you not buy it it is practically a steal in my opinion and probably one of the best things of all it has steam workshop integrated into it and there is already a community effort to bring all the Shadowrun source books to Shadowrun : Returns here is a link for that

If i had any complaints about the game it may be the length of the official campaign which took me about 16 hours to complete left me wanting more and i encountered a few minor bugs but nothing major or game breaking.
TL/DR : Go buy it now and play it.

Highly Enjoyable, with a rather large 'but' or two.
We'll start with the bad, and get it out of the way. The bugs that caused the game to be pulled from Steam are largely fixed... but not totally. Framerate drops that make the game crawl, and even freeze and get stuck in an eternal load, do still occur. Generally while driving the Batmobile around Gotham.
Yet, just as bad is the narrative choices, some of which seem to be ill thought out. Spoilers from here on. Major ones. Seriously, if you care, skip to the next paragraph. First, for some reason Tim and Barbara are in a relationship, engaged even, despite the fact that it was always Richard and Babs that were together. She even still has the Flying Graysons necklace on, pressumably because they originally intended the official/original couple, but decided this was a way to hamfistedly add drama to the game. It works, but it's pointless, and doesn't make much sense. Second is the choice to retire/kill Batman at the end; this has been done far too much in recent Batman stories, from the old comic timeline,  Nu52 for a while, to Batman Beyond, to the Dark Knight Rises, and especially in this case makes no sense. Bruce cannot hang up the cowl, it's one of the most obvious things about him, he will be Batman until a criminal gets lucky or he is too old to stand. Likely the former. It also brings an interesting take on the setting to 'an end'.
End of spoilers.
All that said, the GOOD. We have moved further towards a more realistic look, but not so far as to lose the amazing aesthetic Rocksteady have built through the series. Gotham finally feels like Gotham, rather than a small cutout designed to work with the console limitations, albiet nearly empty of CPU hungry civilians. There is nothing like gliding from a high point in the city, diving and pulling up, while thunder and lightning crash around you and rain pours heavily and runs down your cape. Driving the Batmobile around is a pleasure, and I am actually enjoying the Riddlers races, which I know were a problem for others who felt they were shoehorned in - which they are, i just don't feel that matters much. Combat is fast, brutal, and feels as good as previous games.
All in all, this feels like the magnum opus of Batman games. Roll on Telltale's more story-focused rendition.

It isn't the open-world RPG some of us may have been hoping for, but what's there is a lot of fun.  (It seems to take more cues from the SNES game, but the combat and story depth are massively superior to any previous Shadowrun game.)
And finally, what this game really is, is a suite of tools for users to create their own content.  While the included story is a lot of fun, this game's legs will be in stories that users create and release for free to play through.
Some of the critiques of this game have been fair, but especially for the $20 asking price, it's well worth it to its target audience, and it is way more than worth it in anticipation of the stories we'll soon be able to play through.

Loved too the revamped policy trees, and cosmetic as it might be, the art-deco feel of the UI. As for the music, I still prefer the soundtrack for Civ 4, but that's just my personal perference.
One thing that pulled down the game though was the AI, an aspect already heavily spat upon. At high difficulties it just gets ridiculous. In one memorable play, India was just camping next to me doing nothing for 90 % of the game. Meanwhile the rest of the civs were ganging up on me, while Poland slaughtered them one by one. Not that real-life politics ain't absurd sometimes too, but it gets nonsensical which does compromise overall game enjoyment. Another flaw would be the combat animations. I played the game on a system released four years after the vanilla and still it was unbearable not to turn off combat animations. Firaxis has to look into a better way of managing this when doing Civ 6. It verges on being a bug.

Yeah, this is definitely a game you are going to want to play. There was some debate as to what style of game this is amongst my gaming peers. This was resolved in my opinion by describing this as a fairly perfect video game emulation of the table top gaming experience. It has elements in common with games like XCOM:EU, Dragon Age, Baldurs Gate, and plenty of other aweome games. However, it really stands alone by virute of its comletely intuitive gameplay, deep and yet simple customization system by way of karma points, and a pretty gripping story. The graphics are cool looking for a top town style game, and do a great job of depicting the world in whuich Shadowrun resides. There are plenty of conversation options, and a touch of morality decsion making, but for the most part, all choices lead to the same place.
Overall, I felt this to be a completely engaging game, so much so that the 21 hours or so I put into it only really felt like 8 or 9 hours. I look forward to future expansions and such and am keen to try out the user generated content.

However, it really stands alone by virute of its comletely intuitive gameplay, deep and yet simple customization system by way of karma points, and a pretty gripping story. The graphics are cool looking for a top town style game, and do a great job of depicting the world in whuich Shadowrun resides. There are plenty of conversation options, and a touch of morality decsion making, but for the most part, all choices lead to the same place.
Overall, I felt this to be a completely engaging game, so much so that the 21 hours or so I put into it only really felt like 8 or 9 hours. I look forward to future expansions and such and am keen to try out the user generated content.

This is a great remake. I played the old SNES version years ago when I was but a pup. Shadowrun Returns is a very nostalgiac and great playing game.
Character creation is like you'd expect in a good rpg. Which is to say that it's pretty comprehensive. Class choices are cool and varied. Stat points can be assigned, race and gender as well, hair color etc. but there are also dialect choices to affect your conversation abilities.
Gear and items are very simple. Armor in form of clothing, weapons in the form of pistols, rifles, swords, grenades, what-have-you. Also there are cybernetic implants which have both positive and negative effects on your character.
I love the feel of the game, no voice actors, minimal animation, grid type areas, and something I find kind of refreshing is that there's no forced saving. In other words the only saves you get are the ones the game gives you during area transitions, autosave only. I like that, makes you commit to thinking before running in to battle.
Combat is turn based, X-Com style if you're familiar. Fells pretty good overall, but the chance to hit or miss seems more random than the numbers tell you. Most unfortunate for you caster types is that magic, to me anyway, felt pretty underwhelming. Aside from the typical heal, quite useful, most characters do better with standard weapons when it comes to actually damaging. Mages can buff characters in your party but it's not really necessary.
Some things don't feel as clean as one would hope. One experience I noticed as well as read about others having is the rare occurrence of scripted events interrupting characters during combat. This happened to me I think twice during my whole play-through. You'll be moving a character to cover, or an attack position when a scripted event pops up ( Like an npc telling you how stupid you are for being in this particular place) and stops the action. This ends a turn, the character doesn't continue to the position you've chosen, and I could imagine in some cases one could see a frustrating death coming. Luckily it's pretty damned rare.
Story is a little campy, but that kind of adds to the feel of the game in my opinion.
Like the majority of games out there it's way too short, around 12ish hours, but hopefully Harebrained will put out DLC and the steam workshop is already busy.
Worth the money and time? Yep, play it. Especially if you have experience with the SNES version it's like going home. I can't put in an opinion as far as table top similarity, but I imagine it's more than satisfactory.

I finally got around to playing through this game after picking it up on sale with all the DLC for around thirty bucks. I've been a big fan of the Arkham games since the first one. I was both excited and hesitant to try out this title, given the...issues that existed with the PC release when it first came out. Kind of scary that a game was so bad they stopped selling it for a while, right?
So let's talk about mechanics.
Well, fortunately it seems that they have fixed their technical issues. I didn't have a single crash during my thirty-seven hour playthrough of this title, and the biggest glitch I had was an enemy clipping into the ground when I interrogated them for Riddler's secrets. That's it. Everything else ran smoothly the entire time.
The mechanics have remained more or less the same since the first game, with simple additions and simplifications. Strike, counter, gadget. The enemies are essentially the same, normal thugs, brutes, shields, guns, stun sticks. Now the normal guys can do a charge attack that can't be countered with a right click, which makes them slightly more interesting. You can still counter the charge with a quick batarang, but if they're coming from off-screen, they can get too close and mess up a good combo pretty easily. The main addition to this game, enemy-wise, is the medic. They can wander around the battlefield and pick up enemies you've already knocked out, which can make predator encounters a lot more irritating. They can also give enemies a shock-buff that zaps you if you try to hit an enemy with it. A neat enough addition to the enemy roster.
The big thing in this game, obviously, is the addition of the Batmobile. And yes, it is awesome. You feel powerful driving around in a tank, blasting holes in everything, and taking down enemies. Dudes on foot can be dealt with by running into them (which shocks them instead of smooshing them, which can be entertaining to watch) or blasting with your gun, which becomes nonlethal when an enemy enters the crosshairs. The tank battles are also a lot of fun, with you zipping around the battlefield lining up shots on enemy drones, which come in a few different flavours. Missile launchers, helicopters, and enemy tanks that range from small and weak to big scary robots that can only be approached from behind. The Batmobile handles well, feels fun, and has its own gadgets and boss battles.
The riddler trophies and mechanics are also generally the same. Stand on switch, throw batarangs at targets, but of course there are new challenges based on your new gadgets, and trophies which require the car to handle. There were a few times I was briefly stumped while trying to solve a trophy, including one embarassing time where I spent around fifteen minutes flying remote batarangs around looking for an electrical current before remembering that I had a gun that literally shoots electricity. Not my finest moment.
So that's mechanics talk, let's delve briefly into the story now. I'll start out spoiler-free and jump into spoilery stuff at the very end.
The big bads this time around are Scarecrow, who has gotten creepier since we last saw him in the first game, and the mysterious Arkham Knight. I say mysterious, but his identity is honestly pretty obvious. If you read the comics, or watch any of the animated films, you know who it is. Regardless, even knowing his identity he makes a decent enough villain and counter to you as Batman. The story itself was decent enough, with you traversing the city, fighting dudes, and trying to put a stop to a number of nefarious plans. Won't go into detail for now, to keep it spoiler-free.
A number of other big enemies crop up now and then, either part of the main story or having their own crime spree in Gotham. Even more are added in DLC, which works very well. If you have the DLC, you just need to be a certain percentage of the way through the main story, and the extra villains will appear with their own self-contained stories. Ra's al Ghul, Killer Croc, Mad Hatter, Mr. Freeze, they all pop up briefly to be beaten up and/or helped. Plus the villains in the base game, including Penguin, Two-Face, Poison Ivy, Harley Quinn. Some big names were missing, like Bane and Deadshot, but ah well.
The DLC's didn't really add all that much, just a few extra villain stories, and a few completely self-contained stories that are accessed directly through the starting menu. Not much content, mostly just extra-sized challenge maps with a small amount of story. They range from having only a few fights and/or predator encounters to having a solid half a dozen in Batgirl's story. Nothing big here, but I did enjoy playing as the various characters. Nightwing is as adorable and hilarious as always. No surprise there.
Aight, spoiler time. Anything below is SPOILERS.
So first off, the Arkham Knight is obviously Jason Todd, second and potentially most obnoxious of the Robins, though Damian Wayne puts up solid competition. It's hinted a few times throughout the story, but it's no big surprise. Most fans called it before the game came out, there was even a whole animated film about him coming back and fighting crime in a violent and murderous way. He was a good anti-Batman, though, as most of the villains are kind of old hat at this point.
I think the big twist this time was the Joker stuff. Following the events of Arkham City, with Joker's death (no he apparently did not evade death, despite what many fan theories claimed after AC) and Batman being injected with the joker toxin. Turns out, even the vaunted Lazarus Pit was not enough to stop the disease, which infected Batman and a handful of others who managed to get the Joker's blood before or despite the warning and recall in AC when it was discovered. And this was my favourite part of the entire game. After getting blasted with Joker's fear gas in an early attempt to stop him, the virus manifests as your own personal Joker hallucination that sticks with you for the rest of the game. It is -awesome-. Having Mark Hamill in your head as your own personal Joker that only you can see and hear, to sass you for the rest of the story? I wasn't expecting any Joker at all in this game, and instead he's everywhere I look, full of one-liners and hilarious commentary. Absolutely fantastic.
The other big story thing was Barbara Gordon's death. Psyyyych, in a twist that surprises nobody, she's not dead, it was just a fear gas hallucination. All in all, I think Barbara Gordon was my biggest issue with this game. Not her ersatz death or anything, no. My issue was that in this game she was romantically paired up with Tim Drake, even marrying him after the story events took place, referenced in the DLC. Tim Drake, Babs? Really? WAY TO BREAK NIGHTWING'S HEART.
Aside from that, good game.
If you're thinking og buying this because you liked Killing Floor, look elsewhere. This is not the game for you.

South Park is a tough game to review. From a game mechanic standpoint it doesn't break any new ground. Gameplay is thin, the controls (to fart) are annoying and it's relatively short (15 hours) for what it costs.
If this were any other RPG, it would be widely condemned. But it's South Park through and through, which means you'll both laugh and cringe at the same time. What other game will have you fighting an underpants gnome while trying to dodge a giant ball sack? What game has you crawling through someone's rear end while a gerbil sings to you? Occasionally side-splitting, often head-shaking, the humor in Stick of Truth is exactly like the show.
That's really what you're playing and paying for here. You're interacting with a 15 hour episode of South Park, lovingly nurtured, written and voice acted by Matt and Trey. The RPG mechanics are just an excuse to call it a game. You're playing this because it's just like watching a season of the show. You're going to visit all of the areas you know and love from the series. You're going to the Mongorian grill. You're going to meet up with Jesus. You're going to the wrong side of the tracks to Kenny's House. And you're going to do this as the "New Kid" that fits in perfectly with the rest of the cast of characters for a wild, weird and wonderful time.
If that doesn't sound like it's funny then this game isn't for you. If you find the show rude, crude and reprehensible, then you should run (not walk)away. But if you like the show, if you like the humor, wit, crudeness and everything else that goes on in South Park then you'll enjoy this game as I did.
If you don't, well...respect my authoritah!

This game is absolutely great from top to bottom. The main game is a well written and well paced piece of murder mystery cyberpunk action, made with great writing and interesting characters. The writing is so good, in fact, that even characters that show up just once or twice feel really memorable. The graphic style and musical design are top notch and really help make the experience into a cohesive whole. The gameplay is a solid tactical RPG experience that's fun to play, if a bit on the easy side more often than not.
The few downsides to the game start with the lack of manual saving. The game automatically saves at checkpoints (probably to prevent save scumming like some other tactical games) which can sometimes be frustrating. The locked angle camera usually is okay, but there are times where it's a problem. Some people will call a 12 hour, very linear main campaign a problem too, but I personally think that it's better to have 12 high-quality hours than 20-25 with lots of filler.
So it's not perfect, but it's damned well done. And the inclusion of an editor means that in the end we'll hopefully see a lot more great content from the community.

I have a bit of a love/hate relationship with XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It's got some of the most satisfying turn-based combat I've ever experienced, but at the same time it implements questionably wonky mechanics that can make for extremely frustrating gameplay at times.
For starters, the way the game calculates its to-hit percentages is nonsensical. The numbers you see on screen don't jive with the results -- oftentimes a THC (To Hit Chance) of 100% will miss completely, and you're pretty much guranteed to miss your target if the THC is at anything less than 70%. In addition, character skill doesn't seem to have any affect on overall THC. Percentage seems to be entirely randomly generated, and such poor implementation of THC rules is by far the biggest drawback to the tactical portion of XCOM.
Cover mechanics are also highly questionable. They barely have any affect on THC, and even characters under full cover behind "impenetrable" terrain are liable to take full damage more often than not.
Line of sight rules in XCOM are just plain goofy, and they plainly favor the opposing side in the campaign. I've lost track of the times when a soldier is clearly placed out of sight of enemy units, only to have them shot down in a hail of plasma by an alien halfway across the map.
There are other little niggles. Characters of every rank are way too squishy, some items like smoke grenades and slotted armor are pointless, and randomly-generated events during combat can be unecessarily lethal at times (for example, parked vehicles make for bad cover because they are particularly prone to out-of-the-blue explosions).
Finally, and perhaps worst of all, is the fact that not stringently outfitting your XCOM organization at the beginning of the campaign utterly dooms your chances of winning. Satellites should be an option, but you're forced to use them in order to keep continents from being overrun too early in the game. Not having enough scientists or engineers early on also has the unfortunate effect of ruining your chances at gaining a respectable foothold. Everything has to be perfectly balanced or you lose. That normally wouldn't be an issue in any other TBS game, but the complete randomness of campaign events in Enemy Unknown means that even the most by-the-books setup can be made arbitrarily useless in a matter of a few turns. Playing this game can be an exasperating headache.
Despite all its faults, XCOM: Enemy Unkown is a blast to play. Considering the fact that there aren't enough quality TBS games out there, XCOM really stands out as a  tactical experience. Recommended if you can find it for less than $20.

So there has been a lot of complaining about this game I've noticed and I feel it is unwarranted. This is a fantastically wonderful game. It captures the feel and spirit of Shadowrun beautifully. From the interpretation of the Seattle sprawl to the lingo and even the little things like seeing a Stuffer Shack, it is marvelous.
The game is very linear but thats not a bad thing if you take in the context. Shadowrun Returns is very much a point-and-click adventure game that is more concerned with telling  a story than letting the player have a murderfest. The action is there often enough and is fun enough that  you don't become bored with it and as the story develops in the included module you become drawn into the intrigue that sometimes comes a long with being a runner.
They made character creation simple by giving you the standard Shadowrun achetypes but letting you learn the skills you want. Even Etiquette has a plce here! The equipment is varied enough that you can customize your runner to a degree and so is the actual character creation. The game also comes with a editor pack that allows for you to make your own adventures so the potential this game has is well beyond the price you pay for it.
In short, this is a marvelous reimagining of a fantastic cyberpunk game and I think well worth a buy.

BLUF:  A solid 6 person Co-op arena shooter with good sound, great graphics, no story, and excellent gameplay. 8/10.
Killing Floor 2 is a solid upgrade from the last in the name.  Dark and bloody, the game is at it's heart a co-op 6 player cage-match FPS with a class system called "perks," and an XP system per perk.  The game is brutal, team-work centric, with decent ballance, and challenging extra difficulties.  There are only around 15 maps from the authors, but custom maps are common.
There's some things to avoid.  Don't gamble with real money on boxes and keys if that's not your thing, it's not required to play, but some cosmetics can be neat.  You can get one marketplace item once a day for playing, usually a common, but you can get anything except keys.  Don't listen to others who say the marketplace and key system breaks the game, it's just cosmetic.  The official forums can be poison, avoid them entirely.  The PvP aspect is weak, don't bother.  There are some ballance issues each time they patch or release something new, but they don't overshadow the fun that can be had here if you learn to this play with friends.

PROS:
+ Visuals are incredible, batman and Gotham itself has never looked so good. I personally did not suffer FPS issues the entire time, luckily enough.
+ Gameplay is just as fluid and interesting as it was before, with some changes here or there. More of the good stuff.
+ Story felt like a solid continuation (and conclusion) from the last two games, although the "true ending" being locked behind doing a certain amount of side missions was annoying.
+ Using the batmobile is satisfying, fast, and enjoyable. Really cool to speed through Gotham in it, and see just what you can blast through.
CONS:
- KEEP IN MIND: For many, this game is STILL broken, and the chances of this being fixed are slim to none.
- Major PC port issues that were so severe the game got pulled off steam. Severe FPS issues, graphical bugs, and more. Then the game didn't go on sale for quite a long time despite this.
- Batmobile felt like it was too big of a focus, and at its core the actual vehicle combat was repetitive. Riddler missions are largely replaced with the batmobile as well, which is both a good thing and a bad thing.
- Story was handled somewhat poorly. A huge fakeout death happens that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me the ♥♥♥♥ off because of how it was presented to the viewer. Then, the game kind of spoonfed the big reveal to you.
Overall: If you can run it, it's still a great addition to the Arkham Batman saga. I was mostly satisfied with my purchase. However, as a port, it suffered greatly. Research before you buy.

Dead Space to me is like Super Mario 64 to my Nintendo machine.  I don't know how and why the Dead Space series has slipped over the years, but Dead Space 1 was always the best Dead Space and a genre defining game.  In fact, no one has really created a game where there are space zombies, you fight these things in space, combined with scare and horror with the dread of being alone.  You are truly alone in space.
Dead Space 2 was great too but no where as near as great as Dead Space.  It's one of those games that left an imprint in my recollection of gaming experiences along with Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Super Mario 64, Street Fighter, Goldeneye 64, Lost Odyssey, Valkyria Chronicles, Halo series, and a few others.
The Dead Space Universe is where the heart is.  There's vast potential.  The world of Dead Space is intriguing, and when well written, developed, and executed, it's the definitive space zombie game with a major twist.  But to call it space zombie is a hit from the hilt.  It's a lot more than that.  They're called necromorphs, and they're terrifying.  Horrific.  They terrorize your soul.
The premise of Dead Space is overwhelming with potential possibilities that could bring the series back to life.  Dead Space 4, if it happens, will hopefully revisit the memories of the first game.  It's a must-play, sit in a dark room, with your headphones on video game.  Immerse yourself fully into its atmosphere and it will be one of the best times you've spent playing a game.
Rating: 9.2 out of 10

85% - Welcome Isaac Clarke aboard the USG Ishimura
A missing planet cracker ship, a tiny ship with a crew of five to the rescue, a silent engineer in a desperate search for his lost love, and deadly, scary monsters as welcoming party as you step aboard the ghost ship USG Ishimura. Maybe this is how I can describe Dead Space's story the best.
As Isaac Clarke, the silent protagonist of the game (Presumably he has a sore throat in this episode as he can speak well in Dead Space 2), you have to find your love, Nicole, while you must learn the truth behind the xenomorph infestation plaging the Ishimura, but foremost you must find a way to leave the deadly ship alive and in one piece, which is not an easy task.
Dead Space is a horror game and it is scary at first, but honestly I've met and played with scarier games in my lifetime. Unfortunately the the scary factor of the game is becoming way too predictible as you're progressing with the storyline and the elimination of the necromorphs will become a routine task, especially during the last chapters of the game.
The storyline is well told, the narration is great and the game has enough twists to keep you entertained from the beginning to the end. One of my favorite feature in the game was the H.U.D.s unique presentation, which is definitely new and a great improvement.
The weapons, what you may upgrade by time, are also very-very unique comparing to other games and Dead Space is one of the very few games where you'll love and use the basic weapons just much as you'll use the more powerful ones you'll find later in the game. The graphics of the game is great, however its a bit repetative, but it fits well for the planet cracker ship Ishimura. Dead Space is a horror game, one of the bests in the genre.
I finished it in around 10 hours , but it has some flaws, namely the level design and the tasks you have to complete, which makes the game a bit repetative at times. Still, if you love horror and scary games, Dead Space is your game as its one of the finest in the genre with a unique story, and it is highly-highly recommended for both horror and science fiction fans.

Risk of Rain is a roguelike with some minor platforming elements, and
an option for playing in co-op mode.  The game comes with difficulty levels that
offer a wide variety of challenge in gameplay, as well as artifacts that can
unlock more difficulty options.
You play as a character stranded on a planet, trying to escape by
reaching the teleporter, then stay alive during the 90 seconds it takes to
teleport to safety.  The more time you take to survery your area, the harder
the game gets.  Surviving in the game comes down to a combination of luck and
using passive abilities strategically.  That being said, the longer you take,
the harder the enemy gets, to the point where the quantity of passive abilities
will make no difference.

Dead Space is a Horror/3rd person shooter. I think it should be stated first that this is by no means a survival/horror game. Throughtout the game you are armed to the teeth, even with ammo being limited it just means you have to be strategic with engagements, rather than avoiding encounters as you would in a game like Amnesia: Descent to darkness.
Dead Space takes place in a city-sized space ship where something has gone horribly wrong. The ship has gone dark after sending out a distress signal and our hero Issac Clark along with a small security detail is sent to investigate.
The main focus of this game can be summed up in 3 words "Atmosphere, Atmosphere, Atmosphere". The tone in this game is set wonderfully, and executed masterfully. Distant screams, jumping shadows, and dark hallways give a sense of impending doom throughout the campaign. Dispite my enthusiasm I have to admit this game can only give you proper chills if you allow it to-- it requires you to give it the proper horror game treatment. By that I mean it must be played no earlier than 1am, in a dark room, all alone, headphones on. You kind of have to immerse yourself. But if you let it, this game will wisk you away to a sci-fi world of terror and desperation on par with any other horror juggernaut. Now I'm done heaping praise.
Like I said, since you have plenty of guns the only real urgency you feel stems from ammo and supplies. It reminds me more of games like Resident Evil: Outbreak, where you have to choose to fight or run, rather than Doom 3 where youre supposed to annhilate everything in your way. As you progress, in order to increase difficulty the game kind of shifts it's focus from horror and atmosphere to gunning and being a 3rd person shooter. Though it never forgets the emphasis on atmosphere, it gets put on the backburner near the end.
The Gameply is solid, though takes a little bit of getting used to. This game plays very well on both mouse/keyboard as well as a gamepad. Wether you use an xbox controller or a PS3 controller the game doesnt miss a beat and you get a great control scheme either way. As is customary with any good PC game the layout is completely customizable. Things like hit detection I feel are good but can be sketchy under pressure. There are time where I wasnt sure if it was hit detection or my desperate spray of fire at an encroaching enemy, but i felt like some shots missed that should have hit. It could just mean I'm a terrible shot when im panicking.
As far as performace goes, this game runs wonderfully on my laptop which suprised me, seeing as how my laptop barely meets system requirements. Though, on both my laptop and my PC I opted for using v-sync because of the many flashing lights. And Rather than using the game's v-sync which killed my framerate, I found that if I used v-sync directly though Catalyst(radeon card) my frames stayed locked solid at 30fps.
If you like games where you have to run rather than fight, this game probably isnt for you. If you the kind of game where youre forced to make decisions based on ammo and supplies then this may be right for you.

Risk of Rain is a roguelike with some minor platforming elements, and
an option for playing in co-op mode.  The game comes with difficulty levels that
offer a wide variety of challenge in gameplay, as well as artifacts that can
unlock more difficulty options.
You play as a character stranded on a planet, trying to escape by
reaching the teleporter, then stay alive during the 90 seconds it takes to
teleport to safety.  The more time you take to survery your area, the harder
the game gets.  Surviving in the game comes down to a combination of luck and
using passive abilities strategically.  That being said, the longer you take,
the harder the enemy gets, to the point where the quantity of passive abilities
will make no difference.
This is not a game for those who have never tried roguelikes before;  rather
if you are looking for a challenge, this will entertain you, and even humble you
as you go through the game.  This game respects your time, and I
enjoyed playing it.
I have no problem recommending it.

I have been a fan of the Arkham series since before the first one was even released. I saw the trailer for it and immediately knew that I had to get it the moment it came out. So even after the game was released and I took trips to Gamestop to get whatever I was there to get, I would take like 10 minutes to play the demo on the displayed PS3, just because I thought the combat was that awesome. When Arkham City came out, I didn't get it, don't ask me why because I really don't have a good answer. I guess I just thought that nothing could top Arkham Asylum so I wouldn't even try the game out. Oh boy, was I sorry. Arkham City was perhaps the greatest, if not THE greatest, game in the series. Fast-forward to 2013 and I hear tales of a new Arkham game coming out, and my mind begins to go ballistic because I am so excited at the fact that I get to become the Batman again. By this time, I had gotten myself a gaming PC and was ready to go to play the recently named Arkham Knight on max graphics, only to find out that the game was virtually unplayable on PC. Oh poo.
Anyways, the rest of the story is back up in the first paragraph, but let me tell you, I actually really enjoyed this game, not only for the story, but for the challenge that it brings to the series. I don't want to stay up all night writing this review so I will simply say this, while the story wasn't anything game-changing, just the simple fact that this game wasn't a simple copy-and-paste of Arkham City makes it worth the playthrough. I wouldn't get this game at full price, but I certainly would play it just to get the experience, I definitely haven't regretted it yet!
TL;DR Plays great on newer systems, worth the buy but get it on sale

ok, lets make this short and somewhat sweet.
Gameplay: Very boring, with bland enviroments lacking interest and various places to get stuck. Very small areas, you are never 10 metres away from a loading zone. The weapons lack any realism, feel completely boring to use and overall are to overpowered in the later segments. Using the gravity gun for a portion of the game was a nice diversion for using the source physics engine, but felt a little too watered down.
Graphics: This is a 14 year old game, but the graphics have aged terribly, the textures look overly pixelated and there is 10 tinges of grey used for everything. At the time the graphics were seen as more advanced however.
*SPOILER ALERT!*
Story: A very cliche, predictable plot, which is essentially every zombie movie ever. Zombies takke over dystopian society with corrupt government, rebels trying to fight and regroup. Very predictable
Characters: I think valve have caught onto the fact that if you give a character no character, the audience take to the mysteries and he then has more character. Also you can be lazy in this and not program any noise for the main character. All the other characters were too cliche. Alex is a rebelious teen, She has a loving father who she can no longer see. Kleiner is a stereotypical science nerd with many inventions. Most of the other characters stay to their respective stereotypes.
Overall i think this is just a regular fps, which for some reason made some people hail it as THE GREATEST GAME EVER MADE. A title it obviously doesn't deserve. At its release it had good graphics and somewhat innovative gameplay in the fps genre. It hasn't aged like a fine wine, it has aged like bottled tapwater. If you want the greatest fps ever created, play Goldeneye 007 for n64, or get it on a emulator. Valve  has alot of catching up to do if they want to make half life 3 any where near as good as modern games.
