I was a little late to the party on this one as Windows 10 became my obsession over the summer (though it's more fair to say that joke of an "operating system" befuddled me for the entire summer). I remember reading smatterings of information about how it ran poorly on the PC, but never really checked into it as I thought I'd just decide for myself which version to obtain when I finally got around to buying the game, said event happening right after the "relaunch". So, keep in mind that I never felt any of the launch pain the rest of you may have felt, and that my experience with Arkham Knight was purely with the version that was supposed to actually work on the PC.
Well, did it? Yeah, actually. Worked just fine. So well, in fact, that I had no idea why anyone continued to gripe. When the freebie content arrived in my Steam account for having purchased it by whatever deadline (surprised the heck out of me, had no idea it was coming, just serendipity I guess), I really had to wonder why people were riding Rocksteady so hard on this port, seeing as it played brilliantly on my Laptop.
Yes, laptop. I use a MSI GS60 Ghost Pro (2PE), 16 GB RAM, GTX 870m w/3 GB, and their goofy SuperRAID (which is just two SSDs in RAID0, whooopdie inventory-doo Batman!), though I ran it off the EVO 850 I purchased to replace the HDD. I'm listing specs so that, again, you can take this review from the correct point of view. I ran it @ 1080p with everything maxed and it never dropped below 30 fps (staying around 45-50 most of the time) except for one scene involving an absolute crapton of guys, which I  get...I was sorta pushing it seeing as it was asking for 4GB of video mem. But otherwise it looked and played beautifully.
So, as to the game itself? I liked it a great deal. I think it was a fitting end to the series, as well as an excellent way to do a somewhat Elseworlds-ish "What if Batman up and quit like a baby" thing. I'm quite excited to see where they go with this next, but perhaps they'll just start all over again. Needless to say, I have to personally thank Rocksteady for the games in this series as Batman has been my favorite hero for the majority of my 38 years, and to finally see him done CORRECTLY (or at least as close as necessary to  be awesomesauce) just...well, it just made me very very happy.
The plot itself, without ruining anything, is about par for the course with this series. Most people like Arkham City quite a bit, saying it's the best of the bunch, but I felt the plot there was a bit zany and made no realistic sense. This one goes out of the way to continually say "Oh yeah? Well what if Batman had to fight Godzilla?" kinda things. It is constant over-the-top sequences that will, if you're a true fan, either make you genuinely crack up, or just stare slack-jawed at what just occurred.
Gameplay was about the only thing I felt suffered a bit in this game in that there was a little too much emphasis on the Batmobile. I tend to not like driving with a controller, preferring a wheel as it makes more sense to my brain...so it took me awhile to get on board with the Batmobile. However, once I got the hang of using it as a weapon, it was kinda fun. Still, it seemed too much the centerpiece when Batman and his nifty gadgets should have been more visible. Perhaps they ran out of new ideas for toys and said "Ok, let's make a big toy for the finale". Should have given us the Batwing as well guys :)
The graphics on my settings were superb, and I thought Gotham had never looked better.  The smoke coming off the tires from the new Nvidia stuff was pretty nifty, but I was mostly impressed with how smooth combat was for me in general.
Voice acting was outstanding, and Kevin and Mark deserve a medal for this series. On that topic, I believe the true unsung heroes of the franchise are those that voiced the henchmen and those that wrote their lines. All 4 of the Arkham games cracked me up constantly. I remember in Arkham Origins when you'd pop over a certain combo number and basically turn into the Tazmanian Devil, a henchman would always exclaim "...holy crap!", but delivered so perfectly that it FELT like the guy was actually dumbstruck there was a human being spinning around doing this stuff. But the inclusion of the dialogue  by the henchman that was 100% up-to-the-minute at any point in the story, clever, funny, and absolutely appropriate, made me feel like I was Batman flying around spying on these guys....so bravo....suspension of disbelief achieved :)
So yeah, I liked this game. If you liked the rest of the series, OF COURSE you should buy it. If you haven't played the others, don't start with this one....go play them in order as it will make far more sense, and be more entertaining in general. If you're not a fan of the prior titles in the series, eh, you can skip this unless you need closure somehow, but don't buy it and gripe that it was just like the others...OF COURSE IT WAS...and that made all the difference :)

The amazing sound effects feed this thought of being stalked by a post human space zombie. The sounds are the best part of the whole game. A loose bolt hitting the floor is amplified by the huge ship into an eerie echo in the distance. The overall atmosphere is one of the best so far.
The gameplay itself feels a bit clumsy. Most in game menus are operated with a keyboard instead of the mouse and moving the camera is so slow it makes you lift your mouse from the pad multiple times, unless you're using one of those fancy giant gaming pads. For me, changing the mouse sensitivity didn't do a thing. The game clearly suffered a little while being transported from a controller. The enemies could have used with some visual variety. While acting differently. They all look like either lumb of meat or a burned lumb of meat. The differences are seen clearly only in a distance you don't want to be in order to preserve your life.
While the gameplay is clumsy and should be played with a controller instead of keyboard. The animation quality is top notch. The main protagonist moves naturally. While the jittering movement of the space zombies is both disturbing and facinating. The graphics are a bit outdated for today. But the light effects make up for the little bit muddy textures.

Cyberpunk RPG with turn-based, tactical combat based on the pen and paper RPG for the same name. This game is a successor to the Genesis and SNES Shadowrun games, with references to both throughout and is set around the time of 1st/2nd edition Shadowrun - the 2050s. The soundtrack is actually composed by Sam Powell and Marshall Parker, the composers of the Genesis and SNES games respectively - hardcore fans of the SNES game will LOSE THEIR♥♥♥♥♥♥when they hear familiar melodies and phrases in the midst of some of the games tracks.
That said it's a solid RPG with a great art style, the included campaign ends about 10-12 hours in but is well written and contains every Shadowrun trope there is (cyberware, shamanic totems, decking, runs on corporate facilities, slaughtering gangers, conspiracies, Harlequin, etc.)
More importantly, the fully featured (and almost intuitive) editor it comes with lets you and other members of the community put out their own adventures. You are essentially purchasing not only the adventure that comes with the game but also the framework to play all the stuff the Shadowrun community will be putting together through Workshop.
If you love Shadowrun, cyberpunk, RPGs, turn-based tactical combat and community content this is the game for you.
If you want another triple-A shooter with RPG elements loaded celebrity voice acting, poorly-used military jargon and regenerating health, move along to the next publisher-funded bore.

My roommates and I are thoroughly enjoying Risk of Rain whilst sitting on the couch and drinking beer.  It is a great coop experience as it requires some teamwork and also becomes class-based after unlocking a couple characters.  The rogue-like aspect of the game (always start over after death, unless a teammate can get to another level without dying) makes it frustrating at times, but also makes every situation intense and meaningful.  My favorite aspect of the game is the powering-up of characters by unlocking boxes and getting more potent abilities.  It grants the feeling of progression and makes the odds seem [somewhat] fair as the levels get harder.
This game takes a little bit of time to figure out, but it's very unique, offers great variety with the unlockable characters, and has a surprising amount of depth.  The game mechanics are somewhat similar to a fighting game in that it is a complete button masher, but requires some sequencing of moves to maximize DPS.  I recommend reading some tutorials or watching a playthrough, as you get dumped into the game with nearly no instructions.
After several attempts (and several hours) my roommates and I beat the game on easy, so it's quite difficult, but we had enough fun to want to try to beat it at harder levels and unlock more characters and abilities.
9/10
edit: the 0.4 hours on my record is because of game-sharing with roommate and playing his profile.  Closer to 6 hours of total gameplay.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown (what happened to the hyphen?) is an excellent modern interpretation of that fantastic game, featuring great turn-based tactical combat, fun character progression, a beautiful musical score and above all, that same sense of wonder, dread and emotional attachment to your troops.
XCOM: Enemy Within further expands on this amazing game with a bigger tech tree, a new soldier class and plenty of new enemies to fight, as well as a multitude of new maps to fight them on.. if the XCOM-project isn't destroyed from within.
A must-play for any strategy gamer!

Graphics - 4.0
Not the best looking game, but the style and attention to gore really gives the game it's signature horror feel. You get four limbed mutants, parasite bloated chargers, and slithering zombie scorpions in the first few chapters. I'd love to go into detail, but you should see for yourself. The monsters do not dissapoint.
Sound - 4.5
The audio was the most impressive aspect of the game. Each monster has it's own unique sound made creepier by the echo of a dead spaceship. Along the whispers of some unknown entity, It feels like walking into the Event Horizon.
There's also the satisfying feel of blowing the heads off these mutants that keeps the action exciting and fun. You shoot their limbs off, they cry in agony. You stop to reload, they get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and charge you with a ferocious roar.
I also want to praise the nice touch of adding sound effects for Issac. They're good enough that you really don't need a health bar to tell when you need some first aid.
Control - 2.0
Here's where the game suffers a bit because it takes a bit of getting used to. The third person side view and the weapon selection wheel can be a bit confusing in the heat of the moment. A good example are weapon keybinds. I went with the rifle as my first purchase, which was bound to my '4' key. The last weapon I bought was bound to '2.' It can be changed in settings, but it's made for use with a controller wheel/d-pad. The sensitivity is also kind of off, most likely for controller considerations. The horizontal axis feels accelerated compared to the vertical axis.
Fun Factor - 4.0
Pro : The story is fun and keeps you wondering what's around the next door. Despite the characters whining that there's always something wrong on the ship, you keep wanting to explore and find the cause of all the problems. The missions are pretty varied. Not all of them are go here and press E. One of my favorite missions involves starting up an asteroid defense system while fighting off monsters in a gravity room. That's not even the best part of that mission.
Con: Early in the game, you are given options to sacrifice upgrades to unlock rooms. Some have interesting side plot items. Unfortunately, you don't really see this the rest of the way. You can still explore, but they're just supply rooms.  Seems like a missed opportunity to add replay value or alternate paths. Side  plots items are still there, but they're pretty hard to miss even the first playthrough.
Overall 4.0
I definitely recommend it for a different take on a space and horror games. Despite weak jump scares, it's the atmosphere of a dead spaceship with infested creatures that captures you. Varied mission objectives and satisfying combat keep the game fresh throughout all the chapters.

The game itself is like a Contra RPG, if that makes any sense. Its a side-scrolling action-rpg-rogulike. The item collecting and character classes are the highlight of the game. Stacking items is great fun since these powerups gain interesting effects as they increase in magnitude. Both the characters and the tems grew on me the more I played; elements seen as  "bad" became fun through experience. Lastly, there are Artifacts that can be unlocked that drastically change the way the game is played, from enemies exploding when they die, to granting the ability to select your items! The soundtrack is another highlight.
The negative aspects of the game are largely the past bugs. There have been numerous issues since the games release that have tarnished the experience. The majority of the bugs are now gone, so this isn't an issue to new players. Lastly, hosting a multiplayer game can be surprisingly tricky given that the host has to port forward. This is nothing too special, except methods that work in other games curiously fail to produce the expected result here.
Overall 7/10, leaning towards 8 when played with friends.

If you're like me and you've been aching for a deep and immersive roleplaying experience and actual agency when it comes to solving problems, this game is a steal at $20. Excellent writing, beautiful environments, and a fantastic soundtrack all tied together with engaging combat and character progression.
The campaign will take you about 15 hours to run through, and there's sadly little in the way of extended diversions, and the game is rather linear in how it progresses. There's not much of a sense of an 'open world' that one would expect from this genre, but even still the world itself is one of the most well-realized and vibrant ones I've seen in a long time.
They've got another campaign on the way, and you're going to see plenty of gameplay content coming out of the steam workshop, so I can guarantee you'll have your money's worth in actual meaty game.
If you like RPGs at all you owe it to yourself to grab this game and play through it. You'll be really glad you did.

The Stick of Truth is what happens when you combine the battle system of Super Mario RPG, a loot-and-level upgrade system, Xbox-style achievement hunting, and the crude comedy gold of Parker and Stone. A lot of reviews talk about this being one of the best licensed IP games out there but I think that sells the game short - this is the best comedic game of the modern era. Obsidian did a fantastic job of backing up a great story with great gameplay that doesn't get in the way of the punchline, and that really is key, for there are countless punchlines. Even if you don't know all the inside jokes of the show there are enough culture and gaming gags to make the rest of the people in the house want to know what the hell you are laughing at. Play this game.
Q: How much should I pay?
A: $20 or less. This will be a big seller in any Steam sale
Q: Should I buy the DLC?
A: Absolutely not. The DLC is completely useless. There is more loot then you could ever use in the game and the DLC is all low level loot that will be superseded by the time you are able to use it.
Q: How much play time will I get?
A: A couple of hours a night for a couple of weeks will get ‘er done. People claim 11-15 hours but that sounds like rushing a game that wants you to hang out and have fun
Q: Is there any replay?
A: Only for the completest. Making alternate saves at the start of each quest should allow you to find all the collectibles and show your friends some comedy highlights. You also can start from scratch as a different class if you are into that sort of thing.
Q: Is there any challenge or is this just timing button presses for 20 hours?
A: Set the game to hardcore before you even start. This isn’t Dark Souls. You will destroy this game on hardcore as it isn’t hardcore at all. Do you know what a health potion is? Do you know what buffs/debuffs are? Do you understand that equipping better gear gets you better stats? Can you handle dying a couple of times at boss battles and then respawning right before the boss battle without loss of gear or having to replay sequences? Sure you can!

My roommates and I are thoroughly enjoying Risk of Rain whilst sitting on the couch and drinking beer.  It is a great coop experience as it requires some teamwork and also becomes class-based after unlocking a couple characters. My favorite aspect of the game is the powering-up of characters by unlocking boxes and getting more potent abilities.  It grants the feeling of progression and makes the odds seem [somewhat] fair as the levels get harder.
This game takes a little bit of time to figure out, but it's very unique, offers great variety with the unlockable characters, and has a surprising amount of depth.  The game mechanics are somewhat similar to a fighting game in that it is a complete button masher, but requires some sequencing of moves to maximize DPS.  I recommend reading some tutorials or watching a playthrough, as you get dumped into the game with nearly no instructions.
After several attempts (and several hours) my roommates and I beat the game on easy, so it's quite difficult, but we had enough fun to want to try to beat it at harder levels and unlock more characters and abilities.
9/10

The core of the game is fun, and it's oozing with potential, but Tripwire's glacial pace of updates and stunningly moronic design decisions over the past year have killed any interest I had in the game. While there is more content than there was a year ago, the actual gameplay is far worse, feeling more like a dull slog than a thrilling fight to survive.
It's possible that they'll get their act together later, but their refusal to listen to feedback and apparent incompetence leave me with zero hope that things will change. Avoid this game for the foreseeable future.
For those of you wanting more specific feedback on what is holding the game back right now:
- Far too little ammo across the board, resulting in running dry even if you play near-perfectly. This was always somewhat of a problem, but they inexplicably decided to nerf the spawn rate and usefulness of findable ammo boxes.
- The new resistances system, which does nothing but make enemies bullet sponges in a completely unintuitive manner. Nobody wanted this.
- Terrible, terrible perk balance. Support and Demolition in particular are screwed, and Firebug has only been useful for Microwave gun abuse (spraying fire, like you'd expect it to be good at, is a waste of time and ammo). The worst part about this is that such issues could be fixed with easy number changes pushed out in test patches (it being EARLY ACCESS and all), but they instead tend to wait months for the "big" "free content packs" to even attempt that.
- Teleporting enemies. Have a group of zeds on your tail? Good luck running from them, as they'll respawn before your very eyes at a chokepoint as you try to escape instead of actually chasing you. Also, small obstacles like tables or fences cause zeds to suddenly warp on top of them, making headshots with such obstacles around a fool's errand.
- The addition of microtransaction loot crates adds insult to injury.
- The parry system for blocking incoming attacks with your melee weapon started out a little clunky but useful and rewarding, but it has been nerfed into the ground via significantly reduced overall effectiveness, and making most of the attacks you'd want to parry UNPARRYABLE.
- Sound design used to be great, but bizarre changes to it have made it just ok most of the time and distractingly bad at others. Previously, when a scrake would spawn, it would emit a bone-chilling roar over the current action. Now, it temporarily mutes the ambient metal soundtrack and other sounds before roaring at significantly reduced volume (and with bad timing too, resulting in a sizable duration of almost no sound at all). An abomination announcing its presence should NOT result in a net loss of noise.

The core of the game is fun, and it's oozing with potential, but Tripwire's glacial pace of updates and stunningly moronic design decisions over the past year have killed any interest I had in the game. While there is more content than there was a year ago, the actual gameplay is far worse, feeling more like a dull slog than a thrilling fight to survive.
It's possible that they'll get their act together later, but their refusal to listen to feedback and apparent incompetence leave me with zero hope that things will change. Avoid this game for the foreseeable future.
For those of you wanting more specific feedback on what is holding the game back right now:
- Far too little ammo across the board, resulting in running dry even if you play near-perfectly. This was always somewhat of a problem, but they inexplicably decided to nerf the spawn rate and usefulness of findable ammo boxes.
- The new resistances system, which does nothing but make enemies bullet sponges in a completely unintuitive manner. Nobody wanted this.
- Terrible, terrible perk balance. Support and Demolition in particular are screwed, and Firebug has only been useful for Microwave gun abuse (spraying fire, like you'd expect it to be good at, is a waste of time and ammo). The worst part about this is that such issues could be fixed with easy number changes pushed out in test patches (it being EARLY ACCESS and all), but they instead tend to wait months for the "big" "free content packs" to even attempt that.
- Teleporting enemies. Have a group of zeds on your tail? Good luck running from them, as they'll respawn before your very eyes at a chokepoint as you try to escape instead of actually chasing you. Also, small obstacles like tables or fences cause zeds to suddenly warp on top of them, making headshots with such obstacles around a fool's errand.
- The addition of microtransaction loot crates adds insult to injury.
- The parry system for blocking incoming attacks with your melee weapon started out a little clunky but useful and rewarding, but it has been nerfed into the ground via significantly reduced overall effectiveness, and making most of the attacks you'd want to parry UNPARRYABLE.
- Sound design used to be great, but bizarre changes to it have made it just ok most of the time and distractingly bad at others. Previously, when a scrake would spawn, it would emit a bone-chilling roar over the current action. Now, it temporarily mutes the ambient metal soundtrack and other sounds before roaring at significantly reduced volume (and with bad timing too, resulting in a sizable duration of almost no sound at all). An abomination announcing its presence should NOT result in a net loss of noise.

Bantam: Arkham Guy is the most recent MOBA to come out of Rockstirdy Studios. It features great mechanics, great maintenance, and a PC port that'll knock your socks off. Literally- I've been without socks for 2 weeks!
In this title, you join Bantam, lord of orphans as he teams up with Meowgirl, a Templar, and Mike from Breaking Bad. Wicker-Man steals Mike's daughter, Wheels, from her gaming rig in the clock tower. Mike gets mad and you must stop Wicker-Man before he farts all over Gantam city! So you fight Wicker-Man and suddenly someone named Arkham Guy shows up and starts yelling at Bantam. At first, the guy was so whiny that I thought that Arkham Guy had to be Huffer from the original Transformers cartoon but to my surprise it was none other than Teen Titan!
So Bantam is so upset by the Jokester-Man's death that he keeps seeing him in Dead-Space-like fever-dream sequences where Bantam is seen watching Requiem for a Dream far too close to the TV. What a trip it was! I thought I'd never get through the many sections of gameplay because I was too captivated by the mocap they did for Jennifer Connely.
Anyways, eventually Bantam shoves the Jokester-Man into a shipping crate and leaves him in his mind's version of that huge storage room from Indiana Jones. Bantam then has to reveal that he is actually the Messiah, Bant Wain. The whole world gasps but in the end it doesn't seem to matter.
The story goes on after the story and I haven't gotten too wasted while playing it, so I'd give this game a 10/10 all around. Plus the Bantambile is pretty awesome, I haven't played anything with a Bantambile in it since Crysis 3. GG Rockstirdy, keep pumping out the Bantam games. I haven't played something this good since I plugged myself into an XBOX 360 Slim 20gb console and played Halo Reach with my eyes.
*But seriously, y'all. This is an awesome game with tons of things to do. The base game is rupturing with content and the story is well rounded and has a satisfying end. Ah Shadowrun, I'll start off by saying this: If you're into the Shadowrun universe and games like UFO: XCOM, then chances are that you'll really like Shadowrun returns.
That said, I do have some issues with the game. First and foremost, the music gets grading and tiresome fast. I've played the game for 9 hours and I had to turn the music off, they were clearly aiming for a dark electronic ambience and they do achieve it, but there are simply not enough tunes and a few of them simply sound too much alike.
A second point that I feel must be made, is the fact that the game has cut a lot of corners when making the jump from pen & paper to video game. Shadowrun has always aimed for high realism, but this requires a lot of rules and a lot of depth. I understand that they had to cut a lot of these rules because otherwise nobody would've been able to play the game without 2 hours of tutorial, if not more.
Third point, there are some issues when trying to select certain points to move to in the grid, so I suggest activating the double-click feature, which ends the miss clicks.
Fourth point, the save system blows balls. The game will auto-save whenever you enter a new scene, but you are unable to manually save, this means that if you fail, you have to start all over from the very beginning of the scene, this can be especially tiresome if the encounter is 30 minutes long or you just leveled up before you died.
Fifth point is mostly mechanical, but I still feel  it should be mentioned. There's an issue with scripted events that can ♥♥♥♥ you over; I'll try to explain it: When you move a character through a door and towards cover, the character will stop because and a little dialogue will play. Afterwards your character will be stuck where the dialogue started and if you're out of actions for said character, this can lead to them recieving a lead sandwich. Couple this with the fact that you're unnable to resurrect your main character if his HP hits zero and you can get rather frustrated. This wouldn't be half bad, but when you can resurrect side characters after they hit zero HP it just seems rather silly.
And finally always remember:
Watch your back. Shoot straight. Conserve ammo. And never, ever, cut a deal with a dragon.

There are many differences between a video game RPG and a tabletop RPG run by a GM. A video game RPG we expect certain conventions: random battles to raise XP, walking around a fixed location until we're ready to proceed with the story, and freedom to explore the entire world to a certain point.
In a tabletop RPG, it's almost the opposite: random battles are tedious and most battles are relevant to the plot in some way, you're expected to keep to a timetable to follow the plot, and you probably won't revisit areas you've already visited except for a 'safe house' or two.
What we have here is a video game RPG that acts like, plays like, and runs like a tabletop RPG! There are no random battles, and world exploration is very limited. Side quests are (generally) done immediately when you get them or not at all. There are no obvious good/bad dialogue choices that alter an unseen scale that judges your 'morality'. What we instead have is a very intriguing, atmosphere-driven game with a tightly-focused plot and tactical combat which feels very tabletop-ish.
I enjoy Shadowrun, but I've also played the tabletop RPG and enjoy the setting. A person who buys this expecting something like a Bioware rpg or Skyrim is going to be very disappointed. But if you're willing to give it a chance, the atmosphere and writing will immerse you easily.
And there's a game editor. So you can probably make your own game, if you think you could do better.

The good things I can say about Killing Floor 2 is that it has lovely graphics, sweet gore system, alright shooting mechanics and Tripwire is doing an okay job in informing the community about their work, sharing stuff like previews of weapon models or upcoming changes regarding skills. Sadly, that's about it..
First of all, it is a little over a year after release and we're still missing some of the perks in the game - the Sharpshooter perk was released a few hours before this review was written; it is the fourth added perk and the last one from the set of original Killing Floor perks. We're still missing two (completely new) ones. Considering it takes Tripwire a few months to finish a single one of these perks, I speculate we might see the last ones in early 2017 at best. This is not okay considering how important perks are for enjoyment.
Tripwire has trouble balancing the perks and each attempt to fix the system seems to break something. It can only get worse as the remaining perks come out.
In my opinion the maps are way too small and boring - I particularly greatly miss Killing Floor 1's farm map in which you could easily get lost in the huge field. The sequel's equivalent of that map is incredibly tiny, featuring only a house, a barn and little area around those two buildings.
Welding doors permamently is no longer a thing due to the fact that doors now have their own hit points and will eventually just break, which is a thing due to Tripwire wanting to encourage moving around the map instead of camping in one spot. While I definitely don't think they're wrong in their thinking, the enemies are infamous for, well.. Teleporting. You thought this big brute was behind you? Well, the game has him teleport when too far away, so we'll just put him right around the corner you're about to run by. Fun! Besides, I think they should have explored different ways of fighting camping, such as new Zeds or having the biggest enemies (Fleshpounds, Scrakes) approach that position while already enraged.
A new gamemode was released in which players may fight against each others, taking the roles of Zeds and Survivors! Shamefully though, the gamemode is imbalanced and adding it before PvE balance is achieved only makes balancing the game as a whole even more complicated.
The game now features a strength/weakness system - basically some weapons are good against specific enemies, some are bad against others. It means that a shotgun can no longer one-hit kill a really light enemy, because said enemy is supposed to be 'agile'. While it sounds okay..ish on paper, in reality memorising all the weaknesses is difficult and just unnecessarily complicated, especially because the game doesn't even inform you of the weaknesses. In addition to that, the enemies' resistances are way too strong, making them pretty tanky, annoying, and some weapons just useless. You should be vastly outnumbered by the weaker Zeds, not be forced to waste tons of bullets against the weakest ones 'just because'. Everything being a bullet sponge is not fun.
While I personally don't care much about it being a thing, releasing cosmetic microtransactions using a CS:GO-like crate system while your community is forced to wait yet another month for an anticipated perk is just disrespectful.
The game is in Early Access, but Tripwire doesn't seem to care about that - their updates are a bit rare and.. they release pre-early access copies to the press instead of to the playerbase, which should be able to opt in to help test the update.
Every now and then the playerbase receives a new fully-voiced character to play as for free - while it's really sweet, the quality of the voice actors and their lines is myeh and boring.
EDIT: Now it has come to light that Tripwire is working on a VR-only Killing Floor game, which will be an Oculus Rift timed exclusive. Meanwhile their main game is still far from finished. I think I mentioned something about disrespect, right?
---

The writing is fantastic with plenty of flavor choices as well as ways to complete and objective. You can talk, hack, send a drone, or shoot your way through most siutations and every single one of those paths rewards you equally since the game gives karma (experience) based on completing objectives, not per enemy kill. This system encourages avoiding firefights if you can talk/outsmart your way through, and that's pretty damn awesome.
There isn't a lot of replayability in the main campaign but the game is setup for DLC's and mods. The main campaign is fairly satisfying and sets up for further adventures.
Those who don't mind reading (a lot) and dealing with the often clunky control/ui will find a very enjoyable 10-12 hour game here. Those who grew up on faster paced games with voice actors telling the story and objectives linearly light up may find this a bit jarring.

Aahh , Risk of Rain , where do i start ...
First of all , this game may seem hard at first , but trust me , more and more you play , you will get the hang of it. This game is basically a run-and-gun with rogue-like elements. With 12 classes , each with 4 unique abilities , you wont get bord so fast. And dont forget the items , which are a lot too. The game may have some bugs , which is not nice , but you can get over them. And i almost forgot , everything is randomly generated , so no 2 runs would be the same.
Now , regarding classes , my favorite part of the game. You start at first with only 1 basic class. Yep , only 1 class out of 12. You must do certain things to unlock classes , like killing bosses , reaching a certain level or in some cases even finding the other characters hidden in the game's levels. No 2 classes are the same , each one of them has an unique playstyle and set of abilities . For example , there is the sniper who excels at firing precise shots , being very good for dealing with bosses , but not so good for dealing with hordes of enemies. Or the enforcer , a tank who can stun enemies , or block all frontal damage with his shield.
Now the items. Oh boy , there are lots of items . Some give you a shield , some make your attacks explode . There are activable items who can summon ghosts to fight for you , shoot a lot of missles and so on.
The enemies in this game are well done , every stage bringing some new type of enemy . And also , you can buy drones to help you out in your journey . These drones fly near you and shoot the bad guys or heal you.
And the soundtrack ? Pure genius.
TL;DR Get this game if you like rogue like shooters with lots of classes and items , and most of all , good replay value.

text:
Punishing, but really enjoyable little rougelike with emphasis on fast paced action and easy to learn but difficult to master classes. Each class has it's own set of skills which will significantly change the way you play, but unfortunately only one (out of ten) is available from the start.
As with most rougelikes; levels, items and enemies are procedurally generated and permadeath is enabled but game never feels unfair, since every playthrough offers something new. Due to it's difficulty and random nature it will require speed, precision and adaptability. Luckily there are a lot of items spread out around the level that will provide passive and active bonuses like increased rate of fire or various status effects, as well as more interesting ones which I'm not going to spoil since discovering new item and monster log entries will be your main source of accomplishment in early stages of the game. However as you unlock more drops and get familiar with each class, things will get easier. This is the point where time becomes your biggest enemy (well...besides all the other big enemies). Game implements a timer in the upper right corner that will gradually increase difficulty as time passes, forcing you to find a balance between becoming more powerful and just getting to the next level with all your bits intact. It provides a nice compromise, keeping a challenging gameplay, but still providing the feeling of controling an unstopabble killing machine.
There are some problems on the technical side, like the occasional but gut-wrenching crash that will erase your progress and leave you sobbing, unresponsive controls in menus (especially if you're using gamepad) and problems with online co-op conectivity and Steam achievements. I would also be amiss not to mention brilliant sountrack and appealing pixel art.
All in all, in a sea of rougelikes this one manages to stand on it's own, providing responsive shooting mechanics, hordes of different enemies and items and a great balance between frustrating and adrenaline-pumping gameplay. A great value for money.

I've played since Killing Floor, where a group of friends and I sunk days into the game exploring dedicated servers to modded ones.  I'm a huge fan of the series and I geniunely enjoy playing it.  I was skeptical at first and naturally upset as much as everyone else when they introduced microtransactions and seemed to prioritize it.
I was afraid we were going to have a second DayZ on our hands where they drop the game half-polished and ditch it for 4 years as you cringe over the $35 you spent for a game thats managed by less than a dozen bonobo apes.
They've really pulled through with this game.  The enhancements to melee make playing a Berserker quite fun now.  The transition from the original game's raw stats to choice of skills means you have to consider how you want to play your role.  The addition of brand new perks makes for some interesting team composition (minus survivalist...)
And yet they constantly push out these free updates.  It's not a game made by EA where they rush it broken as ♥♥♥♥ and try to patch it later before giving up.  It isn't like Destiny where a large portion of the content is stuck behind a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t season pass.  Every update always brings me right back.  The implementation of versus is enjoyable, sometimes.  It gave a reason to be level 25 for bragging rights I suppose.  But the recent addition of daily, weekly, and seasonal missions for a chance of cool loot has made the replability of this game even higher.  Adding new weapons, maps with their unique features like changing surroundings or objectives and a new ZED or perk every so often keeps this game interesting.
I've sunk over 300 hours into this game.  I think I can get another 300 hours in easily.

AAA Survival Horror is kind of in a rut and I don't expect to see it coming out anytime soon. The market just isn't what it used to be and AAA studios are running out of ideas. (Hey, Resident Evil 4 was highly successful! Let's model games after that, despite it being the least Survival Horror-y Survival Horror game ever!)
The jump scares in the game got a little bit old after a while and I wish ammo conservation wasn't so easy. (Yes game, I get it. Shooting limbs will save me ammo. It's not hard. Really. I'm unlikely to shoot at the body ever, so stop rewarding me for something so obvious.)
Still, one thing I really liked was situations you couldn't shoot yourself out of. It was possible to make these easier by upgrading your rig, stasis, and oxygen, but they still required skill beyond sharpshooting.
Dead Space also lost a bit of my respect because it had a VERY annoying required mini-game that took me hours to pass the first time. The other mini-games aren't necessary, but weren't that fun in my opinion.
I wish there were more achievements that rewarded you for playing the game in alternative ways. (There's one for only using the Plasma Cutter the entire game, but it was my go-to weapon of choice, and the ability to sell ammo for other weapons and buy ammo for the Plasma Cutter made the Survial Horror aspect of needing to use the weapon you have ammo for basically non-existant.)
I was glad to see that there was only so much you could stuff in your pants. This made parts more difficult, but because you could almost always backtrack to the store where you can store your excess items, it was less impactful.
This is a save point game, which some people don't like, but I think is necessary for Survival Horror as a genre. However, screwing up doesn't necessarily mean going back to the last save. There was some auto-saving, but it only lasted during the current game system. Considering how much you have to do sometimes between saves, this was a godsend every once in a while, especially when having to figure out complex puzzles while fending off space zombies.
Did I like Dead Space? Yes. Did I feel that it heralds a new era of good AAA survival horror games? No. It rehashed too many of the tired tropes to be a glimmer of hope. It's fun, but not brilliant.

Disregarding the troubles this game suffered around its launch date and some time after it, the overall experience was a positive one. Gameplay felt familiar enough to the earlier Arkham titles, but also offered new elements, such as the Batmobile, other playable characters, and the Most Wanted system. Combat stayed mostly the same, offering enough challenge to the one-button masher with several different enemy types, gadget variations, and combat moves to spice up a fairly simple combat system of punches and counters.
Largest issue with the game by far is the framerate. My gear is fairly average (possibly slightly below), resulting in 30 FPS at most, with multiple drops below that. Most notably due to rain and flying rubble.
Regarding the price tag, I'd say it's worth it for an Arkham game. Although the amount of great DLC makes a player hesitant to pay for it after paying for the game itself
So, if you're looking for a great Arkham game after enjoying the earlier titles, or if you want a great introduction to the Arkham series, I recommend this game.

It's also a fun game. I spent around 24 hours on the campaign, doing every side quests (including the DLC quests). Then there is NG+, which makes the game much harder (and a bit more enjoyable). And there are the challenges.
There were times I wanted to spend hours on a video game, and I did on Arkham Knight. There were times I wanted to play a dozen minutes while something was downloading, so I did the challenges.
The gameplay is rewarding, and extremely fun. Yes, they do push their Batmobile down our throat some times, but I still found it very fun to play.

Let me first just start off by saying, THIS GAME WILL KICK YOUR♥♥♥♥♥ This is by far one of the hardest games I have ever played, HOWEVER, it is NOT a rage game. Every death is YOUR Fault. Though, sometimes I swear that the game can turn into a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and start spawning enemies out the butt to Cluster EFF you. This is also a great game, the music is great, the graphics are wonderful, again, another game that is Pixel art, a little overdone nowadays with a LOT of games, but this one looks very pretty! *.*
Now, this game is also quite a time ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I played for the first 2-3 hours BEFORE I unlocked even the FIRST unlockable character! That is INSANE, but I like it, It makes you push yourself to the limits of your skills, those other characters and their silhouettes is somehow one of the best motivations to wanting them unlocked. Now, I HAVE beaten the game....On Easy...and it took me about 10 deaths, and about 4-5 hours, NO JOKE, and even then, about 75% of the characters are STILL unlocked. Even on Easy mode, the game GETS INSANELY HARDER as time goes on.
The Controls are a bit weird, the default is Z for your main attack, X for your next ability, C for your other ability, and V for your last ability, Very odd controls, but you learn to get used to them, it took me quite a while to get used to them myself. Your character BTW is very small on such a large screen but this is a GOOD THING, as there are some MASSIVE enemies wanting to stomp on you and send your butt back ALL the way back to the very beginning of the level. YES, THIS GAME HAS PERMA DEATH, IF YOU DO NOT LIKE PERMA DEATH IN GAMES, KEEP WALKING, THIS GAME IS NOT FOR YOU. However, if you DO like perma death, and having to start over trying to be better than that one time you survived for 20 minutes, then you will cherish this game for years to come.
All in all, this is one INCREDIBLY difficult game, multiple characters, not really much of a story but it doesn't need much of one. Oh! And also, I have to say, this game is not really much of a "Rogue-like" as it claims to be, I have played it about 10 times and have mostly come back to the same levels almost everytime. Sure, sometimes the game will throw you a curve ball and teleport you to a different level three or level two, but eh, who cares?
If you like perma death games which are INSANELY HARD (The scale as far as I have seen it goes from Very Easy, Easy, Medium, Hard, Very hard, Insane, Impossible, I SEE YOU, And finally the last level of difficulty if you survive for like 50+ minutes or something while the game is on Easy mode, is I'M COMING FOR YOU) and you love begging for your life to whoever you pray to, THIS is the game for you!

I've heavily enjoyed this game for a multitude of reasons. However as every game out in the market there are some flaws (Only one major one as of right now that I hope gets fixed soon.)
Pros:
1: There are a large selection of character, each with their own playstyle and abilities. You are sure to find your favorite here as there are melee, short range, and long range characters.
2: The soundtrack is amazing. It fits so well with the game because at its core, you are trying to survive in a harsh world.
3: The levels are diverse and have secrets in them that you will need certain items to get to.
4: The enemies are varied and have their own attack patterns. The wisps for example try to attack you at range while the Golem will try to smash you.
5: Co Op is really fun to play, you have to coordinate with your friends to survive as you do NOT share item buffs. Everyone gets their own items so best to play wisely.
6: The majority of times that you die will because YOU ♥♥♥♥ed up. Either you decided to stay in a fight that you're not prepared for, you spent too long in a level and now the Difficulty Meter is at Hard, or you decided to fight Providence with only 4 items under your belt.
7: The Difficulty Meter is a pretty neat addition to this already great game. The longer you spend in your current run, the harder the game gets. You first have your three base difficulty levels all based on the types of rain, then you have this meter. The difficulty carries through the levels so you have to decide if it's worth spending the extra time in one level to find the rest of the loot or to skip out on it to make the game easier on yourself.
Now for the cons:
1: Co Op connectivity is pretty bad at times. You will sometimes see your friends sliding across the map with their hands in the air.
2: Sometimes a bunch of enemies will just spawn on top of you without warning. That's really aggravating as it feels like that kind of death was just cheap instead of your own ♥♥♥♥ up.
3: Now this is a bug I've experienced as have all my friends but sometimes the map doesn't fully load, as in the art assets will, but the boundaries won't so we've fallen through the floor and into the void plenty of times. This bug is usually at the first level so you won't have a major build most of the time.
So with all that in mind I honestly recommend this game heavily as it's now one of my favorites.

A hugely intense game marred by a bad case of consolitis. Dead Space spawned a whole host of imitators, and for good reason -- it's well-made and placed in a setting original enough to make it stand out from most third-person shooters. Great atmosphere, exceptional surround sound, and ingenious weapon design combine to make a game worth playing through to the end.
Unfortunately, Dead Space suffers from some of the worst console-to-PC translation I've ever experienced. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gamepad controls make movement and aiming more painful than they need to be, and there's a hardware conflict that can cause the gamepad to do nothing but spin the camera in a 360° pattern (something that the devs never bothered to fix through the entirety of the series, amazingly enough). The unchageable FOV prevents me from playing for more than a couple hours due to motion sickness. There's also a bug that causes stuttering when vsync is enabled.
The positives definitely override the negatives though, and Dead Space is a game that should be experienced by horror aficionados and shooter fans alike.

Let me first just start off by saying, THIS GAME WILL KICK YOUR♥♥♥♥♥ This is by far one of the hardest games I have ever played, HOWEVER, it is NOT a rage game. Every death is YOUR Fault. Though, sometimes I swear that the game can turn into a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and start spawning enemies out the butt to Cluster EFF you. This is also a great game, the music is great, the graphics are wonderful, again, another game that is Pixel art, a little overdone nowadays with a LOT of games, but this one looks very pretty! *.*
Now, this game is also quite a time ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I played for the first 2-3 hours BEFORE I unlocked even the FIRST unlockable character! That is INSANE, but I like it, It makes you push yourself to the limits of your skills, those other characters and their silhouettes is somehow one of the best motivations to wanting them unlocked. Now, I HAVE beaten the game....On Easy...and it took me about 10 deaths, and about 4-5 hours, NO JOKE, and even then, about 75% of the characters are STILL unlocked. Even on Easy mode, the game GETS INSANELY HARDER as time goes on.
The Controls are a bit weird, the default is Z for your main attack, X for your next ability, C for your other ability, and V for your last ability, Very odd controls, but you learn to get used to them, it took me quite a while to get used to them myself. Your character BTW is very small on such a large screen but this is a GOOD THING, as there are some MASSIVE enemies wanting to stomp on you and send your butt back ALL the way back to the very beginning of the level. YES, THIS GAME HAS PERMA DEATH, IF YOU DO NOT LIKE PERMA DEATH IN GAMES, KEEP WALKING, THIS GAME IS NOT FOR YOU. However, if you DO like perma death, and having to start over trying to be better than that one time you survived for 20 minutes, then you will cherish this game for years to come.
All in all, this is one INCREDIBLY difficult game, multiple characters, not really much of a story but it doesn't need much of one. Oh! And also, I have to say, this game is not really much of a "Rogue-like" as it claims to be, I have played it about 10 times and have mostly come back to the same levels almost everytime. Sure, sometimes the game will throw you a curve ball and teleport you to a different level three or level two, but eh, who cares?
If you like perma death games which are INSANELY HARD (The scale as far as I have seen it goes from Very Easy, Easy, Medium, Hard, Very hard, Insane, Impossible, I SEE YOU, And finally the last level of difficulty if you survive for like 50+ minutes or something while the game is on Easy mode, is I'M COMING FOR YOU) and you love begging for your life to whoever you pray to, THIS is the game for you!

If you're a fan of South Park you should own this game. More often than not I felt like I was actually wandering around the quiet little mountain town we've grown to love, rather than playing a game. TST has a nice level, combat, and skill system; things seemed farmiliar somehow, but they were unique at the same time. The initial $60 is tough for me to swallow for any game, so when it dropped to $40 I picked it up. To those who thought, or are worried about, it being to short, I couldn't disagree more. It seemed just right, with the window open for expansion in the future... at a cost of delaying of the show apparently, but it was worth it.  I just finished the last of the quests and watched the credits; to my pleasure I can still wander around in a proper end-game fasion. I haven't, however, seen if there is actually anything new or different to do.
The classes have different skills, but all can equip any weapons, items, and armor found; the use of magic is unique to your character and not any specific classes. When playing through I only discovered one decision that may change a single set of quests; a second playthrough isn't even close to out of the question. The humor and incentive of things being slightly different the second time through will drive me to play through again, very soon. It took me just short of 16hrs to finish all the quests (normal difficulty as a mage; I could have easily bumped it up), I found all of the Chinpokomon and other items, but am still missing a friend or two. To put things into perspective, I finished Bioshock Infinite in less time (just over 13hrs) and enjoyed it much less than this, yet it was the "best game of the year"? Please! I am one of the (sadly) rare people that thinks Bioshock was way over rated though. If SouthPark TST was too short, it's only because it was so much fun and I didn't want it to ever end.
To sum it up, if you are a fan of the show, you need to own this game... a fan of RPGs that isn't easily offended should pick it up too, just keep in mind the type of humor you're in for. Either way, you'll have a blast!!

I've been a fan of the Arkham series since the first game so I couldn't wait until Arkham Knight came out. I played it and while I had a good time, it didn't knock my socks off or keep me at the edge of my seat like Asylum, City or even Origins did. While it's a good game, it really abuses the Batmobile mechanic. While the previous games mixed up the stealth and action and both were amazing in their own ways, this game adds the vehicle sections to basically give it three gameplay types: Predator, Combat and Batmobile. But unfortunately Batmobile doesn't stack up to the others.
Don't get me wrong, the Batmobile isn't
, but it's just not as fun as the other two. And unfortunately, the game makes you hop in that car
. Even when it comes to puzzles, you're gonna have to use your car. And the combat with it just is so meh, it's more frustrating than challenging at times and I never feel accomplished destroying tons of enemy vehicles with the Batmobile as I do taking down whole rooms of enemies with Batman.
Far as the story goes, it's..
. Arkham Knight despite having top billing is more or less a subboss the whole game to Scarecrow. And while Scarecrow isn't a bad villain by any means, he didn't really have the gravity or presence that Joker did in Asylum or Protocol 10 did in City. The Arkham Knight as a character was pretty cool, but unfortunately he never seemed to rise to the occasion and more or less stayed pretty basic the whole game. And unfortunately as almost every game in this series goes, the ending felt rushed. As soon as the final confrontation is over, it's like Rocksteady raced out the door to wrap things up. I mean.. c'mon dudes, it's the final game in the trilogy, give me an epilogue that lasts more than a couple minutes at most,
!
But anyway, despite all its flaws, I'd still recommend it. It feels like a slightly above average game that could've been so much more; a solid 75 outta 100 if I had to give it a number. The combat was amazing as always, the stealth was also pretty fun, the enemies varied enough to keep it fresh, but the Batmobile segments unfortunately made the game seem far more tedious than it should've been. And the story while interesting at times, didn't really live up to the hype despite the stakes and just seemed like standard affair. Nothing that happens will really wow or shock you.
In closing, hit this game up if its caught your eye. If you're a casual gamer just looking for a game and this is on sale, this is a safe bet. And if you're a Batman fan, you'll definitely get your money's worth out of this thing.

I've heavily enjoyed this game for a multitude of reasons. However as every game out in the market there are some flaws (Only one major one as of right now that I hope gets fixed soon.)
Pros:
1: There are a large selection of character, each with their own playstyle and abilities. You are sure to find your favorite here as there are melee, short range, and long range characters.
2: The soundtrack is amazing. It fits so well with the game because at its core, you are trying to survive in a harsh world.
3: The levels are diverse and have secrets in them that you will need certain items to get to.
4: The enemies are varied and have their own attack patterns. The wisps for example try to attack you at range while the Golem will try to smash you.
5: Co Op is really fun to play, you have to coordinate with your friends to survive as you do NOT share item buffs. Everyone gets their own items so best to play wisely.
6: The majority of times that you die will because YOU ♥♥♥♥ed up. Either you decided to stay in a fight that you're not prepared for, you spent too long in a level and now the Difficulty Meter is at Hard, or you decided to fight Providence with only 4 items under your belt.
7: The Difficulty Meter is a pretty neat addition to this already great game. The longer you spend in your current run, the harder the game gets. You first have your three base difficulty levels all based on the types of rain, then you have this meter. The difficulty carries through the levels so you have to decide if it's worth spending the extra time in one level to find the rest of the loot or to skip out on it to make the game easier on yourself.
Now for the cons:
1: Co Op connectivity is pretty bad at times. You will sometimes see your friends sliding across the map with their hands in the air.
2: Sometimes a bunch of enemies will just spawn on top of you without warning. That's really aggravating as it feels like that kind of death was just cheap instead of your own ♥♥♥♥ up.
3: Now this is a bug I've experienced as have all my friends but sometimes the map doesn't fully load, as in the art assets will, but the boundaries won't so we've fallen through the floor and into the void plenty of times. This bug is usually at the first level so you won't have a major build most of the time.
So with all that in mind I honestly recommend this game heavily as it's now one of my favorites.

To be honest, I think that the indie "roguelite" genre is a plague that should go away as fast as it can. That being said, a couple good things did come out of it, Risk of Rain probably being one of the best among those, even though it's far from a solid roguelike.
The game's objective is simple: travel through a level, find the teleporter and advance to the next level. Along the way fight enemies, level up and gain items, and unlock new items and classes. The gameplay is extremely simple as there is no inventory or even an item limit (though only one "consumable" item can be carried) and there are no stats or skills to level up. There are no randomized potions or scrolls that might poison you or summon angry demons around you either. Players can move left and right, ascend stairs or ropes, and jump. As you kill monsters you gain a certain amount of money and experience, and the money can be used to open chests or similar items within levels. It resets to 0 at the end of each level though.
Character classes have 4 attacks activated by the ZXCV buttons and mostly play differently from each other. Their speed and similar attributes might also differ. There is only one class unlocked at the start, the rest are obtained via achievements.
There is a relatively small number of enemies in the game, and they all come with various color-coded strength levels. Sometimes enemies will drop Log Books, which will add descriptions for them in the encyclopedia section. Also, each time a never seen before item is obtained, it gets "unlocked", meaning that it can now drop from chests or bosses. The unlocked status carries over to new games, and items also have their encyclopedia section like monsters.
There is a base difficulty selection (easy, normal or hard) and as the player spends time in-game, the "in-game" difficulty  which starts from Very Easy goes up little by little. This affects enemies' strength and numbers.
Despite its problems, Risk of Rain is nevertheless pretty enjoyable and is certainly one of the best roguelites. It is especially good for mutiplayer. Get some friends and slap those monsters.

I've been a fan of the Arkham series since the first game so I couldn't wait until Arkham Knight came out. I played it and while I had a good time, it didn't knock my socks off or keep me at the edge of my seat like Asylum, City or even Origins did. While it's a good game, it really abuses the Batmobile mechanic. While the previous games mixed up the stealth and action and both were amazing in their own ways, this game adds the vehicle sections to basically give it three gameplay types: Predator, Combat and Batmobile. But unfortunately Batmobile doesn't stack up to the others.
Don't get me wrong, the Batmobile isn't
, but it's just not as fun as the other two. And unfortunately, the game makes you hop in that car
. Even when it comes to puzzles, you're gonna have to use your car. And the combat with it just is so meh, it's more frustrating than challenging at times and I never feel accomplished destroying tons of enemy vehicles with the Batmobile as I do taking down whole rooms of enemies with Batman.
Far as the story goes, it's..
. Arkham Knight despite having top billing is more or less a subboss the whole game to Scarecrow. And while Scarecrow isn't a bad villain by any means, he didn't really have the gravity or presence that Joker did in Asylum or Protocol 10 did in City. The Arkham Knight as a character was pretty cool, but unfortunately he never seemed to rise to the occasion and more or less stayed pretty basic the whole game. And unfortunately as almost every game in this series goes, the ending felt rushed. As soon as the final confrontation is over, it's like Rocksteady raced out the door to wrap things up. I mean.. c'mon dudes, it's the final game in the trilogy, give me an epilogue that lasts more than a couple minutes at most,
!
But anyway, despite all its flaws, I'd still recommend it. It feels like a slightly above average game that could've been so much more; a solid 75 outta 100 if I had to give it a number. The combat was amazing as always, the stealth was also pretty fun, the enemies varied enough to keep it fresh, but the Batmobile segments unfortunately made the game seem far more tedious than it should've been. And the story while interesting at times, didn't really live up to the hype despite the stakes and just seemed like standard affair. Nothing that happens will really wow or shock you.
In closing, hit this game up if its caught your eye. If you're a casual gamer just looking for a game and this is on sale, this is a safe bet. And if you're a Batman fan, you'll definitely get your money's worth out of this thing.

The only drawback that I can put out there is the fact that they still do not use 3.0 rules or any real Shadowrun rules at all it's a game specific rule set, which results in the typical samurai power house and makes most other play throughs with any other character lackluster.
You know I'm kind of sad and happy about this game.  Happy that there is another Shadowrun game out there, sad that it seem broken in many ways.
Currently the community is complaining about the save feature, basically the game only has an auto save which happens every hour or more depending on how long you take in each mission. It has it's own set of rules and not much of it makes any sense.  Then theres the game breakers, there are moments in this game where you can definately see bugs pop out of no where for instance NPCs saying Hi !$race.
The big catcher is the huge overlooks aside from the failure at programing the NPCs, they forget things like giving you access to med packs for the last end game mission. There are design mistakes as well, deckers (hackers) are used or in need throughout the game however you can never use an NPC decker that you hire to trigger a skill requirement event (like opening a door). I don't usually tend to play RTS games, but saying that I do enjoy playing them. But out of all the strategy games I have played so far, I'd say XCOM stands out the most. Not only does the game offer a challenging AI as well as unique gameplay mechanics, it also realises that games are meant to be fun. It accomplishes this through the various elements of base and squad management, as well as different missions and contracts. Customisation of your soldiers allows you to customise their looks and edit their names, which allows you to create interesting stories about your team on a desperate mission. Careful planning and well thought strategies are key to beating the game, but it still caters to newcomers to XCOM and RTS's and the hardcore veterans through the four different difficulty levels and it's tutorial. Story is a little bland and battlefields can get repetitive, but that doesn't stop me from regarding this as my favourite RTS. Well worth your money and your time!

Risk of Rain is an stylish pixellated Rougish game, where everything is out to get you.
The general mechanics are simple, kill stuff, get exp, get money, buy items, kill more things with the items you buy... and so on. It's a fun concept. Tonnes of people love those games, and RoR really executed this well, and the Alpha feels polished and stylish with no shortage of little secrets and challenges to keep you running.
It's generally simple, but with 80+ items, 30 enemies and 12 characters with in-depth abilities, 10 artifacts, 6 levels and 3 difficulties to play on. It keeps things fun and interesting and great to pick up with buddies.
But, this isn't a happy positive review. Here are the things setting this game back, but not exclusively, I feel some of these are issues with other very prestigious and polished games.
For one the multiplayer. It's not a great support, in local co-op you are forced to use a gamepad even though there is potentially enough space on the keyboard for two, exp awkwardly all flying to one player, the list goes on. The online multiplayer is just as disgusting. You have to either go up on the internet and search up servers, type in their ip painstakingly into the game, and try again multiple times until you find a game that hasn't started, isn't full and is working (Which is a pretty tight criteria) like, come on guys, you shouldn't have to read a bloody guide to find out how to get in a multiplayer match. But hamachi, as always, fixes this. Just hook it up and play with exclusively your mates or anyone willing to join, but I don't count that seeing it's not ingame software
BUT if you do manage to find a game or set one up with your mates, it's ridiculously fun. The only thing setting it back is its slightly unpolished weapon 'forced sharing'. But that's one probably to be fixed when it comes out of beta so it's unfair to judge it now.
The other problem that players haven't addressed is, is that 'can the developers keep up with the fast growing community of people?' The answer is no, the great risk with these kind of games is that no one will want to see the art style, the mechanics, or anything else to do with the game change when it is released from Beta because that's what makes it familiar and people feel cheaped out that it's 'not the same game'. I know that the wonderful developers making this game understand that, but what's their substitute? THE SAME STUFF.
LOTS AND LOTS OF THE SAME GODDAMN STUFF.
Basically, i'm no gypsy with a crystal ball but I can tell that all they can do do this is polish the bugs, and just keep pumping out more items, more characters, more levels and more enemies. And that♥♥♥♥♥♥gets boring after a while. Basically what i'm trying to say is, sure this game is fun now. You can get some great hours out of it. But it's going to die. Oh that sad, sweet movie cliffhanger. The death of RoR. When the same♥♥♥♥♥♥just gets more and more boring and the once stylish art simply becomes drab. If you've got some money to spare and you're interested, I recommend you go right ahead and jump into it. But people sitting there, rubbing their face staring at a $20 steam card wondering what they should sparingly buy should wonder if they should buy this, or maybe go for something else. You may feel dissapointed soon after and feel it's a waste of money, and that you could've bought this or that instead of it. I'm sorry to hear that but just take the risk if you feel it's a good game.

Super Hexagon is the gaming equivalent of modern art. Where you see a blank square hanging on the gallery wall with a dash of red paint, the critics rave about "the stark presentation contrasting with a bold use of color, challenging the eye and the expectations and slyly satirizing our own feelings of inadequacy." And so it goes with Super Hexagon. Critics rave about its "astounding" minimalism and "elegance." That's because they, as sophisticated consumers of media, "get it," and you, Neanderthal that you are, have no taste.
Well, as a Neanderthal myself, I found it to be a simplistic and hyperactive waste of time with the production values of an Ed Wood film.
On the plus side, the game does bring together some elements of classic gaming: It's got the graphics of Atari's Adventure, the gameplay of Cow Clicker, and the music of a Game Boy game hopped up on meth.
Now, I'm not saying that this game isn't for anyone; if you hate the slow, deliberate pacing and deep, complicated story of Wario Ware games, Super Hexagon may be just the game for you.
I think I paid 30 cents for it and, at night, those three dimes hover in the air over my bed and torment me with their laughter.
There's very little to this game; if this is Super Hexagon, and can only imagine what Hexagon was like.

Half-life 2 came out in 2004. It's 2014 now and the game is still incredibly amazing.

Fabulous game. Replay quality is extremely high. You adventure out as a character in a fairly large world in which you must defeat a boss and find a teleporter in order to advance to the next level.  As time progresses, the difficulty of the game gets harder, raising the spawn rates of the various mobs.  Many tactics must be employed to successfully defeat each boss and the surrounding mobs. On death, you lose everything and start from the beginning with nothing.  The replay quality comes from 4 things: The Monster Logs, Item Logs, Artifacts, and Classes.  I'll start with the classes.  When you first play the game, you are limited to one class: the Commando. As you play the game, you can complete objectives in order to earn the other 9 classes.  This requires that each time the user plays, he must specifically attempt that objective in order to gain that character, giving the gameplay a sense of purpose and a more satisfying playthrough.  Next are the Monster and Item Logs, since I feel they can be grouped in the same area.  The Item Log keeps track of every item you have ever picked up in-game, and if you view it, it will tell you how to unlock items through objectives to allow them to spawn the next  time you play through.  Monster Logs, on the other hand, are random drops from enemies that give you information.  At the game menu, you can view your Monster Logs to see more specific stats on mobs you have collected the Monster Logs of.  Finally, there are the artifacts.  These are hidden throughout the game, and the player must specifically search for them in order to unlock them.  This is one of my favorite aspects, personally, because the time used on searching for each artifact allows the difficulty to raise, resulting in a trade-off: an Artifact for a higher difficulty.
Overall, I find this game to be fantastic, and would recommend it to nearly all gamers.  9.8/10

It's very rare to see a game as simple as Super Hexagon feel like such a fresh experience.  I can't remember the last time I've enjoyed a game this much, either.  Most of my time spent playing games is just used to forget about the sorrow of my sad, pathetic excuse for an existence.  But when I turned on Super Hexagon, some light bulb turned on inside of me.  One that had been turned off since I was a little child.  I was having so much fun playing this game.  I couldn't put it down, and I couldn't stop thinking about it when I wasn't home.
In the game, you control a little cursor that moves around a hexagon.  Press right to move clockwise, and left to move counter-clockwise.  That's all there is to the controls.  The purpose of the game is to dodge incoming lines moving towards the hexagon and to stay alive as long as possible.  There's 3 different levels at first, appropriately labeled as 'Hard', 'Harder', and 'Hardest'.  You can unlock 'Hyper' versions of these levels after reaching the 60 second mark in a stage.
At a first glance, the game seems like it'll be relatively easy.  And then you die right away.  And then you say to yourself "Crap... I can do better than that."  And then you die again.  You repeat this process for about an hour, and realize that you still haven't gotten further than 10 seconds.  You curse the gods and the heavens, go pace around for a bit, and then come back and repeat the process all over again for another hour.  And then somehow you've reached 60 seconds and feel like you have the reflexes of a god.  And even after beating all of the levels, I still can't put this game down.  The game is just so much fun at it's core that I keep playing to try and get better times on each stage.
I should also mention that the music in this game is incredible.  There's only 3 tracks, one for each stage, but they're implemented in a way that helps keep them from being too repetitive.  Whenever you restart a level, the game starts the track from one of three different spots, somewhat giving the player the illusion of progression.  And each song seems to have one melody that only pops up when you're 30 seconds to 60 seconds into a level.  This helps build up tension your first time through, as the music becomes unfamiliar right as you're getting close to beating the level.
If you're the kind of gamer who feels like a game should have a lot of content and things to see, then avoid this game.  You can see 50% of what this game has to offer in approximately 30 seconds.  If you have a little bit of imagination, then pretend the 3 stages you played spin faster and have different background colors.  You've now seen 100% of what the game has to offer, all within less than a minute.  But, if you're a gamer who feels like a game isn't finished until you've completely mastered it, then prepare for hours and hours of fun with Super Hexagon.  This is a game in it's purest form.  No fluff.  No story.  No handholding.  Just... a ♥♥♥♥ing game.  Something that is now exceedingly rare.

Fabulous game. Replay quality is extremely high. You adventure out as a character in a fairly large world in which you must defeat a boss and find a teleporter in order to advance to the next level.  As time progresses, the difficulty of the game gets harder, raising the spawn rates of the various mobs.  Many tactics must be employed to successfully defeat each boss and the surrounding mobs. On death, you lose everything and start from the beginning with nothing.  The replay quality comes from 4 things: The Monster Logs, Item Logs, Artifacts, and Classes.  I'll start with the classes.  When you first play the game, you are limited to one class: the Commando. As you play the game, you can complete objectives in order to earn the other 9 classes.  This requires that each time the user plays, he must specifically attempt that objective in order to gain that character, giving the gameplay a sense of purpose and a more satisfying playthrough.  Next are the Monster and Item Logs, since I feel they can be grouped in the same area.  The Item Log keeps track of every item you have ever picked up in-game, and if you view it, it will tell you how to unlock items through objectives to allow them to spawn the next  time you play through.  Monster Logs, on the other hand, are random drops from enemies that give you information.  At the game menu, you can view your Monster Logs to see more specific stats on mobs you have collected the Monster Logs of.  Finally, there are the artifacts.  These are hidden throughout the game, and the player must specifically search for them in order to unlock them.  This is one of my favorite aspects, personally, because the time used on searching for each artifact allows the difficulty to raise, resulting in a trade-off: an Artifact for a higher difficulty.
Overall, I find this game to be fantastic, and would recommend it to nearly all gamers.  9.8/10
