It's very rare to see a game as simple as Super Hexagon feel like such a fresh experience.  I can't remember the last time I've enjoyed a game this much, either.  Most of my time spent playing games is just used to forget about the sorrow of my sad, pathetic excuse for an existence.  But when I turned on Super Hexagon, some light bulb turned on inside of me.  One that had been turned off since I was a little child.  I was having so much fun playing this game.  I couldn't put it down, and I couldn't stop thinking about it when I wasn't home.
In the game, you control a little cursor that moves around a hexagon.  Press right to move clockwise, and left to move counter-clockwise.  That's all there is to the controls.  The purpose of the game is to dodge incoming lines moving towards the hexagon and to stay alive as long as possible.  There's 3 different levels at first, appropriately labeled as 'Hard', 'Harder', and 'Hardest'.  You can unlock 'Hyper' versions of these levels after reaching the 60 second mark in a stage.
At a first glance, the game seems like it'll be relatively easy.  And then you die right away.  And then you say to yourself "Crap... I can do better than that."  And then you die again.  You repeat this process for about an hour, and realize that you still haven't gotten further than 10 seconds.  You curse the gods and the heavens, go pace around for a bit, and then come back and repeat the process all over again for another hour.  And then somehow you've reached 60 seconds and feel like you have the reflexes of a god.  And even after beating all of the levels, I still can't put this game down.  The game is just so much fun at it's core that I keep playing to try and get better times on each stage.
I should also mention that the music in this game is incredible.  There's only 3 tracks, one for each stage, but they're implemented in a way that helps keep them from being too repetitive.  Whenever you restart a level, the game starts the track from one of three different spots, somewhat giving the player the illusion of progression.  And each song seems to have one melody that only pops up when you're 30 seconds to 60 seconds into a level.  This helps build up tension your first time through, as the music becomes unfamiliar right as you're getting close to beating the level.
If you're the kind of gamer who feels like a game should have a lot of content and things to see, then avoid this game.  You can see 50% of what this game has to offer in approximately 30 seconds.  If you have a little bit of imagination, then pretend the 3 stages you played spin faster and have different background colors.  You've now seen 100% of what the game has to offer, all within less than a minute.  But, if you're a gamer who feels like a game isn't finished until you've completely mastered it, then prepare for hours and hours of fun with Super Hexagon.  This is a game in it's purest form.  No fluff.  No story.  No handholding.  Just... a ♥♥♥♥ing game.  Something that is now exceedingly rare.

Best action horror game in years.
If you somehow didn't play this game yet, WHAT ARE YOU DOING GO BUY IT!
The first order of business is to make sure you follow the on-screen adjuster to turn your brightness down. This makes a fundamental difference in the atmosphere and experience of playing the game. If you don't, it's just a well lit third person shooter where you murder everything with angry curb stomps and plasma.
Dead Space is one of the few "survival horror" titles where other people have admitted to me that the first time they played it, they put it down and couldn't go on because they were "scared". I personally started it, played the first chapter, and refused to put up with it anymore after that because of the degree to which the atmosphere is perfected. Did not pick it back up for 6 months, but I am so glad I did. It isn't necessarily the game or the story that make the game frightening, and it may sound like this is a discredit, but the lighting and sound design alone make the horror atmosphere.
Every hallway and room you go in, you hear necromorphs scurrying through the vents and behind the walls.  You hear them walking around, or you hear objects moving around. Sometimes that ends up being you trolling yourself, because the physics in the game are exaggerated - and glitched on PC especially. If you walk over a limb or a bucket, it will move around on the floor forever and sound like an enemy. The lighting is very well done and the game makes great use of darkness to throw enemies at you - and also to mask the fact that some of them are just scripted jump scares - or to confuse you so that it's harder to see.
One of the best things about the game, and one of the most simple, is the hud. There isn't one.  Health and ammo information is projected from your gun model or player model, rather than having you pause, or block parts of the screen. It's a very basic design decision but it goes a long way towards maintaining your immersion in the environment. It also forces you to be decent at the game because there is no pause. If you need to do view your inventory, you do it in real time while blocking the majority of the screen, so you better not need to heal. That was sort of a fail on Visceral's part, though, and why they put in quick heal in the sequels.
Storywise, no, Dead Space is nothing original. It is simply one of  two modern EA franchises that retells the same story as System Shock (The other being Mass Effect), the franchise they ensured stopped existing after SS2 didn't sell 8 million copies. Anyone who has played those  games can see that, but it does so in an enjoyable and interesting way.....that eventually got retconned and ruined in the 2nd and 3rd games.
I have one major problem with Dead Space 1, and it is the same problem as with RE4. There is a point in time, in the game, where your character transcends from alone and helpless, to alone and a super-Rambo. RE4 did this by accelerating the rate at which you gain money, ammo,and more powerful weapons. Dead Space does this by, admittedly, allowing you to cheat to get Nodes, but giving you Nodes in the first place, and giving you force powers. Kinesis and stasis module don't ruin the game, but they do make it tactical and easily controllable so that you can slay hordes of Necros with some careful playing. You will also eventually pick up so much Force Gun ammo that the hardest (and scariest) parts of the game become a joke, as you simply gravity gun everything to death.
If it weren't for that one problem with the game, I would easily rate it a 10 out of 10 instead of a 9 out of 10. Oh, and the fact that no EA games have Steamworks support so we get boned out of features all console players got - namely, achievements.

Behind Risk of Rain's simple premise and oldschool graphics is an edge-of-your-seat exciting masterpiece in game design that's hard as nails to get the hang of, but thoroughly satisfying once you do. And then you try a different character and the cycle begins anew.
The basic concept is simple: get stronger
than your enemies do. This is easier said than done, of course - the levels, enemies and loot are randomized and there are numerous chance-based decisions and events at play, but after a few deaths you'll slowly learn how to ride the difficulty wave with your chosen character.
The game challenges you to challenge yourself: you can only unlock some of the stronger items (that can give you an edge in subsequent games) by completing hard tasks on different levels or using different characters. Because of this system, striving for certain achievements - albeit still arbitrarily established by the developers - has tangible, noticable benefits on your progress. Plus, the excitement of unlocking something new to play with and the enjoyment you get when you complete the feat is much stronger.
The fact that there is a very thin line between being overwhelmed easily and being an unstoppable killing machine makes the game all the more exhilarating to play - even when you're doing well, you know you can't slack or take your time, or the enemies will catch up to you in strength and/or numbers.
The controls are fluid and the simplistic graphics help you make sense of the chaos that will inevitably ensue once you've progressed far enough. The music is indescribably brilliant and goes perfectly with the visuals and the action-packed nature of the game.
If you can't take being given the short straw by the RNG gods from time to time, if you're frustrated when a game is punishingly difficult after an hour of play, if you can't stand looking at graphics that evoke those of games on Commodore 64, move along, this game is not for you. If these traits don't bother you, you'll get some of the most adrenaline-pumping and rewarding gameplay available in a non-PvP game, wishing other games were as brave with their learning curves as this.

This game is a step down from civ 4 because the developers pushed peaceful victories too much.  If you attack one person, every other person will denounce you and place sanctions on you.  This would be find later in the game but people in medieval times didn't put sanctions on other nations!  An aggressive AI option has also been taken out of the custom game options making it seem to me that the AI never fight any wars.   I also dislike how you can't place more than one unit in a tile.  While stacks of doom were far from perfect, this combat system makes it impossible to fight wars. Personally, I feel that the way the defense mod in civ 4 beyond the sword is how they should have modeled the combat.  In the mod, the more troops you put in a stack, the weaker the troops become in combat. I also don't like how barbarians continue to spawn in the modern era.  In civ 4, barbarians stopped spawning around the medieval era.  I also miss vassal states and wish the new diplomacy Systems worked more efficiently.  Overall, I feel that war in civ 5 was neglected by the developers and made extremely boring and ineffective for successful gameplay.
The positives of this game are good potential for mods, ranged units that are actually ranged and many other concepts such as changing how religions and civics work.  I also like how expansion works and how there are different uses for culture than in civ 4.  However, the fact that domination victories are basically impossible or extremely boring ruins this game for me because with no wars and boring AI what is there to spice up the game?  2/10 hope that take two interactive is taking a step back to go two steps forward.

When all else fails, give all your cities to Gandhi!
...Right?
WRONG! That's not how the game works. In Civ. V, Gandhi is an evil, treacherous person who rips you off in trades and denounces you every single time you settle near him.
Setting aside that, Civilization V is a beautiful game that immerses the player through a series of thought processes. One time you're thinking about where you want your capital to be, another time you'll be thinking about how to save your capital from evil Gandhi.
What with Gandhi you may ask?
Well, I ask the same question you do.
Is Gandhi truly that bad?
The answer is yes.
And it's also yes to this game. This game is full of excitement and strategic thoughts that will keep you occupied for hours. It's a must-buy if you're a big strategy gamer. When I first saw a screenshot, I thought it was the most boringest game on Earth, just moving little troops onto little hexagons. But, when I played the demo, it immersed me in a world surrounded by a true civilization, realizing that I needed to produce pearls for my citizens or set up research agreements with others. Plus, I got to meet leaders in our past history.
I would say 10/10 but because of Gandhi making me rage all day,
9/10 :)

I know this game is quite "old", I think it came out in 2008 or something like that but not only until now I got around to playing it. Dead Space is possibly not a horror game for me, it has some jumpscares and sometimes when a new enemy appeared I kinda freaked out trying to learn how to defeat him. The game itself relies on the dismemberment of enemy limbs in order to kill them, it also features some puzzle "sections" where you need to manipulate gravity and slow down "stuff" using your stasis in order to complete a certain objective. The soundtrack really keeps up the rythm and the action of the game with some intense sections where the music pumps in. Now, as far as I'm aware the PC version was ported from the 360 version and somehow (I doubt it's just me) they forgot to get rid of the mouse acceleration and smoothing which really annoyed me quite some times but once you get used to it, it's all good. Now, for me, the strongest point of Dead Space has to be the story, it's kinda "unique" per say and I really dig into these sort of religion fanatics messing up with alien tech. Another thing I must say is that the developers really put alot of effort into making the game world "realistic", across the USG Ishimura you'll find various advertising panels some of which are different and I feel like those small additions to the world design really make it unique and engaging. I believe I have nothing else to say about Dead Space besides telling you to go give it a try if you haven't played or beated it yet.

I've always been a fan of Soth Park ever since I was a little kid. The over the top lines and jokes that make fun of current events and everything else in the world are great! This game looks exactly like you're in the tv show. You get to create your own character and play through a skyrim meets game of thrones world with all of that southpark humor we know thrown in. Great writing, and all of the companions and characters throughout the game make hilarious comments as you play. I love the combat system, it's turn based but throws in mouse clicks for blocking and extra attacks as well as button mashing and random key pressing for special abilities (keeps the combat kind of fresh rather than just taking a turn). I love the story line as well, it is new and inventive while at the same time making fun of other common story lines in todays games and tv shows. The stick of truth is one of the few games where I actually want to find all the secrets and earn all the achievements where it doesnt feel like a chore or get boring, and it has tons of replayability. My only small dislikes are how short it is for an RPG (roughly 12-15 hours for me) I just wish there could be more or at least a DLC. I also dislike how there are only four classes to choose from. Don't get me wrong I love all four classes and especially the new jew class, but i'd like to see a couple more. In the end this is one of my favorite games and I always come back to it if im in the mood for a good laugh and a quality casual RPG.

A must-have for PC gamers. While Half-Life 1 most certainly hasn't stood against the test of time, Half-Life 2 has aged like fine wine. Even ten years after it's release, the game looks and feels good. Playing as the mute Gordon Freeman, who arrives off the train in City 17, discovers that the city has been taken over by a force only known as the Combine. Shortly after, he meets the protagonists of the game. If I have to make a complaint, it's that none of the characters in Half-Life 2 besides Gordon and the Gman were in Half-Life 1, so you're just supposed to assume that they were there during the Black Mesa incident. To fully understand the story of Half-Life 1, all you have to do is watch the first ten minutes and the last five minutes of the game. I suggest that you skip straight to this one, and if you really want to pick up Half-Life 1 make sure it's less than $5.

Let's begin with the facts. The Stick of Truth is an RPG turn sed combat game with the traditional south park style 2.5D graphics, and the traditional south park concept of boundaries.
You take the role of a new kid in the neighborhood and get drawn into a town wide fantasy role-playing war. Events unfold culminating with someone getting farted on
The game takes you through a miniature open world via a central quest line, with a few other side quests as well to keep you busy. The combat is turn based, pitting you and a buddy against a wide variety of opponents, with a basic class based system allowing you to choose your style of combat such as magical or more hand to hand.
The game, as south park tends to be, is at times so far out on a limb that even the leaves don't grow there. You will encounter at some point: anal probing, anal beads, cross dressing, nudity, sex, crack, exploding farts, Jesus, living turds, completely naked government personnel, Canada, Nazi zombie aborted fetuses, and will perform abortions yourself among many other things.
The game does take a fairly loose approach to the distinction between kids at play and actual real events, but again this is in keeping with the south park style.
If you have no objection to the fairly objectionable content then you're quite likely to enjoy the game, but if you're looking at a south park game in the first place you probably are.

Through out this I am going to make a lot of comparisons to Resident Evil Remake and Alien Isolation, because I want to show you that games made 6 years BEFORE this game and 6 years AFTER this game nailed an oppressive atmosphere with nowhere near the amount of jumpscares as this game.
The Spencer Mansion in Resident Evil Remake certainly had scripted jumpscares, the dogs through the window the second time you went through, the zombies through the window, the hunters through the windows. LOADS of windows. But, it still would have a terrifying atmosphere even without those scares. Just the fact that it gave you about a magazine for every 3 zombies and that you could kill about 2 zombies with 1 magazine meant that you had to find your way around zombies, which meant dodging around them or taking a longer but safer route around the mansion. THAT is survival horror.
But Dead Space, which clearly takes inspiration from Resident Evil Remake, (because what survival horror doesn't?) doesn't take things like the atmosphere. I mean sure, it has scary moments, even when enemies aren't there, but that's just because I'm afraid something will jump out and a loud musical sting will play. I'm not scared of the ship, or the monsters, I'm scared of the musicians slamming there hands down on the piano again.
Alien Isolation, a game that came out in 2014, last year, go 'it'. How to do survival horror without unscripted jumpscares, and having an oppressive atmosphere. The bit when you walk through the synthetic bay, where all the dying 'Working Joe's' go to die. You walk through a corridor with about 10 'Working Joe's' standing idol, and you just know that if you turn your back they'll throttle you, but they don't until 10 minutes later when the game throws 8 shotgun shells, 3 flares, 2 medkits and 6 revolver bullets at you, but that's besides the point.
I do not think that this is a bad game, I just don't think it's a good one either. It takes the claustrophobia and 'survival horror' from RE:R and A:I but they seem a lot clumsier here. Sure you may love this game, but I'll stick with the good stuff until EA get this right the fourth time round.

It is a part of the game that should have been entirely optional for crap like pictures of characters and costumes and other perks, but not a requirement.
2. The ending is just pure crap. I really shouldn't have been surprised by a company that actually kills Batman villians. I won't give spoilers for the endling, but it was a let down. I realize that Rocksteady and DC have presented this as a new story based upon the comics, but that statement that is even more crap. They use all of the actual comic book lore but decide to do something radical like kill a character or other moves that are clearly meant to drive sales and then chalk it up to that lame excuse.

It is a rip-off of an existing Batman comic book character  with a new name and outfit attempting to sell it as something new but pretty much reverts it all back to the comic book story as it plays out.
Other than those three points, the rest of the game play, characters, missions and story are amazing with pretty awesome graphics and sound. Just be ready for a game that takes you on an awesome ride only to end it with disappointment.

The recent negative review surge made me uneasy about purchasing the game. Lucky it just came out on a free weekend so I got to try it. I have not played KF1 but have played other TripWire games extensively and have always enjoyed them. Overall, this is yet another game which I plan on purchasing and enjoying from TripWire. I've gone through and read the reviews and most of them appear to be either out data or harsh critics of the developers and not the game.
The game is quite fast pace and combat is pretty smooth. There is a simple HUD with no crosshair on the screen for hip aiming. All hip fire needs to be estimated, being a TripWire game this wasnt surprising to me. There are quite a few maps, I have clocked about 6 hours as of this review and have only played on several but they seem well though out and each offers different stratagies. Each class is unique and fun to play, medic is my favorite. Though the weapon selection for class specific weapons seems a bit limited. For instance there are only 3 medic weapons to choose from. So in terms of weapon selection the game could be expanded. There are many types of mobs but some of them seem to have over lapping roles like cysts and clots. Stalkers always scare the crap out of me as they are invisible. The game throws alot of mobs at you during waves and you can easily get overwelhmed even on normal difficulty. Where most of my games fail at is the boss fight. I've played 10 games and only have beaten 2 on normal. That speaks for the difficulty.
I recommend this game and give it an 8/10. It has potential and lots of room to grow... I just hope the negative reviews about the company are wrong.

Solid story-telling for anyone who likes turn-based adventures in a role-playing setting. The initial campaign has a fairly straight-forward story with enough flexibility to tackle the minor obstacles to proceed through it in any class or skill-set. It is fairly short and there is minimal deviation from the main plotline. If you are looking for random encounters, tons of sidequests and are all about the loot, this game isn't for you. You only get what you need with a litle room for extras as precaution in terms of item management. As it should be in this game's universe.
The follow-up, Dragonfall, improves upon the the base game considerably. The dialogue is much more thought-out, the characters are fleshed-out better and unique, and there are enough curveballs in the story and variations in your strategy to keep it fresh. It's a bit longer than the original story and the items/equipment/gear options are expanded for the more customized runner. If you are curious about the Shadowrun Universe, this is a great place to start. I pre-ordered before launch, being an original fan of the snes( which is what this game is a spiritual successor to )and genesis versions, so as much as I personally have no problem giving money to this developer at full price, I would still recommend picking up on a sale, and getting the original and the Dragonfall together. This universe was born in the 1980's when pen&paper rpgs were popular, and it's content was ahead of it's time. This is where the "original" Matrix came from.

To get straight to the point: Half Life 2 isn't nearly as good as the original.
The updated graphics and physics engine are nice and all, but when you get right down to it HL2 simply isn't as much fun as its predecessor, even if it is less exhausting. While I never had the problems with limited resources I had in the original, I DID get Opposing Force's annoying habit of constantly introducing new gimmicks that they spend the next half hour showcasing before getting bored and moving on.
Interestingly enough, the other biggest problem I had with the game was the opposite of my issues with Opposing Force: it's too damned easy. Once you get into the swing of things, the combat grows so easy it boils down to white noise, to the point where I was literally no longer paying attention to the fights, just wading forward as an unstoppable juggernaut, which just led me to come to dislike Gordan Freeman's inexplicable supersoldier qualities. In the first game your successes felt like a combination of dumb luck, massive firepower, and the fact that you were the only person in the story who happened to be wearing their powered armor at the time. Here, everyone else just seems massively incompetent. The biggest exception to the boredom factor is just before the finale in the Citadel, where you're fighting through the bombed-out streets of the city with the tripods from War of the Worlds bearing down on you, proving to be the only enemies in the entire game worthy of your attention.
Other than the aforementioned tripods, the Combine are a pretty dull lot though. HL1 had a menagrie of alien invaders, marines who have no qualms about digging their heels in and throwing tanks and machine gun bunkers at you, and Black Ops ninjas, but the Combine mooks just seem to boil down to "gas mask wearing SWAT teams from space" and the occasional alien helicopter. The other aliens have also been cut down to headcrabs/zombies, barnacles, and antlions, which are the only totally new beastie in the game and quickly wear out their welcome as they spend an entire two levels in a row swarming you.
Finally, my list of criticisms isn't complete without mentioning the ♥♥♥♥ing vehicle sections. Take all the boring gunfights that fade into irrelevence, then speed them up and throw in really clumsy controls, and occasionally stop it with the grace of an eight track to get out and unlock a door. They're boring and tedious and full of loud noises that ultimately don't mean a damn thing.
The new engine is pretty nice though, I can see why  a lot of people make games with it.

Having seen the backlash this game received on it's initial launch, I was skeptical to pick it up after it's release in October; especially given that I was running a GTX 760 Ti (OEM) at the time and most of the players leveling complaints had tech in the range of the 900s series.
So, 9 months after launch, with one new GTX 970, and a conveniently timed midweek sale, I tenatively picked up the title to see if it had finally been patched into a stable state, or still as bad as people claimed.
To summurize all my thoughts  before I get detailed: Eh, it works. (EDIT: Since the time of my initial writing, the game has crashed twice, both after using the Batmobile for an extended period of time. Buyer be warned)
During the first few start ups, NVIDIA GeForce Experience refused to acknowledge the game was on my harddrive, and the game itself was posting warnings stating my GPU drivers were out of date and needed to upgraded (something I had doubled checked was done before I had attempted to start it). Undetered, I ran through the graphics options to try and optimize it manually. Right out the gate, the game set itself to it's maximum settings minus a few extra features like ehanced rain and smoke that eat through RAM. Also of note, the game now has a fps selector as well (I keep it at 30fps, I like the cinematic look over smooth).
Now for the game proper, framerate stayed visably stable through my playthrough, save one expectional dip during the now nitorious segment where you call in the Batmobile for the first time. Controls should be familiar to veterans of the series, with combat being more fluid and responsive than the previous entries. The Batmobile is a bit tricky to maneuver at times and the puzzle where you have to rev the engine to power up the generator is a nightmare to do on a keyboard where pressure sensitve buttons aren't a thing. But fortunately you can, for the most part, ditch the vehicle for the classic gliding.
So before I knew it, 2 hours of gameplay had come and gone, and one last question remained: would I recommend the game? I'd say yes. The frame rate issues look nothing like what I saw during the intial release, and the series of patches seem to have hammered the game into a stable state. If you've got the hardware (and maybe a sale going on), and you've enjoyed the previous 3 games, consider picking this up. At its worse, you can ask Steam for a refund.

Half-Life 2 is the sequel to Half-Life,the game by Valve that pretty much wrote the rules for FPSs way back in 1998.
I haven't played very much of this game myself,but I can guarantee that anyone who plays it will end up loving this game,even those that didn't play HL1 before playing this game(like me).
The plot: Gordon Freeman is brought out of stasis by the G-Man,who inserts him in a train arriving at the fictitous City 17,which was taken over by Combine forces.  He eludes the Combine forces and meets Alyx and Barney,and joins the Lambda Resistance.  He gets to Dr. Kleiner's lab and assists them in attempting to get a teleporter to teleport him and Alyx to Dr. Eli Vance's lab. The teleportation fails,and he goes through City 17 on foot to get to Eli's lab.  He arrives at Black Mesa East and meets up with Eli, where he is captured and taken to a combine prison,Nova Prospekt.  Gordon goes through a zombie infested town named Ravenholm and is given a Dune Buggy,which he uses to travel to Nova Prospekt.  Eli,Alyx,and Gordon escape,the combine teleporter they used exploding in the process.  Gordon and Alyx learn they were in a "slow teleport"during which a week has passed. In their absence,the Resistance mobilized against the combine, turning City 17 into a battleground. South™ Park™: The™ Stick™ of™ Truth™ (tm.)™ is one of the best licensed-property games I have ever played, though it's not without its faults.
Let's start with the good stuff. For fans of the show, it's hard to imagine a better use of the license. The designers didn't play it safe and crap out a generic game just to cash in. They took a great hook that was already built into the show (the kids of South Park™ live role-playing RPG-style) and ran with it. This is not a hard-core 100+ hour type of RPG, nor should it have been. Instead, it employs a more simplified style that requires timed button presses for attacks and defense. As a reference point, the gameplay is very similar to the "Mario & Luigi"™ RPGs. This is not only a very good thing, but it also perfectly serves the source material. So while the "RPG" aspects of the game are not particularly hardcore, there is just enough depth to keep it (mostly) interesting throughout. What really take the game to a higher level are the production values. The game itself looks and sounds exactly like the newer HD episodes of the series. Just about every character you could possibly care about makes an appearance, and they're all voiced and written exactly as you would expect. Absolutely no corners were cut in this department - the game really makes you feel as if you are in South Park™, interacting with its characters. The story is also exactly what you would expect out of South Park™. Although the basic premise is very simple - the boys fighting over an ordinary stick™ - the story ultimately progresses in ways you could never have imagined (or perhaps you can, if you've watched enough of the series over the years). The dialogue and voice acting are excellent, and there are plenty of laugh-out-loud moments from beginning to end. There are also tons of obscure references and cameos throughout, seemingly for no other purpose than to make the most hard-core fans chuckle. The whole game really is just a huge South Park™ love fest. In terms of difficulty, the default setting is fine, if a bit on the easy side. If you want more (or less) of a challenge, you can change the difficulty at any point, which is a great feature that should allow anyone to complete it if they put in the time.
Unfortunately, along with all of the things that make the game good, there are also a few low points. Several sections involve slightly complicated "quick time events" (not exactly in the traditional sense, but used here for lack of a better term). Setting aside the fact that these sections seem randomly out of place in an otherwise good game, the real issue is that they just aren't implemented well. The tutorials for each action are executed poorly, which can be frustrating if you don't pick up on what the game is asking you to do, exactly. Another low point comes towards the latter portion of the game, which involves a series of "fetch-quests". While I am sure the intent of this section was to lampoon this tired video game trope, they succeeded a little too much, as it started to get fairly tedious. It also didn't help that at this point in the game, I had already maxed out my character's level, so there was really nothing else to strive for, in an "RPG" sense. It would have been nice if there was no level cap, with enemies scaled to your strength (or something along those lines). Lastly, and this is just a pet peeve of mine, but apparently there are several collectibles that can be missed if you don't get them the first time through - just a warning to those who enjoy collecting things or 100%-ing games.
Overall, my annoyances with the game are fairly minor in comparison to all of the things I enjoyed. If you are a huge South Park™ fan, I think this is a no-brainer. The amount of care that went into making it is readily apparent, and worthy of your money (at least, now that it's only $40 - the original $60 price point was way too much). In terms of length, it's hard for me to estimate, but I would say it will probably take you anywhere from 11-18 hours, depending on how deliberate/OCD you are. It's really hard for me to imagine a South Park™ game ever being done better than this. Needless to say, non-fans should stay away. But for anyone else (assuming you can get into the simple RPG gameplay), it's definitely worth checking out at some point.

Dead Space is one of the best survival horror games of the generation. It's tense, dark, tells its story well (even moreso if you seek out the digital comics that serve as a prelude), and has great combat and controls.
But this is a terrible port.
Even at lowest settings, it's too bright. The framerate is locked at 30 by default. You can unlock it by turning off in-game vsync and then forcing vsync via your graphics card, but this causes the controls to be far too twitchy. Damage seems to scale with framerate, too. Limbs that can be shorn with one shot at 30 fps will take three or four at 60 fps. And if you leave it at 30 fps, the controls feel slow and laggy. I compared it with the Xbox 360 version, which also runs at 30 fps, and that version feels perfect.
If you have no other way to play this excellent game, I guess this will do. But play it on a console rather than on PC if you have any means of doing so.

A fine example of survival horror going more modern, and the only creation in the Dead Space... franchise (ugh)... that had even a shred of dignity or self-respect.
You're better off playing just this one and pretending the rest of those things with the Dead Space logo on it don't exist, for the sake of avoiding a whole bunch of retardation. This is the only one that knew what it was doing. The rest of the franchise went off the deep end and totally lost its touch, forgetting who and what it was and what made it good, and exist solely for the money. At the cost of the soul of the original. The first comic was pretty decent, but everything else got EA'd, for sure.
But back to the actual review: I love that all the HUD is in the game world itself. That, and the game design all around, lends itself well in being atmospheric and immersive. And the curb stomp button. Ah, the curb stomp button. And the slow-motion stasis and telekinesis powers are really cool too. Also, really original and varied weapons that bring different strategies to the dismemberment of your zombie/alien/mutant enemies (my favorite is the Ripper). And that really is just a brilliant game mechanic; you have to literally tear your enemies apart, limb by limb, in order to kill them in this game. This is Gore: The Game right here, folks!
This game stands alone as the Dead Space-iest Dead Space. Quite solid all around, as a third-person shooter and as a survival horror, and definitely worth checking out.

And what a world Valve has created. The dystopian aesthetic feels epic and scope, but it is up to the player as to how to approach it. One thing I should mention about Dead Space is it's a very polished game. The graphics and engine still hold up relatively well, and the lack of heads up display is fairly immersive. At the very least Dead Space still retains good value for money to this day, and if you enjoyed Resident Evil 4 this will appeal to you greatly.

Ever wanted to know what fighting alien invaders would REALLY be like? The answer is "pretty damned suicidal", at least in the beginning when their tech outclasses the hell outta you. Then later it's "OH ♥♥♥♥ THIS IS A NIGHTMARE" when you find they can psionically mind control and panic your squad into killing each other.
Oh but it's not hopeless, seriously. :P You just have to be really careful about how much you expose your guys to danger, plan your gambits well, expect SOME losses (or be a wuss and reload old saves, repeatedly), and exploit recovered alien tech for your own devices - and survival.
Play this if you really want to strategize. If you just want to shoot up aliens without hindrance, go play Duke Nukem or something, seriously, sheesh. But that said it's got a perfect balance between pre-planning and just getting on with the damned game, so don't worry that base and financial management will suck up gobs of time like it did in the original game (if any of you are even old enough to know or care about it).

A game that is not afraid of crushing your resolve (or strengthening it for that matter) with one bad decision. I love this game for the difficulty factor and its contrast to most games released at around the same time. It is a top down strategy game that pits you against a highly advanced alien race invading Earth. The game has a tremendous atmosphere of doom and effectively emphasizes you alone control the strategy for humanity's survival. The pace is aggresive as you hastily choose what technology to research which can impact your team's performance on the field (armor, weapons, and fighter aircraft, all of which are important)
The customization is brilliant, allowing you to recruit new soliders, send them on missions, level them up, change physical appearance, voices, names, and hybrid classes (although limited) if you so choose. You form an attachment with your favorite squad members that are lucky enough to survive for a few missions and it is devistating when they get killed. Playing this game with Ironman (Limited saving capabilites) is an absolute blast and really stresses acting tactically on and off the battlefield.
The unshackled AI in this game can be mercilessly cruel and difficult. When you are successful at a mission it really does feel like an acomplishment, as opposed to give-me achievements for playing normally.

The base game has flaws and is very disappointing coming from a fan of the Genesis game.  However, the combat is nice and the fan made modules make this absolutely worth the price.  Add in the soon to be released Berlin DLC that they are saying includes a more sandbox style storyline and things are really looking up for this game.
Fans of Turn Based RPG tactical combat and/or RPGs in a cyberpunk setting should really consider giving this a try.

This retro-styled game is extremely addictive!  It's a rather difficult platform shooter, a bit like if "The Bindinc of Isaac" were reimagined as a platformer.  You can choose from about a dozen classes, many of which you must unlock through gameplay challenges, and each one has completely different attacks and abilities.
Killing enemies gives you money, which you then use to unlock chests containing a huge variety of items that enhance your character in various ways.  Some may boost your attacking power, others give you defenses or mobility, and a few rare items have unique effects like stopping time, flying, or increasing the money you get from kills.  There are lots of secrets and remote areas only accessible with certain characters, or jetpacks, or other combinations of items, so there's always something cool to discover with each random playthrough.
The enemies get stronger and more numerous as time passes, so the action starts off easy then ramps up to insane fights with you kiting nearly 100 enemies, each with their own unique attacks and behaviours.
You will die.  You will learn.  You will get ridiculously good.  You will read the wiki.  And you will have a RIOT playing it.

I enjoy this game immensely.  It was difficult to get playability information for various machines, so I'll list what I have:
Alienware Alpha
i3 processor
Windows 8.1
5400 RPM HDD (that's the hard drive if anyone didn't know)
16 GB RAM
It initially had horrid display (couldn't see past white flare) so I turned the resolution down to the very lowest, and then it ran.  Hardcore PC gamers would consider it shoddy display, but I'm not picky, and it compares well enough to the XBOX 360 I'm used to.  Point being, it works.
Things to note, if you haven't researched:
Windows 10 is said to need 12 GB of RAM, at least, to play well.
Windows 7 is said to have issues with extended play.
i3 is not the best processor out there, many people recommend i5 for gaming.  So that's impressive.
5400 HDD is neither solid-state, nor 7200.  It's not a very fast drive.  Also impressive.

Proper Review:
South Park: The Stick of Truth is an RPG by Obsidian Entertainment. Its story, script and art style are all true to the show, unsurprising seeing as how the game was written and directed by South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone.
It is obvious that Obsidian Entertainment have played a lot of Paper Mario. Everything in this game, from the timing-spiced turn-based combat system to the battle companions to the interactive world navigation to the equipment upgrades to the cutting injokes about the game itself all bear the halmarks of Intelligent Systems' Mario RPGs. Replace the South Park characters with Mario characters and clean up the filth and this could be a Paper Mario game.
The story sparkles with political satire, unashamedly coarse humour and enough references to make fanboys giggle like lunatics. The script, as well as the art style and animation, make the player feel like they are a part of the show. Games such as Skyrim are made fun of to rib-tickling effect, and the story itself could easily be a story arc in the show.
As a fan of RPGs, I appreciated all the injokes poking fun at RPG staples, such as turn-based battles, Power Points, world exploration and boss battles. These injokes would seem obnoxious if the game was rubbish (it has happened before), but South Park: The Stick of Truth is really fun to play. Taking cues from Paper Mario, your attacks in battle can be powered up with well-timed mouse clicks and keyboard inputs, and you are supported in battle by one of five potential 'buddies', each with their own special attacks. The timing-based attack system means that the combat rarely gets boring, to the point where I actively sought out battles for the fun of it. I found a certain buddy to be somewhat overpowered compared to the others, but this is a very minor criticism.
The sound design is also very good in this game. The music is exceptional, and the audio feedback from attacking and defending is very pleasing. The buddy characters' voice samples, performed by Parker and Stone, are also very entertaining, as they react authentically to the things you do (mostly your farts).
Some have questioned the pricetag of this game, arguing that $60, or your regional equivalent, is too much for a game that lasts "only" about 15 hours. Personally, I hate this mindset. I agree with Totalbiscuit that the games we get these days ought to cost upwards of $100 (or your... oh, you get the idea) on launch, and we are incredibly lucky to get them at the prices we do. I got this game for £40 and loved every minute of it, so I feel that it was worth the money. I can not deny that the cost may seem unjustifiable to some, so you should take that into consideration if you are looking to purchase this game. If you are really bothered by it, wait for the game to go on sale. Also, I encountered a strange bug that sometimes caused my game and sound to start stuttering when I loaded my save file, This fixed itself after several relaunches, but it was annoying when it did happen. I do not know what caused the stuttering, but you should be wary of it.
Overall, South Park: The Stick of Truth is a highly enjoyable game with few flaws. It may seem too easy for  its demographic but if you are looking for an authentic South Park gaming experience, look no further than this game. Go forth, young warrior, on your quest to become... cool.
Good Points:
Excellent story, script and sound
Enjoyable, addictive combat system
Flexible equipment and upgrade system allowing you to tailor your character to suit your play style
Plenty of fun side quests to fill in the time
A goldmine of references
As authentic a South Park experience as you can get
Bad Points:
A little too easy for RPG veterans
An annoying, unexplained bug that occasionally causes the game to stutter upon loading
A certain Jew is a little overpowered
Could have been longer (that's what she said)
May seem too expensive for some

This retro-styled game is extremely addictive!  It's a rather difficult platform shooter, a bit like if "The Bindinc of Isaac" were reimagined as a platformer.  You can choose from about a dozen classes, many of which you must unlock through gameplay challenges, and each one has completely different attacks and abilities.
Killing enemies gives you money, which you then use to unlock chests containing a huge variety of items that enhance your character in various ways.  Some may boost your attacking power, others give you defenses or mobility, and a few rare items have unique effects like stopping time, flying, or increasing the money you get from kills.  There are lots of secrets and remote areas only accessible with certain characters, or jetpacks, or other combinations of items, so there's always something cool to discover with each random playthrough.
The enemies get stronger and more numerous as time passes, so the action starts off easy then ramps up to insane fights with you kiting nearly 100 enemies, each with their own unique attacks and behaviours.
You will die.  You will learn.  You will get ridiculously good.  You will read the wiki.  And you will have a RIOT playing it.

If you're debating buying this game, just do it. This is one of the most innovative and amazing games out there. Made in 2004, but still has amazing graphics and physics, possibly even better than some of the newer games being developed today.

Anyone who is a fan of the original series (XCOM, Terror From the Deep) will find this an awesome reboot. The squad size has been cut down to 5 which may seem like a huge departure from the original but it actually makes you re-think your tactics. Add to that the squad members having defined archetypes (Assault, Sniper, Support, Psionic and Heavy). Each has a skill tree that has minor depth to it where you can choose traits every time your soldier ranks up.
Tactics haven't changed much except that soldiers take cover automatically when you move next to it. Cover does get damaged and will disappear when it takes enough pounding. Research is detailed and captures the spirit of the original as well as manufacturing.
The game does have a storyline and storyline-based objectives that further the story-missions. This addition makes the game a bit more immersive.
The Funding aspect from the original is still present.♥♥♥♥♥♥off countries by not helping them with invasions, abductions or ignoring UFO's that traverse their airspace will result in panic, chaos and ultimately withdrawl of funds from that country. Added to the Funding aspect is bonuses from each country depending on where you choose to base your HQ out of. You also launch satellites (replacing the radar from the previous game) which helps to keep panic down. More satellite coverage also reduces abduciton missions over that country. Also at the end of the month you gain in addition to money either scientists or engineers or both depending on your rating and difficulty.
All in all the spirit of XCOM has been resurrected in this reboot and I highly recommend this game.
PS: There is a multiplayer mode where you go head to head Earthlings vs. Aliens. Super-awesome!

8/10: Likely the best South Park game ever made, though it's simple as RPG's go
I was so excited when this was announced, and starting this game up to see that the graphics were spot-on with the show got me raring to go on my adventure. Finding out Butters was my first new friend in town was just the cherry on top. Even being placed in the role of "silent protagonist" felt funny again simply because of how often South Park pokes fun at conventional RPG tropes over the course of the game.
I ended up playing through the game three times. While I would like to say it's because it's so amazingly well done and fun that I just had to replay it a few times, but to be honest a lot of it was because I'm a completionist and finding every friend you can make in South Park is actually FRUSTRATINGLY tough. This is especially so since it depends on you completing a SEPARATE collection of Chinpokomon, BOTH of which can be missed out on by overlooking them in temporarily available areas! That, and playing through it once felt pretty fast.
Plus, the combat system started wearing thin towards the end of the first playthrough since it often just came down to using your favorite super move as quickly and frequently as possible. Beyond that, prioritizing PP recuperation and ongoing damage (broken bottle ftw) helped me stroll through the game with minimal challenge.
Stick of Truth is full of great references though, whether it's the classic aliens or Hasselhoff or crab people. Honestly, after seein some of the concept art, I wish the nighttime scenarios were more robust. Still, there's no denying that The Stick of Truth allowed me to happily roleplay alongside the cast and characters of South Park on one of their insane adventures.

So, ignoring the whole massive poor condition of the port, I'll quickly say this
It worked for me, BUT IT MAY NOT WORK FOR YOU.
It's not even a question of PC quality, I know people with better PCs who have been unable to play it, and my PC is kinda meddling at best. A 3.4Ghz AMD and Nvidea GTX 770, 6 GB of ram.

However I'd look at other reviews and see what people with a more similar PC to you managed before you buy it, it's almost impossible to say if it'll run for you regardless of your PC.
So for reviewing the game, I'm going to Judge it on the game itself, the port quality is abominable for most, but the game itself is exactly the high quality you'd expect, which makes it's porting woes all the more poignant.
So as for the game. The story has an amazing cinematic approach, sprawling through it's own Arkham universe within the Batman series, with plenty of details and nods to it's lore. The story itself has many twists as you track down the main antagonists and cleverly uses Joker as a way of delivering an internal monologue, that would seem out of place if Batman himself delivered it. With Scarecrow himself being one of the main antagonists, some of the clever twists and techniques we saw in Arkham Asylum come to the fore, driving various plot points and characters and themes towards you, in clever ways.
The gameplay barely improves much upon what you saw in Arkham city or Origins though which is a negative, Rocksteady have previously shown us they're so capable of introducing new mechanics to us, yes there are more characters to play as, and the batmobile. But maybe Arkham city spoiled us, the huge advancements that made Arkham city so amazing are dulled by the time this one rolled around. The Batmobile segments show plenty of potential, which they attempt to show, but it's so simple and repetitive, it doesn't compete with the gameplay which was already here from the prequels.
They added crime map packs to extend the amazing challenge modes and score trials that previous games did, but I feel like there wasn't enough in the base game, there's so much in Gotham, but very little is used outside the main story mode.
I could complain that unlike Arkham city, the other characters were reduced to living out their side stories outside the main story rather than spliced in to create a larger narrative within the game.
The animations and graphics are top quality, but with the condition of the PC port this is a negative, experiencing the vast quality originally given to the game on the PC is (as far as I know) borderline impossible.
There's a lot in this game to justify retail price in full, the problem is the port condition. And it's impossible to recommend because there's no way to tell if anyone can run it, even with a better PC than mine, it has mixed results at best. WB has handled this quite poorly, and if the port was just left to Rocksteady with a larger time frame I'm sure this controversial release would be entirely positive besides the lack of true innovation that Rocksteady has shown before in previous iterations of this sequel. At first I was a bit sad knowing this was Rocksteady ending the series but this game proves they need something new to create something much better.
Overall, IF (big if) this game runs for you, you will be getting your money's worth but it's a huge gamble depending on the price you get it. The game is brilliant and packed with effort and love, and besides a few downfalls like the driving aspect which never got a true chance to prove itself (besides some truly excellent racing puzzles) and the combat reaching it's absolute peak of creativity, and suffering from repetition. It's an excellent game.

As a longtime Killing Floor player, I was a little skeptical of a sequel.
As we all know, sequels don't always live up to their original versions, but I must say that there are distinct improvements on the original Killing Floor in this version.
For one, the graphics are a huge improvement over the original. Zed animations and overall appearance is greatly improved and gameplay in general is much better.
The interface changes were the only thing that kind of "threw me". It's not a bad interface, don't get me wrong, but for someone like me, that's played the original for years, this new interface took a little getting used to.
I did like the "Basic Training" feature, it gives you a chance to get a 'feel' for the new interface and game mechanics without fear of getting "whacked" in a real match. It's well worth doing a couple of times and if you complete "Basic Training" there is a reward:
If you are a Killing Floor fan, I don't think you will find this version a disappointment at all, except for the fact that the Patriarch is missing in the base game. I believe there is a DLC that brings him back, but I feel this is the only "real" screw-up that Tripwire has with this version.
: While I still recommend this game, I have to point out that there is currently no way to run a listenserver on a LAN for this game. If you want to play with your friends, you will basically have to create a public match. That's right, unless you want to go through the "headaches" of downloading the dedicated server files and configuring them, you cannot play a private online or LAN game.
: With the second F2P weekend coming to an end, my attitude toward this game hasn't changed, and neither has the inability to make and play a LAN game without having to configure a dedicated server.
This, in my opinion, is a deal-breaker.
Part of the reason why most people liked the first Killing Floor was the ability to create your own matches without having to configure a full-blown dedicated server. Tripwire has "screwed the pooch" with regards to this functionality with Killing Floor 2.
While I still think it is an improvement over the first Killing Floor, it still leaves much to be desired in the LAN play department. If it wasn't for this, I'd have bought this game already, without it, I seriously doubt that I will buy it.
Sorry Tripwire, but if you can find it in your "heart" to restore the LAN functionality that Killing Floor has, I can guarantee that at least 6 people that I know, including myself, will be buying this game immediately, but not without the old LAN functionality of Killing Floor...

This was a game I thought for sure I wouldn't be caught up in.
I received this as a gift from a friend and upon playing it - it reminded me of Liero from back in the day due to the game mechanics and pixelation sort of graphics. But I got caught in a concept which the game follows. I was beaking my buddy the whole time about power ups and how they were nice in this game but it was lacking physical power-Ups like double jump's. Low and behold two minutes later I get two double jump power ups and my guy is literally jumping across the map. At that point I was in.
The game play itself is good. The concept is you get one life, you run through the levels killing enemies first and fore most to get money to therefore in turn open these chests or "luck" statues for power Ups or items. As you kill you gain experience to level up. Power ups range from being able to double jump, to jumping further, to shooting faster, to shooting through everyone every fourth shot, cool-down time faster, every time you shoot maybe something explodes... literally I don't have enough space in this review to write every single power up out. The player starts with a "commando" character unit first and as you progress throughout the game or the more you play, the more character units you unlock. Every character has their set abilities (four of them) that cannot change but every character has different abilities. Items also have a cool down period just like the weapon abilities characters have, and the nice thing about items is that they are REUSABLE! What makes the game even better is that there is local multiplayer enabled (fakin' rights bud) and online multiplayer (ohhhhh faaakk yeah bud). So I definitely have to give it up to the guy who made this game because he tried thinking of it all. Oh yeah.... and it's controller supported :) (xbox controller as well as Logitech gamepad).
Graphics are graphics as you can see in the preview of the game. To me they look like old Liero touch up's which is perfectly fine but my friend put it better : "This game reminds me of playing the original nintendo". After he said that - that's pretty much what I see now. The impact effects, the multitude of varying enemies with each their own power or attack and health, the backgrounds, the different levels all are nice and easy on the eyes, maybe even appealing to some.
So I've talked quite a bit about this game, and mostly positive as it rightly is. Does it lack anything? Maybe for some. After unlocking a handful of characters I have to ask myself after being able to play for an hour every time I start a new game, what am I playing for? My stats aren't getting saved (I'm not sure if it's supposed to be saved every time you die or every time you simply start up the game) which sort of is irritating considering people like to see their stats. The game pretense is nice, it's all good but there is just that something more missing. Being able to build buildings in game? Maybe perhaps an RPG element where you can choose certain abilities? I think if this game had steam work shop or maybe some free add-ons to add to the game it would be perfect.
I really want to give it my standard rating of 8 which I consider a rating of a good game, however I will have to give it a
RATING 7.1/10.
I feel the rating is fair because once you play this enough, you'll start wondering where is the motivation to play again. Unless of course a friend comes over or wants to play.

Anyone who is a fan of the original series (XCOM, Terror From the Deep) will find this an awesome reboot. The squad size has been cut down to 5 which may seem like a huge departure from the original but it actually makes you re-think your tactics. Add to that the squad members having defined archetypes (Assault, Sniper, Support, Psionic and Heavy). Each has a skill tree that has minor depth to it where you can choose traits every time your soldier ranks up.
Tactics haven't changed much except that soldiers take cover automatically when you move next to it. Cover does get damaged and will disappear when it takes enough pounding. Research is detailed and captures the spirit of the original as well as manufacturing.
The game does have a storyline and storyline-based objectives that further the story-missions. This addition makes the game a bit more immersive.
The Funding aspect from the original is still present.♥♥♥♥♥♥off countries by not helping them with invasions, abductions or ignoring UFO's that traverse their airspace will result in panic, chaos and ultimately withdrawl of funds from that country. Added to the Funding aspect is bonuses from each country depending on where you choose to base your HQ out of. You also launch satellites (replacing the radar from the previous game) which helps to keep panic down. More satellite coverage also reduces abduciton missions over that country. Also at the end of the month you gain in addition to money either scientists or engineers or both depending on your rating and difficulty.
All in all the spirit of XCOM has been resurrected in this reboot and I highly recommend this game.
PS: There is a multiplayer mode where you go head to head Earthlings vs. Aliens. Super-awesome!

Now on with the review. I've graded each section with a letter grade if you just want to skim. And there's a TL;DR summary at the end. :)
So you have all heard about the
problems with this game. Yes; lots of people can't run this game on their computers, and I say that's a terrible shame, because I really enjoyed playing this game myself! This review is focusing on the quality of the game itself assuming your system can run it. Mine could, with only 1 or 2 environments where I noticed any significant lag, but not bad enough that I couldn't complete the game. Yes, shame on WB for how they handled this game, but this review is about my experiences with this game, not on how I feel about how WB should treat PC gamers. OK. We cool? Good.
Along with the other games in the series, this game delivers in a big way! The
is excellent. I think this game has one of the best stories of all of the Arkham Games. And the voice acting and character development is excellent as always. This game drew me in early and kept me invested in the story through to the end. I even decided to 100% complete the game, which I rarely ever do with games. My one minor complaint with the story in this game was that the Arkham Knight's identity was too obvious, but it did fit the story pretty well, so it wasn't too much of an issue for me.
, Gotham has never looked better! The environments are excellent, vibrant, and surprisingly well varied for a Batman game without losing the dark atmosphere surrounding the Dark Knight. The sound in this game, including the music and the sound effects, was truly exceptional. When you are blowing up militia tanks with the Batmobile, you can practically feel the impact of each blast. And taking down Gotham's criminals in hand-to-hand combat has never felt more real.
The only point where I was a little disappointed was with
. It's
, but compared to Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, it wasn't anything special. The Batmobile was done very well, and I had no problems with its controls, but the developers used it way too often. The boss fights were the most disappointing thing in this game. There were a few shining points, for instance, the part when you defeat Scarecrow and the final battle with the Riddler, but there were some characters that deserved a much better boss battle. Without spoiling anything, I was
upset that Rocksteady made one character's boss battle a tank fight, which was far too easy and didn't fit the character at all. Also, while I liked the final fight with the Riddler, collecting ALL the Riddler trophies and solving all the riddles got tedious  once I had completed the rest of the game. I'd still recommend completing the story mode 100% (they give you an additional cutscene at the end that makes it worth it), but be prepared for a lot of frustration getting ALL of the riddles. Now on with the review. I've graded each section with a letter grade if you just want to skim. And there's a TL;DR summary at the end. :)
So you have all heard about the
problems with this game. Yes; lots of people can't run this game on their computers, and I say that's a terrible shame, because I really enjoyed playing this game myself! This review is focusing on the quality of the game itself assuming your system can run it. Mine could, with only 1 or 2 environments where I noticed any significant lag, but not bad enough that I couldn't complete the game. Yes, shame on WB for how they handled this game, but this review is about my experiences with this game, not on how I feel about how WB should treat PC gamers. OK. We cool? Good.
Along with the other games in the series, this game delivers in a big way! The
is excellent. I think this game has one of the best stories of all of the Arkham Games. And the voice acting and character development is excellent as always. This game drew me in early and kept me invested in the story through to the end. I even decided to 100% complete the game, which I rarely ever do with games. My one minor complaint with the story in this game was that the Arkham Knight's identity was too obvious, but it did fit the story pretty well, so it wasn't too much of an issue for me.
, Gotham has never looked better! The environments are excellent, vibrant, and surprisingly well varied for a Batman game without losing the dark atmosphere surrounding the Dark Knight. The sound in this game, including the music and the sound effects, was truly exceptional. When you are blowing up militia tanks with the Batmobile, you can practically feel the impact of each blast. And taking down Gotham's criminals in hand-to-hand combat has never felt more real.
The only point where I was a little disappointed was with
. It's
, but compared to Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, it wasn't anything special. The Batmobile was done very well, and I had no problems with its controls, but the developers used it way too often. The boss fights were the most disappointing thing in this game. There were a few shining points, for instance, the part when you defeat Scarecrow and the final battle with the Riddler, but there were some characters that deserved a much better boss battle. Without spoiling anything, I was
upset that Rocksteady made one character's boss battle a tank fight, which was far too easy and didn't fit the character at all. Also, while I liked the final fight with the Riddler, collecting ALL the Riddler trophies and solving all the riddles got tedious  once I had completed the rest of the game. I'd still recommend completing the story mode 100% (they give you an additional cutscene at the end that makes it worth it), but be prepared for a lot of frustration getting ALL of the riddles. Nevertheless, that made finally punching the Riddler in his stupid face so much more satisfying! I was also disappointed that I couldn't free play as Catwoman or any other character this time around, but with the city designed for the Batmobile, I can understand why, so it wasn't too big of a deal. (But wouldn't it be awesome if Catwoman could hijack any car in free roam and turn the game into a GTA clone? Please someone make that mod. I would even buy it if you charged for it!)
This game is worth playing as part of the series. I'd definitely recommend at least playing Arkham City before this one. Arkham Asylum is still my favorite game in the series, but this game is definitely worth playing if you loved the other Arkham games (and if you have a system that can run it, of course)! That being said, buy it on sale, because WB doesn't deserve full price for how they handled the PC launch and the subsequent patches. The first character given to you when you begin the game has tight controls and a complimentary array of skills to dispatch enemies.
It's a relief that the only protagonist the player is given is so much of a jack-of-all-trades combatwise as it'll likely be the only character you can play for a while as the rest of the game's characters, despite that word feeling wrong, require unlocking.
The aesthetics are wonderful and really create a sense of hopelessness and overcoming adversity vis a vis La Mulana due to their carefully detailed sizes. You will purposefully feel tiny, alone and helpless, but, if you can get over that, you will enjoy crushing things that can sometimes near fill the screen.
Is the game difficult? At first, maybe, but you just need to understand the game's rhythm. Yes, you will be hoarded by enemies, perhaps you will die. But the game is made well enough to make you feel as though you can do more when something goes wrong as if you, the player, have messed up and can do better, each death will usually result in a reason to keep playing.
The game's speed relies on two vastly different paces. One is the adrenaline fuelled 'Hotline Miami'-esque action hero killing-spree and the other is a palate cleansing space between levels for introspection about the masses of murder achieved. All of this is set to a wonderful mellow, yet constantly present, soundtrack written and orchestrated by Chris Christodoulou. I focus quite keenly on the soundtrack of the game as, without it, I feel as though it is a necessary component to this game's unique and refreshing formula without this music, the game would not be the same.
Before you set your fingers keenly to the 'ZXCV' and arrow keys, have a listen to the game's soundtrack. You'll be hearing a lot of it.
My only gripe with this otherwise worthwhile and neatly self-contained experience is the lack of a window when alt-tabbing. Sure, you can alt-tab back in but don't expect to know the game is still running.

Now on with the review. I've graded each section with a letter grade if you just want to skim. And there's a TL;DR summary at the end. :)
So you have all heard about the
problems with this game. Yes; lots of people can't run this game on their computers, and I say that's a terrible shame, because I really enjoyed playing this game myself! This review is focusing on the quality of the game itself assuming your system can run it. Mine could, with only 1 or 2 environments where I noticed any significant lag, but not bad enough that I couldn't complete the game. Yes, shame on WB for how they handled this game, but this review is about my experiences with this game, not on how I feel about how WB should treat PC gamers. OK. We cool? Good.
Along with the other games in the series, this game delivers in a big way! The
is excellent. I think this game has one of the best stories of all of the Arkham Games. And the voice acting and character development is excellent as always. This game drew me in early and kept me invested in the story through to the end. I even decided to 100% complete the game, which I rarely ever do with games. My one minor complaint with the story in this game was that the Arkham Knight's identity was too obvious, but it did fit the story pretty well, so it wasn't too much of an issue for me.
, Gotham has never looked better! The environments are excellent, vibrant, and surprisingly well varied for a Batman game without losing the dark atmosphere surrounding the Dark Knight. The sound in this game, including the music and the sound effects, was truly exceptional. When you are blowing up militia tanks with the Batmobile, you can practically feel the impact of each blast. And taking down Gotham's criminals in hand-to-hand combat has never felt more real.
The only point where I was a little disappointed was with
. It's
, but compared to Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, it wasn't anything special. The Batmobile was done very well, and I had no problems with its controls, but the developers used it way too often. The boss fights were the most disappointing thing in this game. There were a few shining points, for instance, the part when you defeat Scarecrow and the final battle with the Riddler, but there were some characters that deserved a much better boss battle. Without spoiling anything, I was
upset that Rocksteady made one character's boss battle a tank fight, which was far too easy and didn't fit the character at all. Also, while I liked the final fight with the Riddler, collecting ALL the Riddler trophies and solving all the riddles got tedious  once I had completed the rest of the game. I'd still recommend completing the story mode 100% (they give you an additional cutscene at the end that makes it worth it), but be prepared for a lot of frustration getting ALL of the riddles. Nevertheless, that made finally punching the Riddler in his stupid face so much more satisfying! I was also disappointed that I couldn't free play as Catwoman or any other character this time around, but with the city designed for the Batmobile, I can understand why, so it wasn't too big of a deal. (But wouldn't it be awesome if Catwoman could hijack any car in free roam and turn the game into a GTA clone? Please someone make that mod. I would even buy it if you charged for it!)
This game is worth playing as part of the series. I'd definitely recommend at least playing Arkham City before this one. Arkham Asylum is still my favorite game in the series, but this game is definitely worth playing if you loved the other Arkham games (and if you have a system that can run it, of course)! That being said, buy it on sale, because WB doesn't deserve full price for how they handled the PC launch and the subsequent patches. If your PC can't run it, get a refund and try the console version. I'm sure that if you can get this game to work for you, you'll be glad you didn't miss out on it, even though it does have a few flaws.
One other note, I purchased some of the DLC for this game, but it was mostly pretty disappointing. I'd say "Season of Infamy" (4 Extra Most Wanted Villains) and "A Matter of Family" (Batgirl) are worth checking out, but the others are pretty lame (unless you want to mod the game so you can use the characters in free play).

The first character given to you when you begin the game has tight controls and a complimentary array of skills to dispatch enemies.
It's a relief that the only protagonist the player is given is so much of a jack-of-all-trades combatwise as it'll likely be the only character you can play for a while as the rest of the game's characters, despite that word feeling wrong, require unlocking.
The aesthetics are wonderful and really create a sense of hopelessness and overcoming adversity vis a vis La Mulana due to their carefully detailed sizes. You will purposefully feel tiny, alone and helpless, but, if you can get over that, you will enjoy crushing things that can sometimes near fill the screen.
Is the game difficult? At first, maybe, but you just need to understand the game's rhythm. Yes, you will be hoarded by enemies, perhaps you will die. But the game is made well enough to make you feel as though you can do more when something goes wrong as if you, the player, have messed up and can do better, each death will usually result in a reason to keep playing.
The game's speed relies on two vastly different paces. One is the adrenaline fuelled 'Hotline Miami'-esque action hero killing-spree and the other is a palate cleansing space between levels for introspection about the masses of murder achieved. All of this is set to a wonderful mellow, yet constantly present, soundtrack written and orchestrated by Chris Christodoulou. I focus quite keenly on the soundtrack of the game as, without it, I feel as though it is a necessary component to this game's unique and refreshing formula without this music, the game would not be the same.
Before you set your fingers keenly to the 'ZXCV' and arrow keys, have a listen to the game's soundtrack. You'll be hearing a lot of it.
My only gripe with this otherwise worthwhile and neatly self-contained experience is the lack of a window when alt-tabbing. Sure, you can alt-tab back in but don't expect to know the game is still running.

You better have a good rig to run this game, otherwise you're in for some serious lag and stuttering. Even on my mid-to-high range pc, I couldn't maintain sixty on high. But framerate is the least of your problems. The game will not stop crashing. I didn't have this problem when I was starting my save, but after I completed the main storyline and all of the DLC and Most Wanted save the Riddler, I was trying to get all of the trophies and the game continously crashes after ten minutes of play. Again, it was running reasonably well my first 25 hours, but then suddenly I complete the story and everything goes to hell. But that's ok. You're probably wondering why I am still recommending this game.
It's because, as a big fan of the Arkham series, this game is amazing. All of the criticism I heard when going in, about the Batmobile and how it was used too much, and how the story isn't good or whatever people are saying, it proved to be completely unfounded. I REALLY loved this game, and I had a ton of fun playing it. The formula hasn't changed since City, you are still the Batman, fighting arena-style combat against hordes of enemies. There are a couple new types, like the medic, the charging guys, and the big guys that aren't berzerkers but still can't be taken out with silent takedowns (they are pretty annoying). The game is well designed and looks really good, especially because everything takes place in a rainy Gotham at night. I thought the Batmobile was amazingly fun to play and to upgrade, and I felt that it wasn't overused at all. It's only really the side missions that see the Batmobile used a lot, and they were still fun.
There are several DLC missions that help to pad the length of kind-of a short campaign, and I feel that they were worth it to buy. That's why I got the season pass (on sale) and I think I got my money's worth. However, none of the missions were particularly memorable to me. I thought they were ok, but after getting to play them, I don't think I would bother getting them at full price. But if this game is on sale, and you're a fan of the Arkham games or just like Batman, then this game is a really good addition to the series and the franchise in general. If you can handle the performance, at least.
