Civ V - a personal review
I bought this game when it first came out years ago and I have rapidly purchased the expansions when they came out. After over 500 hours of game play I have to admit this game has me hooked. It is very replayable, with random maps providing lots of challenges.
I have previously played CIV since CIV 2 and for me CIV V is the best game, which is very different to CIV IV and I know some CIV IV diehards preferred to stick with the earlier version.
Key differences - Hex map rather than squares - a nice intuitive change which you quickly forget about becuase it just works. One military unit per hex - which makes military units feel more substantial and gets rid of the 'stack of doom' from earlier games. Military aspects of the game feel more nuanced than earlier CIV.
Every expansion has built on and improved CIV V. The religions work nicely and the expanded number of civilisations includes my favourite - Poland. Why Poland - they have stable replacement which is worth building to boost city production, an excellent cavalry unit (Winged Hussar) and they get extra Policies - which is one of my favourite mechanisms of the game.
This game has that 'one more turn' element which is a great plus but also a downside if you are looking for something quick. I like to play on extra large maps which means my games take a long time. Thus I often don't finish a game because I want to try a different map, civ combo.
For me that is fine because it is the expereince of playing the game I enjoy - the journey with its dramatic interactions and elements of discovery are what I look for with CIV. Winning against the AI is not necessarily my goal.
This is a game I wholeheartedly recommend.

Super Hexagon is a cute little game that's very simple in design yet very hard in application. I'm hesitant to call it a rhythm game, but I can't think of anything better to call it. You play as a triangle while some kickin' techno plays in the background. You navigate this triangle around a hexagon to avoid sections of hexagons that are falling towards the hexagon. Later on the hexagon becomes a pentagon then becomes a square (the shape can change between these three forms). The goal is to last for 60 seconds in each of the 6 difficulties. Simple, hypnotic, and addicting, this game is definitely worth the low asking price. I recommend picking it up if you can as you'll find yourself hooked in minutes.

EDIT: Wow, that was a lot longer than I was expecting it to be, haha.  Added a TLDR at the bottom.
This game is hands down the best roguelike game I've ever played.
The developers claim single player is the intended play mode but multiplayer is where this game really shines.  You can select one of three difficulty levels for your playthrough, but easy mode won't save progress.  The gameplay is easy to learn but difficult to master, every character has a unique skillset and every item will give you some sort of bonus and learning how to synergize your skill and item usage is necessary to completing your playthrough because the enemies will grow progressively stronger as time goes on while your growth depends on how much experience you're earning.  It's entirely possible to lose because you took too long to move to the next level where you'd earn experience faster, making quick strategic execution a vital part of anyone's playthrough.  There are three distinct stages of a risk of rain playthrough:
Early game: You scavenge for loot, escape the hostiles, pray that you don't get cornered, and nourish yourself with your own tears.  You will die.
Mid game: If this is the one-out-of-every-twenty playthroughs where you get lucky enough to get past the second level, you'll probably have enough items to begin developing some sort of strategy that helps you kill stuff more gooder.  Maybe you'll have a fleet of drones one-shotting the weak flying enemies and supporting you against the stronger ones, or an item combo like specs+scythe that allows you to heal from doing damage.  Bosses will also begin spawning randomly and dropping items each time they die.
Late game:  In ROR you have the option to return to previous levels, but on the difficulty you're already at, and you can do it indefinitely.  If you choose to do so then you've chosen to become a god of death, demolishing anything in your path.  Elite bosses spawn like basic enemies and items litter the ground.  Most of them are worth nothing because you already have like thirty of them but occasionally you'll find an awesome rare or unique item.  The late game seems like it would be boring and monotonous at first, but returning to where you began and completely obliterating the beasts that once hunted you is anything but.
Now onto more mechanics of the game.
Replay value: High scores, unlockables items, unlockable characters, stats, and lore give you plenty of reasons to keep coming back.  As if that wasn't enough ROR has a system called Artifacts that allows you to set rules when you begin your playthrough so that even the gameplay itself will be unique.  My personal favorites are a combination of three:
- Honor: Spawns every enemy as an elite (has higher health and damage and one of four special effects that make them more powerful)
- Glass: Deal 500% damage, have 10% health
- Sacrifice: items drop randomly from monsters instead of from chests
There are ten in total, each with their own unique effect.  There are also twelve completely unique characters that all have their own different skills and play style.  You start with one and unlock others as you play.
Multiplayer: This is how you play the game for real.  No noobs allowed.  Friendships will be tested, broken, remade, and tested again.  Every human emotion packed into an hour-long episode of shock, relief, and a lot of "one more go"s.  It's awesome in a way that no other game is.
Enemies: Every enemy is unique in a way that requires you to rethink your strategy for every encounter and have multiple backup strategies incase things go awry.  Combinations of enemy types all stacked against you will take your options away faster than you can even remember what your options are, forcing you to develop new strategies on the spot and discover new ways to use your items and skills.  Every single playthrough is unique in the way the enemies are presented and the challenges you're faced with.  Your items provide you with strategies but they're all situational so even if you have the most awesome build you've ever had you can still get destroyed by a combination of enemies that you haven't encountered before.  This forces you to move slowly to preserve your playthrough, but at the same time the clock is ticking, threatening your playthrough with increasingly powerful enemies, and creating a unique tension that I've never seen in another game.
TL;DR: Fast-paced roguelike platformer that's best with friends.  End the game soon and say you beat it or drag it on and destroy everything with hundreds of items.  Uniquely fun and has many opposing mechanics that create tension and must be balanced as you play through your playthrough, and there are plenty of reasons to play it over and over.

Super Hexagon is a cute little game that's very simple in design yet very hard in application. I'm hesitant to call it a rhythm game, but I can't think of anything better to call it. You play as a triangle while some kickin' techno plays in the background. You navigate this triangle around a hexagon to avoid sections of hexagons that are falling towards the hexagon. Later on the hexagon becomes a pentagon then becomes a square (the shape can change between these three forms). The goal is to last for 60 seconds in each of the 6 difficulties. Simple, hypnotic, and addicting, this game is definitely worth the low asking price. I recommend picking it up if you can as you'll find yourself hooked in minutes.

The frame rate fluctuates like crazy while playing with or without v-sync. All in all if you have a good pc i reccommend this game, but otherwise I would stay away from it until you get a better one.  BTW: The story is satisfying albiet a little tedius with the drone battles, but it is a fitting conclusion to the AMAZING Arkham games.

Dead Space is a third-person action-thriller that takes place on the USG Ishimura -- a 'planet-cracker' starship -- in the year 2414. In response to a distress signal sent by the USG Ishimura, the protagonist; an engineer named Issac Clarke, along with four others, are sent to investigate. Upon arrival the crew's ship; the USG Kellion, crashes in the Ishimura dock due to a guidance system malfunction. This prompts the crew to seek out other means of transport as they investigate the abandoned starship in search of answers.
Dead Space is an enjoyable game. It has intense action; impressive presentation and visuals; chilling music; creepy enemies with innovative mechanics; and an overall ominous atmosphere.
Dead Space is a well polished game that is visually striking; and although the missions may become repetitive; the scares somewhat predictable; and the story a bit lackluster, it falls back on it's enjoyable gameplay and haunting ambience.
Recommended -- Check it out!

This unassuming rogue-like indie which at first appears simplistic in both aesthetics and game design quickly proves to be both a deeply challenging and immensely rewarding experience. Featuring a permanent death game mechanic, you take control of one of several unlockable classes, all with vastly different play styles which dramatically change the way you play the game. As your character moves through the five randomly generated levels you gain XP and unlock passive and active abilities which can have a huge impact on how your character performs in combat. One of the most interesting aspects of the design is the concept that time=difficulty. The game begins at "Very Easy" and simply through the passage of in-game time slowly ticks over to "Easy", "Normal, "Medium", etc., there's an achievement for surviving 40 minutes and trust me when I say you won't get there on your first play-through. Once you die, you start again from the very beginning (hence, 'permadeath'), however this is much less frustrating than it sounds and in fact you never feel cheated by the game, chances are if you died it was probably your own fault. With plenty of different classes, secrets and unlockables, there's always something to strive for even if you've beaten the game. Another great example of how indie game developers are creating some of the most unique gaming experiences that are easily on par with AAA titles in terms of both challenge and pure enjoyment.

Dead Space is a third-person action-thriller that takes place on the USG Ishimura -- a 'planet-cracker' starship -- in the year 2414. In response to a distress signal sent by the USG Ishimura, the protagonist; an engineer named Issac Clarke, along with four others, are sent to investigate. Upon arrival the crew's ship; the USG Kellion, crashes in the Ishimura dock due to a guidance system malfunction. This prompts the crew to seek out other means of transport as they investigate the abandoned starship in search of answers.
Dead Space is an enjoyable game. It has intense action; impressive presentation and visuals; chilling music; creepy enemies with innovative mechanics; and an overall ominous atmosphere.
Dead Space is a well polished game that is visually striking; and although the missions may become repetitive; the scares somewhat predictable; and the story a bit lackluster, it falls back on it's enjoyable gameplay and haunting ambience.
Recommended -- Check it out!

-i7 4790k
-GTX 970 (Nvidia Experience settings)
-16 GB of 2133 MHz RAM

Dead Space is one of the first survival Horror games that I had ever played, I got in to it when I was about 13 and didn't think it was going to be that scary, I told myself that the Flood from Halo where probably scarier... Oh how wrong I was. Dead Space is not only a fearful and startling title, it also features some rich gameplay mechanics and an extremely interesting story which gets better as you explore the backstory.
Although I prefer a First Person Perspective in most games, the Third person in this game is done exceptionally well, with weapons using blue laser sights so aiming is calculated much more dynamically and the HUD is replaced by elements on your character, A genius idea seeing as how it's one of the only games that works without a HUD which gives it a level of Depth.
As well as having tremendous graphics for it's time, it is also amazingly optimized, being able to run smoothly on max settings on most rigs, and the sound quality is stunning.
Overall, Dead Space and it's franchise is probably my favorite set if Games. At the time of this review I have already pre-orded Dead Space 3 and I can't wait to play it... if only it where on Steam...

Xcom is an isometric 3D  strategy game with turn-based combat. It has streamlined or removed some aspects of the original game, for better or worse. To me the changes are mostly all positive. Game still feels familiar enough to appeal to many of the veterans.
Xcom gameplay consists of two parts, the tactical combat on the field and little bit of base management. In base management you get limited options to build laboratories, workshops, power generators, satellite uplinks etc. with their different benefits. You can purchase different kind of perks with games currency, you can research new tech, manufacture new items and gear in engineering and sell items you acquire on missions on black market.
The combat itself is really fun, you have different classes of soldiers and you can level them up by completing missions and shooting up aliens. With levels (promotions) you can choose one of two special abilities depending on your soldiers class. Different classes are sniper, support, assault and heavy.
There is a multiplayer option but it's a bit lacking. You can only play 1vs1 matches with your custom made squads. Somekind of co-op would be nice.
Firaxis games really is the master of turn-based strategy with Xcom and Civilization. I recommend everyone to get the expansion pack Enemy Within, even for the first playthrough. Since it doesn't add new campaign but implements new storyline in the orginal games campaign. It also comes with new tech and some new enemies. Another recommendation would be playing with Iron man mode on, when every death of your squad is permanent. Since then game autosaves and you cant save manually. It really adds some great tension to the game.

It's been a while since I played a game where the story didn't try to cram a moral down my throat or overdramatize everything or just overall try too hard. XCOM's story is probably the weakest part of the game overall, but I don't find that a bad thing because instead of boring cutscenes funneling me from wave to wave, enemy after enemy, the story progresses (usually) at your pace; you don't have to do the critical steps to unlock a story-necessary mission until you want to, and when you do, the cutscenes are a nice change of pace from tactical alien-annihilating action.
You start off with a squad of rookies looking to prove themselves for a global council looking to stop the alien invasion. They drop you in, give you basic info, and tell you to have at it, and it tries to keep from shoving too much info at you at the start. There are a ton of cutscenes at the start as you unlock basic features, but they're skippable and the amount of them quickly dwindles as you progress.
Progression is the name of the game in XCOM almost as much as tactics are, and it's nailed here. You level up your soldiers individually, you purchase new facilities for your base, you research new technologies, you buy weapon upgrades... progression in this game never felt forced or too slow. I always was excited to unlock a new tier of gun, a new set of armor, or additional slots for my squad.
With how good the progression is, it's nice to know that the pacing, too, is in most cases very well done. There were a couple times where the difficulty spiked dramatically and took some adjustment, but they were few and far between. For the most part, you feel like you're getting more and more powerful, but the aliens are no slouches; they'll eventually throw tougher and tougher aliens at you in new and interesting combat scenarios.
So it's good to see that the core gameplay itself is wonderful. The turn-based strategy genre is one that seems to be all-too-rare these days, and it's a shame because it's one of my favorite genres in gaming. XCOM excels in this area, with more options for cover, flanking, special abilities, teamwork, medkits, grenades, and elevation advantages than you can shake a dead alien at.
The gameplay consistently shines, and the random number generator seems (mostly) fair, and the game does a good job of giving you the numbers to let you decide whether to take risky shots or not. It also excels at making you cautious; you lose a soldier and they're gone, making all the time you spent leveling them up a colossal waste. They don't lose the items they were equipped with, luckily, which I find is mostly balanced. You can hire new recruits for a small fee, but you'll have to level them up from scratch, leaving you to difficult mid-game missions where you're sending out rookies against tougher and tougher aliens.
The game lasts a reasonable amount of time; I clocked about 20 hours into it before I won on Normal, with quite a bit of saving and reloading. There's a host of options for replayability, and I barely scratched the surface of certain subsystems, but it'll be a while before I replay it. I didn't play multiplayer, either, so I can't comment on that in this recommendation.
Ultimately, XCOM is a well-designed, perfectly executed entry into a genre that doesn't see enough love, and I loved my time with the game. I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who likes a bit of strategy mixed in with their violent alien-murdering.

A competent game that removes the sandbox element of the original X-COM/UFO for a far more linear approach. This results in a game that, while not as overtly cruel and random as it's progenitor, ends up being a bit dull as you approach end game.
That said, combat missions can be tense, especially when using the Second Wave ruleset to force randomness into calculations. However it's hard to escape the feeling that some missions have pre-ordained outcomes, no matter how much you save scum.
It doesn't reach the heights of brilliance achieved by its forefather, but it's one of the few games I've played to completion - and then started replaying - in the past few years, which is something in and of itself.
This game is a great time-kill, and worth the small price for all the time you'll spend playing it, but DO NOT buy this game if you have high blood pressure or a history of violence.

XCOM:EU is an awesome game, brilliantly blending board-game strategy with the cunning of tactical shooters. You take command of a squad of soldiers that must stop an alien menance. Gameplay occurs in turns with intuitive controls, abilities, and movement. Difficulty ranges from fair and balanced to outright masochistic. Soldiers can be customized (name/appearance/loadout/gear) but their deaths are permanent, so if you're planning on perfection (like me) plan you moves VERY wisely. When you aren't in combat you are coordinating the internation response; researching new technologies, manufacturing upgrades, and managing the layout of your HQ for maximum efficiency. Graphics are shiny while not computer-melting and for added flavor there is a short and sweet storyline which is at least enteraining while not exactly revolutionary. Only complaints are line of sight (sometimes your soldiers cannot see an alien despite the fact that Stevie Wonder has line of sight on the damn alien); the randomness of classes (promoted soldiers receive random classes that cannot be changed); and there is no co-op (only singleplayer or online versus). 9 out of 10.

A pleasantly surprising third person shooter. While it isn't quite horror and strays more into cheesy splatter, this is not a bad thing, the atmosphere is still great. The level design is top notch, and is very maze like, similar to Half-Life. Linear, but with wiggle room.
Varied objectives and fun, but not especially challenging, physics puzzles draw you in and help tell the strange story. The goal is always clear, if you pay attention and explore a little, you will never even need to look at a map.
The gore based combat is enjoyable, and the decidedly heavy pacing and unpredicatability helps keep you on your toes.
The store system can feel a bit tacked on, but it works and it helps add a sense of progression to the game.
It does have a few issues with mouse control but if you have a pad, or fiddle with your  mouse settings a bit, this can be overcome. It also helps to disable vsync. But the game is well worth the minor annoyance.
This is a good game and you should play it.

I bought this game for $25, Played with all pre-2016 patches. Hardware: GTX 970, 16GB RAM, i5-4670 running stock clock, installed on SSD. It is straight-up a *shame* that I need to preface my review with any of that.
As a game, this is a thoroughly fine sequel to Arkham City. If you enjoyed City, and you think your PC will run it, you ought to give it a try. The tank combat wasn't as bad as I'd been hearing. I experienced fewer than five crashes over 60+ hours (although they were all hard, "screen goes beige and sound buffer loops" crashes). The "filling the jail" mechanic is incredibly rewarding, until you realize the effort required to 100% Maximum Security. Oh, speaking of which, don't go into this thinking you'll see the "true" ending unless you're a masochist for Riddler gadget puzzles. And if you *are* a masochist for Riddler gadget puzzles, well, the plot just isn't as good as Asylum or City. But... probably better than Origins. Sorry, Origins.
Played with all GPU settings max'ed excepting antialiasing. V-sync ensured no screen tear. Graphics experience was far ahead of Fallout 4, quite a bit behind Witcher 3.
It's really unfortunate that the Arkham series has ended this way, because after I finished the game, I wanted nothing more than to be Batman for another hundred hours. Rockstar nailed it with Asylum and have been making incremental improvements ever since, but with this entry they flew too close to the sun.
If you're still reading this, still unsure, know that Mark Hamill's Joker gets a lot of really fun lines. That ought to tip your scale one way or the other.

I've ticked that I would recommend this game but, if I could, I would have ticked yes AND no. The main story of the game is generally decent and the visual aspect is far beyond what we've seen in previous Arkham games. The high point for me was the general traversal in the game world. In this aspect Arkham Knight is everything I wanted from a Batman game. The Batmobile however, whilst being fun purely as a means of transport, is overused in it's combat sections and puzzle solving, with the Riddler courses being an utterly dispicable addition to the game.
Hand-to-hand combat seems to lack a certain something that was so perfect in the earlier games too. I often felt like I had to use gadgets on enemies before being able to safely strike them. The freeflow rhythm just felt a bit broken.
Challenge maps are another area where the game falls down. Asylum was great for these and City perfected them, but things have changed too much here from the honed formula, and with the inclusion of Batmobile time trials, more tank combat, and god forsaken Riddler racecourse challenges, there's a lot here to dislike.
After all that it may seem strange now that I would still recommend the game, but I do so purely on the strength of the story campaign. In that aspect it is still a great Batman game. It just doesn't deliver on all the extras like we've come to expect.

Civ V - a personal review
I bought this game when it first came out years ago and I have rapidly purchased the expansions when they came out. After over 500 hours of game play I have to admit this game has me hooked. It is very replayable, with random maps providing lots of challenges.
I have previously played CIV since CIV 2 and for me CIV V is the best game, which is very different to CIV IV and I know some CIV IV diehards preferred to stick with the earlier version.
Key differences - Hex map rather than squares - a nice intuitive change which you quickly forget about becuase it just works. One military unit per hex - which makes military units feel more substantial and gets rid of the 'stack of doom' from earlier games. Military aspects of the game feel more nuanced than earlier CIV.
Every expansion has built on and improved CIV V. The religions work nicely and the expanded number of civilisations includes my favourite - Poland. Why Poland - they have stable replacement which is worth building to boost city production, an excellent cavalry unit (Winged Hussar) and they get extra Policies - which is one of my favourite mechanisms of the game.
This game has that 'one more turn' element which is a great plus but also a downside if you are looking for something quick. I like to play on extra large maps which means my games take a long time. Thus I often don't finish a game because I want to try a different map, civ combo.
For me that is fine because it is the expereince of playing the game I enjoy - the journey with its dramatic interactions and elements of discovery are what I look for with CIV. Winning against the AI is not necessarily my goal.
This is a game I wholeheartedly recommend.

In my opinion, Civilization V is one of the best strategy games I've played yet. The mechanics and such are easy to grasp, yet somehow it has some very complex gaming mechanics. The Civilizations that you can play as are very varied, with different abilities and unique buildings and units.
Playing a different civ than usual is the difference between one play style to another. For an example, India has halfed unhappiness for population count, yet double unhappiness for city count, making him a civ which focuses on local growth, along with a secondary focus by the player's choice. Whereas Egypt has a +20% Production Bonus to Wonder Construction. Each civ has a bias, and you can use that bias to your advantage.
If you were lucky, you could be given the best spawn at the start of a match. Coastal, Riverside, Mountains within 2 tiles, Desert within border. This is widely considered the 'best spot' in this game, due to literal access to (next to) everything, including terrain-based Wonders.
There are many more mechanics I could speak of, but it would take too long for a random player like me to document. In a nutshell: Buy this game. If it were up to me, this game would get a solid 9.5/10.

Half-Life 2 was created by Valve in 2004 and still holds up, ten years later. You play as Gordon Freeman, a scientist with a shotgun and a gravity gun! The graphics aren't fantastic by today's standards but you can imagine how great they would have been upon the 2004 release. You get control of a diverse range of weapons and vehicles, facing countless different enemies, from zombies to trigger happy law enforcers. Set in a dystopian world, the game has huge variation in level design and crushing combine soldeirs with a huge metal crate lifted by a magnetised crane never gets old. One of the best things however, is the awesome physics engine this game has to offer. You can use your gravity gun to move objects around you, often rewarding you with the satisfaction of firing a metal disc to take a zombie's head off. This game can be found on the steam store for cheap and will be well worth your money. I say bring on Half-Life 3!

Aliens have invaded earth and it's your job as commander of XCOM to combat the aliens on the ground, learn about their technology and physiology, build up your base and figure out a way to drive them from the earth.
At the strategic level, you build up the XCOM base with a variety of facilities and technology in a manner that is customized by how you want to approach defeating the alien menace.
At the tactical level, command a squad of troopers in turn-based combat to defeat a wide variety of aliens as they terrorize cities, abduct humans, or shoot down their UFOs and assault them on their own ground.  Be careful how you treat your troopers though since they level up as they fight and become incredibly valuable assets that can be painful to lose.
This game is not only worth your money, it is worth your time.  Try out the demo, but keep in mind that the demo is very directed and is only the thinnest slice of what the actual game has to offer.

So i'll be honest, after all the fuss about the PC version i passed on the game until they patched it up. After the January update most people said it was running fine, so i bought the game right away as a big fan of arkham asylum and arkham city (not origins however :)).
The positive:
+ Great detailed graphics wherever you are in the game and it's running 99% of the time on 60fps with occasional drop to 50 in environments really heavy on rendering (i'm running 2500K@4.3Ghz, 16GB RAM and GTX970).
+ Very good story, keeps you on the edge and you feel really engaged. Nice story twists and definitely the best Batman game in terms of story so far
+ Gameplay - smooth gamelay and i mean all aspects - the combat feel natural, the upgrade system is resobable, driving the batmobile was surprisingly easy (usually it needs a lot more time to get used to driving physics in games), cool gadgets
+ Value for money - finished the main story with approx. 60% done after 20 hours. Still feel that i want to fully finish the game, which i didn't do in the previous bat-games
The not so positive:
- I feel i would like to spend less time in the batmobile, mostly it felt right to use it but in some situations/missions the game kinda forces you to use it where i felt it didn't make much sense (like platforming)
That's it. If you love batman or like this type of games, go get it. If you hate WB and rocksteady for f**** up the PC version at launch maybe wait for a -90% price drop, but i think they've already been punished enough..

Reviewers everywhere are loving this game and there is a good reason why. South Park: This Stick of Truth is probably the best game ever created, based on a movie/television show. It also could be one of the best games ever created. You will love South Park: The Stick of Truth if you are a fan of the show. I was not a huge fan, and by that I don’t mean that I didn’t care for it but that I didn’t watch it too often. Even with my limited insight into the South Park universe, I found myself loving this game for its humor and references to the show which is ultimately a reference to current events and pop culture. Let me introduce you to South Park: The Stick of Truth, which I have given a 8.5/10. And yes, as always my reviews are spoiler-free.

Overall, I give South Park: The Stick of Truth a 8.5/10. Why? Because it is so close to being an awesome game, but I don’t know as it has the appeal to be a 9. While I loved it, I don’t know if someone who didn’t like the show would get the same enjoyment. It is also very short, and although there is a ton of exploration to do and a lot of items to collect, I don’t feel the game should be artificially extended in that way. There were also a few characters from the show who were missing or felt very minimalized who I wished to see play a bigger role in the game. (I don’t recall finding “Towlie” anywhere). However, an 8.8 is a highly respectable score for a game that does so much well. This is the best conversion of any TV show or movie to a video game that has ever been done. It oozes South Park humor as if you are just watching an interactive episode. If you are a fan even in the slightest of South Park, you need to get this game.

Continuing sci-fi horror in the style of stories like ‘Alien’ and ‘The Thing’, Dead Space combines all the successful elements of past horror and sci-fi games and combines them into a fantastic experience. Being a huge fan of the South Park TV show I was hugely excited to hear when there was a game being released. Sadly I was always put off by the full price of £40. I waited until this years Summer sale and picked it up for £20 and was not disappointed.
The game takes the style of a turn based combat title, much like Final Fantasy, but it is a much more mellowed down version. I was able to breeze through most combat situations without much attention being paid. The parts of the game which got me scratching my head were trying to work out how to proceed through each puzzle, often at times I had to refer to a walkthrough as I was starting to get a brain hemorrhage.
The graphics and sound throughout the game are exactly the same as in the TV series, so if you enjoy that, you will certainly feel at home here. The ever so crass South Park esk jokes and one liners are here for the world to marvel at.
Story wise, again, very much a South Park episode, you will almost feel like you are watching the show while playing. The length of the main story is about ten hours long, some may disagree but I think that is a little short for a game at full price of £40, but there are plenty of side missions and achievements to go hunting for if that is your thing.
If you are lucky enough to find this game on sale for anything under £20. I would certainly recommend you give it a try if you have ever enjoyed the TV show, however you may not fully appreciate it. Certainly is not worth full price. But for the price I have paid, I still really enjoyed my playthrough.

First off, if you're expecting perfect performance, as you rightfully should, don't. This game doesn't always run that well. However, after the patch, it's more bearable than before. Through my entire play through of the game, it never crashed once. It also stayed at a nice framerate (for my 950 anyway). However, the gameplay is what really makes this game great. It keeps all of the elements from the previous games and manages to mix them into something new. Fighting is still just as satisfying as before, but made better thanks to new types of brutes and medics. The predator encounters have a new mechanic called fear takedowns, which make it much more strategic than before. But I found that the biggest joy of this game comes in the tank battles. They may seem a little out of place, but are fun, fast, and infinitely satisfying. The open world of Gotham is bigger than ever before, and many previous Batman villans make an appearance, even one you wouldn't normally expect...
This is by far the most advanced Arkham game in the series. If you're willing to jump over some performance issues, then prepare to be the Batman one last time.

Have had a lot of fun with this game. Soundtrack is out of this world, and the game is punishing, but not artificially difficult. If you die, it's your fault.
Artifacts let you add modifiers to your game, such as Glass, which gives you a 500% damage boost, but only 10% of your regular health. This, in addition to numerous character classes and items, makes the game have a lot of replay value, with each run being slightly different. Until you get the Command artifact, that is.
My favourite element of the game is the difficulty slider. You genuinely feel rushed, as every few minutes the game gets harder, to the point where in later levels you will find yourself facing randomly spawned bosses from the first few levels. Or maybe that's a bug. I don't actually know :P But playing can become a real hassle later on, where you basically have to get a good ratio of items to time spent, and move on.
You will not beat this game on your first try. That is a given. It is ball-crushingly hard, but in a way where if you play enough, the game becomes much more simple.
Unlocking stuff is fun. Items are fun. Characters are fun.
This review is a bit all over the place, I know, but I'd give this game a solid 9/10. It's the kind of game where I like to hop in, attempt a run or two, and go back to whatever I was doing.

I need to say something important about this review; an important prologue.
I bought Civilisation 5 on release from steam. At the time it had very polished graphics and had an excellent eye-catching UI.
It, however, was extremely unpolished in the gameplay department.  I had played a few games on standard difficulty (for the series; there are multiple difficulty levels in the series' games that reduce or increase the AI's boons). Firstly, resource management and growth was extremely slow and terribly fleshed out; a city surrounded by even the most fertile land would grow so painfully slowly, even when the land was improved. Worse yet, buildings, commonly used in the series to specialise cities and increase their output in food/gold/production etc, gave awful returns for their continued maintenance and had no additional effects beyond offering more science/gold etc. early on in the game.
This, combined with the 1 unit per tile rule (1UPT), a feature a lot of the old fans felt aggrieved by, made me feel like a military playstyle was better than playing a pacifist, builder or diplomat. I chucked most of my gains into military production and swamped cities with vast carpets of doom. The AI of course, could not handle the combat system, and would foolishly chuck units out to die and leave crucial areas undefended. Bad combat AI, however, is normal for the series, but it was made more apparent with the 1UPT style gameplay.
Finally, we get to the part that really ground my gears. The diplomacy was god awful on release. The diplomacy screen would be so vague about how AIs felt about you and you had few diplomatic options to affect relations bar 'declaring friendship', which the AI didn't honestly care about. And speaking of the latter, did I mention that the AI were completely psychotic on release? Even the most peaceful of civs, Gandhi (yes I'm aware he likes nukes in this game series), would declare war despite being half-way across the globe and posessing no military.
A lot of fans and, I believe even a dev at one point, rationalised it that they wanted the AI to be more competitive. Well they certainly bloody succeeded, but all the leaders became devoid of personality and the game presented itself to me as a Skynet Simulator with AIs modeled off anal retentive librarians, every AI hell-bent on loosing their marbles as soon as you so much inhaled near them.  The only AI that exhibited ANY personality differences was Alexander the Great, who would call me up every three turns to abuse me verbally while he stomped all over the city states on his continent.
This was by far, in my opinion, the biggest mistake; make all the leaders homogeneous and you gut a lot of what makes Civ interesting.
The good news is that this has been improved in the amount of expansions added. Civ V is still a military heavy game because of its 1UPT but buildings, policies etc have been marginally improved to fit a more peaceful game style and the AI isn't channeling the irrational rage of a thousand shonen protaganists.
With that in mind I'd recommend it now. But the main point is this, an age old adage: be wary of buying AAA games on release, it was not worth the cash I paid, and it might be more prudent to buy it only if you really have the money to spend/

Half Life 2 was released in 2004, 6 years after the first one. As i said in my Half Life review, the game revolutionized the FPS genre.
It was among the first games to add narrative to its game. To account for the change, it also made the level design very linear. Previously, FPS games would have a very maze like level design.
Half Life 2's budget consisted of $40,000,000. I am not sure how much time and money was spent on the source engine itself, but from the development timeline, it seems that source engine was developed from the very 1999, shortly after release of HL1.
Why do i want to emphasize of the source engine so much? Well, the main goal of the source engine was to provided realistic physics and facial animations.
In the first game a portal opens up from a planet named Xen. You end up destroying the Queen, thus braking the portal link and ending up in captivity of Gman.
The events of Half Life 2 happen 20 years after Half Life 1, somewhere in a eastern Europe town called City 17. Human race got enslaved by Combine, an alien race that was in war with Xen, which got interested in Earth after the events of Half Life 1. Gman decides to send you to City 17 to help the resistance.
The realistic facial animations, and graphics in general that source engine provided really add up to the experience. The character really come to life thanks to those facial animations.
The faces looked very real unlike say, Max Payne. It really took some time for that technology to appear in mainstream games. Sure, by 2004 there were plenty amount of games that would have a very narrative focus, like Fahrenheit (2005) for PS2. But just imagine how much more immersive it would look if it actually tried to focus on facial animations. Half Life 2 had one of the best facial animation techniques, until LA Noire came out. That game used motion capture.
I also felt satisfied with the level the game provided. A zombie town for example. Or a land with arachnid creatures popping out of the sand. The boat chase. Or the one where you have to use the crane to get you car to the other side of the gate. Finally, there is a final chapter with a gravity gun.
Half Life 2 was the first game to feature physics. Because of that it allowed them to explore new horizons.
The game would give the player a gravity gun, which allows you to use objects from the environment to your advantage. You can pick up sharp objects and cut enemies in half with them, or use explosive barrels to lite them up, or simply smash them with something heavy, or even something like tossing back a grenade.
There are also new enemy types. New head crabs types were added. They also decided to improve on the zombies aspect of the game and even added a variety of zombie types to the game. There are also arachnid creatures, sort of like ones from Starship Troopers. At one point in the game, you will be able to control them.
When you are not fighting these guys, you will be fighting the Combine, who use guns. At times you will also be fighting striders, which are 3 legged machines, sort of like the ones from War of the Worlds. Finally, sometimes you will also be fighting small flying drones. Due to their size, you can actually use the gravity gun. They are also sharp, so you can even cut with them.
Thankfully, they decided to dial back on the amount of platforming in this game, though the game had puzzles added, mostly physics related.
The game has a total 13 chapters, which is about 15 hours of gameplay.
Additionally, it also provides a huge mod library. A lot of my favorites came about by being mods of HL2. Games like Chivalry, Natural Selection, Stanley Parable, Insurgency.

A brilliant blend of easy-to-learn / tricky-to-master turn-based combat and base building coupled with macro-management.
The choices you make have short- and long-term repercussions. Outfitting your soldiers with hi-tech armour might keep them alive in their next field operation, but that money might be better spent on a satelitte to appease one of your funding council nations. You might win a battle, only to return to base and find you are losing the war.
The combat plays like a complex game of chess (or Full Spectrum Warrior if you ever played that) - you must out-manoeuvre and out-think the invaders to flank them, provide covering fire, manage your ammunition, move decisively, and take risks. Often your opponents will have superior numbers and superior firepower - your mind and your tactical sense are the best weapons you have against the alien threat.
Cut-scenes and voice-overs from your team of scientists, engineers, and military personnel provide the surprisingly-good narrative; a strong reminder of your objectives and a clever sense of progression.
But for every step you take towards victory, the aliens will take two. XCOM provides a non-stop challenge, keeping the player sharp even on a routine missions and operations.
Recommended for those who enjoy a challenge, strong risk/reward mechanics, and strategy games that require you to make difficult (sometimes impossible) choices.

Aim mode drops your aim sensitivity so much it's almost impossible to use and even adds joystick deadznoes to the mouse control.  Put this all together and you have the definition of artificial difficulty.
It's not even as scary as Doom 3 due to relying entirely on jump scares which the game always warns you about with the music.
I'd say the best part of the game are the zero gravity sections which are pretty fun, but even those are severely hampered by the poor camera which makes it difficult to navigate.  Overall, I can't find any way to recommend this game.

Best purchase on steam without a doubt. An intensely immersive game that I could not stop playing. It started out as just another rogue-like game with a little twist made by a couple of guys who just wanted to make a game. It turned into a game that drives in not only intense difficult gameplay, but fast paced decision making and a strangely immersive plot. The gameplay, made by people who have obviously played or at least heard of Dota 2 and LoL, is like combining a sidescrolling platformer with a moba and a rogue-like. The game stays completely unique with a vast number of items, enemies, and characters. The longer you play the game, the harder it gets.....literally.....the difficulty increases the longer the run. The game feels to work like a rogue-like where the enemies are super overpowered after the first level, but the items you get are even more overpowered. It's like fighting over power on a much larger scale than I have ever seen before in a rogue-like game. The makers of this game put so much time into it that I feel like I'm still not doing the game justice by completing 89% of it. I can't stress how much this game can play with you emotionally (the music writer is a goddamn genius on the last stage). I'm stopping this review here because there is too much to say and I have already said enough, but I highly recommend purchasing this game. It is, and will remain, in my top games list. When Valve Software released Half-Life in 1998, they came straight out of the gate with a game that is now regarded as one of the best and most important computer games ever released. Half-Life not only brought a stronger sense of storytelling and atmosphere into the mainstream of first-person shooters, but also served as the launch point for a huge variety of mods. With this pedigree, Half-Life 2 became one of the most hyped titles of the early 2000s – and managed to live up to the hype. Half-Life 2 revolutionised computer game physics, represented the best in a generation of increasingly realistic graphics and used some of the most intelligent AI code seen to that point.
Half-Life 2 uses the visual medium superbly, with a distinctive architectural arrangement which evokes the crumbling concrete apartment blocks of the Soviet era in Eastern Europe. This contrasts with the futuristic, industrial, metallic aesthetic of the buildings of the Combine, especially the colossal Citadel at the centre of the city, reaching far into the clouds and dominating the skyline. Gigantic screens dot the city, presenting propaganda broadcasts from Doctor Breen and the Combine. The citizens of Earth have been outfitted with the same overall-style clothing, which both invokes a sense of the citizens being unskilled workers and prisoners on their own planet.
Importantly, the game doesn't become overbearing with these details, presenting just enough of them at a time to create a realistic impression of the world after the Black Mesa incident and the Combine invasion. Indeed, Valve's attention to detail seems to be extremely professional, with a polish which shows the artistry that went into the game.
The gameplay demonstrates similar polish. At its core, it continues the same sort of linear first-person shooter action of its predecessor, but brings a set of important improvements which help update the game and make it feel more immersive and visceral. Chief among these was the introduction of realistic physics through the use of the Havok middleware package. The use of realistic physics not only helps immersion through relatively realistic interactions of objects, such as the scattering of objects with explosions or the ragdoll physics of dead enemies, but also plays a big part in the game itself.
One of the biggest and most touted features in Half-Life 2 was the Zero Point Energy Manipulator (also known as the Gravity Gun), a device allowing the player to pick up, move and violently hurl objects around them. This comes in handy at several points in the game, where it can be used to move obstacles out of one's path, use other objects to shield one's self or build impromptu stacks of objects to climb to out-of-the-way places or use the objects as weapons by hurling them into enemies.
However, there are a few instances where the game turns into a showcase for the physics engine and the Gravity Gun. There are a few instances where you must manipulate certain objects in a certain way to proceed and the game seems to go almost as far as to shout out, “This is a physics puzzle!”, which doesn't help with immersion. Luckily, such occasions are few and far between. By and large, the physics manipulations are integrated very well into the game and really help with making the game feel more of an authentic experience.
Another place in which Half-Life 2 feels distinctive is in the vehicular sections. At certain parts of the game, you are required to use various vehicles in order to progress – an airboat used for getting through the canals of City 17 and a stripped-out scout buggy for roaming the countryside outside of the city itself. While vehicular sections in first-person shooters weren't new by that stage, most contemporary games rendered their vehicle sections in either third-person, in imitation of Halo, or in a modified first-person perspective, such as through gun sights. Half-Life 2, on the other hand, steadfastly sticks to its “eyes of Gordon Freeman” first-person perspective throughout.
The vehicular sections in Half-Life 2 are a bit of a love-or-hate beast, since they are quite a divergence from the core gameplay, but I personally love them. They present a sense of speed and exhilaration as you make your way through obstacles, enemies and the scenery around you. There are plenty of stunning set-pieces, such as being chased through the canals and tunnels by an attack helicopter, culminating in a duel to the death near a large dam. There are opportunities to experience the potential of the vehicles as weapons in their own right as you use them to plough through the infantry forces of the Combine. Between that and the use of realistic physics with the vehicle handling, I think that these sections represent some of the best vehicular action in any first-person shooter.
Speaking of set-piece battles, there are some spectacular ones outside of the vehicle sections as well. Alien gunships periodically attack, forcing the player to shoot them down with rockets, steering the rockets past the defences of the gunship as it seeks to shoot down the player's rockets in mid-flight. Even the standard infantry of the Combine can offer some impressive battles, with AI that was at that point very impressive, even if you don't get to see their full potential in the tight corridors of the city.
Half-Life 2 was a graphical masterpiece when it was released, even managing to look distinctly better than its best contemporaries. Surprisingly, the game still looks good ten years after its first release, especially with the addition of HDR lighting in conjunction with the release of Half-Life 2: Episode One. While later games have improved on texturing, especially at close ranges, Half-Life 2 certainly does not look embarrassing, especially given that its architectural aesthetic was so distinctive.
The sound design of the game is similarly impressive. There are realistic sounds for all interactions with the environment, including the meaty sounds of the guns in the game. The sounds of the enemies are all distinctive and impressive, from the muffled radio reports of the Combine soldiers to the screeches of the headcrabs and the groaning of the zombies. The game's music is a peculiar mix of various genres, from rock to techno to ambient, but it is set up very well to create atmosphere.
Given the polish of Half-Life 2 and the way it shines out in gameplay and presentation, there are few flaws which I can point at in the game. Some of the physics puzzles are a bit blatant, while there is a short period after you are forced to abandon the scout buggy where I feel the game slows down a lot in a jarring change from fast-paced action and set-piece battles. The section of the game takes place on the coast line outside of City 17, where alien creatures known as antlions burrow out of the ground whenever you touch the sand on the beach. Cue frustration as you try to either fend off enemies as they persistently attack you or try desperately to stack objects in front of you in what feels like an extended game of “keep off the lava”. The addition of an achievement for getting through this section without touching the sand adds to the frustration; I have the achievement, more out of sheer bloody-minded completionism more than anything else, but I won't be going for it again any time soon.
Despite those occasional flaws, Half-Life 2 is a triumph of first-person shooter design. The polished professionalism shines out as an example of how to do a cinematic game without bogging down the action with overly long cutscenes. The gameplay is tight and intuitive, while the game physics and the strong AI work well to improve immersion. Half-Life 2 is a masterpiece of modern game design and should stand as an example for any developers hoping to develop in the genre.

Half Life 2
Valve
PC
Overview:
Ten years is a long time for a game. Usually you can see its age in the bumps in the character models. The blurriness of the texture when you get in really close. The clunkiness of the controls. This game has very little of that.
Since its release, Half-Life 2 marked the beginning of a new era of PC games. Paired with Steam and the Source engine to back it up Valve through a huge wrench into the way games were published. As a gaming platform, up until now was PC the wild west. There was no need for this middle man. People were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that they had to install this jenky new game installer and it had to be connected to the internet to authenticate that you actually spent money on the game. No one would ever stand for that, would they? PC gaming was officially dead.
But now you had the long awaited sequel to one of the best PC games of all time. It had so much to live up to. And it did.  The Source Engine introduced the idea that a player could interact with all 3D objects. They could break things apart and pick up pieces of those things then throw them around. No one had pulled this off so seamlessly and it became a new standard for games going forward.
The fact that Valve had created a new kind of physics sandbox ment that so much of the games design was based around this principle. In the very beginning the game is walking the player through what everyday life is like in City 17. One of the Overwatch soldiers pushes a can onto the ground and demands you pick it up. If you throw it at the guy he beats you to death. Later you escape by placing a few boxes on top of each other and jumping out a window. This concepts scales throughout the game to the point where you eventually get a Gravity Gun that allows you to toss large objects around like cars, dumpsters and even the thousands of similarly dressed bad guys.
Also this game has incredible scale for the time it was created. Where the first Half Life took place in the same large complex filled with tiny rooms everywhere. This game has you travelling miles from location to location.
Given that fact it should hurt the graphical capabilities of the game. However, Sorce was built to be scaled in quality. Valve is constantly updating and improving it even now which just keeps the game looking fresh. Sure, the character models aren’t the best to today’s standards but the thing about source is it still looks almost picturesque standing still.
Likes/Dislikes:
Pacing is this games middle name. At first the classic painfully long intro guides you along and immerses yourself in the world and the characters. You don’t even get your first weapon until at least half hour in. And then its just a ♥♥♥♥ing crowbar that you must beat someone to death with and steal their gun, like any respectable game would have you do. Each new area lets you play with a new concept. First you are pistoling down guys, then you get a sub-machine gun then you get grenades. Blah Blah Blah. All shooters do this. But HL2 does something different. Next you are driving around in a Boat and are ordered to drive miles back though a death trough to the very place that cause this global♥♥♥♥♥♥storm. Then just as you suspect you’d get an even better machine gun, you are handed a gravity gun and sent into a zombie infested ghost town.
Now this is one of my favorite things about this game is suddenly its like you aren’t even playing a FPS anymore. It survival horror with ton of very sharp things around you and traps you get to set off. Using your guns is now very inefficient and really not worth the cost. Meanwhile a stark raving mad priest is guiding you through this section as if it were another game all on its own. Really it just lets you know that there is now a whole new alternative to just blasting away at every badguy.
Now it’s not all good really. At some point the game decides you need back up and puts you in command of other like minded humans. Unfortunately they are just as dumb as the bugs you command earlier in the game. The will constantly get in your way when there are beams of death coming at you. Really your best bet is to send them down every unexplored hallway to disarm traps or pull aggro from anything that is ready to empty their clip into your face.
Also, really cool physics in their infancy have a price. So many times there are random junk objects in your way and you have to take the time to push them or simply lift it all out of your way. It can get daunting.
Closing:
I regard this game as my third favorite of all time. As far a a game concept goes its near perfect. However the characters are sort fall flat to me in an otherwise ♥♥♥♥ing awesome story. The universe that the game is set in is mostly unmatched only to have been out done with games like Fallout and Deus Ex. Its gruesome and in your face. The human struggle feels real, and heavy. Unrelentingly apocalyptic. It puts you through situations where you’re left thinking “Really, they expect me to do what?” and when you are done you feel like you are changed forever.

XCOM is one of the best games I've played in a long, long time.  It combines tactical gameplay and science fiction quite brilliantly.  You take up the position of the commander of XCOM, a project focused on stopping escalating alien incursions into countries around the world.  As commander you organize squads of special operation soldiers, research alien technlogy and prepare countermeasures against the impending invasion.
It's a careful balancing act, you need to defend countries or they will withdraw their funding from the project.  If enough countries withdraw you fail the game.
There are aliens attacking Paris but all of my veterans are recovering from wounds.
Do I send in less experienced troops and risk losing them or do I let paris burn and france withdraw?
Should I expand my air support network into Asia or should I try to better defend Europe with alien augmented F15?
These are real choices that will haunt you and make the replay valve shoot through the roof.
The tactical portion is great as well, there are times where you have to take the tough calls.  Do I run my best gear assualt trooper in to take out the mind controlling alien(and probably die) or do I let it slowly eat through my ranks as my men turn against me.
I would easily rate this game a 9.5/10 and its more than worth every penny.  If any of what you just read seems like a good concept for a game, you owe it to yourself to at least try the demo.

XCOM is one of the best games I've played in a long, long time.  It combines tactical gameplay and science fiction quite brilliantly.  You take up the position of the commander of XCOM, a project focused on stopping escalating alien incursions into countries around the world.  As commander you organize squads of special operation soldiers, research alien technlogy and prepare countermeasures against the impending invasion.
It's a careful balancing act, you need to defend countries or they will withdraw their funding from the project.  If enough countries withdraw you fail the game.
There are aliens attacking Paris but all of my veterans are recovering from wounds.
Do I send in less experienced troops and risk losing them or do I let paris burn and france withdraw?
Should I expand my air support network into Asia or should I try to better defend Europe with alien augmented F15?
These are real choices that will haunt you and make the replay valve shoot through the roof.
The tactical portion is great as well, there are times where you have to take the tough calls.  Do I run my best gear assualt trooper in to take out the mind controlling alien(and probably die) or do I let it slowly eat through my ranks as my men turn against me.
I would easily rate this game a 9.5/10 and its more than worth every penny.  If any of what you just read seems like a good concept for a game, you owe it to yourself to at least try the demo.

"South Park: The Stick of Truth" is a game you'll enjoy if you like crass humor, because this game has a lot of it! You don't even have to be that big of a "South Park"-fan to enjoy many of those wonderful, hillarious and discusting moments this game has to offer, however, you'll get the most out of the game by watching some of the show's episodes. (Some of the references you don't get because you haven't watched the episode it's refering to might make you want to look it up and watch the episode).
The music is wonderful! The soundtrack has to be one of my favorites of all time, and it sounds very epic. The game has a few references to "The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim" in it, like the main menu looks a lot like the one it "Skyrim", with a dark/black-ish smokey background, a barbaric-sounding choir on some parts of the soundtrack, and other in-game references I won't spoil.
The only negative things I have to say about this game is the following:
1) This is a minor one, but at some times the character you're playing seems to glitch in and out fast during cutscenes. Suddenly he disappears, but before you're able to react, he's back- oh, but suddenly he's gone ag- no wait, he's back again. (You catch my drift.) And also, at some points the voice acting seems to be off. I don't know if my computer is the issue, but sometimes the characters stop talking, but their mouths still move (again, during cutscenes).
2) This one is also just nit-picking. Sometimes during combat, your opponent or even your party member will yell at you for taking too long to decide what attack you'll use. This would be fine if you actually did take a long time to decide, but they might complain 3 seconds after the battle starts! It gets kind of annoying.
3) I think they should've included more interactive events. There's only one point in the game where you'll have to choose between option A and option B, and unfortunately, no matter which one you choose, it won't effect the game very much. It's a shame the developers didn't put more effort into that choice, and more of them would be cool.
4) Most of the side-quests are very short. Most of them are basically like "Go there, get that, then you'll get a mushroom you'll put in a cauldron to get a key." I would've loved to see longer side-quests with more depth. Perhaps the goths could have a long side-quest with a cool plot that would eventually grant you a cool, high goth-status, or something like that.
But these flaws aside, the game is fantastic! It's like you're actually in an episode of the show. And you can customize your character however you want, so you can basically BE in South Park, how cool is that?
If you can't stand classic turn-based RPG-style combat systems, I won't recomend it, but if you do, you definitely should pick this gem up. (Hint: Watch the three prequel/promo episodes called "Black Friday", "A Song of♥♥♥♥♥and Fire" and "♥♥♥♥♥♥s and Dragons" before you play. Especially if you love Game of Thrones. And even if you don't, still watch them).

I've never laughed so much at a game as this one.

Ok, ok, ok, ,...We all know the launch was terrible, but I am reviewing the game as is currently.  I am a HUGE batman fan, and have loved all the arkham games, with City being one of my favorite games of all times.  The map is huge, but sparsely populated.  I actually feel that  Arkham City had more enemies on the streets.  The combat is just as great as the previous installments, and when you do have other characters with you can do dual takedowns which look great, but these moments are not that often.  The gadgets are very similar to the rest of the series, and I feel the emphasis on this game is more combat driven, and less stealth/predator in comparison to the previous entries.  That being said, you have more control on how you want to go about clearing a room of enemies.  I geeked out at the fact you can walk around GCPD, a lab in the Studio area, oracle's office in the clocktower, and even Wayne Tower where Lucius Fox is, but there really isnt much going on there --its fan service mainly.  The story was definetly high stakes, and did get me addicted.  I actually enjoyed driving the bat-tank around, as it reminded me of the Dark Knight Returns Batmobile, and while there are riots in progress, batman might need a riot tank.  However, I HATED the fact that you are forced to use it, and combat it in can be a bit boring after awhile.  If it remained a choice, I may have loved it, but the fact you are forced to use plenty of time in order to progress was irksome and frustrating.
All that being said, I thought it was a satsifying ending to the series, and I was sucked into the story; hardocre batman fans will be pleased.  Yes the launch was terrible, but don't let that force you into missing a great game, that concludes a great series!  I highly recommend this game.

I don't recommend this game, unless you are a diehard fan of the series and can catch the game on sale. I was well aware of the performance issues for the PC version going in, but being a diehard fan I really wanted to play and enjoy this game. I'll admit that the game is gorgeous but only when it's working properly. Some issues I ran into were inconsistent frame rates, dropping down from 60fps to as low as 25fps, stuttering, periods where the game ran fine for 5+ hours, periods where the game crashed every 10 minutes or so.
Not to mention I just built a new PC gaming rig and this game almost killed my brand new R9 380. Had one crash where I got and error message and was booted to the desktop. Thought, ok that's fine I'll just reboot the game up. About 10-15 minutes in I started smelling a burning plastic smell. I had on a pair of headphones so I couldn't hear of my GPU fans were on, crawl under my desk to see that my GPU fans weren't spinning. Opened up HWmonitor and it says my GPU temps are 0 degrees, which I knew was an error right away so I shut off the PC in a panick. Turned it back on and the GPU fans turn on full on 100%. Turned it back off, opened up the side panel and my GPU was like burning hot to the touch. Had to point an external fan to cool it off and waited about 30 minutes or so. Apparently the crash caused my GPU to register that it was 0 degrees, therefore even when it was physically overheating the GPU fans never turned on cause it was reading 0 degrees.
After that point I was so dissapointed and angry that I just rushed through the main storyline to just finish the game, couldn't enjoy any of the other side stuff. Overall a dissapointing experience.

"South Park: The Stick of Truth" is a game you'll enjoy if you like crass humor, because this game has a lot of it! You don't even have to be that big of a "South Park"-fan to enjoy many of those wonderful, hillarious and discusting moments this game has to offer, however, you'll get the most out of the game by watching some of the show's episodes. (Some of the references you don't get because you haven't watched the episode it's refering to might make you want to look it up and watch the episode).
The music is wonderful! The soundtrack has to be one of my favorites of all time, and it sounds very epic. The game has a few references to "The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim" in it, like the main menu looks a lot like the one it "Skyrim", with a dark/black-ish smokey background, a barbaric-sounding choir on some parts of the soundtrack, and other in-game references I won't spoil.
The only negative things I have to say about this game is the following:
1) This is a minor one, but at some times the character you're playing seems to glitch in and out fast during cutscenes. Suddenly he disappears, but before you're able to react, he's back- oh, but suddenly he's gone ag- no wait, he's back again. (You catch my drift.) And also, at some points the voice acting seems to be off. I don't know if my computer is the issue, but sometimes the characters stop talking, but their mouths still move (again, during cutscenes).
2) This one is also just nit-picking. Sometimes during combat, your opponent or even your party member will yell at you for taking too long to decide what attack you'll use. This would be fine if you actually did take a long time to decide, but they might complain 3 seconds after the battle starts! It gets kind of annoying.
3) I think they should've included more interactive events. There's only one point in the game where you'll have to choose between option A and option B, and unfortunately, no matter which one you choose, it won't effect the game very much. It's a shame the developers didn't put more effort into that choice, and more of them would be cool.
4) Most of the side-quests are very short. Most of them are basically like "Go there, get that, then you'll get a mushroom you'll put in a cauldron to get a key." I would've loved to see longer side-quests with more depth. Perhaps the goths could have a long side-quest with a cool plot that would eventually grant you a cool, high goth-status, or something like that.
But these flaws aside, the game is fantastic! It's like you're actually in an episode of the show. And you can customize your character however you want, so you can basically BE in South Park, how cool is that?
If you can't stand classic turn-based RPG-style combat systems, I won't recomend it, but if you do, you definitely should pick this gem up. (Hint: Watch the three prequel/promo episodes called "Black Friday", "A Song of♥♥♥♥♥and Fire" and "♥♥♥♥♥♥s and Dragons" before you play. Especially if you love Game of Thrones. And even if you don't, still watch them).

Without a doubt, this is the R-Rated-iest game I've ever played.  And that's a good thing.
Not only is the spirit of South Park fully intact, but takes it to another (interactive) level.  For an Obsidian RPG, it may be a bit on the short side, but when you're talking about 12-20 hours of South Parky goodness, it's hard register that as a complaint.  I would've liked to be able to see party combat invole more than you and one chosen buddy (perhaps a party of three), but the short-ish nature of the game never causes you to feel you're missing out.  I did find myself sticking to one particular buddy throughout most of the game (Butters) rather than swapping them out a lot.
Some standout game segments include:
I've never laughed so much at a game as this one.
Some downsides... despite the fast travel system (Timmeh!), wandering back and forth in the town can feel like a bit of a drag at times, especially if you're pursuing side quests and collectibles.  (Using a gamepad) The "magic" controls I found to be a bit tedious to perform beyond the basic Dragonshout ability.  The blocking mechanic during combat (which is more or less an absolute must) seemed sluggish at times, or flat-out unresponsive, resulting in a fair amount of lost battles or at least longer ones.  Also, there is an enormous amount of gear in this game, a lot of which doesn't seem to necessarily correlate well with the four basic character classes, so it usually seemed superfluous and unnecessary (that being said, some of the outfits and descriptions are absolutely hilarious).  None of these elements, however, really much detracted from the hilarity and enjoyment otherwise gained.
If you like South Park, and can at least stomach RPGs as a game-form, you will
this game.

Ok, ok, ok, ,...We all know the launch was terrible, but I am reviewing the game as is currently.  I am a HUGE batman fan, and have loved all the arkham games, with City being one of my favorite games of all times.  The map is huge, but sparsely populated.  I actually feel that  Arkham City had more enemies on the streets.  The combat is just as great as the previous installments, and when you do have other characters with you can do dual takedowns which look great, but these moments are not that often.  The gadgets are very similar to the rest of the series, and I feel the emphasis on this game is more combat driven, and less stealth/predator in comparison to the previous entries.  That being said, you have more control on how you want to go about clearing a room of enemies.  I geeked out at the fact you can walk around GCPD, a lab in the Studio area, oracle's office in the clocktower, and even Wayne Tower where Lucius Fox is, but there really isnt much going on there --its fan service mainly.  The story was definetly high stakes, and did get me addicted.  I actually enjoyed driving the bat-tank around, as it reminded me of the Dark Knight Returns Batmobile, and while there are riots in progress, batman might need a riot tank.  However, I HATED the fact that you are forced to use it, and combat it in can be a bit boring after awhile.  If it remained a choice, I may have loved it, but the fact you are forced to use plenty of time in order to progress was irksome and frustrating.
All that being said, I thought it was a satsifying ending to the series, and I was sucked into the story; hardocre batman fans will be pleased.  Yes the launch was terrible, but don't let that force you into missing a great game, that concludes a great series!  I highly recommend this game.

I don't recommend this game, unless you are a diehard fan of the series and can catch the game on sale. I was well aware of the performance issues for the PC version going in, but being a diehard fan I really wanted to play and enjoy this game. I'll admit that the game is gorgeous but only when it's working properly. Some issues I ran into were inconsistent frame rates, dropping down from 60fps to as low as 25fps, stuttering, periods where the game ran fine for 5+ hours, periods where the game crashed every 10 minutes or so.
Not to mention I just built a new PC gaming rig and this game almost killed my brand new R9 380. Had one crash where I got and error message and was booted to the desktop. Thought, ok that's fine I'll just reboot the game up. About 10-15 minutes in I started smelling a burning plastic smell. I had on a pair of headphones so I couldn't hear of my GPU fans were on, crawl under my desk to see that my GPU fans weren't spinning. Opened up HWmonitor and it says my GPU temps are 0 degrees, which I knew was an error right away so I shut off the PC in a panick. Turned it back on and the GPU fans turn on full on 100%. Turned it back off, opened up the side panel and my GPU was like burning hot to the touch. Had to point an external fan to cool it off and waited about 30 minutes or so. Apparently the crash caused my GPU to register that it was 0 degrees, therefore even when it was physically overheating the GPU fans never turned on cause it was reading 0 degrees.
After that point I was so dissapointed and angry that I just rushed through the main storyline to just finish the game, couldn't enjoy any of the other side stuff. Overall a dissapointing experience.

The Stick of Truth would probably cater best to an occasional gamer, who knows a lot about the show, but hasn't necessarily seen all the episodes. Gameplay-wise it's a pleasant surprise, because the turn based combat is sprinkled with the ability to mitigate damage with timed reactions. However, in spite of some tactics present, it can get a little bit repetitive and (at least on normal difficulty) you get OP real quick. The ability to dispose of enemies using the environment in some cases livens things up. From the story perspective, the Stick of Truth is a bunch of references and fart jokes, which would normally be completely fine, but the clever satire and social critique present in the original show is greatly under-represented in the game and along with the simple plot creates a story mostly disappointing to a die hard fan. Without the collectibles and achievements, the game would seriously lack replayabilty. You will still have fun playing it, you'll laugh at most of the new jokes, you'll feel nostalgic and enjoy every little callback to the show, but if you're looking for a deeper gaming experience and/or expect the game to be a real South Park RPG experience, you'll have to squint your eyes to find it. If I were to compare it to a South Park episode, it's definitely not Scott Tenorman, ironically it's not Make Love, Not Warcraft either, but it's a solid Cancelled or Margaritaville level - worth remebering, but not quite legendary.
