Risk of Rain is a retro style game that suits well to those who just want to mindlessly destroy things. It has a variety of unlockable character (which is rare in most games, be it big or small). The gameplay is fun, and it's definitely a fun game to play with a buddy . . . that is if you are lucky to not encounter bugs.
The enjoyment of playing this game is only matched by the multitude of bugs that you will encounter.
Within one night, I have had unlocked characters dissapear 3 times due to the game crashing.
I have experienced monsters showing up on one players screen but not another (meanwhile there are objective that require all monsters to be slain to complete the level) This means you are unable to complete the level if your teammates are dead yet are the only ones who can see the monsters. I have seen invincible monsters, teleporting monsters (the connection between players in RoR is poorly implemented). I have played countless games with said person, in which connection speed is stellar. Additionally, we both openned ports, and made sure firewall was not blocking.
I have experienced falling through the levels, invisible walls, areas that disable your jump. Additionally, I have seen chests(while using the artifact that makes item drops not random) become locked for the player that uses a special key item - only teammates can open the items.
If you really unlucky, you will encounter a bug that progressively uses up memory until you run into a "Out of memory" warning. This will promptly close the game, making you lose all progress(including unlocked characters).
However, most annoying is the ability for RoR to freeze up most of your components if a crash occurs. Alt-tab no longer works, and using ctrl-alt-delete to bring up the task manager doesn't work either, since Risk of rain does failts to then properly alt tab.  (This may be an issue with Windows 8 and Game Maker, however I do not know enough about how GameMaker ports games over to Windows and if it is the true culrpit) I ended up having to sign out of my profile to get the operating system to automatically close any open programs.
This game has a lot of potential, but as of now, it is definitely not worth getting for full price, let alone 25% off. If it goes on sale for 50%+, grab it. But as of now, it just has too many bugs that truly hinder the user experience to warrant buying for anything more.

I enjoyed the game on first release and peaked around the time Firebug was added.  The shooting is great and the first-person animations are top-notch. Then there was a long stretch of very little new content and (later a 50% chance of) an un-fun and unwinnable boss fight that turned me off the game.
Well, I suppose it's only fitting it should rise from the dead having left Early Access.  Class balance is back in a good place now that arbitrary monster resistances have been toned down, and almost everyone (save the pointless Survivalist class) has something to contribute though a bit less so for the boss fights.  Speaking of boss fights, Hans is no longer a solid wall of frustrating instant death.
A fun horde shooter (don't even bother with Vs mode) but be prepared for balance to swing the wrong way sometimes given its history.  Good for a few weeks here and there but not one of my multiplayer mainstays like Battlefield 4, Mass Effect 3 or bigger actions games are / have been.

Risk of Rain is a retro style game that suits well to those who just want to mindlessly destroy things. It has a variety of unlockable character (which is rare in most games, be it big or small). The gameplay is fun, and it's definitely a fun game to play with a buddy . . . that is if you are lucky to not encounter bugs.
The enjoyment of playing this game is only matched by the multitude of bugs that you will encounter.
Within one night, I have had unlocked characters dissapear 3 times due to the game crashing.
I have experienced monsters showing up on one players screen but not another (meanwhile there are objective that require all monsters to be slain to complete the level) This means you are unable to complete the level if your teammates are dead yet are the only ones who can see the monsters. I have seen invincible monsters, teleporting monsters (the connection between players in RoR is poorly implemented). I have played countless games with said person, in which connection speed is stellar. Additionally, we both openned ports, and made sure firewall was not blocking.
I have experienced falling through the levels, invisible walls, areas that disable your jump. Additionally, I have seen chests(while using the artifact that makes item drops not random) become locked for the player that uses a special key item - only teammates can open the items.
If you really unlucky, you will encounter a bug that progressively uses up memory until you run into a "Out of memory" warning. This will promptly close the game, making you lose all progress(including unlocked characters).
However, most annoying is the ability for RoR to freeze up most of your components if a crash occurs. Alt-tab no longer works, and using ctrl-alt-delete to bring up the task manager doesn't work either, since Risk of rain does failts to then properly alt tab.  (This may be an issue with Windows 8 and Game Maker, however I do not know enough about how GameMaker ports games over to Windows and if it is the true culrpit) I ended up having to sign out of my profile to get the operating system to automatically close any open programs.
This game has a lot of potential, but as of now, it is definitely not worth getting for full price, let alone 25% off. If it goes on sale for 50%+, grab it. But as of now, it just has too many bugs that truly hinder the user experience to warrant buying for anything more.

Almost tactically perfect and strategically sound, XCOM features a very polished experience.
Defend the Earth from the stereotypical invaders with ever-evolving weapons and research to even the odds. Build a base, hire more soldiers, train them, mourn them and juggle your priorities. The one-more-turn syndrome at its best. Lots of customisation options will give your soldiers distinct personalities (at least for you) and you'll have to take care of your team if you are to succeed.
A reimagining of very old game that builds on good premises and an interesting story, XCOM will keep you on your toes both on the battlefield and in the Command Room. Higher difficulties offer a painful---but fun---gameplay, complete with permadeath and tough economic decisions. The requirements are flexible enough to accomodate for fairly old systems and laptops.
One thing that deserves to be mentioned: do not expect ancient X-COM mechanics because this is not the same game. Even if somewhat simplified in comparison, this modern tribute never fails to deliver. It is a fine iteration better suited for current times.
If you like aliens, RTTs or strategy board games, you should seriously give this game a try. The expansion Enemy Within is a must; it adds so much to the game that it should be installed and played right from the beginning.
Highly recommended.

South Park: The Stick of Truth has a high production value and puts other South Park games to shame. Although it started out very buggy, the Steam version appears to have been patched enough now to restore the game to its intended glory.
Combat is simple but active (like a Mario RPG), and the variety of items, weapons, armor, and equipment mods makes for a compelling set of base mechanics. But don't expect it to go much deeper than that. The focus here is on the characters, story, and staying true to the franchise, not on combat strategy or (for the most part) exploration.
As has been said by many others, if you like South Park and its brand of humor then you'll like this game. But if you're looking for rich, engaging gameplay instead of an interactive story book then you should probably look somewhere else.

It transitions seemlessly into a Rock Opera in the second half, with this critic hardly noticing the transition. This movie is a fantastic change from the usual Tim Burton film with our second half Rock Opera heroes, Maria Di Forest & Pitt Johnson (Helena Bonham Carter & Johnny Depp). First of all: I'm really dissapointed in the responsibles, who said, that it's ok to release a game, that could be an instant masterpiece, in a state that was sometimes not just messy, but unplayable...The other thing is Arkham Origins.....Don't get Me wrong, it was a good game, but let's be honest, it was just a reskinned Arkham City, with a different story....Because of this Arkham Knight is not as fresh in the eyes of majority of gamers as it meant to be....
To Everyone: THIS IS THE ULTIMATE BATMAN EXPERIENCE. The Story is incredible, brutal, dark, logical, but not easy to get over with, it will stuck in Your head, and You will think about it, don't mention the side stories! They are equally amazing, the only complain about them is the Riddler line, it was too long for my taste, but not a breaking mistake! ...and then the MUSIC, combine it with the design of Gotham and You will see and hear something truly wonderful! The Batmobile is fun, the control is tight, the combat system got fine tuned also, don't expect a revolution, it evolved just as needed.
Without Arkham Origins, 4 years of waiting for a new Batman game would have made Us just as hungry for it as We should be, but with all these mistakes I mentioned before, I'm afraid that many won't even try to play it for long, and if You love Batman as much as I do, You really should give it a chance to prove, because it won't let You down!
Thanks for Rocksteady, THEY made Me Love Batman, and whatever They do next, I'm sure, I will play it! :)

It transitions seemlessly into a Rock Opera in the second half, with this critic hardly noticing the transition. This movie is a fantastic change from the usual Tim Burton film with our second half Rock Opera heroes, Maria Di Forest & Pitt Johnson (Helena Bonham Carter & Johnny Depp). I certainly enjoyed this festive exposition of pure narrative and I'm sure you all will too.

I'd like to give you a fair warning that this is quite a long review with proper detail on why I'm not recommending this game.
I remember the major excitement I had when Killing Floor 2 was first announced as I was a huge fan of the first Killing Floor, and at the time it looked quite promising with great potential. During early access, I was highly intrigued waiting for what's going to come next for the game as time passed. However as time passed, the game kept sinking cause of Tripwire's lack of effort.
Killing Floor 2's Early Access was released on April 21st 2015.
It presented 4 of the main perks; Commando, Support Specialist, Berzerker, and Field Medic. In addition to 3 maps; Burning Paris, Biotics Lab, and Outpost.
Let's start by comparing a few things between both games at that specific time.
Killing Floor 2 is more action-oriented, while the first Killing Floor had the horror atmosphere which made it quite unique and thrilling. However KF2 still had the advantage of being eye-candy with the proper graphics work on the maps and the zeds.
The zeds in KF2 were refined, but I happened to disagree with a couple of zed designs; the fleshpound, and the scrake. While some may say that both are much scarier in this game than in the first, I can quite frankly disagree. In the first game, when a scrake or a fleshpound popped up, you had to be properly prepared as there was no warning as to how many are coming or where they are. In the second game, there's a sound alert for each of them which removes the horror sense of it, and gives you a bit of time to prepare yourself making it easier for players.
Regarding the zed design, in KF2 the fleshpound and the scrake were made bulkier and slightly shorter. Although I agree with the scrake's new design in skin color, I did not understand the need to bulk them up, at least not to this much extent. The fleshpound's skin color in KF2 looks more human like rather than dark and more twisted in the first game which gave the original fleshpound a more intimidating feeling. While some may disagree with that fact, I do not find the KF2 fleshpound in anyway intimidating except in the sense that we know it's a very powerful zed, but not from its appearance.
You can find a reference for the difference between zeds in the first and the second game here
Other things regarding other zeds that I feel slightly disappointed in such as the Siren's scream power with the particle effect looking cartoonish rather than shaking your entire screen similar to the first game. In addition to the lack of audio work when it comes to the Zeds in the second game. In the first Killing Floor, the zeds spoke which gave them their own unique auras or whatever you may call it. It gave them character whilst in the second game, all you hear are normal monster noises which makes you feel like they're just mindless zeds.
Firebug and Demolition perks were later introduced to the game. Needless to say, anyone who played the first game should know how powerful the demo is. In KF2, it's the exact opposite. To summarize, they made the firebug cause more explosions than the demolition man himself.
Regarding the weapon designs in the game, as beautiful as those designs may be, 70 - 80% of those weapons feel like pure mush lacking proper kick to them whether it's in use or regarding the audio. AA12, trench gun, 9 mm, lever action (Winchester), etc. All of them lack the kick/audio eargasm that they used to have in the first game. In addition to the inability to properly use off-perk weapons in the second game which will most definitely get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you by zeds in the game whilst in the first you could get creative with your combinations; Field Medic and Trench gun/Crossbow, Berzerker and Deagles/Flare Pistols, etc.
When micro-transactions were introduced to the game, it was a huge disappointment. As much as people appreciate beautiful skins for weapons, we all considered the fact that good time was spent on this particular 'feature' instead of that time being used on the actual game making it more balanced regarding the perks or the weapons or presenting new content. Instead, they presented players with crates and USBs (Keys) similar to CS:GO where you get crate drops, and you spend 2.49$ to buy a USB to unlock the crate and get a skin. It's a highly useless addition to the game that was not needed yet it was added anyway.
Another update was Versus mode presenting you the option to play as a Zed. I will not deny that I found the mode quite interesting, but it was short lived. The game had been released at the time for almost a year, and it only had 6 perks,  around 6 maps if I recall correctly, micro-transactions, and versus mode. Many fans were voicing their concerns in the forums regarding the game's lack of balance or content and TWI's slow progress with the game. I was shocked to find out from many players that TWI has been banning users for their criticism or for them presenting any kind of negative point regarding the game as well as censoring a lot of posts with no proper reason.
Gunslinger was presented a few months ago giving the game a bit of new life with new content and new weapons with a glorious return of the old beloved deagles in the game.
Outrage filled the forums when many months have passed and TWI has not yet presented any new content regarding the Sharpshooter perk or anything extra. When sharpshooter was finally released, it was released in beta while the game itself is still in early access until now. The content of the sharpshooter raised a bit of skepticism with the rail-gun being highly OP at the beginning of the update, and the sharpshooter's grenade with the function of freezing the zeds, making the grenade a bit unrelated to the sharpshooter's role in the game.
Accompanying the sharpshooter update is a small modification to the boss fights in the second game; adding a health bar to the bosses and making Hans a much easier boss to kill where you have a chance to shoot down his shield before/during his healing.
Today, I have come across one final announcement that pushed me into writing this review. Killing Floor: Incursion.
Killing Floor: Incursion is an announcement trailer for a VR Killing Floor game. At this point, I was highly outraged among many other Killing Floor fans when this announcement was released. Instead of TWI putting all its effort and focus on finishing a great game that once had great potential, they strayed away when the game brought good money from its early access and micro transactions, and started working on different projects.
Rather than listening to what the players want or thinking of ways on how to improve the game, they simply did not.
Killing Floor 1 will always be my ultimate favorite multiplayer game on steam, and I'm sad to say that -in my personal opinion and others'- the second game will /never/ live up to the first.
I definitely do not recommend this game.

Alright, it's probably time to update this from my early access review.
Killing Floor 2 has the potential to be an extremely fun game. However, it frequently isn't. I'll start by saying that if you have a group of friends to consistently play with who don't suck, this is probably worth getting, especially since there are few decent co-op games on Steam that go over 4 players (KF2 supports 6). If you're pretty casual and don't plan to play above Hard mode, this game will be consistently pretty fun until you get bored and move on. Otherwise, here's a list of things that could ruin the experience:
- An exceptionally long grind that can force you to return to lower difficulty settings if you don't level every class you plan on playing evenly
- Level design that's all about new and interesting ways to screw the players over (unless you're playing the PvP and playing as zeds but lol if you're doing that) - and let me give a special shoutout here to waist-high railings that are aggravatingly inconsistent to jump over
- Teammates on public servers being awful (the game scales expecting each player to pull their weight)
- Tripwire deciding the core gameplay doesn't meet their ~vision~ for the game and changing it overnight with no warning (this has happened multiple times)
- Tripwire deciding a glaring issue with the game can wait until their next major content drop (usually months away - they should be out of glaring issues to cause but be ready)
- Getting to the boss wave and the boss deciding to two-shot everyone one by one with melee attacks
- Getting stuck on awkward level geometry and immediately being surrounded by an entire wave of zeds
- Not having the mindset of "losing is fun!" (this is different than "losing can be fun")
I'll finish by saying this game has one of the best gore systems out there if you're using an NVidia card (and still a pretty good one if you're not). If you just want to blow off body parts in slow motion with a shotgun, this game will scratch that itch very well. It'll also just scratch you in unwanted places from time to time because it doesn't know any better. I want to recommend this game but there's so much that can sour the experience and Steam doesn't have a system beyond "yes/no" so for now I'm going to leave it at no.

I've finally completed 100% of the game and unlocked the true ending. Did I enjoy it? You bet!
I've played all of the Arkham Games and I, like many others, wasn't too happy with Origins. Rocksteady is back at the helm for this game and it's GOOD. RS wrote a great story line with excellent scripts for the entire cast. The story is is the best out of all the games in the series and while you definitely expect certain events to happen before they actually do happen the orchestration of the events make you enjoy every second of the story.
Something about Origins' fighting gameplay always felt off to me. Like the beat of a song being screwed up. RS has implemented their trusted combat controls and controlling Batman is as fluid as it was before. Major Batman villains are worked into the story in a non-forced manner and create a fun filler experience during the main story or after you complete the main story to activate the ending. If there's one bad thing there it's that you NEED to do those side-quests to activate one ending. And then you need to 100% the game (including Riddler Trophies) for the true ending. Seriously? Collect all Riddler trophies? I've done it just to do it and I hated every minute of it. I think I spend 10-15 hours on those damn things alone. I felt like Rocksteady spread my cheeks and forced those effing trophies into my happy, carefree world when they stripped me of my trophy virginity. I fear I cannot play any of the other Arkham games ever again without shedding a tear if I see another green '?'. So spare yourself the misery and just look up the true ending on YouTube instead.
The Batmobile is a forced addition into the game and it's a little overdone, but not to the point of boredom. I also feel that the Batmobile sequences are done very well and tight controls make it extremely rewarding when you're up against seemingly impossible odds. It's BATMAN after all! There were one or two times when I was extremely frustrated by a seemingly impossible task, but once I did complete the mission it was one of the most rewarding events in my gaming history. Kinda like when you beat Ganondorf for the first time but without the confusion that followed.
Graphics look great even on Medium settings. It certainly looks as good or better than Origins. I have 2 780 Ti's (not that it matters because this game doesn't support SLI) and I can play on 5900x1080 on medium settings. That's not as good as I'd hoped but still much better than how it was at launch, apparently. If you have SLI cards change the game to be in windowed mode without borders. Somehow it just runs better that way than in fullscreen mode even though it looks exactly the same.
52 hours in, 100% completion, am I going to play NG+? You bet I am. I can't wait to go through the story again. It's that good. Thank goodness the Riddler trophies carry over *shudder*.

Alright, it's probably time to update this from my early access review.
Killing Floor 2 has the potential to be an extremely fun game. However, it frequently isn't. I'll start by saying that if you have a group of friends to consistently play with who don't suck, this is probably worth getting, especially since there are few decent co-op games on Steam that go over 4 players (KF2 supports 6). If you're pretty casual and don't plan to play above Hard mode, this game will be consistently pretty fun until you get bored and move on. Otherwise, here's a list of things that could ruin the experience:
- An exceptionally long grind that can force you to return to lower difficulty settings if you don't level every class you plan on playing evenly
- Level design that's all about new and interesting ways to screw the players over (unless you're playing the PvP and playing as zeds but lol if you're doing that) - and let me give a special shoutout here to waist-high railings that are aggravatingly inconsistent to jump over
- Teammates on public servers being awful (the game scales expecting each player to pull their weight)
- Tripwire deciding the core gameplay doesn't meet their ~vision~ for the game and changing it overnight with no warning (this has happened multiple times)
- Tripwire deciding a glaring issue with the game can wait until their next major content drop (usually months away - they should be out of glaring issues to cause but be ready)
- Getting to the boss wave and the boss deciding to two-shot everyone one by one with melee attacks
- Getting stuck on awkward level geometry and immediately being surrounded by an entire wave of zeds
- Not having the mindset of "losing is fun!" (this is different than "losing can be fun")
I'll finish by saying this game has one of the best gore systems out there if you're using an NVidia card (and still a pretty good one if you're not). If you just want to blow off body parts in slow motion with a shotgun, this game will scratch that itch very well. It'll also just scratch you in unwanted places from time to time because it doesn't know any better. I want to recommend this game but there's so much that can sour the experience and Steam doesn't have a system beyond "yes/no" so for now I'm going to leave it at no.

When Batman Arkham Knight first came out on PC it was a complete disaster; I like many other PC gamers was very annoyed at how poorly it ran and how frequently it crashed; however I was on the lucky side of the stick and was able to complete the game.
On October 28th the Interim Patch was finally released (as well as all the DLC up until that point); the game also went back on sale and things from here started to look up - the game ran much better and there were a lot more options available for PC users such as framerate cap, Anisotropic Filtering, higher quality textures, shadows and lighting. Since Oct 28th the game received an update every month (up until the point I'm writing this review) that would have performance fixes, stability improvements and included DLC that was being released monthly in the Season Pass.
Batman Arkham Knight runs
better than it did on day one; provided you meet the system requirements you should have no issues running the game. Just make sure you have the latest drivers.
I haven't focused much on the gameplay/story side because there are thousands of other reviews out there - I will say this; if you're going to get this game you need the Season Pass; the extra DLC, AR challenges, Story Packs and Skins really adds necessary depth to the game.
I am quite happy changing this review from a negative to a positive - I would also imagine most negative reviews are pre Oct 28th. I'm not endorsing the state the game was originally released in but the fact is it runs a lot smoother; if you are still holding off buying the game just go and get it.
While it may not be the epic finale we deserved it's still a great game any 'Arkham' fan should pick-up.
P.S. I can guarantee people will rate this down because even 7 months later it's still the cool thing to hate on this game.

As do most other games in this genre (survival horror), Dead Space relies heavily on stilted set pieces and triggered events that were supposedly designed to knock the gamers out of their seat. You can smell them coming from a mile away and they rarely amount to a true "horror" experience. Rather, they come off as predictable, annoying, and just simply trying too hard. I don't appreciate these "dire" moments (not enough ammo, low lighting, jumpy music, doors-that-you-KNOW-there-are-monsters-behind-but-HAVE-to-open-by-design) that are so artificial and are solely designed to manipulate you. I REALLY tried to finish this game, but at one point, I was stuck with not nearly enough ammo to clear the level that I was in and I had no intention to go back a few save files and retread the same boring shtick. And I'm supposed to feel "scared" and "horrified" because I don't have anything to defend myself with? Come on!

One of the most challenging games I've played to date, and yet one of the most fun. Dead Space sucessfully combines the horror element of a game with an excellent storyline. It makes you feel like you are completely alone, even though you've got friends talking to you over the radio. And unlike games like Amnesia and Penumbra, it doesn't warn you when there's a monster nearby, so you get a heck of a surprise. And ammo is extremely limited, so you can't just blast through the levels. All of these elements combined actually guide the player to look at their surroundings, which adds even more to the horror atmosphere. Pretty much the only thing I'd change is the level guide that tells you where to go. It would be a bit more fun and challenging if you had to figure out where to go next on your own.

Proof positive that not everything needs to be a first-person shooter (not that there's anything wrong with that).
Okay, fine, details.  You don't have to be familiar with the series to appreciate the concept - nutshelled as "ALIENS WRECKING OUR STUFF KILL THEM TAKE THEIR STUFF STUDY IT TO KILL THEM BETTER" - and there's little pesky plot to get in the way of managing the crisis.  In fact, "crisis management" is probably a better name for this type of game, as it blends sim elements with turn-based strategy to deal with alien threats across the globe.
As hybrid games go, XCOM hits the sweet spot that makes it very easy to keep playing, regularly introducing new mechanics, toys, and threats to deal with.  You'll feel the difference as you unlock new tech, and feel is the right word for it; it's immensely satisfying to start flinging lasers and UFOs right back at the enemy.  Environments are destructible on a Silent Storm scale, meaning you can blast through a wall if doors and windows are inconvenient or too boring.  Rockets and grenades become tools for the imaginative.
It's not always fair, even by hardcore standards, and I would caution against an Ironman run on your first time.  There are too many bugs and interface glitches that can ruin your day in a single turn, sometimes by spawning actual bugs which kill your team then reanimate the corpses to kill the rest of your team.  It's that kind of game.
Here's the bottom line.  Do you like turn-based strategy?  Do you enjoy advancing under overlapping cover, trying to coax foul Xenos into your carefully-arranged chokepoint?  Do you dream of managing base construction so your power generators are linked for redundant bonuses?  Can you live with occasionally fussy movement controls on multi-level missions?  Then go welcome them to Earth already.

For such a simple game, Super Hexagon has incredible replayability.  The concept is simple: make your character (a triangle) dodge the incoming lines.  These walls are coming to the center of the screen from the outside, and all you have to do is dodge left or right.
Easier said than done.  Hop right into the easiest difficulty, which is Hard (also named Hexagon).  Each mode has a hyper mode that is unlocked when you survive for 60 seconds.  Good luck getting there on Hexagonest.
The challenge of this game is very simple, and thus can be very relaxing, if you just sit back, let loose, and don't take it seriously.  Test your perception, reaction time and reflexes, and sensitivity as each mode increases the speed your triangle moves as well as how fast the lines come in at you.
This game can be incredibly fun if you like challenges.  The challenge of it is somewhat like the bullet hell shooters, but more satisfying and less overwhelming.  Definitely much easier with a controller, though.

Risk of Rain is a very hard rogue-like 2D action platformer, with some elements of an RPG game.
So there's a ship - UES Contact Light - it's carrying various chests and stuff. This ship is shot out of its orbit by an unknown being and crash lands on a planet. You survive the crash landing, but for how long?
Basically you start out at your pod's crash site, everything around you is hostile and tries to destroy you while you run and retaliate for your life. Killing creatures gives you coins, and you use these coins to unlock chests that give you items/power-ups. Some of the items are initially locked and to be able to obtain them, you'll have to play the game (see the Steam achievements). The items that the chests give you are randomly selected. Some are more useful than the others. Items' effects stack, so you can attack at 200% rate or have a 50m radius barbed wire to protect you, etc.
You will also run into Shrines. These Shrines will require something from you for a chance to drop an item.
But here's the catch: the longer you play, the harder the game gets. Chests need more coins to be unlocked. Enemies will gain additional abilities, bosses become common spawns.
"It's hard, I get it, but what's the goal of the game?"
The player's goal in Risk of Rain is to get back to the UES Contact Light and get off the planet. To do this, the player must first, pass 5 stages by activating "Teleporters". Teleporters are placed randomly on each map. After beating 5 stages, the player can have 2 choices: teleport to the final level, or revisit the previous ones and get more items (or be killed miserably).
Oh, this game features perma-death, which means dying equals to losing all of your items and having to start over.
While you only have 1 survivor to select at the beginning, there's a total of 10 survivors for you to select after completing certain challenges. Each with their own unique abilites. From the balanced Commando to the highly versatile Huntress.
The artstyle and music are also great additions to the core game. While being 2D, the game looks fantastic with a lot of spectacular particles, and soundtracks that will give you a sense of curiosity.
The OSTs were made by Chris Chistodoulou. Visit his bandcamp
.
TL; DR:
A ship carrying passengers and goods crash lands on a planet with its locals being hostile to anything outside. You are a survivor, fighting for your life. Killing creatures gives you coins and you use these coins to purchase upgrades. The ultimate goal is to reach the ship that crash landed and get off the planet.
Items are given randomly.
The more you play, the harder it gets. With the hardest difficulty being "HAHAHAHA".
That's pretty much it. The replay value of the game lies in its "random item" mechanic and a wide selection of characters.
So, if you enjoy rogue-like, RPG, action, platforming, 2D and suffering, I strongly recommend this game.
Seriously, it's great. Buy it.

Risk of Rain is a game that doesn't ease you into things. you're into the thick of it, right away. No tutorials, no long intro, nada. This is both its greatest strength and its biggest weakness. It makes it insanely replayable, but it also makes it difficult to get into initially. The starting class is very well balanced, but to the point that it becomes a jack of all trades. It does well at everything, but doesnt excell at any particular one either. This is not really a weakness, however, as it introduces a multitude of different playstyles. The biggest strength of the game comes from its replayability. I personally have gotten to the point where I almost never lose on normal difficulty. This means that I go to the very end and beat the final boss almost every game I play. And for those who play this game and know what this is; I don't use boar beach. And yet, even with this being the case, I still have a very high amount of replayability. The highest difficulty is on an entirely different level to the normal difficulty, and thats not a bad thing. It prevents the game from getting stale, as the reason it is replayable is that it always provides a higher challenge for you. You beat the game with your favorite class? Alright, try a harder difficulty, or a different class. The game is only over once you say it is, and it provides enough variety that its pretty difficult to put down. All in all, its a wonderful little game, with a beautiful soundtrack. I thoroughly recommend it to anyone who enjoys challenging games, and I still encourage others to try it out as well. It wont be your favorite game of all time, but it may very well keep you going after it longer than your favorite game.

Batman: Arkham Knight is an open-world action game developed by Rocksteady, published by Warner Brothers, and ported to PC by Iron Galaxy. This game is infamous for its atrocious launch, when it was riddled so much with bugs, frame rate locks, missing features, and general horrible performance that WB felt the need to pull it from shelves and encourage people to get refunds. Now, however, most of the bugs and issues have been ironed out, and it is definitely a fantastic game and an acceptable PC port. Please note that in this review I will be trying not to compare it to previous Arkham games, but I will be using Origins if I do.
The game uses the FreeFlow combat system, as in the previous Arkham games, but this time with new Environmental Takedowns, enemy types, and general combat improvements over previous Arkham games. My main issue with the stealth system in previous games is that it is incredibly difficult, if not near-impossible, to effectively deal with a room full of armed enemies. In Arkham Knight, this issue is addressed by adding a multi-enemy takedown that is earned by pulling off Silent takedowns. The areas have more vertical depth, and you can enter grates from the vantage points. A new gadget, the Voice Synthesizer, allows you to actually order enemies around once you obtain it. The Disruptor has received a major buff as well, now having 4 shots total (after one upgrade), and it can disable even more weapons and environmental objects. The addition of automated turrets adds another layer of challenge in that you have to disable their sensors using the Remote Hacking Device and knock out all the enemies in 60 seconds before it comes back online and guns you down.
One of the strong points of this game is how good it feels to just move around the open world, be it in the Batmobile crushing through buildings and crowds of rioters as you zoom along the streets of Gotham, or flying amongst the tallest buildings and grappling you way to your goal, it just feels good. The Grapnel Accelerator has also received a buff, allowing you to boost yourself 5 times (after 3 upgrades), becoming insanely fast. It can be infuriating, however, to mash your space bar so much every time you grapple to a new location. The mandatory "Open-World-game-collectible-items" are here again in the form of, again, Riddler Trophies. Riddler Trophies will either take the form of items that you merely have to go to the right location to pick up, or rewards for completing puzzles. You can find the location of Riddler Trophies by interrogating Riddler Informants that will randomly spawn throughout Gotham. In previous Arkham games, you could actually take down the Riddler Informant and still interrogate him afterwards, but in Arkham Knight you must keep them alive, which can get infuriating pretty quickly.
Gotham is divided into three islands, Founders Island (The hardest), Miagani Island, and Bleake Island (The easiest). You start out on Bleake Island, but can fly to the other islands any time you wish. You cannot, however, drive the Batmobile to the other islands until you lower the bridges at some point in the main story quest. Each island has a "threat level", which denotes how many drone tanks/checkpoints/watchtowers/quadcopters the main enemy has remaining on each island.
The Batmobile is Batman's personal car that you can drive around almost at your leisure. At almost any point in the game, you can press a button when looking at a street and the Batmobile will be summoned to your location. The Batmobile can also turn into a maneuverable tank by holding RMB, in which mode you are armed with Riot Suppressors (nonlethal rounds), two Vulkan guns, and a 60mm cannon. As the story progresses, you are given more secondary weapons, which you can use after charge is build up by blowing up more tanks in the Batmobile.
I like the Batmobile, I really do. However, the game forces you to use it waaaay too much for my taste, and it starts to feel a bit weird the more you use it. First off, let's just point out that Gotham's streets are full of objects. Boxes, walls, pillars, even those portable toilet things are lining the streets in Arkham Knight. Instead of having these objects as permanent obstructions to the Batmobile, Rocksteady opted to make almost all of these objects destructible with either your twin machine guns, 60mm cannon, or just by rolling over them. This kind of goes against Batman's motto somewhat, as he's incurring enough property damage to probably collapse a building on some poor crowd who went to the "Prometheus Academy of Running Away from Things." On top of that, it just feels like...everything is made of weak foam. There's very little resistance on anything, even solid concrete pillars supporting buildings. It creates this weird feeling of non-substance on the car, something that you never want when designing a driving mode.
Let's face it, it's not a perfect PC port by any means. It will drop to 45 frames per second in some areas. The GameWorks smoke WILL destroy your framerate whenever you rev up the Batmobile. However, I ran with these settings:
and had an overall amazing graphical experience that is well suited to a modern AAA title. The GameWorks Smoke & Fog effect is an absolute waste, So I turned it off immediately, but the other effects actually look quite good and don't have much of a performance hit as far as I could tell.
The game just looks...amazing. By far one of the best looking games ever released, it boasts excellent lighting, wetness effects, reflections, the best rain I've ever seen, particle effects, and cloth on Batman's cape. I have to criticize their off-looking skin effects, however. It's almost as if it's trying to be SubSurface Scattering, but isn't quite there. Nevertheless, it looks great and it runs fairly well on my system (i7 4790k/GTX 970).
At launch, there was a controversy over the PC version missing wetness textures, but I can assure you that they're present now.
The story revolves around the Arkham Knight, a mysterious masked villain who's out for revenge on Batman, and Scarecrow. The Knight is actually a new character created exclusively for this game, which is failrly uncommon to see in a DC game. I won't spoil the specifics of the plot twist here, but
Scarecrow has threatened Gotham with his new batch of fear toxin, and Gotham is evacuated, leaving the Arkham Knight's militia to take control of the city.
I've never really felt intimidated by Scarecrow as a main villain up until now, he's always been just that guy who wears a bag on his head. In Arkham Knight, however, a combination of his redesign and his fantastic voice acting by John Noble (I just have to mention it) creates a genuinely fear-inducing antagonist. In fact, all the characters are very well voice acted.
Overall, the story is very well written and touches on the different characters for just the right amount of time before moving on. Almost every mission feels unique, and they all tie together very nicely.
I would talk more about this game, but the character limit is cutting me a bit short here. Overall, Arkham Knight has fantastic combat, graphics, and story, and overall great side activities and open world. I've explored every inch of this Gotham, and I encourage you to do so as well.

There are still framerate drops, FPS is still stuck at 30 from what I've seen and at one point I jumped through a building and fell into a never-ending hole so I had to reset the game.

How good is XCOM? That's a great question. Playing it made me feel very nostalgic. This is funny, because I've never played a game in the series or anything else like it. the reason it feels so familiar is that it is old-school is its ideas and modern in its execution. You never stop finding new things to build, fix, take care of or customize. The battles of ETs vs XCOM fighters are difficult, but never broken or skewed in favor of either side. To see one of your prized fighters that you've spent hours customizing and caring for blindsided by an alien's laser blast and die is heartbreaking, a feeling I haven't felt since Pokemon Red.
So, in short: a beautifully designed, incredibly addicitng and highly engaging experience that challenges you while rewarding your efforts. Suck it, Starcraft.

Here's a great game if you're into the "Survival Horror" genre (of which I am certainly NOT).  This was my first foray into the genre since Parasite Eve, and I've got to say it certainly delivers.  From the first moment you enter USG Ishimura, you feel haunted by a looming cloud of DEATH that could strike you at any moment.  That being said, you frequently are struck, but the game isn't unreasonable with its shocks and gives you ample time to adjust to situations.  The story is also enrapturing -- as you wander through Ishimura, you can't help but wonder what exactly happened to the inhabitants, even on a personal basis.
If you're into survival horror, you probably have already played/beaten this.  If not, it's a good game to check out with a trainer and cheat codes handy, to eliminate that "I'm going to die" psyche.

Risk of Rain is a game that doesn't ease you into things. you're into the thick of it, right away. No tutorials, no long intro, nada. This is both its greatest strength and its biggest weakness. It makes it insanely replayable, but it also makes it difficult to get into initially. The starting class is very well balanced, but to the point that it becomes a jack of all trades. It does well at everything, but doesnt excell at any particular one either. This is not really a weakness, however, as it introduces a multitude of different playstyles. The biggest strength of the game comes from its replayability. I personally have gotten to the point where I almost never lose on normal difficulty. This means that I go to the very end and beat the final boss almost every game I play. And for those who play this game and know what this is; I don't use boar beach. And yet, even with this being the case, I still have a very high amount of replayability. The highest difficulty is on an entirely different level to the normal difficulty, and thats not a bad thing. It prevents the game from getting stale, as the reason it is replayable is that it always provides a higher challenge for you. You beat the game with your favorite class? Alright, try a harder difficulty, or a different class. The game is only over once you say it is, and it provides enough variety that its pretty difficult to put down. All in all, its a wonderful little game, with a beautiful soundtrack. I thoroughly recommend it to anyone who enjoys challenging games, and I still encourage others to try it out as well. It wont be your favorite game of all time, but it may very well keep you going after it longer than your favorite game.

Before I judge this game on how well of a remake it is, I consider that it is an entirely new game, years from the original. In the same fashion that the Fallout series was adopted into mainstream play with Fallout 3, this continuation of the XCOM series pulls a similar trick. XCOM: Enemy Unknown features excellent gameplay and a pretty neat storyline. The risk/reward of each action is clearly defined and once you have the formula figured out its mostly grinding missions until game completion. Multiplayer is not a feature worth going out of your way for, with the same mechanic as single player in action, however it is still a mechanic worth grabbing a friend or two to enjoy with. The gameplay I give a high score for it is fun, exciting, and held my attention for hours. The PC controls are the biggest negative, with UI reacting poorly to mouse inputs and many options requiring two clicks to register. Menus are sticky and don't update quick enough. The character models are a bit goofy and many visual bugs in solider models and squad customization aggravate me a lot. Despite the visual hitches, the gameplay is solid and stable. One poor gameplay decision can domino a mission quickly out of control, giving this game a tense edge and making every level a risk and a thrill. XCOM:Enemy Unknown is an exciting twist to squad based tactical RPG, adding elements of base building, and over the shoulder run and gun similar to Gears of War. I give this game an 8, with high overall quality at a price I can appreciate, but losing points for many visual and interface bugs.

Risk of Rain is another take on the much beloved rogue-like game genre. Those of you who enjoyed Binding of Isaac and Rogue Legacy will probably also enjoy this little gem.
The graphics are 8-bit, not really that uncommon for an Indie game, but you can still feel the effort they put in them. They're not simply there for the reason a lot of hipster indie game developers use 8-bit graphics, i.e. for the sake of their pretentious artistic integrity. The graphics in this game are like this to convey the feeling of those old but gold and hard as heck games like Castlevania, Metroid and Cave Story. The art direction itself is also really well done. The different levels always give you a metroid-like feeling. They're beautiful, they make you wanna explore them, but at the same time they kind of frighten you, give you the feeling that at any time something bad could happen. And I know I'm repeating myself, but in the end it feels like a subtle hommage to Super Metroid and those kind of games, which in my case I can't have enough of.
The game runs and controls smoothly, the only problem I have is that you always have to pause and then skip the opening animation when you're starting it up. Also the partial support of the gamepad really throws me off, because you can't select your characters with it or look at the items. Can't really say anything about the coop, because I haven't tried it yet, so I won't.
The gameplay itself is also very well executed. You can play as ten different characters, which not only look, but also play differently. From the long-ranged, flexible, but not that much damage dealing Commando to the very close ranged Acrid, they all have their own perks and, of course, disadvantages. Most of them are unlocked if you do something special, so that you have a little motivation to play the game besides just finishing it. The action skills (four of them) you have in this game are almost always active skills, besides the items you pick up. Which brings me to the next point: items/passive skills. All over the map are containers with items that can boost your stats or even give you somewhat active skills. Those can be either that you heal faster outside of combat, have a better attack speed or even launch a mortar while attacking normally. And you can get a special item you can use actively, so you can escape certain dangerous situations. Besides the regular action skill (every character has one special to him) all of the action skills have a cooldown so you can't just go rampage on that poor planet, so a little strategy is needed when dealing with hordes of monsters. Last, but not least, you can change the difficulty from easy to hard if you're in need of a challenge. The further you come in a session, the harder the game gets. And you can collect hidden artifacts if you want to have a little fun while playing. They always grant you certain advantages and/or disadvantages, e.g. that enemies explode on their death or that you deal far more damage while also just having a fragment of your health. All in all it proves that it has a really tight gameplay.
The music in this game also sort of gives me this feeling that only the Metroid series can give me. The feeling you're all alone on a big, dangerous planet. Beautiful, but highly dangerous. It also sounds kind of like the Metroid Prime series, I don't know if they got their inspiration from it, but it's always a plus in my book. It just fits in perfectly with the rest of the environment. The tracks themselves are mostly ambient tracks which compliment the landscape you're in, but in certain situations like boss fights they can also be very aggressive and alarming. All things considered it's a really great soundtrack.
If you still don't know if I'd recommend this game, I do. It has really tight gameplay, looks pleasing to my eyes, has a wonderful soundtrack and high replayability. It's not often you find good rogue-like games like this, so definitely buy this gem of a game.
TL:DR version: If you liked TBOI and Rogue Legacy, buy it, you cheapskate. It's only nine dollars.

Firaxis has done a fine job with XCOM.  Though the general strategy and base-management portions of the game are handled adequately, It's the tactical battles that are this game's strength.  Fans of turn-based tactics games like Fire Emblem and Tactics Ogre should feel right at home.  This game is all about choice and mutual exclusivity; you'll never have the resources to do everything you want and the game offers an array of units that are all equally appealing in their own respects.  There are always multiple via paths presented, and the game favors a patient and thoughtful approach.  I love that.
The game's most glaring issue is the steep learning curve, which isn't the result of the game's difficulty so much as the fact that early on it does a poor job of explaining basic mechanics.  It can take a little while to get your feet on the ground and if you're not picking things up fast enough on your own your first playthrough might be a wash.  (Not a huge deal as the game is relatively short at 15-25 hours depending on difficulty.)  Also, even after the November patch, this game still isn't entirely bug-free.
All in all, it's a solid game that offers a very enjoyable experience, but it's a little rough around the edges.

Risk of Rain is another take on the much beloved rogue-like game genre. Those of you who enjoyed Binding of Isaac and Rogue Legacy will probably also enjoy this little gem.
The graphics are 8-bit, not really that uncommon for an Indie game, but you can still feel the effort they put in them. They're not simply there for the reason a lot of hipster indie game developers use 8-bit graphics, i.e. for the sake of their pretentious artistic integrity. The graphics in this game are like this to convey the feeling of those old but gold and hard as heck games like Castlevania, Metroid and Cave Story. The art direction itself is also really well done. The different levels always give you a metroid-like feeling. They're beautiful, they make you wanna explore them, but at the same time they kind of frighten you, give you the feeling that at any time something bad could happen. And I know I'm repeating myself, but in the end it feels like a subtle hommage to Super Metroid and those kind of games, which in my case I can't have enough of.
The game runs and controls smoothly, the only problem I have is that you always have to pause and then skip the opening animation when you're starting it up. Also the partial support of the gamepad really throws me off, because you can't select your characters with it or look at the items. Can't really say anything about the coop, because I haven't tried it yet, so I won't.
The gameplay itself is also very well executed. You can play as ten different characters, which not only look, but also play differently. From the long-ranged, flexible, but not that much damage dealing Commando to the very close ranged Acrid, they all have their own perks and, of course, disadvantages. Most of them are unlocked if you do something special, so that you have a little motivation to play the game besides just finishing it. The action skills (four of them) you have in this game are almost always active skills, besides the items you pick up. Which brings me to the next point: items/passive skills. All over the map are containers with items that can boost your stats or even give you somewhat active skills. Those can be either that you heal faster outside of combat, have a better attack speed or even launch a mortar while attacking normally. And you can get a special item you can use actively, so you can escape certain dangerous situations. Besides the regular action skill (every character has one special to him) all of the action skills have a cooldown so you can't just go rampage on that poor planet, so a little strategy is needed when dealing with hordes of monsters. Last, but not least, you can change the difficulty from easy to hard if you're in need of a challenge. The further you come in a session, the harder the game gets. And you can collect hidden artifacts if you want to have a little fun while playing. They always grant you certain advantages and/or disadvantages, e.g. that enemies explode on their death or that you deal far more damage while also just having a fragment of your health. All in all it proves that it has a really tight gameplay.
The music in this game also sort of gives me this feeling that only the Metroid series can give me. The feeling you're all alone on a big, dangerous planet. Beautiful, but highly dangerous. It also sounds kind of like the Metroid Prime series, I don't know if they got their inspiration from it, but it's always a plus in my book. It just fits in perfectly with the rest of the environment. The tracks themselves are mostly ambient tracks which compliment the landscape you're in, but in certain situations like boss fights they can also be very aggressive and alarming. All things considered it's a really great soundtrack.
If you still don't know if I'd recommend this game, I do. It has really tight gameplay, looks pleasing to my eyes, has a wonderful soundtrack and high replayability. It's not often you find good rogue-like games like this, so definitely buy this gem of a game.
TL:DR version: If you liked TBOI and Rogue Legacy, buy it, you cheapskate. It's only nine dollars.

Unfortunately, a game that relies on living with tough outcomes *needs* to be cleaner. Losing your favorite soldiers because you made a mistake is one thing. Losing him/her because of a rare-but-frustrating glitch almost ruins the experience. Despite the bugs, I still enjoyed the game and would recommend it to anyone who loves sci-fi/strategy, even if they're new to turn-based games.

Batman Arkham Knight is an action-adventure game developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Warner Brothers, coming out on PS4, Xbox One and PC in June 2015.  The game is run using the Unreal Engine 3. The PC release of Arkham Knight brought plenty of controversy and issues.  The technical issues on the PC release almost forced Warner Brothers to suspend sales on the game in order for them to address the issues people were having. The game was re-released on Steam in October 2015 after a few patches in order to solve the technical issues.  Sadly people still reported problems with the game forcing Warner Brothers to offer full refunds on the game regardless of whether you met the regular criteria or not.  To this day, the developers are still working on technical issues which people are having.
Before I start my review, I would like to point out that I played this game on a mechanical hard drive, with one nVidia 970 (my second one is being RMA’ed right now!), playing at 1080p with graphics turned on and the majority of the nVidia graphics options turned on as well.  On launch of the title, Warner Brothers recommended that the game be installed on a solid state drive, so as you read the review, please bear all of the above in mind.
Game play in Arkham Knight is again, the same as its predecessors; this shouldn’t be taken as a negative thing though, as the game play is absolutely stellar. The combat system is as fluid and easy to grasp as ever, with some new and interesting combos and special take downs being introduced, such as double take downs when you are working with a partner on some missions.  Some new gadgets have been introduced, a remote controlled batarang which can scan the area for information, and a voice synthesiser, that mimics other character’s voices; this gives you plenty of different ways to use such as ordering enemies around and opening voice controlled locked doors.
The major new game play mechanic that has been added in Arkham Knight is the Batmobile.  You are able to summon the Batmobile to your location when you are on foot or gliding in the air. The Batmobile has two different mods that can easily be used at any time: Pursuit and Battle. Pursuit is the regular movement mode with little on offer in terms of firepower, as you are traveling from A to B. Battle mod turns your Batmobile into a death machine; as you utilise all of the weapon systems on board. The Batmobile can be upgraded using the points you are rewarded with for levelling up as well.
Graphically, I was really impressed with how the game looked. The high resolution textures and rain effects are all stunning.  All of the characters look almost life like, and you can really appreciate this when you get close up shots on their faces; so much detail has gone into the modelling and texturing, to the point where you can see the blackheads on the Joker’s face! All of the game’s animations are done very well too; the Arkham combat system has a very fluid feel to it, so they need to be spot on or else it would just look out of place.
The plot within Arkham Knight is probably my favourite of the series so far. It is the last episode in the Arkham series, so takes place after origins, Asylum and City. I have not read the comic book series so I missed out on a lot of the plot in between the games but the game does do a good job of trying to fill in the gaps.  Arkham Knight introduces a few new main characters to the fold if you haven’t read the comic books too, such as Robin, and a more starring role for Barbara Gordon. With plenty of the other regulars returning, such as Cat-Woman and Alfred. You will encounter plenty of the super villains, Scarecrow, Penguin, Two-Face, Riddler, Poison Ivy, Harley Quin, and of course, the Joker. One new villain, Arkham Knight also has a starring role and has an important storyline plot attached to him as well.
Difficulty can be scaled depending on how hard you set the game. I felt the medium setting to be just enough challenge without hitting the brick wall. None of the boss battles in Arkham Knight are just generic fist fights, each of them uses a unique mechanic which adds some variety to the game.
As with its predecessors’ the open world aspect of the game does a very good job of filling in lots of “blank space” with plenty of side missions and collectables to find. Most Wanted missions, Riddler's Revenge, collectables and AR challenges makes the optional part of the game full to the brim with content. You are also able to unlock different endings to the game by completing the side missions as well, giving you more incentive to continue playing after finishing.
I have been playing for about twenty five hours so far, this has allowed me to finish a handful of side missions and the main story in the game. I will definitely be dropping a few more hours into completing the rest of the most wanted missions in order to unlock the alternative endings, but I can’t see myself wanting to collect the hundreds of Riddler items again after my fiasco with the past two games with them!
Now, onto the technical issues.  As I said above, I am using a single nVidia 970 and the game was installed on a mechanical hard drive. The majority of the time the game was running around 57-60 fps. There are moments where the frame rate will drop to 30 for no good reason. I can understand if it drops on more graphically intensive scenes or when there is a lot happening, but it can sometimes happen when you are in a building with very little going on. Maybe this would have been different if I was using SLI, but even then, it has been reported the SLI makes no difference to the performance. Taking all of this into consideration it seems I was on the lucky side and the pure power in my machine seemed to pull it through to an acceptable playable state.
My conclusion of Batman Arkham Knight may come as a controversial one, but like all of my reviews it is my honest and truthful opinion. I am going to highly recommend Arkham Knight. The game play and interesting compelling story make it a definite worthwhile play through.  I would only recommend this game to people who have a bit of meat in their rig to play it though, unless you are willing to sacrifice some of the graphical fidelity, please bear in mind all of what I noted in the technical issues section of the review and make your judgement on purchasing the game on that if you are on the fence. The game’s retail price on Steam is £34,99, I would also recommend that you don’t purchase it for that price, either get it from another source (definitely not GEE 2 AAAA hint hint hint hint) or wait for one of Steam’s sales as this game will go on sale for less than £20, and more than likely even more now.

Allow me to be very frank here: XCOM: Enemy Unknown is the game that'll make you feel as if you are saving the world.
As you might have guessed, this is a turn-based strategy game where Earth is attacked by aliens, and you're the commander of the XCOM Project: An elite army of people who you can micromanage to death by picking their names, customising their armour and their layouts... It isn't the most in-depth system in the world, but it has its place, certainly. All this is done in the first major part in the game you'll be spending a lot of time in: XCOM HQ. Basically, this is a view of your main base. Here you'll assign research to be done, build expansions, make new weaponry, select missions, overview how loyal countries are and more. Then, after fiddling around here, you'll go on a mission.
The missions are your standard turn-based combat games, but hot damn it's stressfull. Aliens are extremely powerful, especially early on and on the harder difficulties, and reckless play is punished by... Well, by the death of your precious soldiers. Though the combat has its bugs and certainly could be deeper, it's good.
Now, that's the basic premise of the gameplay... Where did that "Saving the world'-feeling-thing, come from, then? Well, the story isn't much more complex than that: You save the world, so that's not too much of innovation... So, what could it be? Well, firstly, the gameplay, of course: You get attached to your soldiers (especially when you name them), you chew off your fingers in the tense combat, and when you select which soldiers you'll be taking on missions the most epic music plays, giving you the feeling as if you were the CEO of the damn world.
Words can't properly describe it. XCOM might lack some polish, but makes up for it. A definite must-have.

Batman Arkham Knight is an action-adventure game developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Warner Brothers, coming out on PS4, Xbox One and PC in June 2015.  The game is run using the Unreal Engine 3. The PC release of Arkham Knight brought plenty of controversy and issues.  The technical issues on the PC release almost forced Warner Brothers to suspend sales on the game in order for them to address the issues people were having. The game was re-released on Steam in October 2015 after a few patches in order to solve the technical issues.  Sadly people still reported problems with the game forcing Warner Brothers to offer full refunds on the game regardless of whether you met the regular criteria or not.  To this day, the developers are still working on technical issues which people are having.
Before I start my review, I would like to point out that I played this game on a mechanical hard drive, with one nVidia 970 (my second one is being RMA’ed right now!), playing at 1080p with graphics turned on and the majority of the nVidia graphics options turned on as well.  On launch of the title, Warner Brothers recommended that the game be installed on a solid state drive, so as you read the review, please bear all of the above in mind.
Game play in Arkham Knight is again, the same as its predecessors; this shouldn’t be taken as a negative thing though, as the game play is absolutely stellar. The combat system is as fluid and easy to grasp as ever, with some new and interesting combos and special take downs being introduced, such as double take downs when you are working with a partner on some missions.  Some new gadgets have been introduced, a remote controlled batarang which can scan the area for information, and a voice synthesiser, that mimics other character’s voices; this gives you plenty of different ways to use such as ordering enemies around and opening voice controlled locked doors.
The major new game play mechanic that has been added in Arkham Knight is the Batmobile.  You are able to summon the Batmobile to your location when you are on foot or gliding in the air. The Batmobile has two different mods that can easily be used at any time: Pursuit and Battle. Pursuit is the regular movement mode with little on offer in terms of firepower, as you are traveling from A to B. Battle mod turns your Batmobile into a death machine; as you utilise all of the weapon systems on board. The Batmobile can be upgraded using the points you are rewarded with for levelling up as well.
Graphically, I was really impressed with how the game looked. The high resolution textures and rain effects are all stunning.  All of the characters look almost life like, and you can really appreciate this when you get close up shots on their faces; so much detail has gone into the modelling and texturing, to the point where you can see the blackheads on the Joker’s face! All of the game’s animations are done very well too; the Arkham combat system has a very fluid feel to it, so they need to be spot on or else it would just look out of place.
The plot within Arkham Knight is probably my favourite of the series so far. It is the last episode in the Arkham series, so takes place after origins, Asylum and City. I have not read the comic book series so I missed out on a lot of the plot in between the games but the game does do a good job of trying to fill in the gaps.  Arkham Knight introduces a few new main characters to the fold if you haven’t read the comic books too, such as Robin, and a more starring role for Barbara Gordon. With plenty of the other regulars returning, such as Cat-Woman and Alfred. You will encounter plenty of the super villains, Scarecrow, Penguin, Two-Face, Riddler, Poison Ivy, Harley Quin, and of course, the Joker. One new villain, Arkham Knight also has a starring role and has an important storyline plot attached to him as well.
Difficulty can be scaled depending on how hard you set the game. I felt the medium setting to be just enough challenge without hitting the brick wall. None of the boss battles in Arkham Knight are just generic fist fights, each of them uses a unique mechanic which adds some variety to the game.
As with its predecessors’ the open world aspect of the game does a very good job of filling in lots of “blank space” with plenty of side missions and collectables to find. Most Wanted missions, Riddler's Revenge, collectables and AR challenges makes the optional part of the game full to the brim with content. You are also able to unlock different endings to the game by completing the side missions as well, giving you more incentive to continue playing after finishing.
I have been playing for about twenty five hours so far, this has allowed me to finish a handful of side missions and the main story in the game. I will definitely be dropping a few more hours into completing the rest of the most wanted missions in order to unlock the alternative endings, but I can’t see myself wanting to collect the hundreds of Riddler items again after my fiasco with the past two games with them!
Now, onto the technical issues.  As I said above, I am using a single nVidia 970 and the game was installed on a mechanical hard drive. The majority of the time the game was running around 57-60 fps. There are moments where the frame rate will drop to 30 for no good reason. I can understand if it drops on more graphically intensive scenes or when there is a lot happening, but it can sometimes happen when you are in a building with very little going on. Maybe this would have been different if I was using SLI, but even then, it has been reported the SLI makes no difference to the performance. Taking all of this into consideration it seems I was on the lucky side and the pure power in my machine seemed to pull it through to an acceptable playable state.
My conclusion of Batman Arkham Knight may come as a controversial one, but like all of my reviews it is my honest and truthful opinion. I am going to highly recommend Arkham Knight. The game play and interesting compelling story make it a definite worthwhile play through.  I would only recommend this game to people who have a bit of meat in their rig to play it though, unless you are willing to sacrifice some of the graphical fidelity, please bear in mind all of what I noted in the technical issues section of the review and make your judgement on purchasing the game on that if you are on the fence. The game’s retail price on Steam is £34,99, I would also recommend that you don’t purchase it for that price, either get it from another source (definitely not GEE 2 AAAA hint hint hint hint) or wait for one of Steam’s sales as this game will go on sale for less than £20, and more than likely even more now.

In risk of rain, you play as the sole survivor of a space-faring vessel that crash landed on a strange, alien planet, along with all it's goodies. I suppose maybe it was the space postal service, because that sh** ain't ever gettin' delivered now.
In risk of rain (you'll feel the pain) Your goal on each map is to find the teleporter while taking out swarms of aliens hell-bent on murdering you, then activating the teleporter on the map, setting off a larger boss mob and even MORE aliens hell-bent on murdering you. You are required to Survive for X amount of time after you activate said teleporter as well as kill all the remaining aliens on the map the spawned endlessly and rapidly during said countdown.
Along the way on your journey, you'll encounter several chests from your downed spaceship that you'll have to purchase and use to have any chance in hell of surviving. Items purchased have a wide variety of effects ranging from freezing time to making your character move faster, jump higher, attack faster, etc. Generally speaking, the more expensive the chest, the better the item quality.
In addition to these special items your character has four abilities that have a cooldown/rotation before they can be used again. Each skill falls under a category: damage dealing, specialization, evasion, and/or crowd control. Using all of them to their fullest, as often as possible is going to be the key to your survival. along with the previous mentioned item gathering.
As your current game playthrough progresses, the enemies become more and more difficult. There's a bar in the upper right corner of the screen. As time progresses, it fills more and more. The difficulty you play on controls where the difficult starts. Don't think you're terribad for deciding to start playing on "Drizzle" and/or "Very Easy", especially if you're new. I've seen games where the difficulty ramped up to "I SEE YOU" and "HAHAHAHA"
As you gain progress in what is sure to be many playthroughs, you may unlock additional classes to play as. Each class has its own unique playstyle and different ways of surviving on the planet. For example, while the commando, the default starting class is a sort of well-balanced jack of all trades, the sniper class focuses on damage dealing and can possibly kill bosses on a single hit of a fully charged, perfectly reloaded, droid scanned boss with their "steady shot" ability.
In addition to unlocking new classes, you also unlock new items and/or artifacts that can be used to inject control (command artifact), Offense over Defense (Glass), or insane difficulty into your various play-throughs (Glass + Spite)

Dead Space has just about everything I want out of a game.
The combat gives you an over-the-shoulder view as you attempt to 'tactically dismember' swarms of aliens.  This idea forces many gamers to throw a learned concept:  Aim for the head.
A key point for me in any game is the plot, if the plot is engaging, I love the game almost instantly; Dead Space is no exception.  The plot pick ups pretty fast into the game, only to hit a low point through the middle, as it sometimes feels like you're walking around the ship without a purpose.  Fortunately, it picks back up near the end, and can even leave you shocked at times
Now we get to my faveorite part of the game:  the ingenious HUD.  The fact is, there isn't one.  Your health can be seen as part of a 'RIG' on your back, but EVERYONE has a rig, which adds to the immersion.  Ammo is viewed above the gun as you aim.
There's also an upgrade system that works surprisingly well.  It's based off of power nodes (cont. in comments due to space)
