Risk of Rain, where to even begin...? The ship you were on was damaged greatly by an unknown assailant and you crash-landed on a planet with lots of incredibly very hostile lifeforms... and you got stranded incredibly far from the wreck. Luckily, the ship you were on was a cargo ship: everything in it was "unfortunately" also stranded, and you can bet your life on the fact that those now-misplaced goods will be the most valuable things you'll need in order to attempt to leave the planet.
Risk of Rain (RoR from now on) features preset stages with some randomization, where monsters litterally pop from the ground every now and then, boxes have to be properly paid for (with the spoils of popping monsters) in order to get your hands on their sweet contents and portals have to be found in order to traverse the hostile world as you try to get back to your damaged ship. But be ready: once you activate a portal and wait for it to "charge up", a powerful monster boss appears. After a set amount of time charging the portal, no more monsters appear and you must eliminate all the threats remaining in order to move on with your quest for safety.
In RoR you can have up to 10 different character choices when you start the game. The default and starting one, the Commando, is pretty well balanced and intersting to play, but the other 9 are more specific in their gameplay as to what you should be doing and what you'd favour getting boosted by the various items you can find. Some are more challenging to play with than others, most definitely, and some are much harder to unlock than others. Also to keep in mind is the fact that you can collect throughout the different stages game-changing artefacts that WILL make or break the experience of some of the characters.
I can confidently say that I had the least fun time of my life playing the Enforcer, a human-riots-specialized shield-wall with some area-of-effect options and side-defined damage mitigation skill, and loved playing the Mercenary, a ninja-like sword-wielding blur of speed that can avoid damage with two of its skills. Noteworthy mentions are the easy-mode Engineer, the run-and-gun Huntress and the only-with-item-choosing-artefact Sniper that can litterally one-shot the final boss (or make you run into a bug where you make the final boss nigh-invulnerable, and doing 2 damage per attack for more than 15k hp can take well over 30 minutes with the wrong items). Acrid and H4NDY (or with an A, don't remember) are also interesting in their own way, and the Miner is incredibly complex in terms of mobility and self-preservation. And there's also the Bandit, which feels a little underwhelming if you get it after you unlock the Huntress; just saying.
The items you can find on your journey to the ship are also very much unique in their functions, or in certain cases there's a relation between a more common white item and a not-as-common green one (such as critical hit chance), but each and every item has a purpose and an ideal synergetic relation to each of the characters (or a broad spectrum of characters, such as happens with Paul's Goat's Leg, which increases move speed: everyone should have it). Items' effects stack, some with better results than others (you can't have more than 100% chance of a critical hit, for example), and some items are not really worth stacking unless you have no choice on the matter (I'm looking at you, Golden Gun). Bosses also drop unique items on rare occasion that might be just the extra edge you needed to stay alive or kill something better. And every enemy type, all the bosses included, have a chance to drop a monster log that will let you get some insight as to the world you've crash-landed on... and perhaps even the reason behind the attack on the ship, spoilers which I won't reveal.
Naturally, RoR has a major flaw: it's inherent quality is that you will benefit the most of it the more you play it and replay it, but at some point you will have unlocked everything and found out the strategy that best fits you or your playstyle with whichever character you chose. And by that point, you will have seen pretty much all that the game has to offer, barring unlockables that you might not even need or will end up not really picking up once unlocked. You'll still have fun playing the game, but you will feel like you need to forget about it for a while to make it worth booting it up again; this is especially true once you reach a point where you've been alive for over 2 hours stacking items to the point of glitchyness and automatic downscaling of settings just to let the game run properly... Fun fact: I once became so overpowered that I just left my character unattended on a level and had a heavy lunch, only to find out an hour later that I was not only still alive but with tons of new crap uncollected to make me even more overpowered. Of course, I went for the final boss afterwards, since I had "taken the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it" and any sense of challenge with it.
You may be pleased to know the game has online multiplayer, as well as local multiplayer, and you can choose repeated characters (which is a good thing, considering a group of 4 people playing without anything unlocked would render the option moot). Playing online with your friends is fun, but one thing that happened significantly often with even someone on the same LAN as myself was a slight desynchronization of the game, including enemies that existed for one of us and not the other and, most annoyingly, the position or even the existence of items. This is more frequent the more items you start stacking up, of course, since more things have to be synchronized to begin with, and especially with area-calculated things happening (such as high amounts of Barbed Wire). In short, online is FUN, but only if you accept that really bad/annoying things may happen as part of the experience.
I do have to say that there are some really
bugs. I, for one, hate with a passion just how unclickable the difficulty can get to be with overlapping texts and whatnot. There should also be a back button on the multiplayer screen, forcing you to instead use the escape-key menu, or at the very least a "no, wait, I've selected a character but I really changed my mind and want to select another one" button in that menu. Textboxes may and will innevitably get stuck, be it trying to read how a skill is scaling or hovering some other annoying thing while in-game. And I find it so anti-climatic, the lines that the final boss spews, for their oh-so-annoyingly consistent typo all across the game (can't remember which it is, but I know it also happens on the descriptions and flavour texts of some of the items, since it is actually an English rule that is being broken); I can say that it's one of the reasons that every time I clear the game again I feel like I need to cool down and not play it for another week.
Having mentioned all the relevant things, how much do I recommend it?
, that's for sure. RoR certainly feels unique enough in the sense that I know no other game that makes me feel good about commiting genocide on some lizard people, allows me to essentially fly with a continuously executed jump-slash as a ninja and invariably laugh at seeing over 1 million damage per shot when playing the sniper as it should always be played.
The price seems fair for what it is, but ideally you should try to get it at a 50% discount. I also recommend a 4-pack if you think at least two people you know would enjoy playing the game with you, even if you only play with one of them at a time.

Dead Space has just about everything I want out of a game.
The combat gives you an over-the-shoulder view as you attempt to 'tactically dismember' swarms of aliens.  This idea forces many gamers to throw a learned concept:  Aim for the head.
A key point for me in any game is the plot, if the plot is engaging, I love the game almost instantly; Dead Space is no exception.  The plot pick ups pretty fast into the game, only to hit a low point through the middle, as it sometimes feels like you're walking around the ship without a purpose.  Fortunately, it picks back up near the end, and can even leave you shocked at times
Now we get to my faveorite part of the game:  the ingenious HUD.  The fact is, there isn't one.  Your health can be seen as part of a 'RIG' on your back, but EVERYONE has a rig, which adds to the immersion.  Ammo is viewed above the gun as you aim.
There's also an upgrade system that works surprisingly well.  It's based off of power nodes (cont. in comments due to space)
Your brain does everything for you after 10 hours.

So, I waited until January 2016 to purchase the Arkham Knight.  I've been waiting for a long time for the game and I was initially diappointed to find out that there were so many issues with the PC port, so I waited.  And waited.  Finally, I found the game for less than $25 and leapt at the opportunity.
I'll just say it.  It's incredible.  The issues have all been fixed, near as I can tell since I never experienced them first hand.  The graphics are stunning.  The story has kept me on the edge of my seat for hours.  As a fan of all the Arkham games (I enjoyed Origins, but not nearly as much as the first two, being a different studio), this one does not disappoint.  I'll go ahead and break it down.
Pros:
Graphics
Storyline
Gameplay (both in difficulty and variety)
Voice acting (I love having Kevin Conroy back as Batman.   As well as a few other returning voice actors)
Cons (of which there are few):
There have been a few moments of clipping where the game freezes up for a moment, but always recovers with no issue, after just a few seconds.
I would like to see less Batmobile gameplay and more Batman gameplay, but I can deal
I have yet to finish the main storyline, though I'm close, and plan on powering through some of the DLC afterwards as well, but as of clocking 33 hours so far, I have zero big complaints.  I only have praises for this game.  Even though I didn't pay the full price, knowing now that it functions as well as it does after the patches, I would gladly pay it!  Kudos to WB for getting the PC port sorted out and playable to a miraculously enjoyable level!

+ Game is long and the city is bigger than ever. Excellent graphics.
+ Improved UI and controls all around. Now the game pauses when you pick a gadget and you can change your current objective marker in less than two secs.
+ No BS challenges that are impossible to complete after a while like in Arkham Origins. You can get achievements related to gameplay whenever you want without having to restart the entire story. + The Batmobile, although it's frustrating to drive it at times.
+ Music is as good as in previous games.
+ Some cool plot twists as always.
+ You can change your character in pretty much every challenge.
+ Batman has even more moves than before, although Rocksteady pretty much ignored any improvement made by WB Montreal in Arkham Origins.

- The Riddler thropies and whatnot are always a negative due to how dense that quest is (Required to get the true ending).

If your looking for a review on this game you\'ve come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you\'ve come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you\'re using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don\'t forget to scrape the bowl as you\'re doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

So the Arkham Batman series come to an end with this game. Did it end on a high note? Well let take a look.
Just a head up, *SPOILERS* from all Arkham game may be in this review. You have been warned!
Arkham knight is an open world game that put you in control of Batman. Dealing with the aftermath of a Gotham without Joker, Batman must face the Scarecrow. Scarecrow threaten to release fear gas across Gotham unless Batman can stop him. As you can guess, all the citizens have left, leaving Gotham full of nothing but criminals at this point. Not to mention Batman must also face a mercenary army being led by the Arkham Knight, who seem to know a lot about Batman.
If you been played any of the Arkham game then you can already know how these games play, but here a quick recap. These game is like a modern 3D beat'em up with a counter feature. You can go through these game with button smashing but you'll miss some of the fun of chaining combos and attack with your gadgets. One new thing this game introduce is the dual take downs. Whenever Batman is fighting enemies alongside allies (Nightwing, Robin, and Catwoman) they can perform a dual take down where they beat the tar out of a poor enemy who is in your crosshairs. The combat is solid and feel really nice.
Their 2 main enemy types, regular grunts and heavy grunts. Regular grunts are easy to take down with a punch. The only thing that make them difficult is when they got weapons like guns, cattle prods, shields, medic packs (to revive enemies), knives, and etc. Heavy grunts require you to stun them before you can dish out damage on them, and they can come with weapons such as knives or shock gloves.
Another new feature is the batmobile. This allow you to move Gotham quickly and run down foes or use it to perform a vehicle take down in a fight. The batmobile also transform into a tank (yea thats a thing) and you can do battle with the Arkham Knight unmanned tank drones. The batmobile handle fairly well although it feel too slippery when doing power slides.
Also predator mode make a return where the enemies all have guns and you must take them down stealthy to avoid being shot to pieces. One new feature is fear take down. Where Batman move at lightning speed and quickly take out 3 or more opponents before they can even react. This is achieved when a meter is filled, by doing silent take downs.
This game is like Arkham City and Origins. The only different are a bigger map, Batmobile, and fear take down. Now that not a bad thing. Those games was solid and this only add onto it. Really this was a great way to end off the Batman Arkham series.
Also the DLCs are good, but short. All expansions can be done in like an hour or 2. So if you get them, get them when they are on sale or if you can buy the deluxe edition on sale like I did. Otherwise you may find yourself cheated if you bought the DLC at full price.

How To Make a Basic Butter Cake from Scratch
Makes one 2-layer cake
What You Need
Ingredients
1/2 cup unsalted butter, softened (plus extra for greasing the pans)
1 1/2 cups sugar
3 large eggs
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
3 1/2 teaspoons baking powder
1 1/4 cups whole milk
1 teaspoon vanilla
2 1/2 cups buttercream frosting, such as basic buttercream
Equipment
2 9-inch round pans
Stand mixer or hand mixer
Measuring cups and spoons
Cookie scoop or measuring cup, for dividing the batter
Instructions
Heat the oven to 350°F.
Sift together the flour, baking powder, and salt. Set aside.
Prepare the pans: Rub the bottoms and sides of the cake pans with a little butter, shortening, or baking spray. Make sure to get into the corners and all the way up the sides. Flour the sides and bottoms of the pan by scooping a bit of flour into the pan, then shaking and tapping to coat the bottom and sides of the pan with flour; dump out the excess. Alternatively, cut out a parchment round and use this to line the bottom.
Beat the butter and sugar until fluffy and light. Cream together for about 3 to 5 minutes on medium spread (see above notes for more information).
Add the eggs one at a time. Beat until the batter is very smooth and creamy-looking. Adding the eggs one at a time gives them a better chance at incorporating into a smooth batter. Be sure they are room temperature so the batter does not appear curdled.
Beat in half the flour, salt, and baking powder. Add the sifted dry ingredients with the mixer running at low speed. Continue to mix until incorporated.
Beat in the milk and vanilla. Alternate adding in the liquids with the dry ingredients so the milk has a chance to be absorbed without needing to overmix the batter. Stream in the milk with the mixer on low until combined.
Beat in the remaining flour mixture until just combined and no more visible flour remains. Stir a few times with a spatula to make sure no more flour remains on the bottom of the bowl.
Divide the batter between cake pans. Use a scale or mechanical ice cream scoop to evenly divide the batter. Smooth the tops with an offset spatula. Drop the pans against the counter to shake out air bubbles.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes: When done, the cake should be puffed like a pillow, golden, and pull away from the sides of the pan. When done, a toothpick inserted into the center of the cakes should come out clean.
Cool for 15 minutes in the pan. Run an offset spatula around the cake to make sure it's completely loosened from the sides of the pan.
Flip the rounds out of the pan, remove the parchment lining, and flip right-side up to cool completely.
Once cool, frost and assemble the cake with the buttercream.

However one askpect about the hud and movement, is that your health and stasis modes, etc. are all placed on the back of Isaac's suit, allowing you to be able to be able to take in the entire enviornment without any health bars or maps getting in the way. The only downside is that alot of the aspects of it are "A-B" type objectives, alot like in super hero games or prolonged GTA mission. The Dead Space Franchise will be a long series to come no doubt. I give Dead Space a [9.0]

Super Hexagon is a simple game, made to test your patience. No, really. That's all it is. It consists of the player attempting to safely navigate their way through a plethora of 'chambers', which are just pre-created patterns thrown together randomly. Despite it's simple mechanics and design, Super Hexagon may drag you back into another try through it's almost hypnotic music and visual effects. You must survive 60 seconds on the first three levels to unlock three more challenging versions and then complete the newer levels to successfully 'beat' the game. This is a great game for killing a few minutes or if you're on the go as it's available on iOS and Android. If you're a fan of challenging games that requires patience and good reaction time, I recommend you pick this up.

It's been years and years of playing CIV V and still by far it is the best strategy Sid Meier's done. ...yes, including all post CIV 5 games they have released. If for some reason you still don't have it go and get it now. You will not regret it.

The original allowed stray bullets to cause damage, this remake does not.  This makes a huge difference. While the main media outlets' coverage of the game has been  universally stellar, a quick jaunt over to Enemy Unknown's Game Hub shows that the fan response is actually polarized.
This is a game that will convert new people and comfort some players of 1995's UFO Defense with its similar structure and design conceits – but it's also a game that has the potential of severely disappointing whoever has grown to consider the original formula as being a benchmark by which other squad-based strategy games should be judged.
You have to come into this with a single thing in mind : this is its own beast. Enemy Unknown is not trying to be UFO Defense, it's trying to magnify those parts of the original game that made the experience so memorable and to eliminate some of the things we've forgotten were pure and simple cruft; essentially design-based clutter that had no real purpose or place in the grand scheme of things. The inventory is simplified, the action point system is replaced with a two-move system that turns the on-field missions into games of high-stakes and live-ammo chess, and the interface is made friendly and digestible to new players of the franchise.
Rest assured, this is still tactical combat at its finest, and the base management segments are as meaningful as ever, even if the younger generation might consider them to be something of an unneeded lull between missions. The truth is these moments of introspection are absolutely vital, as they allow the player to experience the game's admittedly simple narrative – Roland Emmerich would be proud – and to graduate from a desperate band of surviving soldiers and scientists to the world's first, best and last line of defense against the alien threat. The difficulty curve can be rather surprising, things turning steep once Commander Bradford lets you loose in the first of your truly randomized missions, but this inverted approach creates a sense of rising potency and power that's unlike anything any recent strategy game has managed to deliver in recent memory. Everything you do paints a bit more of the bigger picture, with your usually matter-of-fact scientific, military and engineering-related advisors sometimes waxing philosophical in the face of the sheer devastation.
I don't advise you buying into the associated DLC, however. At five bucks a pop, it's a lot to ask for an extra hairdo and helmet and a new uniform color. If the game's visuals were any more central to the experience, I'd almost make a comment about a certain horse armor pack..

Risk of Rain is a game you will try and fail in. Then try again and get a little further. Then try once more and get not quite as far as the first. There's a lot of elements to this game that are random. The biggest of which is the item drops. The quality of the items, the rarity and quantity are randomly generated. That not only makes Risk of Rain feel random, but also makes it challenging. For some reason I'll get further and last longer with worse items. Makes me think I'm on my game! The randomness can feel frustrating or unfair at times, but it adds major replayability.
There are a lot of pros and cons, but just know... Risk of Rain is a fantastic game. There are different characters you play as and unlock. You also unlock droppable items through achievements and tasks. The characters all play incredibly different. I believe there's 10 different options. In the game you'll spend the majority of your time dodging and platforming - trying to trick the AI into not being able to get to you. The difficulty also ramps up for every 5 minutes you play (up to 60mins). So ideally you'll clear the level, get all the items and kill the boss all in one sweep. That's usually not the case, since you have to kill enemies to gain money to unlock a chest.
A major flaw I've seen is the multiplayer. It has huge potential for a fun multiplayer experience but they missed it just a bit. You can play with 4 players in one screen. That screen does not get split. You must travel CLOSELY with your companions. I'm uncertain if online multiplayer allows you to split off. That's not the flaw, however. The upgrades are how you get more powerful. Only one person can pick up the upgrade, and upgrades are not shared. So you can either choose to split the upgrades between you and your buddy/ies and all be weaker, or have one person pick up every upgrade and have the others feel useless. This can also add some tactical measures to the game as well. If you know the upgrades well enough, you can give the ideal upgrades to the different classes and maybe be stronger as a unit then you would be with one godinator and 3 scrubby nubbies.
I'm tempted to say this game is ALMOST too challenging, but it wouldn't feel like an accomplishment if it were easy to make it to the end, now would it? I've played maybe 30-40 runs and completed once or twice. Damn it felt good when I beat it.
Play this game. Beat it with every class. Be my hero.

On balance a brilliant game and a worthy reboot! Endless fun has been had re-living my early gaming experiences brought up to the modern standard.
Inspired by the old Microprose game of the same name from 1994, "UFO: Enemy Unknown", Firaxis have had a go at revitalising the series;
The graphics look very nice, even on my low end card (hd3600 256mb) and the class mechanic is a nice touch, if somewhat arbitrary!  Enemy Unknown is rather simple to get into and the tutorial is very helpful for those new to the series.
There are, however, several things missing from the original. All the core mechanics are still there, just not in quite so much depth. Which is a shame as the scope of the original was massive with intricate levels of detail and micro management which are sadly lacking in this reincarnation. Most notably the inventory system which is essentially non-existant now.
Indeed many elements have been "streamlined", Firaxis' buzzword for removing anything likely to reduce it's accessability to the masses, in particular our console bretheren. I do wish it was little more faithful to the original, but i understand the decision.
Grumbles aside, my thanks go to Firaxis for remaking my favourite series! X-COM Enemy Unknown (2012) is a great choice for a tactical gamer who enjoys turn based, squad level combat. Those with a hatred for turn based combat should try the demo before casting this game into the Abyss.

Risk of Rain is a rogue-like that offers a few interesting twists on the genre, but utlimately this game doesn't give the player a compelling reason to keep going back into the rain-stained void.  I'm going to keep this short and just discuss the two main design errors that kept me from enjoying this game.
The first strike against this game is that it has a very skewed difficulty skewing.  As time progresses in Risk of Rain, the enemies grow in numbers and strength.  The early portion of this timer makes for an exciting experience that forces the player to formulate a careful balance between farming and progressing through the initial levels.  If the scaling maintained this logical, linear progression, Risk of Rain would be brilliant.  The problem is that near the end of the timer enemy statistics are hyper-inflated to the point where the game becomes slow, dull, and almost impossible to survive.  No matter how lucky or unlucky one is in their item drops, eventually they will reach a point where progress is slowed to a crawl due to insanely inflated HP pools and huge damage numbers.  Here's the critical reason why this is so bad: Risk of Rain is a game about kiting.  You must be able to whittle the horde as you kite across sections of each map, and when you can't effectively kill anything after multiple loops, things go badly.  Difficulty can be punishing yet rewarding, or it can be merely punitive.  Risk of Rain's difficulty starts as the former but quickly morphs into the latter.  Either the enemies need to be slowed in their evolution, or the player needs better scaling ratios.
The other problem with the game is that a large portion of the character kits are badly designed for the engine in which they inhabit. Risk of Rain is a game mostly about kiting, but only a few of the characters' kits are actually able to do this with any efficacy.  The varying roster brings a welcome diversity to the game, but any initial excitement about new characters quickly begins to fade once the player begins to realize that only about three characters are actually worth playing when attempting more difficult and longer runs.  The developers seemed to have forgotten that the game requires constant kiting, and as a result you'll find throughout character diversity many kits that inhibit or restrict one's ability to kite, and the damage compensation for the restricted movement isn't nearly enough to make it worth the sacrifice.  The Huntress is an example of a character that is designed with the game's core mechanics in mind.  Her speed, fast cooldowns, and movement are unparalleled, and playing this character augments all of the postive aspects of the game.  Kiting the flood of enemies is a rush and most mistakes can be assigned to player error. The Bandit is an example of a poorly designed character -- weak mobility, long cooldowns, and no true edge in damage.  The Bandit either would need more movement or much higher damage ratios to be a character that is worthwhile.  Perhaps many would argue that they enjoy this hieratic approach to character rosters -- and some might even enjoy the extra challenge of a poorly designed character -- but I would have liked to seen multiple playstyles designed around the mobility required in Risk of Rain.
There's a few other problems with the game, but those are the two main things that kept me from going back to it.  The initial struggle of balancing farming v. progression was addicting and compelling, but this experience was quickly ruined by an atrociously designed end-game.  The thrill of unlocking characters, too, was diminished once one understood that only three have well designed kits. It's an interesting game that will be exciting for a few hours, but if you've played other Rogue-likes, you'll soon see the design errors that hold it back from true greatness.

I never thought I'd be among the folks hating on this game, but I am. Here's why.
PC Specs:
Intel i7-3770
AMD R9 380 4GB
12GB DDR3/1333 RAM
256GB Samsung 850 Evo
Resolution run: 1366x768
Latest drivers and game patch(es) used. (Jan 15, 2016)
FPS: Mostly 30FPS. Batmobile trips dip below 20FPS on occasion. Every so often, there is a jarring transition to 60FPS, and then down to 45FPS. This game, beautiful though it is, isn't optimized for the PC. Honestly, I'd imagine drunk monkeys could optimize this game better than Rocksteady/WB.
Lag Spikes: Proceeding large explosions, Arkham Knight will often simply pause as it does whatever calculations it wants to run. These spikes are brief, but unpleasant, and make the game appear more broken than it already is.
Glitches: The only glitches that I have run into is Batman getting stuck on stuff and the controls not responding. Ledges are particularly bad in this game. It's a flashback to some of Origin's problems, and I can't say I'm thrilled.
The actual game:
Meh. It's okay. The Batmobile is alright, although it ruins the feel of "I'm a lone wolf, saving a dark world," changing it to "I'm Iron Man in a car." The story is bland, although helped be better lipsync, and more anguished expressions on all parties involved. The map is fine. Mostly it feels like you are defending the world's largest overpass or roadway instead of a city, though. Reasonably large, not too much to complain about. Overall, a mediocre game, helped along by good memories of Arkham City and Asylum.
Also, I have the season pass, as well as the base game. It isn't worth it. Most of the DLCs are essentially horse armor. Buy each individual DLC that is interesting instead.
In conlusion, unless you have a powerful rig, don't mind running on low resolutions, dealing with annoying bugs and terrible FPS issues, forget this game. Just forget it. Including the ~$90 of DLCs Rocksteady/WB is selling for it.
EDIT:
Since my review, I've gotten my hands on a PowerColor HD 7990 6GB, which is a monster 3-slot card. It's rated to be between 150%-200% (1.5-2x) as fast as my old 380 4GB. It's essentially two crossfire'd HD 7970s. While Arkham Knight can't properly make use of the second card, most of the FPS drops are gone, as well as the calculation-before-explosion bits. At 1366x768, it benchmarks at 90FPS average, 60FPS min, 150FPS max with all settings maxed + Nvidia enhanced rain. As you'd imagine, this makes the game much more enjoyable to play. I may try getting into this game after they patch it a few more times, now that most of the FPS issues are fixed.

I'm normally not that into strategy games, especially when they're turn based. Somehow they feel slow, and I just want to unwind without thinking about things too much. But Xcom managed to pull me right in. It succesfully mixes turn based strategy with a bit of management, and,... guess what ? It's great fun !
Xcom uses a certain graphical style, which reminded me a bit of Team Fortress 2. It's not super detailed by any means, but I still liked the clean look of things.
The combat is brilliant, with the camera zooming in when a certain action is taken. It makes the combat feel exciting. Completing missions and killing enemies will level up your soldiers. You'll learn to take care of them, because when they're a higher level some of their abilities might just save you and your squad.
The story is nothing special, but the way the whole game is executed is just amazing. You'll have to make some difficult choices (concerning building certain items/facilities and the missions you choose to accept), none of which are right or wrong.
The sounds and music also add to the atmosphere of the entire game.
Also, for a single-player game it's surprisingly lenghty as well. It should take most players well over 20 hours to complete, especially if you mess up your first few games (like me).

After nearly 30h of gameplay I can say that this game is actually pretty okay. Worth 49,99€? Not really no, but if it comes on sale and you like the Batman franchise, pick it up.
First off - lets start with the gameplay. The story is great, apart from the mainstory you kind of doing the sidemissions automatically, which are referring to the mainstory as well. It's a darkish kind of scene with roughly all villains coming in the missions.
Groundcombat system is great, detective mode really feels useful and isn't timeconsuming at all once you get used to it. Combo's feel really natural to make and aren't complicated at all.
Driving is a bit different in this game - it doesn't feel right at all. You almost instantly will prefer flying over the batmobile. Driving the batmobile gives insanely performance issues as well, framedrops as hell from smooth gameplay to 5-10 fps drops.
To talk a bit more about performance - indoors and groundscenes are really doable and acceptable framerate. Don't expect to get 100fps or more constantly in this game. I run other similar games (Mad Max) at 120fps easily, whilst at Batman it's 55-60fps constantly (Batmobile 40fps with framedrops to 5fps). If you think this will annoy you - don't pick it up, you're forced to use the batmobile at some points.

Risk of Rain is a rogue-like that offers a few interesting twists on the genre, but utlimately this game doesn't give the player a compelling reason to keep going back into the rain-stained void.  I'm going to keep this short and just discuss the two main design errors that kept me from enjoying this game.
The first strike against this game is that it has a very skewed difficulty skewing.  As time progresses in Risk of Rain, the enemies grow in numbers and strength.  The early portion of this timer makes for an exciting experience that forces the player to formulate a careful balance between farming and progressing through the initial levels.  If the scaling maintained this logical, linear progression, Risk of Rain would be brilliant.  The problem is that near the end of the timer enemy statistics are hyper-inflated to the point where the game becomes slow, dull, and almost impossible to survive.  No matter how lucky or unlucky one is in their item drops, eventually they will reach a point where progress is slowed to a crawl due to insanely inflated HP pools and huge damage numbers.  Here's the critical reason why this is so bad: Risk of Rain is a game about kiting.  You must be able to whittle the horde as you kite across sections of each map, and when you can't effectively kill anything after multiple loops, things go badly.  Difficulty can be punishing yet rewarding, or it can be merely punitive.  Risk of Rain's difficulty starts as the former but quickly morphs into the latter.  Either the enemies need to be slowed in their evolution, or the player needs better scaling ratios.
The other problem with the game is that a large portion of the character kits are badly designed for the engine in which they inhabit. Risk of Rain is a game mostly about kiting, but only a few of the characters' kits are actually able to do this with any efficacy.  The varying roster brings a welcome diversity to the game, but any initial excitement about new characters quickly begins to fade once the player begins to realize that only about three characters are actually worth playing when attempting more difficult and longer runs.  The developers seemed to have forgotten that the game requires constant kiting, and as a result you'll find throughout character diversity many kits that inhibit or restrict one's ability to kite, and the damage compensation for the restricted movement isn't nearly enough to make it worth the sacrifice.  The Huntress is an example of a character that is designed with the game's core mechanics in mind.  Her speed, fast cooldowns, and movement are unparalleled, and playing this character augments all of the postive aspects of the game.  Kiting the flood of enemies is a rush and most mistakes can be assigned to player error. The Bandit is an example of a poorly designed character -- weak mobility, long cooldowns, and no true edge in damage.  The Bandit either would need more movement or much higher damage ratios to be a character that is worthwhile.  Perhaps many would argue that they enjoy this hieratic approach to character rosters -- and some might even enjoy the extra challenge of a poorly designed character -- but I would have liked to seen multiple playstyles designed around the mobility required in Risk of Rain.
There's a few other problems with the game, but those are the two main things that kept me from going back to it.  The initial struggle of balancing farming v. progression was addicting and compelling, but this experience was quickly ruined by an atrociously designed end-game.  The thrill of unlocking characters, too, was diminished once one understood that only three have well designed kits. It's an interesting game that will be exciting for a few hours, but if you've played other Rogue-likes, you'll soon see the design errors that hold it back from true greatness.

Whenever you start a new story, whether it is a book, a game, a movie, or a tv series, you sometimes become so fond of it, it makes a void in your heart. As you read, watch, or play this trilogy the void begins to fill, and you are comfortable. And when you reach a point where the series ends, the void is filled and you feel complete until you find another story. But if the story isnt finished, wrapped up, or completed, the filling of the void stops, and you feel anxious for the next part and it is a very uncomfortable feeling. Sometimes, your mind forces you to search for this missing area in the void by looking up the next release date or if they will continue the series. But if you don't find the information to satisfy this feeling, it gets worse. Your mind begins to wonder and think what if? ...what if?... ...what if?... and it will not stop. It's even worse if it is a story you really love or like. It leaves nothing but a constant stream of thoughts of what if? what if? what if? and HALF LIFE is responsible for those two words bouncing around in my head and until it is completed or information is available on its release or when it will come, i will be forced to scower the internet while those two words ring in my head! Tormenting my very soul and giving me the feeling that my life has no meaning. what if? what if? what if? what if?
It has ruined my life. 200/10 would think what if again.

Quite a few gameplay elements have been streamlined, simplified, and made adaptable for console play.  This in turn, makes the game a bit dull and less tactical in nature.  However, its overall delivery is solid and shows a lot of promise should a sequel be planned.

There are quite a few annoying bugs that bothered the hell out of me such as being able to shoot (more importantly, being shot at) through walls and objects.  Overall though, good game but could improve greatly with a sequel.

I'd pay ~$25 for it with all the DLC included.
The main story quest is absolutely amazing, but I wouldn't pay full price for it because the side quests are universally awful (and you have to complete 100% of them, including the Riddler's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to actually get the ending cutscene to play).
The real problem with the sidequests are that they are almost all glorified pixel hunts, with the Riddler stuff being particularly bad.
Most of his riddles are impossible to do without Google.  This isn't because its hard to figure out what you're looking for - once you actually find the object all of them are fairly obvious - but rather because it will send you out to look for a 10 pixel by 10 pixel piece of debris in a giant, multilevel area filled with similar debris.  The game is also *extremely* particular about where the camera has to be pointed for it to count you having solved the riddle - oftentimes just having the camera centered on the object isn't enough, which adds to the frustration of wondering whether you are looking at the correct pixels or if the seemingly obvious answer was just a trick (hint: it never is, you just looked at it from the wrong angle).  In previous games they were done much, much better.  Also some of the Riddler objectives (in particular his sonar minigames) are fairly buggy.
The DLC is also quite underwhelming as of January 2016.  Most of it is just the same pixel hunt garbage from the other sidequests and most of the DLC quests could be done in less than 5 minutes were it not for the fact that they run you all over the city in your search for pixels.
That being said the Mr. Freeze DLC is some of the best content I've experienced in a game, hence why the game is worth it if you can get it bundled with the season pass for ~$25 during a steam sale.  I honestly wouldn't get the game without the Mr. Freeze DLC just because of how amazing it is and how much of the Batman story you miss out on if you don't have it.

I'd pay ~$25 for it with all the DLC included.
The main story quest is absolutely amazing, but I wouldn't pay full price for it because the side quests are universally awful (and you have to complete 100% of them, including the Riddler's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to actually get the ending cutscene to play).
The real problem with the sidequests are that they are almost all glorified pixel hunts, with the Riddler stuff being particularly bad.
Most of his riddles are impossible to do without Google.  This isn't because its hard to figure out what you're looking for - once you actually find the object all of them are fairly obvious - but rather because it will send you out to look for a 10 pixel by 10 pixel piece of debris in a giant, multilevel area filled with similar debris.  The game is also *extremely* particular about where the camera has to be pointed for it to count you having solved the riddle - oftentimes just having the camera centered on the object isn't enough, which adds to the frustration of wondering whether you are looking at the correct pixels or if the seemingly obvious answer was just a trick (hint: it never is, you just looked at it from the wrong angle).  In previous games they were done much, much better.  Also some of the Riddler objectives (in particular his sonar minigames) are fairly buggy.
The DLC is also quite underwhelming as of January 2016.  Most of it is just the same pixel hunt garbage from the other sidequests and most of the DLC quests could be done in less than 5 minutes were it not for the fact that they run you all over the city in your search for pixels.
That being said the Mr. Freeze DLC is some of the best content I've experienced in a game, hence why the game is worth it if you can get it bundled with the season pass for ~$25 during a steam sale.  I honestly wouldn't get the game without the Mr. Freeze DLC just because of how amazing it is and how much of the Batman story you miss out on if you don't have it.

I am generally skeptical of Early Access games, so I was initially hesitant to buy Killing Floor 2 before it was fully completed. The development quality and overall fun I've had playing Tripwire Interactive's earlier games -- Red Orchestra, Dwarfs?!, and the original Killing Floor, were what convinced me to go ahead with my purchase, and I haven't been disappointed.
Killing Floor 2 is basically a model of what an Early Access game should be like. When I first got the game it was highly playable, with plenty of content to keep me interested in coming back to the game. It's received fairly regularly content updates in the ~9 months I've had it, including weapons, characters, enemies, levels, and game modes. It's still not out of Early Access, but it feels and plays pretty much like a fully finished game, and has for awhile.
The game can best be described as a brutal, gory, wave-based co-op FPS with a focus on teamwork. It has loads of community content, including many vanilla and popular custom levels from the original game. The controls and immersive feedback of the weapon handling is something Tripwire is known for, and the weapons themselves feel powerful and rewarding to use. The soundtrack is an excellent mix of metal, industrial, and dark ambience.
I even bought several copies of this game to play with my friends. I haven't regretted my purchases. Highly recommended.

Turn-based tactical games are a genre dominated by remakes. They're still remaking Jagged Alliance 2, which came out 14 years ago. It'd be stupid of me to get down on this game for trying to innovate, but I'm not really sure that the innovations are what I wanted. In this case, they took Full Spectrum Warrior's puzzle-like focus on cover and movement. From a tactical perspective, I agree that the changes they made are solid ones though not really suited to the genre. Their plot and strategic choices, however, fall pretty short. The satellite mechanic is straight-up dumb. The reduction to a single skyranger was a needless and hamfisted way to introduce GROWN-UP DECISIONS to a game that's been largely stripped of them. While I like the increased guidance in some scenarios, it makes some moments feel awkward and mechanical, where previously they felt spontaneous and terrifying.

Overall, I like this game. I've been playing Cibilizations since Civ 3. It's by far my favorite computer game.I like that it is turnbased and I can play it at my convenience. I can pick it up and leave it and not suffer any ill effects of downtime. It has days and weeks of replayability, months and years even. It takes me a month or so to play a campaign in my 'spare' time. There are numerous different leaders to play with, each having distinct differences that affect gameplay. Each civilization has it's own special building and unit or other feature distinct for them. There are different victories that are available to suit different personalities. If you are combat driven, Domination victory. If you are passive there is the culture victory. If you are political there is the diplomatic victory. I really enjoy the abundance of replayability this game offers.
One thing that I would change is the resources vs. tech imbalance. For instance, there may be no horses in your realm but to get to further techs you have to research horseback riding. The same with ironworking. Also, Civilizations in the past were molded by the terrain and resourses available to them, not the other way around. You could pick England and get thrown onto a map where you are landlocked and then your special unit is wasted. Or you could be Ghangas Khan and not have horses. I would like to see a civilization game that offers options for tech based on what resources you have available and ability to change your ruler, or pick a ruler after the first age. For instance if I have horses direct my studies toward better horsemen. If I have Iron THEN study swordsmen. If I have access to water tiles THEN study shipbuilding. Instead I have to waste turns studying  something I can't use.
Overall though, I really enjoy playing. Each start gives new challenges from terrain, opponents, and resources (or lack thereof)

Half-Life 2 is a game in Valve famous game series Half Life. But how is the game like. HEre is a review dummies.
Story:
You start off as an Ex-Employee from Black Mesa, known as Gordan Freeman (Sounds like Morgan Freeman). As some of us know, Gordan was in an expirement gone wrong until it opened a portal to another world. Because of this, Gordan had to fend off all the Aliens (even the zombies are aliens). One Alien Race known as the Combine took over the world. Wallace Breen joined the Combine to save people but nobody belived in him so they all rebelled. This created a war. A few years after Gman abducted Gordan Freeman, he set him out on a journey. After everybody realized Gordan Freeman was there they started helping. In the game, Gordan's main goal is to get to the citadel to shut down some weird portal with the help of many friends, such as: The Rebels, Antlions, Father Griggory, Alyx Vance and much more! Unlike most games, you seem to have feeling for most character such as the antlions and stuff. Each character has something special in them to make them  charming and all.
Graphics:
The Graphics are pretty standard and look much better the CoD which is great.
Level Design:
Like all games, each level needs to be designed goodly. In half life 2, all levels are designed to make you feel like you are in an actual place with actual stuff. Props and vents especially help do this. but sometimes, I feel like alot of things are purposley made in a certain way for the character to advance or go the other way. Sometimes, parts can be confusing and other stuff.
A.I.:
A.I.s are also pretty important in any game. In this game, they are good and bad. They are good because they never block your way and move out for you. But sometimes, this cant be a pain in the butt. It's easier to navigate through the friendly Antlions rather than the rebels.But otherwise, it's good.
Gameplay:Most Important Part! Now gameplay is where the game suceeds. The player is always kindve sorta told where to go at points just by looking around. Now, Gordan Freeman can carry up to 10 different Guns at once! Because of all the guns, you can add more varierty to your style. Now, Gameplay varies each Chapter. In the first Chapter, you are starting off with no guns at all but getting to one location. Thats it. But it gets better! Next, you get to expiriement with the airboat and solve LOTS of puzzles! the 3rd is about learning to fight for survival against zombies while learning the shotgun mechanics and traps with the gravity gun. The 4th is about the Jeep and Antlion Stepping. The 5th gets you to command Antlions! The 6th lets you play with the combines own turrets and defending. The 7th is about squads. The 8th is a full time combine assault with  powered Gravity Gun OF DEATH. the 9th is the Finale. Each chapter with different game styles is great for varying the gameplay by alot!
Conclusion: Half-Life 2 is a great game and was definantly worth the weight.

Be the Batman. With this proposal, Rocksteady launch the final masterpiece of the Arkham Trilogy. And holy ♥♥♥♥, it really delivers. After the events of Arkham City, all the crime stopped for a moment at Gotham, but in the amazing and unique intro sequence, everything changes and a mayhem starts in Gotham, that is in most part evacuated. Now, Batman must stop Scarecrow and the Arkham Knight, a mysterious foe who led a mercenary army composed of even drone tanks and all kind of war machinery. They seek to unleash a toxin in Gotham and they must be stopped at all cost. That’s where we start. The story become even more complicated and something very weird happens, but that weird thing is one of the best things in the game.
. The story do not disappoint and there is a lot of plot twists, good character development and a good ending for the Batman Arkham Trilogy. Cliché, but it was the only way. The only bad point about the story is the identity of the Arkham Knight, a good mystery that It’s revealed in a disappointing and obvious way. The villains are awesome as ever, with their own side missions that must be completed to reveal the true ending. The side missions are fun and it's a good excuse to complete them all to reveal the true ending. Batman is back with all the previous gadgets, alongside new. Man, there's a LOT of gadgets and predator levels are even more awesome with more freedom to take down your targets, with ambient interaction. Also, the great "show" of Arkham Knight, besides all os this, the Batmobile. Now you can command the "car-tank" with a lot of weapons, in combat mode against lots of drone tanks and other vehicles or in normal mode to complete challenges and travel trough the city. In my opinion, it's fricking amazing to control the batmobile, the battles are fun and sometimes challenging, but sometimes some parts in the story demands too much the Batmobile. There is some overuse, but the fun is the same. It's badass. It's epic. The scenario is destructible and all that mess in battle or driving through the city is an amazing feel. You will face bigger tanks that will act as bosses for the game. Ok, they are good fights, but are the only present boss fights in the game, besides a certain one. I would like fistfights like the other Arkham games too. That was disappointing. Alongside the side missions, there is the well-known extra challenges and the collectibles, the riddle trophies to face the Riddler. Along with the epic story, Batman Arkham Knight have one of the best graphics i've ever seen, with amazing rain effects and lighting. Combined with the epic soundtrack, AK it's one of the most cinematic experiences of 2015. It's beautiful to see and to play, with an easy and upgraded gameplay from Arkham City with some new interesting combat mechanics. The Arkham series combat is on it's top form. With a lot of upgrades and skills to unlock for Batman and Batmobile, it becomes even more formidable. Another thing is the art direction and the open world in Gotham. Really amazing, and Gotham feels alive with chases in the street and all the bandits. Spectacular. The only real bad thing about the masterpiece it's the performance. It launched really bad and now after patches and patches is more okay, but still not acceptable. My rig managed to run without any problems with everything on high at 40-60fps, but on lower rigs...a disaster.

I am a simulation and training professional, I do "serious games" so whilst not a programmer, I can look at strategy games and see where they are coming from with a professional eye. That said, I was a fan of the original Xcom, and Terror from the deep, so it was going to be hard to like a remake. Xcom Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within are not remakes, they are concept enhancements. It is a very good example of taking the best features and applying them with new technology of the day and some new Ideas. It is still turn based, it is still time unit based. It still has place the base and build the base. It has soldier development, which is so important to hook you. All mine are named after family and friends as soon as they have a specialism. I give them cool outfits and laugh when they get assigned nick names/call signs that are just so appropriate to my family. The tension when the top squad is in sickbay and you send out the new team on a hard mission is great and a sign of how effective buy in is. great telling the family member you just turned in to a zombie and I had to kill you. What could be better? Well I would like to assign call signs myself, be able to pick up dropped equipment and be over burdened as in the original Xcom. Bigger maps, more maps, a map editor and the ability to play from the Alien side so we could have whole campaigns of player versus player. That's it, add those and you have reached turned based heaven rather than pushing at the pearly gates. thank you for not disapointing my hopes and for confounding my fears with respect to the original Xcom. 1/ A legitimately funny game - funnier than a good 60% of South Park proper;
2/ Turn-based combat I not only enjoyed, but took seriously and implemented strategically;

I somehow managed to finish the main story and left it at that, hoping they would fix it in a few weeks so I could play some more. When they re-released the game and DLC I gave it another shot and the game was unplayable because of all the stutters, so I gave up. I thought they would NEVER fix the game. As a fan of the first two batman series I really looked forward to this game (Didin't play the the third part). When it became apparent that it was very poorly optimized I waited untill it was patched and started playing with patch december 17th.

Conclusion

Probably one of the better PC games to be made from a liscenced property since......"Beavis and Butthead in Virtual Stupidity" maybe?   It perfectly translates the look and tone of the TV show to a video game format.  Which isn't to say it's perfect, though, either as an RPG or as a piece of "South Park."  As an RPG, the game mechanics are there for a good amount of depth.  Attacks do different types of damage, special moves often involve the stacking of various status effects to do maximum damage, and enemies have different vulnerabilities. So theoretically the game's mechanics could be used to design some fairly interesting fights.  Unfortunately, even on the hardest difficulty fights are incredibly easy.  Special attacks do so much damage that you usually don't have to worry about what type of damage you are doing, to the point that one wonders why the designers bothered implementing the various damage types and status effects at all.  I can't think of a game that would benefit more from a fan made difficulty mod than this as the potential for depth is there in the game's mechanics, it's just that the designers never really tap into this depth in combat design.
As "South Park" the game is much better, although it does suffer from the repetition of way too many jokes from the TV show.  This is especially troublesome in instances where these recycled bits come from later in the series run and thus were never that funny in their first incarnation (see, for example, Morgan Freeman gets a freckle).  However, the game does have many inspired moments all its own (a sex scene fight that I won't go into detail over lest I spoil it sticks out in particular) and ultimately part of this is probably due to the length of the game's development more than anything (Parker and Stone canabalized a good deal of the game's storyline in their Game of Thrones themed, three part episode last season, which ended up stealing the game's thunder somewhat.  I suspect some of these jokes would have had more impact had the game been released first, as it was originally planned).   Most importantly, though, even if the jokes occasionally fall flat, the game works first and foremost as a narrative.  The game's central conceit of basing an RPG around kids playing fantasy dress up is brilliant and Parker and Stone are good enough at adapting their story telling and humor to video games as a medium that it kind of makes me wish that they'd write an original RPG.
In the end, this is a solid, if uninspired, RPG despite its gameplay flaws and, taken as a whole, represents "South Park" at its most epic and comprehensive. Parker and Stone haven't tried to go this big, in terms of the scope of the series, since "Bigger, Longer, and Uncut."  Given that the game reaches so much farther than the show has in years, it's slightly easier to forgive the overreliance on recycled material.

Killing Floor 2 is the much awaited sequel to the 2009 game Killing Floor. Killing Floor 2 picks up not long after the "story" of the previous game ended. Killing Floor 2 ramps up the gore, the graphics, and game speed.  Gone are the slow moving ZEDs that just shambled along towards you, replaced by faster, more aggressive ZEDS that will keep you on the edge of your seat and your eyes peeled for all threats. Graphical settings have been cranked up, as animations, textures and maps look more modern, destructible lighting and you can even paint entire sections of the levels red with the blood of the ZEDs. Each perk now has 10 perk skills that you can choose from every 5 levels alongside the passive bonuses for each level you gain.

While the game has been in early access for over a year, we've gotten a decent amount of content added to the base game.  3 new perks, 5 new maps, and 20 new weapons with unique perk and knife combos for each. The upcoming release of the sharpshooter perk will add another perk and 4 new weapons. I know this might sound like not much for over a year of early access, but you have to remember that TWI isn't a huge company with a ton of employees at its disposal such as EA, Activision and others.  Weapons weren’t pre-made so the delay in content is them creating them from scratch.
Tripwire added Workshop support to Killing Floor 2, meaning easy access to tools to create content for the game, such as custom maps, weapon skins, ZED skins, and much more. This being added has lead to Tripwire allowing community members to post weapon skins and cosmetic items to be posted to "Curate" on the workshop. While cosmetic micro-transactions are a "hot button issue" in the early-access period, they allow the developers to give back to the community members creating custom content, but also help to pay for future content.
Tripwire added a Vs survival PvP mode that allows you to take control of many of the zeds with unique attacks not present in the AI ZEDs. Spawn as a Siren? You can not only scream at players, bite them but you can also "separate" a specific player with a vortex attack that temporarily immobilizes enemies and requires them to have teammates help them to free them.  A downside is the balance of the PvP mode.  While fun initially, it tends to get frustrating after you play it for a while. An example of this is if you're a ZED going against a team with a zerk, it almost feels like you're "useless" to the point that once ZED time triggers, you'd be better off suiciding via console to not give them the cash that's inevitably going to come from killing you as a human controlled ZED.
Tripwire is working on game balance so that there isn't one specific strategy that is required to beat the game on the higher difficulties.  These include adjusting ZED behavior/mechanics, and a recent ammo change for almost all weapons. No longer do perks struggle to keep shooting the entire wave, conserving ammo in fear of running out.
On the negatives side, I think there are some perk unbalances, such as Zerk being almost a vital perk for most teams to complete a game on the higher difficulties.  Having zerk walls at major choke points makes the game a bit easier, leaving only the big ZEDs as an issue deal with. Support specialist, while buffed immensely with the recent ammo changes, generally gets lost in the "perk shuffle" not frequently seen even now.  I feel like if they could nail the perk balances it would be a much more enjoyable game.
The recent live-update system allows TWI to be able to tweak things on the fly without the need of a major patch or content update.  TWI is actively tracking many stats for the game,changing things to better the experience based on the stats they see. While maybe not always the best changes or well received, they are making a concerted effort to keep a close eye on the balance of the game.

I really wanted to like this game, so I've given it a good run of play and a lot of chances to improve before writing a review. I really enjoyed Killing Floor 1 and thought it was great value for money. I think I paid $10 for it, and got 400 hours of play out of it, through interesting mods, piles of great custom maps, plenty of servers, and of course interesting player classes and a nicely balanced diffculty curve that my friends and I gladually climbed. Killing Floor 2 cuts right back on a lot of that.
I bought KF2 in early access because I enjoyed KF1 so much and wanted to support the guys who made such a fun game. I've had it for what's got to be coming up on a year now, and they've done very little with the game in that time. There is a paltry selection of official maps, which is my cheif complaint. This kind of game lives or dies through the ability to freshen things up by playing regular new maps. They're decent, but there's nowhere near enough. On top of that, there are very few servers that run custom maps. It gets very bland, samey and tedious going over the same few maps on every server.
Next there's the character classes. This is a minor complaint, but they've all been simplied and streamlined since KF1. The carrying capacity and small number of weapons for each class really limits players and doesn't allow any real space to customise your loadout to your particular play style. You pretty much just go for the top weapon and that's it. I feel like KF1 gave you a bit more freedom to match weapon loadout to your preferred play style for a particular character, and I expected KF2 to give more freedom there, as a sequel, not less.
Then there's the difficulty curve, which is a big problem. It's just stupidly unbalanced. My friends and I have progressed through normal and hard, and both of those are too easy for us now, but the next rank: suicidal, is just silly. And that's not even the hardest difficulty. We're damn good players, but it's frustratingly hard, to the point of draining the fun from the game.  So we're stuck in this no-man's land where hard is too easy and suicidal is so difficult it's not worth it. The game needs major balancing, but the patches are few and far between. It's like trip wire have just given up and are content to make money off of DLC and microtransactions while leaving the game in early access forever. Levelling up your character to 25 doesn't help either, since the level 25 perks are universally almost useless for each character class, which is bizarre. You'd think that achieving top level with your character would warrant a big reward, but the focus on 'Zed-time' means you -might- get two seconds worth of use out of this perk every 30 seconds or so if you're lucky, and the bonuses are pretty poor. It adds almost nothing to the game.
With the current state of the game's balance, the lack of maps, and the VERY slow rate of patching and updates I honestly can't recommend this game unless it's on sale really cheaply... and even then I'm not sure tripwire deserve to be rewarded for leaving this game and its players in limbo.

Really drags you in once you try it. I couldn't help myself and just went on playing with the purpose to reach 100% achievements, however stopped at 97% with few monster logs missing. It has an enormous replay value, which sadly ends once you unlock some artifacts (Kin, Glass, Command, Sacrifice) and items (infusion, chargefield generator).
Once you get them, starting on a lemurian map, grabbing early infusion and stacking on barbed wire soon makes you and unstoppable ball of death and after 30 minutes of farming you always beat monsoon regardless of the character choice.
That kinda killed the fun for me, as I couldn't just go back to the regular style of playing after trying that. All in all though, the point where you can possibly roll through the maps every time you play start after you've played for some 20 hours or so already (if you are fresh new to the game), probably less if you've played it before or read the wikis a lot.
Before that I still had lots of fun, trying to survive, which is not always that simple. If you play it the regular way, your every gameplay will be different, some items will make cleaning the levels a breeze, while other sets will push you to change your strategy in order to prevent your painful death. The graphics might be a little archaic, but I think it synergizes well with the game overall and it actually looks pretty neat. The background music is prefect as for a space survival game, it fits well with the atmosphere of being on another planet, alone. Another great thing about the game are the monster logs, which I found very well written and enjoyable to collect and read.
RoR doesn't escape few minor bugs like item containers (the always come in three and you can buy only one item) sometimes spawn all in the same place, so you can't even really see what you might get or some items not working properly sometimes (looking at you Imp Overlord's tentacle), but it's nothing gamebreaking. For me, the most annoying issue was the FPS rate in later stages of the game, I mean, I don't really have a gaming rig (yet), but for a game that doesn't involve any too complex graphics, I think it should run smoother rather than lowering my details to the minimum and the FPS rate dropping to 20-30 (which also affects the clock, so the in-game time is not the same a real life time).
Still, for such a low price, this game is well-worth buying. It costs like 3 euro, when there's a discount running, which is a funny price for the fun I've had, especially with the AAA games having 5-10 hours of gameplay with no replay value at the cost of 40 euros. I recommend it to everyone who likes games with roguelike elements and is a completionist freak like me.

Risk of Rain is a somewhat Roguelike platformer. The game consists of five stages. Each stage is selected at random from a choice of ten to fifteen maps per stage, with the maps being variants on two or three actual landscapes. For example, for the first level, you will find yourself either in the Ancient Forest or in the Dried Lake, and each one of those has several variants.
Throughout the game, enemies spawn and attack you, the type of which are determined by the map you're on, and the number of which are determined by how far the game timer has progressed. It starts at Very Easy, Easy, Medium, and Hard, and eventually progresses to I SEE YOU, I'M COMING FOR YOU, and HAHAHA.
At around HAHAHA, you might start having two or three boss monsters spawning with the normal enemies at random.
As if this isn't bad enough, you're pretty fragile and horribly, horribly outmatched by the unending waves of enemies you face. Your weapons are laughably weak in comparison to your foes' attacks, and the fact that there are Elites and Phantasms which ramp the power up to even more ludicrous heights only makes the game more inherently unfair.
You kill enemies to collect currency and experience. Experience gains you levels, with the usual "make everything better" that comes with levelling. Coins can be used to unlock treasure chests or sacrificed at shrines.
The items you gather will make your life a little easier. Not much. Sometimes, negligibly so. But enough negligible boosts can really stack up after a while.
This game follows the Goldeneye model of achievements. Each achievement you earn comes with an in-game unlock - some will unlock items that will be able to drop from thereon out, some will unlock new characters, like the specialized and challenging Sniper, or the adorably toxic Acrid.
All in all, I have ground my face against this game for hours and hours, have only won a handful of times, and have loved nearly every minute. This is not for the Facebook Games generation, this is for the motherfudgers who thought Contra was a good time, even if they never could get anywhere without the Konami Code.

Killing Floor 2 is the much awaited sequel to the 2009 game Killing Floor. Killing Floor 2 picks up not long after the "story" of the previous game ended. Killing Floor 2 ramps up the gore, the graphics, and game speed.  Gone are the slow moving ZEDs that just shambled along towards you, replaced by faster, more aggressive ZEDS that will keep you on the edge of your seat and your eyes peeled for all threats. Graphical settings have been cranked up, as animations, textures and maps look more modern, destructible lighting and you can even paint entire sections of the levels red with the blood of the ZEDs. Each perk now has 10 perk skills that you can choose from every 5 levels alongside the passive bonuses for each level you gain.

While the game has been in early access for over a year, we've gotten a decent amount of content added to the base game.  3 new perks, 5 new maps, and 20 new weapons with unique perk and knife combos for each. The upcoming release of the sharpshooter perk will add another perk and 4 new weapons. I know this might sound like not much for over a year of early access, but you have to remember that TWI isn't a huge company with a ton of employees at its disposal such as EA, Activision and others.  Weapons weren’t pre-made so the delay in content is them creating them from scratch.
Tripwire added Workshop support to Killing Floor 2, meaning easy access to tools to create content for the game, such as custom maps, weapon skins, ZED skins, and much more. This being added has lead to Tripwire allowing community members to post weapon skins and cosmetic items to be posted to "Curate" on the workshop. While cosmetic micro-transactions are a "hot button issue" in the early-access period, they allow the developers to give back to the community members creating custom content, but also help to pay for future content.
Tripwire added a Vs survival PvP mode that allows you to take control of many of the zeds with unique attacks not present in the AI ZEDs. Spawn as a Siren? You can not only scream at players, bite them but you can also "separate" a specific player with a vortex attack that temporarily immobilizes enemies and requires them to have teammates help them to free them.  A downside is the balance of the PvP mode.  While fun initially, it tends to get frustrating after you play it for a while. An example of this is if you're a ZED going against a team with a zerk, it almost feels like you're "useless" to the point that once ZED time triggers, you'd be better off suiciding via console to not give them the cash that's inevitably going to come from killing you as a human controlled ZED.
Tripwire is working on game balance so that there isn't one specific strategy that is required to beat the game on the higher difficulties.  These include adjusting ZED behavior/mechanics, and a recent ammo change for almost all weapons. No longer do perks struggle to keep shooting the entire wave, conserving ammo in fear of running out.
On the negatives side, I think there are some perk unbalances, such as Zerk being almost a vital perk for most teams to complete a game on the higher difficulties.  Having zerk walls at major choke points makes the game a bit easier, leaving only the big ZEDs as an issue deal with. Support specialist, while buffed immensely with the recent ammo changes, generally gets lost in the "perk shuffle" not frequently seen even now.  I feel like if they could nail the perk balances it would be a much more enjoyable game.
The recent live-update system allows TWI to be able to tweak things on the fly without the need of a major patch or content update.  TWI is actively tracking many stats for the game,changing things to better the experience based on the stats they see. While maybe not always the best changes or well received, they are making a concerted effort to keep a close eye on the balance of the game.

I really wanted to like this game, so I've given it a good run of play and a lot of chances to improve before writing a review. I really enjoyed Killing Floor 1 and thought it was great value for money. I think I paid $10 for it, and got 400 hours of play out of it, through interesting mods, piles of great custom maps, plenty of servers, and of course interesting player classes and a nicely balanced diffculty curve that my friends and I gladually climbed. Killing Floor 2 cuts right back on a lot of that.
I bought KF2 in early access because I enjoyed KF1 so much and wanted to support the guys who made such a fun game. I've had it for what's got to be coming up on a year now, and they've done very little with the game in that time. There is a paltry selection of official maps, which is my cheif complaint. This kind of game lives or dies through the ability to freshen things up by playing regular new maps. They're decent, but there's nowhere near enough. On top of that, there are very few servers that run custom maps. It gets very bland, samey and tedious going over the same few maps on every server.
Next there's the character classes. This is a minor complaint, but they've all been simplied and streamlined since KF1. The carrying capacity and small number of weapons for each class really limits players and doesn't allow any real space to customise your loadout to your particular play style. You pretty much just go for the top weapon and that's it. I feel like KF1 gave you a bit more freedom to match weapon loadout to your preferred play style for a particular character, and I expected KF2 to give more freedom there, as a sequel, not less.
Then there's the difficulty curve, which is a big problem. It's just stupidly unbalanced. My friends and I have progressed through normal and hard, and both of those are too easy for us now, but the next rank: suicidal, is just silly. And that's not even the hardest difficulty. We're damn good players, but it's frustratingly hard, to the point of draining the fun from the game.  So we're stuck in this no-man's land where hard is too easy and suicidal is so difficult it's not worth it. The game needs major balancing, but the patches are few and far between. It's like trip wire have just given up and are content to make money off of DLC and microtransactions while leaving the game in early access forever. Levelling up your character to 25 doesn't help either, since the level 25 perks are universally almost useless for each character class, which is bizarre. You'd think that achieving top level with your character would warrant a big reward, but the focus on 'Zed-time' means you -might- get two seconds worth of use out of this perk every 30 seconds or so if you're lucky, and the bonuses are pretty poor. It adds almost nothing to the game.
With the current state of the game's balance, the lack of maps, and the VERY slow rate of patching and updates I honestly can't recommend this game unless it's on sale really cheaply... and even then I'm not sure tripwire deserve to be rewarded for leaving this game and its players in limbo.
